en: Oṃ, salutations to the Supreme Self. An Exposition of the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* Commentary on the Vaiśeṣika Darśana.

Viśvanātha Pañcānana, in his commentary on the verse ending with "the cognition of non-unity and unity is called *buddhi*," states in the *Vidvatsūkti*: "The knowledge of an indefinite unity [in a substrate] gives rise there to the number 'plurality' (*bahutva*), which is distinct from 'duality' (*dvitva*) and so forth; and by that [number], this [cognition] is expressed—so says the author of the *Kandalī*. And Mahādeva Bhaṭṭa, in the *Sukṛtavallī*, has stated: "The view of the author of the *Kandalī* is that 'blue' is superimposed upon the object," and so forth.

Desiring to determine what the *Kandalī* commentary is and who its author is, even within the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha*, I observed in the *Śrī-tattvadyotana*—a compendium of the Māyāvāda school—that it says: "The followers of Bhaṭṭa and the Vedāntins declare that substance is ninefold," and "Śrīdhara Ācārya [says] that blue color is superimposed. Having seen this, I inferred that this very work is the commentary on the *Vaiśeṣika-bhāṣya*, that the *Kandalī* is the path [of this commentary], and that Śrīdhara Ācārya himself is the author of the *Kandalī*. This has been confirmed by authorities such as Śrī Rudra Svayambhū, who stated: "The *Nyāyakandalī* is a commentary on the *Bhāṣya* of the first chapter; its manuscript exists in the library of Paṇḍita Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha Śāstrin, the former professor of Nyāya at the Royal Government Sanskrit College in Vārāṇasī. (1)

Regarding the manuscripts belonging to the tradition of his son, which were deposited in the fourth row at Ikṣmadaha, he who considers himself their discoverer should state with what specific time [the copying] was completed; let him declare that he passed away to the other world at a particular time, while remaining deeply distressed in mind.

Thereafter, for the delight of those devoted to the Vaiśeṣika system, although the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*—accompanied by the commentary *Kiraṇāvalī* composed by Ācārya Udayana—was already printed and had begun to circulate, [the author remarked]: "By Udayana alone are the established conclusions regarding effects realized, not by mere desires;
for deer do not enter the mouth of a sleeping lion."

Having begun thus, and having reached the region of Kashmir, he was sent back once more to our presence; he obtained one copy of the *Kiraṇāvalī* and a second one, which had been procured at the instigation of the scholar Paṇḍita Baṭṭa Śrī Bhīmaśarman residing in Vārāṇasī. Then, having resolved that the printing of this work could be undertaken with these two copies, he set about it.

In the meantime, at the request of the eminent presiding officer of the Royal Veṅkaṭeśvara Pāṭhaśālā in Vārāṇasī, the distinguished scholar and historian Śrī 100 Mukhya, the noble gentlemen brought from their own private library two manuscripts of the *Nyāyakandalī*—the meritorious legacy of the late Śrī Gurubundarasāheba Mahāśaya, who appeared in his own country and time—and presented them for the first two of the six systems of philosophy.

Thus, among the four manuscripts beginning with the one from Satya, the manuscript titled *Praśastapādabhāṣya*—an ancient Vārāṇasī copy—was designated as the first by Paṇḍitamaulibhavara-maśarman. The *Kiraṇāvalī-bhāṣya*, brought from Kashmir, was considered new and was designated as the second. A fragmentary, modern manuscript from Puṇyapattana, full of errors, was designated as the third. And the fourth was prepared from the [remaining] portions.
Having adopted what was beneficial as composed by himself in the Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter, he [composed] the fourth [chapter].

Therein, regarding the first, second, and third [chapters], one should grant the manuscripts; those written with transpositions of words or letters in the cited manuscripts or in the *paramādeṣu* (corrupt/variant) manuscripts—wherein in the *paramādeṣu* manuscripts, parts such as the *vīṇīṣā*, due to being far removed by worms and the like, have been lost or obscured, and which are supplied with appropriate readings there and there, indicated by marks and so forth—and wherein there are variations in reading (*pāṭhabheda*) due to the scribe’s negligence (*yogakṣematva*).

However, having kept in mind with great effort that the manuscripts were copied from the very last manuscript of my own collection and were thus prone to errors, omissions, and corruptions, I fearlessly undertook the task of editing them.

Regarding the third manuscript, which contained the readings of Śrīmat Kullūka, Śrīdharasvāmī, Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇubhaṭṭa, and Maṅgaṭumba, I began the printing after first collating it with four other manuscripts.

Although there are instances in the third manuscript (Ādyupustaka) where readings are either deficient or excessive, that manuscript maintains a consistent state of textual deficiency from its beginning up to its conclusion; however, prior to this deficiency, the manuscript remains as it was found, as if in its original state. Therefore, it is probable that this [manuscript] was once complete.

There exists a commentary on the *Prathama-pāda-bhāṣya* by the teacher Jamadagni-maṭṭācārya, which contains refutations [of others]. Furthermore, this other work, titled the *Vārtika*, was composed as a supplement to the *Bhāṣya* according to its meaning; having been written with a compassionate gaze, it elucidates the chapter on the *Kaṇḍu-śāsana* (the section on the injunctions regarding scratching/itching), which—though appearing redundant due to its repetition of the *Bhīṣma-niṣeva*—is indeed meaningful when understood through the lens of Śaṅkara Miśra’s extensive labors over a long period of time. This wise man has thus brought to completion that which had previously been commenced.

Although there are hundreds of commentaries on the *Nyāyakandalī*, none of them possess authentic manuscripts. [Regarding the sounds: the battle of the jewel-wedding (*ratnavivāha-saṃgrāma*), the sound arising from the conch (*śaṅkharavya-haranināda-sambhava*), the circle of crows (*kākacakra*), and the emergence of the *caicam*;

the sound of the conch blown by the washerman (*yarajaka-śaṅkha-nināda*), the rising of the nectar-like sound (*amṛta-mukti-ṣaṇādi*), and the wind to be understood as being blown from the conch-instrument (*aśaṅkhavādya-parvavat-uddhūyamāna-vāyu-bodhya*).
"I stand before the feet of my guru; I am merely a sound, indistinct.

Having bound the meaning of the sentence in a dream by Padmanābha, [the commentary] was composed. "In the form of a mendicant who has taken up the life of a celibate student (brahmacārin) for the sake of the body, the Lord of Mahīśūra, facing toward the instruments of his practice, expounded [the text]. "The jar-like form that transcends the deities who are the mothers of the body—therein, the three worlds are established as the qualities of consciousness, ever-present."
Having addressed Vasumātṛ, he describes the city as a region of suffering,
where women with bodies and limbs grown stiff from the intense heat of the sun have lost their senses.
There, the illustrious Vāmadeva, having embraced the lotus [of the heart], remains free from dependence as his passion has subsided;
he is a man who has become one with knowledge and austerity, and among those on earth who have cast off darkness, he is known by the name Śivāsana.
Of Śivadāsa, the illustrious Mahādeva, an ocean of virtues,
the best of kings, was always like a protector of the earth with palms joined in respectful salutation.

Doubt and the other [mental afflictions], having attained the capacity to endure the splendor of the lotus feet of the Lord—which are the eternal support for those whose minds are well-disposed toward Him—became like bees once more;
yet, O Ocean of Charity, they depart with their own happiness, accompanied by confidence and adorned with the arts of the Vedas, possessing the virtues of mendicants.
Having received the name Kālodeva through the power of devotion,
he became a master of those [pearls] produced from the shells of the ocean, which had previously belonged to the wealthy.
He who, having known this Brahman as the eternal divinity through wisdom, has fixed his intellect upon that which is not Brahman,
though he may be engaged in the study and recitation of the Vedas— O All-Knowing One, you are the bull among sages, the abode of all desires.

7. This work, known as the *Nyāyakandalī*, which has been elucidated by the vision of its seal [the author] after explaining the reality of the non-existence of time, contains marginal notes (*ṭippaṇī*) and other additions by those born of the lineage of Kaṇāda. Whatever is deficient in this manuscript has been extracted; whatever is slightly incorrect has been corrected by me, and whatever sentences were incomplete have been completed. For the sake of clarifying the initial manifestation, it was prepared for the purpose of a manuscript of the *Bhāṣyaja* (the commentary) regarding the subject matter of Rudra and Śukī. Nevertheless, having examined it thoroughly, its true nature has been established according to my own judgment.

In the course of work, one may encounter various readings—whether from one's own ancient manuscripts or others—that are deficient in parts, such as missing portions or those found within royal libraries and so forth, which must be compared with great care.
Generally, even in ancient manuscripts written on birch bark, variant readings caused by the negligence of scribes are encountered due to differences between individual books.
Likewise, it is not hidden from the learned that variant readings are sometimes also found due to the differing opinions of commentators.
This being the case, even the two variant readings first encountered remain unknown.

Such being the situation, although the readings of the *Kandalī* author are obtainable, and although they are found in available manuscripts of the *Bhāṣya*, yet because of the presence of erroneous readings in the commentaries such as the *Ānandācintā-ṭīkā* that have been encountered, and because of certain differences from the text in the *Kandalī* manuscripts—including the presence of additional material—it has been necessary to occasionally emend and extract the correct readings from the printed edition.

In the first manuscript, although the *Bhāṣya* was present alongside the *Ṭīkā* and the *Mūla*, in this eleventh manuscript, the *Mūla* and the *Ṭīkā* were found as separate texts; the scribe, out of pride, claimed they had been spoken by his lineage. However, since the readings in this manuscript generally accord with those of the author of the *Kandalī*, I have established the *Bhāṣya* readings in the *Mūla* as they appear in that manuscript and in the various commentaries (*pratīka*), while other variant readings are presented for reference.

Now, regarding the Nyāyakandalī commentary on the *Mūla-bhāṣya*: although many manuscripts were available, among those accessible, four manuscripts bearing the mark "Saumūtahāra" were found to be superior. However, that [text] was written according to the readings current in the region of Kaśmīra; therefore, for the sake of determining the true nature of the scripture, we have first undertaken great effort to establish the Kaśmīrian version.

Furthermore, I have been properly assisted by the most venerable and esteemed teacher, the excellent preceptor Paṇḍita Śrī Raghuvarya Miśra, and by the noble Ācārya Mahāśaya Vai-kaunāśa Candragupta, through their deliberations, commentaries, and other scholarly contributions at the Khāraṇakhīśvarāñjī Saṃskṛta Pāṭhaśālā.

Therefore, having now tasted this difficult work—which is like the flow of nectar—according to a gentle style, and having purified it with the sight of the lineage through the removal of faults such as errors and omissions by means of my own keen intellect, I pray to the illustrious Lord Viśveśvara that the compassionate scholars may look upon me, a base person of wicked nature, with favor.

Although the biographies of the authors of these works are generally not available—due to the fact that poets, disciples, and grand-disciples have described them in various ways; due to the difficulty of ascertaining the truth from hearsay, false rumors, and baseless gossip spread by others; due to the lack of proof through various means of valid cognition such as inference based on names shared by many persons; and because even the names of the authors themselves are often subject to doubt and require investigation—it goes without saying that this is the case for the ancient great seers (maharṣis), such as those belonging to specific lineages and clans, as well as for others who were like seers. Nevertheless, I shall describe them exactly as they are found and according to the traditional readings.

Regarding the application of Vedic scriptures therein, it is certain that the great sage Bharadvāja appeared at a specific time and in a specific place; yet, although his lineage is not clearly established, it is inferred from the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa* lexicon—which states "Kaṇāda, Kāśyapa, Sama"—that he was born into the *gotra* of Kaśyapa, the son of Maṅgala, and is thus known by the name Cakrapāṇidatta, being a descendant of Dalhaṇa.

Moreover, it is described in the *Vāyupurāṇa*, in the section on the *Pratiṣṭhā-khaṇḍa*, chapter 23, within the dialogue between Maheśvara and Prajñākhaṇḍa, that during the many transformations involving the transposition of phonemes (*varṇavyatyaya*), the illustrious Kaṇāda, an incarnation of Śiva and the best of the twice-born, attained the status of a disciple under Khaumaprabha. From this, it is understood that Kaṇāda, the knower of the three times, remained as a disciple of Khaumaprabha.
For instance: Brahmā said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Friend of the Universe, Maheśvara!"
O Mahādeva, praised by the world, these [goddesses] are knowers of reality for you.
O great sage, at what time and during the emergence of which age are the twice-born seen by you as possessing a universal form and a vast body?
O Mahādeva, knower of reality, by what application of truth or by what yoga of meditation can [the Self] be seen by the twice-born?
The Blessed One said:
"They do not say that he who [practices] through austerity, yoga, the duty of giving, or even the merit of sacred fords, or through sacrifices, [attains the goal]."
I cannot be seen by mortals even through the study of the Vedas, nor through reflection, nor through ritual offerings; for there is nothing higher than meditation.
Jñāya, Nārāyaṇa, and Viṣṇu, the eternal Lord of the World—
here in the future, I shall indeed be renowned by the name Jñārya.
Having the bow for his arm, four arms, ten arms, and four faces like the sky,
he will always become the year and manifest as sacrifice in many ways.
It is both active and quiescent, eternal and non-eternal, moving and unmoving.
Listen also to these: Dvāpara and Kali constitute the four ages (caturyuga).
The four quarters of an age consist likewise of faith and sacrifices.
When that Kālakūrma and Varāha have been established, and when the Lord Viṣṇu, the son of Nārāyaṇa, shall become known; |||
Then you too, O Lord of Gods, shall become the master of the four Vedas;
you shall be the Lord Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, worthy of homage in the world of Brahmā.
Then, through my yoga, half of him was liberated by the king’s mind;
they were mutually moistened toward one another by the power of passion.
Having seen the worlds of moving and non-moving beings, their bellies became emaciated;
having attained supreme wonder and awakened through meditation by means of human [insight], they [proceeded].
Then, situated within the interior of a lotus, you— the eternal Padmanābha—
shall attain abundant prosperity when meditated upon at the junction of the feet of the Lotus-Born during the kalpa.
O Lord, when this entire Vārāha-kalpa has come to its end,
the great command of Viṣṇu, Time, once again brings about the destruction of the worlds without fear.
A son named Bhṛgu Vaivasvata will be born as the ninth.
Then indeed, through my inquiry during that kalpa at the end of the age,
I shall become the great sage named Śveta, endowed with supreme intelligence.
When you have arrived at the delightful peak of the Himalayas, that best of mountains,
my four disciples shall then become devoted to Śiva.
Śvetana, Śikhaṇḍin, Śvetāsya, and Śvetalohita—
these four were great-souled Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas.
Then, through their celibate discipline, they shall attain supreme austerity for the sake of Brahman;
by my grace, they will reach that state from which a return is difficult to obtain.
Furthermore, O Lord of Gods, in the second Dvāpara age,
there will be a lord named Vyāsa Kṛṣṇa, the son of Prajāpati.
Then, for the sake of the welfare of the world, I shall become known by the name Sutāra in that Kali age, for the purpose of bestowing grace upon the people.
Nevertheless, those sons of mine shall be known by the names Dundubhi,
Śatahūpa, Ṛcīka, and Kṛtumān.
And so forth. Thereafter:
"When the All-pervasive Lord [is present] again in the sixth exhalation of the Dhūti for the sake of the Earth, then I too shall exist there by the name Lokācintī."
But my disciples shall be divine, self-possessed through yoga, firm in their vows, highly fortunate, knowers of reality, and world-renowned.
"Sudhāmā was like one free from passion (viraja), pure and indeed invisible," and so forth. Following that: "When Vyāsa Parāśara was the lord of the earth under the sixth Indra..."
Even then, I shall exist by the name Bahiṣmān.
Having reached the Puṣya Druyavaṭa in that Kali age at the end of the Yuga.
Nevertheless, those sons of mine shall be most righteous:
Ulūka, Vedaśiras, Vajreśa, and Hrāmbalāyana.
For they shall go to the eastern forest of asceticism to attain the most excellent yoga.
200. In the village of Khārviṣyantīya, during the reign of Kṣamāvat, there will be a tiger named Jñānakathya, rich in asceticism.
Then this sixteenth best of the twice-born shall become one perfected in the eightfold path,
a soul of yoga, world-renowned through the power of Prabhāvatī.
Nevertheless, those sons of mine shall be rich in asceticism:
Abupada, Kṣaṇada, Uttuṅga, and Bandhu.
Those of yogic nature, great souls, stainless and pure-minded,
having attained the yoga of Maheśvara, have then departed to the mark of the heart’s splendor.

Regarding the statement in verse 203, "They shall become sixty-four," even so, by the declaration "Nevertheless, they shall be my sons," it should be understood that Śikhidhvaja alone is being addressed in this manner.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction: on one hand, his birth in the lineage of Aṅgiras is heard of in the *Bharata*, the *Purāṇas*, and other texts; yet, according to the aforementioned method, his birth in the lineage of Kṣaya and his subsequent birth [in another] would be inconsistent.
Furthermore, the statement of Śiva to Pārvatī found in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the *Padma Purāṇa* can only be explained through figurative usage (*upacāra*).
For instance: first, indeed, the Śaiva, Pāśupata, and other systems were spoken by me alone; thereafter, they were spoken by the members of the assembly whose minds were possessed by my power.

"Kaṇāda, however, [expounded] the great Vaiśeṣika scripture consisting of six [categories], and likewise Gautama [expounded] Nyāya, while Kapila [expounded] Sāṅkhya. Thus, in the Devībhāgavata as well as in the Śrīmadbhāgavata, here and there, the fact that the name of the most compassionate Great Sage (Maharṣi) is not concealed from the learned is clearly indicated by the mention of his name.
This was stated in the commentary on the first and sixth quarters [of the *Brahmasūtra*].

"To the Lord of Yoga, who, adorned with the eightfold yoga and possessing great power, spoke the Vaiśeṣika Śāstra—that one of crooked views—to him, out of compassion, I bow. By Śabara and the teacher Sūdayana, as well as Uddyotakara and others, many [arguments] were set forth in their respective Nyāya treatises.
For this very reason, it was also stated by Rājaśekhara in his commentary on the *Nyāyakandalī*: (1)

It is said that here, having first composed this [work] as a mere introductory thread for those of dull intellect, the Lord himself, acting with compassion toward the wretched, directly perceived all categories—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—and distinguished them.
Thereafter, out of compassion for the great world, he composed the aphorisms (*sūtra*) which are the secret means for understanding those six categories.

Regarding such matters, the various readings, omissions, and additions that appear in the commentary on the *Kaṇāda-sūtra-ṭīkā* are inferred from oral tradition to have arisen from differences in the opinions of the commentators and from the negligence of scribes.

Since there is a similarity between the *Rāvaṇabhāṣya*, the *Bhāradvājavṛtti*, and the *Viṭhaṇabhāṣya*, it will be established that the prohibition of [certain] views and distinctions is intended for the future.

The Blessed One and Praśastapāda, keeping this very point in mind, composed a commentary (*bhāṣya*)—intended to explain those [categories] by way of the purpose of the treatise and so forth—in order to refute specific fallacies (*viśeṣa-dūṣaṇa*). Therefore, even through that [commentary], the refutation of the distinction between fallacies and so forth is not possible. Consequently, the current prevalence of teaching and studying fallacies occurs only through the addition of false embellishments consisting of difficult-to-answer sophistries (*duruttara-mithyākṛti*) intended to disparage specific points; in the absence of such [embellishments], the application of fallacies would be impossible.

Regarding this, first of all, there is no definitive certainty as to at what time or in what region the author of the *Bhāṣya*, Praśastapāda, appeared; nevertheless, it is stated here according to the accounts of the learned.
In this context, the *Bhāṣya* states: "The refutation of the views of those who maintain difference [is established] by means of scripture, number, and perception.
In the commentary (*Ṭīkā*) on this by Jitāri, it is explained that Udayana’s statement—"those very things mentioned previously are the specific types of perception"—is the intended interpretation.
And the author of the *Kiṣpāvalī-bhāṣya* has stated: "He says, 'labdhaścana me,' according to the *prātaranuvāka* and *anurūpa*;
however, in the *Bhāṣya*, there is the sense of 'ādhipati' (sovereignty)," as explained by Pradyumnasiṃdhuya.
In the *Nyāyakandalī*, Śrīdhara Ācārya states on page 120, line 6: "In that regard, having first established [the point] through well-known examples, he says:

'of the sense organs, beginning with the ear. And on page 267, line 1: "'They declare the creation... Furthermore: "'It is clearly stated in the Śruti that in the process of manifestation, the group of sentient beings is the lowest; therefore, someone is clearly the creator.'"
Thus it was commanded by the father.

And likewise, in the *Baudhāyana-sūtra*, in the section on the *Pravara* (lineage), within the *Kāhirakhaṇḍa* and the *Gautama-sarga*, the name of Praśasta is recited as having eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*).
"Praśasta had five sons, all of whom were rich in asceticism (*tapodhana*)."
Thus it is stated even in the *Śivadr̥ṣṭi* in the inquiry regarding devotion;
likewise in the *Nyāyakandalī*, page 24, line 2: “In the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*,” and so forth.
Similarly, at the end of the *Guṇaratna*, page 266, line 29: “Therefore, I have here explained [the text] according to the path of the author of the Bhāṣya.”
For this very reason, it was stated at the commencement of the second year’s study in the *Nyāyakandalī*:
"Having respectfully received the *Praśastabhāṣya* from Umāpati,
and having written the beautiful *Nyāyakandalī* based on the pioneering work of Śrīdhara, I am now completing it."

Thus, in the *Upaskāra* on the *Vaiśeṣika-sūtra* (6a. 2 ā. 13 sū.), the venerable Miśra states: "The author of the *Praśastapāda-bhāṣya* also says that this [perception] is not a different kind of cognition among the cognitions of the learned.
By this, it is shown that "Praśasta" is the primary name of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, while terms such as "Prādeśin" are merely figurative.
For a detailed account, one should consult our *Līlāvatī-jayantī-kiraṇāvalī-prakriyā*, composed at Vārāṇasī.
Thus, by this very fact, it is possible that the author of the Bhāṣya as well is ancient.

As for the passage from the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* stating, "This [perception] is the direct perception (pratyakṣa) of those such as Asadādi; however, for yogins, it is [the perception] of things not within our range of vision," and so forth—that should be understood as referring to what is self-evident according to the perspective of ordinary people (*laukika*).
For this very reason, it says: "This is the direct perception of those such as Asadādi."
For non-yogins, [the perception of] taste and so forth is merely false.
He speaks of the yogic direct perception [as follows]: "But for those who possess the sixfold [powers] and the twofold [qualities]," etc.
Thus [it was stated] by Śrīdharācārya in the Nyāyakandalī. This means that the sixth [sense], the eyes, is the direct perception of fire.
He states the direct perception of yogis: "of the sixth and the twofold" means "the exposition of the sixth [chapter] concerning yogis."
This is for the sake of those who practice meditation (*dhyāyin*).
Thus, in the *Kiraṇāvalī*, a commentary on the *Nyāyamukha-candrā*, because this treatise—

which consists of a dialogue between teacher and disciple— is composed according to its own nature with a worldly intention, the *Bhāṣya* statement, "Inherence is to be inferred by the intellect through perceived sense-faculties," is consistent.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the earlier commentary which states: "By means of the mind, there arises in the Arhat the perception of his own self, as well as of other non-existent things, time, atoms, air, the mind, the qualities, actions, universals, particulars, and inherence inherent in those [entities]"; thus, there would be a self-contradiction for one who asserts otherwise.

Furthermore, if one were to assert that this very [entity] is eternal and divine by virtue of being delimited by all time and all space, then even for Kaṇāda, there would be no valid means of knowledge—whether general or specific—to establish the existence of the earth, based on such sūtras as "The mark [of the earth] consists of six forms and eight times two" (VS 2.1.18) and "From marks that are eight times two" (VS 4.2.4).
Moreover, in the *Adhyātmarāmāyaṇa*, in the first canto of the Bālakāṇḍa, at the beginning of the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada:
"Having prostrated before Him, I said: 'O Brahman, you are the source from which everything arises.'"
Having spoken thus, the consumer of oblations (Agni) replied to Hṛṣīkeśa.
17 || "O Sage, Śaṅkara knows the entire majesty of the Śrī Rāma Gītā;
Girijā knows it likewise, and so does this supreme Veda."
Therefore, I shall speak a little; it cannot be told in its entirety.
By knowing this, there arises the awakening to reality through the cessation of the fluctuations of the senses and the mind.
If [the opponent] were to argue thus, even Brahmā’s omniscience and divinity would not be established; therefore, enough of this digression.

Now, the consideration that this work is a commentary (*bhāṣya*) is introduced as being extremely difficult. Modern Vaiśeṣikas, however, say: "Some claim that the *Praśastapādabhāṣya* (the commentary on the Vaiśeṣika-sūtra) was composed for the sake of facilitating the study of the text; that is incorrect. This is their powerful argument against its status as a commentary: "That by which the threads are woven together with cloth following the pattern of the threads [is a commentary]."

"Those who know what is to be produced (bhāvya) recognize that even while weaving their own cloths, [the cloth] is yet to be produced," because the reality of the characteristic of being "to-be-produced" is not perceived therein. It is clear that "that which is to be produced" refers to the portion [of the work] yet to be made;

furthermore, even for the sake of proficiency in effort, [Vasubandhu] pointed out in his own composed treatise the entry into the *Saṃgraha* [Abhidharmasamuccaya], but he did not do so by way of its being "to-be-produced," since it is impossible to speak of that [work] as something yet to be produced.

"Having bowed with devotion to the Lord who is the cause [of all], the wise Kaṇāda will hereafter proclaim this compendium of categories, which is full of great compassion. [This is followed by the objection: "In these [verses], there is mere redundancy because the subject matter is already established," and so forth.

The objection that these [qualities] cannot be cultivated because they are incompatible with other qualities to be cultivated—since cultivation is impossible for that which is light due to the contradiction between being light and being something to be cultivated—is here resolved:
this inclusion of "non-existence" (amaḥ) under the first category is for the sake of the cloth; it has been determined, however, that it is not something to be cultivated.

For the sake of clarifying the meaning of the effort [involved], it is stated by the followers of Kaṇāda that [the effect] is produced from the cause; for it is not perceived as having the same form as the initial state.

And at the beginning, it is said: "Thus, by those who have seen the purpose of the effort, [it is established] that the cloth and so forth are always present in the threads and the like," as concluded by the final line.

If it is argued that the determination of the meaning [of the *Bhāṣya*] is due to the proficiency of effort in other texts, then [we reply]: because the state of being a *bhāṣya* (commentary) is indicated by the mention of the *bhāṣya* at the end of the sequence, and because it has been established as a *bhāṣya* by the final verses and so forth, as well as by those who expound the meaning of the *Citsūtra*, the modern Vaiyākaraṇas—who investigate its status as a *bhāṣya*—are indeed correct.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "In his own composed work, he did not indicate the entry into the *Saṃgraha* as a *bhāṣya*," even here the tradition of the activity [of the author] is consistent; for the Sage spoke the *Śāstra* for the sake of the world's *Śāstra*.
I shall compose a treatise for the purpose of turning away those who possess the knowledge of the insignia of the lineage.

Since this has been stated by the teacher Udaghoṣakāra, even according to the later view of Ācārya Ākhyāttamiśra—who, in the absence of that *Bārttika*, [asserts] that [the term "object"] refers to the meaning of the suffixes within the *Nyāya* treatise—[the objection does not apply].

Furthermore, if they read "yaś ca śabdānuśāsanam" at the beginning of the *Mahābhāṣya*, then because it is stated in three thousand [verses], it would lack the status of a *bhāṣya*; consequently, Kaiyaṭa’s statement in the introduction to the *Bhāṣyapradīpa*—"In the *Mahābhāṣya*, an examination of usage"—and Nāgeśabhaṭṭa’s statement—"Having exerted great effort in the *Pātañjala-Mahābhāṣya*"—would both result in being nothing but the ravings of a madman.

In the *Kiraṇāvalī*, Udayanācārya states, "Having raised the objection that the sūtras would be redundant because the Bhāṣya is too extensive," and immediately following that, he says, "And because the *prakaraṇas* and so forth are but parts [of a whole].
Therefore, this is not merely a *prakaraṇa*, but a complete treatise (*śāstra*).

For this very reason, the following passages are consistent: in the *Kiraṇāvalī*, "In order to adopt the practice of the virtuous at the commencement of a treatise (*śāstrārambhe*..."); in the *Nyāyakandalī*, "The deity of those who desire protection at the commencement of a treatise (*śāstrārambhe rakṣimatāṃ devatām*..."); and the passage from the *Kandalī*: "And when there is engagement with reality, the treatise would be both composed and honored; therefore, wise persons, desiring to begin a treatise, utter [the name of] its deity at the outset and state the purpose of that word as a response to the inquiry regarding the apprehension of the meaning of the words. Thus, the text of the *Kandalī* is logically established.

Thus, when the teachers have established that this work—which consists of a compendium for grasping the meaning of the words—is indeed a *bhāṣya*, the definition of a *bhāṣya* will be rendered consistent, according to the verse:

"Where the sūtras are explained by means of words following their proper sequence, and its own words are also explained, those who know the *bhāṣyas* recognize that as a *bhāṣya*. This is what will come to pass.
For instance:

regarding the consistency of the statement "wherein the sūtras are described," the teacher Uddyotana has explained it according to the words of the *Kiraṇa*: "By means of sixteen words, [the nature] of the elements is explained. "We shall explain the dharma that is not cold by means of the elements; for that dharma is the first attainment (*prathamasiddhi*) which subdues the heavy [obstacles]."

By that statement, the fourth [chapter], which concerns the soul (*ātman*), has been explained. Furthermore, in the *Bhāṣya* it is stated: "In the section on the specific qualities (*guṇaviśeṣādhikāra*), the specific qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth are established. The section on the specific qualities is the second chapter (*adhyāya*).
And likewise, it is stated in the *Kiraṇāvalī*.

In the *Nyāyakandalī*, it is said: "The word 'na' is used in the sense of exclusion (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*). It demonstrates that very meaning with the passage beginning, "Because a specific distinction is observed in the word," and so forth.
He demonstrates his approval of the excellent meaning and the excellent formulation [of the verse] by means of the words "Thus, by means of the external [world], etc.
(tathā bāhyair yādinā).

Indeed, in the *Kiraṇāvalī* and also in the *Nyāyakandalī*, wherever the categories (*padārtha*) are defined, the aphorisms (*sūtra*) from the *Bhāṣya* have been cited by teachers such as Śrīdhara and Udayana;
however, we shall present them here.

Nor should it be suspected that there is no commentary on all the *sūtras* here because such a commentary is not perceived in its entirety; for the Great Sage Patañjali has provided explanations for all the *sūtras* in the *Mahābhāṣya*. Were this [work] not so, its greatness would be far removed, and its very status as a *bhāṣya* would be untenable.

Now, one might object: "If it is argued that just as the entire definition of a *sūtra*—characterized by brevity, clarity of meaning, and so forth—is possible when applied to each individual word, and thus the meaning of 'clear' (*su*) is described [in relation to each], so too, since the entire definition of a *bhāṣya*—beginning with 'yajati' and so on—is possible when applied to each individual word, this [text] should be considered a *bhāṣya* through its application to each."

Since the entire [text] is characterized by the aforementioned defects, the meaning of the *sūtra*—beginning with "the understanding of the words" (*padānām anvayaḥ*) and so forth—is explained either together with the word "yajati" or its own constituent words are explained; this is stated as an alternative (*vikalpa*). Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "those who know the Bhāṣya understand that the nature of the *ākṛti* is called the *sūtra*," there is no non-occurrence of the plural number (*bahuvacana*), and thus these [explanations] should be construed according to what is possible; hence, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

And if the meaning of *su* is described [as follows], then the remainder of the commentary on *yajati*—consisting of the explanation of *su*—is for the purpose of stating the injunction (*pravartaka-ukti*).
Thus it is said in the eighteenth chapter of the *Parāśara Purāṇa*:
"The analysis of words (*pada-ccheda*), the statement of word-meanings (*padārthokti*), the syntactical resolution (*vigraha*), and the construction of the sentence (*vākyayojanā*)..."

"An explanation [consists of] objections and resolutions; it has five characteristics. By this [definition], since even the statement of word-meanings (*padārthokti*) is an explanation, a commentary (*bhāṣya*)—even one that merely states the word-meanings as they appear—is indeed a commentary because it performs the task of explaining.
Here, each element, such as the division of words (*padaccheda*), is itself a characteristic.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for a work like Rādhāmaṇi’s *Bhāṣya*, which performs the division of words and so forth, to be considered a commentary, since it would lack some of these characteristics.

Furthermore, it is untenable for the *Brahmadṛṣṭi-bhāṣya*, which sets forth the meaning of the "Seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) as expounded in the *Kārikās* composed by the teacher Gauḍapāda, to be considered a mere commentary (*bhāṣya*).

In the *Paṭa* [of the Vaiśeṣika], regarding the aphorism "color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are the qualities" (*hūparasagandhasparśāḥ saṃkhyāḥ parimāṇāni pṛthaktvaṃ saṃyogavibhāgau paratvāparatve buddhayaḥ sukhaduḥkhe icchādveṣau prayatnāśca guṇāḥ*), there is the following commentary (*bhāṣya*): "The qualities—namely color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort—are those mentioned by Kaśyapa; and when the sixteen beginning with gravity, fluidity, velocity, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and sound are added, these constitute the twenty-four qualities."

Moreover, in the *Bhāṣya* on the definition of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), it is stated: "Just as the twenty-fourth dimension [of the soul] is produced by a substance, and as the spherical dimension (*parimaṇḍala*) is [produced] by a substance, so too elsewhere, conjunctions born of action and the like are said to be produced; however, the conjunction between the skin and the mind is distinct from the substance, because of the cessation of its existence. And in the section on inference (*anumāna-prakaraṇa*), the *Bhāṣya* states: "Where there is no cognition characterized by the aforementioned [conditions], or where the property (*dharma*) is perceived in a contrary manner, that does not constitute a mark (*liṅga*) for the comprehension of the object of inference; this is what the author of the Sūtra says."
"Agni, divya, janapada, anaḍuh, śvan, and ratha are designated [with specific suffixes] when following the word *anu*. This applies elsewhere as well.

"And its own words are explained," the connection of which is as follows in the *Nyāyakandalī*: "It explains by means of *jyotsnā* (moonlight), *paśu-bādha-vena*, and so forth; it explains by means of *manaḥ-svapnena*."

By the words "that which is intended to be explained," and so forth; by the words "it acts for another purpose," and so forth; and by the words "the moonlight," he explains the sentence and demonstrates the non-existence of particulars within perception and inference. Thus, since he has himself described his own terms in this manner on many occasions, everything is consistent.
In the *Nyāyakandalī* commentary on the *Padārthadharmasaṅgraha*, titled *Patrikā*, Rājaśekhara states in his *Śabdamālā*:

"In this system, it is said that the Lord himself, having first manifested his power for the sake of those seeking knowledge who had been overcome by negligence, taught the categories (*padārtha*) characterized by the sixfold nature of existence, as perceived through both direct perception and inference.
Subsequently, out of compassion for the world, he composed the *Sūtras* consisting of concise aphorisms regarding those very categories, intended for the wise."

When those [lineages] had perished, Bhārgava Saṅkara, having entered the first *skandha*, established a *kṣetra* (domain) that was neglected due to the removal of the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) from the station of Maheśa. Therein, the various modes of conduct (*vṛtti*) were brought to completion.
One such mode of conduct is called *Jyotsnānī*; its teacher is Jyotsnāvidyācārya, who is skilled among men.
The second [commentary], however, was composed by Nīlakaṇṭha, based on the *Nyāyakandalī*;
the third was indeed composed by the teacher Mudgala;
and the fourth was composed by the teacher Vāmana, who meditated upon the seat of the individual soul (*jīvāsana*).
Furthermore, Śrīdharadeva [states] in his *Nyāyakandalī*: "This profound commentary on their truths is more ancient than those [others]," and so forth.

Here, in this fourth commentary on the *Bhāṣya*, Rājaśekhara’s intention is not that each preceding work is older than each succeeding one; for he mentions the "commentary named *Śuklā* or *Dakṣiṇā*" without referring to it as the "first," and because he has shown a partiality toward the *Upasnigdhā*.

If, however, priority is determined by relative antiquity, then since the *Kandalī* and the *Kiraṇāvalī* are later than the *Līlāvatī*, it is impossible for the *Vaiśeṣika* [of Praśastapāda] to be more ancient than the *Līlāvatī*, because Śrīmat Sīturu [Udayana] did not incorporate [the views of] the *Kandalī* and others [into his work].
Thus, for now, the *Kandalī* and the *Kiraṇāvalī* are established as being respectively ancient and modern.

In this regard, after Udayanācārya had composed the *Kiraṇāvalī* up to the end of the "Testing of Intellect" (*buddhinikaṣaṇa*), Śrīdhara Ācārya composed a complete commentary named *Nyāyakandalī* on Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya*, which he completed by adding [the section] titled "The Denial of the Next World" (*paralokanirākaraṇa*). Scholars understand that the work was brought to completion by him personally as a supreme Vaiśeṣika, having provided a commentary on the path of the *Kiraṇāvalī* from the beginning up to the end of the "Testing of Intellect," without merely presenting a shadow [of the original].

In accordance with this very point, we have demonstrated that Udayanācārya’s overturning of the earlier treatises was based on the instructions of Śrīdharācārya, for the purpose of [clarifying] the meaning of the *Kiraṇāvalīmudrikā*.

In reality, however, whether the *Nyāyakandalī* was composed by relying upon the *Kiraṇāvalī*, or the *Kiraṇāvalī* was composed by relying upon the *Nyāyakandalī*, the sequence of priority cannot be determined, as it is clearly understood through the mutual correspondence between the two works.

And so, certain statements cited as authoritative in the *Kiraṇāvalī* are illustrated by the author of the *Kandalī* with some degree of explanation, while others are presented merely as they appear in the *Kandalī*, such as the form "nirayaikaḥ. Therefore, it follows that one should examine the *Kandalī* by relying upon the *Kiraṇāvalī*.

However, because this *Kiraṇāvalī* is loose compared to the *Kandalī*, and because it was stated that even after the *Ghana* commentary on the earlier *Ṣaṣṭhīkinī*, there is no possibility of examining the *Kiraṇāvalī* due to its loose exposition, and furthermore, because [the *Kiraṇāvalī*] is refuted by Śrīdhara’s *Avadhīna*, the examination of the *Kiraṇāvalī* occurs by relying upon the *Kandalī*.

However, as long as even the name of the world’s threads is not perceived in a single instance, so long—despite the absence of certainty regarding priority and posteriority—it is possible for there to be non-duality through the five [factors] that are properly distinct yet conceived as prior and posterior, such as those held by the teachers Kṛṣṇa, Udayana, Akṣapāda, and others, because of their lack of dualistic affliction; thus, why should we not proceed toward the higher door with firm resolve?

The venerable Śrī Dharaṇīdhara Ācārya’s mother was Cacchokṣā (or Cacchoṃkṣā) and his father was Baladeva. He resided in the village of Bhūriṣṭhudrigra, to the south of Rāḍhāpura in the Goṅga country, which lies beyond the western ocean of the Vaṅga region. Inspired by the poet Pāṇabuddhāraka, he composed the *Nyāyakandalī* commentary in the year 693 of the Śaka era (corresponding to the Vaiśvānara saṃvatsara). This is evident from the following verse cited therein: "In the city of Cārvīdṛṅga-Rāḍhā, a holy field for the twice-born..."
In the village called Bhūriṣṭhuddrita, there was one named Bhūriṣṭhudri, who was a refuge for people.
The moon of the Kali age became a laughingstock for the worshipers of Kṛṣṇa,
like a Brahmin who has become an old husband to the moon that brings joy to the world.
Therefore, he became a great ocean of the jewels of pure virtues, a tree upon which the creeper of knowledge depended;

named Baladeva, he was one whose clear intention was like the festive waters flowing from the streams of various rivers of wisdom. Born into the lineage of Viṣṇu, whose fame was the nectar of reality, his wife was the auspicious Gṛhamedhinī, who possessed inconceivable and stainless qualities.
Upon that tree, which possessed a beautiful shade, was in full bloom, had many branches, and served as a refuge for birds,
there grew a small tree called Śrīdhara, towering high among the directions.

This *Nyāyakandalī*, which is like an oblation, has been offered by me— having been first scorched by the fire of knowledge— unto this oneness of the six categories, which is worthy of being approached until the very end of existence.
This Nyāyakandalī was composed by Śrī Śrīdhara, the son of the venerable Cintāmaṇi Miśra known as Pāṇḍura, at the command of Nyāyācārya Bhaṭṭa Śatānanda. (893)
Other works composed by Śrīdhara Bhaṭṭācārya, which are cited in the *Nyāyakandalīvyākhyā* as follows:
the *Tattvabodha* (or *Tattvaprabodha*),
and the *Tattvabodhādinī*.
And there is the *Saṃśaṭīkā*.

Śrīdhara Svāmī, the author of commentaries on the *Bhagavadgītā-nibandha*, the Purāṇas, the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata*, and other works, is indeed distinct from this Śrīdhara. Furthermore, Mīṭhara and Dhāraka are none other than those called the authors of the *Kandalī*;
even there, there are differences in their names.
At the end of each stream of meanings, there is indeed this stream of meaning;
for the highly learned perceive it as if running in the forest at its very root, by means of the cause that renders [the subtle] gross.
O people, for the sake of specific names,
you should know that the sequence of knowledge established by tradition has been taught by the venerable Śrī Tharāvaya.
Moreover, even things such as the lordship over Śrī and Kṣīrārṇava are perceived as false merely through names; how much more so when they are seen through the difference of Vedic texts?
This is a certain explanatory commentary by Śāṅkṛtika.
This reading is found in the first manuscript.
This reading is found in the first and second manuscripts;
this reading is found in the first, second, and third manuscripts. The same applies further on as well.

Since the investigation of the category of substance (*dravya-padārtha*) is established solely within the scope of the single subject, and likewise the commentary (*ṭīkā*) also constitutes that very subject, the connection between the root text (*mūla*) and the commentary should be made by linking the first page of the root text with the second page, should one desire such a synthesis.
The same applies hereafter as well.

Now, the index of the relationship between the *Kaṇāda-sūtra* and Praśastapāda’s *Bhāṣya*. In the Section on Enumeration (*Uddeśa-prakaraṇa*): Having prostrated—*marīcayaḥ* (rays); substance (*dravya*); cause (*hetu*); in reality (*tattve*)—the Vedas; the collection (*caya*); qualities devoid of [substance] (*niṣprātānu-guṇāḥ*); twenty-four qualities (*caturviṃśatirguṇāḥ*); moreover, the internal nature (*utave-cātmyantarīya*); the definition of generality (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇe*); eternality and so forth (*nitya-tvādi*); only directions (*deśā eva*); inherence (*samavāyaḥ*); sixfold (*ṣaṭ-kataḥ*). In the Determination of Generality and Particularity (*Sāmānyaviśeṣanirūpaṇa*): [The text continues with further categories.]

In the examination of the *eṇā* (antelope) and other [qualities], there is the non-perception of the unseen void-footedness in the two middle [states]; the sixth case-ending indicates dependence on what is seen; the deficiency of the visible and so forth; the desire of qualities (*guṇa*) to depart; the agency of the visible and so forth; the causality of effects in impermanence, like the possession of causes; the dual-location of causality; the seen and the unseen; the generality; the specific reality in the two foundations; the dependence on the protector and the seen; the consciousness in the state of having relatives; the expansion in consciousness and the spatiality of space; the calves of the earth; the fourfold nature of substance; the threefold possession of touch; the threefold fluidity; the heat and clarity of the two; the possession of qualities across the three times by the elemental self; the fourfold possession of qualities by the indivisible self; the oneness of space; the causality of direction and time; the impulse in consciousness; thus, in the summary of the description of earth, the number of earth-natures; the smell of the *tittiri*; the single form of color and taste; the touch and fluidity; she is indeed the threefold collection of the two; the sugar, the clay, and the stone; the three-born, the egg-born, and the sky-born; the object of perception by the senses—thus ends the [section on] objects. In the examination of air: air is known from the word; it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); its time is the same; the sense organ is the skin; the object is touch; its leadership of the world through the wind; the vital breath is equalized; in the twenty-two-fold description, it is to be understood in the scriptures; likewise discipline; at that time it remains; thereafter it remains; it remains in that very place; thereafter it remains—such is the cognition of doubt. In the examination of space: divisions of space; sound; determination; the determination of sound; the extension in the sky; magnitude in expansion; in the examination of time: time is that time; the cause of all worldly transactions; its division; its establishment in space; in the establishment of time; in the examination of direction: due to the impossibility of a cause for direction; its establishment. In the examination of the self: the self is the intention of the self; its happiness and sorrows; by that, the self is approached through sound and so forth; it is inferred by the body; and by the vital breaths, etc., because of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Its qualities: the qualities of the senses and the elements; in the examination of the mind: the mind is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); its qualities: conjunction, disjunction, throwing upwards, drawing back, difference from sound; in the thrown—the previous commentary; from thrownness, priority and posteriority; the state of being a latent impression (*saṃskāra*); not all—wholeness; and from the location of action; these are common—substantiality; due to the absence of a cause, it is for another's sake; due to possessing qualities, it is substantiality; and due to perception—thus ends the examination of substances.

In the determination of qualities: color and the rest have the nature of being instrumental causes; color, taste, and [tangible] form are qualities of material objects; intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, and gravity are qualities of the self; number is a quality common to both; and conjunction consists of multiple factors. This is the purpose [of this section].

Qualities produced by each of the [three] primary qualities (*guṇa*); qualities mentioned in the *Rigveda*; numerical qualities; those designated as sound; those designated as number; those designated as cognition (*buddhi*); those beyond the senses of the householder; preceded by the knowledge of the fickle; preceded by cognition; born from the conjunction of cognition; born from the action of conjunction; sound and disjunction are born from [conjunction]; preceded by the cognition of priority; consisting of the same genus as form; to be understood starting from the thumb and so forth for the seven-fold state; on the back, in the row, the commentary or the aphorism (sūtra) 99–22... ... the knowledge of pleasure and taste 100–3|4... the knowledge of conjunction and taste... 11|12 cognition—knowledge of taste... 16... knowledge of form and taste. 20|21 Conjunction and accumulation are the nature [of these]. 101–3|4... the causes of heaviness... 9|10... the causality of form... 102–1|2... the causality of cognition as an instrumental cause 4|5... the non-causality of conjunction and accumulation 12... the nature of excellence and manifestation 16|17. ... the reality of the location of conjunction and cognition; therein, form is fourfold: it transforms through vision, having various forms such as white and so on; it is innate, moving according to its own will, and is perceived by the eye; taste is to be grasped by the tongue, transforming through vision, consisting of the three [sweet, sour, salty] and the six flavors such as bitter and so on; smell is to be grasped by the nose, transforming through vision, consisting of grapes, juices, and so on; they are explained as non-pervasive. For the purpose of the completion of expansion, the root *spharya* is used; the suffix *-ti* is added; *sphukṣuh* and *ahaṅkāra* are the two types of form; the stream is threefold; non-pervasive, heavy, and light; in the process of the production of cooked [color] (*pākaja*) in earth-atoms and so on, when the unity of the raw jar is manifested, there are disjunctions among them; that which is to be disjoined is the destruction of conjunction; upon the destruction of conjunction, manifestation occurs; in that destruction, they are born again; immediately after that, they are released; therein, there is no manifestation of form and so on, nor is there cessation. The determination of number: the rule of one and so forth; but a substance consists of multiple substances.

"Consisting of new individual manifestations"—thus there would be inferential cognition. "No, because it is a term denoting a specific [quality], as in 'in the past'. But this is not the understanding [of the author]. In the determination of dimension (*parimāṇa*), [it says] "dimension and shortness. Among those, there are only two: the large (*mahat*) and the minute (*aṇu*). Likewise, in the case of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) of air, the conventional usage of "shortness" occurs due to weakness. This is established in the middle section of the sixth book. As for the statement "that which goes to the end and does not go beyond," in the determination of separateness (*pṛthaktva*), [it says] "separateness. In the determination of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), one should determine it by way of similarity, as it is so.

Because of the statement "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), the section beginning with "Now, how [is it] of those... and ending with the completion of the discussion on *prakaraṇasama* (the counter-argument based on the similarity of the case) concludes the examination of disjunction (*vibhāga*). In the examination of distance and proximity (*paratvāparatva*), the section beginning with "The cause of disjunction is preceded by atoms... and ending with the completion of the discussion on *prakaraṇasama* concludes the examination of the cause of distance. As for the cause of distance, however, according to the manner of the section beginning with "That [cause] is one of two [objects], being superior in sequence," there is a different meaning regarding the refutation of the [opponent's] position.

In the definition of *buddhi* (cognition): "This cognition," "with respect to this," "ascertainment"—these are synonyms. And because it is not restricted [to a single object], it is its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). In the definition of *saṃśaya* (doubt): "Doubt" is that which has many causes. In the definition of *viparyaya* (error): "Error" is also a form of cognition. In the definition of *anadhyavasāya* (indefinite cognition): 152—(First Half) It is similar to the nature [of doubt]. *Anadhyavasāya* also occurs. Nyāyakandalī Commentary: Having prostrated before the Lord, the cause of the world, who is without beginning or end, whose will is ever-true, and who possesses eternal and unimpeded knowledge.

Salutations to that Blessed One, the Supreme Person, whose nature is wisdom, who has shattered all bonds, and whom those with minds one-pointed in meditation perceive as stainless, non-dual, and beyond destruction, even when their mental activity has ceased.

At the beginning of the treatise, the author praises the deity and the teacher who composed the treatise, and he pays homage to the previously mentioned subject. Regarding the word "having prostrated" (*praṇamya*):
it is the established custom of the learned that at the commencement of a work, both the deity and the teacher are saluted.
Furthermore, the fruit of the salutation is the pacification of obstacles; it is not a direct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is assisted by the intellect of the practitioner.

Even another [deity] is not necessarily assisted at the commencement of an action, since assistance occurs only at that time for the sake of beginning and completing the undertaking without obstacles, and because the fruit is directed toward a superior state.

Now, is it the case that the pacification of obstacles occurs only from the salutation (*namaskāra*), or does it also occur from something else? It is not a fixed rule that it occurs only from the salutation, for even when a salutation is present, works such as the *Nyāya-bhāṣya* and the *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya* have been completed. And when it occurs from something else as well, then its inclusion as a rule would be subject to the fault of being superfluous (*vaiyarthya*). This is explained: the pacification of obstacles occurs only from the salutation, because it is included at the commencement of the work with the determination of its efficacy (*śakti-nirṇaya*).

If it is argued that no salutation was made by the authors of the *Nyāya-bhāṣya* and *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*, but rather that such a perception is merely based on the tradition of those who claim omniscience, [we reply]: No; for even if there were doubt regarding the lack of contradiction with the sacred texts (*āgama*), one who possesses the conviction of being a virtuous person (*śiṣṭa*) does not fail to engage in meritorious actions simply because of such uncertainty. Furthermore, if these two [authors] had not been restrained by their own teachers—those who were supreme in removing suffering and who possessed direct knowledge of the truth—then this lack of possibility would not have occurred. This is explained and demonstrated in the commentary (*vyākhyā*).

By means of a question posed by one who perceives the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), there is merely a salutation preceded by devotion; for indeed, even the fame arising from the production of dharma has no other source than our ultimate refuge. For this very reason, although a salutation has been performed, works such as the *Kādambarī* remain incomplete because the excellence of that [salutation] is being diminished due to the absence of a specific salutation. Furthermore, even when a salutation is performed here, it is employed with the intention of making known that it occurred at a prior time, in view of its disregard for the connection with the subject matter to be treated later. This is done to bring about syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with that [later subject], and not because its status as occurring at a prior time is being restated (*anūdyate*), nor is it a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), since there would be no purpose in such a case.

By the word "cause" (*hetu*) used without qualification, he asserts that [God] is the cause of all things by virtue of his universal nature. By the word "Lord" (*īśvara*), he denotes a specific deity, because this term is well-known in common worldly usage, and because this scripture aims to incorporate meanings established in the world. By the word "sage" (*muni*), he refers to one who possesses a mind purified by the lamp of knowledge of the pure self, and who is endowed with tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, and the realization of the meaning of the Vedas; for the word "sage" is seen in common usage in the sense of one who has "measured" (*munitavān*) the past and the future.

Having obtained this through the feet of Kṛpāda, and having daily performed this worship worthy of the venerable one—characterized by the restraint of the senses and the company of the assembly of sages—one speaks thus out of compassion, or rather, out of devotion, as an expression of the possibility of such a sign.

"This indeed is its name"—thus Praśastadeva has performed the mention [of the work] by means of that word; however, this is not stated as a logical argument for teaching the specific excellence of its composition, because the excellence of its composition is already understood simply from the fact that it is accepted by the learned (*hājana*) through its integration with words such as "mantra. If it is argued: "There is no utility whatsoever for this treatise on *kṛpā* (compassion) by means of this [mention]; yet, by that much, the excellence of his own machine-like system is established"—[we reply: the excellence of one's own system must necessarily be established by being preceded by that [other system], and thus this composition also serves as a means (*upāya*), since it is possible [for it to lead to the goal]. If it is further argued: "Since Praśastadeva’s authority is merely presumed, the possibility of human error is still present"—[we reply: it was previously established that trust in humans regarding what is seen in brief is based on the author's own nature; furthermore, engagement with a subsequent composition occurs only through corroboration by another person. Thus, even in the case of a composition made by Praśastadeva, engagement will proceed without obstacle provided there is a vision of what was seen in brief. Therefore, nothing is established by this [mere] mention of his own system preceded by that [other system]. The salutation to *kṛpā* (compassion) is established [as follows]: in the sequence [of the verse], "attaining the state of the inner self for the sake of the six qualities" refers to the natural state of the immediately preceding characteristics. Moreover, the previous desires were settled by their own inherent momentum; this [new] one has arisen as something unprecedented. There is no connection to bondage, and liberation and bondage reside in the same substratum despite the difference in their objects; and he who sets out [on the path] becomes desisted once he has attained [the goal].
When Prakṛti has ceased its activity due to the discernment of the difference between Prakṛti and Puruṣa, the Puruṣa’s abiding in its own heart is called liberation (mokṣa). In that regard:

If it is argued that since the *prakṛti* has activity as its inherent nature (*pravṛtti-svabhāva*), it is impossible for it to remain indifferent, and thus its activity is necessitated by the purpose of the *puruṣa*; and that once this [purpose]—discriminative discernment (*viveka*)—is fully known, that activity ceases because the task has been accomplished; [we reply: To what [agent] would this apply? Since the *prakṛti* is insentient, it lacks the capacity for intentional action. Just as even when an undertaking has been completed based on a verbal command, one resumes that very same activity again, so too, even when discriminative discernment has been accomplished, she will resume her activity in the same way, because an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) is imperishable.
Others, however, maintain that [the cessation of activity occurs] because the *prakṛti* consists in the manifestation of eternal, unsurpassed bliss.
That conventional usage [is set aside] because it is about to be refuted. Therefore,
it is logical that the ultimate cessation of what is harmful to that [conventional usage] is the supreme attainment (*mahodaya*).

Regarding that [objection]: "What is the proof for the determination that the six [categories] destroy suffering? Is it the witness [pramāṇa], such as [the inference] 'because it possesses a nature that is eternally severed from bondage'? That is incorrect, because diseases and the like are warded off by independent [means] such as medicinal herbs and so forth.
"We ourselves, being indeed bodiless, are not touched by the pleasant or the unpleasant"—such passages from the Vedānta are our authority.
If it is argued that this is not so because an authority must have as its object a thing already heard (i.e., previously known), we say no, because [the self] is not known through perception.

Now, if it is thought that a statement whose object has already been apprehended through hearing would be merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*), and therefore not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it depends on another means of knowledge and lacks the status of being the most effective instrument of proof (*sādhakatama*), we reply: no, for repetition does not consist in the restatement of what has already been known, since that would lead to the undesirable consequence that even perception and the other means of knowledge would be repetitive. Rather, repetition consists in making known an object already apprehended. In this regard, if the Vedas were repetitive, they would have to be so by virtue of being objects of other means of knowledge such as perception. But since their object is not the domain of those other means of knowledge, how could they be repetitive? Furthermore, there is no doubt regarding what is previously apprehended from them, unlike the case of memory, because there is no requirement for a prior apprehension. For this very reason, even human speech is a means of valid knowledge; for it does not convey its meaning by first establishing its own validity, but rather conveys the meaning directly, independent of any other operation, since it is required only for its own production. Indeed, the natural capacity of words is directed toward word-meanings, and the natural expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and proximity (*sannidhi*) of word-meanings suffice for their mutual syntactic connection (*anvaya*). Thus, just as in the Veda, the word is independent of other means of knowledge—this is the section concerning the definition of the subject matter (*uddeśya-prakaraṇa*) in the treatise on grammar and the nature of substance.

The principle stated in the *Nyāya*—that "words such as 'smell' (*ghrā*) and so forth denote both worldly and Vedic objects, for there is no distinction in the power of the word"—is accepted by me. However, the pursuit of the actual state of things (*vastu-rūpa*) regarding their essential nature (*svarūpa*) is like the case of perception, where the object is understood through the absence of sublation (*abādha*) despite the presence of defects; it is a cognition that excludes what is non-existent. This is the general direction [of the argument]; the detailed exposition should be seen in the *Iṣṭasiddhi*.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the authority of a word lies in its [denoted] effect (*kārya*) and not in its own form (*svarūpa*), because the capacity of words is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in the context of worldly usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding things to be accomplished? Therefore, the Vedāntas do not have their purport in the [Brahman’s] own form. [Reply: This is not so; for we observe in common worldly usage sentences whose purport is indeed the own form of a thing—for example, when one prompts another toward the mere pleasure of transformation (*pariṇāma-sukha*) while simultaneously dissuading them from the process of transformation itself.

Although the instruction regarding engagement and withdrawal is indeed the meaning of the sentence, [it is said] so that there may be the attainment of happiness in the final transformation and the cessation of what is unpleasant in the final transformation; for a person engages spontaneously upon perceiving sweetness and desists through aversion upon perceiving unpleasantness—what need is there there for the capacity of words or for dependence on instruction? For the scripture itself says later on: "The wise man engages in what is beneficial and desists from what is harmful."

If it is argued that this [sentence] is of such a nature because it is employed with the intention (*abhisandhi*) of inciting activity (*pravṛtti*) or cessation (*nivṛtti*), [we reply: although there is indeed an intention regarding activity and cessation, it is by virtue of being a *producer* (*janakatva*) rather than a *designator* (*pratipādakatva*). For the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of a word lies precisely in its object as it has been stated. If, however, because a sentence is employed with the intention of activity or cessation, the status of being "verbal" (*śābdatā*) were to apply even to things that do not exist, then both the cognition of a substratum (*āśrayabodha*) and the production of satisfaction (*tṛpti*) would have to be the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Furthermore, since perception (*pratyakṣa*) occurs with the intention toward some purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the purposeful action of activity and so forth would have to be the object of knowledge (*prameya*) in that domain. If the Vedāntas were intent on activity by way of being producers, then upon the realization of the true nature (*svarūpa*) from them, one would engage in meditation and the like; yet, when the pure self-knowledge—free from conceptual constructions regarding objects—arises for one thus engaged, liberation (*apavarga*) would result. However, it is not necessary that the operation of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇavyāpāra*) must always aim at activity or cessation. This is because, even when a prior desire is obstructed and does not arise, the inquiry of seekers concludes in the determination of the thing itself (*vastupariccheda*). Nor is it the case that words have their power (*śakti*) only toward things that are already existent, for we observe the acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) even toward things not yet connected. Just as in the statement "The bee is drinking honey in the bowl of the *prokṣitṛ*," where the meaning of the word "bee" is understood as referring to the agent of honey-drinking among those things whose forms have arisen in the past, so too in the case of the *kākṣeptviṣu* (those who throw at crows), one understands the word "bee" as denoting the agent of honey-drinking through the speaker’s conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) based on a lineage of transmission. If you say this is so, [we reply: no, because of uncertainty.

Is the learner’s comprehension of the speaker’s intention derived from observing linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), or is it through instruction (*upadeśa*) based on the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with well-known words, or by means of the word’s own form? There is no certainty here; for if there were doubt, how could comprehension occur? Furthermore, comprehension would not arise regarding the meaning of a word unless it is connected to what has been previously stated; otherwise, one would not grasp the true nature of the word’s meaning. Moreover, the meanings of words such as "madhukara" (bee) vary according to the person—whether they are understood literally or as having a contextual significance—because they have fallen under the sway of various circumstances. If it is argued that in Vedic sentences, where the cause of the word-meanings is their intended purpose (*tātparya*), the mutual connection of those meanings will be based on their requirement for action (*kriyākāṅkṣā*), we reply: in cases where there is an absence of action, the connection between the word-meanings expressed by the words—which constitute a collection of words—is based solely on their mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), conditioned by their fitness (*yogyatā*). Thus, even in the sentence "The king, the crest-jewel of the Kāśīs, gave [something]," the sentence-meaning is indeed understood. Or rather, in that case, it may be due to the concealment of the unexpressed verb *asti* (is). But this is of little consequence; let us return to the subject at hand.

In this context, since there is no separate inclusion of properties (dharmas) independently, the inclusion of the categories themselves (padārthas) is obtained through the very words that denote the properties of those categories.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that a compendium (saṃgraha) devoted to the properties of categories (padārtha-dharma) is the cause of great prosperity? Anticipating this doubt—that no effect can arise without the communication of the meanings of words—the author states the following, demonstrating how the compendium, as the means for investigating the properties of categories, is the cause of great prosperity through a traditional succession (pāramparya).

The knowledge of the true nature of the six categories—substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—through their similarities and differences, is the cause of the supreme good.
"Substance, quality," and so forth.

That which is called "substance" (dravya) is a state of being; its existence (sattva), its commonality (sādharmya), and its property (dharma)—that is, its similarity—and its difference (vaidharmya)—that is, its dissimilarity—these similarities and differences constitute its true nature (tattva). Knowledge of that [true nature] is the cause of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa).

Happiness born from the enjoyment of sense objects is fraught with much suffering even for merchants and others; and even if one attains heaven, it shares the same nature [of being impermanent] and is subject to degrees of excellence. Thus, while one person may possess heaven, another may hold the sovereignty of heaven; therefore, because of the fear of falling from that state, it is beset by suffering and cannot be determined as the ultimate good. Absolute cessation of suffering is the certain good, because it involves the total destruction of all suffering through the absence of further experience. The cause of this is the knowledge of the true nature of the categories, beginning with substance (*dravya*).
By this, that which was stated by the Blessed One—that liberation is characterized by the cessation of specific qualities—is not contradicted.
For when there is the destruction of the specific qualities, the self remains in its own nature; it is not [the self] that is destroyed, because it is eternal.

Nor is this [cessation of suffering] not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), because the complete cessation of suffering is the supreme human goal. If it is argued that it is not a human goal because it does not procure all forms of pleasure, [we reply: even pleasure, due to its perishability, its being accompanied by many calamities, its being produced by means, and its being attended with effort, is always overcome by suffering; thus, because it is mixed with poison, it is cast into the category of suffering as something transitory. Whose [is there] the identity of the goal and the means? [The answer is: "of substances and so forth" is the connection [to the phrase] "for the sake of figuratively designating self-knowledge as the non-impelling cause."
It is also explained according to the sixfold division as substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*).
This is because the subject matter of the enumeration has the same scope as the sixfold division.
Among these, substance is enumerated first, because it is the most important in terms of its meaning for all [categories].
Qualities (guṇas) are mentioned immediately after substance (dravya) because they possess a greater number of specific actions.
Action (karman) is enumerated after qualities because it invariably conforms to them.
Generality (sāmānya) is mentioned after action because it arises momentarily.
Since inherence (samavāya) is included within all [categories] by virtue of being held among the five categories, it is mentioned specifically among the particularities (viśeṣa).
The absence of a separate enumeration for non-existence (abhāva) is because it belongs to the category of non-being (abhāva-padārtha).

Regarding the six beginning with substance (dravya), others say there are six sense organs; however, when there is a multiplicity of means to the highest good (niḥśreyasa), the knowledge of substance and the rest is established as the means to that end, since the knowledge of the means and the goal is achieved through their independence.
From the manifestation of the impelling force through the principles, Umādevī [arises].

Now, if it is argued that since the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the means for achieving the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), dharma is not the cause, then [the author] replies to the objection raised by Sucarita—that "dharma is that which, when satisfied, brings about the accomplishment of the highest good"—with the words: "Only from dharma, manifested by the injunctions regarding the principles (*tattva*). The intention is this: the highest good arises solely from dharma; the knowledge of the principles, such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, is the means for achieving the highest good precisely because it is a cause of that dharma.

When external and internal objects have been known in their true nature, one who has become dispassionate through the perception of their defects ceases all striving; for it is logically established that the self-nature [is not produced] from that which is its improper source. Furthermore, for one who practices the knowledge of the self—having washed away the defects of objects by means of the impressions (*vāsanā*) arising from the Vedas and Smṛtis and refusing to take them up again—there arises supreme dispassion and imperishable liberation, because of the eventual occurrence of the absolute release from the body for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is fully matured.

When the objects of the senses have been seen, the relinquishment of the eyes, ears, and other organs occurs through a specific quality of the self (*ātma-viśeṣa-guṇa*) that is preceded by the perception of the defects of objects and is characterized by a non-returning intention (*abhisandhi*). This relinquishment of the body and so forth from the self is caused by that specific quality of the self which is preceded by the perception of the defects of objects and is characterized by a non-returning intention; this we shall explain in the section on liberation (*mokṣa-adhikāra*).
