Dharma alone does not directly bring about the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) until it is favored by the will of the Lord; therefore, this was said: "from the *bhāvas*. Here, "impulsion" (*codanā*) means the impulsion of the Lord, which is a particular form of the Lord's will. "Manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) is the state of being directed toward the commencement of an effect. From both—the manifestation of the Lord's impulsion (which is the state of being directed toward the commencement of an effect) and that which is manifested by the Lord's impulsion (which is made to face the commencement of an effect by a particular form of the Lord's will)—the supreme good arises. This is the construction of the sentence. The word "and" (*ca*) conjoins the fact that the six categories taught in the treatise on substances (*dravya*) and so forth are also causes of the supreme good through Dharma.
Thus, having understood that knowledge of the six categories is the means to liberation, he asks a further question in order to investigate the specific distinctions among each of them.
Now, what are the categories such as substance and so forth, what is their denotation, and what is their mutual difference?
In that regard, substances are ninefold—earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind—as these have been declared to be the [categories of] generality, particularity, and inherence;
for no other existence is mentioned apart from them.

Now, what are "substance" and so forth? One should apply [the questions]: "What are substances? What are qualities? What are motions? and so on. This is because, according to the meaning of the treatise, when the substratum (*dharmin*) is known, its attributes (*dharma*) are known; therefore, there is a separate inquiry regarding the attributes, beginning with "And what are they? and so forth.
Furthermore, the word *ca* here signifies conjunction (*samuccaye*).
He states the answer with the words "therein," and so forth.

Among those [categories] beginning with substance (*dravya*), the substances—earth and the others—are presented by means of the term "substance" (*dravya-sañjñā*), the term "generality" (*sāmānya-sañjñā*), and the term "particularity" (*viśeṣa-sañjñā*), as well as by their respective individual, non-common designations such as "earth," "water," and so on. To the question, "Are there only these many, or are there others as well? he replies: "only nine."
Now, one might object: since the capacity for the other two [types of knowledge] is absent when the characteristics of the nine are stated, it should be understood that "only nine" is redundant.
This is not so.

When nine [categories] have been defined, one might wonder whether others are not included because they do not exist, or because even if they existed they would be useless, and thus the doubt as to why these alone are the objects of definition (*lakṣya*) would not be removed. This is because a definition, being true only in the sense of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-mātra-satya*), lacks the capacity to establish the absolute non-existence of other things, since its function is merely to differentiate [the object] from what is not of its own kind. To resolve this determination, this very enumeration of the specific number of the observed categories has been made by virtue of that [definition’s] capacity; otherwise, how could one understand from the instruction that there is no further division beyond these that there are *only* nine? To this, he says: "Not beyond nine," and so forth.

Apart from those nine, there is no other great poison; it is the cause of distress in all water-substances and odors. If it is argued that another [substance] is designated by the term "poison" because it functions in a twofold manner—namely, through the conjunction of atoms of water-substances and atoms of darkness (*tamas*), and through internal states such as pride, intellect, and so forth—no one says this.

If it were argued that because there is no deviation regarding the touch of a substance possessing form within the substance of darkness, and because a substance possessing touch necessarily possesses the property of resistance, then a person moving in the dark would encounter resistance; and furthermore, in a great mass of darkness, the parts of that [darkness] existing as minute fragments would be perceived—this is incorrect.

Just as the existence of objects such as a pot, which are perceived by means of cognition through the senses of sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch, is established by the force of valid cognition even when they are not directly present, so too is the substance of darkness established by its atoms of darkness.

Therefore, it is otherwise conceived: are the atoms of darkness (*tamaḥ-paramāṇavaḥ*) possessed of touch or devoid of it? They are not possessed of touch, because no effect possessing touch is ever perceived that would result from them, and because there is no possibility of their being another substance possessing touch—which would lead to the undesirable consequence of [darkness] being a non-substance (*adravyatva*). If this is argued, then why is it not postulated that the atoms of air (*vāyu-paramāṇavaḥ*), being devoid of the defect of non-substantiality, do not initiate an effect possessing color? Or rather, why has this not been postulated by some: that even from a single atom, through the removal of defects, fourfold effects are produced?

If it is argued that atoms, which are accessible only through their effects, are not produced from those [other] substances because there is no evidence for it—then, in that case, how could even the atoms of darkness (*tamas*) be intangible? For we observe a lack of pervasion (inconsistency) in the principle that a substance with tangibility cannot originate an effect-substance that lacks it. If you argue that a cause is postulated in accordance with what is observed in the effect, and that it is not logical for the effect to be otherwise due to a deficiency in the cause—[we reply: No, we are not opponents of other causes; rather, we say that this is not a substance because its nature is untenable and because it is perceived as an absence.

In that case, this would be perceived as the very absence of existence, for it is impossible for it to appear in the form of blue; moreover, even when one is moving slowly, there is the perception of a blueness characterized by the description of traveling a great distance. Furthermore, in a corner of a house, when the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is present, the absence is apprehended as a qualifier conjoined with it, not independently; and when darkness is being apprehended, there is no other [object] present, nor is the cognition one whose face is turned toward a counter-correlate. Therefore, it is a positive entity (bhāva).
Nor is it the case that the mere non-perception of light is called "darkness" by virtue of being directed outwardly, for it is described as such because of the appearance of a black form.

Therefore, this is a particular kind of entity which, in the absence of light, is perceived everywhere as superimposed under the name "darkness. Furthermore, during the day, there is the powerful impression of a bluish luster on the surface of the eyeball.
But when existence and non-existence are restricted to a specific location, then there arises the cognition "this is shadow" with respect to a blueness superimposed at a distance.
For this very reason, upon seeing two eyes, one designates the large area of shadow as "shadow"; thus, even for us, there is the perception of blueness in that shadow.
And in the case of an uncovered [surface], even though there is an excellence in the manifestation of the object, it is difficult to establish; as it has been said:
Nor is there any darkness in that which is merely a semblance of light, nor is it a vast radiance;
and because the shadow resides within the wood, its qualities of wandering and circularity are ancient [inherent properties].
And because objects such as a fig tree are perceived as being either distant or near;
furthermore, a shadow that follows the body could not exist [as a real entity] by virtue of its substantiality and other such qualities.

Furthermore, regarding its "badly-formed" nature (*durūpatva*): in some instances, such as in shadow, it possesses a connection with blackness and movement; and because it abandons odor, wherever there is an absence of light, there the perception of form is produced.
And as for [qualities] such as priority (*paratva*) and the like, they are not admitted [there].

In that case, the cognition produced by the absence of light is what constitutes darkness; and since the capacity of the eye is not directed toward light in that darkness, it would experience that [darkness] just as the absence of light itself is its own nature.

[Objection: "In that case, there is a contradiction with fluidity; for darkness is defined as the absence of the manifestation of qualities and actions that are perceptible. [Reply: There is no contradiction. Since darkness is perceived as an entity (*bhāva*), it is an entity. Even the Lord (*Īśvara*) is like the self (*ātman*) when seen through the lens of merit; however, He does not differ from the liberated selves (*muktātman*) by way of a distinction of qualities, because He is independent of the production of the three qualities (*guṇa-traya*). Nor is He distinguished by the liberated selves.

The qualities (guṇas) are sixteen as stated by Kaṇāda: color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort.

By the word "and" (ca), those taught by Akṣapāda are included: heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, momentum, mental impression (saṃskāra), unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa), and sound; thus, there are twenty-four qualities, including velocity (vega).
The qualities beginning with color (rūpa) are those mentioned by Kaṇāda; these were restated by the author of the Sūtras through the words "color, taste, and so forth" (rūparasādyādi).
Furthermore, those such as heaviness (gurutva) and others which are not explicitly mentioned by name but are well-known in the world as being qualities have been included [by the word "and," *ca*].
Thus, there are exactly twenty-four qualities.
However, those [other types of yoga] such as the sixteen-fold yoga, the subsequent Kāṇabhujīya, and so forth, are included within these.
Furthermore, even for one who is powerful, there is an exertion toward the supreme self through the remaining [means], and this is indeed what is intended.
For one who practices dharma, there arises a loftiness of intellect.
Desire is the wish to cause others to experience suffering;
it is the intellectual deficiency of one who is dogmatically attached to [false] principles;
it is the state of being unfit for the highest good or for receiving spiritual grace—and so forth.

By the word "fourfold," there is an inclusion of each according to its respective application. "Impression" (*saṃskāra*) is a designation for velocity (*vega*), mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*).

But if this is so, there would be a lack of distinctness [among them], because velocity, mental cultivation, and elasticity would be one due to their sharing the single universal (*jāti*) of "impression-ness."

In that case, the notion consisting of the form "it is not twenty-four substances" has ceased; for, just as in the case of property and possessor of property, there is no such thing due to their identity, so too there is no absence of the class-property of non-substantiality.
Although it is devoid of qualities, because it possesses common attributes, there is the conventional usage "the cognition of the jar" through metaphorical designation.
There are exactly five types of action: upward throwing, downward throwing, contraction, expansion, and locomotion.

By the inclusion of "locomotion," the upward flaming of fire, the horizontal falling of water, the bending of a tree, and so forth, are merely specific varieties of locomotion and do not constitute distinct classes of action.
He classifies actions [as follows]: "Throwing upward," etc. He states how many there are among them:
"Only five.
Now, since there are also [actions] such as whirling and so forth, how can there be this restriction that there are "only five"?
To this he says: "Because of the inclusion of 'going' (gamana)."
Because of the inclusion of "going," there are only five actions;
the others are included within these,
such as whirling, ejecting, contracting, and so forth.

The meaning is that since even whirling and so forth are specific types of going—namely, subdivisions of going—and not distinct classes [of action], it is established that the restriction "only five" is valid, because these too are included by the mention of "going."
Generality (*sāmānya*) is of two kinds: the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*), which serve as the cause for the cognition of inclusion (*anuvṛtti*).
Among these, the higher is "Being" (*sattā*), because its scope is vast; and since it is the cause of inclusion alone, it is exclusively a generality.
"Substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and the like are lower generalities, because their scope is narrower than that of "Being."
In the same way, because it also serves as the cause for the cognition of "tiger," the universal also receives the designation of a "particular."
He speaks of the universal. He explains that the universal is of two kinds;
he thus states its twofold nature itself.
"Supreme and beyond the supreme" (*paramāparam*): the particle *ca* has the sense of emphasis; thus, the meaning is "supremely beyond the supreme" alone.
He describes its nature:
Regarding the phrase "the cause of the cognition of conformity":
that from which the mutual conformity of the individual entities (piṇḍa) following upon the threads is perceived is the universal (sāmānya).
To the question "What is that? he says: it is the highest universal (paraṃ sāmānyam).
"Because it has a supreme object.
Here he states the reasoning:
"Because its scope is vast."
The meaning is that it has a wider range of objects (*bahuviṣayatva*) in comparison to [the narrower categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*).

Furthermore, because it is the cause of persistence (*anuvṛtti*) alone, substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and the like are indeed universals (*sāmānya*); for they are the cause of the very cognition of their own substratum.

Even though [substance-ness] thus excludes itself from universals and so forth, it nevertheless cannot exclude its own referent from them, because even those [universals] possess the nature of being the referents of the word "existence" (*svarūpasattāśabdārthatva*).

Furthermore, by the term "bound intellect" (*baddhamedhā*), what is intended is the state of being a cause for subsequent conceptualization (*anuvṛtti*). Therefore, there is no fault even if it is not a cause for the initial conceptualization. Some claim that since worldly people do not engage in linguistic usage regarding the objects of the various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as they are perceived by those means, there is no other [single] means of valid cognition.
That is incorrect.

Because prior to the unity of the means of valid cognition, there is an absence [of such usage] even when there is multiplicity; and because, like a donkey's horn, there would be an absence of anything to be grasped, resulting in the fallacy of mutual dependence.

If the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were itself an object of apprehension, then existence (*sattā*) would have to be established by a means of valid cognition; furthermore, since that momentary object of apprehension would require another means of valid cognition to apprehend it, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). In this view, one should not abandon the reality of the means of valid cognition simply because it exists; rather, the very nature of the thing itself is what is intended by the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). Even for those who assert that things like pots possess a universal existence (*sattā-sāmānya*), the unity of form in a pot and so forth is untenable. Since a thing devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is impossible—given that all things such as pots would be subject to total destruction and non-existence—what could possibly exist? This is the point being investigated.

Since the individual forms of each jar and so forth are distinct, how can there be a cognition of a single form and the application of a single word toward them, given that no relation [of the word] has been apprehended with respect to those individuals? If, however, there exists a single cause for them, then our desired conclusion is established.

If it is argued that—just as in the case of one who has seen a single cow-individual (*gopiṇḍa*), a cognition arises regarding another individual that conforms to what was previously seen, whereas no such prior cognition exists for mountains and the like based on a mere perception of stability (and thus why should a universal be postulated here?)—is it that there is no non-conceptual experience (*nirvikalpakānubhava*) regarding mountains and the like, or is it that it simply does not exist yet? If you reject the universal because of the absence of non-conceptual experience, then you must also reject "cowness" (*gauḥ*); for between those two—the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and the black cow (*bāhuleya*)—there is an absence of similarity among all [individuals].

Now, even if there were no experience of the intrinsic nature [of the universal] at this time, that would be unproven; for it would follow as a logical consequence that all those [cognitions] would be equal to the conceptual construction of the absence [of the universal].
This is due to such specific [reasons].

In the case of individual cows (*gopiṇḍa*), because there is a persistence of the universal through the cognition of belonging to that same class (*tajjātīyatā*), there is an inclusion of the universal. However, in the case of mountains and the like, because there is no inclusion of a universal through the cognition of being "large" (*mahīdharatva*) and so forth, the genus (*jāti*) does not recur [as a perceived entity], just as one has the cognition of a string of pearls in a heap of gems.
By this, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is also refuted in its entirety.

Since there is no causal efficiency in that which is imperishable, and since existence is defined as having causal efficiency, if that existence were to depend on another causal efficiency for its own existence, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, it would follow that all things are non-existent, or else they would result in being [mere] substances (*dravya*) and so forth.
The meaning is that, with respect to *sattā* (existence), [the categories of] substance-ness (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*) are not its objects.

Likewise, with respect to substance-ness and so forth, earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth are subordinate; with respect to those, pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth are subordinate; with respect to quality-ness and so forth, color-ness (*rūpatva*) and so forth are subordinate; and with respect to action-ness and so forth, rapid throwing (*śīghropakṣepa*) and so forth are to be explained as subordinate.
Some maintain that because there is no commonality in the cognition "river" for one who is traveling on land and one who is traveling on water, substance-ness does not exist [as a universal].
That is not so;

for even in the case of a substance, since the cognition of those two [qualities] is possible through the difference of their own-nature (svabhāva), the very cognition of the difference of own-nature is the cognition of substantiality.

Even though [the quality of] being a substance (*dravyatva*) and so forth exists in motion (*calana*), there is no cognition of it; likewise, there is no cognition of it in sequence (*krama*). However, in the case of *hrasvatva* (shortness) and so forth, because the universal of quality (*guṇatva*) is not perceived due to the absence of a manifesting mark (*liṅga*), the apprehension of the individual (*vyakti*)—just as in the case of the apprehension of the universal—is also a cause for the cognition of that [quality]. Just as the universal of Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇatva*) is manifested by the word "birth" (*yoni*) even in Caitra, nevertheless, Brahminhood—which is understood merely through the birth arising from the cause of being a pure Brahmin—is grasped by the senses as distinct from the blind and others, because it persists through the observation of its complete pervasion (*atyanta-vyāpti*). But when the eyes and other [senses] are directed toward the parents and the offspring, then pure Brahminhood is supported; at that time, one is cognized as "you are a Brahmin" by perception itself. For instance, one who is well-versed in the science of examining forms perceives the distinction of the blood-born caste through direct perception, and not otherwise.

It is not the case that there is no distinction between types of passion merely for that reason, nor is its existence imperceptible; as for the claim that because women are by nature fickle, their purity is difficult to perceive, that too is incorrect.

For those who are well-trained, such perception is easily accomplished, and since many methods have been taught for the nourishment of their passion and so forth, their passion is indeed observed even when unexpressed.

Substancehood (*dravyatva*) and the other categories, because they are the cause of the exclusion of their own objects even from heterogeneous things, obtain the status of "particulars" (*viśeṣa*) as well—not only the status of "universals" (*sāmānya*) due to being the cause of inclusion, but also the status of "particulars" due to being the cause of exclusion; such is the implication of the use of the word "also" (*api*).

What is meant is this: in the case of substancehood and the rest, the term "universal" is used in its primary sense, because the definition of a universal—namely, being the cause of inclusion—is applicable to them.

Furthermore, the word *viśeṣa* (particularity) is also used as a definition in the Bhāṣya: "That by which its own substratum is distinguished—that is, excluded from everything else—is a *viśeṣa*. However, this definition applies to other types of particularities as well.
Particularities (viśeṣas) are the ultimate entities residing in eternal substances;
they are the causes of absolute differentiation, and thus they are entirely unique.
"Particulars (viśeṣa) are ultimate and reside in eternal substances.
They reside only in eternal substances; those which belong to atoms are the particulars.

By the phrase "in eternal substances," there is an exclusion of substance, quality, action, and generality. For while substance, quality, and action reside only in substances, they do not reside in eternal ones alone.

Universals, however, exist neither in substances alone nor as eternal entities alone; otherwise, there would be no exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of cognitions, words, and so forth, because those [universals] would constitute the very essence of all eternal substances.
Now, a doubt arises: are these [particulars] merely specificities (*viśeṣa*), or do they possess a form like "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and the like?
To this, he says: "They indeed... and so on.

The word *khalu* signifies certainty. The meaning is that those particularities (*viśeṣa*) which belong to eternal substances and their qualities are certainly particularities alone; they do not also become universals (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, this is because they serve as the cause—by way of being the reason—for distinguishing [their own substrates] from others at all times (*atyantam*), even when those substrates are otherwise indistinguishable.
As it is stated later in the Veda: "That which is to be eaten by the Brāhmaṇas is above them."
Inherence is that relationship which is the cause of the perception here [in this world] of those established entities that have been heard of and which serve as the substrata.
He defines the nature of inherence (*samavāya*):

"Of those whose establishment is not heard" (*śrutasiddhānām*). "Establishment not heard" means non-separate establishment; that is, the absence of separate existence for two related entities, or their not being supported by separate substrata while remaining apart from one another. The relation between such two things whose establishment is not heard is inherence, as in the case of the threads and the cloth.

Although the threads inhere in a substrate distinct from the cloth, nevertheless, because the two do not exist apart from one another, they lack the state of being supported by separate substrates; for the cloth has the threads themselves as its substrate.
However, where two related substances exist with separate substrates due to their mutual separation, there is "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*).

As in the case of the sense-organ of touch and the body—the body, indeed, is supported on its own substrate which is a substrate distinct from that of the sense-organ of touch even when the latter is absent—therefore, between those two, there is conjunction (*saṃyoga*), not inherence (*samavāya*).

However, for eternal things, there is no "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*), which means either separate existence or the capacity for separate existence; those two which lack this are "non-separately established" (*ayutasiddha*). The relation between them is inherence (*samavāya*), as in the case of space and its quality, or substance and the property of being a substance. If it were merely stated that "the relation between non-separately established things is inherence," then the relation between attributes (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), characterized by the nature of cause and effect, would also result in being inherence, because those two—the attribute and the substratum—are non-separately established. To exclude this, the Teacher [Praśastapāda] added the phrase "of things that serve as substrata."

But [the relation] of parts (*pada*) with ether and so forth is not [inherence], because that [relation] is already excluded by the term "non-separate existence" (*ayutasiddhi*), since it is defined as a relation between eternal substances that are inseparable. Likewise, the relation between the non-ether and the word "ether" would be inherence; to exclude that, [it is said] "the cause of the perception of 'here'. For if it were merely the denoted-denoter relation (*vācyavācakabhāva*), that [perception] would be excluded, since in that case the object is known [merely] as "this," but not as "this is here. [The term] "the cause of the perception of 'here'" excludes the relation to the entire locus for those things that serve as the substrata for the Teacher's [teaching]; to exclude that, [the phrase] "of non-separate existents" (*ayutasiddhānām*) is used.

Now, some analyze the term *ayutasiddhi* (inseparability) as follows: does it mean "not established separately" (*yuto na siddhaḥ*) or "established together" (*yutaḥ siddhaḥ*)? If it means "not established separately," then since there would be no two substrata (*dharmiṇoḥ*), of what two could there be a relation? On the other hand, if it means "established together," even so, what kind of relation is there? For a relation exists only between distinct things, such as a bowl and a jujube fruit; [they argue] that this [relation] is not [one of] separateness.

For this [entity] does not exist as non-distinct, nor is it unestablished, nor does it fail to enter [into relation], because we accept its association with what is unreal. Nor is it established as unjoined with its own nature; for if there were a single essence, there would be only one object to be pervaded, since non-penetration is characterized by the absence of mutual exclusion. And that object is not such [a unity] in the ultimate sense, because those two forms appear as mutually distinct, and the definition of difference is precisely the manifestation of two distinct forms.
Otherwise, the establishment of difference and non-difference would be untenable.

Therefore, even though there is a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svarūpabheda*), the phrase "of those that are mutually established" means that they consist of a distinct application characterized by mutual dependence.

This being the case, a relationship is not untenable, because the difference in intrinsic nature is possible; for, as in the case of fire and a mass of iron, a relationship is impossible without mutual dependence.

Now the specific distinction is stated: in other systems, *prakṛti* and the rest are connected with the whole (*piṇḍa*), but here, even while not yet arising at the time of its own cause, it is connected [with the whole], just as the action of moving is connected with the earth; enough of this. Now, why are there exactly five categories? Because there are no others beyond them, and because of the non-existence of anything else. Since "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is not perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its object is essentially void.
As for the sixth, its general characteristic is that its object consists of a qualified self-nature (*viśiṣṭātmaka*).
However, a definition may be contradicted, as for example: "Substance is that which is the substratum of qualities";
"Quality is that which possesses generality and is devoid of qualities, and is intermediate between conjunction and disjunction, and is not a cause";
"Action is that which resides in a single substance, is devoid of qualities, and is the independent cause of conjunction and disjunction."
Generality (sāmānya) is the cause of mere cognition [of similarity].
Particularity (viśeṣa) is the cause of absolute differentiation. Inherence (samavāya) is the relation of locus and located between two things that cannot exist separately.
All phenomena have been established by you as being devoid of a substratum.

Since it is not possible to speak of properties (*dharma*) in the absence of substances (*dravya*), he demonstrates the multiplicity [of properties] by means of the property itself within the section on "Non-existence" (*abhāva*).
Thus:

having previously, by means of the aforementioned text, set aside the properties while considering the possessors of properties (*dharmin*), and having summarized the discussion of the possessors of properties through their conjunction, the intention now is that the properties themselves are being pointed out.

Although the classification (*vibhāga*) of substances (*dravya*) and the other categories was performed previously, it was stated that the enumeration (*uddeśa*) has also been accomplished; for the purpose of enumeration is fulfilled merely by the mention of their names. Furthermore, since the categories (*padārtha*) are established by the treatise, they possess the properties of being denotable (*abhidheyatva*), cognizability (*jñeyatva*), and nameability (*prameyatva*).

Although *dharma* is not distinct from the word and its referent (*padapadārtha*), since they are not *dharma* in relation to one another according to that [conventional] understanding; nevertheless, for the sake of fully comprehending their respective status as substratum (*dharmin*) and property (*dharma*), he provides a separate enumeration: "the word" refers to the denotative expression.

The capacity [to be perceived] (*śaktitva*), the state of being perceived by oneself (*svadṛṣṭatva*), and the state of being capable of attainment (*śakyaprāpti*) establish that whatever is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a given entity, that very thing constitutes its suchness (*tathāvidhatva*).

Furthermore, the state of being denotable (*abhidheyatva*) is the fitness for being conveyed through verbal expression; this too is simply the essential nature of the entity, since the essential nature of an existent (*bhāvasvarūpa*) itself is designated as "cognizability" (*cetyatva*) and "denotability" (*abhidheyatva*) according to different states (*avasthābheda*).
And elsewhere, the reality of the dependent is ceased by both.

And "being dependent" is perceived through the state of being reliant on another, not through the perception of inherence (*samavāya*), because that [inherence] is absent in inherence itself. Furthermore, he states that this state of being dependent does not exist in certain entities—namely, atoms (*paramāṇu*), space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*diś*), self (*ātman*), and mind (*manas*)—by saying, "except for eternal substances."

However, for those who maintain that inherence (*āśritatva*) is distinct from the property itself, since it would be a single entity, this [inherence] would fail to pervade all things individually; thus, if they wish to establish that inherence resides in imagined things such as "milk" and so forth, then because its existence is merely imagined, the cognition of it as having its own nature would be untenable. On the other hand, for those for whom inherence is simply the very nature of the entity itself, there is no fault, because—just like the nature of wealth—it lacks the capacity to be a cause for further production. Furthermore, it is illogical to claim that inherence is purposeless, devoid of nature, and lacks the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), for such a thing cannot exist.
The five categories, beginning with substance, possess both the state of being inherent and the state of being inherent in [another].
He establishes the common property (*sādharmya*) of the categories beginning with substance (*dravya*) and ending with particularity (*viśeṣa*).
"Inherence-possessor-ness" (*samavāyitva*) is the mode of existence characterized by inherence (*samavāya*).
"Multiplicity" (*anekatva*) is simply their own nature (*svarūpa*), which consists in being distinct from one another and mutually exclusive.

If it were stated simply "of substance and so forth" (*dravyādīnām*), then inherence (*samavāya*) would also be included; therefore, it is said "of the five" (*pañcānām*) with respect to their properties.
And if it were stated simply "of the five," it would not be known which five; for that purpose, it is specified as "of substance and so forth."
The five categories beginning with quality (guṇa) are likewise devoid of qualities and devoid of action.
He states the common characteristics (*sādharmya*) of the categories beginning with *guṇa* (quality) and ending with *samavāya* (inherence).
Regarding the phrase "of qualities and so forth":

"the state of being devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇatva*) means being characterized by the absence of qualities; "the state of being devoid of action" (*niṣkriyatva*) means being characterized by the absence of action, as stated in the *Bhāṣya*. Just as an absence can serve as a qualifier—as in the expression "the smoke which is the basis for the fault"—so too is it here.

If it is argued that "this non-existence is a qualifier because there is no relation between existence and non-existence," [we reply: there is no qualified cognition regarding existence; therefore, we shall postulate a relation for that purpose, provided that one considers a qualifier to be necessarily related.

The three—substance and the others—possess (1) a connection with existence (*sattā*), (2) the state of being qualified by generality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*), (3) being denotable by words whose objects are established by their own convention (*svasamaya*), and (4) being the agents of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).

The connection of the three—substance and the others—with existence (*sattā*) is their relation with the universal *sattā* by way of inherence (*samavāya*); this constitutes the commonality of substances, qualities, and actions.
How these possess a connection with *sattā* has already been established.
However, the following point is now being investigated here.

Is this relation with existence (*sattā-sambandha*) with that which already exists or with that which does not exist? If it is with that which exists, then since it has already attained existence through its relation with *sattā*, there is the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), for *sattā* would require another relation to exist. Furthermore, if the relation were possible with that which does not exist, then *sattā* would also exist in things such as a donkey’s horn. First, in the case of eternal things, [the relation] is untenable because they do not undergo any change of state. In the case of non-eternal things, it is precisely their prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) that renders them incapable of producing the effect of existence.
Nor is there the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of [existence] to things like a donkey’s horn, because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for their production is absent in anyone.
There is also another common property (*sādharmya*) of the three categories beginning with substance (*dravya*), namely, "this" (*ayam*).
And [the definition] includes "possessing universals and particulars.

Because they are the causes of inclusion (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so forth are the universals and particulars; their inherent connection with substances and the like is precisely *samavāya* (inherence).
And [the definition includes] "being denotable by the term 'own-convention' (*svasamaya*)."
The convention established by the Vaiśeṣikas themselves for their own usage in the treatise is as follows: "Substance, quality, and action are to be understood from the word.
By this, the three—substance and so forth—are expressed by words that are denotative through description (*nirūpaṇavacanīya*).
Likewise, merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and agency (*kartṛtva*) [are expressed].

Furthermore, the status of being the substratum for both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) belongs to the three [qualities]. For instance, just as the earth is the cause of merit and demerit when it is being given away or when it is not being measured;

and just as conjunction is the cause of fluidity, as in the case of the body of a man with tawny hair; likewise, the effect of both is seen, as in the case of something that is both pleasant and extremely loathsome—other examples should be inferred in this manner.
The statement "the state of being the agent of dharma and adharma" is precisely what is called their innate capacity (śakti) toward the production of dharma and adharma.
Now, one might object that the universal (jāti) is also a cause of the two; however, this is not so, because it [the universal] cannot be delimited by its own substratum, the individual (vyakti).

The properties of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*) are indeed restricted to having a cause (*kāraṇavattā*). That is to say, for those substances (*dravya*) and so forth which have an impermanent cause, the properties of being an effect and impermanence are not subject to doubt. When it is stated that "being an effect" consists in inherence (*samavāya*) in its own cause, prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), or conjunction with a heavy substance (*ghanasaṃyoga*).
That is correct.

Since [the effect] would not manifest immediately upon the disjunction [of its causes], the acquisition of its own nature depends upon causes; therefore, "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is the definition because it is all-pervasive.
Some maintain that impermanence (*anityatva*) consists in the existence of a real entity characterized by the presence of constituent parts (*prakṛty-aṃśa*).
That is correct.
The world understands that "the world is impermanent" (*anitya*) as a reference to its activity and its head (i.e., its nature), and not from a quality like wickedness (*khala*), and so forth.
Others say it is because of its connection with arising and destruction.
That is incorrect.

For origination does not exist in prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), because it is well-known in the world that this [prior non-existence] is eternal; therefore, its causality consists in the destruction of its own destruction.
As it has been said:
In some cases, a general action is stated for the purpose of expressing destruction.

Although destruction does not exist at the time of the entity itself, there nevertheless occurs a cognition of its cessation established by other means of knowledge, as seen in the qualifying expression "the pot is impermanent" resulting from such a response; likewise in common worldly usage, one says, "having heard that the body is perishable, [I shall act] with constancy."
And the state of being an effect [is established] for all things other than spherical dimension and so forth.

"And being an effect [is the property] in all cases except for spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and so forth. "Spherical dimension" refers to the dimension of an atom (*paramāṇu*). By the word "and so forth," one should include the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), the omnipresence (*vibhutva*)—which is absolute magnitude—of ether, time, space, and the self, the dimension of the mind (*manas*), priority and posteriority, the dimension of the final product of a binary compound (*dviṣṭha-prakṣama-antyāvayavi-parimāṇa*), and so on.

Setting aside these [qualities], although substance (*dravya*) possesses the status of being the three types of causes—namely, the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), and the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*)—whereas qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*) do not possess the status of non-inherent or inherent causes, nevertheless, this commonality has been stated as an ornament by way of their status as efficient causes.
And the state of being a substance exists elsewhere than in eternal substances.
"And substantiality [belongs] elsewhere than from eternal substances.

Now, it was stated that "dependence belongs to jars," so is this not a repetition? It is said in reply: "It is not a repetition, because dependence as characterized by being a substance has also been established.
That is incorrect.

Since it is possible for universals (*sāmānya*) and the like to be dependent by virtue of being characterized by substance (*dravya*), there would likewise be a statement of similarity regarding the objects that are substances and so forth. Therefore, this [phrase] must be explained as follows: "except for eternal substances" (*anyatra nityadravyebhyaḥ*). The definition of substance is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); thus, the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*) other than those [eternal substances] are also included.

By excluding eternal substances and the ultimate particulars other than them, the dependence upon substance is the common property (*sādharmya*) of the three—substance and the rest—and not of others; for they are excluded from the category of substance due to their dissimilarity.

The three [categories] beginning with generality (sāmānya) possess existence in their own right, the characteristic of being cognized by the intellect, the state of having effects, the state of having causes, the absence of further generalities or particulars, eternity, and the state of not being denotable by the word "object" (artha).
He states the very sublation of universals (*sāmānya*) and the rest by means of their completion:
"of universals and the rest.

Existence as their own self is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) which belongs to universals and the rest; that alone is their existence, not a connection with [the universal] *sattā*, for such is the function of words.
The meaning is that by this, the three—beginning with generality (*sāmānya*)—are stated to have the common property (*sādharmya*) of being devoid of generality.
Because it is impossible to alter this in any other way, there is no absolute non-apprehension of existence within generality.

Even regarding particulars, since it has been stated that they possess universality, doubt is possible; therefore, for the sake of certainty, one must pursue the particulars, which leads to an infinite regress. Furthermore, even if [universals] were admitted, the undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpatti) would arise because inherence (*samavāya*) would also have to be accepted for their production. Since "existence" (*sattā*) pervades universals such as "cowness" by virtue of possessing its own universal, the cessation of that [universal] through its opposite constitutes its destruction. Thus, there is a continuous application of "existence" to universals and so forth. However, this is merely a superimposition of existence upon them based on the common property of having their own nature (*svarūpasattva*). If that were so, one might object: "Then this is a false cognition. To this, who indeed would say "no"? It is an error (*bhrama*), yet there is a single continuous application [of the term]. The nature of a substance is not separate from its own form, because its own form is real. Let the continuous application of the cognition [of existence] in substances and so forth also be caused solely by the superimposition of existence. This is not so, for if that were the case, there would be a suspicion of superimposition even regarding primary [existents]; however, this is not the case, because while sublation (*bādhaka*) is possible regarding universals and so forth, it is absent in the case of substances and the like.

Regarding the phrase "having cognition as their defining characteristic" (*buddhilakṣaṇatvam*): those for whom cognition alone is the defining characteristic—that is, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—are "those characterized by cognition. This is said in contrast to categories such as the "universals" (*sāmānya*), where it is stated that cognition alone is the defining characteristic and nothing else; whereas in the case of [categories] such as "substance" (*dravya*), it would follow that other effects thereof could also be the means of valid cognition. Alternatively, they are called "characterized by cognition" because, when milk is being consumed, [the substances therein] are indicated—that is, perceived—by means of that cognition.
That is incorrect;
since substance and the rest are also characterized by their own cognitions, this would have to be stated as a point of dissimilarity [from universals].
Furthermore, being non-produced (akāryatva) and independence from causes—which constitute non-existence—is certainly not a fault in the case of a universal.

Relying on the persistence [of the cause] at the time of manifestation when it has reached full growth, and given the absence of a cause, [inherence] is perceived—just like pervasion (vyāpti)—during examination by one who is engaged in the production of a jar through an auxiliary that is not its own self. Thus, inherence is also established as non-produced (*akāryatva*), because there is no sequence involving the prior collection of its constituent parts. For if the inherence of a cloth were to exist prior to the cloth, how could it be a relation in the absence of a related entity? If, on the other hand, it were produced simultaneously with the cloth, then the cloth would lack a substratum (*anādhāratva*).

Now, even if there is such a persistence [of the universal], the cloth nonetheless remains non-substantial; moreover, it is not logical for an effect to be without a substratum. Therefore, inherence (*samavāya*) is beginningless.
Furthermore, since the particulars (*viśeṣa*) are neither effects nor powers, they are established as being distinct from substance, quality, and action, just like universals and inherence.

Regarding their lack of causality, there is an absence of both inherent and non-inherent causality; however, this does not prohibit their status as instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*), since their functioning as instrumental causes—such as in the case of cognition—is indeed possible.
The other two [particularity and inherence] are devoid of commonality, particularity, and inherence.
Among universals, there is no further universal named "universal.

Furthermore, since universals do not exist in prior non-existences, nor in absences, nor in particulars or inherences—and since it is logical that there be only one [universal]—then how is the recurrence of the cognition "universal, universal" to be explained regarding universals?

The application of the terms "particular" (*viśeṣa*) and "one" (*eka*) occurs due to the influence of limiting conditions (*upādhi*), such as multiplicity and inherence (*samavāya*), since it is possible for everything to produce cognition that is entirely free from verbal expression.

Regarding eternality, if there were a cause for destruction, then even though the universal (*sāmānya*) has perished, the notion that it is subject to destruction—such as through being struck down—is merely an error; for what has been set in motion will indeed be accomplished, and thus a contradiction with pervasion (*vyāpti*) is raised. As for inherence (*samavāya*), however, because every effect is perceived [as inherent], its uncreated nature is accepted.
Furthermore, the non-eternality of words regarding objects, as well as the non-eternality of words regarding their own conventional meanings, are the proofs for these [positions].
Vaḥ [is used] at the end of the sixth case.

All nine substances, beginning with earth, possess substantiality (dravyatva), the capacity to originate within themselves, the possession of qualities (guṇavattva), the state of being opposed by their effects and causes, and the possession of ultimate particularities (antyaviśeṣa).
Now he defines the commonality (*sādharmya*) of substances alone.
Regarding the phrase "of earth and so forth":
the connection or relation of earth and the other [elements] with the generality (*sāmānya*) of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is what he calls the result of the action.
"Of the nine as well. Here, the word *api* (also/as) carries the sense of *api-śabda* (the particle "also").
By this, it is indicated that among these categories of substance (*dravya*), there exists a distinction characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
The ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "substance" (*dravya*) has been examined.

Here, someone says: "The connection with substantiality—that is, inherence in substantiality (*dravyatva-samavāya*)—is the definition of substance, and that [inherence] consists of the category of 'cattle' (*paśu*). Another replies:

Activity is desired for all [categories], and likewise inherence; nevertheless, the definition of substance (*dravya*) is observed through the distinction of its qualifying characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), namely "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*). For instance, although space is conceptually divided, the difference in its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is seen solely through the ear. This meaning of the sentence should be understood as follows: just as the ear is not the definition of space, nor is conjunction (*yoga*) the definition of substance, but rather "substance-ness" itself is its capacity, which serves as the definition. This is not explicitly stated by the *Yogasūtra* when determining the nature of the earth and so forth as a sign (*liṅga*). Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "Earth and the other [elements] are distinct from others because they possess 'substance-ness'; those things that do not have a distinction from these [others] do not possess 'substance-ness,' just like color and the rest."
Therefore, because it consists of non-doubt,
he states another reason for the sublation of substances:
"the state of being of the nature of the self within itself."
The meaning is: "the state of being the substrate for moments inherent in itself.
Possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*) refers to the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) with qualities.
This is necessary for establishing the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) of substances from qualities and so forth, as it would otherwise be impossible.

The state of being non-opposed by either effect or cause: for a quality (*guṇa*) is sometimes destroyed by its cause, as the first sound is destroyed by the second sound; sometimes it is destroyed by its effect, as the final sound is destroyed by the penultimate sound; and sometimes it is destroyed by other effects, as in the case of conjunction with a subsequent [sound]. Substances (*dravya*), however, are neither destroyed by their effects nor by their causes; thus they are non-opposed by effect or cause. Regarding eternal substances, this non-destruction by cause is simply the absence of destruction by a cause. As for non-eternal substances, while destruction by cause is possible, there is no destruction by their own effect; rather, destruction occurs by something else—this is the distinction.
Likewise, "possessing other particularities" means being endowed with other particularities.
And non-dependence and eternity [belong] to [space and time], except for the substances that have limits.

Regarding the properties of being non-dependent (*anāśritatva*), inherence in produced substances (*kṛtidravyasamavetatva*), and eternality (*nityatva*)—which consist in being devoid of destruction—if these are sublated in some substances, then one might ask: "Is this the case for all [substances]? To this he says:
"By others than the indestructible substances.
The meaning is that, setting aside the indestructible substances, non-dependence, eternality, and so forth apply elsewhere because they possess other specific qualities.
The meaning is that it is not only the previously mentioned qualities of the earth and so forth, such as being a *yakṣa*, but rather [the qualities of] non-dependence and permanence as well.
[The reason for the inference] regarding earth, water, fire, air, and ether is their multiplicity and possession of a lower genus.
Explaining the mutual similarities and dissimilarities of the substances beginning with earth, he says:
"Of earth, water, fire, air, and ether.
"Multiplicity" refers to the distinction between each individual manifestation.
"Being devoid of non-earthness" means being connected with the genus (jāti) such as earthness (pṛthivītva) and so forth.
Earth, water, fire, air, and mind possess activity, corporeality, priority, posteriority, and velocity.
Earth, water, fire, air, and mind possess the qualities of having action, being corporeal, having priority and posteriority, and possessing velocity.
Having action (*kriyāvattva*) is the connection with actions such as moving upward and so forth.
Being corporeal (*mūrtatva*) is the state of possessing a limited dimension (*parimāṇa*).

Remoteness (*paratva*), proximity (*aparatva*), and possession of velocity (*vega*) consist in the inherence (*samavāya*) of remoteness, proximity, and velocity. Some maintain that remoteness and proximity do not exist [as distinct qualities], because the conventional usage of "remote" and "proximate" is caused solely by time and space through their connection with conjunctions and conjunctions-with-conjunctions. This is not so; for even when such connections with conjunctions and so forth are present, the cognitions of "remote," "proximate," "far," "near," and so on still arise in relation to the body, despite the presence of those [connections]. Thus, remoteness and proximity do indeed exist.

If it is argued that the cognition "this is true" arises with respect to two lumps situated in one direction, then [we reply] that even in the case of a convention, it must depend on conjunction and so forth, because a distinct cognition arises without any difference in the objects themselves, yet there is a difference in the objects.

If it is argued that the Vaibhāṣikas do not consider velocity (*vega*) and other such qualities to be anything more than the mere possession of action (*kriyāvattā*), and that their usage of the term "action" is merely due to the observation of its causal function, [we reply: this is not so. For even when actions are observed as mere conventional designations—arising in uninterrupted succession—one perceives through direct experience a transformation (*pariṇati*) that is distinct in each moment, whether it be prior or non-prior; moreover, the Vaibhāṣika position itself admits this. Furthermore, in the world, there is a clear cognition of the distinction between the destruction of an action and the persistence of momentum, as evidenced by the common perception: "He goes with speed."
Space, time, direction, and the self possess omnipresence, mutual contact, and the property of occupying the same location as all things with which they are conjoined.
Regarding the statement that space, time, direction, and the self are all-pervading (*sarvagata*), and so forth:
here, by the word "all" (*sarva*), the corporeal substances previously mentioned are intended in relation to the subject at hand.

All-pervasiveness (*sarvagatatva*) is conjunction with all locations; however, this does not mean that space and the others are reachable by everything, because they are devoid of action (*niṣkriya*).
"Mutual conjunction" means possessing a dimension equal to that of the four infinitesimals (*paramāṇu*).
"Occupying the same location as all conjoined things" means that space (*ākāśa*) is the substratum in the same location for all these conjoined corporeal substances (*mūrtadravya*);
the same should be explained for the directions (*dik*) and so forth.
Although space and the like do not serve as the substratum for all things that possess conjunction— since a substratum exists by virtue of being non-distinct [from its own locus]—
nevertheless, because it is the substratum of all conjunctions, it is called the "substratum of all things possessing conjunction" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
It is precisely in this sense that its "all-pervasiveness" (*sarvagatatva*) is restated here.
For in that case, it was stated that conjunction is taught with all [the elements] together;
here, however, it is said that it is the substratum of all of them.

The five elements, beginning with earth, possess the properties of being elemental substances (*bhūta*), being the material causes of the sense organs (*indriya-prakṛtitva*), and possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣa-guṇa*) that are not perceived by other senses.
The elements beginning with earth and ending with space are maintained and designated through their mutual exclusion.
This refers to "the elements beginning with earth."

The state of being an element (*bhūtatva*) consists in being denotable by the word "element" (*bhūta-śabda-vācyatva*). This singularity is established through the application of multiple individual words such as "earth" and so forth, just as the application of dual number and so on is established through the connection with the generalities of "Devadatta-ness," "sensed-organ-ness," and "specificity. Just as the word "element" is applied to earth and the other [elements] by virtue of the generalities of "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so on, so too is the word "element" applied to space (*ākāśa*) by means of its individual determination. Thus, the cognition "an element, an element" is permeated by that word because it is based on a limiting condition (*upādhi*) consisting in being directly perceptible and being denotable by the word; just as there is the cognition of "Devadatta" and so on in relation to Devadatta and others.

Some maintain that the nature of being a sense organ (*indriyatva*) is the commonality of the sense organs' essential character, and that the sense organs do not inhere in the primary elements (*bhūta*), because they function as perceivers; for their fundamental property is the state of being a perceiver, just like a lamp.
This is incorrect, because there would be no perception of obstructed objects.
If a lamp and the sense organs were perceivers [in the same way], then an object obstructed by a wall or similar barrier would also be perceived, since there would be no resistance.

If it is argued that the perception of an object not obstructed [by distance] is due to a general capacity (*yogyatā*), then: first, the sense organ certainly possesses the capacity to grasp its object at that time, since it perceives objects that are not obstructed. Furthermore, the capacity of the object—consisting of its magnitude, being composed of multiple substances, and other such specific qualities—does not cease even when there is an obstruction; its presence in space remains exactly as it was. Now, if it is thought that the absence of an obstruction (*āvaraṇābhāva*) is also a cause for the cognition of an object, just like the absence of doubt (*saṃśayābhāva*), this is not so. For even when an obstruction exists, the absence of obstruction has not ceased, since the cognition "the absence of obstruction has occurred" does not arise; thus, the absence of obstruction cannot be the cause.
This is not sound.

For an obstruction is observed to possess the nature of obstructing the very object that stands in opposition to it; for instance, a door or the like obstructs water or sunlight by means of its luminous [constituents], yet it does not negate its own mere existence. Thus, this inference establishes that the eye is an illuminator of what is already reached [by its rays]: "The eye illuminates objects that are not separated [from it], because it is an external sense organ, like a lamp, or because it is an external sense organ, like the sense of touch."

[Objection: If that were so, then even a distant object would be perceptible, because of this dependence on rays; for visual rays, having traveled a long distance, grasp objects situated at a distance. Precisely because it has been stated to have a real cause, why is the elemental nature (bhautikatva) of the sense organ not established? For its existence is possible through rays, just as in the case of a lamp. And just as rays, by means of their own repeated expansion and through the effort of their conjunction, abide together within their very parts.

In that case, because the object is apprehended in its entirety—including all its specific qualities—the apprehension is "with recollection" (*smṛti-sahita*). However, when the substratum (*dharmin*) is apprehended as qualified by its own nature alone, without the intervention of [recollection], it is an "apprehension without recollection. If it is argued that whatever moves reaches its destination sequentially, depending on causes other than its own action—just as the simultaneous perception of the branch and the moon is a causal effect—[we reply]: no, because the operation of the sense organ is extremely rapid. This simultaneity is caused by the rapidity of the apprehension, like the appearance of a circle [of fire] from a whirling torch; it is not a real simultaneity.

Now, it might be argued that in the case of a living being, there would be no perception of smell, sight, or touch, for otherwise those [perceptions] would not be possible; since the sense organ is supersensible (*atīndriya*), its contact with the object cannot be directly perceived. However, when there is a cognition of continuity—whether through the contact of a supersensible relation or otherwise—just as there is the apprehension of an object connected to the body, so too does an uninterrupted cognition arise. But just as there is the apprehension of the number six and so forth, so too is there an interval.
Thus, [the elements] possess specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are each perceivable by one of the external senses.

The specific qualities such as color and so forth, which are to be grasped by each external sense organ—such as the eye—and by virtue of possessing those qualities, [the categories] beginning with earth are [defined].
Therefore, these qualities are also graspable by their causes; consequently, their being graspable by each single sense organ is unestablished, just like the term "external" [in the definition].
This should be explained according to the nature of each individual sense organ.
If the four possess the nature of being real entities (bhāva) by virtue of their substantiality (dravyātmakatva).
Regarding the existence of the four as being of the nature of substance:

in the case of the four—earth, water, fire, and air—their state of being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to substance is precisely their own innate power (*nijā śakti*). Being possessed of its own nature is the inherence of its own nature (*svarūpasamavāya*).
The three [substances] possess perceptibility, possession of form, and liquidity. (1)
The three possess perceptibility, possession of color-form (*rūpa*), and fluidity.

Perceptibility belongs to the three—earth, water, and fire—in the sense that they appear in cognition produced by the sense organs; it does not, however, consist in their conjunction with causes such as magnitude (*mahattva*). Possession of color-form exists because of the continuous production of the sense organ's [perception]. Now, one might object: "But the self (*ātman*) also possesses perceptibility. True; however, it was stated that "the three" possess it with respect to the external senses.
Likewise, "possessing color" is the inherence of color;
"fluidity" is another quality named fluidity.
Both possess heaviness and flavor.
Gravity belongs to two [substances].
Gravity is a distinct quality belonging to both earth and water.
Because of its presence, the designation "heavy" is applied to earth and water.
And "possessing taste" (rasavattva) is the inherence of taste; the meaning of "and" (ca) is that it is not only heaviness (gurutva) but also possessing taste that [belongs] to those two.
The elemental selves possess specific qualities.
The possession of specific qualities by the elemental selves (*bhūtātman*). The conjunction with specific qualities belongs to the elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether.

"Specific" (*viśeṣa*) means differentiation; those things, such as color and so forth, which are capable of effecting differentiation—that is, the exclusion of their own substrates from others—are called "specific qualities" (*vaiśeṣika*); the possession of these belongs to the elemental selves. Furthermore, the state of possessing fourteen qualities belongs to the conscious, fluid, and vital selves.
The state of those whose nature is earth and water consists of fourteen qualities;
the conjunction of fourteen qualities belongs to those whose nature is earth and water.
The state of those whose nature is space consists of specific qualities residing in one part of a dyad.
He states that for ether and the self, there exists a connection with specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that reside in a single part of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).
He says: "of ether and the self.

Since specific qualities also exist in earth and the other elements, he specifies those which reside in a single part of a dyad; furthermore, those specific qualities belonging to ether and the self possess the nature of being destroyed immediately after their production (*āśutaravināśitva*), and this is established by the mention of residing in a single part of a dyad.
Regarding space and time: they possess five qualities and serve as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for all things that arise.
He states that "in space and time" there exist exactly five qualities—number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction.
Thus he says: "In space and time."
Not only do these two possess five qualities, but they also serve as the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) for all produced things in relation to their respective effects.

Now, one might ask: how is it to be understood that space and time are the efficient causes of all produced things? If it were the case that space is also a cause [of sound] by virtue of being the locus of the specific quality of sound, then [the argument] would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because we observe expressions such as "born in the house" even when there is no actual causal basis, based merely on conventional designation. To this, it is replied: [The text continues with the formal response.]

Indeed, since the production of all things occurs through the specific restriction of the categories as indicated by reality, through the specific restriction of the particular doors for the manifestation of entities, and through the specific restriction of time—if it is argued that specific place and time are not causes because there would be no production of effects at any time or in any place due to the absence of causes everywhere and always—then this must be addressed: those things which serve as causes exist in a particular place and time, and their capacity to produce arises only therein and not elsewhere, because the assistance required for the generation of the effect is provided by the causes specifically in relation to those particular places and times.
And this alone is the causality of place and time, namely, that an effect arises in one location and does not arise in another.
[Likewise,] there is the conjunction of adventitious fluidity with the two, water and fire.
There is the conjunction of adventitious fluidity with the two, water and fire.

"Occasional fluidity" (*naimittikadravatva*) refers to both that which possesses occasional fluidity and the occasional fluidity itself. If it is argued that "by this [fluidity], there is a conjunction of the two [earth and] fire; and because of the destruction of the fire by its weak potency (*durbalaujas*), there is no negation [of earth]; for those who are afraid, just as weight and strength diminish during a disease, so too in gold and other substances being melted, [earth] is perceived through its inherence in the fire," [we reply]: No, for there is no absolute negation of the earthly substance here, since its reduction to ashes is observed, whereas such [reduction] does not occur in the case of [pure] fire.

For this very reason, even gold and the like are indeed earthy; thus, even if one were somehow to favor [the opponent's view], the argument that "being earthy while possessing the nature of a substance that is perishable, harmful, and liquid" [is the definition] has been refuted by this [definition of fire] as having fluidity, heat, light, and so forth.
Even if it is argued that gold and the like are earthy because they possess the state of being liquid, perishable, and harmful, and because they are substrata of gravity—this is incorrect.

Is there the perception of heaviness (*gurutva*) therein? Since it is a quality (*guṇa*), even when the state of being a quality has passed away, there remains the doubt that moisture (*sneha*), fluidity (*dravatva*), and so forth might be the causes of its manifestation; thus, this doubt is not dispelled. Even if one were to argue that [the opponent's position] is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the opposing side, that too is merely a partial indication (*diṅmātra*) presented here as a refutation of the proponent’s claim, following a brief sequence of arguments.

By means of this very principle (*ṛta*), he says "thus" (*evam*) to the disciples, indicating that in all categories of objects, even while they are being refuted by oneself, their correctness (*sādhutva*) must be stated as something to be understood through verbal testimony (*śābda*) and so forth, and thus it is to be investigated.
In this way, it should be stated for all cases; and the dissimilarity by way of reversal should also be stated—thus there is no confusion of substances.

Regarding objects that have not been perceived, their definitions do not apply because they lack an objective basis; and regarding objects that have not been attained, there is an absence of the cognition of reality due to the absence of its cause. Therefore, for a treatise (*śāstra*) engaged in the systematic exposition of categories (*padārtha*), its activity consists of the "goal" (*upeya*), namely enumeration (*uddeśa*) and definition (*lakṣaṇa*). However, the rule (*niyama*) pertains to critical examination (*parīkṣā*).

When a definition has been stated as described, if the ascertainment of reality does not occur because of an intermingling with other purposes, then the procedure of critical examination is set forth for the sake of eliminating the objections of others.

However, where the determination of the true nature [of the subject] occurs solely through the force of the definition and the statement [of the purpose], there too it is useless to resort [to a separate inquiry]. For even for one who desires the scripture to proceed in various ways, there is no investigation of the purpose and so forth; why? Because those are understood from the mere mention [of them].
Thus, regarding works composed by the authors of the Vedas, the necessity of undertaking a detailed commentary is not to be questioned.

*Uddeśa* (enunciation) is the naming of categories by means of their designations. *Lakṣaṇa* (definition) is the characteristic feature of that which has been enunciated, serving as the means for the knowledge of its essential nature. *Parīkṣā* (examination) is the investigation of that which has been defined according to its definition. There is no end to the subject matter once it has been enunciated, because it is comprised by its specific qualities and characteristics; for instance, the definition of earth is stated separately among the substances in order to establish a rule regarding the grammatical coordination of words.

Furthermore, when substances are distinguished, there must be specific characteristics for them; otherwise, they would be indistinguishable. You have enumerated the substances as earth and so forth, and you will later describe their specific distinctions among substances, qualities, and actions. Therefore, this undertaking is begun for the purpose of defining those specific characteristics.
Now, in this non-Vaiśeṣika treatise, a point of divergence is indicated.
Regarding the phrase "now here":
previously, the dissimilarities (*vaidharmya*) among substance (*dravya*) and the other categories were stated in mutual relation to one another.
Here, however, in this particular section, the defining characteristic (*vyāvartaka-dharma*) that distinguishes each individual substance among the seven is being described.

Regarding the phrase "of each one," he first states the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) of earth according to the order of the subjects, by means of two grammatical derivations involving *bahuvrīhi* compounds—namely, *śaṅkha-pratyādi* and *praty-anta*—which result in the removal of the two suffixes.
Earth is so called because of its connection with the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*).
It possesses color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, substance-ness, viscidity, number, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, and mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
These specific qualities, beginning with color, are established under the section on the specific qualities of substances.
Gravity is established by the mention of the number six;
heaviness is established by the teaching of falling;
and fluidity is established by the separate mention of fluidities.
From the statement "only the subsequent [moment]," it follows that it is a conditioned formation (*saṃskāra*).
Odor exists only in the three [realms].
Visible form (*rūpa*) is of many kinds, such as white and so forth.
Taste is of six kinds, beginning with sweet;
smell is of two kinds, fragrant and foul;
touch, being neither hot nor cold, is produced by maturation.
That [substance] is of two kinds:
eternal and non-eternal. That characterized by atoms is eternal.

The effect-characterized [quality], however, is non-eternal. It is distinguished by stability and the arrangement of its constituent parts, possesses a multiplicity of subordinate universals (*aparajāti*), and provides various benefits through effortless striking and non-striking. Furthermore, its effect is threefold.
That which is designated as body, sense-faculty, and object.
The body is of two kinds: born from a womb and not born from a womb.

Among these, disregarding that which is not born from a womb (*ayonija*), that which is recognized as belonging to the *ṛṣis* and gods—such as the body of Ṛbhu—is produced from atoms accompanied by a specific merit (*dharma-viśeṣa*).
The multitude of Buddhas and beings, as well as bodies of torment (*yātanā-śarīra*), are produced from atoms accompanied by a specific demerit (*adharma-viśeṣa*).
That which is produced from the falling together of semen and blood is "born from a womb" (*yonija*).
That which is the object of that cognition consists of the womb-born and the egg-born.
Among humans, cattle, and deer, it is womb-born;
among birds, reptiles, and fish, it is egg-born.
The sense organ that manifests odor for all living beings is the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇa*), which is composed of earthy atoms because it is not overcome by water.
Its object, however, consists of substances and so forth; it is threefold—namely, as manifest color-form (*rūpin*)—and serves as the basis for the olfactory perception.
Among these, the regions of the earth, such as walls, wood, flowers, and so on, are the forms of the substance earth.
Stones include rocks, gems, diamonds, and so forth; immovable things include grasses, medicinal herbs, and trees.
Earth is so called because of its connection with earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*).

For those who smell the earth with their own hands do not conventionally refer to it as "earth" when it is merely heard of; therefore, for the sake of establishing conventional usage regarding objects connected to the self, this unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is stated:
"Earth is so called because of its connection with earth-ness."

This [entity] should be designated as "earth" because it is connected with earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*); whereas that which is not designated as "earth" is not connected with earth-ness, such as the ether (*ākāśika*).
And this [entity] is not unconnected with earth-ness; therefore, it should be designated as "earth."

Alternatively, for one who hears in the world that "this is earth" but does not know its true nature (*svarūpa*), and for whom it remains hidden, the unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) of earth is stated in order to establish its true nature as distinguished from things of the same and different classes. That which is designated as "earth" in the world is earth because of its connection with the universal *pṛthivītva* (earthness). As it has been said: "Definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) serve the purpose of excluding [an object] from things of the same and different classes, just as the words 'hand' and 'staff' [exclude the person from other things]. Therefore, it is replied that categories such as "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth need not be defined for each individual substance; for those that are not well-known do not require definition there, as it would be purposeless.

Even for that which is not identical to its own nature (*svarūpa*), a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is heard [in scripture] for the purpose of establishing a specific conventional usage (*vyavahāra-viśeṣa*) and for the purpose of defining a particularity (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of what is already known in a general sense.
