Now, if this were so, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding the purpose of a "definition of a definition" (*lakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇārtha*). [This is not the case], because the substance (*dravya*)—as in the statement "Earth is high"—is subordinate (*guṇabhāva*) [to the quality].

If it is argued that [the earth] is inferior because it is preyed upon by tigers, we say no; for that which is not perceived would be utterly non-existent, or else there would be no perception of it at all. For instance, two islands follow after cows with their heads and feet, yet they do not tolerate these two [tigers] attacking them. Moreover, one who destroys the vision of all cannot be countered.

Furthermore, because [the earth] possesses speech through its living beings, such as the wind and the mute, it is established that even the fact of being composed of atoms preceded by the practice of distinct odors constitutes the specific difference of the earth from the others. Thus he speaks while demonstrating this.
Regarding the phrase "color, taste, and smell":
because there is no application of the word "and" (*ca*) as a separate particle, each of the qualities beginning with color is understood to be individually connected with earth.
Thus, he states that the qualities pervaded by the nature of color are intended to reside in earth.
And [the word] *gate* [is used].

The detailed exposition of qualities (*guṇa-vinirdeśa*) is established by means of substances (*dravya*) through their occurrences; this second chapter, which belongs to the section on the detailed exposition of qualities, is for the sake of making that [exposition] manifest in this [treatise]. In that [chapter], color, taste, smell, and touch are established as existing in earth (*pṛthivī*), and they are presented by the particle *ca* (and) in the statement: "Earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch. Because it consists of four words, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "after two numerals... [Pāṇini 5.2.42].

Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and action—these qualities belong to the earth through inherence in substances that possess form. Because they are fourfold (in their application), number and the others are metaphorically attributed to the earth; thus, their existence in it is established. If these were not present in substances possessing form, then their perceptibility through inherence in them would be difficult to maintain, as it would contradict [the observed facts]. Gravity is inferred from the description of falling.

From the teaching that "falling occurs due to weight in the absence of a counteracting conjunction," it is implied by the word *duścakra* (bad wheel) that the earth, which is connected to falling, possesses weight; for that which belongs to a different locus cannot be the cause [of the same action].
From the statement regarding its similarity with water, [the earth] possesses fluidity.

Because of the statement that "there is no distinction between wax, lac, resin, and stones that have holes [in terms of their fluidity]," and because of the statement that fluidity is common to [the earth] and water, it is stated that the earth possesses occasional (naimittika) fluidity.
The term "weak" (*mṛdu*) is used as a designation for what is to be conceptualized (*vikalpya*).
Because of the mention of subsequent action (*uttarakarma*), it is [called] *saṃskāra* (impulse).

Since that action of giving and taking is not [inherent], but rather due to the impulse that causes it to be so, and likewise because of the subsequent quality, by the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated here that in this earthly substance (*pārthivadravya*), impulse (*saṃskāra*) is the cause of action; thus, it is made known that there is velocity (*vega*) in earth, because it is the cause for the cognition of what is not [otherwise] present.

And we shall demonstrate how a single barley grain [is affected] by the process of ripening; it is like a scattered scent. This is the meaning: that it is merely a common property according to its measure.

If it is argued that there is a smell in a separate substance because of the perception of a foul odor in a fragrant bladder (vastu), we say no; for that quality is perceived through its inherence in an earth-substance. If it is argued that the certainty [of its existence] is based on the effect itself, then even in the absence of that [earth], it arises from contact with the air. Just as color belongs to the three [elements], so too, by comparison with what is not external, that very [smell] belongs to the earth alone, as the Vaiśeṣika says: "Color is of such a kind. Even black [color] is to be understood as being stated [to exist] in variegated things and so forth.
The meaning is that white, yellow, and other various colors produce a variegated effect (*citra*) from the variegated itself, and not from anything else.
In a single surface, various forms are presented through the distinction of individual manifestations.
Even in a single jar, there is a convergence of many kinds of disordered forms, wherein the atom is pervaded by the expansion of various types of forms.

If it is asked how this is so, it is explained as follows: Just as in the case of a jar, there is no such restriction that its color must be exclusively white, nor exclusively black; rather, it may be black, white, green, and so forth. Nor is there a rule that only one of these colors exists and not the others, since each is observed individually and all are seen together.
Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that because they are mutually contradictory, none of them can ever arise at all.

Furthermore, there is no perception of a "variegated form" (*citrarūpa*) that is distinct from the individual forms, because a defective cognition lacks the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*).

Nor do the many parts, when combined, appear as a single variegated mark; for if one were to imagine that the whole (*avayavin*) is perceived in this way, it would follow that the same would apply elsewhere, leading to the collapse of the very concept of a "whole. Therefore, all that is perceived by them is merely the collection of those [atoms], which—due to following the nature of various causes—consists of black, white, and green components, and is thus designated as "variegated."
If it is argued that this is because of contradiction, since the existence of two [opposites] in one [locus] is impossible, then it is as the ancients have already said:
"That which is both one and variegated is even more variegated than that."

What contradiction is there between blue and other colors? It is not their non-existence [in one another], for that would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya) in the inference of the existence of one from the non-existence of the other. If it is argued that "contradiction" consists in being different from one's own nature (*svarūpa-anyatva*), that is true; nevertheless, even so, there is no separateness (*apṛthaktā*) for a variegated form (*citrātman rūpa*), because its manifestation through the efficacy of diverse causes has been established by perception itself, which is renowned to all the world. If it is argued that, since the cloth—the substratum—is on one side, there would follow the consequence of perceiving only the variegated form residing in it, because that [cloth] is a single entity; [we reply: otherwise, even though the various forms are perceived through repeated practice whose capacity was acquired from distinct [experiences], they serve as the cause for the perception of the variegated form, and that [perception] is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in other cases as well.

If that is so, then in a substance possessing various colors, there can be no perception of a variegated color, because there is no perception of the colors of its parts. Who indeed says that it is not so? For the color of an extremely subtle object is not perceived in isolation; however, for that which is perceived in isolation, even colors that are not of such a nature are perceived. But for one who maintains that there are many variegated colors occupying a single locus, there would necessarily be an absence of blue, yellow, and so on; for when two or three [colors] perish, a color that is not distinct from them cannot be the producer of another color.

Now, if a single variegated well were to be commenced there, that same [principle] would apply elsewhere as well, because there is no distinction; for a variegated substance is not a manifold [collection], because it possesses the nature of a variegated substance like a conch-shell or a cloud, just like any other substance. That [well] is indeed a single composite substance (*avayavidravya*), because it is a composite substance, like the form of any other composite substance.
The refutation of the previous position also applies here to the statement "the taste is white";
for if it were a substance by its very nature, it would be a definition of earth.

He states [the following] to dispel the doubt that the mention of "consciousness" (*caitanya*) is merely a description of the essential nature of earth alone by means of its primary quality: "Smell is a substance.
He demonstrates that very fact of being a substance as follows:
Regarding the phrase "surabhi-sura-bhijñā" (the cognition of the fragrant):

"asurabhi" refers to another odor that is contrary to a fragrant smell, perceived as disagreeable upon contact with certain substances and so forth; it is not merely the absence of fragrance, because it is experienced as a positive entity (*vidhirūpa*) and through its own specific effort.
Furthermore, that odor which is perceived as intensified is nothing other than a particular degree of the fourth dimension (*parimāṇabheda*), and thus is not mentioned separately.

Alternatively, it is because "non-fragrant" (*asurabhi*) is defined as that which is simply pleasant and fragrant, yet distinct from [the specific quality of] fragrance. He demonstrates its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) to fragrance just as he did for "non-god" (*asura*). Thus, he says: "Its own [quality] is this."
Regarding the touch produced by heating (*pākaja-sparśa*), its definition as a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) to earth is stated for the purpose of inference.

Although touch, like color and taste, possesses the property of being produced by heating (*pākaja*), there is nevertheless no mention of color and taste as being produced by heating because their difference [from touch] can be established otherwise; for what is intended here is the demonstration of a third [distinctive] characteristic. Therefore, among those things that are not produced by heating, such as rigid objects (*stabdha*), the fact that touch is produced by heating is established through inference: "The touch in rigid objects is produced by heating, because it is a touch belonging to an earthy substance, like the touch of a jar and so forth. Furthermore, even the touch of a jar and the like is produced by heating, because—while being perceptible by a single sense organ—it is a quality of a substance, like the fluidity residing therein.
Right here, the author states the determination:
"It is both eternal and non-eternal.
He speaks by way of statement, making known another mode.
He states what is eternal and what is non-eternal:

that which is characterized as atoms is eternal, whereas that which is characterized as an effect is non-eternal. In both cases, the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) has the sense of "essential nature" (*svarūpa*).

Regarding the existence of earth whose nature is that of atoms, what is the proof? It is inference: [earth] has the dimension of an atom as its cause, because it is the cause of the dimension of a final product-substance (*kāryadravya*), whereas in other cases [of dimension], it is not the cause of a dimension.
Or rather, that which is the limit of knowledge—that from which there is no further division—is the atom (*paramāṇu*).

For this very reason, [the atom] is eternal, because while being a substance, it is partless, like space (*ākāśa*). Or rather, not all atoms are [eternal], because in the world, when an effect is produced, the measurement of its parts is perceived in relation to the measurement of that effect. Sound is its part; that will be the atom. Or if even that [sound] does not exist, because of the existence of further parts, then there would be no end to the series of parts, since there would be no ultimate limit to those parts. Consequently, since all things are equally produced from infinite causes, there would be a merging [of all measurements] due to the addition of measurements; what room for doubt is there regarding the equality of the nature of number? This is because of what has been stated.

There exists, indeed, a distinction in the measurement of objects; therefore, it is established that the dimension of the atom (*aṇu*) is a dimension belonging to an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*). Thus, the eternal atom is proven. And that [atom] is a single producer; for if a single eternal thing were not an effect, there would be the production of the existence of an effect, since there would be no cause for its production. Furthermore, if the effect were destructible, it would perish upon the destruction of its substratum, because there is an absence of any cause for destruction such as the destruction of the substratum or the disjunction from the substratum.
This [argument] is characterized by a contradiction in its pervasion (*vyāghātavyāpta*) and is not established.

For here, in the case of "largeness" (*mahattva*) and "substantiality" (*dravyatva*), one observes the capacity for both substantiality and the production of an effect in the dimension of the self (*ātmaparimāṇa*) due to something other than substantiality.
In the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), both substantiality and the production of an effect are generated because it possesses largeness, just like a jar.

First, there is the contradiction regarding the status of a single [atom] as a cause: if [it is argued that] an atom is not commenced by its nature as a substance (*dravyatva*), then how is a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) commenced? Furthermore, one should not observe a fixed rule that a dyad is commenced only by two [atoms]. Since it possesses a minute dimension (*parimāṇa*) and because its causal multiplicity and destruction are not established, there is no restriction on the number [of atoms].
Sometimes it is commenced by three, which is called a triad (*tryaṇuka*); sometimes it is commenced by many, and sometimes by few—such is the conceptualization according to one's preference.

Nor is there any confusion regarding the effect; for as the number of causes increases, so too does the degree of its large dimension (mahat-parimāṇa). Nor does it follow that only dyads (dvyaṇuka) would be the originators of a jar, because they originate it solely for the purpose of producing its large dimension. In this very way, the earth characterized as an effect is produced through the sequence beginning with dyads; and it is non-eternal, because the cause for its destruction—namely, the disjunction of its constituent parts—is possible.
He joins together the interval between the earth, characterized by its effects, and its impermanence with the word "and" (ca).
"Khā" means freedom from doubt regarding one's own [nature].

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), qualities such as being capable of sustaining life (*prāṇiśaktatva*) are included. For those who are ignorant of the Vaiśeṣika doctrine regarding the imperceptibility of atoms, there is a distinction from direct perception (*akṣapratyakṣa*); and because of the distinction of the imperceptibility of grossness (*sthaulya*) and so forth, they [the atoms] are distinguished by those [qualities]. Possessing a multiplicity of lower universals (*aparajāti*), the manifestation of universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) occurs in both [atoms and compounds]. Because universals such as "atom-ness" (*paramāṇutva*) are not perceived, their arrangement (*vyūha*) occurs in such and such a way that, through those [arrangements], further universals arise from those initiations.

Now, one might object: "Since the earth, characterized by its effects, produces for a person who gazes upon it according to his desire the imitation of all atoms—which is itself characterized by its effects—then how is it that this [earth] is not created by an unseen force (adṛṣṭa)?
To this, he says: "Just as from a seat," and so forth.
This means that just as various services such as a seat and the like, which are produced by many [factors], are characterized by their effects for those who desire them.
He, however, adds another function of this [mind]:
"the object.
He demonstrates the very difference in function as follows:
"Body," and so forth.
The designation "body, sense-faculty, and object" applies to this triad of effects.
The state of being possessed by an enjoyer pertains to the body; for it arises from that [enjoyer] in every individual body, like the thumb [as a mark of a person].
The first [category] is the body (*śarīra*), because it possesses a knowing person (*jñātṛpuruṣavat*); such a substance is a sense-organ (*indriya*).
A substance distinct from the body and the sense-organs, which serves as the means for the self's experience, is an object (*viṣaya*). He explains the classification of bodies:
It is both born from a womb (*yonija*) and not born from a womb (*ayonija*).

"Womb" (*yoni*) refers to the union of semen and blood; that which is born from that is "born from a womb. That which is the opposite of those two is "not born from a womb. He demonstrates this very point by saying, "In that regard, [there is] that which is not born from a womb."
Among those two types—born from a womb and not born from a womb—the body not born from a womb does not arise from the union of semen and blood.
To the question "Of whom? he says: "Of the divine sages (devarṣis)."
And this is for the sake of the deities and the sages (*ṛṣi*).
Since the production of a body occurs even in the absence or depletion of semen and blood—which are causes characterized by limited, excessive, non-pervasive, or deficient natures—he says:
"from those impelled by a specific merit" (*yarmaviśeṣavaśitebhyaḥ*).

"Distinct" (*viśeṣa*) means that which is distinguished; thus, "distinction in dharma" (*dharmaviśeṣa*) refers to a preeminent quality, one superior even to those things beneficial to reality. This is the intended meaning: just as the atoms of the body alone are the cause [of its specific nature] and not the semen and blood, so too, because of the destruction of its activity through disjunction and so forth, there is no production of the body by atoms that have undergone transformation (*pākaja*). Nor is there any distinction among the atoms of semen and blood, since they are indistinguishable from other atoms standing nearby. Furthermore, in this case as well, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is the cause for the specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*) produced in the effect.
And just as it is possible for bodies not born from a womb to arise from atoms through the assistance of specific types of gems, so too [is it possible in other cases].

Now, it may be argued that in the case of the production of a body, you yourself have observed a rule regarding the priority of semen and blood; therefore, just as the production of a body from sound or a magical illusion is untenable because it lacks the independence of real substances and contradicts other means of valid cognition such as the ego-sense, so too should the production of a body from a womb be understood. However, even if one observes that the bodies of insects and the like exist independently of semen and blood, there is still no certainty established regarding the rule that the production of a body in specific locations must necessarily be preceded by semen and blood, due to the doubt as to whether this is because of the absence of a particular unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), or whether it is merely a consequence of being born in a specific location.
By this, the inference of an obstructer (*bādhaka*) has also been fully refuted, because its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is doubtful.
Whatever else remains to be said, we shall explain it on the occasion of the examination of yogic perception (*yogipratyakṣa*).
Now, he states that by a specific kind of demerit (*adharma*), a body not born from a womb (*ayonija*) comes into being:
"of those with nud-born births.

Those with nud-born births are gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like; their *yātanā* means affliction, torment, or suffering. For that purpose, a "body of torment" (*yātanā-śarīra*) is produced from atoms (*aṇu*) impelled by a specific kind of demerit.
But here, it is indeed well-known in the world that he speaks of the body as born from a womb,
saying: "born from the union of semen and blood."

"Semen" (*śukra*) and "blood" (*yoṇita*): their "conjunction" (*saṃdvipāta*) is a specific kind of union; that which is born from this is called "born of the womb" (*yonija*). From the semen of the father and the blood of the mother, through their conjunction, the body of a human being arises in the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the six elements—earth, water, fire, air, ether, and consciousness—from the destruction of the previous color and other qualities and the production of new, similar qualities, proceeding by way of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth. This is the entry of the self and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) [into that body]; however, there is no immediate sequence between the production of the body and the dependence upon semen and blood.

In this regard, the mother’s food-essence (*mātṛ-bābāra*) is transferred to the fetus through the four pathways. Furthermore, according to the principle of the division of action (*kriyā*) among the atoms that initiate the formation of soot (*kajjala*), even within the body of soot, there is a great abundance of many atoms. Thus, by the process of conjunction with the atoms of food—which, being non-substantial (*adravya*) and active (*kriyāvat*)—the production of the body begins through the coming together of these atoms that initiate the soot. This conceptualization is observable daily in the body.
As for the measure of the body, what is its proof?
[The soul] is also [limited] by measure (*parimāṇa*): because a large measure cannot be fully contained within a substratum delimited by a very small measure.

If it is argued that "the body becomes the substratum at whatever size it may be," then whether the body is the substratum during the production of other bodies through the assistance of food and so forth, or whether the body exists simultaneously with those [other bodies], in either case, there would be the perception of multiple bodies of smaller or larger measures, just as [multiple] threads and the like exist in a jar and so forth.
But this is not so.

Therefore, [it is established that] prior to [the production of the body], there was a minute dimension (*praṇu*) in the bodies under dispute; for they possess distinct substrata of dimension due to having inferior and superior dimensions, like the dimensions of a jar and a bowl.

Furthermore, the dimension in the bodies under dispute perishes precisely upon the destruction of its substratum, because it is a dimension, like the dimension of a jar destroyed when the wall of clay [that formed it] is destroyed.

If it is argued that the identity of the body is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), we say no; for that [recognition] can be accounted for as having similarity as its object. Furthermore, since a cause for the cessation of cognition—such as the non-production of subsequent cognitions, internal appropriation, or extreme exhaustion—is always possible, just as in the case of individual flames and the like, the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) is itself subject to subversion by way of reasoning.
He shows the manner of that [subversion] with the words:
"It is of two kinds."
The explanation is that "dvividha" (twofold) means that which has two modes.
"Jarāyu" is a designation for the womb; that which is born enveloped by it is "jarāyuja" (viviparous). That which is born after bursting an egg and being enveloped by it is "aṇḍaja" (oviparous).
Another says that the "sheath" refers to the viviparous sheath and the egg-born sheath;
[the former] is from the mother's back and so forth,
while the latter consists of humans, horses, and the like.
"Paśavaḥ" refers to goats, as seen in such scriptural injunctions as "one should sacrifice a goat at the Anūbandhyā rite" and "one should sacrifice ten animals dedicated to Prajāpati.
"Mṛgāḥ" refers to the black antelope and similar species; their bodies are born from a womb (jarāyuja).
And this is intended as an illustration;
for other quadrupeds are also born from the womb (*jarāyuja*).
Birds are well known.
Reptiles are serpents; their body is egg-born (*aṇḍaja*).
Even though it says "hundredfold," this is not for the purpose of restriction, because others as well, such as fish, are egg-born.
They say [this refers to] the sense-faculty (*indriya*).
Regarding the term "faculty" (*indriya*):
among the twenty-six [elements], that faculty which perceives odor within the category of odors and sounds is distinct from the others.
Since no restrictive rule is obtained to the effect that this alone is the olfactory faculty and no other earthly substance is so, he says [the following] for that purpose.
When the elements such as water have perished, there is the grasping of the other [element], namely the earth, by means of its own constituent parts.

This [earth] is commenced by those [parts] which, having their capacity obstructed by water and the others, are distinct from the [ordinary] cognition arising from that [obstruction], such as the perception of foam and bubbles; thus, it is designated as "smell" (gandha) and so forth, being capable of manifesting [its qualities].
This very [earth] is what is intended by the term "grasping" (drāṇa), according to its function.

The self smells the odor by means of this [organ], and thus the very perception of odor in its substance is the proof [of the organ's existence]. Since an action must be accomplished by an instrument (karaṇa), and since that [perception] is not found in the eyes and other organs, it follows that even though it is a sense-organ like the hand, the proof for its being restricted to odors alone among the [objects] such as form is its specific indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Just as in the case of the statement "the scent of saffron," where the occurrence [of the scent] manifests the scent of saffron together with its own inherent scent, so too the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) is an organ that possesses its own inherent scent; it is not the perceiver of its own scent, because that [scent] is apprehended by that very [organ] itself. As it is with the sense of smell, so it is with the senses of taste, sight, and touch. By the force of this analogy, it is understood that for all elements (*bhūta*) without exception, their status as an organ consists merely in the cognition of their own specific quality (*svaguṇa*). However, the organ of hearing has sound as its quality;
therefore, sound is perceived by that [organ] alone.
By the word "tu" (but), he shows the distinction of the object from the body, the sense organs, and their respective specificities; he demonstrates this difference with the words "the object is...
This is a restatement of the common nature [of the object] as that which serves the purpose of the excellence of knowledge and so forth.
"Having grasped the lower characteristic of the *ghṛtābhāṇa*," means:
in the nature of the lower [levels] and so forth of the *ghṛtābhāṇa*. Among those, he determines the former by way of its own form.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):

there, all such features as the high and low ground of Bhūmadevī, as well as the trees and so forth previously mentioned, are all of the nature of *mṛtsnā* (fine soil), meaning they are composed of earth.
He now describes the breaking of stones (*pāṣāṇabheda*).
"Stones" refers to pebbles and rocks; "gems" refers to sun-crystals and the like.
The *vajra* is the thunderbolt and the diamond. Grasses have roots for their feet.
Herbs (*oṣadhi*) are those that perish at the ripening of their fruit, such as wheat and other grains.
Those trees which bear fruits from the wood (vanaspati) are the *kovidāra*, the *kapūta*, and so forth.
The creeper (*latā*) is well known.
Those called "creepers" (*avatanāḥ*) are branches that descend; they include the *kaitakī*, the *bījapūra*, and others.
Those which bear fruit without flowers are *vanaspati*s, such as the *udumbara* tree and others.

However, there is no specific activity arising from their own will that constitutes "stationariness" (*sthāvaratva*). Furthermore, because the state of being a sentient being (*sattva*) does not exist for those two [trees and creepers]—since another form of consciousness (*citta*) can arise even after death—the designation was not made by means of this [sentient] consciousness.
Water possesses the six qualities beginning with form (*rūpa*).
It possesses taste, color, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, and faculty (*saṃskāra*).
Their establishment is as before.

The venerable Śuklaguru [taught] that [reality consists of] parts whose meanings are self-luminous; and speech, which is of the nature of the cognition of those [parts], is established as having the status of a substance. Sentences, as before, are of two kinds.

Because of the existence of both the eternal and the non-eternal, the sentence (*vākya*) is indeed an effect (*kārya*), and it is threefold, having as its objects the body, the senses, and the external world. Among these,

the body and the senses are capable of experience (*upabhoga*) precisely through their own inherent nature, as will be explained later, and by means of the [elements] beginning with earth, which are called "blooming" (*puṣpa*).

The sense organ (*indriya*) among the ten sense organs is that which manifests itself; it is composed of the same substance as water (*jalāvayavaiḥ*), produced from taste (*rasaja*), and is not intended for consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Its object (*viṣaya*), however, consists of coldness, dew, frost, hail, snow, and so forth.
Now, he states its definition:
Now, [the definition of] the self is that which is neither produced nor subject to destruction.
Here too, as before, the purpose of the definition is either for the sake of conventional usage or for the exclusion of similar and dissimilar classes. However, this point must be clarified here.

The distinction between the categories of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as direct perception and the rest, is established for another by means of their definitions, because that which is not already understood cannot be made known [otherwise].

The distinction among categories is characterized by mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva); and since this non-existence consists in both that which is the entity and that wherein it is absent, it is grasped through the apprehension of both. Otherwise, if there were no restriction regarding its own nature, negation would be impossible—as in the case of "a cow is not a horse."

In this regard, what is the point of the conjunction of *vaḍūla* (the tiger) and *upadrāhu* (the wolf)? From the beginning of the section until now, it has been established that there is no possibility [of their coexistence], for *vaḍūla* and *upadrāhu* are mutually distinct and both are faulty. Thus, when there is the perception of the state of "I" and so forth as being mutually distinct, there is no contradiction; rather, in the desire to know things as they truly are, when there is the investigation into the abandonment of existence and the abandonment of non-existence, non-existence itself is the distinction (*viveka*), because [it is] thus that one desires [to know].

This [non-existence] resides in two distinct things, but difference is not a mutual absence (*itaretarābhāva*). Rather, difference is the individual intrinsic nature (*prātyātmika-svarūpa*) of an object, as if it were a spatial location. Or, difference is that by which the two categories [of substance and quality] are perceived; for when the universal (*jāti*) and the substance (*dravya*), etc., are perceived, each is experienced as distinct. Thus, for example, a cow does not proceed from what is being perceived as a horse, nor does it recall the word "horse"; and the cognition of the horse is restricted to its own specific nature. Therefore, the cognition of mutual non-existence is necessarily determined by the apprehension of each thing through its own respective essence.

And it should not be said that if the very nature [of the object] is what is perceived, then why posit mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), for even in that case, there is the cognition of the object of negation. Furthermore, it is not only the difference (*vaidharmya*) that has arisen which is grasped by the means of knowledge; as for what was stated previously—that the distinction between the two is redundant—he says "humrāve" (in the following) to demonstrate this.
In this case, honey, flowers, and so forth are to be made the causes immediately following the substance;
the position of the eastern [schools] remains as before.

The meaning is that just as the existence and apprehension of qualities such as color and so forth—which have moisture as their cause—were previously established in the case of earth, so it is here as well.
And thus, it was previously stated that sound, taste, touch, and smell reside in the [respective] elements as their fluids.
However, it is more appropriate that the presentation of these as "common" (sādhāraṇa) refers to their being present in all [elements], beginning with earth.

For, since the qualities such as form (rūpa) and so forth—which are common to earth and the other elements—are explained without distinction as having specific limits of qualities mentioned in a non-uniform manner, it is precisely by this [explanation] that their status as "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) is established.

Whiteness and so forth; for whiteness itself resides in the heart, as does sweetness in taste and fearfulness in touch. If it is asked how this is so—given that there is a distinction between the substratum (āśraya) and the quality (guṇa) residing within the heart—it is because, having brought those qualities forth from their respective substrata, one describes them according to their actual state; furthermore, once they have been thus defined, they conform to the nature of their own substrata.

If it is argued that those [waters] do not possess a sweet taste because they are transformed by fire like molasses and the like, we say no; for a taste distinct from pungent, astringent, bitter, and salty is actually perceived. The transformation by fire in the case of molasses and the like, however, is due to the presence of an excellence of sweetness.
This implies that viscosity alone is the specific property of water.
Viscidity belongs to water as well.

Now, this [fluidity] exists even in earth, as in the case of ghee in oil; yet it does not exist everywhere, such as in the case of stones, bricks, wood, or clods of earth. As for that fluidity which occasionally occurs in substances like ghee and oil, it belongs only to those parts that have reached a state of suffering due to the heat of the fire; just as the fluidity of ghee and oil [is temporary] when they are melted by fire. However, the property of moisture (leha) belongs to water everywhere, because it follows the presence and absence of that [moisture] in all cases. Likewise, among things not measured by the instruction [of scripture], there is stability in those of the size of a *tarkṣaṇuka* and so forth, and there is heaviness in those measured by the *hrasvatā* [unit]. Even in that case, stability belongs to those whose roots are firmly established, while heaviness exists in those that possess weight.
And fluidity is innate (*sāṃsiddhika*).
It is not only through the Vedas that the extreme fluidity of water is established as being inherent by its very nature;
rather, in the case of milk and oil, that [fluidity] is perceived through contact with their substrates, because it is observed only to a limited degree in some instances.

He states that water, like earth, possesses internal differentiation and is therefore subject to liquefaction: "And those [waters]," etc. Waters, being of the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*), are eternal.
The intrinsic natures of effects, however, are impermanent; and effects are manifold,
even where there is assistance as previously described.

Just as the earth has a manifold function designated as body, sense organ, and object, so too does water. In this regard, the meaning is that while the earthly body is both womb-born (*yonija*) and non-womb-born (*ayonija*), the watery body is exclusively non-womb-born; this is the distinction.
But the human body is not composed of those [two elements], because the quality of odor is perceived therein; rather, it is composed of earth, as he says:
"In the world of the wind.
This body is thus established as having water as its constituent essence through scriptural authority.
He said that such a body— consisting of the collection of substances, resembling a water bubble, fit for being carried away by Viṣṇu, and comparable to a flower on the neck—
is [transient] even at the time of its enjoyment, because it is nourished by earthly elements.

The body, which consists of a specific conjunction and is merely nourished by the constituent parts of earth, may exist for the sake of utility at a particular time; therefore, because it is called "the self's body," the constituents of earth are the instrumental cause. When the substantiality of the self's own parts is obstructed by their conjunction, that which possesses a specific form is called a "body," meaning it is not primarily composed of water bubbles.

As for those who assert that the body has the dead animal as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), for them the body would have no [specific] destination, because the destination of the cause is of a single place-nature. Furthermore, it would follow that there is also a conscious ego-sense (*cidahaṃkāra*), since multiple ego-senses are possible among the causes; yet this is not observed. Therefore, the body could not possibly have the dead animal as its material cause (*prakṛti*), nor could it be composed of earth, water, and fire alone. For the same reason, it could not even have earth, water, and air as its material cause. It would only be so if it had earth, air, and ether as its material causes, and if there were a uniform conjunction of color and taste.

Regarding the nature of air, space, and primordial matter (*prakṛti*) as being non-eternal, the scriptural statements such as "fire is immortal" and so forth should be applied according to their respective contexts.

Furthermore, it does not follow that a body would lack sensory capacity (*akṣatva*) simply because it has the dead animal as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), since a distinction is established through the difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāvabheda*).

If it is argued that the human body consists of earth because it possesses odor, and that the perception of qualities like intensity is obtained in atoms down to the ninefold division [of the body]—and that this perception ceases upon destruction—the answer is that it occurs through "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*).
"The sense organ that makes taste known belongs to those possessing six senses.

Regarding this, [the author] asks: although the sense organ that makes taste known in those possessing six senses consists of the essence of the water-element (*tajjala-avayava-sāra*), why is it not this [water-element] itself that makes taste known, rather than the aforementioned substance?
To this, he says: "Because of the arising and ceasing of consciousness" (*vijñāna-janmi-mṛteḥ*).

The collection of causal factors for the production [of the sense organ] consists of the constituent parts of the earth and consciousness; these constituent parts of the self are distinct from other substances. Therefore, this sense organ, which is produced from a specific originating substance, is not a separate substance, because there is no such production of it as a distinct entity—this is the meaning.

By this, it is inferred through the observation of a fixed rule that the gustatory sense organ arises; the perception of taste is itself the proof [for its existence], since an action must be accomplished by a cause, and because [the self] possesses the nature of being a knower of taste among the qualities such as compassion, like the saliva and other substances in those who experience pleasure.
He speaks thus for the purpose of defining the object:
The object (*viṣaya*), however, is the sixfold [world]:
the river, the ocean, snow, hail, the stone of the cloud, and so forth; it is called "the object" because it is to be enjoyed as a means for meditative worship (*upāsana*).
Fire is that which manifests itself through its own nature;
it consists of color, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, fluidity, and faculty (saṃskāra). Its establishment is as previously explained.
Among these, its color is white and luminous.
Heat alone is the tactile sensation (*sparśa*).
That too is twofold, because of its existence as both atoms and their effects. And the effect consists of the body and so forth.

The eye, which is the organ of sight for all living beings, is located in the solar world (*ādityaloka*) within the body; due to the influence of earthly elements, it is incapable of drying up or consuming [its object]. The eye is composed of fiery (*tejomaya*) parts because it is not overcome by other [elemental] components.
The object of the eyes is the twenty-fourth [tattva].
It is elemental (*bhautika*), supernormal (*divya-anudbhūta*), and space-born (*ākāśaja*).

Among these, the elemental consists of things produced from wood, stone, and so forth, which are capable of producing heat, water, and light, and are effective for sweating and other such functions; the supernormal consists of the sun and so forth, or the enemy of darkness (fire) and so forth; the space-born consists of gold and the like, for the purpose of transforming food and drink into its constituent juices and so on.
In this regard, the perception of taste arises from the combination of the [taste] with saliva.
"Because it is related to fire-ness (*tejastva*), it is called 'fire' (*tejas*).
The explanation is as before.
He shows that, just like fire-ness, the application of the term "atom" (*aṇu*) to color, visual perception, and so forth is likewise useless.
"Form," and so forth.

"Their establishment is as before" means that just as the existence of form and the other [sensory objects] is established in earth because they are mentioned among the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), so too is their existence established in fire.
And so it has been said:
"Fire also possesses color and touch;
however, that which establishes qualities such as number and so forth is stated to be common [to all]."
It draws out its form and becomes that very form;
namely, white and luminous.
While the color white exists in both earth and water, it is not luminous; however, the color white that illuminates its own nature exists only in fire—thus it is specified.

In some cases, the color of the book is perceived as either red or black; however, having set aside that [perception] due to its lack of application, there is everywhere only the perception of pure whiteness, just as in the case of the circle of light from a lamp or a gem, or upon seeing the moon.
As for the statement "the touch is only hot," [it refers to the fact that] the touches of earth and water are respectively hard-soft and cold-not-hot-cold.
Since the touch of fire is indeed hot, [the definition] is redundant.
Just as with earth and water, fire is also of two kinds; this is included by the term "atom" (*aṇu*) within the compound. It is associated with that.

From the *Aṇubhāṣya*, it follows that light (*tejas*) is also twofold: as effect (*kārya*) and as non-existence (*abhāva*). Regarding the effect, that which is produced from the body and so forth is the body itself; and that which is designated as the "object" (*viṣaya*) is indeed the effect of light alone.
The body is indeed not born from a womb, as in the case of the light of the sun.

Now, because it consists of fire (*tejas*), that body, being composed of fire, is predominantly hot on the outside; and because it is suitable for the practical activities of scattering and spreading, it is fit for experience. For instance, the earthly constituent exists in the form of minute particles.

The intention is that, because there is no distinction between the atoms of light—which serve as the instrumental cause for the accumulation of earthly particles—and [the other elements], their nature as light constitutes a specific capacity for being experienced; thus, in terms of the common characteristics of a body, it is not merely characterized by external heat.
Regarding the sense organ: "The sense organ is the eye, ear, and mind.
That sense organ which manifests the darkness within living beings is said to consist of the two types of light.

Why should this alone be the sense-organ (indriya) consisting of the eye and ear, and not other substances of light? This is the [implied] objection. [The answer is: Because of its extreme necessity as the cause. Those parts of light whose capacity is restricted to the regions of earth and ether constitute the eye; therefore, because of its distinctness, this organ is the manifester of color-form (upādhika-vyañjaka), and no other such thing exists that could perform that function. Thus, the very same principle that applies to the cause applies likewise to the effect; this is the proof.
Its nature as light, however, is established because, among its qualities such as color and so forth, it invariably manifests color alone, like a lamp.
This [eye], moreover, is assisted by that [light]; thus, it assists only that which has been assisted by light.
Therefore, it does not grasp its own object, nor is it itself perceived.
That which is designated as "object" (viṣaya) is fourfold.
That whose designation is "object" is the fourfold product of fire.
He demonstrates this very fourfold nature:
"Bhoḥ, abhiṣya," and so forth.

The word "tathā" (thus) has the sense of determination (*nirdhāraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "bhaume kāṣṭhacayasambhavam": that fuel (*indhana*) which arises from a heap of wood is said to "originate from that" (*tat-samutpanna*), because there is no production of something independent [of its cause]. The mention of "wood" (*kāṣṭha*) is for the purpose of illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), since grass, shrubs, and so forth are also causes.

In the "lotus-born" (abja), there is fire—a specific activity characterized by that [nature], possessing its own properties; it cooks at the time of boiling and so forth. Cooking is the production of a different quality (*guṇāntara*) not distinct from the previous form. Boiling is the destruction of oiliness and fluidity. From the word "and so forth" (*cchādi*), one understands the bursting of flames, the raining of water, burning, and the accumulation of various activities such as heat, sweat, cold, and rain. Furthermore, the thief (*caura*) who moves about at night, consisting of lightning and the like, is the outflow of light; this is introduced by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word "thief. Thus, by the word "and so forth" (*cchādi*), the thief consisting of lightning and other such things is to be understood as an extraction.

The fire (*tejas*) present in the stomach arises for the purpose of transforming the consumed food into its constituent juices (*rasa*) and so forth; it is the cause of the transformation of the consumed food by means of the process of digestion.
And space (*ākāśa*) [is the cause] in gold and the like.
Space refers to a particular location; within that, the fiery substance (*tejasaṃ dravyaṃ*) is produced in gold, silver, and so on.
Regarding the fact that gold and other such substances are of the nature of fire (*tejas*), scripture (*āgama*) is the authority;

this has been stated in the Nyāya-śāstra. [Objection: In that case, there would be the perception of the qualities of odor and taste, as well as the perception of a quality that is incapable of being experienced by a non-experiencer (*abhoktṛ*). To this, he says:
"So be it.

Because of the invisibility of the yogis, due to fear, the kings [cause] gold and other substances suitable for forming a mass within the heart-lotuses of the kings—which have been seized by the light of atoms of the earthly elements—to originate. And because of the absence of a vision of reality, these [substances] such as taste and so forth are perceived.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion.

If it is argued that we do not perceive gold and so forth as being "this lotus in the heart" because there is no other substance apart from the perceived lotus in the heart, [we reply: this is not so, because there is a continuous recollection based on the non-perception of individual marks such as "this is a pot," since for everyone, the object of cognition is merely the pot and so forth. If it is further argued that due to a difference in verbal expression, only what is proximate is connected [to the cognition], then even when Caitra and others are proximate, let the distinction of blue and so forth remain as it is, produced by verbal expression.

Alternatively, if it is argued that because a transformation based on verbal instruction (*vācanā-pariṇāma*) does not arise from the apprehension of an external object as being merely independent of itself—and because, due to the non-establishment of its being like wood and so forth, it is impossible for the distinction between blue and other such things to be like wood and so forth, this must therefore be a mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)—then [we reply]: even now, for one who conforms to an external object present before oneself, it is not possible for it to be like wood and so forth; thus, a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*) distinct from the jar and other such objects must be postulated, which serves as the cause for awakening a specific verbal cognition that is otherwise obstructed.

By means of that which, while being non-manifest through the manifestation of another, clearly manifests itself as a single entity, there arises a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding objects such as jars; for these are necessarily apprehended by a single sense-faculty.

Furthermore, objects such as jars consist of parts that are mutually dependent; since each part is beyond the reach of the senses, how can there be for you this perception whose object is the unity of those two [the whole and its parts], given that they do not exist? If it is argued that atoms, though individually beyond the senses, become perceptible through their conjunction with the mind, the sense organs, and so forth—because of their collective suitability—[we reply: even if there were suitability due to such conjunction, the nature of extreme minuteness would still be absent. Moreover, mere suitability for conjunction would imply that the mind and the sense organs themselves should also be perceptible, as there is no distinction between them in that regard.
Now, even if it were granted that atoms are not beyond the reach of perception, how could they, being individually extremely subtle, produce the appearance of something gross?

If you argue that these atoms arise as visible objects through their lack of interval, or else perish due to their deficiency, then we ask: among these many [atoms], does a single gross form arise at that time, or is it perceived through the superimposition of something already existing in some of them? If it arises, it cannot emerge as a single unit. If it is perceived while not existing, then it is an illusion; yet an illusion is distinct from non-illusory cognition. How then can a single gross object be established by those [atoms]? Furthermore, it is not logical for consciousness to possess reality in that regard, because the perception of "grossness" and "largeness" would result in the absurdity of its existence depending solely on what is seen. Therefore, this notion of a single gross object—which appears as the object of all the senses—is an unfounded misconception, even when examined through inference.

[Objection: Is there not an external object established by cognition that is conventionally designated as "existent"? If [you say] there is no external means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then consider this: when the hand is being filled with a jar, the body does not tremble; or when the foot is being filled with a jar, the body does not tremble without it. Thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharma*). [Response: This is not so, because there is no fixed rule. When the cause for moving the hand exists, then that hand moves, but the ear does not, due to the absence of a cause. However, when a cause for the movement of the ear also exists, then the ear indeed moves; there is no other way. Thus, where is the contradiction? If the hand moves and the ear does not, then the non-difference between part and whole (*avayavāvayavinor abheda*) is established. It is not the case that "separate subsistence" (*yutasiddhi*) consists in having different substrates (*pṛthagāśrayāśrayitva*), nor in being mobile and immobile. Even when a substance moves, a quality may remain immobile; yet they are still "inseparably established" (*ayutasiddha*) because they lack separate substrates. Furthermore, even if part and whole were non-different, they would not have "separate substrates," and thus there is no "separate subsistence. As for what was said regarding the imperceptibility [of the whole]: "If one substrate is covered, the whole residing in it is not perceived; if the substrate is not perceived, the whole is perceived"—this leads to the conclusion that a single quality or atom would be perceived upon perceiving its parts. That too is incorrect. When one substrate is covered, there is no covering of the whole; thus, it is refuted by the very denial of its own [existence]. When some parts are covered, the whole is perceived through the perception of those uncovered parts, because it is non-different from all of them. As for the claim that a gross perception does not arise from the perception of many parts—that is because there is no cause for the perception of the magnitude (*parimāṇa*) of the perceived parts. And where there is no perception of parts due to the absence of the collection of conditions for color (*rūpa-sāmagry-ādhāna*), there the whole is not perceived, as in the case of a mountain submerged in water, which is not seen. The argument that "if one part is red, then the whole must be both red and not-red, since another part is not red"—this is untenable because there is no contradiction. Redness is the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with a coloring substance; non-redness is the absence of that. Both can indeed exist in one place, because conjunction is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*). This is another sublation: Does the whole reside in each part by way of a single portion (*ekadeśena*) or in its entirety (*kārtsnyena*)? Since there is no other part, it cannot reside by a single portion, as there is no "portion" distinct from the part itself. If it resides in its entirety, then like the wind, it could not reside in other [parts], because its nature (*svarūpa*) is delimited by its residence in one substrate, leaving no room for other parts; and since it has no other nature apart from that. To this it is replied: What is this self-contradictory statement—"it resides by a single portion and in its entirety"? Such a thing is not even known to oneself, let alone to others. Nor is the mode of subsistence established for either [part or whole] by way of "portion" or "entirety," because those two do not subsist [in that manner] and because such a mode of subsistence is not the cause of perception. When something resides, it resides in its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*) by a mode of subsistence characterized by the relation of substrate and resident (*āśrayāśritabhāva*). And it is not contradictory for one thing to have multiple conjunctions. For instance, in a variegated cognition (*citrajñāna*), there are conjunctions with the forms of yellow and so on, even when the form of blue is present; yet there is no division of that [cognition] into parts. Otherwise, if it were impossible for one thing to grasp multiple forms, your own theory of variegated cognition would be undermined. Nor is it the case that because it is a cognition, the forms are not inherent in it, for that would contradict the experience of variegation. Just as in a cognition where the parts are not perceived individually, there is an inclusion of other elements, so too for a single gross entity: when one part is seen, it is not the case that the one is not in the many places. Thus, in the absence of consciousness, the fact that one has multiple conjunctions is established by the logic of both [part and whole].

Thus, where there is one [cause], there is only one [effect]; where there is one immovable light, likewise, where there are many causes, there are many [effects], as in the case of many fruits on a branch or many immovable lights. These two contingencies have been rejected.

Since its own manifestation is established through itself, first of all, a single cognition exists by way of its own production with a distinct nature among multiple objects, sense-faculties, and mental attentions; likewise, a single atom exists by way of its production through conjunction among multiple directions with subtle distinctions. Even so, it will exist in the atoms through the medium of inherence (*samavāya*), and thus it will not be manifold, nor will it be the cause for the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the atom] would occupy the entire object; this also refutes the objection.

If there were no composite whole (*avayavin*) and the world consisted merely of atoms, then in establishing that properties, their substrates, and substance-ness (*dravyatva*) exist, there would be no cognition because it lacks a support; thus, even if perception were established by the destruction [of the object], this verbal [objection] would be weak compared to the counter-position. If it is argued that "perception is erroneous," then let it be so; if it is argued that "this is done by presenting a sublater (*bādhaka*)," then there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayitva*): the validity of the sublater depends on the error of perception, and the error of perception depends on the validity of the sublater. However, this logic does not apply to perception, as no such sublater is observed. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to say that what is characterized by the world as being effective for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is erroneous with respect to its own appearance, for if it were, the very cognition of blue and so forth would also result in being erroneous. Thus is the refutation of the sublater.

Even atoms (*paramāṇu*), though they are to be inferred from their constituent parts, must be treated [in this manner]. If it is argued that the sixfold nature of an atom is contradicted because of its simultaneous conjunction with six [other] atoms, then what is this so-called "simultaneous conjunction"? Is it the simultaneous production of one atom together with six other atoms, or is it simultaneous conjunction? As for simultaneous production, even if it were possible—though it is already rejected on the grounds of the simultaneity of causes—what contradiction would there be? However, if it is simultaneous conjunction, that too is not untenable; for conjunction among substances does not have spatial parts (*aṃśu*) as its object. Even in the case of space (*ākāśa*), which is partless, such [conjunction] exists because of its nature as a substance. Furthermore, if there were another internal part within a part, then since conjunction and so forth would be restricted to a mere atom, it would follow that it is imperceptible. Rather, [conjunction] has the essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone as its object. Thus, even in the case of a partless atom, although it is a single substance, the occurrence of conjunction in six directions simultaneously is not contradictory, because it serves as the cause for [the formation of] a single location. Therefore, there is no rejection of the reality [of the atom]. Wind is established by the existence of air.
It possesses touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and faculty (saṃskāra).
Its touch is neither hot nor cold, and it is not produced by heat (apākaja).
This is established from the enumeration of its qualities.
Because they are crushed by words and because they are repeated, [the terms] such as "sattra" and "saṃkhyā" [denote] substances;
because they express substances and actions, [the term] "saṃskāra" [denotes] a preparatory rite. And this [saṃskāra] is of two kinds: that which has an effect and that which does not.
In that regard, the fourfold characteristic of the effect consists of the body, the sense organ, the object, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Among these, the body is exclusively non-womb-born (*ayonija*) for the liberated ones in this world; it is composed of earthly particles or aqueous particles and is capable of experience.

The sense organ is that which perceives touch for all living beings; it is the tactile sense (*tvagindriya*), which is not produced by the accumulation [of particles] from the earth, and it pervades the entire body.

The object, though its touch is being perceived, is an invisible substance characterized by the conjunction of touch, sound, and fluidity, which possesses the capacity for the propulsion and support of clouds and other such things.
Although it is imperceptible, its manifold nature is inferred through "coalescence" (*sammūrcchana*).

Coalescence, moreover, is the meeting of two winds of equal velocity that are extremely pure and devoid of secondary qualities; this too is inferred from the upward motion of those two winds, which possess constituent parts, and that [upward motion] is itself understood through [the observation of] flowing and so forth.

Prāṇa, being the single cause for the impelling and other functions of the bodily fluids and the watery elements within the body, receives the various designations such as vyāna and so forth due to the differentiation of its activities.

Having explained all [substances] beginning with earth through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), at this point in the exposition of the remaining substances, he explains [the term] "wind" (*vāyu*) in accordance with the context, because the three moments characterized by both the permanent and impermanent types have been introduced.
"Wind is that which possesses its own connection" (*svābhisambandhāt*);
the explanation is as before.
The *sattva* quality describes the qualities (*guṇa*),
such as touch and so forth;
here too, the explanation is as before.
The touch of the wind is primary; he demonstrates this by saying "touch.
In the atoms composed of the five elements, which consist of the defects [of the earth], there is the awakening to reality within their own functions.
However, because touch is not produced from disjunction (*apakṣaja*), it is distinguished [from sound].
Or, if [the air] were not produced from disjunction, then even when a connection with a striking object is observed—as in the case of an echo—it would be impossible [for the air to be perceived].
Furthermore, this touch has been stated to be distinguished by the qualification "being neither hot nor cold," which also excludes the touch of water.

And this [series] is doubled; they say that the sequence of the meditative life-span (dhyānāyuḥ) and the contacts (sparśa) is found in the aphorisms (sūtra), because of the connection with the qualities (guṇa).
Because of the subsequent mention of "air" (vāyu) among many, "space" (kha) and so forth are the numbers.

When formless [substances] are perceived, numbers and so forth do not appear as qualities; because of this misconception, the multiplicity of numbers and so forth is stated regarding those that are unperceived. Otherwise, there would be a misconception of their non-existence everywhere.
From the statement "the action of grass," it follows that there is "disposition" (saṃskāra);
for by the statement "the action of grass arises from conjunction with air," the disposition of air is demonstrated.
Since there is no lack of justification for action being the cause of the conjunction of that [self] with its opposite,
he says, "And this," because otherwise the designation of its distinction would be untenable.

The word "and" (*ca*) serves to clarify that the intellect (*buddhi*), being external to the [internal organ], is referred to as "the five sense organs" by way of direct perception (*pratyakṣatvena*).
The meaning is that not only are earth and the other elements twofold, but this [intellect] is also twofold; that is to say, they are so because of the production of effects.
Regarding the phrase "the external false thicket," they say it consists of the body, the senses, the objects, and the vital breaths. Among these,
the determination is made by birth with respect to the body.
"And not a body" means that it is indeed non-uterine;
the meaning is that while it is a terrestrial body, it is both uterine and non-uterine.
"In the world of the Maruts" is a locative compound denoting location.

Through the assistance of the earth-based [elements] beginning with the earthly, which serve as the instrumental causes (nimittakāraṇa), there is a connection to the utility of being an earthly body, indicated by the state of being stable and compact through conjunction and so forth. As for the sense organ, it is that which perceives touch among the specific qualities of space.

The meaning is: that sense organ which perceives touch among the specific qualities of touch belongs to the earth, because it is not accepted [to belong] to others; thus, by the statement of its unimpeded specific quality, its stability is established, and therefore the sense organ must consist of a specific touch and so forth.

First, its description is given for the purpose of perceiving the sixfold touch. Its nature as a cognition of air is established because, among [the objects] such as form and so forth, it is intended to be known specifically as touch, like the wind that manifests the thumb or the fingers.
In this regard, it pertains to the entire body as well.

Because its function—the perception of touch—is present everywhere, the designation "skin-faculty" (*tvagindriya*) is applied; it is called the skin-faculty because it is the faculty located in the skin, through a metaphorical transfer of the term to its locus. Some maintain that since all the seats of the other faculties are pervaded by the skin, and since the apprehension of color and so forth exists in the skin when it is unimpaired, the skin-faculty perceives not merely touch, but [all objects] within its own sphere.
That is incorrect;

for it would entail the consequence that there is no first [sensation] elsewhere. Furthermore, since the difference in capacities is not established by the difference in the ten states of the internal organ (*manas*), it would follow as a consequence that there must be a difference in the sense organs by some other means.
Thus, he states that the instruction regarding the restriction of the determination of objects would be purposeless.
Regarding the phrase "the object, however":
the object (*viṣaya*) is that which serves as the locus for the non-apprehension of an object—such as whiteness—which is currently being perceived.

As for the proof that [wind] is the substratum of the action, some maintain that it is indeed perception itself, since the cognition arises precisely from the awakening of wind through the operation of the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*).

In this regard, it is logical: because one perceives the meaning of another element (dhātu) designated as the tactile faculty (*sparśendriya*), in direct perception (*aparokṣajñāna*) it is only touch that appears, and nothing else. As for the cognition "this is wind," since that is a locus of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), it is an inference based on the destruction [of the object] once the touch previously indicated has been apprehended. This is because the eye alone is observed to perform the functions of smelling and so forth; and while the auditory organ might lead to the recognition of wind through the perception of its specific qualities, even that recognition is merely an inference since it leads to the apprehension of its substrate. However, by means of the tactile organ, nothing other than the qualities of sound, smell, taste, and so forth would appear.

The inference—"Air is perceived as having touch, like a jar"—is sublated by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), just as the inference based on faith regarding tranquility (*praśama*) and so forth is sublated by its own lack of tranquility. This is because the state of being a substance possessing touch is pervaded by the state of being visible (*cākṣuṣatva*); since visibility exists in jars and the like but is absent in air, this inference—which attempts to determine the perceptibility of air—is invalid. Therefore, he sets forth the following [reason] in his mind to demonstrate its lack of authority:
"Touch, sound, and conjunction are the inferred marks (*liṅga*)."

The term is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has touch, sound, conjunction, and disjunction as its characteristics. This touch which is perceived as being devoid of heat and so forth is not visual, because it is a touch belonging to earth and the like, just like other touches; nor can it be argued that this heat is merely superimposed upon the earth, as in the case of the wind that is touched [but not seen], because the touch being perceived is invariably observed together with the perceived heat. Furthermore, since there is no lack of tangibility here, this touch is not non-perceptual, but is indeed terrestrial.

This [tangible quality] does not belong to water or fire, because it is neither exclusively hot nor cold, like the touch of a jar or similar objects; nor does it reside in earth, fire, ether, time, or space, since touch is observed to be invariably concomitant with corporeality (*mūrti*). Furthermore, if the mind possessed touch, it would follow that it, like atoms, must consist of an aggregate of substances. But this is not the case. Therefore, it does not exist in the three [other elements] either. Consequently, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), that in which this [touch] inheres is air (*vāyu*).

The word "go" (wind) is also its [the air's] indicator: that sound which, through the shaking and trembling of leaves, produces the *śuka-śuka* noise, belongs to this [air], because it is a conjunction with a substance possessing touch (*sparśavaddravya-saṃyoga*), given that it is a sound produced by striking—like the sound of a bamboo being struck—and because it is a sound. That [substance] which possesses touch is air (*vāyu*). Since ether (*ākāśa*) and the others lack touch, and since earth, water, and fire possess touch, if they were the cause of that sound, it would follow that they are perceptible (*pratyakṣatva-prasaṅga*).

It has been stated that [the definition] includes "being related to a substance possessing touch," in order to exclude sound produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-śabda*). [The argument is as follows: The stability of clouds and the like, which is a state of rest resulting from the speaker's intention, is a substratum for conjunction with a substance possessing touch; because it exists while lacking causes such as a hand, like a leaf resting on water. That substance possessing touch in which this [stability] resides cannot be the triad beginning with earth (i.e., earth, water, and fire), precisely because they are not perceptible. Thus, another substance is established.

Regarding the stability of the lords of arrows and the cutting of moving objects, there is an absence of causes such as effort; furthermore, the specific trembling of hunters and others is produced by conjunction with a tangible substance. This is explained in the context of the wind and its odor.

If it is argued that there is an inconsistency (vyabhicāra) because of earthquakes—just as there is movement and trembling in the flow of a river or in reeds due to their being specific types of action—the answer is no, because those have other causes. However, in the case of [trembling] produced by conjunction with a tangible substance, the reason is simply "being a specific type of action"; this is the proof, and thus there is no inconsistency.

Now, is it not the case that the very same substance which is inferred by touch is also inferred by sound and so forth, and that there is no inference of a different substance for each respective mark? Why then is this said as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): "Air is characterized by the marks of touch, sound, and motion"? This is the means of valid cognition: since the occurrence of sound and the rest is possible precisely through the substance inferred by touch—namely, space (*ākāśa*)—the postulation of a separate substance would be futile. Such being the case regarding air, one should perceive its qualities.
"Having the nature of moving obliquely" means that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is movement in a diagonal direction.

This refers to the impelling of clouds and so forth, their being led here and there, their holding [in place], and the obstruction of whiteness; these are included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) among those things observed at the time [of the action].

By the phrase "clouds and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes villages, fields, and the like, because these too are moved by the wind. Here, when there is doubt regarding the perception of water in various [places] such as the sky—which are objects of inference—that [doubt] serves as the means for the absence of the object; that is, the absence of water in that [place], which is the self-nature of that [absence].

Even "obstruction" (*sammūrcchana*) is not understood; therefore, he says: "Obstruction. It is a specific kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*) occurring between two winds moving in opposite directions, which causes a mutual impediment to their motion. By means of this [obstruction], the production of wind is inferred to be absent; for when there is an absence of such conjunction, there is an interval of space between two substances possessing fluidity as they move, which constitutes the absence of obstruction. This means that it occurs between two winds whose motions are in opposite directions.
The convergence of two [substances] with unequal velocities does not occur, because one would displace the other; for that reason, it says "of equal velocity.
Furthermore, thinking that just as there is diversity and agitation even when [the qualities] are non-existent in conjunction, so too is conjunction [non-existent], he says "velocity" and so forth.
There is also a fallacy regarding velocity.

It is inferred that there is a distinct substance possessing parts (an *avayavin*) because of the mutual obstruction of two substances moving in opposite directions, as stated in the root text; for when no other cause is possible, a substance whose nature is to move transversely possesses such motion due to the shaking of the earth and so forth, like the unseen substance (*adṛṣṭadravya*).
Although one should have said "of two substances possessing parts," the expression "of two substances possessing parts" was used to avoid the contingency of error.
Nor is it for the purpose of grasping the whole (avayavin) as an object, nor for the sake of apprehending the prior and posterior states of the flow;
because an atom (aṇu), by its very nature, lacks the capacity for simultaneous duality, even its movement [is impossible]. Thus, stating that their atomicity is preceded by those conditions, he says:
"It is inferred by the movement of grass and so forth."

He describes the nature of that which is called *prāṇa*, which is practiced in the world and in the science of yoga (*yogaśāstra*) and is well-known: "Prāṇa is within the body. Both within the body and in the movement of the wind (*vāyu*), it is called *prāṇa*.
Its functional activity is described as being the cause of stimulation and so forth, produced merely by acts such as protection.
Regarding "rasa," even in the context of the digestion and preservation of food consisting of subtle and gross names, it is this very specific substance that is grasped.

"Excrement" (*mala*) refers here to urine, feces, and so forth, as well as other bodily constituents such as bone and blood. It is the cause of their impelling, independent movement, and the drawing together (*vyūhana*) [of the body], which serves as the reason for inferring the existence of a controller.
Regarding the determination of its presence at that time or at another time, he says:
"Like a potter's wheel."

[Objection: But are not the animal, the brahminical, and the bodily [vital breaths] heard of in scripture? To this he replies: "Due to the difference in function. The *vyāna* is so called because it leads the vital energy (*ūrg*) of both the fool and the wise man; the *apāna* is so called because it leads the essence of food (*rasa*) toward the stomach and the like; the *udāna* is so called because it leads [the breath] upward for the purpose of perceiving hunger and the like; the *prāṇa* is so called because it exits through the mouth and nostrils; and the *samāna* is so called because it rises for the sake of digesting the food consumed.

Because everything is seen as identical through the act of leading [into oneness], it is not real that these possess the nature of sacrificial animals; rather, this is a conceptual construction for the sake of the liberation of those who have entered into the state of identity with the One.
Now, here the procedure for the creation and conventional usage of the four great elements is being stated.
