At the end of a hundred years according to the measure of Brahmā, at the time of Brahmā’s dissolution, for the sake of the rest of all living beings who are weary of the cycle of transmigration, when the activity of the imperceptible atoms residing in all bodies—which bind the vital breaths, the senses, and the gross elements—is suppressed by the will of Maheśvara, the Lord of all worlds, then, through the cessation of the conjunctions of those atoms resulting from the divisions of the atoms that are the causes of bodies and senses—effected by the sequence of yogic powers arising from the will of Maheśvara—their destruction occurs down to the level of the ultimate atoms. In the same manner, the gross elements of earth, water, fire, and air also undergo destruction, each preceding one being destroyed by the subsequent one in this very sequence; thereafter, the separated atoms remain, and the selves (ātman) persist for that same duration of time, retaining their qualities of merit, demerit, and mental impressions.

Then again, for the sake of the experience of living beings, following the will of Maheśvara to create, and depending upon the conjunctions [of atoms] through the acquisition of activity inherent in all substances, motion arises in the atoms of air; from their mutual conjunctions, beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), a great wind comes into being and remains increasing in volume.
Immediately after that, in that very same wind, from aqueous atoms, by that same process, the great ocean comes into being.
Furthermore, immediately after that which has dissolved, within that very ocean, a great mass of fire arises from fiery atoms through the process beginning with dyads and so forth;
it remains blazing, ignited by certain flames.

Thus, when the four great elements have arisen, through the mere volition of Maheśvara, from atoms of fire and water combined with earth-atoms, he produces the Great Egg (Mahādaṇḍa); and within that, having produced the Grandfather of all worlds, Brahmā, together with the entire universe, he appoints him to the task of creating progeny.

And he, commissioned by Maheśvara, endowed with supreme knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty, having understood the ripening of the karma of living beings, created from his mind the Prajāpatis—his sons—along with the groups of Sanu, Devarṣis, and Pitṛs; and having created the four castes from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet, as well as other various classes of beings, he joined them with wives suitable to their status, whether born of sexual union or otherwise, noble or otherwise.

Having explained in detail the substances such as *śakti* (potency) and others which possess the quality of origination, their production—which is useful for [understanding] their effects—is now being set forth. The destruction of the four [elements] beginning with earth must be described; here, dissolution (*laya*) is described for the sake of its opposite. It is begun in this manner for the purpose of description, following the sequence of succession.
Regarding the phrase "of four":

although the commencement of the gross body is said to be the method (prakāra) for both its diminution and destruction—and thus it might seem that one [method] is stated for all four—nevertheless, this is not so, because these two [processes] are described as distinct in each case within the verbal expression. Just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice the *kapiñjala* birds," where the plural number is understood from the singular hearing (*ekāśruti*) yet only three are accepted, because the purpose is fulfilled by the plurality being the governing factor (*tantra*), so too here, the phrase "of four" is used despite the singular hearing.

When "of the four" is stated, the aforementioned quartet—body, sense organ, object, and vital breath—is understood by the intellect as the effects of air among the four principles of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Now, if that were so, would not the subsequent destruction of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) fail to be asserted, since they are atomic? It is not so; for a specific term has been employed, meaning that the manner in which the subsequent destruction of the great elements occurs is precisely what is being described. And the meaning of the word is that their destruction continues through the entire sequence of production beginning with dyads.
Even for *draṇukas*, two gross bodies might be admitted;
however, since the intention is merely to explain the meaning, he first describes the body after the five [elements]. [He says:
"By means of measurement in the woods."

Fifteen of our *nimeṣas* constitute a *kāṣṭhā*; twenty *kāṣṭhās* constitute a *kalā*; fifteen *kalās* constitute a *nāḍikā*; thirty *kalās* constitute a *muhūrta*; thirty *muhūrtas* constitute a day and night (*ahorātra*). Fifteen days and nights constitute a fortnight (*pakṣa*); two fortnights constitute a month; two months constitute a season (*ṛtu*); four seasons constitute a year (*saṃvatsara*). Four years constitute the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*); four years also constitute the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*). The northern course is a day for the gods, and the southern course is a night for the gods. Likewise, a day and night of the Asuras consists of four years. Twelve thousand years multiplied by sixty constitute a *caturyuga*.

By this measure— that one day of Brahmā consists of a thousand cycles of the four yugas— at the end of three hundred years, he describes the instruction on the method of dissolution, which is distinct from the aforementioned visible [creation]:
at the time of Brahmā’s liberation (apavarga), whether at the time of creation or dissolution, even when there is application toward non-self-objects— namely,
among living beings who are distressed by various sufferings such as hunger and thirst within the limited confines of bodies and the like.

For the sake of the Great Lord (Maheśvara), whose self-nature is eternal and consists of pure knowledge—who for a certain period has been traveling upon the path of suffering due to the intense affliction of his own body and who now desires to withdraw it—the commencement of a physical body occurs at the time of that [desire], and immediately thereafter follows the cessation of the senses, which is the obstruction of their power and their relinquishment. This results from the dissolution of the conjunctions of those factors consisting of the body, the senses, and the great elements, which are rooted in the vital breath and consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

In that [process], there is indeed the non-arising of the future bodies, sense organs, and gross elements, and the destruction of those already known. For this, there is the conjunction of the Great Lord’s will with the qualities of the self (*ātma-guṇa*), along with [the influence of] karmas. The Great Lord’s will—characterized by the desire to withdraw [the world]—arises; it initiates the grasping of atoms. There is a twofold cause: the Great Lord’s will and the conjunctions with the qualities of the self. From these arise [the effects]; from those karmas born of the conjunction of the Great Lord’s will and the qualities of the self, [the world is produced].

Regarding those atoms which are the indirect causes for the production of bodies and so forth, there occurs a disjunction among the atoms. At that moment, the motion of the atoms ceases due to their own momentum; upon the cessation of motion, their action ceases, and they perish as atoms. The destruction of those bodies and sense organs proceeds through the sequence of the destruction of dyads and so on, until it reaches the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).

Regarding that which was stated by someone—that for living beings who are free from longing for the body and so forth, there may be a fulfillment of their desires through means consisting of eternal knowledge (*vidyā*)—this is the remedy for those creatures. Although this has been said, [it remains true that] while the infinite unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) of infinite selves ripen in succession, some come to an end of experience due to the power of what has been seen, some are currently experiencing, and others are oriented toward experience; such is the case.

The statement that "simultaneous existence of the body and so forth is not possible for all [beings] engaged with sense-objects" is refuted. When the cessation of the fourfold [elements] is declared at the time of Brahmā’s liberation, he says that there is no such destruction of the great elements (mahābhūtas), because the term "cessation" is used figuratively due to the similarity between their rising and setting and the rising and setting of the senses. It refers to the dissolution of the portions of their own momentum (saṃskāra).
It is exactly so.
Just as the destruction of the body and the sense-faculties occurs down to the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*), so too does it occur for the great elements (*mahābhūta*) in this very same sequence.
Through the sequence beginning with the activity and disjunction of atoms, this [destruction] occurs in this subsequent aggregate (*skandha*) just as before.

"The destruction is as before" means that when water has ceased [to exist], there is the destruction of earth; when fire has ceased, there is the destruction of water; and when air has ceased, there is the destruction of fire. This is the meaning.

Then, the atoms situated on the back [of the dissolution] remain for a period of one hundred years of Brahmā in that extremely subtle state, which is characterized by a lack of manifestation as before, until the time of their own emergence. Even though they have returned to a state of cessation, because of their eternity, they do not cease to exist; rather, by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), they abide within themselves according to the sequence of the "former" and "again" mentioned previously.
Thus, having explained the process of reabsorption (saṃhāra), he speaks while explaining the process of creation (sṛṣṭi):
"Then again," and so forth.

Although at that time there is no [individual] soul denoted by the word "prāṇa," nevertheless, because they possess the fitness described by the term "living beings" (prāṇin), the Lord of the Assembly (Saṅgheśvara) develops a desire to create—a wish to bring about the arising of the experience of pleasure and pain within those who constitute the locus [of those souls]. Immediately thereafter, the unmanifest power (śakti) residing in all souls becomes active.

Although the desire for the remaining attributes (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-icchā*), which is directed toward various objects arising simultaneously and is engaged in their assistance—such as the directions, time, and so forth—is conducive to the purpose of action, nevertheless, prior to the emergence of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) at that time, this [desire] sometimes results in withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and sometimes results in creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
When it is for the purpose of withdrawal, then, in accordance with that, the power to be favored (*anugrāhyā śakti*) arises characterized by restraint and neutrality (*udāsīnya*).

When there is a manifestation of its own [nature], then there is the acquisition of power (*śakti*), which is the operation toward the production of its own effect. Once the power is acquired, they are said to have "acquired power" (*śaktilabdha*). This is a case of prior placement (of the compound member) according to the rule governing words such as *āhitāgni*, just as in the expression "one who has given knowledge" (*dattajñāna*).

In those beings who are connected with the supreme self-power that is to be attained and is to be favored, there arise from the conjunctions of the selves with the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) actions within the atoms of air; the atoms of air are the material cause (*samprāpti-kāraṇa*), while the sixfold causal complex consisting of the conjunction of the self-atom—which is difficult to establish and devoid of an objective referent—is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*).

Thus, when karma arises, mutual conjunctions of those wind-atoms (pavanaparamāṇu) occur; from that conjunction, dyads (dvyaṇuka) are produced there, and subsequently triads (tryaṇuka), and in this sequence the great wind is generated, swelling in the sky (ākāśa) and, due to its extreme velocity, possessing an intense upward agitation.

Immediately thereafter, from the very same atoms of water within that wind, a great ocean is produced through the same sequence beginning with dyads; being nourished and due to the absence of any obstructing factor, it spreads everywhere and flows forth. Immediately after that, within that very ocean, a great earth—consolidated and characterized by a stable nature—is produced from the atoms of earth.

Immediately thereafter, in that very great ocean, a vast mass of intense heat arises from fiery atoms through the process beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth; because it has become like a pillar piercing through [the waters], it remains as if it were an island (*dvīpa*).

Although there is a natural opposition between the two distinct sides, nevertheless, due to the power of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭavaśena*), their relationship as support and supported is not untenable.

In the manner just described, once the great elements have arisen, by the mere volition of Maheśvara and from the six waves of fiery atoms accompanied by earth-atoms, a great substance—the Great Divine Body—is produced in the form of a *śiṃśumāra*. Earthly components are first introduced; thus, it ascends outwardly in height. Within that condensed body, he creates the worlds and their inhabitants, including the noble personage who possesses all qualities, and having produced them, he appoints him to the duty of procreating offspring, thereby establishing the law for beings through his own wisdom.

And he, appointed among the Brahmins, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, [performed] hospitality toward the Brahmins, and through knowledge, the meaning of the Vedas, and discernment—through knowledge, discernment, and discernment—he properly attended to them with the conduct of a Kṣatriya. Through knowledge and hospitality, he correctly understood the instruction of dharma for living beings; through dispassion, he proceeded with the five-fold [discipline]; and through his own merit, he will enjoy the fruits of action.
Having known the ripening of the karma of living beings...

"Vipāka" means ripening by way of being pierced; "karmavipāka" means the ripening of these actions—that is, knowing that the fruit of action will inevitably come to pass. Having known this, He joins [beings] with actions corresponding to their nature through the agency of Prajāpati Dakṣa and others—[namely] from Manu (the son of the Creator), from the group of divine sages and ancestors, from the gods, from the best of the Asuras, from the Brāhmaṇas born from the mouth, from the Kṣatriyas born from the two arms, from the Vaiśyas born from the two thighs, and from the Śūdras born from the feet. The intention is that these [actions] are heard of and seen as being most excellent, such as the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice and so forth, which remain within the self until the time of experiencing their fruit. Furthermore, He joins them with knowledge, austerity, and desire for objects corresponding to those very actions—meaning that whatever kind of action one has, He endows them with corresponding knowledge and so on. The intention is that He does not act through mere illusion (*māyā*), but rather through the conviction [of the law of karma]. (2)

Or rather, as some indeed declare: "He acts out of compassion for living beings, or because He is incapable of restraint, or because He is devoid of mastery. This is not the case, for He is independent and possesses all desires. Therefore, His engagement in the creation of the world is untenable.
To this, the answer is:
"For the sake of the experience of living beings."
The intention is that the activity of Parāśakti is not motivated by her own self-interest.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If this were so, she would create a world consisting solely of happiness, since it is not prompted by any [selfish] purpose. This objection is answered by the statement: "Having brought about the ripening of the karma of living beings."

The meaning is that even though the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is active, He does not make [the world] consist of nothing but pleasure, because He possesses agency over that which is devoid of Viśvakarman’s utility.
Nor is this so if He acts out of compassion, for His nature is such that, by means of generating detachment (*vairāgya*), He is the cause of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*).
If He were to act solely through the instruction of *dharma*, He would have no purpose of His own; thus, I refute the objection that this implies the defect of Him being a non-Lord (*anīśvaratā*).
[The opponent argues: "He connects [beings] with the excellence of knowledge through the primary vehicle, the *ṛks*, the *kūpas*, and the *yajñas*.

For if the Lord were to bestow fruits upon those who possess merit (*dharmavatām*) in accordance with their actions, he would be subject to partiality (*kṛpaṇa*). [The author replies: This is not so. For a master does not grant specific rewards to his servants in accordance with their fitness simply because of his own power; rather, it is because he establishes conventions (*saṃketa*) for words among living beings who have deviated from the true meanings of words. If you argue that verbal communication (*śabdavyavahāra*) is thus untenable, this objection is groundless even against a non-Aryan.

For it is said that among human beings, those who are born with auspicious marks and whose speech is clear through the observation of grammar from the womb onwards act with purity; yet, one does not remember the specific experiences of a previous birth.

For the sake of the propagation of progeny, the human beings—those born of Manu—performed sacrifices; they were not born from a womb. Having perceived the relationship between word and meaning through the performance of various rites, they established the entire linguistic usage of words and their referents. Like friends meeting after a deep sleep, they recalled [the conventions] due to the clarity of their memory, and many among them engaged in mutual transactions. Regarding these transactions, it is said that for the living beings existing at that time, who were proficient in the linguistic usage of their own kind, the understanding of the relationship between word and meaning arose through a continuous succession of such usage (*vyavahāra-paramparā*). This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, what is the proof for the existence of a Creator? It is both scripture (*āgama*) and inference (*anumāna*). [The inference is as follows: The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are preceded by one who possesses the power of creation, because they are effects; whatever is an effect is preceded by one who possesses the power of creation, just like a jar. And the four great elements are effects; therefore, they are preceded by one who possesses the power of creation. If it is argued that the state of being an effect is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of earth and the other elements because no prior effort is perceived, we say: no, for that is incorrect, because they are shaped (*saṃsthita*). Whatever is shaped is an effect, just like a jar; and earth and the others are shaped; therefore, these too are indeed effects.

Now, it might be argued that the operation of inference, which depends upon the apprehension of a pervasion (*vyāpti*), requires the cognition of the effect-ness (*kāryatva*) [of the sprout]; and this is indeed desired, since at the time of the cognition of an agent in the case of a jar and so forth, the observation of a sprout and the like is seen to be pervaded by that [cognition]. Nor is it logical to claim that sprouts and the like are also the subject (*pakṣa*), for the distinction between the subject and so forth occurs only at the time the inference proceeds based on a previously grasped pervasion, when there is an opponent's position. But in our case, because it is always beset by the logic of the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*), the very apprehension of the pervasion cannot be established—this is what has been stated.

To this, it is replied: if, because length [of movement] is impossible and so forth, there is an absence of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), then even the inference of the self as an enjoyer—established through perception and based on the general property of moving from one place to another—would not be established. For in that case too, at the very time of apprehending the pervasion by observing Devadatta and others reaching another location, there is the perception of mere living beings reaching other locations in places such as the ocean. Alternatively, if it is argued that although movement to those specific locations is not perceived, there is no sublation of the apprehension of the cause of pervasion—namely, the observation of repeated instances (*bhūyodarśana*)—because the argument is not equally applicable there.

Alternatively, Caitra, even if the agent is not established by way of being an authorial principle (*ācāryarīti*), it is possible for his specific nature to be perceived—just as in the case of the first sprout and so forth—and thus the efficacy of repeated observation, which functions without contradiction, is not impaired; this is the same [in both cases].
Moreover:

O sir, what is being established by inference? Is it the creator who is being established, or is the earth, the twinkling of an eye, or the momentary nature [of things] being established by means of [the example of] lightning and so forth? For that which is created similar to lightning and the like is not non-different from those things; nor can it be said that the effect, such as the earth, is of that very same nature, for it is impossible to establish a similarity with the creator seen in the example because of the momentary destruction of lightning. Indeed, the creator is not pervaded by the specific object [lightning], since at the time of establishing the pervasion, if one does not depend on the cognition of that [specific instance], then when proving a general property, even the momentary nature of the earth and so forth would be a particularity, just like the arising of lightning; for there is no lightning in a general property that is devoid of particulars.

If it is argued that there is no generality (*sāmānya*) in lightning, we reply: it exists by virtue of being an effect, since it possesses the nature of fire and so forth. For if one were to overlook the generality of fire even though it is pervading (*vyāpta*), then there would be no generality in lightning; this is because a thing devoid of specific qualities (*nirviśeṣa*) cannot be related [to anything], and because that which lacks specific qualities cannot persist. Now, if it is said that the essence of the substance-fire and its qualities constitutes the pervasion (*vyāpti*), and that the presence of the five properties (*pañcadharmatā*) constitutes the generality in lightning—then, by the force of the rule of pervasion and the presence of the five properties, the intended particularity (*viśeṣa*) exists in lightning as well, characterized by the very nature of smoke and fire.
Otherwise, what utility would there be for the fivefold nature [of the reason], and what pervasion (*vyāpti*) could be grasped by inference? [The answer is: none at all.
If this is so, then it is the same in the case of the inference for God (*īśvarānumāna*), because there is no difference in the underlying attachment.

Now, it might be thought that even in the case of the inference of a specific [creator], just as there is no contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*), so too there is no such contradiction regarding the specific non-duality of the self. For a distinction based on place, time, and so forth is indeed observed among particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). However, in the inference of God (*īśvara*), a specific [creator] is not established because of contradiction with valid cognition. To explain: here, being preceded by a body cannot be proven as the means of proof; for if a body were required, then since the capacity of the agent depends upon the thorough knowledge of the instruments and materials—such as the collection of sense organs and their respective substrates—the status of being a creator would be impossible.

The fact that [the world] is not preceded by a body—that is, its dissimilarity to sound—the author will explain later. An agent first ascertains the nature of the causal factors; then he desires, "I shall accomplish this by means of this"; then he exerts effort; thereafter he applies the instruments to the task; then he presides over the causes; then he acts. Thus, while initiating the undertaking, he acts by applying himself to the effect. Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that even in the production of an effect, there is a prior intelligence (*buddhi-pūrvaka*). Since the means for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—such as the authoritative scriptures—is available for the apprehension of all conditions, it cannot be discarded on the grounds of its multiplicity. If one abandons the capacity for purposeful action when it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then one must also abandon intelligence itself, which is its correlate. Furthermore, the absence of a body would result in an extreme lack of intelligence, making liberation impossible. If it is argued that one who is ignorant of the various materials, instruments, and so forth, is incapable [of creation], how is this known? It is because such a thing is not observed. Just as in the case of Caitra, the nature of the object of knowledge (*prameya-svarūpa*) is not [simply] the body, but rather the specific desire characterized by direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*) that brings about the suitability for the production of the effect; thus, the body is merely the locus for the operation of that specific perception according to his will.

Because the universal of "being preceded by an intelligent agent" (buddhimattva-pūrvakṣaṇa-sāmānya) is established even in the absence of either specific qualification—namely, being embodied or being unembodied—and because an inference based on such a universal is seen to be valid, no one is defeated when employing a universal as a probans for a specific conclusion, such as proving the existence of a body or horns. For example, it is like someone who, having obtained a specific sword, attempts to apply its function toward the indivisible ether. If you, however, are not satisfied without a refutation of the inference, then consider this: in the inference that [the world] is preceded by an unembodied agent, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is sublated by the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends it; thus, the pervasion is damaged at a later time. Furthermore, the intended specific qualification of "unembodied-ness" does not contradict the fact of non-deviation (*avisamvāda*); therefore, this is merely an internal variety within the category of non-deviation. This is the summary of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Here is the rebuttal:

Is being an agent (*kāryetva*) identical to having a body (*śarīritva*), or is it the state of being the prompter of a causal factor whose capacity has been observed? It cannot be that being an agent is identical to having a body, for that would entail the consequence of agency even for one who is inactive during deep sleep and the like; rather, it is the state of being the prompter of a causal factor whose capacity has been observed.
Since the production of an effect occurs when that [prompting] is present, agency is established even in the absence of a body, as in the case of the self’s prompting of its own body.

If it is argued that there exists for him [the soul] a body acquired through its own karma, and that this very body serves as the means of impulsion, we reply: true, such a body exists; however, it cannot be the means of impulsion because action within oneself is a contradiction. If it is further argued that he impels by means of another [body], then even for God (Īśvara), there would have to be another atom to be impelled.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in one's own body, because volition and effort exist, and because there is no existence [of these] in what is other than the body, the body possesses the status of being a means for its own impulsion by way of generating volition and effort? [Reply: This is not so, because the body functions solely for the purpose of bringing about those very volitions and efforts which are to be realized; however, at the time when the impulsion is actually being performed, since the volition and effort belonging to the subject (the self) are not dependent upon the body, the body is excluded from the pervasion (vyāpti) as a cause. For we observe that the activity of the body—which is not being subsisted upon—is capable of performing a conscious action only when it is characterized by volition and effort alone; thus, while the body is an instrument, volition and the like are the causal factors, and this establishes the existence of God (Īśvara).

If it is argued that desire (*icchā*) and effort (*prayatna*) have a limit because they are inherent in a body and thus require something else [as their substratum], whereas those two are seen to be natural in other cases and thus do not require anything else; and if it is further argued that there is no contradiction in the eternality of intellect (*buddhi*), desire, and effort—just as we observe that qualities such as sound in a well and so forth, though entering into their substratum, still possess both eternality and non-eternality in respect to the substance itself—then this objection against the doctrine of God (*īśvaravāda*) is refuted by the supreme authority of the scriptural evidence (*liṅga*). Beyond this, the Lord is the ultimate authority.

If it is argued that those whose purposes are distinct from their own selves will proceed toward the ultimate goal, we say no; for those who do not know the object of their own senses—which arises from their own decay—there is no production of a body.
This is because there is no such cognition for all [of them], due to the absence of this [body].

If it is argued that for these selves, there is a pervasive consciousness in all [bodies] due to multiplicity, we say no; for that which exists through its true nature is merely the innate connection with a body.
One should know that all this is the Self; all this passes away into the Self.

If it is argued that because of the cessation [of activity] within the body, consciousness rests solely within itself and does not become extroverted—[we reply: since it is all-pervasive, its connection with objects is never severed; and since it is eternal, what logic is there for the suppression of that which has the nature of illuminating objects? If you say that "non-suppression" means that no other logic [applies], then how is the apprehension of objects by embodied beings accomplished? If you ask why these [objects] are not immediately withdrawn from it, what is this specific distinction? Just as the object of sensory perception is grasped, so too the attainment of objects by consciousness—which is not grasped by the senses—is not established here. Even if pervasiveness were granted, because there is an absence of grasping all things, and because it would follow that everything would be an object of the senses, there is no direct cognition of objects for disembodied selves.
And so some say:
"The Self-existent pierced the openings outward;
therefore one sees with the eyes turned away, and not the inner self."

And since there would be no attainment [of effects] if those [atoms] were not conscious, one must postulate some other entity beyond them—a creator by nature who consists of the production of jars and so forth—who is ignorant; for non-conscious things cannot possess the state of being a master without the presence of consciousness.
Is he one or many? We say: he is one.

If many [beings] were non-omniscient, they would lack the capacity [to create], just as those who are ignorant of the means lack the power to produce an effect such as the destruction of the world. However, if they were omniscient, there would be capacity in only one, while for others it would be useless; furthermore, there is no reason why multiple beings should possess sovereign power over a single reality, which might lead to the non-production of the effect at times. Since all possess sovereignty in accordance with the intention of the One, there is dependence [on Him]; it is not like a monastic community or a council where sovereignty is shared. When there is no conflict among all [beings] in accordance with the production of the effect, each individually lacks true lordship.

Thus, since the specific agent established by the particular nature of the effect is omniscient, there is no perception of any distinction [in him] based on reasoning; therefore, false cognition lacks reality. In the absence of false cognition, there is no passion or aversion rooted therein. Due to their absence, there is no activity produced by them. In the absence of activity, there is no merit or demerit to be accomplished by it. Due to their absence, there is also an absence of pleasure and pain resulting from them. Furthermore, because of the constant presence of the fourfold states of existence (*caturbhava-saṃvṛti*), even latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) do not persist. Thus, some maintain that the Blessed Lord Īśvara is one whose substratum is free from all defects.

Others, however, maintain that the self (ātman) is nothing but the intellect (buddhi), and that its power of action consists precisely of such things as desire, effort, state, form, and activity; they say that this [intellect] is the locus of qualities. But is it bound or liberated? It cannot bind itself by means of bondage, for it is not an agent capable of such action, since even the capacity for action is absent. Nor can it be liberated, for liberation consists in the application toward the severance of bondage. It must therefore be eternally liberated, as the knower of truth, Patañjali, has said: "Īśvara is a distinct Puruṣa, untouched by the afflictions, actions, fruits of actions, and latent impressions, and whose will is directed toward isolation (kaivalya) and freedom from the guṇas."

Since ether, time, space, and self each possess a single individuality (*ekatva*), there is an absence of subordinate universals (*aparajāti*); thus, they have only the primary designations (*saṃjñā*) such as "ether," "time," and "space. Among these, the qualities (*guṇa*) of ether are sound, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.

(4) Sound is not a quality of tangible substances such as fire or air, because while being perceptible by the senses, it does not arise from the qualities of its causes, it does not persist as long as the substance itself, and it is perceived elsewhere than its substratum.

It is not a quality of the self, because it is perceptible by an external sense organ, it is apprehended by different individuals, it does not reside in the self through inherence, and it is perceived as distinct from the fingers.
It is not a quality of space, time, or the internal organ, because it is perceived by the auditory organ and lacks the characteristics of cognition.
By process of elimination, being a quality, it is the mark for the cognition of space.
Its unity is established because there is no distinction in its mark, namely sound. Its numerical distinctness is established from the diversity of cognitions thereof.
From the mention of its manifestation (*vibhava*), it possesses the highest degree of magnitude (*paramamahattva*) and is a universal (*sāmānya*).

From the mention of its being the cause of sound, it possesses conjunction and disjunction. Because it is heard to possess qualities (*guṇavattva*) and because it is not pervasive (*avitata*), it is a substance (*dravya*).
Furthermore, it is eternal because there is no cause for it that is either similar or dissimilar in nature.

It serves as the instrument for all living beings in the perception of sound by way of being the auditory organ (*śrotra*). The auditory organ, moreover, is the cavity of the ear; it is the substrate for the dharma that brings about the experience of the causes of sound. And because of the deficiency in the causal connection for its plurality—which would otherwise follow from the eternity of the object—it is singular.
By means of the ultimate limit of accumulation (*saṃcayāgramena*) of the three beginning with space (*ākāśa*), there is a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) [from the other categories];
this is stated as "of space, time, and direction.

Because space, time, and direction are each singular, there is no lower genus (*aparajāti*) for them, since such a genus would be contradictory to the distinction between individual instances (*vyaktibheda*).

Furthermore, in the absence of a secondary genus (*aparajāti*), the designations "space," "time," and "direction" are technical (*pāribhāṣikī*) names; the meaning is that they do not have a secondary genus as their cause, unlike the case of "earth" and so forth. Even though there is no difference in the nature of being a name, the distinction is as follows: a name is technical when it is uttered by convention without a [corresponding] cause, such as the name "Devadatta" applied to an object according to its actual fact; whereas a name is causal (*naimittikī*) when it is uttered by taking a specific cause into account. This is the differentiation.
Now, he speaks for the purpose of defining each [element] individually:
"In that regard, the qualities of space.

Among those three [elements], the qualities of space are sound, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction; its specific difference (vaidharmya) from [the other elements] is its suitability for possessing qualities such as sound.

Now, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of space as the locus of notes such as *ṣaḍja*? If it is argued that perception itself is employed, and that Patañjali has stated that the ascent through the four stages consists of five [elements], and that there is no perception of a locus restricted to a specific place—that is incorrect. For neither the invisible nor the visible possesses visual perceptibility (2). When considering the perceptibility of a suitable locus, no other visible object appears apart from the circle of the world-system (*lokamaṇḍala*). Therefore, having presented a residual inference (*pariśeṣānumāna*) regarding the nature of space as the locus of the *ṣaḍja* note, he negates that sound is a quality of any other substance. He says: "Sound... [and so forth].

If that which is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of its own substratum is not a quality (*guṇa*), then sound is not [a quality], because it would follow—like a cloth or a pot—that it is something other than a quality of the self (*ātmaguṇa*). Therefore, like pleasure and so forth, it is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) belonging to its own substrate. One should not suspect that, since its status as a specific quality has not been determined, it might instead be a general quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*); for, by virtue of being perceivable by an external sense organ, its status as a specific quality is certain, just as in the case of color and so forth, due to the presence of both generality and particularity.

In the atoms of earth, there are specific qualities possessing touch (*sparśavat-viśeṣaguṇa*) which enter into the category of visual qualities (*cākṣuṣaguṇapraveśa*), yet because of their atomic nature (*paramāṇutva*), they are not perceptible; thus, even their destruction does not constitute a flaw regarding perceptibility. As long as something is visible, sound does not exist, for it perishes in its ultimate substratum, such as space (*ākāśa*); therefore, like pleasure and other such qualities, it is not a specific quality possessing touch. Consequently, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) among the atoms of earth and the rest, since all of them perish through conjunction with fire at the final atom; thus, the condition "while being perceptible" (*pratyakṣatve sati*) must be understood as following [the definition].
He states another reason:
"The perception [of sound] occurs even elsewhere than its substratum.

If sound were a quality residing in the sense organs of touch, its connection with the ear-canal (śaṅku) would be obstructed; yet it is perceived elsewhere, at a distance, in the region of the ear-cavity. Furthermore, there is no possibility of confusion with the qualities of other things [in that location]. Therefore, sound is not a quality residing in the sense organs of touch.

If it is argued that sound is perceived in the sky [ākāśa] by means of the auditory organ (śrotra) as it is conjoined with the *śaṅku* [the auditory canal], because of the doctrine of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the auditory organ through its entry and initiation, then there would be no distinction in perception between what is near and what is distant. If it is further argued that even though the organs are all-pervading (*vyāpaka*), they are constrained by a cause located in front of them, and thus—being fashioned as conducive to the apprehension of objects—they manifest the object; and since the apprehension of the object occurs at that time, the state [of the argument] remains the same. To this we reply: the apprehension of objects by the organs is based on the scripture (*śruti*). Since the organs and their respective objects are simultaneous, the other [theories] are useless and lack any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, the property of being audible (*śrāvaṇatva*) is not perceived in the meanings of the word "going" (*gati*), as it is in the case of sound; nor is there any arrival of a quality (*guṇa*) by abandoning its own substratum (*svāśraya*). Nor can sound be produced in the intervening space by the gift of the arrow, because we observe that when a quality is seen to reside in its own substratum among the objects of touch, it does not produce another distinct particular quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*); and because a substance situated on the arrow is perceived through qualities such as the production of sound in the arrow and the ear. Moreover, there is no perception of what is unattained, as this would lead to undesirable consequences. Therefore, if sound were a quality of the arrow, it simply would not be perceived.

And there is the perception of that [sound]; therefore, its status as a quality of a distinct substance is refuted. For while it would have to be perceivable by the ear through the production of a subsequent sound within the space it occupies, here [in our experience] it is perceived as residing in the conch.
This determination that it is a quality of space is stated because it is perceptible by an external sense organ.

The ear is not a non-external sense organ, because it necessarily illuminates external objects; since sound is its object of perception, and because that [sound] has passed away, it is not [perceived] as its object. Therefore, the meaning is that sound is not a quality of the self, just as color and so forth are perceived by external sense organs but are not qualities of the bodiless self;
for this reason also, sound is not a quality of the self, because it is perceivable by another self, which means it is produced within bodies belonging to multiple selves.

Indeed, the manifestation of sound produced by the playing of a lute or flute is perceived by one person who has provided the illustration, and it is also perceived by another person standing at a distance who hears it; however, pleasure and the like are not perceived in this way. Thus, due to the dissimilarity between these [external sounds] and the qualities of the self, sound is not a quality of the self, because—like color and so forth—it does not inhere in the self. If it is argued that its non-inherence in the self is unproven, [we reply: no, because, like color and the rest, it is perceived as something external, whereas the qualities of the self are understood to be internal.

Furthermore, this [sound] is not a quality of the self (*ātman*), because it is perceived as having a different locus from the cognition produced by the sense organ of sight and others. Indeed, whatever is a quality of the self is perceived as having the same locus as the "I-notion" (*ahaṅkāra*), as in "I am happy" or "I am suffering"; however, sound is not perceived in this way, and therefore it is not a quality of the self. If it is argued that there is indeed the designation "I am speaking," that is true; however, that occurs through the connection with its action, and not by virtue of being dependent on it as a quality. This is because there is no such thing as a continuous stream of the cognition of a substance [in the case of sound]. [The opponent replies: "Then [sound] must be a substance. [The author answers: No, because time and the mind are qualities.
"Because it is perceptible by the ear. What is meant by this?

Those conjunctions and so forth which belong to the two [atoms], the soul, and the mind are not perceptible by the ear; however, this [sound] is observed to be such. Therefore, it is a quality of those [elements]; it is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the two [atoms], the soul, or the mind. Since you maintain that this is indeed a specific quality, he says: "And it belongs to them."
Regarding the Vaiśeṣika-sūtra-bhāṣya-ṭīkā:
"Sound is not a quality of the two [atoms], space, or the mind, because it is a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa), like pleasure and so forth. This is the formal argument (prayoga).

If it is argued that there is accumulation by one [cognition] regarding a single object and its expenditure by that same one—since the determination of that expenditure is accomplished by that very [cognition]—we reply: Is this because there is no result when the object is known by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) after it has been established by one, or because it is useless for the person? It cannot be that there is no result, for even in subsequent continuous cognitions, there is the manifestation of that expenditure. Nor is it useless for the person, since everything corresponds to its own nature; for instance, in the case of a pleasant experience, there is indeed pleasure, and even in the case of pain, there occurs a repeated perception through the senses, as with a son who is extremely dear.

Alternatively, even if it is by this very [means], nevertheless, there is no futility in the operation of the power of the preceding cognition as a cause for the subsequent one, because its purpose is fulfilled precisely through the determination of the object already perceived. For the result of the previously perceived [cognition] does not become non-existent; rather, every other [subsequent cognition] has as its result merely the determination of the object within the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since its status as an object is established through causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). If it is argued that once [the object] has been determined, the second [cognition] lacks the status of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*), we say no; for in respect to its own specific effect, that [second cognition] is indeed the most effective instrument. Otherwise, a cognition occurring in a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*) would be invalid due to the lack of a distinct object. Furthermore, because each individual cognition is produced in succession according to the force of time, there is no failure to produce a valid cognition. Nor does this lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), for they say that the process ceases when the goal is attained.
Now, one might object: "Even if sound is not a quality of substances such as earth and the rest, what does that have to do with space? To this he replies: "By elimination (*pariśeṣāt*).

Sound is a quality, and a quality cannot exist without a substance possessing that quality (*guṇin*). Since it is not a quality of earth and the other [elements], and no other substance exists, therefore, by elimination, space is the substratum for the quality of sound. Thus, the sense organ [of hearing] is the means of cognition (*liṅga*) for establishing the substratum of space; this is the meaning.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
Sound is a quality belonging to another substance, because, while being a quality, it does not reside in substances that lack qualities such as those of earth and the other [elements].

That which is not a quality belonging to another substance does not, while being a quality, fail to reside in substances that lack qualities such as those of earth and the others—just like color and so forth; this is a negative inference (*vyatirekī*).

From the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the six substances, the fact that space has sound as its quality (*śabdaguṇatva*) is already understood. Now, for the purpose of establishing its qualities such as number (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth, he says: "Because there is no distinction in the mark (*liṅga*), namely sound.

This means that by requiring sound as the mark, one understands that "of all [substances]"—thus supplying the genitive case—and thus one supplies exactly what was required, because of the force of the sequence of the words.

Now, it may be argued that even in the case of sound (*śabda*), a diversity [of types] is possible since gradations such as high and low are observed; however, by that [diversity], its status as a *liṅga* (inferential mark) for a miserable person is not established. Rather, it is by virtue of being a quality (*guṇa*)—as something distinct from that—that it is capable of leading to the understanding of the Veda. This is because, since a single [quality] cannot be non-pervasive, there is no contradiction in the observation of differences such as gradation in sound due to a difference in causes.
Consequently, because it conforms to that [singularity], there is a single application (*ekaprayukti*).
That is to say, because it conforms to oneness, there is a single application.

If, however, because the sequence of expressing distinctions is the very life-breath of the sentence-meaning, all these [words] possess this unity, then by that [unity], even though there is separateness, they say "this is one" (*idam ekatvam*); for who could not speak thus? Furthermore, they say that unity is indeed the word itself and not a specific number (*saṃkhyā-viśeṣa*).
For them, the co-occurrence (*saha-prayoga*) in the expression "one jar" (*eko ghaṭaḥ*) would be untenable, because it would be a mere repetition of the same thing.

Even for those who claim that the distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) of entities is indeed intrinsic, it would follow that a conceptualization of distinctness could occur even in the absence of a recollection of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogi*), just as there is a conceptualization of oneness (*ekatva*). But this cannot be the case, because distinctness is conceptualized as "distinct from this" or "distinct from that," which implies a sequence. Therefore, the two [oneness and distinctness] are identical. Regarding the statement "the supreme magnitude" (*paramamahatparimāṇa*): since it is established that space possesses magnitude due to its being a locus of defects, the supreme magnitude of space is established by the statement of the author of the *Vṛtti*: "Space is great by virtue of its being an object."
And if that [space] is of supreme magnitude because the Self or Viṣṇu is its referent, then this [space] is also of supreme magnitude for that reason.

If it is argued that the all-pervasiveness of space (*ākāśa*) is established by its being heard everywhere—since sound is produced everywhere [and] because an effect cannot arise in the absence of its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), such that if space were not pervasive, sound would not be produced everywhere—[we reply: Sound produced in the atmosphere and in the sky is inferred to exist on the earth, because it is sound, like the first sound on the earth; furthermore, the inherence of the sound in the air and the sound in the earth in a single object must be understood through their relationship as cause and effect, since there can be no non-coincidentant inherent causality (*vyadhikaraṇāsama-vāyikāraṇatva*).

From the statement that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) are the causes of sound—specifically from the sūtra stating that "sound is produced from conjunction and so forth"—it is declared that conjunction and disjunction are the causes of sound, which is a quality of space (*ākāśa*). Therefore, conjunction and disjunction are established as residing in space, because there can be no non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) located in a different substratum.
Consequently, [space] is a substance (*dravya*), because it possesses qualities and is not dependent [on another].

For [the opponent argues]: "The mind is a substance because it possesses qualities, like space; and because it possesses qualities, it is a substance, like a jar. But this is not so, for space is a substance despite possessing qualities, and because it is non-dependent (anāśrita), like an atom.
Furthermore, it is eternal because of the absence of causes—both homogeneous and heterogeneous.
This means that there is an absence of its homogeneous inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), its heterogeneous non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), and its instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa).
"It is the cause for the perception of sound by all living beings.
[Objection: But if this were so, then everyone would perceive all sounds, because space is common to all without distinction. To this, he says: "The ear, however... [is the specific cause].
What, then, is the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) therein? He says: "The auditory faculty, moreover...

That by which one hears is the *avaśana*; and that which is both *avaśana* and a cavity is the *avaśanavivara*. That very region of space within which sounds [are perceived] is designated as the auditory faculty, because sound is not perceived outside of it.
He states its qualification with the words "caused by sound," and so forth.
Experience—meaning the feeling of pleasure and pain—is caused by sound; that [experience] is bound by Yama and Yamī, who bring it about, and thus consists of the six elements.
Consisting of destruction.

That sense organ which perceives a specific quality graspable by the external auditory faculty must possess that quality as its attribute; for example, the eye, which perceives color, has color as its substrate. Likewise, since the ear is the perceiver of sound characterized in such a manner, it is determined that it too possesses sound as its quality and is the locus of the nature of sound. Therefore, space alone is that which possesses the quality of sound. Although it is all-pervading, sound is not perceived everywhere, because the sensory capacity of living beings is restricted by the force of their unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) and the specific development of the power of the instrument [the ear]; for instance, although the self is omnipresent, its function of smelling occurs only in the region of the body, and not elsewhere, because the body is the locus of experience.
Otherwise, there would be an inequality in its [the auditory organ's] functioning.
Now, even so, there might be the perception of external sound; [anticipating this objection, he says: because of the opening of the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*).
"And of that" means:

even though that ether (*ākāśa*) is eternal, one should contemplate the connection with the first [of the six] elements—the two threads of *yamī* and *yamaī*, which are the binders—by way of non-return.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion.
Time is the indicator for the inquiry regarding priority, posteriority, duration, action, utility, and the user of utility.
Since there is no other cause for the arising of those [notions] which are distinct from previous cognitions with respect to their objects, time is the cause therein;
this is because it is established that time is not the cause of the arising, persistence, or destruction of all effects.

It is the cause for the conventional usage of [time units] such as the moment (*kṣaṇa*), lava, nimeṣa, kāṣṭhā, kalā, muhūrta, day-and-night (*ahorātra*), half-month, month, season (*ṛtu*), solstice (*ayana*), year, yuga, kalpa, manvantara, dissolution (*pralaya*), and great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

Its qualities are action (*kriyā*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and disjunction (*vibhāga*). Its being the indicator of time (*kāla-liṅgatva*) is established by its [invariable] association with all [these qualities]. Its oneness is proven.
Distinctness follows from its conformity to that [cause].

From the statement "time is the cause," there is the dimension of supreme magnitude (*paramamahat-parimāṇa*). From the connection with priority and posteriority based on the cause, there is conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Because it is presided over by that [Lord], it is called "half of the tree" (*drubhāga*).

Since its status as a substance possessing many parts and its eternity have been established—just like space—even though it serves as the delimiting factor for distinctions such as time and direction, there is a metaphorical attribution of multiplicity to it, due to the differences in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the origination, persistence, and cessation of all effects, just as in the case of a wheel of fire (*alātacakra*).
The proof for the determination of time is as follows:
regarding "time," when there is something posterior, there arises the cognition "this is posterior" with respect to it;

and when there is something prior, there arises the cognition "this is prior" with respect to it. The cognition that manifests both the posterior and the prior, as well as the cognition of simultaneity, the cognition of non-simultaneity, the cognition of "long duration," and the cognition of "short duration"—these are the indicators of time.

[Objection: Since time is not perceptible, there can be no apprehension of its pervasion with [notions] such as "prior" and "posterior"; therefore, how can it be an inferential mark (*liṅga*)? To this, he says: "Not so. For, regarding the objects of those notions—simultaneity and so forth—which are distinct from previous notions and distinct from the notions of substance and so on, there exists no other cause for their arising.

This is so: regarding substances and the like, cognitions of "prior," "subsequent," and so forth arise; yet substances and the like are not their cause, because those cognitions are distinct from them. Furthermore, there is no production of an effect without a cause; therefore, time must necessarily be the cause.
Some maintain that the usage of the notions of "prior" and "subsequent" regarding a youth and an elder is based on the direct perception of the movement of the sun; however, that is incorrect.

Furthermore, because there is no cognition of the words "young" and "old" in relation to the revolution of the sun, they lack the status of being verbal designators; or, if they were to serve as the cause [of the distinction], it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Others claim that their state as the sixth [case] constitutes simultaneity (*yogapadya*);
that too is incorrect.

If it is argued that, since time is not accepted as a distinct entity, the sixth relation (*ṣaṣṭhabhāva*) must be explained as the mutual non-connection of the factors of action (*sādhana*) within an activity—that is, the meaning of the sixth case—[we reply:

this is untenable because such a relation is not perceived among those things that are established [as distinct], and because if those possessing a sixth relation were indeed correlates (*pratiyogin*), it would result in the impossibility of time being imperceptible.
Furthermore, cognitions such as "simultaneous" and "non-simultaneous" regarding the sixth relation must also be accounted for.

If it is asked, "Since time is indivisible, how can there be a distinction between cognitions? [the answer is: Due to the difference in the substrata of the cognitions, the apprehension of a jar-cognition occurs through a knowledge that has as its object its arising and destruction; by means of the time that effects this, the cognition of priority and posteriority (*parāpara*) is produced. Similarly, by means of that which possesses the function of grasping the moments occurring in succession, the cognition of simultaneity (*yugapat*) arises. And by means of that which effects the apprehension of one's own nature through the sequence of activities existing within the interval between the production and destruction of the effect, the cognitions of "long" and "short" arise. These should be explained according to the circumstances.
Now, it may be argued that the distinction between the suffixes *aṅ* and *ap*, as well as their temporal application, is based on various specific causes;
however, because these [suffixes] would have to share the same essential nature [as the base], such [distinction] is impossible.
For there can be no absolute difference, nor can there be the production of space (*gagana*).

Nor is there an absolute difference [between the cause and the effect], for they are drawn together from different locations; rather, the distinction lies in the prior absence of causal efficiency in the case of the jar's non-existence, which serves as a qualifier. Furthermore, if it were argued that the production of something occurs because of its being located in two places (*dviṣṭhatva*), then at whatever time the qualified cognition arises, the causality of time would remain unestablished; it would not function as a qualifier like a staff or other such objects.
The same applies to the self (*ātman*).

For cognition, whose sole nature is apprehension (*vodha*), when it attains another object without depending on anything else—just as it does with its own object—an "inherence" (*anvaya*) is postulated. When two substances are perceived through a difference in their states, time is inferred as the cause of that [perception]. This is because, according to the view of those who maintain the reality of cognition (*jñaptimataḥ*), there is a unity in the cognizer; thus, there is no contradiction in a qualifier being presented by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For example, as in the case of "the silver in the mother-of-pearl," or "the ground containing the golden pot. However, in the case of jars and the like, since they are perceived at a distance or through a difference in state, once the connection with the time of perception is known, the simultaneous cognition of them arises; subsequently, their qualification by time is understood. Thus, there is no fault.
It is the cause of the arising, subsistence, and destruction of all effects. Now, he states the reasoning:
"Because of its concise teaching."

The meaning is that time functions as a cause in those instances because of designations such as "the time of arising" and "the time of destruction," which refer to the arising and so forth of things.
He also mentions another effect of it:
"similarity of color" and so on.

A fourth part of a *nimeṣa* is a *kaṣa*; two *kaṣas* make a *lava*; and a *nimeṣa* is defined as the time taken for a slight sound or a slight scratch, and so forth—this is to be understood according to the treatises on calculation (*gaṇita-śāstra*).
Thus, while the duration [of time] is established, he describes its qualities:
"its qualities," and so on.
Since time is a substance, its connection with number and other qualities is established; however, in order to explain its specific characteristics, he says:
"Because there is no distinction in the marks of time.

This means that time is the cause of the non-distinction among the marks of time—namely, the cognitions of simultaneity and so forth—since there is no other means of proof for a difference in time itself.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the very difference in cognitions, such as "simultaneous" and so forth, is what establishes that difference [of number]? [Reply: It is not so; for even when there is a difference in time, a difference in cognition would result due to a difference in auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).

Because that [difference] is not mentioned, [the author says] "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*). If oneness were to follow from separateness, there would be a restriction based on externality; therefore, the establishment of separateness follows from oneness and the like.

By the statement "time [is designated] in respect to the effect" (*kārye kāla*), the author indicates through the phrase "possessing the dimension of supreme magnitude" (*paramamahatparimāṇam*) that time is designated as the cause. Thus, the dual meaning is that the designation "time" applies to the cause, and time is the substrate for cognitions such as simultaneity. By this, time is characterized as all-pervasive; the intention is that it exists within all things, whether past, middle (present), or future. Furthermore, by the teaching of its priority (*paratva*) and so forth in relation to its causes, it is established as conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
In the sūtra stating that "priority and posteriority [arise] from priority of cause and priority of effect," the term "priority of cause" denotes a connection with temporal succession.
By this, its primary nature as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is established.
This is what is meant by the statement: "the apprehension of the substance and so forth."

Since that conjunction is produced, it is necessarily perishable; therefore, disjunction is its destroyer, for all things possess the nature of being perishable. Thus, although time possesses the quality of distance through disjunction, because it is itself indivisible and indestructible, its substantiality and eternity are established—just as space is a substance because it possesses qualities and is non-dependent, so too is time; and just as space is characterized by the absence of homogeneous and heterogeneous causes, so too is time.

To the question, "Since time is one, how can there be such designations as 'that' and 'this'? he replies: "Because of the non-distinction of the marks of time. Since the marks of time—such as priority, posteriority, and so forth—are non-distinct in that they serve as indicators [of time], it is established that time is essentially one, even though it is designated as manifold through metaphorical usage. Thus, despite the unity of time, the designation of its multiplicity arises from the figurative application of diversity.

[The divisions are] commencement (*upakrama*), which is the beginning of all actions; completion (*parisamāpti*), which is the cessation of action; persistence (*sthiti*), which is the abiding in its own nature; and cessation (*nirodha*), which is destruction. Furthermore, there is application (*praṇayopayoga*), which is the designation of difference and manifoldness (*nānātva*). Just as a single ground is designated as "blue" due to the difference of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as crystal or the color blue, so too time (*kāla*) is designated as "time of [the sun's] movement," "time of action," or "time of cessation" according to the difference of its limiting conditions. This is the meaning.

To demonstrate that while the relation of time to an action is not real when time is viewed as a mere cause for perceiving an entity, rather it is the relation of time to action that is real, he provides another illustration: "The cook.

Just as this person receives the designation "cook" or "reader" due to his connection with the actions of cooking and so forth, so too does time [receive its designation] through such [actions] as beginning; for time is distinguished by the diversity of its specific cognitions.
Space (dik) is characterized by the notions of "east," "west," and so forth.

Having established the east as a reference point, that from which these ten notions arise—namely, "this is to the east," "to the south," "to the west," "to the north," "to the southeast," "to the southwest," "to the northwest," "to the northeast," "above," and "below"—with respect to corporeal substances alone, is space.
This is because it depends upon other causes [for its cognition].

In that regard, the qualities of space—number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction—are established as being like those of time. Although space is a single substance because its indicative marks are non-distinct, the wise have established ten directions for the sake of the practical conventions of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and worldly affairs. These are the tenfold conceptualizations of the divisions of space, beginning with the East, which are mentally apprehended through specific conjunctions of the divine Sun as he revolves clockwise around Mount Meru; these regions, presided over by the world-protectors (Lokapālas), are established as the ten directions.
Furthermore, they receive their names from the presiding deities:
Māhendrī, Vaiśvānarī, Yāmyā, Nairṛtī, Vāruṇī, Yāmyā (again), Kauverī, Aiśānī, Brāhmī, Nāgī, and Dhrauvi.

Demonstrating that time possesses the characteristic of having simultaneous beginning, middle, and end, whereas space possesses the characteristic of having prior, posterior, beginning, middle, and end, he says:
"In the directions, there are prior, posterior, etc., and middle and end.
That direction which has prior, middle, posterior, etc., as its middle and end is described as such.

He demonstrates this very point of injury: by means of the eastern direction (*pūrvedik*), he shows that there is no spatial extension (*nāvayivatva*) for this substance, nor any distinction of prior, posterior, middle, or end, because its own inherent measure is concealed. Therefore, it is said: having established the eastern direction as a limit, that which exists prior to, or posterior to, or between [other] substances is a "direction" (*dig*), since from it the prior, posterior, middle, and so forth arise.

In the sense of "this is prior to that," the designation "prior" (pūrva) is used because of the rule extending the application of the nominal stem's meaning. Now, one might object: since priority, posteriority, and so forth are effects, a cause is inferred; but how is it certain that this cause is *diś* (space/direction) alone? To this he replies: "because no other cause is possible."

A substance consisting of parts is not the cause for the beginning, middle, and end [of a process], because if the substance were merely present in some state or another, it would follow that those [stages] could not occur.

Furthermore, even if two substances were the cause of each other’s production through mutual dependence, there would be the same fault [of infinite regress]. Moreover, if direction were the cause of qualities, actions, and so forth, there would be no specific cognition regarding qualities, actions, and the like that are devoid of those [substances]. Therefore, that which serves as the cause for such [cognitions] is *dik* (direction). When one uses the ablative case in expressions such as "this is from that," it is because otherwise the [notion of] spatial distance would not be established. Nor is this merely a conventional usage; rather, it is an imperceptible [entity] dependent upon direction, and not a substance, since all [substances] are indistinguishable in that regard.

Even though she is immortal, it must be stated that she is the cause of death through Viṣṇu, who brings about time. To establish that she possesses qualities and that her presence is perceived as water, he says:
"But her qualities," and so forth.
These [qualities] are like time.

Just as the unity of time is established from the specific distinctions residing in time, so too is the unity of space established from the specific distinctions residing in space; and just as distinctness is established in time because of its support [of those distinctions], so it is in space. Just as time possesses the dimension of infinite magnitude (*paramamahatparimāṇa*) because of the statement "time is the cause," so too space possesses the dimension of infinite magnitude because of the statement "space is the cause. Furthermore, since all its effects possess the nature of being preceded by their material cause (*upādāna*), just as the quality of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) has been demonstrated for time even though it is subordinate to its cause, so it is for space as well. And just as disjunction (*vibhāga*) is established in time because it is the cause of the destruction of conjunction, so too is it established in space through its various locations.

[Objection: Is it not the case that a specific property residing in the directions (*diṅniṣṭhaviśeṣa*) is not established, because the distinctions such as "east" and "west" are merely relative? And thus, it is logical that there is a plurality of directions. [Reply: No.

Since they are of a single nature and refer to a single object, the distinction between east, west, and so forth exists for those who rely on the proximity or distance of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For if there were indeed a plurality of directions, then whatever is in the east would also have to be in the west; and if you say that this is because the word "direction" applies to all individual instances, then in that case, everyone would have all perceptions regarding everything at all times.

But this is not the case. Therefore, there is only one direction; the difference in cognition arises from the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). For instance, when a substance situated near the sun is in conjunction with the eastern region, it is designated as "east"; when that same substance situated near the sun is in the interval between [the east] and the south, it is designated as "southeast. Similarly, when a substance situated near the sun is in conjunction with the western region at sunset, it is designated as "west"; and when it is in the interval between those two, the designations "northeast" and so forth arise in relation to the substance situated in conjunction with the midday sun. Thus, the diversity of cognitions is logically established.
Furthermore, the cognition of a forest is based on the conjunction with the sun;
yet,
since there is no conjunction with each individual [tree] and it is impossible for an undivided whole to be the cause of such a cognition, this very [cognition] remains inexplicable.
"Because of the distinction between two types of limits.

Since the unity of direction (*diś*) is established, the great sages have assigned ten conventional designations—such as "eastern" and so forth—to it. [The objection is: "How can these be otherwise? [The answer is: They are designated as such because they are perceived in that way. These directions are occupied by the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), Indra and the others; in the vicinity of those regions of space, there occur conjunctions and disjunctions, and from these, the usage [of the names] arises accordingly. For instance, the region where the sun first appears is called the "eastern" (*prācī*).
It flows downwards, thus it is *avācī*; it flows westwards, thus it is *pratīcī*;
it flows upwards, thus it is *udīcī*.

As Viṣṇu, the Earth, the Sky, the Ancestors, and the Gods revolve clockwise around me as I rotate clockwise, for what purpose were these six designations established? [The answer is: For the sake of worldly prosperity and tradition; this very tradition is known for the purpose of practical conduct (*vyavahāra*), not through the application of the speech of those facing west.
Herein also is the self-definition: traditional conduct (*smārta-vyavahāra*) includes such statements as "An Ārya Brāhmaṇa eats," and so forth.
Worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*) consists of such [injunctions] as "Go first" or "Look to the south," and so forth.
Once [the world] was divided into ten sections, the ten directions were then established by the learned through figurative usage (*bhakty-upacāra*).
He states that in the *Māheśvara* and other traditions, these do not refer to objects that have perished, but rather they function because they are based on names and other underlying causes.
"Following the name," and so forth.
This belongs to Mahendra, thus it is *māhendrī*;
this belongs to Vaiṣṇavana, thus it is *vaiṣṇavanarī*—in all such cases, the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is to be understood accordingly.
First, there is the Self, which is regarded as the very nature of the Self.
Its ultimate reality is established through the auditory organ and the others, which are inferred from the non-perception of sound and other objects;

for, since instruments such as axes and the like are seen to be employed by an agent, and because [the sense organs] are well-known to operate upon objects such as sound, it is inferred that they must likewise have an agent who employs them.
[Consciousness] does not belong to the body, the senses, or the mind, because [the body] is merely a material entity.
Consciousness does not belong to the body, because it is an insentient effect like a jar, and because [consciousness] is impossible in a dead body.
It does not belong to the senses, because they are instruments, and because we observe recollection even when the senses are impaired or when objects are absent.

Nor can it be the mind, because if the mind were independent of other instruments, there would be the consequence of simultaneous perception and memory, and because the mind itself functions as an instrument. By the method of elimination, since it is the effect of a self, the self is thus established. Furthermore, with respect to the activities of engagement and withdrawal—which consist in the capacity to attain the beneficial and avoid the harmful and which inhere in the body—the self is inferred as a conscious controller residing within the objects of experience, possessing effort like a charioteer who directs a chariot by means of the vital breaths and so forth.

How is it that when the air has taken possession of the body, one perceives a certain agent who—like a master of the house through the observation of modified actions such as inhalation and exhalation, and through the regulated action of the winking and opening of the eyes like a skilled artisan; who, like a householder through the cause of fatigue, thirst, and the movement of the limbs; and like a child in ancestral houses and fields through the impulse of mental activity—is recognized as a certain observer of both [senses], since he is known by the modification of the tongue observed upon the casting of a morsel of food into the mouth immediately after the perception of visual objects?
