The possessor of qualities (guṇin) is inferred from the qualities of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort; and these are not qualities of the body or the sense organs. Why? Because they are expressed by the same term as the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra), because they reside in a specific location, because they do not cease as long as the substance exists, and because they are not perceptible by the external senses. This is likewise true for sound, since it differs from the sounds of earth and other elements. Its qualities are cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression (saṃskāra), number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.
Within the section on the marks of the self (ātmaliṅga), those beginning with cognition and ending with effort have been established.
Dharma and adharma [are qualities of the self] because it is stated that they are not causes for the qualities internal to the self;

mental impression (saṃskāra) [is a quality of the self] because it is stated to be the cause for the arising of memory; number [is a quality of the self] because of the statement regarding its specific determination; separateness and non-exertion [are qualities of the self] likewise; and individuality (paratva) and relativity (aparatva) [are qualities of the self] because of the statement "and so too is the self."
Conjunction [of pleasure and so forth] occurs because they are produced from contact with *sattva*;
disjunction occurs because they cause that [contact] to perish.

He states these [categories] for the purpose of establishing them, so that the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) may lead to the highest good (niḥśreyasa), while the knowledge of objects (viṣayaprajñāna) serves as the instruction on the cause of saṃsāra.
Regarding the term "ātmatva":

*ātmatva* is a universal (sāmānya); the conventional usage of the term "ātmatva" occurs by way of being directed toward that [universal]. This [usage], namely "this belongs to this," is also a case of difference (vaidharmya).

[Objection: Is it not the case that everything [that exists] is pervaded by being cognizable through some form (*ākāra*), and yet there is no cognition of anything having the form of a self (*ātman*)? Since its pervader is not perceived, the self is refuted just like a water-jar; thus, how can there be a determination of its properties (*dharmanirūpaṇa*)? [Response: Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states "tathā" (so it is), demonstrating that there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the self because perceptual non-apprehension (*pratyakṣānupalabdhi*) is established otherwise, and there exists a proving proof, namely inference (*anumāna*). The term "distinctness" (*vailakṣaṇya*) refers to the absence of fitness for perception (*pratyakṣopalabdhi-yogyatā-viraha*).

Therefore, for the householder, the auditory organ and so forth are established through inference based on the non-perception of sound by the self as an instrument; for [sound] is inferred to be a momentary sequence because it is an action, like the action of piercing.
This is stated in the passage beginning with "It is done," etc., because the instruments such as speech are incapable of producing an effect [without such organs].
It is not apprehended by anyone through direct perception, just as an effect such as speech is pervaded by a single agent;
and since the instruments, such as the ear and so forth, must be employed by someone, that which is their employer is the Self.

Although there is no direct connection between the ether (ākāśa), which constitutes the sense of hearing, and the self because it consists of three forms, nevertheless, the self exercises its agency over it through the medium of the internal organ and so forth—just as a hand, by means of a staff, brings about contact with an iron ball. Furthermore, the senses such as hearing function as instruments because they apprehend specific objects, like a lamp.

Although the self is perceived as the agent, the locus of the conjunction with the various instruments, and the possessor of ownership— conditioned by its own specific functions through the eyes, the mind, and so forth— it is nevertheless inferred as the prover (the knower) based on the intention of the senses whose activity is unknown,
and based on the established cognition regarding sound and other objects.
That is to say, although the cognition regarding objects such as sound is well-known, the prover— the knower— is nonetheless inferred.
Knowledge exists within the self because it is an action, like the action of cutting; and that which is manifested is the self.

If it is argued that this [self] knows this by itself and not through another, is this [self] eternal or does it perish every moment? If it is eternal, then pleasure and so forth would be eternal from the very beginning. If, on the other hand, it is momentary, there could be no memory of what was experienced long ago, because of the difference [between moments] at every instant. As for the claim that there is memory of what was experienced in a previous moment due to the causal relationship between cause and effect—whereas there is no memory of what was experienced long ago because the causal relationship between the preceding and subsequent moments is absent—that is incorrect, because both the body and the [supposedly] preceding and succeeding moments are insentient.
Therefore, that [argument] is untenable.

In the absence of a self (*ātman*), because the relationship between cause and effect cannot be ascertained, at the time of the cognition of the cause, the cognition of the effect is yet to come, and at that time, the cause has already passed away. Furthermore, since there is no single observer distinct from these two, who could perceive the causal relationship between them occurring in succession?
Now, if it is thought that the embodied intellect (*buddhi*), which is self-supporting, perceives its own causality—which is not distinct from itself—as its object.

If it is argued that the subsequent cognition also grasps its own cause as its object and, being non-different from it, grasps its own status as an effect; and that although causal and effectual natures are each individually experienced, they are determined by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through the exclusion (*apoha*) of what is not experienced—alas, this is a fabrication of an elaborate hypothesis! For even if [the cognition] is restricted to its own self-nature, how could it perceive "this is my cause" or "this is my effect," given that there is no mutual concomitance? Even if [causality] were established by means of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it would not be determined, because it does not follow upon actual experience.
Let it be granted that knowledge belongs to another; however, its substratum must be either the body, the sense organs, or the mind.
To this, he replies: "Not of the body, the sense organs, or the mind.
The word *caitanya* (consciousness), defined by the characteristics previously stated, is connected here with the term *niṣiddham* (denied).
He states why consciousness does not belong to the body, the senses, or the mind: "Because of insentience" (*acetanatvāt*).
This means because they lack the status of being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of cognition.
To this, he states the reason for the non-pervasion [of consciousness by the body] through the phrase "na śarīre" (not in the body).

Consciousness does not belong to the body because the body is an effect of the elements, like a jar; whatever is an effect of the elements is not conscious, just as a jar is; and the body is an effect of the elements; therefore, it is not conscious. (1)
The author states the internal argument:
"And because it is visible.

By the previous statement, "because consciousness is impossible in the body," it was intended that consciousness does not exist as long as the substance [the body] exists; consciousness is not a specific quality of the body, because it does not persist as long as the body is perceived by the eye, just like conjunction.

For this very reason, their causes as well must be insentient; for if they were sentient, sentience would likewise exist in their effects, just as it exists in the primal matter (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, there would result a plurality of knowers within the body, and consequently, defects such as the absence of a restrictive rule regarding the activity of the single self and its vital breaths (*prāṇa*) would follow.
[Objection: "The sense organs are not [sentient], because they are instruments. [Response:
The sense organs are sentient, because they are instruments, like a staff.

And he states another reason: "In the case of impaired [faculties]. When the sense faculties (*indriya*) have perished, an object previously experienced is remembered; yet, it is not logical for there to be memory when the experiencer has perished. Therefore, cognition is a quality of the sense faculty. Furthermore, memory is observed even when the external object that was previously experienced no longer exists; and since the external sense faculties function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*), memory cannot belong to them. Thus, in the absence of such [external] faculties, experience itself would not occur; the meaning is that because one does not remember what was experienced by another, [experience must reside in the same locus as memory].

For this very reason, the object also does not possess consciousness; for there is no possibility of remembering that [consciousness] with respect to the object, and for this reason as well, the object lacks consciousness, because pleasure and so forth—which are produced by that [object] and have it as their content—are experienced by the self, and because [the object] lacks the specific nature of being presided over by a conscious Lord. Nor can the sense organs or the objects be considered conscious, because there is a distinct appearance of "I see color," "I touch what is touched," and "I smell fragrance," which is preceded by the individual perceptions of each respective sense organ; for there is a difference between the eyes and other organs and the colors and other objects.
Furthermore, since it is untenable for the quality of the mind (*manoguṇa*)—which is cognition (*jñāna*)—to be both omniscient and eternal, he says:
"Nor [is it] the mind.

If the mind were insentient like the eye and other organs, it would require another instrument to perceive objects such as sound; thus, others explain the nature of the self (*ātman*) as distinct from the body and the senses.
There should be no dispute regarding this: that which is the mind (manas) is unfit for [simultaneous] action, and that mind which is the instrument of cognition is composed of eight parts.

Now, if it does not depend on another instrument, then the simultaneous occurrences of perceptions in two or more locations would belong to a single entity due to the simultaneity of its causes. However, if there is dependence on another instrument, then because that [mind] is atomic, it cannot be present in all the sense organs at once; thus, the simultaneous occurrence of perceptions would be impossible.

Now, if there were an absence of internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the sense organs would have to function simultaneously, because there would be nothing to require [sequential] dependence. However, if there is a dependence upon organs, then since those [organs] themselves lack the capacity for simultaneity, their manifestation arises sequentially.
It is argued that "one eternal entity cannot produce effects both successively and simultaneously.
That is incorrect.

Because simultaneous action is impossible, and because there is no inference [of the mind] at a time other than that [of perception], and because its existence is not observed apart from its causal activity,
they say that cognition is not a quality of the mind, since the mind itself is an instrument (*karaṇa*).
This is because of its status as an instrument in its own right.

The mind is not the agent (*manas-cetanā na bhavati*) because it is an instrument (*karaṇatvāt*), like a jar or similar objects. If it is argued that the mind’s status as an instrument is firmly established because its being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth is accepted, [we reply: if the mind were an effect, then for the cognition of pleasure and so forth—just as in the case of the cognition of color and so forth—there would have to be another primary instrument for the act of cognition, since an action is impossible without an instrument. And this being the case, since both [the mind and that other instrument] would be instruments for the purpose of perceiving the six notes (*ṣaḍja*, etc. and so on, [the opponent's position fails]. Furthermore, this [mind] is not [the agent], because it possesses form (*mūrtatvāt*); thus [the author] concludes.

If knowledge is not a quality of the body, the senses, or the mind, then what follows for the establishment of the self? To this he replies: "By elimination" (*pariśeṣāt*). Knowledge, being an effect, must be the effect of some inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Since its subsistence in the body, the senses, and the mind has been refuted, and since no other external things possess the capacity—by logical principle—to be the cause of knowledge, knowledge is therefore the effect of the self by elimination. Because it is the effect of the self, the self is established through that knowledge; such is the conclusion.

Is this not entirely incoherent, since you are propounding this chapter on the basis of its being a treatise on logic (*vāda-śāstra*)? To explain: existence (*sattva*) consists in causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and that is pervaded by either succession (*krama*) or simultaneity (*yugapad*), because there exists no other mode besides these two, which are of the nature of succession and non-succession. For succession is the state of multiple causal activities occurring at different times, while simultaneity is their occurrence at a single time. Nor is there any other mode apart from the one and the many, because the presence of one among two mutually exclusive properties necessarily implies the exclusion of the other. Furthermore, for that which is not subject to temporal duration, succession is impossible, as it would have to function simultaneously.

If it is argued that this and that [entity] produce their effect sequentially because they obtain sequential auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), since the non-existence of their capacity does not cease even at another time;
then they reply:

If the auxiliaries do not produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the entity, they are not to be depended upon, as they would be ineffective. If, however, they do produce it, is that [excellence] distinct from the entity or non-distinct? If it were distinct, then—given the impossibility of its being either eternal or non-eternal—the production of the effect from something distinct from the established entity would result in the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and thus it could not establish the status of the entity as a cause. This is because such a distinct excellence would already be established [as a separate cause].

If you argue that the cause possesses its generative power because of an excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), then if that excellence does not produce another excellence, what kind of assistance is it?

And if it does produce one, what is the remedy for infinite regress (*anavasthā*)? The saying that "the excellence produced by auxiliaries is the source of non-deviation" is well-spoken; however, the claim that "an excellence non-different from the entity itself is constructed by the auxiliaries"—since there can be no relation between that which is neither assisted nor assisting—is not at all sound.

Because there is no further arising of an entity that has already arisen previously. For if it is argued that the prior entity, while remaining as an unaltered nature, is born with an added excellence (atiśaya), this is refuted by the [doctrine of] momentariness (kṣaṇikatva). Now, what do the auxiliary causes (sahakārin) do even for a momentary entity? Nothing at all. Why then are they designated by that name? What purposeful activity (arthakriyā) is performed by them?

For indeed, it is the individual phonemes existing in their final state that are capable of producing the effect; what need have they for mutual dependence? In that case, their proximity to one another would be a superfluous cause, since the necessity of their presence is already established by the requirement of the object to be produced. Nor does the totality of causes produce the effect at that time, because there is no fixed rule regarding their causal efficiency due to their lack of substantial reality (*avastutva*). If each cause were individually capable, they would each produce the effect separately; why then do many perform a single act? It is because their causes are such that they bring about the power to accomplish a single purpose, even though they are distinct.
We, however, are speakers of the nature of reality as it has been perceived, not of the great flood of former traditions.

If it is argued that when one [cause] alone has performed the effect, what further use are others? We reply: they do not perform what has already been done; rather, while one is performing it, the others also perform it. If it is asked, "Since each is individually capable, what is the utility of [other] causes?", we say: True, they are not individual causes. If this were so, then when lightning flashes, it would be impossible for a single effect to arise from multiple [causes], because the difference in effects must have a cause in the difference of the effects themselves. To this we reply: The difference in effects arises from a difference in capacity (*sāmarthya*), not from a difference in the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). Being an auxiliary factor consists precisely in the production of a single effect.

Therefore, if there is a specific characteristic (*varṇika*), the successive performance of functions by entities in a sequence is possible; however, for that which lacks such a characteristic, purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) in a sequence is difficult to establish. Likewise, simultaneous performance is also difficult to establish, because the nature of that which is capable of performing those effects does not persist beyond that time. There is no performing of what has already been done, and nothing further remains to be done by it, since the entire collection of effects has been produced all at once by that which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*). Consequently, it does not produce another [effect] at a later moment.

If, on the other hand, this [entity] were to arise at that time as something non-existent, it would do so in the absence of any causal activity; thus, because the two pervading properties—succession and simultaneity—are not perceived, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), and everything is necessarily established as momentary (*kṣaṇika*). This being the case, the inference of momentariness for a person is as follows: "Whatever exists is momentary, like the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*) at the time of their manifestation. To this, it is objected: "There is no fault regarding momentariness, because that is its very nature."
It should be understood that for him, the status of being an object is untenable.

If it is argued that a momentary entity is excluded from the nature of reality because it lacks both succession and simultaneity—just as a horse’s horn lacks succession and simultaneity—and that this exclusion from reality follows from its exclusion from succession and simultaneity via the subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) of its momentariness; we say no. For when momentariness is perceived, it is impossible for the word [denoting the object] to be perceived as excluded from it. Just as when a person is being perceived, one perceives the absence of external trees [in that specific location], so too, when a non-momentary substance is perceived, the absence of the nature [of reality] would have to be perceived due to the absence of succession and simultaneity. However, for you, there is no such thing as a "non-momentary" entity that could serve as the locus of exclusion, just as a ghost (*piśāca*), though unperceived, is perceived as excluded from a pillar in the form "the pillar is not a ghost. If it is argued that the same will apply here, we say no, because the exclusion [of the ghost] is preceded by the perception of the other object (the pillar) and the prior non-perception of the ghost, which constitutes the absence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) through the possibility of perceiving the other object. Furthermore, since a ghost is merely a conceptual construct (*svarūpa-vikalpa*), it is impossible for it to be perceived as excluded from that [pillar]. If it is asked how, then, the cognition "the pillar is not a ghost" arises, we say: it is not a negation of a relation (*saṃsarga-pratiṣedha*), but rather a negation of identity (*tādātmya-pratiṣedha*). And this proceeds on the basis of admitting the substantiality of a ghost that is already established as having the nature of a pillar, and not otherwise.
As it has been said:

"To whatever extent a particularity exists through identity, all of them are made non-characteristic by the perception [of the object] being characterized. Likewise, the cognition of a pillar, which is restricted solely to the essential nature of the pillar, is the cause for the exclusion of what is not that [pillar]. If the pillar were a *piśāca*, it would be known as having that [ghost's] nature; however, the cognition does not apprehend the nature of a *piśāca* in the same way it apprehends pillar-ness. Therefore, "this is not a *piśāca*."

Now, if it is argued that there is nothing whatsoever—neither non-variegated nor variegated—that exists apart from blue and the other colors, but rather that the non-variegated is so called because the color blue and so forth, which were the objects of a previous cognition, are superimposed through the power of a subsequent cognition as being distinct from the color blue and the rest; ... [the argument continues] ... [the opponent claims that] the non-variegated is merely a conceptual construct arising from the synthesis of various colors perceived in succession.

And being established as distinct [moments], such that "it is a merchant," for you, there is the cognition of existence and non-existence through the contradiction of succession and simultaneity regarding blue and so forth. If this [present object] is perceived by virtue of having been previously perceived, then it would have to perform its present causal function exactly like its previous one, or else perform its previous function right now; it could not perform them successively, because it is contradictory for a single entity to be both an agent and a non-agent.
Nor could it perform all [functions] only as before, because that would entail non-existence due to its being devoid of its present causal function.

In that case as well, is the object of the reason for reality [its] outflow (*āsrava*)—is it superimposed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā-samāropita*) or is it concentrated (*samāhita*)? It cannot be a real object, because the momentariness of blue and other such things is not real. Therefore, one who desires a real causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) from inference must bring forward a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of determining the nature of the logical mark (*liṅga*). Consequently, every object established by a means of valid cognition is seen to be real and not merely a product of conceptual construction; otherwise, there would be no non-perception of what is perceptible, and thus the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established. Furthermore, for one who does not know [this], the reason would be unestablished due to the contradiction with other treatises regarding [the object's] unity and so forth. Thus, the reason is not real.

And some [opponents] claim that because there is a sublation [of existence], the state of being momentary follows from the state of being existent; for what other [property] could exist between momentariness and existence? Why [is this so]?

Because [the opponent argues that] even though "lightning" is not a reason merely by way of its non-recurrence [in the subject], the state of being a branch or the like is accepted as a reason; and since they themselves have established that in a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatireki*), existence does not belong to that which is impermanent and momentary—therefore, if it is argued here that "existence" is a reason with a deviation from the contrary (i.e., it exists in non-momentary things), we reply: no, because [the reason] is faultless. This is the consideration of the reason "existence."

Since momentariness is not established as a reason even for that [existence], and since no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is observed to demonstrate pervasion (*vyāpti*)—just as a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) does—it would have to demonstrate it within the twelve sense-bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) alone; for pervasion proceeds by way of each individual object, and there is no observation of anything beyond the twelve sense-bases, nor is there any other means of valid cognition regarding them.

If it is argued that the cognition of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is also inseparable from the cognition of the proof of the relation [between momentariness and existence], and therefore, while the apprehension of the pervasion occurs generally through the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with existence, existence itself serves as the reason for the particular case—this is not so. For there is no cognition of a universal devoid of particulars; even when the particulars are set aside, since neither momentariness nor the general property of existence is being cognized, it is not logical to say that "momentariness is cognized" in the same way as blue and other [colors] through the dissimilarity with existence.

If it is argued that because the subverting proof (*bādhaka*) does not apprehend the pervasion of momentariness by imperceptibility, there is still the cognition of momentariness as the very nature of the thing (*vastu*), we say no. This is because the identity (*tādātmya*) of the excluded particular—which is merely an imagined distinction—is itself non-perceptual. Furthermore, identity is experienced through inference; since there is identity between the two natures of the thing—momentariness and existence—there is also identity between the two pervasions as they are manifested through that identity. We say no, because the identity-pervasion between the thing and its nature is unestablished. Or, if it were established, the subverting proof would be redundant. Moreover, when the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between two pervasions is determined, there is no establishment of the thing itself, because there is no difference between the thing and its non-thing (its nature), and because [the thing] is not independent.
As for the argument that it is improper because it is a different property—

that having demonstrated the pervasion by a subverting proof in the case of a jar, the demonstration of momentariness in the case of sound based on its existence [therein] is nonetheless a means of proof due to the difference in the objects—
regarding that too, this is the reply:

Just as in the case of a jar, even with respect to sound, there is no contradiction in the removal of sublation; thus, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is untenable. Nor is the non-momentary [entity] capable of being observed, for it is only when there is association with auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) that the production of an effect is possible. An entity does not possess the nature of an independent causal factor; rather, its capacity is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), such that the effect arises only when the auxiliary causes, whose efficacy follows from those concomitances, come together. Thus, even for a stable [entity], action occurs sequentially, because an effect dependent on multiple causes cannot arise from a single one alone.

Nor is it logical to claim that [the cause] is not a causal agent because the production of the effect occurs due to the predominance of factors such as existence (*sattva*) when there is dependence on many contributory causes; for [otherwise], one could not define the self as a substance (*dravya*). Indeed, since the production of an effect is observed through the inference of its form, it must possess causal agency. For if it were merely a cooperative factor (*sahakāritva*), then—due to the absence of a restrictive cause—such cooperation would exist equally in the production of lightning, water, or a sprout from a rice seed. Furthermore, cooperation does not bestow any excellence upon the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the entity itself, but rather resides only within the cooperative factors themselves.

Furthermore, if it is argued that although these [auxiliaries] lack the capacity for cooperation (*sahakāritva*) and possess no excellence (*atiśaya*), yet their mere presence constitutes a destruction [of the causal state], then because the effect would arise from that [destruction], there would be no distinction between the states; consequently, the distinction between producing and non-producing causes, as well as the granting of results, would be untenable. If one were to say that this is merely a change of state (*avasthāntara*)—since a sword, a staff, a vehicle, a snake, or a path require other intervening factors to produce pleasure, pain, cognition, or the self—then, if the merchant’s analogy holds, perception would be erroneous; and if that [perception] does not arise, the merchant’s analogy would fail. Thus, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśrayatā*).

Furthermore, it is not the case that (1) the very production of perception is the cause of its destruction, since [perception] persists until the occurrence of another cognition; thus, the conceptualization of its production and destruction in such a manner is logical. (2) Destruction is without cause, and it is nowhere observed that even a seed is the cause of itself.

A seed that produces a sprout does not possess the nature of a seed [at that moment], because it is a seed, just like a rice-seed that has become a sprout. Since a partless entity cannot possess both agency and non-agency, these two aspects are untenable; therefore, this [argument of yours] is trivial.

Just as fire possesses both the status of being an agent (*kārakatva*) with respect to burning and the status of not being an agent (*akārakatva*) with respect to cognition, yet there is no difference in its own nature (*svarūpa*), so too a single entity possesses both the status of being an agent and the status of not being an agent due to the presence or absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri*). If it is asked, "How can one thing be an agent for one [effect] but not for another, even though it is an agent?"—here, the natures of things (*vastusvabhāva*) must be understood through the method of exclusion (*apoha*).

But as for us, we do not perceive their capacity in a place where they are not employed due to the existence of a remainder; therefore, since we have accepted that very capacity as being distributed [among them], we are not subject to reproach.

Even in your own position, only lightning, water, and the seed possess auxiliary efficacy (*sahakāritā*) toward the production of the sprout, and not other things. What cause for this is there other than the nature of the entities themselves? If it is argued that the seed and the others are each individually capable and do not require mutual assistance, then for what purpose does the farmer sow the seed in soil that has been prepared and pour water upon it? If you say that they depend on one another so that from them—each individually—the capacity to produce a sprout is generated, [we reply: the seed was already produced by its own causes as something capable of generating the capacity to produce a sprout; what then is the use of earth, water, and so forth? Or, if it is incapable, then even with their presence, those factors would be of no avail, because the seed’s nature has not been abandoned. If you argue that the seed’s inherent inability to initiate a new state while remaining in its own place is obstructed by lightning, water, and so forth, then let it be so; however, non-production from the incapable remains, while production from the capable is difficult to obtain due to the absence of such a cause.

Nor is non-existence (*abhāva*) the existence of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); rather, the second moment is the non-existence of the preceding moment. As for the conventional usage [of "non-existence"], even though there is a distinction between the preceding and succeeding moments, there is no contradiction regarding their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Just as a jar might undergo cessation along with another jar that ceases at a different moment, so too it ceases along with that which has an independent cessation. This is because the second moment lacks the status of being a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for negating the first moment, since it merely possesses a particular excellence within its own specific characteristic.

If one understands the nature of things as momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), then from the arising of the cognition "the jar does not exist," there follows the cessation of the negation of its own production; its non-abiding is the non-stability of the entity, and its perception is the non-perception of the entity—this is logical because of their mutual contradiction.

Furthermore, if everything exists, there can be no momentariness of an entity, because for an entity that is perishable by subsequent cognition, there would be no necessity for another entity [to cause it] since it would depend on other causes.

And thus it is observed that the destruction of a produced jar occurs only after a long time due to the blow of a mallet or similar instruments; whereas the destruction of the jar, being itself a positive entity, would—according to your view—result from the production of shards or a void following the blow of the mallet, which is an objection not yet raised.

Since existence (sattā) and non-existence (asattā), bondage and liberation, and so forth, are measured within the wheel of the six categories, there is the possibility of the permanence of the existence of a variegated jar even when its prior resistance is destroyed; and since that [existence] is countered by the blow of a mallet or similar means, what aversion can there be toward the counteraction of an entity? Furthermore, because non-existence is perceived as a real thing just like existence due to its status as cause and effect, and because it is established by perception and other means of knowledge as having the nature of the negation of a real object.

If the nature of that which is to be known and expressed were such that even in the case of what is produced, its "existence" (bhāvatva) perishes—perishing because it is no longer perceived—then by the exclusion of a single entity established by valid cognition through its mutual difference from others, the investigation of universals (jāti) is also excluded. Furthermore, because the momentary destruction of each other [entities] constitutes the multiplicity of their own-nature, as in the case of an atom, whatever else is said is merely the appearance of an object; thus, the designation "the jar is perishable" would be applied metaphorically (upacaryeta) by both means, through the desire for those two distinct properties.

For this very reason, O Noble One, its manifestation does not occur in all places, nor does it have any inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Since there is no such thing as an inherent cause for its existence, where has an effect ever been seen to exist without a substratum? Thus, it is observed that [absence] does not inhere in a jar because the jar is absent; nor does it inhere in the ground, because both [the jar and its absence] would then be present simultaneously. How, then, is it perceived in a restricted location? It is solely due to the restriction of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). The nature of absence is such that when its own form is negated, it appears as if inherent in that which is conjoined with what is inherent (*saṃyuktasamaveta*), just as something inherent appears in that which is inherent. The qualifier is merely to be excluded (*apohya*); however, it possesses neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*), because it is devoid of both.

Thus, it is established that non-existence (*abhāva*) is the opposite of existence (*bhāva*), yet there is no contradiction in cognition; for even in the case of "non-snow" (*ahina*) and "snow" (*tuhiṇa*), there is a contradiction between them—namely, the absence of snow in non-snow and the presence of snow in snow—but this is a mutual contradiction, not a contradiction in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), because there is no contradiction with another [nature] qualified by its own form.

Furthermore, as for what was previously stated—that the so-called "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) does not depend on any other probans—that too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), being designated as "purely negative" (*kevalavyatirekin*); for if it were of such a nature, there would be no distinction of time.
This same fault applies even if it is based on the connection with conditions (*sāmagrī*).

For [the destruction] necessarily subverts the cause of passion; since that [destruction] has a fixed time, there is no increase of it at that time because it is the locus of passion. Furthermore, in the case of lightning and so forth, there are causes of destruction that have fixed times; since it is impossible to obstruct them always and in every way, one [cause] necessarily remains fixed. And at another time, by the very fact of its necessity, it is figuratively said to destroy the entity when it arises. This same analysis applies even to the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*). All this is observed for the sake of the object of qualities and so forth, even across different times, because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of what was previously perceived upon perceiving it again.

Surely this cognition does not illuminate the existence of an entity persisting through prior and subsequent times; let it be explained that this is not a single cognition, because the sense organ, being the cause, has a present object and does not apprehend a prior interval of time. Furthermore, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), born from a prior experience, is restricted to that specific object and does not touch upon a subsequent time. Nor is there any other single thing existing at that moment which could have both as its object and produce this cognition.

Furthermore, this single cognition [would have to be] distinct due to a difference in its own nature: for "this" is perceptibility, while "that" is non-perceptibility; and perceptibility and non-perceptibility are mutually contradictory. They cannot coexist in one [thing]; therefore, these two designations, having a dual nature, must refer to two distinct objects. To this we reply: first of all, from this cognition, a single reality delimited by prior and posterior time is indeed perceived. That this [perceived thing] is not its object is contrary to experience (*saṃvid-viruddha*).

Since that which consists of smell does not take a single object as its support, this consciousness must be accepted as having both objects as its domain due to its capacity for the manifestation of signs; and scholars postulate a cause even if it is not perceived, for the sake of producing an effect that is being experienced, but they do not deny an evident effect simply because the cause is not perceived—lest they be accused of denying the world, the two eyes, the self, and so forth.

Therefore, although each [factor] has as its object a specific aspect belonging to the side of a particular sense-faculty, nevertheless, this single effect called recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) will arise as something possessing causes; and by virtue of the capacity of both causes, it will come to have both as its objects and will attain the status of perception (*pratyakṣatā*), because it conforms to the capacities of both the object and the sense-faculty. Nor is it the case that what is incapable individually remains incapable even when combined, for even though the various painful sensations were individually non-existent, they are not perceived when there is merely their mutual proximity.

It is well-established that where the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is distinct, the effect must likewise be distinct; therefore, its status as direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) or indirect cognition (*aparokṣatā*), characterized by having an object that is either proximate or non-proximate, will not be contradictory. For this very reason, even though the sense organ does not exist at every moment, there is indeed direct perceptuality regarding a previous time, because it is an object of sensory cognition and because direct perceptuality is invariably concomitant with that alone. Now, [we turn to] the definition of the self (*ātman*) within the category of substance (*dravyatva*).

Even that [cognition] which has been established as having a delimited object and sense-faculty determines it only at the time of the preceding moment and so forth, and not at a future time, because of the absence of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) as a cooperative cause.
Nor does there arise the consequence of occasional occurrence for a single entity existing in both times; rather, for one who conceives of both times therein, it is conceptual in nature.

When an object is perceived, its nature as a "word" (or entity) is not differentiated by multiple qualifiers, just as Caitra’s nature as a "parasol" or a "book" is not distinct from his being a "parasol-and-book-man," nor is there any distinction when he is sequentially designated by two words for two different times. There is no difference in the case of one thing being delimited by both qualifiers, because the past state remains indistinguishable [from the present]. Therefore, recognition—which apprehends a single substantiality persisting through differences of place, time, and state—prevents the notion that the destruction of entities is inferred by means such as non-perception. If it is argued that this is merely a false perception, we say no, because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).

If it is argued that clear contradiction (*bādhaka*) is the obstacle here, [we reply]: when there is a correct cognition (*pratyavabodha*), the inference arises because its object is not sublated; however, if the cognition regarding that direction is itself sublated, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). But this does not apply to perception, because it is non-injunctive and non-additional. In cases such as a flame, there is no conflict, as perception has a general object while inference has a specific object; thus, the prohibition of the arising of inference by means of perception is sufficient. Whether the capacity for obstruction is established by perception or through the clear refutation [of the contrary], if that [inference] does not arise, it is due to a lack of awakening.

If it is argued that when one perceives "this is blue," there is also the perception of "this is momentary" because the nature of being blue and so forth are inseparable from its momentariness—such that there is no separate cognition of the latter, and thus when blueness is grasped, momentariness is also grasped due to the non-apprehension of any difference between them, and in this way the object is not established by another means of knowledge—then [we reply]: this is a groundless excellence of intellect, which explains and asserts something that is not produced by any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaja*). It is like a mirage; for the determination arising from the power of perception cannot be overturned by the establishment of firmness through any other perception, nor by any other means of valid cognition.

Alternatively, if at the time of the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), it is not determined by that very [awareness] that "this is blue, it is thus," then it would follow that there is self-awareness (*ātmajñāna*).

If it is argued that perceptual cognition, being momentary, may indeed discern its own form existing at the same time as itself, and may exclude what is external to that time, exclude what is amorphous and non-deviant from that time, and exclude what is connected to another time; and that it grasps its own momentariness as the state of persisting for only a single moment—this is merely striking wood with an axe.

Cognition does not even apprehend itself; how much less can it apprehend that which stands in the same time as itself? Or, if it were to apprehend it, [you would have to admit] that what did not exist previously will not exist later—thus, for one who accepts the apprehension of a time characterized by the destruction of present cognition and the arrival of future cognition, there is the exclusion of other times within the delimitation of the present time. This is because of the contradiction between two states of being (*bhāva*). However, the non-exclusion of that which relates to another time is like a woolen thread or a sprout; this is explained in the *Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā* regarding the principle of the one being many.

This has been explained by us almost in its entirety in the *Tattvaprabodha* and according to the method of the *Tattvasaṃvāda*; thus it is not elaborated upon here. Furthermore, even if all [moments] were reduced to the status of a courtesan (i.e., devoid of continuity), whose would the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) be? If it is argued that it belongs to the possessor of knowledge, that is untenable because a continuum (*santāna*) that is eternally obscured from such [possession] is impossible. Now, if transmigratory existence is not the connection with various bodies and so forth belonging to a single entity, but rather the non-interruption of the possession of knowledge, then that is not inconsistent even with momentariness.
That too is without substance;

for there is no evidence that the knowledge of fire arises from the knowledge of smoke, since fire is observed to arise not only from things of the same class [as itself] but also from things of a different class, such as from wood and grass.

Now, the established principle is that whatever possesses a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) whose presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are strictly concomitant with a certain thing, and which is subordinate to it, is the producer of its own kind. Furthermore, cognition possesses the excellence of having consciousness as its nature; however, this does not exist in the elements such as earth and so forth. Therefore, since it is established that this excellence of his is the cause for producing its own kind, it follows that the knowledge of the embryo must be preceded by another instance of knowledge, because if there were a deviation from the cause, the consequence would be the loss of the effect's regularity.
But even that is without substance.

Just as the excellence of fire’s burning power—characterized by its capacity to burn, its being produced by burning, and its nature as a burner—arises from its very essence as fire and not from its being of the nature of *uṣman* (heat), so too the excellence of the eyes and other senses in having consciousness as their essence does not allow for the postulation of a conscious cause [for them] originating from fire. Therefore, there will be no proof of a previous birth.

Furthermore, even the existence of another birth is not established; for there is no evidence that at the moment of death, one cognition must link itself to another cognition by means of the final cognition of the body. If it is argued that there is proof—namely, that whatever exists in a state of being a complete cause necessarily produces its effect, just as a seed in a state of being a complete cause for a sprout produces the sprout, and the final cognition is likewise in a state of being a complete cause—this is not so, because this is contradicted by the final moment of a flame and similar phenomena.

If it is argued that, because the final flame—characterized by the exhaustion of the oil, the wick, and so forth—is incomplete due to the deficiency of its causal conditions, [the analogy fails], then for the final cognition as well, it is unproven that the remaining causal conditions are deficient when one is afflicted by the indifference toward death; thus, the primary point—that there is no future world if momentariness is accepted—is established.
Having understood that [the soul] is bound, he stated another means of proof:
"That which inheres in the body. By this, the cessation of movement in the body—which is subject to effort—is inferred from its rapid attainment [of a new state].
It has been stated that the activity directed toward water and so forth, which serves the purpose of that [desire], is "effort" (āyāma) inherent in the body.

Furthermore, the activity and cessation directed toward the body as apprehended by the sense of hearing, which serve the purpose of that [desire] and are capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, constitute "effort.

Here, "beneficial" (hita) is pleasure and "harmful" (ahita) is pain; their "attainment and avoidance" mean the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful. The inclusion of cognition, perception, and volitional effort is due to their being pervaded by the constant presence of these two [attainment and avoidance].
The statement of an illustration regarding the activity of a chariot:

[The movement of the body] is preceded by effort, because it is a specific action, like the action of a chariot; or, [the body] possesses that which exerts effort, because it is a substance characterized by specific action, like a material object. Furthermore, through the medium of the movement of its constituent parts by means of the wind, there occurs the activity of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful.
"And by means of breath, etc."—it should be understood that one possessing effort (the self) is inferred by means of breath and so forth.

By the phrase "by means of breath, etc.," there is an inclusion of the various types of evidence from the *Sūtra* (Nyāya-sūtra 3.1.18–24), namely: inhalation and exhalation, the movement of the life-force (*jīvana*), the movement of the mind, the modifications of the sense organs, and pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, all of which are marks (*liṅga*) of the self.
He demonstrates that the vital breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*) serve as a mark [of the Self] by means of a question: "In what way? He says, "contained within the body.

This wind, which cannot be obtained from any other source, is seen to perform an action contrary to its own nature—namely, the actions known as inhalation and exhalation—when it is modified as the two breaths called *prāṇa* and *apāna* while contained within the body.

Therefore, one who possesses effort and is encompassed by the body is inferred; for he impels the air through effort, otherwise there would be merely the state of being modified air. The example is like that of a bellows in operation. By the phrase "encompassed by the body," the fact that [the movement] is preceded by desire is shown, because the air is impelled by effort based on a desire for some purpose within the body, just as in the case of a bellows.
Therefore, it is determined by means of its two kinds of actions and so forth.
By the action of closing and opening [the eyes], and by smelling, the agent of the act of seeing is to be inferred.

The closing of the eye (*nimeṣa*) is the action that causes the conjunction of two things not previously joined; the opening of the eye (*unmeṣa*) is the action for the purpose of separation. By means of that action, the body's agent of seeing is inferred to be possessed of effort (*prayatnavat*).
"The opening and closing of the eyes of the Seer (Īśvara) are pervaded by the effort of the wind and are restricted for the purpose of turning the eyelids.
By this, he declares [the Seer's] dependence upon will.
The body is controlled by the effort of the agent, because it is conjoined with a substance whose opening and closing of the eyes are dependent on will, just like the Seer.
He describes the sequence of the signs of life:
"of the body," [it is said];
"growth" occurs at every stage.

Furthermore, because the body and the food are the causes for the plurality of those two [growth and nourishment], and because they are subject to chance, it is inferred that there is one who possesses effort.

The growth and nourishment of the body are produced by one who possesses effort, because they consist of the conjunction of the body with food that undergoes growth, just like the growth and nourishment of a house through its conjunction with food.
If it is argued that there is an inconclusiveness (vyabhicāra) due to growth and so forth occurring through rain and the like, [we reply] that even those are created by the Lord (Īśvara).

But bulls and the like do not possess the nature of space (*khātman*), because it is impossible for that which is incapable of pervading [space] during the day to have a connection with its own self at night.
By this, he introduces the sequence based on the mark of arrival (*āgati*).
He does so by means of the passage beginning with "the desired" (*abhimata*).

The desired object is that which is perceived by the power of representation (*vijñapti*). When there is a cause for its arousal, such as the eye and so forth, the mind—denoted by the term "mind" (*manas*)—is conjoined with it through that [cause] as its instrumental condition (*nimitta*).

Just as a lamp shines within houses or in various places, so too, from the movement of this body, an agent who possesses effort (*prayatnavat*) is inferred; he is the mover and the door-keeper of the mind.

The mind is impelled by one who possesses effort, because it performs an action caused by a connection with a desired object, like a stone held in the hand of a door-keeper. However, even when impelled by a substance or other factors, a connection may occur with something undesired.

Immediately after the arising of a visible form (*rūpa*) within the range of the visual faculty, a transformation of another sense-organ, the gustatory faculty, is observed through the sequential pursuit of taste (*rasa*). Therefore, let there exist a single substratum (*dravya*) distinct from the substances [of the qualities], which is inferred as the locus of both color and taste. This is the cognition of the sense-object, which is not [merely] the two [qualities] themselves.

What is being said? Upon seeing the form of some liquid fruit, there arises a desire for its taste due to the recollection of that taste previously experienced as concomitant with it; from that desire, an effort arises which, depending on the conjunction of the self and the mind, produces a modification in the gustatory faculty. This modification of the gustatory faculty is inferred—like the throwing of water by a branch—and would not occur if the sense-faculty itself were consciousness. Furthermore, in perception, the object is restricted; since there is no recollection of taste upon seeing a form when the concomitance of color and taste has not been previously perceived, yet a modification of the object does occur, there must therefore be some distinct entity other than the sense-faculty which, having seen the form, recollects the taste.

If it is argued that [the soul] will exist through efforts inherent in the body, we say no; for since the body is established as distinct [from the soul] even in the cases of children, the elderly, and those who have fainted, it would follow that one could not remember what was experienced in childhood during old age.
Furthermore, the Person (puruṣa) is inferred not only by the previously mentioned reasons, but also by conch-sounds, pain, desire, aversion, and so forth.

This is because pleasure and the like—which are the objects of the cognition "I am happy" or "I am miserable"—are shown to be the causes of multiple cognitions, such as the grasping of the tip of a goad, the movement toward restraint, and the single act of cognition, as is perceived in the awareness that "pleasure and the like belong to the object of the cognition of the tip of the goad."

If it is argued that the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) regarding the body does not extend to another's body because it lacks the power [to do so] that it possesses over one's own body, we say no, for this leads to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

If the notion of "I" regarding the body were the cause [of its application] in one's own body, it would likewise apply to other bodies; however, it is not perceived to be so, just as the notion of a "pot" and the like applies to one's own body but not to the bodies of others.

If there were even the cognition "I am," it would not be a cognition of the self, because [the self] does not function as a remainder [of the body]. However, regarding the distinction created by the differentiation between self and other, the cognition produced by that [distinction] is not due to the body being the self; for if the body were the self, [the cognition] would not exist even when [the body] is internally perceived. Therefore, it is not due to the sense organs being the self, because the sense organs are beyond the reach of the senses, and because this [self] would otherwise result in being perceptible through the non-perception of signs or words. Consequently, pleasure and the like are also not objects belonging to the body or the sense organs.

However, that which is inferred is its very nature: an indivisible state described in the treatises on happiness as the arising of pleasure, the cessation of pain, and so forth. This is directly experienced by every embodied being within themselves, yet it is not perceived [as residing] in the body or the senses; thus it has been stated that pleasure and the like do not have those as their objects. He states another argument: "Because they exist in specific locations" (*pradeśavṛttitvāt*). It is observed that pleasure and the like possess location-specific cognition, as seen in such expressions as "there is pleasure in my foot" or "there is pain in my hand."

Furthermore, because there is an absence of being perceivable by the body and the senses, and because their specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) do not occur as pervasive occurrences (*vyāpyavṛtti*), pleasure and the like are not specific qualities of the body and the senses, since they are pervasive occurrences.

Those which are specific qualities of the body and the senses are observed to be pervasive occurrences, such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; however, pleasure and the like are not pervasive occurrences in that manner. Therefore, they are not qualities of the body or the senses—this is a negative inference (*vyatirekī*).

The sound that becomes a quality (*guṇa*) of that which is perishable, non-abiding, designated by name, and has reached the range of the sense of hearing, is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because it arises from the manifestation of that [name]. Furthermore, pleasure and the like are not qualities of the body or the senses, because they deviate from the rule; by contrast, visible form and the like serve as the illustrative examples. Moreover, this reason [of being perceived] is not a valid probans for proving excellence in the qualities of the senses, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of sound, which is a quality of the ear.

For this reason as well, pleasure and the like are not qualities of the body or the sense organs, because they are not perceived by the external senses. The observed course regarding the qualities of the body and the sense organs is that those which are not perceived by the external senses—such as gravity and so forth—are distinct from those which are perceived by the external senses, such as color and so forth; however, pleasure and the like are different from both categories. Therefore, they are not qualities of those [two]. Since their status as qualities of the body and the sense organs has been refuted, it is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that they are qualities of the self (*ātman*).

Now, it may be argued that pleasure and pain are modifications (*vikāra*), and thus cannot belong to the eternal self (*ātman*). Even if they did occur, the self would not cease to be eternal, because there is no falling away from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the self through conjunction, disjunction, or destruction. For an eternal entity, modification consists in the destruction of its own nature or the production of another nature; however, the cessation of one quality and the production of another quality is certainly not a falsity [of the substance]. So what is produced for this eternal self by the occurrence of pleasure and pain?
Their experience regarding their own objects.
When the experience of pleasure and pain exists, what benefit could there be for this [self] which possesses neither excellence nor deficiency?
This very thing is the benefit to the self and this alone is its excellence: that in its presence there is the state of being an experiencer of pleasure and pain.
The same applies to the word "I" as well.

Just as the self is inferred through pleasure and so forth, it is likewise inferred by the word "I" (*ahaṃ*). In both worldly and Vedic usage, the word "I" is employed in connection with the self; however, it is not a qualifier of its attributes, nor is it logical for its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) to be the denoted object, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.
As it has been said:
"No word ever denotes itself."
Therefore, that Self is what is to be sought after.
Now, one might object: "Could this [word 'Self'] not be a designator of earth and the other elements? To this he replies:
"Because of its distinction from the words for earth and so forth."
Whatever word expresses the same object as another word is placed in grammatical apposition with it, as in "the substance is earth.

However, the word "I" lacks such co-referentiality (samānādhikaraṇatva) with words that denote earth and so forth, because expressions such as "I am earth" or "I am water" do not occur; therefore, this [word "I"] does not have earth and the like as its object. But surely, this [word "I"] is seen to have the body as its object, as in "I am fat"?
No;

for there is the usage [of such expressions] as "I know" and "I remember. Furthermore, the body's status as the substratum of knowledge and memory has been refuted. Therefore, the application of that term [the word "I"] to the body is by way of secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), based on its being an auxiliary to the self, just as there is the designation "this is my excellent servant" with respect to a servant.
This being established, he describes the qualities of the self with the words "And its qualities," and so forth.
He demonstrates that the impressions (saṃskāra) follow upon the cognition of the intellect and other faculties within the self.
Regarding the section on the marks of the self (*ātmaliṅga*), it is established that [the qualities] beginning with cognition (*buddhi*) and ending with effort (*prayatna*) are the marks.
By the phrase "the section on the marks of the self," he indicates the sūtra beginning with "vital breaths, inhalation, exhalation, etc. [NS 3.1.28].
This is because merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are not causes for the qualities belonging to another self, due to the restriction [of causality to one's own continuum].
This is established by the statement: "Because the qualities of one self are not the cause of [the qualities] of another self.

In order to determine the investigation of the effect—that a substance-quality residing in one person produces a quality in another following its own cessation—this was well-stated by the author: "Because the qualities of one self are not the cause of the qualities of another self.
This is the meaning of it:

Because qualities belonging to one self, such as number (*saṅkhyā*) and so forth, lack causality with respect to the qualities of another self, such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, it is illogical for the intellect (*buddhi*) and its attributes (*dharma*), which reside in one place, to initiate [effects] in another.

By this [argument], it is established that merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are qualities of the self; otherwise, their status as the means to pleasure and so forth could not be explained through their connection with the self.
As for latent impression (*saṃskāra*), it arises from memory.

From the conjunction of the self and the mind, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) brings about memory and pleasure. Regarding memory of what was previously experienced, experience itself cannot be the cause because it has long since perished; nor can the absence of experience be the cause, as an absence, being devoid of any specific excellence (*niratiśaya*), cannot account for the diversity of memories such as those of Pradyumna and others. Anticipating this objection, it is stated: "Therefore, some excellence must have been produced in the self by the experience, from which memory arises"—this is the postulation of the latent impression.

However, for those who claim that memory is the cause [of recognition] even in the absence of an experience of non-destruction, it would follow that a light, a tree, or the like, once destroyed, could still serve as the means for attaining fruits such as heaven; thus, the necessity of performing ritual acts (*anuṣṭhāna*) would be undermined.
The statement regarding "distinction" (*vyavasthā*) refers to number.
The meaning is that by establishing distinction through various substances, the proof of plurality is established, thereby demonstrating the non-identity of the self (*ātman*).

Now, what is this established order that results from a plurality of selves, such that there is no recollection of [experiences like] knowledge, pleasure, and so forth? For if there were a single self, then just as one remembers what was experienced during childhood upon reaching adulthood—thinking, "I had pleasure" or "I had pain"—everyone who has entered into another body would likewise remember it;

yet this is not the case, as stated by those who have experienced it. Therefore, there are distinct selves for each body. Just as all space is one, yet the distinction in the perception of sound is established due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the ear-cavity, so too is it with the individual soul (*jīva*) due to its [apparent] difference.

If it is argued that the distinction between experiences and so forth arises from the difference in bodies, this is a mistaken presentation. For, just as there is a restriction [of experience] for each individual due to the specific arrangement of the ear-cavities—which are the causes of perceiving sound and which possess the necessary causal conditions—the restriction in the apprehension of sound follows from the fixed location of the soul within them. However, in the doctrine of a single self (*ekātmya*), since the aforementioned restrictions would apply to the body as a whole, in the absence of bodily distinctions, what basis could there be for the restriction in the arising of pleasure and pain? This is because even the mind and sound would be common to all.

However, for one who holds that there are multiple selves (*nānātmānaḥ*), although all selves are connected to all [bodies] in reality, experience is not common to all. Whichever body is produced by the karma of a particular self, that body alone is the locus of experience for that self, not for all others. Furthermore, even though [the body] is capable [of being used by all], that which was performed with a particular body belongs only to that [self], not to another. Thus, the restriction regarding other bodies arises from the restriction of subsequent karma; this process is beginningless (*anādi*). Now, suppose the following view is held:
Even though the supreme self (paramātman) is one, it must be admitted that there is mutual difference among the individual selves (jīvātman).
This is incorrect; for if there were difference from the supreme self, the doctrine of non-duality (advaita) would be destroyed.

Furthermore, this contradicts the reasoning that the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) are not distinct selves, based on the scriptural statement: "Having entered by means of this living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me evolve names and forms.

If it is argued that the distinction between the individual soul and the supreme self is created by ignorance (*avidyā*), then whose is this ignorance? Is it Brahman’s, or rather that of the individual souls?
It cannot belong to Brahman, because Brahman is by nature pure and enlightened, and thus has no connection with ignorance.
The statement that "ignorance has the individual soul as its locus" is intended to avoid the fault of mutual dependence:
namely, that the differentiation of souls is caused by ignorance, while ignorance has the differentiated souls as its locus.

If it is argued that the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) is beginningless because the soul is supported by ignorance, [we reply: this is untenable, as the distinction between the individual manifestations of ignorance and the soul is like that of the seed and the sprout; there is no ultimate self-nature (*ātmābhāva*) in their mutual relationship. Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the individual manifestations of the seed and the sprout, they stand in a relationship of mutual causality. However, the individual soul is one and the same throughout all millions of cycles of existence (*bhavacakra*). For one who has been born in various wombs—such as mother, son, grandson, and so forth—there is a similarity in the specific manifestation [of the soul], and through the experience of particular foods in those various births, there arises a sequence of inference based on the specific foods consumed in previous lives. Thus, the attainment of the body for the enjoyment of experiences, such as the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), results from the distinction between the soul and ignorance, while the distinction between the soul depends upon that [ignorance]; thus, they are mutually causal.

If it is argued that because the individual soul (*jīva*) is also beginningless and eternal, it is non-different from Brahman—and therefore, based on the authority of such scriptural passages as "Everything shines after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined," it must be said that this entire universe, which is the beginningless and eternal reality of Brahman, merely appears within all bodies—then [we reply]: if that were so, the established distinction of the four orders of life (*cāturāśramya*) would be undermined, and the doctrine of the plurality of selves (*nānātmānaḥ*) would be rendered obsolete. Thus, the view that the primary non-difference [of the self] has a secondary (figurative) meaning is the direction of our argument.

Furthermore, even on the view that there are multiple selves, there is no total cessation of *saṃsāra* at the end when all have been liberated in succession, because there is no exhaustion of the infinite [selves], as they are neither more nor less than one another.
As the venerable Vṛttikāra has said:
"For this very reason, while the wise are being liberated, [the world] remains continuous."
Even in the Brahmakhaṇḍa, because living beings are infinite and numerous;
Mutual non-excess and non-deficiency are appropriate in the case of that which possesses measurement;
however, in an immeasurable reality, their impossibility is certain.
Thus, it is indeed distinct.

From such statements as "the selves are established as manifold," distinctness is known by the learned because it follows the number [of the objects]; thus, the substrata are delimited by distinctness. Likewise, from the statement "and the self," it follows that it possesses the dimension of the supremely great (*paramamahat-parimāṇa*).

Because of its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*), the Self is great and similar to space; from such conformable statements, since the Self is all-pervasive like space, it is accepted by the learned as having the dimension of the supremely great (*paramamahat-parimāṇa*).

Furthermore, the all-pervasiveness of the Self is understood from the statement that it exists even above the unseen water and the unseen fire, for those two are indeed produced by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

Furthermore, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in that [soul] cannot be the cause of those two [pleasure and pain] if it were not perceived [in them], for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Nor is it possible for an unseen force experienced by the self to have a connection with external substances; thus, it follows that its presence everywhere occurs through its connection with its own substrate.
Consequently, the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the self—characterized by its connection with all corporeal substances—is established.

If it is argued that combustion occurs from fire by its very nature (*svabhāva*) and not from the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), then we must ask: what is this so-called "nature" in the effect? Is it fire-ness, or the capacity to burn, or some specific visible quality? If it were the first, then combustion would occur even in a mass of iron, since that too possesses fire-ness. If, on the other hand, the nature is defined as being produced from a specific heat, then this combustion would not occur in lightning and the like, which are produced without such [heat] and are impermanent. Alternatively, if the opponent’s position is that there is some nature belonging to fire and fuel—such as exists in wood or lightning—by means of whose continuity combustion is observed, then what is the cause for this aversion [to our view]?

For that [motion] whose sequence has gravity, velocity, or effort as its cause—such as the upward throwing of hands by human effort—the sequence does not have gravity and so forth as its cause, because of their absence and because the effect is contrary to them.

Therefore, it is logical that in these cases, such as the upward movement of water, the horizontal movement of wind, and so on, the sequence is produced by the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self (*ātman*), since gravity and other such causes are absent; this is just like the sequence in the upward throwing of hands produced by human effort.
Because pleasure and the like belong to all fields (*kṣetra*), there is conjunction [with the self].

Since qualities of the self such as pleasure and so forth are produced by conjunction with the mind, conjunction in the self is established; for that which effects pervasion cannot be a non-inherent cause.
Because it is the destroyer of that [conjunction], there is disjunction. Regarding this, others say that the mind is black.
Because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the cause of destruction, passion (*rāga*) is established as being momentary.

This is because, since the self (*ātman*) and the mind (*manas*) are eternal, there is an absence of the cause of destruction, namely "destruction by departure" (*apāya-vināśa*). Furthermore, while the self remains eternal, for one who perceives the self as eternal, there arises attachment to the objects of pleasure and aversion toward the objects of pain; from these arise activity and cessation, from which come merit and demerit, and from those comes *saṃsāra*. Thus, liberation (*anirvāha*) is not achieved.

If it is argued that, since there is no self (*nairātmya*), "I" do not exist at all, and thus it cannot be specified whose suffering it is, then in the absence of any activity and so forth for one who is free from passion and hatred, the undertaking [of action] would be impossible—this is not so; for even in one who perceives a permanent self, passion and aversion do not cease upon seeing the defects of sense-objects, and thus their arising occurs. This is the point.
Because of its association with the mind, [the self is established].
Even when the self, the sense organs, and their objects are present, since we observe the non-arising of cognition, pleasure, and so forth, another instrument is inferred.

Because hearing, seeing, and other [perceptions] are observed to arise [successively], and because there must be something that perceives pleasure and so on which are not grasped by the external senses, there exists an internal instrument (antaḥkaraṇa).
Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
From the statement that effort and cognition do not occur simultaneously, the oneness of each individual body is established;
distinctness is likewise established for this very reason.
Because it expresses the state of being that [substance], it possesses atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*).
Because it expresses the proximity and distance (*aparatva-paratva*) of that [substance], it possesses conjunction and disjunction (*saṃyoga-vibhāga*).
Because it is mobile, it possesses priority and posteriority (*paratva-aparatva*) as well as mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
Because it is not composed of atoms (*aścadhatvāt*), it is not a substance (*adravyatvam*). Because it possesses action (*kriyāvattvāt*), it is incorporeal (*amūrtatvam*).
Because it would entail having a common physical form (*sādhāraṇavigrahavattvaprasaṅgāt*), it is not a substance (*adravyatvam*).
(7) It is for the sake of another because it is an instrument;
it is a substance because it possesses qualities;
and it is characterized by impurity and so forth due to the influence of effort and the grasping of what is perceived. (8)

Thus ends the category of substance (*dravya*) in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*. Having first described the self (*ātman*) because of its association with effort (*prayatnatva*), he next states, for the purpose of defining the mind (*manas*): "The mind is that which possesses the property of mindness (*manastva*). The explanation is as before.

The universal called "mind-ness" (*manastva*) is postulated because individual minds (*manovyakti*) exist as similar; for it is observed that when individuals possess a common form, there exists another universal, as in the case of jars and other objects where there is the property of having a common form.
