Since the mind possesses such a universal due to its nature as an individual mind, there is a connection with such a universal. Thinking that its definition and proof are necessary while the mind is not yet understood, he states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
"When there is contact between a real self, the sense organs, and their objects..."

First, regarding the self: although there is a simultaneous conjunction of all the sense organs with their objects, and even though the sense organs are present, a sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) occurs; nevertheless, while one object is being perceived, other objects do not give rise to the sixfold cognition and so forth. It is observed that these arise upon the cessation [of the perception of the first]. From this observation, an instrument (*karaṇa*) other than the conjunction of the self, the sense organ, and the object is inferred, because through its presence the production of cognitions occurs, and through its absence they do not. Thus, even when there is a conjunction of the self, the sense organ, and the object, the production of the effect depends upon another instrument.

Even though it possesses its own form (*svarūpa*), because it does not produce an effect [on its own], it is like the principle of reality (*tattva*) and so forth; and that which serves as the meaning of its constituent parts is the mind (*manas*).

What is the proof here that at the time of the perception of one object, there exists a contact between the sense organ and another object which is the basis for that perception? [The proof is: because they are seen to be under the control of the sense organs, at the time of perceiving a visible object, odors and other qualities are also brought into contact with the nose and other organs, because they are situated in proximity to those [organs], just like the perceiver and other factors. He states yet another proof:
"Because it manifests the object upon the completion of the auditory process.
Memory is directly produced by a sense organ because it is a form of knowledge, like the knowledge of seeing and so forth; yet it is not visual.

Since the sense organs such as the ear are external gateways, memory is observed to arise only when there is activity of the ear and other senses. Therefore, that sense organ which is the instrument of this [memory] is the mind (*manas*).

The inference of another instrument is not based solely on the reason previously stated; rather, it is also because of the existence of pleasure (*sukha*) and other internal objects—which are assisted by the external senses and are fit for compassion—that that [instrument] is inferred. Thus he says: "By the external senses...

The cognition of pleasure and so forth is produced by a sense organ, because it is a direct perception (*aparokṣapratīti*), just like the cognition of the self (*ātman*); and that which is that sense organ is the mind (*manas*).

If it is argued that pleasure and so forth are of the nature of cognition because the eyes and other senses function therein as their instrumental causes (*adhiṣṭhāna-kāraṇa*), and that these pleasant sensations are apprehended by means of another cause, we say no; for if pleasure and pain were essentially cognition, it would follow that there is no distinction between them.

Furthermore, there is a mutual distinction between these two [pleasure and pain], for even though they share the nature of being forms of cognition, their respective forms as pleasure and pain are mutually contradictory. Nor can these two have a nature non-different from consciousness (*vijñāna*), because they arise from the form of a specific instance of knowledge (*jñānavyakti*). Therefore, since pleasure and pain arise due to the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and follow a sequence of other suitable denotations, the lamp is not a valid example for self-cognition (*svavedana*). If it is argued: "This is not so; for consciousness (*bodhi*) is known by the person and made known by the eye, and knowledge is its activity (*kriyā*). Yet, it does not itself act as its own cause, nor does it become both the object (*karman*) and the action (*kriyā*). Just as for the proponent of the Self (*ātmavādin*), the Self is the agent that illuminates its own qualities during its own perception, so too is knowledge the instrument (*karaṇa*) and so forth," We reply: No, because there is no contradiction. The state of being an object (*karmatva*) belongs to the Self insofar as it is the objective domain of the act of knowing; and because of its independence (*svātantrya*) in that very act, it possesses agency (*kartṛtva*). There is no contradiction in this statement regarding its independence. However, the states of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) and being an action (*kriyatva*) are mutually exclusive, as they belong to distinct entities—the cause and the effect—and there is no identity between them. For example, the lightning and the rising [of the sun] are distinct. Thus, [the lamp cannot serve as an analogy].

Thus, being caused by another (paraprayojyatā), being not caused by another (itaraprayojyatva), and being an agent (kartṛtva) are mutually contradictory; since these would rest upon the very nature [of the self], it is not logical for them to coexist as the Naiyāyikas maintain. Now, he states that the mind is not the instrument of cognition: "The reason is self-awareness (svasaṃvedana); rather, for that which has self-luminous nature, its very arising is self-awareness.
This too is now examined.

What is this manifestation? Is it of the object or of itself? If it is the manifestation of the object, then because that [manifestation] arises from the object, there would be the fault that the meditator does not perceive it within his own yoga, since the perception belongs to the object. If it is the manifestation of itself, then that very thing which is the object of manifestation is also the manifestation; thus, the identity of the action and its cause remains as before.
Nor is there any illustration to show that the very arising of a thing constitutes an action upon itself.

Even though, in establishing self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), one might argue that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the person are like a lamp and its light— such that when the lamp is manifesting, the objects are manifested by that manifestation, just as two jars are manifested by the light of a lamp, and color-forms (*rūpa*) and so forth are manifested by the light of cognition— therein, if cognition itself is intended to be the manifestation of the object, then the claim that "color-forms and so forth are manifested by that [cognition]" is unproven (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the sense-faculty (*indriya*). Furthermore, if the manifestation of the object is something other than cognition and not cognition itself, then there is a lack of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*), since a lamp, which is the producer of cognition, lacks the quality of being the manifestation of the object.
By this very [argument], the following point is answered: its self-consciousness is not the perception of the object;
for there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) of cognition itself.

Rather, in the seeing of an object, it is the arising of consciousness that occurs. Even when one does not doubt the cognition, the awareness of its mere arising is what they would call the "cognition" (*saṃvedana*) of the object.
If it is asked, "How can there be the cognition of one thing by another that is distinct from it?"—is it because a jar possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastusvabhāva*)?

This being the case, it is not so that everything is cognized, because [the cognition] arises through the restriction of its own causal capacity, having a nature determined by a specific object and being subject to a specific manifestation.

Others, however, say this: "When the visible object is manifest through conjunction with cognition, it is manifested because it has the nature of being manifest; and since the self is the locus of manifestation, it too is manifested, like a lamp or like sesame oil," thus they attempt to refine their position.
That too is incorrect.

When the cognition "the jar is" is perceived, there is no apprehension of the knower and the act of knowing; and when those two appear [in the form] "I know the jar," that consciousness is a mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) characterized by the knowledge of the knower and the knowledge of the object, but it is not an appearance resulting from the actual entry of the knower and the knowledge [into the cognition itself], because both are unperceived within the mind. Thus, when the mind is thus situated, one demonstrates its qualities.
By the words "its qualities" and so forth,
[the author] states that even the connection with qualities such as number belongs to the mind among its specific attributes;
he thus explains the inclusion of number.

By the words beginning with "prayatna" [the author] addresses the view that there is one mind per body; having refuted this single-minded position in the *Khaṇḍana*, the author of the Sūtras stated: "Because of the non-simultaneity of effort and the non-simultaneity of cognitions, there is one mind per body. By this, the oneness of the mind per body is established. If there were a plurality of minds, there would be simultaneous cognitions and efforts due to the multiplicity of conjunctions between the knower and the self; however, a sequence of cognitions is observed, because when one is occupied with another object, no other object is perceived, and once that occupation has ceased, it is perceived—thus, there is no simultaneity.

Thus, even regarding efforts (*prayatna*), the sequence [of cognitions] would otherwise be different, because for one who is striving in one place, activity in another is possible, and because simultaneous action occurs. Therefore, the mind (*manas*) is one. Indeed, when the reality is one, as in the case of the conjunction with the twenty-sixth principle (*tattva*), it is logical that there is only one cognition and only one effort. As for the perception of the diversity of actions, that is due to the nature of the momentary wind (*kṣaṇavāyu*), and not because of a Sāttvika simultaneity; rather, it is because the capacity of that very cause is inferred through the rapid succession of effects in a single location.

If this is so, then how is it that the Drāviḍa teachers have stated that "the appearance of multiple objects occurs simultaneously," and why do they maintain that their own body is impelled and sustained at once?
It is not so;

for in this case, there is no prohibition against a single cognition having multiple objects as its support through a process of synthesis (*saṅgraha*). However, when there is a distinction of cognitions (*buddhibheda*), there is no such simultaneous appearance, because each individual cognition is restricted to a single object.

Thus, just as a single cognition can have multiple objects due to a particular effort, so too there is no point that is untenable regarding the application of an effort that is not contradictory to its cause for the impelling and sustaining of the body.
Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) also exists here;
for it is established that separateness follows from number alone—this is the meaning.

Its distinctness is established by its own nature, just as [the distinctness of] space is established by its own nature; likewise, since it is designated in relation to the self, it is said that "the mind is atomic because of its state [of being so designated].
Therefore, it is proven that the mind has an atomic dimension.
This is because the properties of being an eternal substance and lacking spatial division (*vibhaktvābhāva*) are invariably concomitant with the dimension of an atom (*aṇuparimāṇatva*).
The absence of spatial division is established precisely by the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions;
for if the mind were all-pervading (*vibhu*), there would be simultaneity of cognitions regarding color and other objects in contact with the various locations of all the sense organs at once.

Now, if it is argued that when objects such as a jar and so forth—beginning with those possessing only one sense-organ—are simultaneously in contact with the eye through the impact of the mind, cognitions do not arise all at once because the contacts of the self, the senses, and the objects are simultaneous; and that therefore it must be postulated that the single conjunction of the self and the mind lacks the capacity to produce multiple cognitions at once—then this is equally applicable even if the mind is atomic. Therefore, even given its atomicity, a more reasonable position must be stated. That is now explained: [The opponent says: "If the mind were atomic, how could there be simultaneous cognitions when multiple objects are in contact with the senses? Since the contacts of the self, the senses, and the objects occur simultaneously, cognitions would arise all at once. To avoid this, one must assume that the single conjunction of the self and the mind lacks the power to produce multiple cognitions at once. [The author replies: This objection applies equally even if the mind is atomic. Therefore, even though the mind is atomic, a more logical explanation must be provided. Cognition of the self, the senses, and the mind arises from their mutual conjunction; in the absence of such mutual conjunction, there is no perception of the qualities of the self, such as knowledge, pleasure, and so forth, because of the absence of a non-conjunctive cause (*asamprayoga-kāraṇa*).

If the conjunction of the self and so forth were the non-inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) of knowledge, then knowledge would arise only when this [conjunction] exists, since it is asserted that the production of qualities occurs through the application of even a non-conjunctive cause acting upon a specific location. Furthermore, if the conjunction of the self and the sense organ were the non-inherent cause of the whole, there would be no production of auditory knowledge, because there is no conjunction of the self with the ear, which consists of space (*ākāśa*).

Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no perception in external regions due to the non-arising of auditory cognition; therefore, since the self-object conjunction and the self-sense-organ conjunction are not refuted as being non-inherent causes [of cognition], by the method of exhaustion (*pariśeṣa*), the self-mind conjunction is established as the non-inherent cause. Since this is not possible if the mind were all-pervading (*vyāpaka*), its atomicity (*aṇutva*) is established, just as it is for cognition, pleasure, and so forth. Moreover, because of its fiery nature (*taijasatva*), the mind possesses power (*śakti*); thus, it alone determines the purity of the mind. Now, by the expression "separateness of conjunction" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva*), both conjunction and disjunction are indicated.

Now, because it possesses conjunction and disjunction, is not inherent in sound, is produced by conjunction, and has conjunction with another body as its cause, the mind is established as a substance; it has been stated that it possesses disjunction from the previous body and conjunction with another body. Therefore, its conjunctions and disjunctions are proven. Furthermore, priority and posteriority and momentum are established through prior production.
Since there is no [other] object [of comparison], its corporeality is established; therefore, like a jar or similar objects, its possession of priority and posteriority is proven.
Its number is neither two nor many;

its number is one. Since the mind, while being distinct from the body, is the producer of cognitions regarding all objects—just like the self—it is established that it is not composed of substances of the same class [as those objects], precisely because its cognitions are diverse. Furthermore, because it possesses activity, it is corporeal.
Although this has been stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa regarding its corporeality due to the demonstration of its atomicity,
[it follows that] it would possess the nature of a substance (dravyatva) because of the consequence of having both common and specific qualities.
Furthermore, if the mind were the body, this body would become a common locus of experience for all.
But this is not the case;

for, in accordance with the conceit of being one, its activity and cessation are observed at all times. Therefore, although the mind has been refuted as being atomic and conscious, this is stated again on account of [the opponent's] illumination. Having established that it is not the Self, he says:
"Because it is formless, it is an atom"—
this means it is the instrument for another's experience.
Because it possesses qualities, it is a substance, like earth and the other elements.
It should be understood that [the movement] is preceded by the operation of grasping through effort and so forth.

In the case of movements preceded by desire and aversion, as well as those preceded by the life-force (*jīvana*), it should be understood that what is grasped by effort moves swiftly from one place to another; likewise, what is grasped by the non-swift [life-force] moves swiftly from the body at death to another body.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion. [This concludes] the method of investigating the two kinds of pure logic (*nyāya-mīmāṃsā*).
It serves as the cause for the clear cognition of the various substances belonging to the shrines.
Thus ends the section on the category of substance (*dravya-padārtha*) in the *Nyāyakandalī* commentary on the *Padārthadharmasaṃgraha* by Bhaṭṭa Bhīmā.
Now follows the definition of the category of quality (guṇa).

All qualities, beginning with color (rūpa) and so forth, possess the properties of being qualities, being distinct from others, residing in substances, being devoid of further qualities, and being devoid of action.
Oṃ, salutations to Bhuśuṇḍi, the bestower of knowledge, who reclines upon the serpent Śeṣa as his couch,
and who brings great bliss to the breasts of Lakṣmī.
Having explained the category of substance (*dravya*), he speaks in order to define qualities (*guṇa*):
"of the qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth.
The term "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) is a generality (*sāmānya*); the connection with that [generality] belongs to the qualities—this indicates their mutual association.
This is also a statement of the dissimilarity [of the subject] with other categories:
the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) residing in color and the rest is apprehended individually by one who possesses the Ratnacintāmaṇi jewel.

As for the fact that it is not apprehended at first because it is distinct from action (*karman*) and so forth, even then, since there is the possibility of similarity with those who contemplate the self independently [of qualities], the mention of "the qualities such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth" is merely a statement of their essential nature. The word "all" is intended to indicate pervasion. Their "residing in substance" (*dravyāśritatva*) means being subordinate to substance; this is a statement of their mere property (*dharma*), and not for the sake of grammatical non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), because they can exist in relation to both substance and action.

In the pure [substance], there is the state of being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), which is the state of being free from qualities. This is because, within the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the qualities themselves—that is, in their own selves—there is no presence of other qualities, nor do they originate them; for instance, among color and the rest, no further color or the like is perceived, and there would otherwise be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, the conventional usage of terms such as "the color of the cow" or "the sound of the cloth" occurs only when the substance exists, and is thus merely figurative (*upacāra*).
Number and the other categories do not reside in the substratum of color and the rest, because they are qualities, just like color and the rest themselves.
He states another essential characteristic:

"the state of being devoid of action" (*niṣkriyatvam*). If it is argued that when a substance moves, its qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth also move, [the answer is] no; for there is an absence of action in space (*vyoman*) and other such things despite their being impelled with great force by something possessing momentum, whereas action exists in sound and the like. Thus, even though corporeal things are devoid of action apart from the moon (i.e., as a general rule), the cessation of action in qualities such as color is established through the power of the relationship between the substratum and the superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), despite the presence of corporeality. Now, therefore, follows the determination of the similarities and differences among the three groups of qualities.

Regarding these, the one called Rāmacandra says: "Just as existence itself does not go to the substratum by means of the action of the substratum—because if it did, it would follow that when the jar moves, the [universal] 'thrown-ness' (kṣiptatva) would also move."
Color, taste, smell, touch, priority, posteriority, weight, fluidity, viscidity, and velocity are the qualities of corporeal substances.
To demonstrate their mutual similarity and dissimilarity, he says:
"Form," and so forth.
These are the qualities of material things alone, not of immaterial things.

For instance: in earth and the other three [elements], there are the qualities of number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, and velocity; in mind, all these except for color-form (rūpa); in taste, all except for color-form; in earth and water, fluidity; in earth, water, and fire, viscidity; and in earth alone, odor.
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, and sound are the qualities of the formless.
He describes the formless qualities:
"Intellect, pleasure," and so forth.
Intellect and the others, up to volition (*bhāvanā*), are the qualities of the self.
Sound is the quality of space.
Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction are qualities belonging to both [substances].
Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction are qualities common to both; they are qualities of both the corporeal and the incorporeal.
Conjunction and disjunction have as their effects two qualities each; they are dependent upon more than one substance.
Conjunction, disjunction, number, duality, action, and so forth are dependent upon multiple substrata.
For example, just as disjunction is distinct from conjunction and is not non-dual [in its occurrence], such is their dependence on multiple substrata.
Likewise, this applies mutually to the cognition of duality and the rest.
However, those terms included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), such as "threefoldness" (*tritva*) and the like, depend upon many [entities] as the case may allow;
furthermore, based on the etymological derivation that the word "many" (*aneka*) means "that which is not one," it is common even to pairs and other such groups.
Sound is that which is perceivable by a single sense organ.
Sound is perceptible by a single sense organ.

The term "sounds" refers to dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, existing only as individual manifestations up to the ultimate atoms; however, sound does not exist pervasively in both [the cause and the effect] like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), meaning that it does not reside in dyads and the like in the same manner as conjunction does.

Color, taste, smell, touch, priority, posteriority, weight, fluidity, viscidity, velocity, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, and sound are the qualities common to both [substances]. [The author] defines the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*):

"color, taste, smell, etc. A *viśeṣa* is that which distinguishes; those qualities which serve that purpose are the specific qualities, such as color and the rest. For these indeed distinguish their own substratum from others, whereas number and the other qualities do not, because they lack such a distinguishing character (*viśeṣa*). However, whatever distinction exists among them should be understood as functioning for the sake of distinguishing their own substratum.
Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, occasional fluidity, and momentum are the general qualities.
Number and the other general qualities are qualities that reside in their own substratum and in the substrata of that substratum; they do not reside in the specific substrata of their own substratum.
Therefore, the dimension of those qualities does not serve as the determinant of atoms. No.
Because it is common to other kinsmen;
if the effort toward the substance of power is a specific quality, then by that [effort] there is occasional fluidity.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are each perceivable by a single external sense organ.

Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are each perceivable by one external sense organ; the external organs are the eye and so forth, which are like the spokes of an external wheel, and by them, form and the other objects are apprehended individually.
Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, fluidity, viscidity, and speed are perceptible by two sense organs.
Number and the others, ending with velocity, are perceptible by two sense organs.
Just as the cognition "this is two" occurs through the eye, it also occurs through the tactile organ; thus, among the pairs beginning with number, they are perceptible by both.
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort, however, are apprehended by the internal organ.
From cognition (*buddhi*) up to effort (*prayatna*), those [qualities] are graspable by the internal organ; the meaning is that they are perceived by the mind (*manas*).
Some maintain that cognition is inferable and is grasped by the instrument of knowledge (*jñānakaraṇa*);
that is incorrect.

Because there is no inferential mark (*liṅga*), [the soul] is not established through a faulty means. An external mark is not [the proof], because it is fallible. If it is argued that "being known" (*jñāteyatva*) is the mark, then if [this] consists in being the agent of knowledge or being the object of knowledge, it is not cognized when the knowledge itself is being cognized as belonging to the self, because the cognition of the relation and the cognition of the probandum are distinct. Furthermore, what specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) could serve as its mark? Even for a specific quality such as "markness," its status as a cause of inference would depend upon its being known.

Now, you might think that immediately after its own arising, a certain state called "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) is produced in the object by cognition, just as "cookedness" is produced in rice grains by cooking; and since this is a property of the object, it is apprehended simultaneously with the arising [of the cognition].
That is incorrect.
[For] the investigation of the nature of the object is distinct from the investigation of the nature of the cognition.
It is not so.

For while the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) is inferred solely through the absence of such-and-such a cognition, manifestness (*pratyakṣatā*) is not perceived in this way. Furthermore, this quality of being immediate and the fitness for the linguistic usage of "cognition" and so forth—these too are merely relations to a cognition; they are not further properties of a property (*dharmottara-dharma*). Just as when an object is known there is "known-ness" (*jñātatā*), so too when "known-ness" itself is known, there would have to be another "known-ness," leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is argued that this "known-ness" is self-luminous (*svaprakāśā*), then that is simply an aversion to the nature of cognition.
In reality, that which is qualified by the three times and is otherwise unperceivable is perceived through cognition as being uninterrupted by the present time.

Some maintain that the state of being uninterrupted by the present within the triad of times is "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), and because it is produced by cognition, it serves as its inferential mark (*liṅga*).
That too is of no consequence.

For the state of being uninterrupted in the present is simply the non-distinction from the present time; and this [temporal character] of the object is inherent to it and is not produced by cognition, but rather is perceived.
Even he who maintains that cognition is to be inferred from the "cognizedness" (*vedyatā*) of the object should be questioned as follows:
Does this "cognizedness" inhere in the self or in the object? It cannot be in the self, because consciousness (caitanya) has been denied there.

If it inheres in the self, then what other cognition is there that belongs to the self? If its cause is characterized by the activity of the knower, then is that [activity] eternal or non-eternal? If it is non-eternal, then its cause must also be stated at the time of its production. If you say that the contact of the object, the sense organ, and so forth—the conjunction of the knower and the mind—is its cause, then let that same causal complex be the cause for the production of the cognition of the object; what is the use of another inference?

Now, if it is understood that this [consciousness], being eternal, produces the occasional cognition of an object by means of occasional auxiliary factors such as the contact between the sense organ and the object, then we reply: the production of the cognition of an object is established from the very collection of causes pertaining to the internal self (the *adhyātma*); thus, the postulation of that [external consciousness] is useless, since the comprehension of the object, the comprehension of reality, and worldly discourse are all accomplished through the cognition of the object itself.

Now, it might be argued: "Cognition produced by objects, sense organs, and so forth, inheres in the self alone; for if the self were not composed of innate knowledge, then, given its insentience, the inherence of cognition would occur in the sense organs and other such causes due to their specific nature as causal factors. To this we reply: that is not so.

Since the restriction [of cognition] is established by the very nature of things (*svabhāvaniyama*), just as threads, although they are not cloth, possess the inherence of cloth in them due to the restriction of their genus as "thread" and not in husks or other things—so too, because of the restriction of the genus "self" (*ātmatva*) in selves which consist of consciousness, there will be a restriction of the inherence of knowledge [in them]. By this, that which some say—that self-cognition is the innate consciousness (*caitanya*) of the self—is also refuted, because it would follow that even this [innate consciousness] would be subject to the appearance of an object to be cognized.

If it is argued that its concealment is caused by ignorance (*avidyā*), then what [concealment] could there be for Brahman itself? Furthermore, in the case of an effect that is eternal and self-luminous, the notion of concealment is illogical. Nor can there be the manifestation of anything else while that [Brahman] remains concealed, because its manifestation is established for all through the scripture stating, "Its speech is the all-accomplishing power" (*vibhāṣā*). If it speaks, then since the ignorance residing in all beings has been destroyed, ignorance cannot exist; for it does not perish in the *Atharva* [Veda]. If that were so, the light of knowledge would not be the cause of its wonder, and thus there would be no liberation. Moreover, it is impossible for that which is partless to have a partial manifestation or a partial non-manifestation.
Heaviness, merit, demerit, and mental impression are cognizable by the sense of hearing.
Heaviness, merit, demerit, and mental impressions are beyond the senses;
the meaning is that they are not perceived by any sense organ whatsoever.
Non-produced [qualities]—namely, the ultimate minute, the subtle, magnitude, unity, individual separateness, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, and velocity—are preceded by the qualities of their causes.
The qualities beginning with color (rūpa) and ending with touch (sparśa), when not produced by cooking (apākaja), are preceded by the qualities of their causes.

Those qualities of the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of their own substratum are the precursors of the qualities such as color in the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and so forth; that is, the color and other qualities of a cloth are invariably preceded by those [qualities] because they arise from the production of those qualities. For if it were otherwise, there would be no cause for the production of any quality whatsoever in the cloth. By this, the argument that "the white color of a single [substance] is recognized everywhere" is refuted.

Because the initial state [of the atoms] is impossible due to the absence of a self (ātman), recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) therefore has only the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. The specific qualities such as color and so forth produced by baking (*pāka*) are not known to be distinct from those residing in the atoms as their inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Therefore, the term "not produced by baking" (*apākaja*) is included in order to exclude that case.

Having determined that in the production of lightning and the like there is both dependence on the qualities of the cause and independence from the qualities of the cause, and that the color and other qualities of the water-atoms and so forth do not possess the nature of being produced by baking, there is no figurative application (*upacāra*) of the term to them.

Just as the cognition that [the water in] a mirage is preceded by the qualities of its cause is a statement of its own nature and not for the purpose of establishing [its reality], because it is possible for occasional fluidity and velocity to exist even without being preceded by the qualities of their causes;
so too, in these two cases, the state of being preceded by the qualities of the cause should be understood as being contradicted by the water and other things situated at the top of the head.
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, and sound are preceded by qualities that are not their own causes.

Cognition and the rest, ending with sound, do not have the qualities of their own substratum’s inherent cause as their antecedents; because they are eternal qualities, they do not originate from the qualities of that which is their inherent cause.

Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and sound; the dimension of cotton, the subsequent moment [of a substance], conjunction, incidental fluidity, priority, posteriority, and those produced by heating—these are born of conjunction. Intellect and the rest are born of conjunction:
intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression are born of the conjunction of the knower with the self.
Sound is born of the conjunction of the *maitrīka* drum and the stick.

The distinction is as follows: the subsequent conjunction (*uttara-saṃyoga*) produced from the triad of conjunctions known as "middle" (*madhya*) in the case of seeing what has been seen and so forth, is a conjunction born of conjunction (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*), which is the conceit of conjunction; or rather, it is the state of being seen through an instrumental cause. Visibility, audibility, and the properties of priority and posteriority are born of conjunction with space, time, and substance. Furthermore, even in the case of the pervasive inherence in a collection of earth particles, [qualities such as color] are born of conjunction with fire. This is the analysis.
Conjunction, disjunction, and velocity are born of action.
Conjunction, disjunction, and velocity are born of action;
the first two, conjunction and disjunction, are born of action.
Sound and the subsequent division [of the ether] are both produced by division.
Sound and the subsequent disjunction are both produced by disjunction;
the distinction is that the initial sound is produced from disjunction as well, whereas the subsequent disjunction is produced from disjunction alone.
Remoteness, proximity, duality, and disjunction, among others, depend upon cognition.
Remoteness, proximity, duality, and disjunction, among others, depend upon cognition.
Thus, as stated, cognition is the non-material (efficient) cause;
by the word "etcetera," qualities such as triad-disjunction and so forth are included.
Color, taste, smell, and non-hot touch, even though they reside in a single substance, are in earth; likewise, these qualities in water are initiators of their own kind.
Substances beginning with color (rūpa) and ending with viscidity (leha) initiate effects of their own kind.

Among causal substances, the effect-substance possesses [qualities] such as taste (rasa), while smell (gandha) and the rest are distinct from their own; from viscidity arises viscidity, and from magnitude (mahattva) arises magnitude—this is how the application [of the rule] is to be understood. Sound, however, initiates another sound within its own substratum; in that case, one should consider only its status as a cause, but not its status as an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause), otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of eliminating the distinction between being a material cause (*upādāna*) and being an instrumental cause (*nimitta*) for heterogeneous things that produce a single genus.

If that is so, then it follows that color-form and the rest are causes of visual perception and the like, but they do not initiate [their own] homogeneous effects apart from those; thus, [the opponent's position] remains unestablished.
Pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort originate from causes of a different genus.
Pleasure and the rest do not originate from causes of their own kind: pleasure is the cause of desire, pain of aversion, desire and aversion of effort, and the remainder [effort] of action.
If it is argued that pleasure in the son produces pleasure in the father, otherwise his joy would be inexplicable—this is without substance.

For when a father experiences pleasure by seeing his son’s pleasure through the latter’s laughter and so forth, that pleasure arises in the father; yet in such a case, the son’s pleasure is not the cause [of the father’s pleasure]. This is because it is not delimited by the same time. Rather, the process is that the cause is the cognition directed toward that object [the son’s pleasure], which is characterized by affection (*snehika*).

Conjunction and the rest, disjunction, lineage, gravity, fluidity, heat, viscidity, cognition, sound, and the specific qualities of the elements, as well as the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*), originate both from homogeneous and heterogeneous causes.
Conjunction and the other [qualities] are initiators of sound; they initiate both similar and dissimilar kinds [of effects].
From conjunction arises a subsequent conjunction of the same kind.
In the case of a double thread, length and so forth arise from the number "one" belonging to the qualities of the cause, as well as from disjunction and other factors.

In effects, from the number "one" arise the numbers "two" and "many"; from [the quality] of minuteness arise minuteness and largeness; from gravity arises another gravity and so on up to another lightness; from fluidity arises another fluidity and viscidity; from heat arises another heat;
from color arises color such as minute-color and so on; from cognition arises cognition and mental impression (saṃskāra);
from merit arises merit; from pleasure arises pleasure; from demerit arises demerit and pain; and from mental impression arises mental impression and memory.
Cognition, desire, aversion, volition, and effort are inherent in their own substratum and are initiators [of action].
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, mental impression, and effort—these, inhering in their own substratum, initiate [their effects];

they exist by themselves and likewise produce their effects. Furthermore, while intellect produces duality and so forth—which are qualities of the self inhering in another—and even other specific qualities of the self, it produces them only as inhering in its own substratum, and not elsewhere.
Color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, and effort originate [their effects] in other things.
Color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, number, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, and effort originate [qualities] in other things.

Colors and the rest, as they exist in their constituent parts, originate color and the rest in the composite whole according to their possibility; likewise, efforts inherent in the self are the cause of motion in hands and so forth.
Conjunction and so forth, number, unity, separateness, fluidity, velocity, dharma, adharma, and form are the initiators of action.
Conjunction and the others are initiators in both cases;
they are initiators both in their own substratum and elsewhere.

Furthermore, that present conjunction initiates a cloth in that very [substratum]; whereas the disjunction from the sense organ initiates the cessation of the self; and the disjunction between the bamboo slivers and space initiates sound in the space. Moreover, the number "one" residing in the parts initiates the number "one" in the whole in its own substratum, the space; and the number "two" and so forth initiates [its respective number] in its own substratum. A dyad initiates a dyad in its own substrata, such as the dyads and so forth, because it is one of the categories known as quality, substance, action, or name.

Furthermore, heaviness, fluidity, and velocity residing in the cause do not initiate [their effects] in the effect; rather, they produce action in their own substrata. Likewise, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) [produce] pleasure and pain in the self, while cognition, action, and so forth [arise] in other things such as the sense organs.
Gravity, fluidity, momentum, effort, merit, demerit, and specific conjunctions are the causes of action.

Gravity and the like are the causes of action. From gravity comes falling; from fluidity comes flowing; and from velocity and the like comes gliding along. Thus, the specific nature (*viśeṣa*) is that while merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are distinguished by actions such as sacrifice and the like, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) itself is the distinction—that is, a specific conjunction (*saṃyogaviśeṣa*). Conjunction is characterized by pushing (*nodana*) and striking (*abhighāta*). It will be explained later that velocity (*vega*) is also a cause of action.

Color, taste, smell, non-hot touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, and momentum possess the nature of being causes of generality, particularity, and inherence.

Color and the rest, up to sound, are inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*). An inherent cause is that which possesses the property of being inherent; moreover, the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is defined by its proximity (*pratyāsatti*), which consists in inherence in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa-samavāya*) and inherence in that which assists the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇopakāri-samavāya*). For pleasure and the like, the self (*ātman*) is the inherent cause; and the contact between that [self] and the mind (*ātma-manaḥ-saṃyoga*) is their non-inherent cause. [Objection: If that were so, then merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) would also be non-inherent causes. [Reply: No, because it is not determined that those two have the capacity for the production of all the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self.
For instance, from non-dharma (adharma) arises non-happiness (duḥkha), and from dharma and karma arise happiness (sukha) and dharma;
likewise, the deviation of each [of the other categories], such as knowledge (jñāna) and so forth, should be demonstrated.

In all cases where there is a capacity of ten thousand, the conjunction of the four [factors] is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) by virtue of this specific distinction; disregarding that, because the cognition of the cloth inheres in the threads which are the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the cognition, the cognition of the threads is the non-inherent cause of the cognition of the cloth, and not taste and so forth, because their capacity is determined by the exclusion of other distinct entities produced from them.

The same [analysis] should be applied to taste and the other qualities as well. Furthermore, it is stated that among those produced by cooking (*pākaja*), there is also the status of being an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇatva*). These properties should be understood as residing in atoms. Regarding color, taste, smell, non-hot touch, and dimension, their status as non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇatva*) arises from their inherence in the same object as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because they depend on the power of the cause and initiate similar effects in the product. As for sound, its status as a non-inherent cause arises from its inherence in the same object as the inherent cause; since it is a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), it initiates another sound within space.

Regarding number and quality, which were stated to be causes by virtue of possessing causality, their status as causes in the effect is according to their respective order: because [number] initiates unity, substance-ness, and action; and because [quality] illuminates its own substratum and that which resides in two substances. Furthermore, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression (bhāvanā) possess the nature of efficient causes (nimittakāraṇa).
And the fact that desire and the rest are efficient causes means that they possess exclusively the nature of efficient causes.
Conjunction, disjunction, hot touch, heaviness, fluidity, and velocity possess causality through their perception.

Conjunction, disjunction, hot touch, gravity, fluidity, and velocity possess causality through being non-inherent causes, inherent causes, and instrumental causes; this is the meaning. For instance, in the production of sound, the conjunction of the drum and the stick is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), while the conjunction of the drum and space is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
Thus, in the case of division, the division of the two [substances] is the efficient cause (nimitta), while the division of the space within the pot is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa).
Hot touch is the non-inherent cause of hot touch, and it is the efficient cause of qualities produced by baking (pākaja).
Gravity is the non-inherent cause of falling in its own substratum.
Upward motion and downward motion are not the efficient causes for the production of action;
the same should be applied to fluidity and velocity as well.
Remoteness, nearness, duality, dual inherence, separateness, and so forth are not causes.
Remoteness, proximity, and so forth are not causes [of cognition].
These are neither non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) nor efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of duality, separateness, and the like—specifically the three types of separateness—as well as the atomic dimension (*paramāṇu-parimāṇa*) and the ultimate large dimension (*paramamahat-parimāṇa*).
Conjunction, disjunction, sound, and the specific qualities of the self reside in a limited portion [of their respective substrates].

Conjunction, disjunction, sound, and the specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) reside in a limited portion [of their substratum]. "Residing in a limited portion" means residing non-pervasively; that is to say, they exist in some parts of their own substratum and do not exist in others.
But is this not improper?

Just as the existence and non-existence of a single entity in different locations is not untenable, since its existence is perceived through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too is its non-existence perceived. For instance, the conjunction of a large jar with its front and back [surfaces] is perceived, as is its absence on the ground; for while the ground is perceived by the intellect, the conjunction is not perceived everywhere. Nor can it be said that the conjunction and its absence belong merely to the parts of the ground, because the absence of the back surface is perceived in relation to its own specific location. If the conjunction belonged only to the location and not to the whole object possessing the location (*pradeśin*), then since even a location is a "possessor of location" relative to its own sub-locations, conjunction would occur only in partless atoms. But such a conjunction is not perceptible; thus, this inquiry ultimately concludes within the very examination of conjunction. Furthermore, just as no single object is established by the distinction between the heart and other parts, so too, whether by way of conjunction or its absence, the identity of the two is established, and the sensory organs are accepted as being in agreement.

Because there are twenty-two [atoms], conjunction occurs through their mutual approach; yet, since those two [atoms] are respectively perceived and unperceived, and because it is also unperceived due to its being cut off by a density that is as subtle as the weightiness of form and so forth, it lacks pervasiveness (*avyāptatva*).

In this way, sound also does not pervade space, because for you [the opponent], it is perceived and not perceived simultaneously due to the difference in substances, or else it occurs successively; for just as fire and other things are non-pervasive because they are perceived and not perceived both inside and outside [the house], how then can there be action in horses and other animals through merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)? If it is argued that these two [merit and demerit] operate either within or successively [in the body], we say no, because even though they are not present there [in the horse's body], they serve as the cause for the movement of their own substratum along with its parts.

Just as when the eye has moved away from its object, the conditions for the visual consciousness of Caitra—which was previously conjoined with that visual object—are no longer present, so too should this case be understood.
The remaining [faculties] do not pervade their own bases.
The remaining ones do not pervade their substratum.

Those other than those already mentioned are the "remaining" ones; the meaning is that they do not possess the quality of pervading their substratum, as conjunction and the like do not act as pervasive [qualities].

The color, taste, smell, touch, temperature, dimension, unity, individuality, number, duality, conjunction, disjunction, fluidity, gravity, and viscidity that are not produced by fire possess existence as long as the substance exists (*yāvad-dravyabhāvitva*).

The quality of existing as long as the substance exists (*yāvaddravyabhāvitva*) pertains to color and other qualities produced by non-heat (*apākaja*). As long as the substance exists, these qualities—color and the rest—are present. Since color and other qualities produced by heat (*pākaja*) perish even while their substratum still exists, they are distinguished as "non-produced-by-heat" (*apākaja*).
And the remaining [faculties] exist as long as the substance [endures].
The remaining qualities exist as long as the substance itself.
This means that qualities other than those such as color produced by cooking do not persist for the duration of the substance; they perish while the substratum still exists.
Each of all the qualities, beginning with form (rūpa), receives the designation "derived" (upādi) due to its connection with a lower-level generality (aparasāmānya).
In order to demonstrate the mutual distinctness of the qualities (*guṇa*) one by one, he says:
"Of form and the rest" (*rūpādīnām*).

Those qualities of which form is the first—because each of them is associated with its own specific cognition, such as "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth—they come to be designated by such names as "form" or "taste."
The designations "form" and so forth, produced by lower universals such as "form-ness," constitute the specific dissimilarities of each individual form and so forth.

Some maintain that the universal *rūpatva* (the nature of form) does not exist; this is incorrect, because the cognition "this is form, this is form" recurs across the various distinctions of blue, yellow, and so forth. If it is argued that this recurrence is due to the fact that the four [elements] are unmodified, we say no; for they are not perceived by the eye as "form. Indeed, the cognition in question would only arise after the perception of those [elements], and thus it would have them as its cause. Furthermore, if the inability to perceive them as such were their inherent nature, then since that nature persists extensively in blue and the other colors, let it be so. What is the consequence? If there were a contradiction with each individual form, the recurrence of the cognition would not occur, just as it does not when the cause is absent. Therefore, the universal must exist as a recurring entity.

Taste and the other qualities are also explained in this manner. Among them, color (rūpa) resides in four substances: earth, water, fire, and air. It is perceptible by the eye, exists in various forms such as white and so forth, and is eternal in the atoms of water and the like. In the case of earthly atoms, it is not incompatible with the conjunction of formless [atoms]. In all effect-substances (kāryadravya), it arises preceded by the qualities of its causes and perishes only through the destruction of the whole (avayavin).
Because it is the cause for the existence and so forth of all categories of objects (*padārtha*), [the author] first defines *rūpa*.
Regarding that, *rūpa* is fourfold;
among those qualities (*guṇa*), *rūpa* alone is apprehended in four ways, and not by any other sense organ.
Nor is "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) itself apprehended in only four ways; how then can this be a point of dissimilarity regarding form?
No, for this is intended as a specific quality (*vaiśeṣya*) of it, and thus it has been stated that such a designation does not apply here in the present context.
The dissimilarity from common substances, however, consists precisely in their possessing generality (*sāmānyavattva*).
[This applies] to earth, water, fire, air, and ether.
It exists only as "earth, water, fire, air," and so forth.
Of the four substances:
that in which a substance exists, as well as its qualities, actions, and generalities, are perceptible;
it moves through the eyes.
The cause for the apprehension of objects by the eye through form is manifold, such as white and so forth;
that which has many varieties, such as white and so forth, is of such a kind.
It is eternal in the atoms of water and so forth;
it is eternal in the atoms of water and in the atoms of fire;
and it is not incompatible with the formless conjunctions of the atoms of earth.

And we shall further explain that the conjunction of the formless [air] is the destroyer of the color of the earth atom. In all effect-substances, the color residing in the effect-substance is preceded by the qualities of its causes; that is, it is preceded by the qualities of the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of its own substratum.
It perishes precisely through the destruction of its substratum.

Even for the destruction of an effect-substance, the non-destruction [of the cause] is the very reason; therefore, it cannot be said in a primary sense that "its destruction results from the destruction of its substratum," as if referring to the simultaneous destruction of both color and the substance, because of the absence of such a cause.

First, through the process of disintegration and so forth of the substance, there occurs the destruction of the substance whose nature is the effect experienced through conjunction; why then is the destruction of its color not [the result] of the destruction of the cause? If the production [of color] were from the destruction of the disjunction of the parts that constitute the cause of the substance, then the colors of the potsherds would also be destroyed from that same [cause], as there is no distinction. Therefore, it is logically established that first there is the destruction of the substance, and subsequently the destruction of the color due to the absence of its substratum; this sequence is thus justified.

However, those who maintain the identity (*tādātmya*) of color and substance, and assert that the cause of the substance itself is the cause of the color, should be asked this: does the color of an atom (*paramāṇu*) produce another color or not? If it does produce it, does it produce it within itself or in its own substrate, the atom? If it does not produce it, or if it produces it either within itself or in its substrate, then since no color would arise in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), the world would be perceived as devoid of color, taste, smell, and touch. Thus have I reflected upon the world.

Now, since that which does not exist at the time of the commencement of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) cannot be made to endure, it must be admitted that the well (*kūpa*) arises there only after the dyad has been produced; for an effect devoid of a self-nature (*nirātmaka*) cannot arise.

Thus, if identity (*tādātmya*) were the case, then because the previous defect would remain, your own tradition also holds that when a jar is situated in a pit, the well and so forth emerge from the force of the fire and are thus produced. Furthermore, this is the established principle: that for whatever self-nature there is no arising, and for whatever accidental properties there is no cessation, there can be no production of that [self-nature].
Nor do I suspect that there is an absolute separation between the two, as in the case of a well, because [the ear] is a distinct substance;
rather, it is due to the inherent nature of things, just like a jar. Thus, enough with this verse composed by one of heavy intellect.
Taste is that which is apprehended by the sense of taste.

It is a quality of earth, water, and fire; it is the cause of life, nourishment, strength, and health; it assists the sense of taste; and it is divided into the distinctions of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent.
Its eternality, non-eternality, and production are also like those of color (rūpa).

In the context of defining the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that are perceptible by the external sense organs and serve as causes for substances, immediately after describing taste (*rasa*) and smell (*gandha*), and having explained color (*rūpa*)—which is characterized as being perceptible by the eye—the author now explains taste:
"Taste is that which is grasped by the gustatory organ.
Among the qualities, taste alone is what is grasped by the gustatory organ, and that which is grasped by the gustatory organ is indeed taste.
The power of earth and water exists only in earth and water;
it is the cause of life, nourishment, strength, and health.

Life is the maintenance of the vital breaths; nourishment is the increase or accumulation [of the body]; strength is a particular kind of enthusiasm; and health is the absence of disease—of which rasa is the cause. This, however, is to be understood from all the medical treatises (vaidyaśāstra).
It is the collaborator of the sense of taste.
The internal taste (*svagatarasa*) is an auxiliary factor in the perception of external tastes.
It is divided into the distinctions of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent;
the meaning is that it is established as being of six types according to these distinctions, beginning with the sweet.
And its production as eternal or non-eternal is like that of color (*rūpa*).

Just as color is non-eternal in earth-atoms, being destroyed by the destruction of the substance [composed] of other [atoms], whereas it is eternal in water-atoms, perishing through the destruction of its substratum due to the absence of the qualities of an effect such as color—so too is taste (*rasa*).
Odor is that which is apprehended by the sense of smell;
it functions within the earth element, assists the olfactory organ, and is either fragrant or foul.
Its production and other characteristics are explained as before. Odor is that which is apprehended by the sense of smell.
Odor alone is perceivable by the sense of smell;
that which is perceivable by the sense of smell is odor alone.
But how is this restriction established? It is established through the restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Such is the nature of odor that it is perceived by the sense of smell alone; it is not perceived by any other [sense], because for those whose vision is impaired, there is neither a positive injunction nor a negative prohibition [regarding its perception]. It functions within the earth; it exists only in the earth and nowhere else.
Smell is the auxiliary cause for olfactory perception. The smell inherent in its own substrate is the auxiliary cause of olfactory perception.
There is a distinction based on the distinction between pleasant and unpleasant odors.
The [processes of] origination and so forth have been explained here as well, just as before.

Just as taste—due to its conjunction with the atoms of earth—is subject to origination and destruction, and as an effect it perishes through the destruction of its commencement following the sequence of the qualities of its causes, so too is odor.
Furthermore, this [odor] possesses no permanence whatsoever.

Tactile sensation (*sparśa*) is that which is apprehended by the sense organ of touch (*tvagindriya*). It resides in the qualities of cold, heat, and lukewarm water (1); it causes the contraction of the skin (2); it conforms to color-form (*rūpa*) (3); and it is of three kinds, distinguished as cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold.
Furthermore, its eternality and non-eternality are to be determined as before.
It is perceptible by the sense-organ of touch.
The sense-organ located in the skin is the "tactile organ" (*tvagindriya*); by that alone is touch perceived, and not by anything else.
Its function consists of the qualities of hot, cold, and tepid water.
This function is indeed perception alone; it is the preparer of the skin. Touch is the auxiliary for the tactile faculty in the apprehension of its object.
That which conforms to form (*rūpānuvidhāyin*)—that is, following, accompanying, and conforming to form—is coldness; for that form which is cold necessarily possesses six states.

It is of three kinds due to the distinction between cold, hot, and neither-cold-nor-hot. However, the attainment of these two extremes is due to a particular conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*), not by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it is perceptible by both sense organs.
Even in this case, the determination of permanence and impermanence is as before:
there is perception of a distant taste but not of its odor, because the latter lacks permanence.
The process of the production of qualities born of heating (*pākaja*) in the color and other qualities of the atoms of earth:

When a substance such as a jar, which is composed of many parts, is processed by fire, either through the agitation caused by the final impact or otherwise, qualities are produced successively within the atoms that constitute it. From these [qualities] arise disjunctions; from the disjunctions, the destruction of conjunctions; and from the destruction of conjunctions, the effect-substance perishes.

When that has perished, in the independent atoms, due to the conjunction with fire and depending on the heat, there occurs the production of qualities such as color and so forth, which are born of heating, as described.
Furthermore, upon the destruction of the [earlier] substances such as the dyad, due to the conjunction with fire and the state of being heated, qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*) arise.

Immediately thereafter, through the conjunction of the soul (*ātman*) with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) which is dependent on the enjoyer, action arises in the atoms where the baked qualities have been produced; from their mutual conjunction, an effect-substance is produced in the sequence beginning with the dyad.
And therein, the production of color and other qualities occurs through the sequence of the qualities of the causes.

Furthermore, neither the arising nor the destruction of all colors is possible in an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), because its existence in the present life is understood through the observation of universal emergence, and because pervasion is impossible even through the entry of atoms due to the destruction of the effect-substance.

He explains the determination of the production and etymological definition of the color and other qualities of earth-atoms (*pārthivaparamāṇu*). Regarding the phrase "of the earth-atoms' color and so forth": although atoms themselves are indeed the earth, nevertheless, because of the long-standing convention regarding the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), they are called "earthly" (*pārthiva*); that is, these atoms are the cause of the earth. Those which are their color and other qualities—of those produced by heating (*pākaja*)—the production, etymology, and method are being stated.

[Objection: "In that case, the non-determination of the destruction of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and so forth would not have been promised [as the subject matter]. [Reply: Not so; for by the word "manner" (*prakāra*), that too is understood. For instance, he demonstrates that very manner—namely, the manner in which color and other qualities arise from baking (*pākaja*), and how others arise from the destruction of preceding ones—by the passage beginning with "of the jar and so forth which are to be produced. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), cloth and other such things are included.
"Of a non-originated substance" means of a substance that has not been produced as an effect.

Since atoms connected by the cause of baking are mentioned in succession, and since there are no atoms belonging to a jar or other such things that possess conjunctions with a non-originated substance, he says "of those which originate it" in order to exclude that possibility.
The meaning is "of the constituent parts of that [object], such as a jar.
He states that the atoms which constitute the jar and so forth are causes through a succession of steps, beginning with the impact of a stick and so on.
Thus he says: "from the impact of a stick," etc.
The specific conjunction of the constituent parts of an earthly atom is either impelled or [natural]; this will be explained in the section on action (*karma*).
By that action, there occurs a destruction of the conjunction capable of being destroyed by action; and upon the destruction of that conjunction, the effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) perishes.

From those [motions] arise the disjunctions of the atoms from their constituent parts; from these disjunctions follows the destruction of the effect-substance, such as the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth. When that has been destroyed, while the atoms remain independent, there occurs the destruction of the efforts of the atoms directed toward shadow and the like, caused by non-eternal conjunctions and other factors depending on heat. Then, again, from another [motion] independent [of the previous], qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) arise. Regarding the production of qualities produced by heating in independent atoms, the proof (*pramāṇa*) is the observation of the substance being devoid of all qualities such as color and the like, which is not conducive to the effect.

The color and other qualities of atoms exist within substances as constituent qualities that are conducive to the production of effects; this is because they possess the nature of being initiatory qualities, as seen in the case of earth and so forth.
Furthermore, the production of another color even when the previous color has perished is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The movement of color and other qualities is due to the initiation of subsequent colors and so on; for instance, red and other colors are initiated in a triad (*trasareṇu*) because it possesses color and other qualities, just like the color and other qualities of earth and so forth.

Since the prior destruction of color and other qualities in atoms has already been established, the same cause of destruction remains operative even in external objects, because no other [cause] is possible apart from the non-perception of the cognition of those [qualities]. Furthermore, it should not be understood that the cause of the destruction of color and other qualities is exactly the same as their cause of production; for the production of color and other qualities arises from one thing, while their destruction is brought about by another. Therefore, regarding atoms, both the production of color and other qualities independent of the acquisition of something else, and the destruction independent of the acquisition of something else, are refuted.

The destruction and production of the color and other qualities (*rūpa*) of an atom do not have a single cause, because they are the destruction and production of color and other qualities, like the destruction and production of the color of a thread. It is the same for the intermediate [stages] and so forth. When jars and other substances have been produced, there will be experience (*bhoga*)—to be inferred from pleasure and pain—in their effects; those who possess such experience are "experiencers" (*bhogin*). Today, for them, through the conjunction of atoms characterized by the restraint of Yama, the qualities of color produced by heating (*pākaja-rūpa*) and odor arise sequentially within these atoms.

From those [atoms], there occurs the mutual conjunction of those atoms; from that, the substance *dvyaṇuka* (binary atomic compound), the *tryaṇuka* (ternary atomic compound), and so forth are produced in this successive order, by which means the effect-substance such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) arises.
And in that process, color and other qualities arise preceded by the qualities of the causes.

For the sake of the quality of color in the *dvyaṇuka*, starting from the atoms, and from the cause of the *dvyaṇuka* to the cause of the *tryaṇuka*, in this sequence, the production of color and odor occurs in the jar and other objects.
Furthermore, number and the other qualities are produced by heating (pākaja), because they are observed to be non-eternal.
[Objection: But even in the case of its own destruction, no difference in character is perceived.
[Reply: True.
Nevertheless, its being produced by heating (*pākaja*) is established through inference.

This has been demonstrated regarding earth, water, fire, and air. Following the production of qualities through heating, motion arises in the atoms, but not simultaneously with the causes of grossness and so forth. For it is observed that in a substance possessing color and other qualities, there occurs a motion that serves as the cause for the commencement of an effect-substance possessing color and other qualities; thus, motion arising in an atom is seen to possess color and other qualities, because it is a motion that serves as the cause for the production of an effect-substance possessing color and other qualities, just like the motion that produces the conjunction which initiates a jar.
Now, why is it not assumed that the production and destruction of color and other qualities occur independently [of the substance] within the very substance that is the effect?

For jars and other objects are perceived in cooking, in fire, and in the presence of all medicinal herbs; they are recognized as possessing qualities independent of one another even at different times, such as "these are those same jars. To this he says: "And not...
He states the reasoning:

"Regarding the passage beginning with *sarveṣv avayaveṣu* and so forth: since there is no conjunction—characterized by being non-pervasive—that exists within the whole (*ghāṭe*) while residing in all its internal and external parts as something inherent (*samaveta*) and capable of causing destruction, it follows that the production and destruction of effect-substances (*kāryadravya*) and the like would not occur; this is the meaning. Even if, on account of the word *tat*, a plurality of composite substances (*avayavidravya*) were thereby established, there would still be no entry into the interior [of those composites] because they consist of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Therefore, the claim that [the whole] pervades [its parts] is not contradictory; to this, he replies:"
The subtle entry and so forth as well.

Atoms do not possess internal space (*khāntara*), because a substance is devoid of such properties. If atoms possessed internal space, they would be non-originated, as there would be no conjunction of that atom; and since a conjoined part has already been refuted, even inherence (*samavāya*)—which occurs between two entities through conjunction in some part and non-conjunction in another—would necessarily involve internal space. Let conjunction itself be devoid of properties; this rule does not hold. What is perceived in gross substances is not perceived elsewhere. The notion that there is internal space in dyads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth is untenable due to their unsuitability for perception; thus, the previously mentioned conceptualization stands.

Therefore, jars and other such objects are indeed internal [to space]; there is no entry of atoms as small as their interior until there is an interpenetration of the constituent parts of the hand and other instruments.

Regarding "from touch" (*spṛṣṭeḥ*): in a substance, because of the resistance (*pratighāta*) of one substance against another substance at its tip, and because of the occurrence of action and so forth when the parts are being disjoined, there is no destruction of the conjunction that constitutes the substance itself; thus, the destruction of the substance [occurs]. This is the manifestation of the quality of being produced (*kṛtaka*). Furthermore, in the case of effect-substances, the destruction of color and other qualities does not occur from anything other than the destruction of the [effect-]substance through its own destruction; rather, their production is seen to arise from the qualities of the causes. Therefore, the production and destruction of color and other qualities in a jar due to contact with fire and so forth is not to be postulated [as independent]; rather, the color and other qualities of the jar perish only through the destruction of their substratum. Since the color and other qualities residing in an effect-substance belong to the same category as those in a cloth and so forth, [it follows that they arise from the qualities of the cause]: moreover, the color and other qualities of a jar and so forth are produced from the qualities of the causes alone, because they are color and other qualities residing in an effect-substance, just like the color and other qualities residing in a cloth and so forth. Furthermore, since the well-known existence of the prior substrates is established, how could there be a state of confusion regarding their location? Nor is it logical for the two categories of "fitness" (*yogyatva*)—namely, the capacity to be perceived and the capacity to be the object of cognition—to coexist in one place, due to their mutual contradiction. Therefore, let this be a different conventional usage arising from the cessation of the previous day's [usage]. Likewise, if there is the production of another substance from the destruction of the previous substance due to the destruction of the causes, and if the state of the qualities of the causes remains, then there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), which is observed in all cases despite the difference in form, such as in the case of a flame. Even as the effect is perishing, its destruction occurs gradually; for a jar does not reside within the atoms in a way that it would perish instantaneously when those atoms are separated. Rather, it is begun through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth. Its destruction occurs only after the destruction of the dyads and triads and so forth, and until that destruction, perception certainly exists. It is logical that the previous [atoms] perish perceptibly, and others arise in their place through the sequence of dyads and so forth, possessing the same number and dimension. Thus, there is the removal of the old and the addition of the new; and when the objects of the senses are entirely distinct, then non-perception arises because of the non-production [of the new], and in the next moment, upon the destruction of the previously arisen parts, there is the production of another substance. In this way, the commencement of the subject matter of the beginning occurs, and as many as were the constituent parts of the previous substance, so many are the constituents of the subsequent one; thus, its dimension and number are logically established.

The process is as follows: at one and the same time, there is the destruction of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), the state of being in the process of destruction of the triad (*tryaṇuka*), the state of having been destroyed of the black color and so forth, the state of being produced of the disjunction born of disjunction in the atom, and the state of being produced of the red substance that is in the process of being produced.

Then, at another single moment, there is the destruction of the triad, the state of having been destroyed of its effect, the destruction of the black color and so forth, the production of the disjunction born of disjunction, the state of having been destroyed of the conjunction, the state of being produced of the red color and so forth which is in the process of being produced from the substance that was in the process of being produced, and the state of being destroyed of the conjunction that was the cause of the transformation of the black color and so forth.

Then, at one and the same time: the destruction of that effect, the state of that effect being destroyed, the arising of the subsequent conjunction, the production of the red and other qualities, the destruction of the conjunction that was the cause of the destruction of the black and other qualities, and the arising of the action that initiates a substance in the second atom.
