Then, at another [simultaneous] time: the destruction of that effect, the state of that effect being destroyed, the production of the subsequent conjunction, the state of the destruction of the action, the disjunction, and the disjunction produced by disjunction, the arising of the action in the second atom, and the arising of the disjunction.

Then, at that time, there is the destruction of that effect, the state of that effect being destroyed, the destruction of the action, the disjunction, and the disjunction produced by disjunction; and simultaneously, there is the production of the action and the disjunction in the second atom, and the state of the conjunction with it being about to perish—this is one moment.

Then, there is the destruction of that effect, the state of that effect being destroyed, the destruction of the action and the conjunction in the atom, and the state of the subsequent conjunction being in the process of arising—this is one moment.

Then, at one and the same time, there is the destruction of that effect, the state of that effect having been destroyed; the production of a subsequent conjunction of one atom with another atom, the state of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) being produced, and the state of the disjunction and the action being destroyed. Then, [at the next moment], there is the destruction of that effect, the state of that effect having been destroyed, the production of the dyad, the state of the triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth being produced, and the destruction of the disjunction and the action. Thereafter, in the subsequent moment, other qualities are produced in the dyad, preceded by the qualities of the cause. This entire process of conceptualization applies to all dyads.

However, in the case of triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth, action need not be considered [as the cause]. This is because when many atoms (*paramāṇu*) are produced through simultaneous conjunction, there occurs a conjunction of an atom that is the cause of one triad with an atom that is the cause of another triad; from that, there arises the conjunction of a triad with an atom that is the cause of yet another triad. Furthermore, number (*saṃkhyā*) is the cause for the conventional usage of "one," "two," and so on.
Moreover, it resides in a single substance and also in multiple substances.

Among these, regarding that which resides in a single substance, its properties of being eternal or non-eternal, and its necessity or lack thereof, are like those of the color and other qualities of water-atoms and the like.
But duality and so forth, up to the highest number (parārdha), reside in multiple substances.
Indeed, its production arises from unities devoid of a cognition of multiple objects, and its destruction results from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi).
How so?

When, due to the observer’s perception, there occurs a conjunction of two substances belonging to the same or different classes, and upon the arising of the cognition of the generality of unity (*ekatvasāmānya*) inherent in that which is conjoined and inherent therein, a single enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises—having as its object the two unities and being directed toward multiple objects—then, depending on that [cognition], duality is produced in the two substrates of those unities. Subsequently, the cognition of the generality of duality arises with respect to that [duality]. At the very moment when, due to that cognition of the generality of duality, the enumerative cognition is in the process of perishing, the cognition of the quality of duality arises from the generality of duality, its own nature, and the cognition thereof; this constitutes one and the same time.

Therefore, now, at the moment when the quality of duality is about to perish due to the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānya*) is destroyed; this is one and the same time as the cognition of the substance (*dravyabuddhi*)—in the form "these two substances"—is arising from the perceived qualities of duality and the cognition thereof.

Immediately thereafter, there is one moment when the cognition of the two substances arises, the duality (dvi-tva) is destroyed, the cognition of the quality of duality is in the process of perishing, and the mental impression (saṃskāra) is arising from the cognition of the substances. Immediately after that, from the cognition of the substances, the cognition of the quality of duality is destroyed, and the cognition of the substances is also destroyed by the mental impression. By this, the production of triad-ness (tri-tva) and so forth is also explained. Even in the case of unity, the production [of the cognition] occurs when the cognition of the object as "one" has ceased; or its destruction occurs through the destruction of the enumerative cognition (apekṣā-buddhi).
In some cases, it is due to the destruction of the substance. How so?

When a part that serves as the substratum for unity is destroyed, at that very moment the cognition of the universal "unity" arises, the separation of the constituent parts from one another is effected by the action [of destruction], and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is produced.

Then, at the very same time that the destruction of conjunction [of the two atoms] occurs due to disjunction, duality arises; from the destruction of conjunction follows the destruction of the substance, and the cognition of the universal [duality] arises. Then, at the very same time that the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is destroyed by the cognition of the universal, duality is destroyed by the destruction of the relative cognition. This has been explained according to the "slayer-and-slain" (*badhyaghātaka*) theory. However, if there were contradiction characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), it would follow that the cognition of the substance could never arise. How so?

Because the destruction of duality occurs simultaneously with the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) at the same time as the cognition of the quality [duality], there would follow the undesirable consequence that the cognition of the substance—namely, "two substances"—which depends upon that [duality], would not arise.

If it is argued that "it is like inferential knowledge; from mere cognition," meaning that just as in the case of "that which has come into being" (*asaṃve bhūtasya*), there is inference from mere cognition even in the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*), so too, despite the destruction of the quality, the perception of the substance would occur from the mere cognition of the quality—[we reply:
No.
Because it is the cognition of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*).

Indeed, the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣyajñāna*) cannot occur without a direct relation to the qualifier. And thus says the author of the Sūtras: "Of the inherent [cause]... and so forth, which is to be inferred. He states that your cognition and [the cognition of the qualifier] are related as effect and cause.

But it is not the case that worldly cognition arises from non-worldly [cognition]; therefore, the presentation of the object is not logically tenable, as in the example "space possesses sound. However, there is no fault in this, because just as three cognitions arise rapidly [in succession], so too do they arise in the production of the cognition of duality and so forth.
If it is argued that the same fault applies even in the "killer-and-killed" (badhyaghātaka) model, one might think:
"In that case, even under the killer-and-killed model, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-arising of the cognition of substance."
How so?
[One might argue: "Because the destruction of the cognition occurs simultaneously with the production of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) by means of the cognition of duality.
This is not so.

Since the cognition of the whole (*samūhajñāna*) alone is the cause of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*)—because it is the cognition of the final [member] that serves as the cause of the impression—and not the extraordinary cognition (*alaukikajñāna*), there is no fault.

If it be argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of the simultaneity of cognitions (*jñānayogapadyaprasaṅga*), thinking: "Surely, when cognitions stand in the relation of the 'slayer' and the 'slain' (*badhyaghātaka*), there follows the consequence of their simultaneity," we say:
no.
Because it is denied that two [cognitions] which are not perishing can coexist.

By the statement regarding the simultaneity of cognitions, the simultaneous arising of two cognitions and the simultaneous existence of two non-perishing [cognitions] are both denied; for in the case of the contradiction between the bound and the slayer, there is neither the simultaneous arising of two cognitions nor the simultaneous existence of two non-perishing ones.

Regarding those who, though learned and possessing great erudition, hold adverse views and oppose our own philosophical positions, he says: "Number is that which [accounts for] the usage of 'one' and so forth.

"Usage" (*vyavahāra*) refers to the linguistic convention concerning the object of knowledge and the means of knowing; it is that by which such usage is carried out. Thus, "usage of one and so forth" refers to the cognition and the verbal expression of "two," "three," and so on. That which is the cause of such cognition and verbal expression is "number" (*saṃkhyā*).
The cognition of "one," "two," "three," and so forth, being a qualifying cognition, is associated with the mere substance because it is a qualified cognition;
or alternatively, having analyzed even the word [itself], the logical connection is that its status as a reason is due to its being a qualified word.
[Objection: But surely this cognition has form and other [sensory objects] as its object?
No, because the substance (*sattva*) is not of a different character [from its qualities].
For if the cognition were distinct from color and the other qualities, it would be "blue," "yellow," and so forth; rather, it would be "one," "two," and so on.

Let it be then that [the cognition] is without an object, since there is no existence of anything distinct from pleasure and so forth; but how then has this form—such as "one," "two," or "many"—arisen?

If you say it is because the consciousness of one who has not ceased ignorance transforms into that [form], then let that [transformation] apply equally to the forms of blue and so on. For there is no logical distinction between the nature of the cognition and its numerical form by which we could understand that one is produced from a single [cause] while the other is produced from many. Nor is there any such distinction: that the form of blue is non-dual, whereas the numerical form is dual.
Regarding that conventional usage:

since there is no evidence for the non-erroneousness of even the blue aspect, there is no correspondence whatsoever between those two [the aspect and the object], because they are restricted to a single cognition and because of their momentariness.
For this very reason, there is also no causal efficiency (kriyā) in destruction.

Furthermore, since each individual cognition, being concentrated solely on its own internal form (*svākāramātra*), lacks the capacity to differentiate between preceding and succeeding cognitions, there can be no external correspondence (*bāhyasaṃpratipatti*) by which the perception of a correspondence with the form seen in reality could be established; for even in the case of six [cognitions] acting as a collective, a correspondence is established only when they are of the same kind, whereas it is observed that this occurs only occasionally even among those of different kinds.

Furthermore, even if the cognition were produced by an object, the non-illusory nature of the blue form would not be established. For the determination that it is produced by that [object] occurs only when the object has been revealed by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the cognition of the form is known through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Alternatively, if one accepts that the object is established solely from the cognition of the form, then the object would be established from the cognition of a non-illusory form; however, the establishment of the non-illusory nature of the form depends on the determination that it is produced by the object, which results in a circular argument (*anyonyāśrayitva*).

Furthermore, imperishability exists even for the form of number, which is not grasped by the cognition of the form "blue"; and since there is no possibility of sublation regarding the non-reality of clouds, it is difficult to maintain [the reality] of blue and so forth, because those [clouds] are remote from their own nature. Therefore, in all cases, there is only the awareness of the mere form. If it is argued that even in the case of many [objects], they are described as such within a single cognition, and thus there is no cognition [of them] as being like blue and so forth—[we reply: if the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which arises dependent on independent inference regarding a non-external object, occurs only occasionally, then the occasional occurrence of the form of blue and so forth would be established by that cause alone; if that were the case, the conceptualization of blue and so forth would not proceed. If it is argued that the form of the cognized object also does not have an occasional occurrence because it conforms to an external object, then number must also be postulated, because its application is established through specific usage.

Although it was stated that number does not exist as something distinct from substance because it is not perceived separately, that too has been answered: since substances such as mutual difference and so forth are not perceived even when they occupy the same location as the substance, it is possible for [number] to be perceived through its own specific perception.
In this way, the distinction from color and so forth is also explained regarding substance, since even the perceived color is shown to be the very nature of the substance.
Thus, having established number, [the author] now demonstrates its divisions;
that [number], moreover, is both residing in a single substance and residing in multiple substances.
That which has a single substance as its substratum is *ekadravyā* (single-substance-based);

that which has multiple substances as its substratum is *anekadravyā* (multiple-substance-based). Prior to the production of sound—whether it be single-substance-based or multiple-substance-based—it is known through perception to be like the generality of light (*prakāśasāmānya*). In that regard, concerning the production of sound based on a single substance or multiple substances, the determination of the permanence or impermanence of sound is established by means of the color and other qualities of atoms such as *khaliba*, which are themselves perceivable as single-substance-based.

Just as in the case of the atom of *baliśa*, fluidity, taste, and touch are eternal, while number, action, and configuration are non-eternal; and just as in the case of the destructible *baliśa* atom, qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and the rest are non-eternal and perish due to the destruction of their substratum, yet they possess eternity through the excellence of the qualities of their cause—so too it is with the number and other attributes of a single substance. However, duality (*dvitva*) and the like, which belong to multiple substances, are dependent on others (*parāyogata*). Duality and the rest are produced by two or more substances; they are dependent on others, and because they are perceived by the sense organs, they are brought about for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), being thus dependent on others.
The word "tu" (but) serves to demonstrate that, unlike number (*saṅkhyā*), which resides in a single substance, duality (*dvitva*) and so forth are characterized by residing in multiple substances.

Indeed, it is indicated that this [number] possesses a multiplicity of substrata, just like unity (*ekatva*); otherwise, there would be the destruction of its nature as a qualifier and the non-establishment of its dual character. The particle "khalu" is used for emphasis; the meaning is that even for that unity, there is indeed a restriction, namely that it is the quality of being one in each individual substance.
And [the phrase] "in unity and unities" belongs to the *dharmārthīya* [compound]; otherwise, the cause for the production of duality would not be postulated.

[The term] "accompanied by" means "accompanied by that cognition which is devoid of an increase in multiple substrata. The word "multiple" (*aneka*) does not apply to a single thing, since it is observed to apply to two or one; rather, it refers to that which is accompanied by the cognition regarding multiple objects.
This very point is established by means of a series of questions, beginning with "How? and so forth.

When, at a certain time, there occurs a contact between the eye of the conscious self and a jar of the same class (the object), as well as with a cloth—a jar of a different class—and when the quality of "graspability" inheres in that which is conjoined with the eye, a cognition arises regarding the generality of "oneness" (*ekatva-sāmānya*) which inheres in those two [the jar and the cloth]. It has been stated that the knowledge of a qualifier is the cause of the knowledge of the qualified; since the generality of oneness is a qualifier of those two [objects], it is precisely that knowledge which is being considered here. Furthermore, since visual cognition does not arise without a sense-object contact, the impossibility of a relationship other than "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyukta-samaveta-sambandha*) for the generality of oneness is shown by this demonstration of the relationship.

Thus, when knowledge arises, because of the commonality of being the "root-villager" (mūlagrāmakatva), there is a connection with the number one; from the lack of knowledge regarding that [connection], a cognition arises which expresses the state of having a single quality belonging to multiple substrata, due to the internal presence of the quality of oneness.

Since it is impossible for both [the sense organ and the internal organ] to reach the object simultaneously, and because there is no cognition of a second [object] when one alone is always perceiving its object, the absence of that [second perception] serves as the distinguishing mark. Rays of light emerge from the eye and perceive the object together with the sound; just as in the case of a lamp situated within a house, [light reaches objects through] apertures, so too the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the cause of the experience of sound. Because there is no outward exit due to the connection with the object, its connection with multiple locations of the senses is the cause for the arising of knowledge.

This being the case, although cognition indeed occurs simultaneously with respect to multiple objects due to the completeness of its causes, only one [cognition] arises therein, because the soul’s conjunction with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has the capacity to produce only a single cognition at once.

For this very reason, when the aforementioned soul is manifested in such a way that it serves as the basis for multiple cognitions, the conjunction of the soul with the internal organ—which possesses a multiplicity of clear impressions (*saṃskāra*)—is capable of producing a single recollection of multiple objects.
Even if a single cognition were to arise from a soul possessing multiple qualities, what does that matter?
Thus, these two [entities] initiate duality through the practice of oneness by means of a cognition that has them as its object and their own individual qualities.

In this process, the two objects are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the two qualities are the non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the cognition having multiple objects is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). When a single cognition arises from two qualities, duality is initiated by those two identical natures; such is the illustration of a single cognition.

Due to the impact of the sense organ, the object, time, and the intellect, as well as the impact of the ear, there is indeed a temporal distinction between cause and effect; thus, the production of cognitions and so forth occurs because of their relation to prior and subsequent times. This is not an extraordinary or unestablished fact, since we observe the production of that sound from broken pieces [of a vessel]. Nor is it the case that production is never seen even in external objects, for by accepting that "that-ness" (tadatva) is merely a specific quality (*vaiśeṣya*), the capacity to produce cognition is distinguished in both types of sounds.

If it is argued that since the nature of both [the two objects] consists of qualities, their manifestation as a duality is established, and thus the cognition is inseparable from that possession [of duality]—this is not so, because it would lead to the consequence of lack of restriction (*aniyama*). For if duality were not born of cognition, it would be perceived by another person as well, just like atoms and so forth, due to the absence of a restricting cause. But if it is born of cognition, then the restriction is logically established: it is perceived only by the one whose cognition makes it known.

The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: Duality is produced by cognition, because it is necessarily perceived by a single cognizer; whatever is necessarily perceived by a single cognizer is produced by cognition, just like pleasure and so forth. And duality is necessarily perceived by a single cognizer; therefore, this too is produced by cognition.
[The author] now defines the cause for the perception of the property (dharma) that arises from duality.

"Then again," [means]: after the production of duality (*dvitva*), knowledge arises with respect to that generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānya*). Even for one who is ignorant [of the specific], the cause is indeed the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasambandha*). The word "again" (*punar*) is appropriate with reference to the generality of yakṣahood (*yakṣatvasāmānya*). The generality of duality is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the quality of duality; and a cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) does not arise when the qualifier has not been perceived. Therefore, as the cause of the cognition of the qualified, the knowledge of the generality was described first.

Now, even regarding the cognition of two, the cognition of duality itself—qualified by the generality of duality—is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); and for the existence of that [cognition], the cognition "two substances" is the means of valid knowledge.

Since the cognition "two substances" is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), it is preceded by a cognition of its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñānapūrvaka*), just like the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*); thus, when the cognition of the quality (duality) is inferred, its being preceded by a cognition of its own qualifier is likewise established, as it too is a qualified cognition.
However, there are those who maintain that the cognition of the qualifier and the qualified arises from a single [simultaneous] cognition.

The refutation of their argument is as follows: Who indeed is capable [of such a claim]? For the sense of smell does not grasp an object within the domain accessible to the eye, nor does it take up a substance. Therefore, because the mode of being a perceptible object (*pratyakṣatva-prakāra*) is dependent on the restriction that it must be a direct perception characterized by substantiality (*dravyatva-prakāraka*), the mode of being a perceptible object—just like number (*saṃkhyā*) and so forth—is not the cause of sensory-produced recognition (*pratyabhijñā-pratyakṣa*), which has as its object a cognition colored by the form of non-substantiality (*adravya-rūpa*). Likewise, they study [the following]: "Sound-ness (*śabdatva*), which is not grasped by the ear of a student, is produced; this causality, being of the nature of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of substances, is not the object [of that cognition]. Thus they pacify [the objection].
Even that is not contradicted, because it is free from defects.

If cognition were capable [of grasping both], then it would be possible to establish a distinction such that one part of the object is produced by the act of grasping and another part is prior; however, this [cognition] is a single, undivided whole. If it grasps both the odor and the substance, then it follows that the odor is visible and the substance is accessible to the sense of smell, because their status as objects of the resulting cognition is uniform, and thus their perceptibility by those respective senses would be identical. Nor is it possible for the mind—due to its atomic nature—to avoid being an organ [simultaneously] for the distinctness of qualities; therefore, even against one's will, one must accept that the odor is first grasped by the nose, and subsequently, by the eye acting as an auxiliary to that [nasal perception], this specific cognition is produced which has only the bare particular (nirviśeṣa) as its objective support.
And likewise, this same principle applies elsewhere even to the cognition of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).

The cognition of a qualifier under dispute has as its objective support only the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), because it is a perception produced by the power of the cognition of the qualified object, like the cognition "fragrant sandalwood.
The phrase "because it is a perception" is intended to exclude [the case of] the *itikartavyatā* (the procedural means).

Now, if the mere nature of the substance (*dravyasvarūpamātra*) were the objective support (*ālambana*) for the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣyajñāna*), then even when the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is absent, there would be such a cognition. Alternatively, if it is argued that because the qualifier is the producer [of the cognition], the cognition of the qualified arises only when it is present—even so, since this is merely the nature of the substance, there would be no distinction [in the cognition]; for there can be no other distinction in a cognition except through a distinction in its object. Nor could it arise from a non-valid source (*apramāṇa*).

We do not say that the object of specific cognition (*viśeṣajñāna*) is merely the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the substance; rather, it is the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*). And this "qualifiedness" (*viśiṣṭatā*), which appears in the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*) as something distinct from the essential nature, is indeed not perceived there as a separate category (*padārtha*), nor as the conjunction with a staff. Thus, in the cognition "the man with a staff," it is precisely the mutual exclusion (*itaretarabhāva*) that is perceived as distinct, and its differentiation consists simply in being delimited by the staff. For this very reason, the qualifier is called the "excluder" (*vyavacchedaka*).
For a staff (*daṇḍa*) distinguishes a person from others precisely by means of its own being delimited [by the person];
and this alone is its utility as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Even a secondary indicator distinguishes [the object], but it is not the cause for the cognition of its own mere being delimited [by that object]. For just as in the case of "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), the state of being delimited by a staff is cognized in the person, it is not so in the case of "one with matted hair, honey, and milk" (*jaṭā-madhu-payas*); there, the state of being delimited by matted hair is not [cognized] in the one characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*). Furthermore, the predominance of the person [over the staff] follows from the usage of the suffix *ini*, which disregards any excellence [of the staff] over the two signs (*liṅga*).

If that is so, then the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) would not be real; furthermore, what would be the object of cognition? In the case of [the expression] "the destruction of the jar," is the connection real? Enough with this elaboration; [this has been addressed] in the summary verses regarding the perishing entity.

When both [the cognition of the universal and the cognition of the quality] lack a further object of apprehension, it is called "cognition of such a kind" (*evambuddhi*). Because that [cognition] is a cognition of a dual-natured universal (*dvirūpasāmānya*), the universal of dual form is the cause of destruction; because it is related to the quality of dual form, the cognition of the quality of dual form is the cause of production. Thus, the cognition of the dual-natured universal itself is the destroyer of the non-cognition and the producer of the cognition of the quality. Therefore, the very production of that [quality-cognition] is metaphorically designated as the state of perishing for one and the state of being produced for the other; this is the conceptualization of identity between that which is perishing and that which is being produced.

Therefore, the destruction of the cognition [of the specific property] is itself the cause for the destruction of the two-fold form, because that [destruction] is not perceived as long as the cognition exists; thus, by this very fact, the destruction of the cognition is the state of perishing for the two-fold form.

As it is said, "In the case of a duality of qualities, [destruction occurs] due to a distinct cause," just as the destruction of the cognition of absolute non-existence follows from the destruction of the body when auditory perception has ceased.

Furthermore, the cognition of the two-fold quality is the cause for the destruction of the cognition of the general property of the two-fold form, because there is a contradiction between the cognition and its opposite.

Likewise, since the substance-cognition is also the cause [of the quality-cognition], at the time of the arising of the cognition of the quality, there would be the state of being produced for the [substance-cognition] under consideration and the state of perishing for the other.
This refers to "the connection with the cognition of the two-fold quality.
The construction is as follows: the cognition of that two-fold quality and the connection [between them].

Immediately after that, the time [is as follows]: the arising of the cognition of two substances, the destruction of the two forms [of the substance], and the state of the cognition of qualities being on the verge of destruction.

Although duality does not exist at the time when the cognition "two substances" arises, it nevertheless serves as its cause; for the nature of a cause consists in its producing an operation corresponding to the production of the effect, since one cannot demand the continued existence of the cause at the very moment the effect is produced. But what need has this [duality] for existing at the time of the effect's production? And what operation is there distinct from the cause itself? It is not so with *śakti* (potency), because it lacks causal agency (*akārakatva*). Its operation is thus: it is the very cause of that [operation]. Nor is it the case that *śakti* is not a causal factor, for its causal agency consists in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), as there is no intervention. Otherwise, in the case of an arrow released at the moment of striking a target, the arrow—having already ceased due to the impact of the string and other factors—would lack agency regarding the piercing of the target occurring in a subsequent moment.

Immediately thereafter, from the cognition of the substance (*dravya*), there arises the destruction of the cognition of the quality (*guṇa*) and the state of the impression (*saṃskāra*) being produced; then follows the production of the impression and the state of the cognition of the substance being destroyed. In the subsequent moment, from the impression, there occurs the destruction of the cognition of the substance. Furthermore, the impression serves as the cause for the destruction of the cognition of the substance because it has that [cognition] as its object, since this would otherwise be inexplicable. By this, the production of the cognition of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also explained. Thus, by means of this sequence of the production and destruction of two forms, the production of consciousness and so forth is explained; he demonstrates this very process in this manner.
Even in the case of unity, the cognition of multiple objects arises from the cognition of many; and its destruction follows from the destruction of the cognitions of those many.
By this, the production of a hundred cognitions and so forth is also established. This concludes the definition of number as a quality.

Each individual impression (*saṃskāra*) is released by its own specific qualities according to their sequential attainment; because they do not arise simultaneously, there is no confusion. Even though the final cognition consists of eleven qualities—including the three hundredfold conventional usage—it is nonetheless a single synthesis of all conjunctions. When a single recollection arises regarding multiple objects, it is designated as "recollection" (*smaraṇa*). Furthermore, in the subsequent cognitions that are explained [as being] of this nature, one hundred cognitions are produced, or rather, all of them are indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they have as their object the knowledge of the three [factors] conjoined with the two [types of] impressions of all substances.

When many substances have been destroyed, at the end there arises a cognition consisting of a multitude [of atoms], such as "this is a hundred jars" or the like, which is produced from those specific [atoms] that remain after the destruction. Some maintain that because of the absence of a cause—whether it be the visual perception or the large-scale conjunction—the conventional usage [of the term "jar"] occurs solely within the range of the atoms and so forth.

Others, however, disregarding the conception of the fivefold nature within past [moments], maintain that the sense-bases (*āyatana*) consist of past substances alone, because they are brought forth by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). This excludes things such as a pair of moments which are absolutely non-existent, since they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). As for past [substances], there is no powerful obstruction of their existence in time; nor is it the case that they have been discarded, because when they are deposited in memory, they acquire the capacity to perform many functions consistent with their own momentary nature, thereby making possible their status as inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

And this being so, it is not the case that everything exists in the manner it is perceived, because [the nature of things] is established according to how they appear; for even if the past were capable of producing [an effect], and even if its status as a cause of manifestation were possible, the postulation of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) would be useless—this is not so, because [the cognition] presents that [past object] by way of having its form imposed upon it through the impossibility of its remaining in its original state without decay. However, the establishment of the latent impression occurs only when there is such a postulation.

Likewise, at the time of the cognition of a subsequent letter, even though the preceding letters have perished, they certainly possess the status of efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) in the cognition of the manifestation, clarity, and so forth; and just as this is the case, some understand them to possess the status of inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) as well. Furthermore, it is difficult to deny that the mind—which possesses latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—has the capacity to produce direct perception (*pratyakṣānubhava*) regarding external objects, even when its stability as a material cause for manifestation is weak.

This being the case, it is not the case that [the destruction] follows another kind of cause, because it conforms to the operation of the external sense organs. When two objects are clearly perceived, a second [cognition] arises; in that case, the destruction of this [first cognition] occurs solely from the destruction of the non-apprehension (*abuddhi*) characterized by its clear manifestation. However, when the first [cognition] still exists, its arising does not occur merely from the destruction of the non-apprehension; in some instances, its destruction may also result from the destruction of the substratum (*āśraya*). They say that when one substance possesses both substantiality and quality, there is no apprehension of "two," and thus [the cognition] is destroyed. In some cases, it is from the destruction of the substratum.
Explaining how this is so through direct perception (*akṣa*), he says: "Where... and so forth.

At the time when an action arises in a substance possessing a single quality (ekaguṇadravya) without its destruction, at that very same time, a cognition of oneness (ekatvasāmānya) arises with respect to that single quality and the [substance's] unity. In the subsequent moment, destruction is brought about by another inherence of action and quality; from the movement of the generality of oneness, there arises a cognition of motion and so forth. Then, at the very time when the conjunction that initiates the substance is destroyed due to the disjunction from both [parts], it follows that even in the cognitions of the parts and so forth, there occurs the destruction of the substance due to the destruction of the conjunction, and the production of the cognition of the two-fold generality (dvividhasāmānya). This is the desired sequence of time.

Then, at the time when the destruction of the subsequent cognition occurs due to the cognition of the two-fold universal (*sāmānya*), there is a destruction of the two-fold [number] because of the destruction of its locus and so forth, but not a destruction of the non-human (*apaiśāca*) cognition, for that is the cause; it is simultaneous.

Here, although the cognition "two substances" arises, there is no purpose served by the production of a duality that has already perished; nevertheless, the arising of an effect attained through the capacity of its causes does not depend upon a [prior] purpose, and thus an investigation into its production was undertaken.

Indeed, here at the time of the production of duality (*dvitva*), the destruction of the preceding cognition by subsequent cognitions and so forth has been demonstrated; and that is possible only if there is a mutual opposition (*virodha*) among those cognitions. Regarding this opposition, some maintain it consists in their occupying different moments (*kṣaṇabheda*), while others maintain it is non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*). Among these, I accept the former, as in the case of [the destruction of] a jar by a hammer-blow. This is an excellent garden—such is the nature of the cognition of duality itself.

Regarding the definition of contradiction as "the moment of destruction of one substance" (*dravya-pradhvaṃsa-kṣaṇa*), it is correct and reasonable to hold that a second cognition arises and, in the subsequent moment, destroys the preceding cognition.

However, if contradiction is defined by "non-coexistence" (*sahānavasthāna*)—whereby the arising of one cognition is the destruction of another—then since two substances would exist simultaneously, the non-arising of cognition would be impossible; therefore, the intention is that contradiction characterized by non-coexistence is not tenable. He states the following to refute this:
Regarding the phrase "How so? and so forth:

For, according to the position that [two qualities] cannot coexist, since the cognition of the absence of duality would destroy the duality at the very moment of its production, the duality would have already perished; and if the duality were destroyed simultaneously with the cognition of the quality, then the cognition "these two substances possess duality" could not arise at a later moment due to the absence of its cause.
To this, it is replied:
"Regarding the phrase 'to'dyakabuddhi' (the cognition of today): it refers to the cognition of duality. [The objection] 'it would not be sufficient,' etc., [is addressed by the following]."

If all of this were so, it would not be acceptable, for instance, in the inference of a person from a particular sound, where the cognition itself—characterized by the sound—is the mark (*liṅga*); even though that [sound] has ceased to exist and is no longer present, it serves as the mark for a specific person who exists in the past. Thus, even in the absence of the physical mark, the cognition arises from that very cognition of the mark. Similarly, at the same time as the cognition of the quality, duality (*dvitva*) perishes; yet, even though it has perished, the cognition "two substances" would arise from that mere cognition [of duality] alone.

Another, however, explains that the rain-producing action (*varṣakarma*) of a being who has attained speed through speech and mind is the inferential mark (*liṅga*). Thus, even in the absence of the rain-producing action as a mark, there is inference from the mere cognition of it.

This is not so; for here the rain-producing action is not the mark. Even if it were, its absence would indeed exist at that time, because that which has been brought about by its own cause and conforms to the reality does not perish. Therefore, this [explanation] is the same as the case of cold and rain.
He states the rebuttal:
"Not because of the cognition of a specific quality.
This means that the production of the cognition "there are two substances" occurs from mere cognition alone; this is because it is not for the sake of anyone's non-cognition.

Let it be that there is knowledge of the distinction; nevertheless, how does it arise from mere cognition? To this he says: "The determination of number is not [possible] through qualities. That is to say, a qualifier is the very nature of the qualified (*viśeṣya*), that which colors the qualified, and the cause for the cognition of the counter-correlativity of destruction (*dhvaṃsa-pratiyogitā*) in the qualified.

Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is non-existent to possess the quality of being an attractor (*anurañjaka*) or to be the cause of the cognition of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) of destruction; therefore, the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣyajñāna*) cannot occur without a prior cognition of the relation between the qualifier and the qualified. Thus, since the cognition of the qualified does not arise without a prior cognition of the relation between the qualifier and the qualified—because [otherwise] it would follow that there is no external object—it demonstrates that the meaning is difficult to establish. He shows this by saying:
"And so he says."

Because the inherent [quality], the inhering [substance], the delimitors, and the delimited qualities are the causes that delimit, there arises in some cases the cognition "in a substance" and in others the cognition "a substance"; these two cognitions of qualifier and qualified stand in a cause-and-effect relationship and possess the nature of cause and effect. By this, the author states through refutation that the qualifier possesses the property of coloring [the mind].
The point is that this does not exist for that which is non-existent.
He speaks of the distinction by filling out the gap with the word "prior" (*puraḥ*) to the cognition of the qualified, regarding the cognition of cloth and so forth as an intensified cognition.
"But it is not so," [he says].
An elevated cognition does not arise through a distinction of the mark (*liṅga*) for the sake of removing the subordination of the mark to the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*).
Therefore, they are expansions of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).

The meaning is that, when the word *nehi* is added [to the sūtra], the cognition "it is indeed in the substance" (*vai dravye*) is not equal to [the cognition] "it is with knowledge" (*jñānena saha*).
At the time of the cognition "it is indeed in the substance," even duality does not exist; how then could there be a grasping of it as qualified by that?
No.

Since duality exists in the substance during the moment preceding the arising of the cognition, even though all [the factors] possess the state of being in the preceding moment, there is indeed a distinction: "duality is in the substance" occurs in the moment prior to the arising of the cognition; thus, its status as a subordinate factor (upasarjanatā) is certainly established.
However, this must be stated here:

In the cognition "it is indeed a substance," just as the substance appears, so too does duality appear as a subordinate factor (*upasarjanībhūta*). However, it is not logical for a non-existent duality to appear; therefore, at that time, the cognition of the qualificand (*viśeṣyajñāna*) would have to be a cognition of something else entirely, since it would lack that [duality] as its objective support (*ālambana*) due to the absence of such a thing. To this, he replies: "Not from a prior cognition."

At the time of the cognition of the substance, duality has not yet perished; however, because the cognition of duality—which preceded it—and the cognition of the substance arise so rapidly, there is a failure to perceive the interval between moments, leading to the misconception that both duality and the substance appear in a single cognition. In reality, however, the meaning is that first there is the appearance of duality, and subsequently that of the substance.
Now, he provides an example consistent with the subject at hand, beginning with "Just as."

Just as from [the perception of] sound, a jar, or a letter, there arise sixteen cognitions—namely, the cognition of sound, the cognition of space, and the cognition qualified by sound—so too, for the sake of explaining the cognition qualified by duality and so forth, what has been said? Just as in the case of the cognitions of sound and the like, there is no misconception regarding the moment because it is not perceived due to its extreme brevity (*āśupatana*), so it is likewise with the cognitions of duality and substance. Furthermore, the claim made by some—that if the sequence were otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [duality] arising from the cognition of the substance—is incorrect; for this holds true even under the "killer-and-killed" (*vadhyaghātaka*) model. This is explained in the section on the killer and the killed.
By the passage beginning with "vyāmnatam" [it is said]:

if, when duality is destroyed due to dependence on the cognition of qualities, the cognition of the substance does not persist, then that [cognition] would be untenable even under the theory of the "slayer and the slain" (badhyaghātaka). He refutes this as well by means of this [argument].

At the time when the cognition of sublation (bādhā) arises, there is the destruction of the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) and so forth caused by that cognition of sublation. Furthermore, because it acts as a cause for the sublation of the previous [cognition], duality is produced; likewise, the residual impression is not the destroyer of that [duality]. Therefore, the production of the residual impression and of duality, and the destruction of the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitvasāmānyajñāna*) which is arising—these occur at one and the same time. Subsequently, at the time of the production of the cognition of the generality of duality, because the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*) is the cause of its destruction, the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) and the state of duality being about to perish occur at one and the same time.

Therefore, the destruction of duality—which is useless for the cognition of qualities—results in the non-arising of the cognition "two" that depends upon it at a later moment; thus, the same fault applies even to the "slayer-and-slain" (badhyaghātaka) theory.
He offers a resolution: "No, because the cognition of the aggregate is the cause of the mental impression (saṃskāra)."
Regarding the phrase "wherever he repels," and so forth:

the meaning is that the cognition of a collection—specifically the cognition of a substance qualified by the quality of duality—produces a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), whereas an extraordinary cognition (*alaukika-jñāna*) or an indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) does not; therefore, there is no destruction of this [collection-cognition] by the latent impression.

Regarding the claim made by someone that there is a specific fault [in our position]—namely, that if the cognition of the substance qualified by its qualities (*guṇaviśiṣṭadravyajñāna*) is the cause of the subsequent cognition (*apūrvajñāna*), then the nature of the two qualities (distinct from the substance) would be the object of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); whereas if the nature of the unqualified substance were the object of the means of knowledge when the cognition arises and perishes—that is, if the cognition vanishes, then in this view, simultaneous existence (*sahāvasthāna*) would never be attained, and consequently, there would be no "application of cognition" (*jñānopayoga*)—that is incorrect.
This is because [the opponent] might think, "The cognition is produced," and so forth.
I shall provide an explanation of this.
With the words "nanu" and so forth, [the opponent] objects; [the author] replies with "no.

Furthermore, the co-existence of the knowledge of the object to be destroyed and the destroyer within a single moment is not a fault, because it is not subject to the refutation based on the argument that "the application of cognitions would be simultaneous. This is because the objection regarding the presentation of the object to be destroyed has been negated.
He demonstrates this very point:

by means of the simultaneous occurrence of the application of knowledge (*jñānopayoga*), it is shown that [the soul] does not perish as it did previously, and thus its simultaneous existence is not negated.
Furthermore, in the case of the "slayer and the slain" model (*badhyaghātakapakṣa*), the application of knowledge does not arise simultaneously; therefore, there is no simultaneous destruction.
Co-existence [is impossible] because even in a single moment, when one [entity] has arisen, the second has already perished; thus he says, "not...".
The word *iti* indicates the conclusion.

"O sir, this [notion] that 'two' is established by all [means of knowledge] is utterly inconsistent; for duality is untenable because there is no proof for it. If you say that the cognition 'two' is the proof, we say no, because the defining characteristics [of such a cognition] are absent. For if the two objects to be grasped by the cognition were non-existent, they could not be either a direct experience (*anubhava*) or something else; thus, in both ways, it is untenable, because what has already arisen lacks duration, and what is yet to arise lacks existence. If you argue that past objects are graspable by cognition because they are its producers, we say no, because they lack presentness, which would lead to the absurd consequence that even the sense organ is a grasper [since it was a producer]. As for the nature of the producer, the formal inference (*anumāna*) is as follows: whatever possesses the specific nature of being a producer, it is not like the sense organ and so forth, because the effect arising immediately after it lacks the status of being an object of cognition. If you ask, 'What then is the "nature of being a producer" known to be?', then once again the status of the sense organ as a producer falls back upon us, since there is no distinction between them. If you say that the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of the cognition itself is the nature of the other [the object], we reply: it is illogical to say that the self-awareness of one thing is the nature of another. This is because a nature cannot be unknown, especially in the case of specific entities."

Now, it has been said that consciousness does not possess the nature of joy or sorrow; therefore, its self-awareness (*svarūpasaṃvedana*) alone constitutes the cognition of an object as it truly is, such that this [consciousness] is similar to the object.

Indeed, there is no such over-extension [of the argument], for it is not [determined] by the object in that manner. Furthermore, what is called the "object-directedness" (*arthonmukhatva*) of knowledge is simply its own singularity, and since there is no duality between knowledge and the object, it is not restricted to the object. Nor is it the case that the object [is determined] by knowledge, because otherwise [the relationship] would be impossible. And because both are mutually restricted, the relationship of perceiver and perceived between them necessarily requires a rule of uniformity (*ekarūpya*).
Furthermore, cognition regarding past and future objects is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because [the object] has not attained the status of being a cause.

If it is argued that there is a restriction on the relationship between object and subject such that the restriction of the state of being perceived and the state of perceiving constitutes the rule, then—since the state of being an object is simply the state of being perceived at a certain time, and the state of being a subject is simply the state of perceiving at a certain time—if their mutual restriction were such that whatever is the cause at one moment is the same thing at the subsequent moment, then everything would appear as a mere void.

If it is further argued that this restriction is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of cognition even when it is not produced by direct perception, then if that nature were without a cause, the restriction itself could not be established.

Now, if [it is argued that] because of the causal factor, the deity is the supervisor, what is the use of determining its intrinsic nature? We do not perceive that it conforms to that [nature]. Furthermore, it is said: that which produces and brings forth cognition is of such a nature for him, and not otherwise; for there can be no reliance on the eye alone, as cognition would perish [without form]. Otherwise, since mere consciousness devoid of form would be indistinguishable in all cases, the determination that "this is blue" and "this is yellow" would be untenable; consequently, there would be no cognition of the specific distinctions of objects.

For this very reason, they say that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which possesses the form of the object; and it is this [cognition], produced from the eye and other [senses], that connects [the self] with the specific [object] consisting of knowledge, and not the common sense-faculties and so forth.
As it has been said:
"It is not the dull sense-faculty that connects this [self] with the object."
Therefore, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the apprehension of the object of cognition (prameya) is its having the form of that object.
And it has been said elsewhere:

"Indeed, it is not logical that its cognizability [occurs] through determination alone, because that [determination] is common to all external objects; rather, similarity entering into it [the cognition] would connect it with the external object. To this, it is replied:

What purpose is served by a cognition possessing a form (*sākāra-jñāna*)? Does it apprehend the object, or its own form, or both? It cannot be both, because this blue [object] is always perceived as having multiple forms and aspects. Furthermore, it is not logical for an object to be inferred by means of cognition; for at the time when the object's own nature exists, it lacks conformity to the cognition, and at the time when the cognition conforms to the object, the object’s existence in the present is impossible. To claim that the present existence of an object is experienced by a momentary cognition is a contradiction of your own tenets, since that [momentary cognition] is itself what is to be grasped. Even if one were to concede that a specific cognition necessarily makes a specific object known and not everything—since there is no such identity (*tādrūpya*) between them—it has already been stated that neither "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) nor identity is a sufficient ground for such a determination.
If it is argued that the restriction to the form of that [object] is the cause, why does one cognition of blue not apprehend another blue object of the same form?

If it is argued that the nature of being an object of cognition (*grāhyatva*) is not something that can be imparted [to an object], even so, a single cognition of blue would have to be the apprehender of all blue objects, because there is no difference in their possessing that form (*tadākāratva*). Furthermore, since the status of being an object of apprehension cannot possibly exist through either its production from that [object] or its similarity to it—[otherwise] the sense faculty and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) would also be apprehenders, for cognition is produced from them as well; and in the case of an object, such apprehensibility would require both a restriction to the grasping of a specific object and the nature of being of the same kind [as the object].

Now, as for the view that the assistance of the object (*viṣaya-sahakārin*)— which consists in the non-inert nature of cognition (*ajaḍa-svabhāvatva*)— is the specific regulator by which cognition grasps the object and not the sense-faculty or the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because both the assistance of the immediately preceding condition (insofar as it aids in establishing the determination of the specific form) and the nature of being consciousness (which is the assistance of the immediately preceding condition insofar as it brings about the character of awareness) are common to all cognitions, whereas the non-inert nature of its own constitution is possible only when there is the form of blue in the cognition of blue; and since this alone is the regulator, cognition grasps the object through this much distinction— that too is without substance.

If it is argued that the purpose of specifying the *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition) as having the same object is this: that which imparts the form of blue and so forth to the consciousness is alone its apprehended object (*grāhya*), whereas in a continuous stream of consciousness (*dhārāvāhika-vijñāna*), the immediately preceding condition does not produce the form of blue and so forth; rather, just as in the case of [the cognition of] a jar, because that [form] arises [simultaneously], one correctly perceives through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the nature of consciousness is indeed the possession of the form of cognition itself—[we reply: those who postulate that "that which imparts the form of blue and so forth is the apprehended object" do not [accept] any other [factor] as such. Rather, the restrictive factor is the necessity of the very nature of being an apprehended object. If it is the case that this restriction exists due to the necessity of nature, then let it be so; for consciousness arises as having the nature of cognizing an object restricted by its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*). Even so, [the form] belongs to all substances by the necessity of their own nature, and not to the sense organs and so forth; thus, the form is not the cause [of the cognition]. For the act of cutting has the tree as its cause, such that it is connected with the tree and not with the axe; rather, there is such a nature between this [act] and the tree that it is restricted to this [tree] and not to another. Otherwise, the determination of "all cognition" would be undermined.

Because it is based on the cultivation of that which is ungraspable, its causal efficacy is not perceived. Now, if [the object] is not cognized by a cognition through its branch-like [aspects], but rather only its own form is [cognized], then—though it is non-deviant and unwavering—it is not grasped from the perspective of worldly experience, nor is there a determination; for conceptual construction (vikalpa) is established as such, and even if the activity of apprehension occurs here, it does not serve to establish perception as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, while perception is the subject at hand, one who abandons self-contradiction and adopts the nature of the cause brings about a great deal of confusion.

If, however, direct perception itself is what cuts through [the object], and likewise conceptualization is also incapable because of the absence of a cause; and if it is argued that the form of cognition—having its own cause—is established as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when it is struck by the object, then what now becomes of that statement regarding the gross form arising from a difference of moments and its externality? Therefore, the gross appearance within consciousness belongs to its own nature, not to the object.

Since [the object] is fixed as a single entity, the arising [of multiple cognitions] is not possible. Now, if it is argued that even when not being displayed, it is perceived at some time by someone from some cause as having a certain form—like a woman [seen in a dream]—or that it will exist as such, this is replied to: furthermore, in the theory of forms (*ākāravāda*), the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous forms of cognition is not easily established, as has already been largely demonstrated.
Moreover, in that case, the form of the external object would necessitate the postulation of many causes over a long period of time.
If it were understood that whatever is the form of the cognition (*buddhyākāra*), such is the cause of the form of the object (*grāhyākāra*), then [the objection would hold].

However, as long as the object is not distinct from the cognition, such a perception is impossible, because the determination of a cause depends upon the ascertainment of its suitability for producing the effect. Thus, the theory of forms (*ākāravāda*) is not refuted. Furthermore, being a cause is not the defining characteristic of the apprehended (*grāhya*); nor is the difference in form the cause, since that lacks the defining characteristic of being apprehended. Therefore, let it be concluded that there is no object of experience for the cognition.

Even if it were granted that there is no object distinct from cognition, since an insentient thing does not manifest by itself and we do not perceive any other illuminator for it— because at all times only a single form is perceived—
nevertheless, if there is an illuminator, then an object that is itself unmanifest and of an unmanifest nature could not be manifested by it.

That which has manifest illumination is unmanifest, just as an object obstructed by a wall or the like; and the external object of another [cognizer] has unmanifest illumination. Furthermore, that which illuminates another must be similar in kind to it in its own manifestation, just as a lamp [illuminates other objects while being itself manifest].

And since cognition is the illuminator of another, it is understood—by the principle that "only consciousness that is itself manifest can illuminate an object"—that cognition possesses the capacity to illuminate an object only when it is itself manifest.

If that were so, then because of the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), there would be non-difference between the object of cognition and the cognizer, just as in the case of the omniscient one and his knowledge. For difference is pervaded by the absence of the rule of simultaneous perception; since blue and yellow are not necessarily perceived simultaneously, the rule of simultaneous perception is contradictory to the absence of such a rule. Thus, through the perception of what is contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), the rule of difference—which is pervaded by [the absence of] simultaneous perception—is excluded, and the opponent is defeated; thus he is established in non-difference. This is the "piercing by contradiction" (*pratibandhyaviddha*). Furthermore, the word *ṣaṅ* (six) does not mean simultaneity (*yogapadya*); rather, it must be explained as "coming from the same sense-organ" (*ekākṣa-kṣetra*). Otherwise, one might say: "Bring the six cows," or "Enter the six caves. Moreover, since the "sixfold state" is merely a conceptual construct (*ābhimānika*) and not a specific causal qualification, it is not taken up [as a valid reason]. In the case of the fallacious example, the "cutting of a sword" is a conceptual construct, not a real unity of the two blades. Just as all things perish gradually along with their own nature, there is no production of the qualities and words in all living beings. Nor can it be said that this is "not unsteady" or "not the Lord," for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). The simultaneous perception based on the conceit of being visible is not a visible fact; likewise, in the case of the eye, it is restricted to the two eyes, yet each is not perceived individually. What then is intended? The rule of simultaneous perception is not based on the conceit of identity among names, nor is there simultaneous perception of consciousness with every continuum (*santāna*), because it is possible for everything to appear at some time as mere self-awareness (*svātmamātra*). Nor is it the case that at that time there is no possibility of all things appearing to everyone. Just as a cook is seen by the eye, so too, whatever is known by a cognition is not different from it—just as the self is to knowledge. If they were different, blue and other objects would not be knowable by that cognition, because there would be no cause for the restriction [of the relation], namely identity (*tādātmya*). It is said: because there is no restrictive factor, if one thing were knowable by another unrelated thing, there would be no peace. Since the pervasive cause of restriction—the relationship—is not perceived when there is difference, the negation of difference and so forth is understood. Thus, knowability is pervaded by non-difference, and the connection of the reason is established.

By this, the non-difference of even the cognition having the form "I" from [the object] is established. That which appears as a separate nature in these cognitions of external objects is an error, like the appearance of two words for a single thing in a single word. Thus, [cognitions] such as "I am indeed the primordial Brahman" and so forth are also based on that [same principle].
As it has been said:
"In the final consciousness, which has differentiation as its intrinsic nature, two kinds of objects are seen within.
Now, if this cognition arises bearing the forms of blue and so forth while external objects exist, what is its cause?
As it has been said:
Now, this [cognition] which has the form of the perceived object is qualified by that [object];
whether that [object] comes from something external or otherwise, it does not fall within the scope of investigation.
Furthermore, they say:

"If it is asked what the cause is for the existence of external objects appearing in forms such as blue and so forth, [we reply: such a thing is not perceived, because the object (*artha*) is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). If it is argued that it must be inferred through its effect, which is cognition, then let one rather infer the diversity of potencies belonging solely to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), by which it is consistent with the cognitions in dreams; for in those cases, there is no efficacy in objects separated by space and time, as they do not exist."

But in that case, there would be no manifold cognition either; for since cognition is unitary, it would be impossible to distinguish it from perception, and if cognition were to differ according to each form, then because each cognition would be restricted solely to its own respective form, there would be no apprehension of all forms as distinct from those individual cognitions.
To this we reply:

One should not first produce [the object] as a Buddha, nor should one manifest it, because that would contradict the nature of consciousness; furthermore, for that which is insentient (*jaḍa*), manifestation is impossible. Therefore, one should produce it as being essentially of the nature of cognition (*jñāna*). Nor is there a difference in cognition due to a difference in forms, because there is no difference in form within each individual [cognition], just as blue is a single [entity].

The form [of cognition] consists of the nature of blue; likewise, the very nature of variegation (*citratva*) in a single [cognition] is its form. It is within that very cognition, which constitutes its own essence, that everything functions in its entirety, or else it does not function at all; it does not function partially, because that [cognition] is partless (*nirbhāga*). As for these parts that appear as mutually distinct, they do not constitute a variegated whole; thus, no causal effect is possible. A gross form (*sthūlākāra*) should also be established by this same line of reasoning.

In this regard, some maintain that just as a gross [object] is metaphorically designated as "cognition" because it possesses various parts—since it is impossible for that [cognition] itself to possess multiplicity—the form of cognition existing within a single cognition is indeed one and gross; however, distinctions such as sequential or non-sequential must be established as specific features of consciousness (*saṃvit*).

Others, however, having accepted that even the form of cognition—which appears due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is incapable of withstanding analysis, they assert its ultimate reality.

And thus, whatever is a cognition has an external object, just like the cognition of dreams and so forth; and because it is a cognition, the cognition of pillars and the like [must have an object]. For the state of being without an object is invariably concomitant with the absence of the nature of being a cognition, as seen in dreams and such; since the very nature of a waking cognition is its status as a cognition, if it were to abandon the state of being without an object, it would thereby abandon its own nature.

Now, if all cognitions were without an object (*anālambana*), then the cognitions of the locus (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would likewise be without an object. Thus, due to the absence of the locus, the reason, and so forth, the operation of inference (*anumāna*) would be impossible. If it is argued that they do have objects, then there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*) from the reason. This is not so, because those [cognitions] which appear to have external objects function merely as causes for the occurrence of knowledge consisting of mere conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti-mātra*). For instance, the perception of phonemes (*varṇa*) arises from the letters inscribed on a palm-leaf manuscript; and since the phonemes convey meaning, the object itself is also real in its own right.

It is true that they are real, yet they do not convey [the object] in its actual form; rather, they convey it by superimposing a form such as "crow" (*kāka*) and so forth upon it. Thus, the utility of the effect resides in what is unreal; this constitutes the first part of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). As for what was stated previously—that there is no connection with an external characteristic (*bāhyalakṣaṇa*)—that is not the meaning. In the convention of the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*), the substance characterized externally would not be graspable, and thus there would be no apprehension of it there. If it is argued that even for something graspable, like a *piśāca* and the like, there is non-apprehension due to a delusion regarding its own nature, and that the proof of non-existence follows from the non-apprehension of what is otherwise capable of being grasped—then how can its capacity (*yogyatā*) be free from contradiction?

For that [object] is not graspable by the intellect; if it were perceived as a real entity, there would be an incompatibility with the definition of being graspable. Furthermore, an object is not graspable by itself, and cognition is restricted to its own self-nature; thus, the fact that anything other than that [cognition] is ungraspable is established merely by this. If it is argued that it is ungraspable simply because there is no graspable object, then that is a matter for doubt.

Moreover, regarding what you have stated concerning the perceived, you must explain: what constitutes the apprehensibility (*grāhyatā*) of the form of cognition? It cannot be its being a cause of cognition, for it is not distinct from it; nor can it be its being the possessor of the form, because two forms would then have to be experienced; nor can apprehensibility consist simply in being of the nature of cognition, because even during deep sleep, although there is the experience of the "mass of cognition" which is of the nature of cognition, there is no apprehension of it as an object.

If it is argued that its very state of being necessarily cognized constitutes its "graspability" (*grāhyatva*), then there would be an absence of the form of the cognition itself, because [the cognition] would be abandoned due to being bound by another cognition. If it is further argued that this results in the attainment of fitness for practical activity (*vyavahāra-yogyatā*), then the same fitness would apply to the external object as well; for instance, when one says "this blue is indeed yellow," the speaker grasps or rejects the external object itself, and not an internal form—thus, for one who does not know [otherwise], the definition of the graspable would be inapplicable. If it is asked how something produced in one thing can possess fitness for the practical activity of another, the answer is: because of the restriction imposed by the nature of the cause of its own form, it is produced with a nature conducive to the practical activity directed toward that object. This is established by reasoning.
By this, the objection beginning with "the Vedas" is also refuted.

Even though [the object] arises solely through the restrictive power of the cause, which is the nature of cognition (*jñāna*), and because it is subject to doubt—despite the fact that what is insentient (*jaḍa*) cannot be manifest—nevertheless, this must be examined with the intention of [showing] that it does not have manifestation as its essence, and with regard to the possibility of doubt concerning lightning and the like; for there is no royal decree stating that the perception of manifestation will not occur for the insentient. Just as an action is connected to and differentiated by two factors, so too the action of cognition is connected to and differentiated by two. For even the restriction of apprehension involves the bringing forth of objects and so on; since the restriction of the apprehension of blue and such arises precisely by taking up the state of cognition being cognized both by itself and by another, while accompanied by doubt.

If it is argued that because external objects do not exist, cognition cannot be the perceiver of another [object], then the proof of the non-existence of the external would entail the loss of the very reason for that argument; and if that [non-existence] were established, then its status as a probans for the absence of an object would result in a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). Let that [circularity] be; what is the use of this? If it is argued that the necessity of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*)—as in "this is blue"—is established because at that very moment there is the experience of the internal experience of that [blue], and thus the necessity of simultaneous apprehension is established once the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of cognition is proven; then we ask: what is the proof for the establishment of self-cognition? If it is argued that whatever is manifest is self-manifesting and independent of another, like a lamp; [we reply: there is a contradiction in a lamp producing the cognition of such an object, and since that [contradiction] is produced by the lamp itself, it does not depend on another lamp, as that would be redundant. However, for its own perception, it does depend on eyes and so forth. If this is your intended meaning, then let it be so. Alternatively, if "being a manifester" is what you intend by cognition, and therefore it is independent of another at that time, then that is an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) probans.

If internal cognition (*pratyātmaka-prakāśa*) is self-luminous, then just as a conch shell or similar object is covered [when not perceived], so too for that which is covered there would be non-manifestation; yet because it is self-luminous, its form exists as if directly perceived—thus a contradiction is established. As for the argument that "because it is not an object of cognition" (*apratyayatvāt*), that too is worthless, because the example is unestablished. Furthermore, even words like "self" (*sva*) and "dream" (*svapna*) do not manifest their own nature as being self-luminous, since they are used as designations for things superimposed with an external character; otherwise, the novelty of the cognition's own nature would not occur. Moreover, since names such as "self" and so forth are applied based on how things appear, otherwise even the experience of what was previously seen or died would not be grasped, as there would be no rule governing the arising of that [recognition]. Furthermore, if the external does not exist, what is it then that is perceived in a restricted form as "this is blue"? If you say this is the form of the cognition itself, then because the subsequent awareness perceives [the blue] without perceiving [it as] cognition, if it were the form of cognition, the perception would have to be "I am blue. If you argue that because the forms of cognitions of blue and so forth differ individually, one person has the perception "I" while another has "this is blue," [we reply] that there is no fixed distinction between the form "I" and the form "blue" within the cognition of blue.

And so, if one is perceived as "I," then another is perceived as "you. If it is argued that in one's own self-awareness there is the manifestation of "I," then does the awareness of another also exist? If it is argued that even through one's own craving, the apprehension of difference occurs due to delusion, then why would the difference perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) not belong to anyone [as real]?
