When two dyads—one earthy and one watery—consisting of a cause and a non-cause, are mutually conjoined, such that the earth atoms are the causes of the earth dyad while being non-causes of the other watery dyad, and the water atom is the cause of the watery dyad while being a non-cause of the other earth dyad; from the conjunction of these two, a conjunction arises between the earth atom (which is a non-effect) and its effect, the earth dyad, as well as with the water atom (which is a non-effect). Similarly, a conjunction arises between the water atom (which is a non-effect) and its effect, the watery dyad, as well as with the earth atoms (which are non-effects). In this manner, the production of substances occurs.
What is the reason?
Being asked what the proof is for the conjunction of dissimilar atoms in the case of the dyads (dvyaṇuka) composed of earth and water particles, he states the proof:
"By that which is conjoined with the cause."
An earth atom is conjoined with a water dyad because it is conjoined with the cause [of that dyad], like a thread conjoined with a jar.
For this reason, even the first atom must be stated to be the object of action (*prayojyatva*).

Since an effect is conjoined by that which is conjoined with its cause, the mobile earth dyad is conjoined with the water atom which is conjoined with its cause; and the water dyad is conjoined with the earth atom which is conjoined with its cause—this is the conclusion.

Now, one asks: "How is there a connection between the earth-dyad and the water-dyad, which are connected respectively to their own non-causes and to each other's causes? For the earth-dyad is connected to its own non-cause—the water-dyad’s cause, namely a water-atom—and the water-dyad is likewise connected to its own non-cause—the earth-dyad’s cause, namely an earth-atom; how, then, is their mutual connection established? He provides the answer: "Of those two atoms... [and so forth].

The conjunction produced by the conjunction of an earth-dyad with a water atom, and the conjunction produced by the conjunction of a displaced dyad with an earth atom—by means of these two conjunctions between the earth and water atoms, there occurs a mutual conjunction of the two dyads.
Here too, the previously stated principle applies: "the effect is conjoined with that which is not its cause, by means of that which is conjoined with its cause.
Thus, it has been stated that conjunction is of three kinds.
Some maintain that this is because even an eternal conjunction is possible; he refutes that [position], saying:
"There is no unproduced conjunction, because it is not mentioned separately, like the spherical [atoms]."

Since all the great sages have taught that there is no conjunction of atoms (*ajaḥ saṃyogaḥ*)— as it is not mentioned separately by way of question or answer in any of their instructions— it does not exist, like a flower in the sky;
for this very reason, he refutes [the opposing view].
Regarding that which is produced:
in the proposition that "conjunction is not unproduced," it is not further argued that "unproduced conjunction does not exist," because [that would be] purposeless.
Now, one might object: the conjunction between atoms and space is eternal, because both of them are eternal and thus lack the capacity for being produced.

As for the fact that this was not stated by Kaṇāda, it is because it is a point of contention (*pūrvapakṣa*) arising from error; therefore, he says: "by means of atoms, [there is] of ether and so forth. Even though its root has been explained as being absent, if one considers the moment delimited by conjunction and disjunction—whether due to the absence of both the root and its opposite, or whether the root exists—the atom is simultaneously perceived. Likewise, even in the case of ether, conjunction and disjunction with the atom are objects of cognition; since these two do not exist as pervading or non-pervading [respectively], there is no permanence to the conjunction of the atom and ether.

First, this inconceivable [objection] has been refuted by the Lord: that there can be no mutual conjunction or counter-action among all-pervading entities (*vibhu*) within moments other than their own; nor is it produced by the action of both, because they lack the desire to grasp one another;
nor is it born of conjunction, for in effects, a conjunction born of conjunction occurs between a non-cause and that which is conjoined with the cause.
And this is not possible for all-pervading entities, because they are eternal.

Furthermore, there is conjunction for them; for even with a substance that has a spatial form (*mūrta*), [space] is always conjoined, because it possesses conjunction with substances having spatial form, as is understood through the analogy of a cloth. And since that [conjunction] is not due to a variety of causes, this statement—that "conjunction is unborn" and does not exist—is untenable. To this he says: "Of those residing in two. Conjunction is observed only where there is separate existence (*yutasiddhi*). Since separate existence is absent in space and so forth, conjunction does not exist there; thus, by the absence of the pervader, conjunction also cannot be the cause.

Furthermore, the proof stated to establish conjunction is not a valid means of proof, because it applies equally to both sides; for it asserts conjunction between each of the all-pervading entities (*vibhu*), yet we shall likewise refute that through reasons and examples. If it is argued, "Let there be [conjunction] for both by means of a means of knowledge, since such [conjunction] is not perceived," we say no; for if one of the two—conjunction or disjunction—is eternal, the other is impossible, and thus neither is established due to their mutual exclusion. Now, as for this lack of separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*), since it does not exist, conjunction is not found between the two; to this, he replies: [The text continues with the refutation of the opponent's position regarding the nature of conjunction and the impossibility of its existence.]

Furthermore, "separate existence" (*yutasiddhi*) consists in the separate existence of either one of two things; however, for eternal things, there is no separate existence of either one by way of mutual exclusion from the other. This is because this [separate existence] does not exist in the case of space and so forth, which reside in both [loci]. Let it be that for all [non-eternal things], conjunction exists until their disjunction.

Due to the force of action in either one [of two bodies], even that conjunction of an inactive [body] is destroyed by a disjunction inherent in the same substrate as that [conjunction]; thus, the conjunction of each of the two [bodies] occurs, and their mutual destruction arises solely from their mutual disjunction.

Although conjunction exists at the time of disjunction, nevertheless, their coexistence is not obtained because of the obstruction caused by the disjunction that has already arisen or by the non-arising of that [destruction]. In some cases, the destruction of conjunction also occurs through the destruction of its substratum; how so? In reality, while conjunction exists, even when the collection of qualities in the constituent parts of either [body] undergoes disjunction, [the conjunction is destroyed].

Regarding the production of action: because of a specific cause, that action brings about the state of being superior, inferior, and so forth; through the division of two visible objects, there is the destruction of their conjunction; upon the destruction of that [action], there is the destruction of the conjunction dependent upon it, because when both substrata remain in that same state, the conjunction is no longer perceived.
Disjunction (vibhāga) is the cause of the cognition of separation;
it is also the cause of the separation of sound.
Disjunction is non-attainment preceded by attainment.
And that [disjunction] is of two kinds:
produced by the action of one [of two things], and produced by the action of both; and disjunction is [further divided into] disjunction [from conjunction] and [absolute] disjunction.
Among these, that produced by the action of one or produced by the action of both is like the splitting of a bamboo stalk.
That which is produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja*) is of two kinds: from the disjunction of the cause and from the disjunction of the effect from its non-cause.

Regarding the first, when an action has arisen in a cause that possesses specific effects, it produces a disjunction from another constituent part but not from a location such as space; whereas when it produces a disjunction from a location such as space, it does not [at that same time] produce a disjunction from another constituent part—such is the established rule.

Therefore, the action of a part initiates disjunction from another part; from that disjunction follows the destruction of the conjunction that originates the substance. When that [conjunction] has perished, there is an absence of the effect due to the absence of its cause; thus, there is the destruction of the composite whole. At that time, the disjunction between the two causes—having as its own nature the time characterized by the destruction of the effect, or depending on the state of the parts—initiates a disjunction of the very part possessing motion from a location such as space (ākāśa) that was conjoined with the effect, and not from a part devoid of motion. This is because, in the absence of a cause, there would be no production of a subsequent conjunction, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of the action being non-consummated. However, that action of the substance does not produce a disjunction from a location such as space at that time, because the moment for its initiation has already passed; yet it certainly produces a conjunction with another location, since there is no lapse of time for an action whose conjunction remains unimpaired.
How [is it] also from the disjunction between the cause and the non-cause?

When, following a disjunction produced by the internal accumulation of action arising in the hand, a disjunction is initiated that is perceptible through the sensation conducive to disjunction, and then a conjunction is initiated in another location—at that time, those disjunctions between the cause and the non-cause initiate disjunctions between the effect and the non-effect with respect to the direction toward which the action is oriented and facing which the effect is about to arise; and subsequently, from the conjunctions between the cause and the non-cause, they initiate conjunctions between the effect and the non-effect.

If the production of the disjunction of the effect follows immediately after the disjunction of the cause, and the production of the conjunction of the effect follows immediately after the conjunction of the cause,
then surely it would follow that the parts and the whole are simultaneously subject to the same motion.
This is not so.
This is because of the thorough understanding of *yutasiddhi* (separate existence).

Furthermore, that [separate existence] is defined as the necessity of both or either one of two things possessing separate motion; whereas for eternal things, it is inherence (*samavāya*) in separate substrata.

In the case of the tactile sense-organ and the body, there is no possession of separate motion, but there is inherence in separate substrata; thus, their mutual conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is established.
In the case of the ear and sound, although there is no other substratum, conjunction and disjunction are established because one of the two possesses separate motion.
However, since the threads and the cloth are non-eternal and lack another substratum, there is an absence of mutual conjunction and disjunction between them.
Furthermore, since direction and the like do not possess separate motion, there is an absence of mutual conjunction and disjunction among them.

The destruction of every disjunction, however, is momentary because it has a subsequent conjunction as its limit; thus it is momentary. But disjunction is not merely the cessation of conjunction, for [as stated] in the *Guṇagrantha* on disjunction: "Why does the destruction of disjunction not occur, just as in the case of the cognition of being conjoined? Because there is no continuous connection of the separated [object], and because that [disjunction] does not exist when those two substances are conjoined. Thus, it is momentary.
In some cases, destruction occurs precisely through the destruction of its substratum. How so?

When a motion has arisen in one part (*aṃśu*) of the cause of a two-threaded cloth (*dvitantuka*), and it effects a disjunction from another part, at that very same time a motion arises in the other thread; and from that disjunction, there is the destruction of the conjunction that constitutes the nature of the substance. Then, by the motion of the thread, a disjunction from the other thread is produced—this constitutes a single moment of time.

Therefore, at the very moment when the destruction of the conjunction of the threads occurs due to disjunction, at that same moment, the destruction of the threads occurs due to the destruction of the conjunction; and when those [threads] have been destroyed, there is the destruction of the disjunction from another thread which was dependent upon them.
Thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that no further disjunction of the threads could arise, because of the absence of a disjunction of the cause.

Consequently, since there would be an absence of conjunction in that which possesses conjunction with another location, and because a contrary quality is thus impossible, the fault arises that [the substance] would exist for only a moment as its substrate, and that what is inherent in an eternal substance would itself be eternal.
How so?

When an action produced by the conjunction [of two atoms] causes a separation from one part while it is still in conjunction with another, at that very moment an action also occurs in the other atom. Then, at the same time that the destruction of the conjunction constituting the substance [the dyad] occurs due to that separation, a separation from the other atom is produced by the action in that second atom. Then, at the same time that the destruction of the conjunction of the dyad and the atom occurs due to that separation, the destruction of the dyad occurs due to the destruction of its conjunction; when that [dyad] has been destroyed, there is the destruction of the separation from the atom which was dependent upon it. Consequently, because the quality of disjunction exists only as long as the substance exists, the permanence of the separation from the eternal [atom] is established.
It should be understood that there is a distinction between the disjunction of the two principles (*tattva*) themselves and the disjunction from another principle.

Because the substratum has perished, the disjunction of the two principles itself is destroyed, but the disjunction from another principle is not. Therefore, a subsequent disjunction arises through its own momentum, just as the disjunction of the body from space arises from the disjunction of the atom from space. At that very moment, the action, having produced conjunction, perishes; thus, there is no fault.

Alternatively, at the very moment when the disjunction from another thread arises, action is produced in that same thread; then, from that disjunction from another thread, there is the destruction of the conjunction that initiated the substance [the cloth], and by the action in the thread, a disjunction from another thread is produced—this constitutes one moment.

Then, from the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the thread, and from its destruction, there is the simultaneous destruction of the disjunction and the action residing therein.

When there is a conjunction between the thread and the vīraṇa grass, the two substances being destroyed, the destruction of the disjunction between the thread and the vīraṇa occurs through the aforementioned process involving the destruction of the substance and the conjunction.
Since disjunction is preceded by conjunction, he states the following in order to define it immediately thereafter:
"Disjunction is the cause of the state of being separated.
Here too, the explanation is as before.

If it is argued that "the absence of conjunction results in the effect of disjunction," then why is there no production of the absence of conjunction when disjunction is absent? If it is asked whether this is brought about by action (*karman*), [we reply] that we observe the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) for the destruction of one quality by means of another quality. Furthermore, the causality of qualities is observed in the destruction of qualities; therefore, in this case as well, another quality must be postulated.

Furthermore, if there were no conjunction (*saṃyoga*), then even the presence of qualities such as manifestness (*udbhūtatva*) would have to be perceptible; yet this is not the case, for even when [the parts] are disjoined (*vibhakta*), there is no perception of it due to its very nature of being imperceptible. If it is argued that the cognition appears despite the absence of light, then since disjunction (*vibhāga*) cannot be denied, there would likewise be an appearance of the cognition of the object itself.
He demonstrates its effect:
"It is said to be the cause of sound and disjunction."
The meaning is not merely that what is divided causes the division of sound;
rather, when a sound is being recited, that sound which arises from you (the speaker) must have disjunction as its cause, because it is a sound, like the sound produced by the snapping of fingers.

Nor can it be produced by conjunction, because there is an absence of such [conjunction] here; therefore, just as in the case of a jar, it must be produced by disjunction, and its manifestation is brought about by that disjunction.
We shall explain later that disjunction (*vibhāga*) is the cause of disjunction.

Its definition is stated as "non-attainment preceded by attainment. Just as the negative particle (*nañ*) in the term *adharma* refers to another quality (*guṇa*) that is opposed to dharma, and not to the mere absence of dharma; so too, the negative particle in *aprāpti* (non-attainment) refers to another quality opposed to attainment, and not to the mere absence of attainment. The meaning of the sentence is this: disjunction is that specific quality opposed to attainment which exists when attainment has previously occurred.
What is established? Is it that the previously mentioned [conjunction] serves as a cause for disjunction, or is its function merely to maintain [the state]?
We say it is merely maintenance.

For if conjunction were the cause of disjunction, then immediately after the conjunction of two [substances], that very disjunction would arise, which would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-production of the substance.

If it is argued that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) acting as a cooperative cause (*sahakārī*) is the cause [of disjunction], then—given that the capacity [to produce disjunction] is inseparable from [the action itself] based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—let action alone be the cause, not conjunction; for even when that [action] exists, [disjunction] does not necessarily occur. Furthermore, there is a rule of temporal priority: action precedes the production of disjunction, and conjunction precedes the production of separation, because disjunction has a nature that is the opposite of conjunction.
The phrase "having reflected" (*vicintya*) is stated to indicate a distinction.
Here too, the word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of "having reflected."
There is disjunction produced by the action of one [of two things], or disjunction produced by the action of both.

Among these, accepting that it is produced by the action of one alone—just as in the case of conjunction, where the conjunction of a moving thing with a stationary thing is born of the action of one—so too is disjunction. Or, just as conjunction produced by the action of both occurs only when there is mutual movement, so too is disjunction.
The phrase "but disjunction produced by disjunction is of two kinds" uses the word "but" (*tu*) to state a distinction between this and what was previously mentioned.
There is a twofold division of disjunction: one arises from the disjunction of two causes, while the other arises from the disjunction of an effect and its non-effect.
Furthermore, the disjunction resulting from the disjunction of causes is described by the phrase beginning with "kāryādiṣu" (in effects, etc.).

When a cause that has arisen from action occupies a delimited space—that is, when it produces a disjunction that destroys the substance-initiating conjunction between that part and another part—it does not at that time produce a disjunction from a location such as space; and when it produces a disjunction from a location such as space, it does not at that time produce a disjunction from another part. This is the established rule.

Therefore, the action of a constituent part initiates disjunction only from another constituent part, because there is a rule that an action which is the cause of disjunction from space does not produce disjunction from another constituent part; hence, the action that initiates disjunction from another constituent part produces disjunction only from that other constituent part, and not from a location such as space.
This is the intended meaning.

The agency of [the hand] in the disjunction from space and so forth is pervaded by the non-production of a disjunction that is contrary to a conjunction consisting of a substance; and the production of a disjunction contrary to a conjunction consisting of a substance is contradictory to the non-production of a disjunction contrary to a conjunction consisting of a substance. Therefore, when something is perceived in this manner, and its state of not producing a disjunction contrary to a conjunction consisting of a substance is ascertained, its agency in the disjunction from space and so forth is also ascertained through that medium.
This is just like the pervasion of smoke being pervaded by fire.

If it is argued that there is no pervasion (vyāpti) because there is no possibility of deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the agency of producing divisions such as space, and because [such agency] does not initiate divisions that are contrary to conjunctions consisting of substance, we say no; for no deviation is observed.

Since no deviation is observed between the two—namely, the occurrence of motion upon the earth and the absence of coexistence—just as in the case of a diamond (*vajra*), where although both "stoneness" (*pāṣāṇatva*) and "metalness" (*lohatva*) are present, metalness is absent in wood and other such things despite the presence of stoneness; likewise, no deviation is seen between the agency of dividing space and the non-production of a specific division. Even if one were to suspect that such a deviation might have occurred or will occur in the future, it would imply that the coexistence of these two—which are neither the subject nor the pervader—is perceived as being caused by some external limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Even so, it is not the case [that there is no pervasion], because conditions (*upādhi*) are not perceived. For if deviation (*vyabhicāra*) were to occur even when [conditions] are unperceived, then pervasion would be non-existent; since this undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*) follows, it has already been stated that the certainty of pervasion is established. Thus, the talk of inference in this world revolves as before. If the action of a part produces disjunction from another part and not from a locus such as space, what is established by that? He says: "For from disjunction comes the destruction of conjunction, which consists of substance."

The meaning is that if [the self] were the agent of the division from space and so forth, then because a specific division would not arise, the destruction of the conjunction constituting the substance would not occur. He asks what would happen if that conjunction were destroyed, and then says: "In that case... (tasmin).

When that conjunction—the cause consisting of the grove and so forth—is destroyed, then by the principle that "in the absence of the cause's operation, there is an absence of the effect," there occurs a disjunction of the parts. Once the whole has been destroyed, what happens when [the parts] are destroyed? To this he says: "Of the existent" (*sataḥ*).

When the substance has perished, there is a disjunction of the two parts which are its causes; having waited for a specific time characterized by the destruction of the effect, or for the parts to become independent, it initiates a disjunction of the active part from the space such as ether that was conjoined with the effect.

As long as the effect-substance has not perished, the self-originated [disjunction] lacks the capacity to serve as the locus for the first [subsequent] disjunction; thus, disjunction from the location of the whole is not possible. Having considered either the time characterized by the destruction of the effect within that lineage, or the independent collection of parts, he asks: "What is the reason? regarding the claim that "the disjunction arising between two causes produces disjunction only in that which possesses motion. He replies: "Not in that which is devoid of motion, because of the absence of a cause."
But since disjunction arises from disjunction, it would be a sequential efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*);

and because that [subsequent disjunction] is absent, disjunction would not be possible for that which is devoid of action. Therefore, he says: "If there were no production of a subsequent conjunction, there would be the consequence of impossibility."

For action generally accomplishes some human purpose by means of a substance that, through a subsequent conjunction, has reached another location. In that case, if there were no division from the location of the aggregate of effects—such as space and so forth—due to the pervasion of power, then, because the obstructing factor residing in the previous location would not have ceased, the qualities reaching the other location would fall [unimpeded], or else the wind and so forth would be experienced as having no spatial extension.
But this is untenable.
Therefore, they say that division occurs precisely within the power itself.

This [disjunction] of two unchanging [substances], which would be like the division of space and so forth, is not possible as something transferred through non-distinction. As was stated previously, since the action of the quality of conjunction occurs in a sequence, what contradiction is there in one part of that sequence? For what reason should one abandon the production of disjunction—which is observed to be the cause of separation—and instead resort to the unseen capacity of disjunction as the cause of action? To this he says: "But it does not produce disjunction from the parts of that [substance] or from places such as space, because it arises at the same time as the sequence consisting of those [parts]."

For just as, from the successive [actions], an inherent nature arises—by virtue of being the cause for the substratum of those parts—which manifests its own existence as a state of disjunction in the moment immediately following its own production, and not in any other moment; and since that time of its existence as disjunction has already passed at the time of the production of the second moment, there is no production of a state such as conjunction. Therefore, it does not perform the movement to another location either, because of the intervention of multiple moments. For this reason, he says:
"It effects conjunction with another location."

Just as from successive actions (krama) there arises time consisting of disjunction (*vibhāga*) in the moment immediately following its own production, so too there arises time consisting of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with another location in the moment immediately following the cessation [of the action] that occurred in the previous location. Since the substance situated in the previous location has attained another location, and since the passing away of that time consisting of conjunction has not yet occurred—that is, it has not been transcended—it would follow that this is indeed the time of those [actions]. Therefore, the conjunction with another location is produced by the very actions themselves. Consequently, because there is no passing away of the time consisting of conjunction belonging to that which has not yet performed the conjunction, it does not perform a conjunction [again], nor does it perform a disjunction. And thus, because there is no absence of what has already been performed, and because a substance cannot arise without a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), it is established that disjunction is the cause of the arising and other effects of this [substance].

The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the present topic. For those who wish to understand how disjunction preceded by the disjunction of causes and non-causes is itself brought about by depending upon a disjunction, he asks: "How [is it] even from the disjunction of cause and non-cause? He provides the answer:
By means of a regional ruler and so forth.

When, due to a cause, a sequence of production occurs in three [substances] held in the hand—specifically, when, following the disjunction from the hand's substratum, there arises a disjunction from space-points such as those occupied by a crown or other ornaments—and at that time those disjunctions between the cause and non-cause do not initiate conjunctions with other space-points; then those disjunctions between the cause and non-cause are the disjunctions of the hand (the non-cause of the body) from the space-points of ether and so forth which are non-causes of the body. Furthermore, with reference to that direction in which the conjunction of the parts of the effect must be produced in the form of the effect itself, there arise, through the disjunction of the cause and effect, the disjunctions of the hand (the effect) from the space-points of ether and so forth which are non-causes of the body.

Since the disjunction of the body is observed from that very place—such as a wall—from which the disjunction of the [hand] occurs, and since this [disjunction] is seen to be the effect of the action of the body, it cannot be the effect of the action of the hand because the body is then devoid of action; thus, the difficulty of [proving] deviation is avoided by observing the [necessary] concomitance.
Therefore, it is stated that the cause is the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause.
The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "ether, etc. (*ākāśādi*) is for the purpose of indicating the purity of space and so forth.

For this very reason, the plural number in the phrase "from the divisions" (*vibhāgebhyaḥ*) is intended to signify their manifold branches, because of their multiplicity. Furthermore, since the division from a location such as a wall and the subsequent division of the body are perceived simultaneously in a single cognition, the assertion that these two stand in a relationship of cause and effect is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That is irrelevant;
for at the time of the hand's division, there is no cause for the production of a division of the body.

Nor does an effect arise from an incomplete cause, and it has already been stated that the action of the hand is not the cause [of the body's division]; therefore, the conclusion shown in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* is untenable.

If it is argued that inference is accessible [only] for a mere moment, whereas the sense-faculties are simultaneous, and that in perception there is no arising of inference at all because its object is not uncontradicted—how then can the validity of perception be established in accordance with that [inference]? [We reply: This is like piercing the layers of a lotus petal; the ground of the "kṛtalakṣa" mark is [established] because it does not contradict perception.

Now, you might think that an inference is urged there because it contradicts perception, such that the sublation of the object by this [inference] would be certain; however, in this case, even though it is impossible for a single sense organ to grasp a hundred words with extreme distinctions, it is possible for perception—which grasps simultaneity—to function as the probans (*liṅgin*). Furthermore, there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is well-known to all the world: "Cognitions are distinct when separated by a very great distance, but not when merely separated. Therefore, since the causal complex for perception is present, an inference can indeed arise.

And since there is no deviation in this case—namely, that action does not produce disjunction—the inference of sequence is well-established, because the means of valid cognition that grasps the pervasion is too remote and because perception would otherwise be inexplicable.

For this very reason, the sublation of perception by means of an inference is suspected; for indeed, a perception that has already ceased is both objectless and incapable of exerting influence prior to the occurrence of [the subsequent cognition]. Since it subsequently ceases to exist, its sublation cannot be reached. Thus, whether strong or weak, it is devoid of assistance from an objectless state. Therefore, just as in the case of the grasper of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no sublation among perceptions [by another perception]; rather, it is only when there is a sublation of perception by means of an inference [that sublation occurs].

And thus, the Buddhas consider that by the very inference "I am situated in two [places]," it is indeed more powerful; for they maintain that inference is indeed stronger than even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

However, because direct perception is accompanied by a multiplicity of cognitions, there is no simultaneous apprehension of another [object]; therefore, when the object is sublated by that [perception], the operation of inference does not occur. Why, then, is the absence of perception (*pratyakṣābhāva*) postulated as a sublating factor in this case? It is because of the specific nature of the conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*) regarding this object.

The meaning is that it makes known something contradictory to what is already established; and since this is the very nature of reasoning (*yukti*), there is no possibility of its occurrence here because it would involve the production of a totality of reasons. Indeed, because these two [cognitions] exist by way of mutual exclusion, there is a contradiction between them. Thus, when there is a contradiction between the cognition of existence and the cognition of non-existence due to a conflict regarding their objects, the conceptualization of the relationship of sublated and sublator occurs. What is sublation? It is the removal of the object.

Now, one might object: just as in the case of an illusory cognition of silver and the like, even when another cognition has arisen, that [silver] necessarily appears; since its silver-ness does not exist at all, what is it that is being negated? [The answer is: It is for the purpose of removing the specific relation [of the qualifier].

If you say that when consciousness manifests, [silver] appears as "existent" (*sat*), then it is true that it appears; however, this manifestation does not constitute a verbal appropriation (*śabdāpahāra*) because it is simply a fact of experience. For that which has manifested does not become non-manifested by way of its actual status (*vastuvṛttyā*). Even though silver is non-existent there, it is presented by cognition as if it were existent. If you argue that its "qualification" (*viśeṣaṇatva*) consists merely in establishing an external contradiction to what was shown by that cognition, then once the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the silver is established, what harm is done to the cognition of silver? For this [cognition] has no operation toward the cause of the silver’s persistence; rather, it has already accomplished its own manifestation. Thus, what is sublated (*bādhyate*) by the previously established [fact]? When asked, "What is the harm?"—the answer is: the harm is that the nature of the subsequently arisen cognition of silver is perceived as being non-conformable to reality (*ayathārthatā*).

[Objection: "In that case, sublation (*bādha*) would simply be the removal of the result (*phalāpahāra*), because knowledge is conducive to practical activity (*vyavahāra*) only when it is not a cognition of something unreal. [Reply: Not so. For the removal of the result is necessarily concomitant with the removal of the object (*viṣaya*). Furthermore, it is not the case that all knowledge is restricted solely to its result; for knowledge arises from the desire of a person and is dependent on other factors, such as the prior force of past impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), even when it does not produce [an action] based on that desire.

Even though there is a desire for the result (*phala*), nevertheless, because the result is dependent upon its object (*viṣaya*) and the desired [result] is dependent upon knowledge (*jñāna*), it is precisely the sublation of the object that constitutes the sublation of the knowledge, not the sublation of the result, since the latter is necessarily concomitant with the sublation of the former. Enough of this elaboration; this has been established in the *Saṃgrahaṭīkā*. Following the discussion on division and non-division, he demonstrates the connection regarding the conjunction-born nature of that which was promised when asked about what arises subsequently.
[He says: "Immediately after that."

Therefore, immediately after the disjunction produced by that [initial] disjunction, due to the conjunction of the hand—the cause of the body—with space and the points of space such as the eastern direction, there is no commencement of the conjunctions of the body—the effect of the hand—which is itself inactive, with space and the points of space such as the eastern direction; for the action of the hand is the cause of its own substratum reaching another location. The word "destruction" (kṣati) signifies the completion of the sequence. Now, if it is argued:
Regarding the word "yadi" (if):

if the disjunction of the effect, the body, were to occur immediately after the disjunction of the cause, the hand, and likewise if the conjunction of the effect were to occur immediately after the conjunction of the cause, then it would not be simultaneous with that [cause] at the seventh moment. And this is because, such being the case, the observed [phenomenon] would be inconsistent with its status as a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

Separate existence (*pṛthaksiddhi*) would mean mutual independence, as in the case of substances, qualities, and actions. If the body were separate from the hand, then when the hand moves, the body should also move; likewise, it would possess conjunction and disjunction with the earth.

If conjunction and disjunction were not produced by the action of the two [the hand and the body], then when the hand moves, the body would not move; consequently, it would follow that the body possesses independence [from the hand]. He refutes this, saying:
"No."
"O friend, [the term] 'yutasiddhi' has not been established [as a valid definition], because the [actual] state of *yutasiddhi* (separate existence) has not been abandoned.
The meaning is that you have not understood the nature of *yutasiddhi* as it truly is.
He states its definition in the following verse.
Separate existence (*yutasiddhi*) consists of two things being established separately as distinct substances, or the capacity for inherence that does not cause mutual conjunction or disjunction.

In the case of two atoms, it is the possession of separate motion; or, in the case of either one of them, it is the separate motion [of one relative to the other]. This, however, pertains to eternal substances.
[Examples include] the cutting of thirst, and shadows.

In our view, "of eternal [substances]" (nityānām) is to be understood as meaning that for eternal substances alone there is "separate establishment" (yutasiddhi). However, for non-eternal [substances], "separate establishment" is inherence (samavāya) even when they are conjoined. For two non-eternal substances—or for either one of them—inherence in a different substratum by means of mutual exclusion constitutes separate establishment; that is, the state of being supported by different substrata through inherence. As for example, in the case of a yarn and space, or of two yarns, it is the state of being supported by different substrata.

Although one of the two may indeed have separate motion, nevertheless that separate motion is not taken [as the definition of separateness] because it is explained as having only eternal things as its domain.
Why then is it not said that even for non-eternal things, separateness (*yutasiddhi*) consists simply in separate motion? To this he replies:
there is no separate motion of the skin-organ and the body; however, since they exist in conjunction within their constituent parts (*āpya*), their mutual conjunction is established.

If, however, "separate existence" (yutasiddhi) were defined as the separate motion even of impermanent things, then because there is no separate motion between the sense of touch and the body, they would possess non-separate existence (ayutasiddhatā). Consequently, their mutual conjunction could not be established, since that [conjunction] is pervaded by [the absence of] separate existence alone. Therefore, the meaning is that for impermanent things, separate existence is not separate motion. Since the two [types of] substrata do not exist at all in the case of eternal things, the state of being supported by separate substrata does not occur among them; rather, because they possess separate motion, their mutual conjunction and disjunction are established. With the intention that for these [eternal things], separate existence is indeed separate motion, he says:
Since there is no mutual dependence between the egg and space, and because one of them possesses separate motion, conjunction and disjunction are established [between them].

Previously, it was stated that even in the absence of separate motion, conjunction is possible between the sense-organ of touch and the body when they stand in the relation of substratum and dependent; thus, for non-eternal things, "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*) consists in having separate substrata, not in separate motion. This point has been supported by the example of the two horns on a cow's head; it now demonstrates the absence of conjunction and disjunction when, due to the impossibility of either possessing separate motion, there is an absence of separate substrata.
Regarding the phrase "of those two" (*tatpuṣṭyoḥ*) and so forth:

although there is certainly no conjunction or disjunction between the two substances when they are pure or when one of them is nameless, because disjunction is preceded by conjunction, he says "of direction and so forth" (*digādīnām*) to indicate that there is merely their own inherent existence.
To this extent, [the argument] regarding sound, conjunction, and its qualities [is refuted].

The body does not go when the hand goes; to this extent, there is no notion of corporeality [in the hand]. If, however, the hand and the body were to have the relationship of separate substratum and superstratum, then these two might possess the notion of corporeality; but that is not the case, because the hand is a constituent part (*avayava*) of the body.
As for destruction, it occurs in all cases because disjunction (*vibhāga*) is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*).

One might raise the objection: "How is it established that disjunction—whether produced by action or produced by another disjunction, whether residing in the cause or in the non-cause—is all-pervasive and yet subject to extremely rapid destruction?
To this, [the author] replies: "Because of the absence of a subsequent conjunction.
That is to say, disjunction is pervasive because it ceases upon the occurrence of a subsequent conjunction, just as the destruction of a jar occurs when it meets with a hammer.

However, while the division (*vibhāga*) perceived by the observer is indeed without limit, it nonetheless has a subsequent conjunction (*uttara-saṃyoga*) as its limit. Immediately after that subsequent conjunction, the destruction of the [original] conjunction occurs; therefore, the subsequent conjunction is the destroyer of the [original] conjunction. Since there is no pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the division, this very point establishes that [the definition], and not the word "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).

Just as a conjunction arises from the mutual division of its own two substrates, a division does not arise from the mutual conjunction of its own two substrates alone; rather, it arises from the conjunction of its substrate with something else as well.
For instance, when a liquid is separated from a substance by a person, that disjunction arises either from their mutual conjunction or from the person’s conjunction with another location.

If this is so, then it is not established that disjunction is non-pervasive with respect to subsequent conjunction, because the action that initiates it brings its own substratum to another place, thereby causing the cessation of the previous designation [of "conjoined"]. Now, one might object: even this [cessation] occurs upon the destruction of all conjunctions of the substratum; thus he says:
"Like the persistence of conjunction and disjunction.

Just as [the notion of] conjunction persists even when it is delimited by its own substratum, there is no persistence of disjunction once a conjunction with another location has occurred for that substratum; therefore, its cessation occurs merely through the removal of the conjunction. He concludes:
"Therefore" means that in some cases there is destruction even without [the destruction of] this [substratum]. The question arises from the desire to know how this is so.
The answer is as follows: "When" refers to the following:

when the capacity of the thread—the cause of the two-fold body—is exhausted, and the quality of disjunction initiates the conjunction and disjunction within itself, at that very same time, the effect—namely, the destruction of the conjunction that originated the thread—must also occur in the other thread. When that occurs, the disjunction from the other thread is produced by the action of the thread; thus, these events constitute a single moment.

Then, at the time when the destruction of the conjunction of two threads occurs due to disjunction—at that very moment, from the destruction of another conjunction, there is the destruction of the thread originated by them; when that thread has perished, there is the destruction of the disjunction between the [other] thread and the [remaining] thread, because its substratum has perished, just as the cause for the destruction of wood into ashes is the fire. Now, however, it is recognized again.

"Everything [arises] from that. The destruction of the previous disjunction is the subsequent disjunction; [this occurs] when the thread, possessing potentiality, undergoes all disjunctions and non-disjunctions with points of space and so forth, because of the arrival of the disjunction designated as "wood.
If the subsequent disjunction were not conjoined, what would follow? Thus he says:
Regarding the word "tataḥ" (thence):

because no subsequent division arises, the prior conjunction with the ether—which acts as an obstacle—is not removed; consequently, a conjunction with another spatial location does not occur for the pot. For this reason, since there is an absence of a subsequent conjunction of the substance and its qualities, there would be a sequence [of states] persisting over time until the destruction of the substratum, at which point it falls due to the removal of the cause of its support. Thus, the defect is that what inheres in an eternal substance would itself be eternal. The question "How so? is asked to clarify this.
He states the answer with the words "when" (*yadā*).

When the first corner [of a dyad] produces a spatial interval and so forth in the atom that constitutes its own self, at that very same time, it [produces them] sequentially in another non-compositional atom conjoined with the second corner.

Then, at the very moment when the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) perishes due to the disjunction and destruction of its two constituent atoms, and that dyad having perished, the disjunction between the dyad and the atom—which was dependent upon it—also perishes. Consequently, since there is no further limit (*kāṣṭhā*) to this disjunction, no new disjunction of the atom from space or other locations arises. Thus, because the prior conjunction has not ceased, and because the subsequent conjunction—which would be a contradictory quality (*virodhiguṇa*) acting as the cause of destruction—is impossible, the motion inherent in the eternal atom would be eternal by succession.
This, first of all, refutes what was stated previously.
"Disjunction [arises] from the disjunction following the production of the reality [of the effect].

The rule is this: when an effect is produced in a cause, it produces a disjunction of its own substrate from every other point of space, etc., occurring in a sequence, but it does not produce a disjunction from the location of space, etc. [itself].

Because that which does not produce a specific disjunction (viśiṣṭavibhāga) is pervaded by the non-production of successive spatial divisions [from space] and so forth, and because there is no other constituent part [to obstruct it], it indeed produces all [subsequent disjunctions] with whatever is conjoined to its own substratum, as there is no contradiction. Therefore, at the same time as the disjunction from another thread occurs in the two threads that are the cause of the double-threaded cloth (*dvitantuka*), those qualities [of the threads] initiate all the disjunctions with whatever is conjoined to the threads. And they say that this disjunction [from space] remains until the thread reaches the state of space; due to the destruction of the substratum, the disjunction between the two threads itself is destroyed, while the disjunction from the subsequent object [the cloth] remains in the threads.
If this is so, what follows? To this he says:
"From this," meaning from the non-separation of the two [atoms] from space, just like the non-separation of long space [from its parts].
Just as, for example, from the sequential disjunction of the drum from space arises the disjunction of the sound from space;
so too, from the sequential disjunction of the yarn from the shuttle arises the disjunction of the yarn from space—this is the illustrative point.

It is logical that from the disjunction of the sense-organ (e.g., the eye) from Indra [the deity] arises the disjunction of the body from the sense-organ; let this be so with the intention of referring to its own conventional usage.

If it is argued that [the soul] is directly perceived in the body because of the presence of breath and so forth, we say no; for there is no absence of bodily injury and the like [that would prevent perception]. How could there be a division of the soul from the body even through a division of the body? Now, since the body pervades its constituent parts, and since the senses and so forth are likewise [pervasive], when a finger or the like is amputated, the designation "body" does not cease because the collection of parts such as the fingers remains. Thus, when a division occurs—such as the cutting off of a finger—the previous conjunction which acted as an obstacle ceases, and a specific action proceeds; having produced a subsequent conjunction, the body then perishes. This is what he says.
Regarding "its establishment": because the substratum of the manifestation, the upward movement, and so forth has been destroyed, the disjunction perishes.
It perishes.

Simultaneously with the production of the disjunction from another thread, action arises in that very thread whose parts are being divided; then, from that disjunction, there is the destruction of the conjunction that initiated the thread. By that action, there occurs the disjunction of that thread from the other threads and so forth—at this same time. Immediately thereafter, due to the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the thread initiated by it. And from that destruction, there follows the production and destruction of the disjunction and the destruction [of the conjunction] initiated by it.
Regarding that point where it was raised that there is eternality for that which is eternally active, no formal rebuttal was stated there, because its meaning is extremely well-established.

For in the case of effects such as wood and the like, due to the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors, one observes that they do not produce all types of disjunctions—such as the manifestation of spatial divisions or illumination—because their capacity to act as agents of disjunction regarding the sense organs and so forth is conjoined with the nature of suffering and the production of conjunctions that obstruct yoga. However, in the case of an atom (*paramāṇu*) which is non-self (*anātman*) and conjoined with Brahma’s action, at the very moment of its disjunction from Brahma, it indeed produces all disjunctions simultaneously with respect to the space-points of ether. From that disjunction, when there is a cessation of the conjunction between atoms and a subsequent conjunction occurs, the destruction of the action initiated by that [conjunction] necessarily takes place. When a conjunction of similar kind (*samānajātīya-saṃyoga*) occurs and a substance (*dravya*) is produced, the destruction of the disjunctions occurs through the destruction of their substratum (*āśraya-vināśa*). On the other hand, when a conjunction of a different kind (*vijātīya-saṃyoga*) occurs and no substance is produced, the destruction of the disjunction occurs through both the destruction of the conjunction and the destruction of its substratum. Thus, the connection is established through the effect.
Thus, when there is a conjunction between the two threads, since no new substance is produced, [the effect arises] due to the previously mentioned cause, namely action.

At the same time that action arises in the two constituent [atoms] of the reality, there is an action in the *vīraṇa* grass; then, from the other side of the two sprouts, there is a disjunction, and by means of the action in the *vīraṇa*, all disjunctions are produced with its disjoining part, the thread, and the point of space. Then, from the disjunction of the atoms, there is the destruction of the atomic conjunction; and from the disjunction of the *vīraṇa*, there is the destruction of the conjunction between that [grass] and the *vīraṇa*, as well as the conjunction between the *vīraṇa* and space. Then, from the destruction of the atom-destruction, there is the destruction of that [conjunction]; and from the destruction of the atom produced by the conjunction of cognition and from the destruction of the subsequent moment-producer, there is the destruction of the destruction of the thread and the *vīraṇa*. This is the process.
Remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) are the causes of the cognitions of "remote," "proximate," and so forth.
These are of two kinds: produced by space (*dikkṛta*) and produced by time (*kālakṛta*). Among these, that produced by space depends upon a particular direction.
That which is produced by time (kālakṛta) indicates the distinction of age.
Among these, the production [of spatial direction] caused by space (dikkṛta) is now described. [Next is its] destruction.

When two objects situated in one direction possess a multiplicity of conjunctions through their connection [to a common point], a perceiver, having seen a grove from the south, produces a perceptual cognition regarding that which is the substratum of priority: "This is distant. From that, due to the conjunction with a spatial region that is remote in relation to the observer, there arises the production of priority (*paratva*).
Likewise, when the situation is reversed and one sees the nearer object, a cognition of proximity arises regarding the other, which is the substratum of posteriority (*aparatva*): "This is near."
From the conjunction with a spatial direction that is further away in relation to that [near point], the production of "remoteness" (aparatva) occurs.
Regarding those produced by time as well:

when two persons of equal age—one young and one old—are standing in front of a house, and upon seeing the wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth of the elder, a certain observer, having seen the younger person first, develops the cognition that the elder is more distant.

From the conjunction with a further spatial division of time relative to that [prior] one, there arises the quality of "remoteness" (*paratva*). Furthermore, having perceived an elder and seeing a youth, a cognition of proximity arises;
from the conjunction with a nearer spatial division of time relative to that [prior] one, there arises the quality of "nearness" (*aparatva*).

Destruction [of distance], however, results from the destruction of both the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) and the two conjunctions. First, regarding destruction by the destruction of the relative cognition: when, in the case of a jar, the cognition of the universal *ghaṭatva* (jar-ness) arises, at that same time the relative cognition begins to perish; and simultaneously with the arising of the cognition of the universal, there is the arising of the cognition of the quality of "priority" (*paratva*), because these are the causes for the destruction of the relative cognition. Thus, it is one and the same moment.

Then, from the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), there is the arising of the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*). Then, due to the destruction of the relative cognition, while the quality is in the state of perishing, and simultaneously with the cognition of the quality, the true nature of the substance, and the self-love, the cognition of the substance (*dravyabuddhi*) is in the state of arising; this is one moment.
Then follows the arising of the cognition of the substance and the destruction of the quality.
How [does it happen] also through the destruction of conjunction (*saṃyoga*)?

Simultaneously with the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), an action arises in the substratum of "remoteness" (*paratva*); by that action, a disjunction from space and the material object is produced; and from the relative cognition, the production of "remoteness" occurs—this constitutes one moment. Then, there is the production of the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) and the destruction of the conjunction between space and the material object. Subsequently, at the very moment when the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*) arises, the destruction of the quality occurs due to the destruction of the conjunction between space and the material object.
How [also] does it occur through the destruction of the substance?

When action arises in a constituent part that serves as the substratum for "remoteness" (paratva), at the very same time that it produces a separation from another constituent part, the relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) arises. Then, at the same time that the destruction of the conjunction occurs due to the [resulting] disjunction, remoteness is produced. Subsequently, from the destruction of the conjunction comes the destruction of the substance; and from its destruction comes the destruction of the quality (guṇa) residing therein. How, then, can there be destruction even from the destruction of the substance, the relative cognition, and the quality?

When action arises in a constituent part that serves as the substratum for "remoteness" (paratva), at that very same time, the relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) arises; by that action, disjunction from another constituent part is produced, and the production of remoteness occurs—this is one moment.

Then, at the very same time that the destruction of the substance-constituting conjunction occurs due to the disjunction from its own constituent parts, the cognition of the universal (sāmānyabuddhi) arises; immediately thereafter, the destruction of the substance follows from the destruction of the conjunction, and the destruction of the relative cognition follows from the cognition of the universal—this is one moment.
Then, from the destruction of the substance and the relative cognition, the destruction of remoteness occurs.

How [is it destroyed] even through the destruction of the substance, conjunction, and so forth? When an action has arisen in a part of the substratum of "remoteness" (paratva) and effects a separation from another part, at that very same time, the production of the cognition of priority (apekṣābuddhi)—which is the cause for the production of the quality—occurs within the mass. Then, at the very moment that "remoteness" arises, there is the destruction of the substance-constituting conjunction due to disjunction, and by the action of the mass, a disjunction between the two parts of the mass is produced; thus, these occur at one and the same time.

Then, at the very moment that the cognition of generality (*sāmānyabuddhi*) arises, at that same moment, due to the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance, there is the destruction of the aggregate (*piṇḍa*); and from the destruction of the aggregate, there is the destruction of the conjunction of the aggregate. Thereafter, simultaneously with the cognition of quality (*guṇabuddhi*), due to the destruction of the aggregate and the destruction of the conjunction of the two aggregates, there is the destruction of "remoteness" (*paratva*). How [is it destroyed] also from the destruction of the substrate (*āśraya*), which has been employed by the conjunction and the cognition of relative distance?

When "remoteness" (*paratva*) arises, then action occurs in the substratum of that remoteness. At the very same time that the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of remoteness arises, the disjunction of the two lumps is produced by the action of the [original] lump. Then, at that same moment, the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) follows from the cognition of the generality, and the destruction of the conjunction of the two lumps follows from the disjunction; thus, these occur in one and the same time. Subsequently, due to the destruction of the conjunction and the relative cognition, there is the destruction of the quality of remoteness within the group of five qualities. This concludes the determination of remoteness and nearness (*aparatva*).
There is also destruction through the simultaneous destruction of the three types of causes: the inherent, the non-inherent, and the instrumental.

When the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises, at that same time action (*karman*) occurs in the constituent part of the mass; then, at the very moment action produces a disjunction from another part, the relative cognition and the production of "priority" (*paratva*) occur. At that same time, action also occurs in the mass itself. Then, from the disjunction of the parts, the destruction of the conjunction that initiated the mass occurs; and by the action of the mass, a disjunction from the other mass is produced, while the subsequent cognition (*dāsānyabuddhi*) arises—all this constitutes a single moment.

Then, from the destruction of the conjunction follows the destruction of the mass; from the disjunction follows the destruction of the conjunction of the two masses; and from the cognition of the universal follows the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). Thus, all this occurs simultaneously through the destruction of the three causes—the inherent (*samavāyi*), the non-inherent (*asamavāyi*), and the instrumental (*nimitta*)—and thereby the destruction of "remoteness" (*paratva*) occurs.

"Remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) are established by the usage of the terms 'remote' and 'proximate. Remoteness is the cause for the designation and cognition of 'remote,' while proximity is the cause for the designation and cognition of 'proximate'; thus he demonstrates them by means of their effects."

Just as conjunction with space (ākāśa) regarding doors and so forth is the cause of the designations "prior" and "posterior" according to their respective locations—as is the case with the self—so too, although conjunction and the like are non-inherent causes (asamavāyikāraṇa) of priority and posteriority, there must be the recognition of another efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa), because a specific cognition cannot exist absolutely without a specific cause. Furthermore, both types [of priority and posteriority] are mutually dependent upon one another.
In that same way, that twofold nature—priority and posteriority—is of two kinds; this is the determination of their distinctions.
He explains that [the cause] depends on something else to some extent; he says this because of the observation of differences in effects.
"Produced by two" (*dvikṛta*) refers to that which is produced by both [time and yoga]; thus, there is that produced by time and that produced by yoga—this is the twofold [classification].
That which is produced by the conjunction with a mass of time is "produced by time.
One should understand that the distinction between these two has been established based on the difference in their effects; thus he says:

that which is produced by action (kriyākṛta) indicates a connection with two [actions], whereas that produced by time (kālakṛta) indicates a difference in age. Furthermore, priority produced by action (kriyākṛta-paratva) makes known the distance from the observer, while posteriority (aparatva) makes known the proximity to the observer. However, the distinction is this: priority produced by time (kālakṛta-paratva) represents the object's being characterized by a long duration of time, and posteriority (kālakṛta-aparatva) represents its being accompanied by a short duration of time.
In that regard, the possibility of such a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—even concerning that which is produced by speech and that which is not so produced—is thus refuted.
If one asks, "How so?", he provides the answer:
"In a single [instance]."

Since priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) cannot exist between two objects situated in opposite directions, it is stated that they must be "situated in one direction. When two objects are situated in the same direction—whether east or west—the distance of one from the other is determined by its conjunction with a point of space that is itself conjoined with and inherent in a more remote location. Because there is a multiplicity of such "conjunctions with what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*), the object possesses a greater number of these conjunctions than the other; this constitutes its "externality" (*bahiṣkṛta*) or "greatness" (*mahattva*). Consequently, that object is considered more remote than the other object. Thus, when the operation of priority is about to arise in an object possessing a multitude of conjunctions, the notion of remoteness first arises in that object. Then, depending upon that intermediate notion of remoteness, and through a conceptual process involving the multitude of conjunctions as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), priority is produced in the object which serves as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

Having rendered the distant object—which possesses a multitude of *saṃyuktasaṃyoga*s (conjunctions with what is conjoined) relative to its own cognition—visible to the eye, the mind arises directed toward that [object] which is excluded from the range of perception due to those *saṃyuktasaṃyoga*s. Taking that excluded mental state as an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), and by means of a conceptualizing process (*vikalpaveśa*) characterized by the non-perception of further *saṃyuktasaṃyoga*s, there arises in the lump (*piṇḍa*)—which serves as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*)—the quality of "remoteness" (*paratva*), produced by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

If it is argued that there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) because the cognitions of "external" (*bahiṣkṛta*) and "remote" (*viprakṛṣṭa*) are mutually dependent, we say no; for there is no mutual dependence. It is not the case that the cognition of "remote" arises by first perceiving the object as "external," nor does the cognition of "external" arise by first perceiving the object as "remote. Rather, having perceived the mass (*piṇḍa*) as accompanied by conjunction and ownership, the cognition of "remote" arises with respect to that which possesses a collection of conjunctions.

Previously, having perceived in a mass (piṇḍa) that which is accompanied by conjunction and accumulation, there arises through its cause a cognition of "external" in that which possesses conjunction and ownership; thus, these two do not depend upon one another.
How then [is this] for those produced by time?
First, the production of priority and posteriority produced by space has been explained; the question is: how is their production likewise [effected] by time?
"Conjunction [is restricted] to two things existing in the present time.

This means that when two things, or even one single mass, are being moved past [a fixed point], priority and posteriority do not arise; for that reason, it is specified "existing in the present time."

When two objects, such as a staff-bearer and a crow, situated in indefinite locations like a village or elsewhere—whether standing near or far away—are perceived simultaneously by a person, there arises in the cognizer a desire to know their relative distance characterized by time. Based on the qualities [of proximity and remoteness] observed in the causes of those objects, and having inferred through the measure of the staff-bearer, the crow, and so forth, that they occupy mutually distinct times, one forms the cognition "the staff-bearer is older" or "the crow is younger. This determination of priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) occurs within the category of qualities in relation to that cognition; it is said that, depending upon that cognition, the terms "prior" and "posterior" are applied accordingly.
Due to the conjunction with time-hatred as the non-inherent cause, the quality of "remoteness" (paratva) arises in that very elder, having made the younger person the proximate one.

A cognition of proximity arises; depending upon that cognition, through conjunction with a temporal division characterized by fewer revolutions of the sun—which is termed "remoteness"—there occurs the production of remoteness. Regarding the two substrates, the young man and the old man, the lesser degree of conjunction with time is what should be understood as "nearness," and not as a property of the individual entities themselves, for those perish every moment. Since they are produced, their destruction is inevitable, and since that destruction cannot be without a cause, [the author] states the cause for the destruction of priority and posteriority:
"the power of destruction."

The destruction of priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) occurs through seven modes: from the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), from the destruction of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), from the destruction of the substance (*dravya*), from the destruction of both the substance and the relative cognition, from the destruction of both the substance and the conjunction, from the destruction of both the conjunction and the relative cognition, and from the destruction of the substance, the relative cognition, and the conjunction.
The destruction resulting from the destruction of the relative cognition is explained as follows:
once priority has arisen, at the very same moment that the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of priority arises.
The word *tataḥ* here takes the suffix *tasil*, which is prescribed for the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhy-arthe*).
At this very same time, the "relative cognition" (*apekṣā-buddhi*) is in the process of perishing, as it possesses the nature of being a cause of destruction.

Generally speaking, there is a single moment [in which] the cognition of the universal (*sāmānya-jñāna*), the relation with that [universal] (*tad-sambandha*), the universal of "priority" (*paratva-sāmānya*), the cognition of the universal of priority (*paratva-sāmānya-jñāna*), and the relation with the quality of priority (*paratva-guṇa-sambandha*) exist; from these, the cognition of the quality of priority (*paratva-guṇa-buddhi*) arises. Thus, they are simultaneous.

The cognition of the generality of "remoteness" (*paratva-sāmānya-jñāna*) is the cause of the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣā-buddhi*) and the cause of the arising of the cognition of the quality (*guṇa-buddhi*). Therefore, while that [cognition of the generality] is being produced, the relative cognition is in the process of being destroyed, and the cognition of the quality is in the process of arising. Then, in the subsequent moment, there is the destruction of the relative cognition and the arising of the cognition of the quality of remoteness. Following that, due to the destruction of the relative cognition, the quality is in the process of being destroyed. At this same time, from the quality, the cognition of the quality, and their relation, the cognition of the substance (*dravya-buddhi*) is in the process of arising; thus, all these occur simultaneously.

The destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is the cause of the destruction of the quality; the cognition of the quality is the cause of the cognition of the substance; and the destruction of the relative cognition and the production of the cognition of the quality would occur simultaneously. Therefore, the state of being in the process of destruction of the quality and the state of being in the process of production of the cognition of the substance would also occur simultaneously. Consequently, there would be the production of the cognition of the substance qualified by "priority" (*paratva*) and the destruction of the quality of priority. When the question is raised as to whether the destruction of priority and posteriority (*aparatva*) also results from the destruction of their conjunction (*saṃyoga*), he says in reply: at the very same time as the relative cognition, an action (*karman*) arises in the object (*piṇḍa*), which is the substratum of priority.

In the next moment, by that same action, a disjunction is produced between the two parts of the substrate of priority, and simultaneously, the cognition of relative reference (*apekṣābuddhi*) and the production of priority (*paratva*) occur; this constitutes one point in time.

Then, once priority has been produced, the cognition of the universal of priority (*paratvasāmānya*) arises, and simultaneously, the conjunction of the two actions and their disjunction are destroyed; this constitutes another point in time.

Thereafter, at the very moment that the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*) arises from the cognition of the universal, at that same moment, priority is destroyed due to the destruction of the conjunction of the two throwing motions and the two fragments—not because of the destruction of the cognition of relative reference, for the cognition of relative reference is also destroyed at that very time.
He explains how destruction occurs even from the destruction of the substance:
"in the parts that are the substrata of remoteness."

The substratum of "remoteness" (paratva) is a substance that is yet to come into being. When that [substance], having arisen in sequence, undergoes destruction, at that very same time the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) arises. Then, simultaneously with the disjunction (*vibhāga*), there is the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance. At that same time, "remoteness" arises from the relative cognition. Subsequently, from the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the substance; then, from the destruction of the substance, there is the destruction of the quality (*guṇa*) residing therein. At that very moment, from the knowledge of the generality (*sāmānya*) of remoteness, there is the destruction of the relative cognition. Furthermore, from the destruction of the two moments, there is the destruction of the conjunction of the two fingers. Thus, these two possess the nature of being causes for many subsequent states.

How [is it destroyed] even by the destruction of the substance, the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), and the conjunction? At the very moment that [the relative quality] arises sequentially in a part of the substratum of "remoteness" (*paratva*), at that same time the relative cognition arises, and by means of action, the rotation of other parts and so forth is produced; the production of "remoteness," however, occurs at one and the same time. Then, at the very time when the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance occurs due to the disjunction of destruction, at that same time the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of "remoteness" arises. Subsequently, from the destruction of the conjunction, there is the destruction of the substance; and simultaneously with the arising of the cognition of the generality, there is also the destruction of the relative cognition—thus they occur at one and the same time.

Then, due to the destruction of the substance and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), there is the destruction of "priority" (*paratva*). Each of these two is a cause for the destruction [of priority] individually; for this reason as well, it is so. Furthermore, the determination of one or the other specific [cognition] is also a cause for the destruction of both. [This is stated] in the passage beginning with "also from the destruction of the conjunction with the substance," and so forth.

How does destruction [of distance] occur even from the destruction of the substance-conjunction? When the rotation of another part and so forth arises successively in a part of the substratum of "remoteness" (*paratva*), at that very same time there is the simultaneous production of the cognition of sequence (*piṇḍakrama*) and the non-apprehension (*upekṣābuddhi*).
