Then, at the very moment that "remoteness" arises, at that same time, through the disjunction of destruction (*pradhvaṃsavibhāga*), there is the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance; and by means of the sequence of the [original] mass, a disjunction is produced between the two parts. Thus, all this occurs in a single moment.

Then, at the very moment that the cognition of the universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*) arises, at that same moment, due to the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance, there is the destruction of the aggregate (*piṇḍa*); and from the destruction of the aggregate, there is the destruction of the conjunction with the aggregate. Subsequently, simultaneously with the cognition of the quality (*guṇabuddhi*), the sense organs have a cognition directed toward the qualities within the two aggregates. Due to the destruction of the conjunction with the aggregate, there is the destruction of "priority" (*paratva*). However, the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is not the cause [of the destruction of priority], because it is possible for the cognition of the universal to arise at that very same time.
There is also destruction [of distance] due to the simultaneous destruction of both conjunction and the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).

When "remoteness" (*paratva*) arises, at that time there is motion in the substance which is the substratum of that remoteness; then, at the very same moment that the cognition of the generality (*sāmānya*) of remoteness arises in the substratum of remoteness, a disjunction between the two forms of the mass is produced by the motion of the mass. Thereafter, from the cognition of the generality, the relative cognition is destroyed, and from the disjunction of the two forms of the mass, the conjunction of the two forms of the mass is destroyed—this constitutes one single moment. Subsequently, from the destruction of both the conjunction and the relative cognition, the destruction of remoteness occurs.

At that time, however, the destruction of the substance itself does not occur; therefore, it is not the cause [of the destruction of relative distance]. Rather, there is destruction through the destruction of the three types of causes: the inherent (samavāyi), the non-inherent (asamavāyi), and the instrumental (nimitta).

To the question—how is the destruction of "remoteness" (paratva) brought about by the simultaneous destruction of these three, namely the inherent cause, the non-inherent cause, and the instrumental causes, which consist of the substance, conjunction, and the cognition of relative dependence?—the author provides the answer with the words "When...
(*yadā*).

All of this occurs simultaneously due to the simultaneity of its causes; and consequently, from the destruction of the three causes—the inherent, the non-inherent, and the instrumental—there follows the destruction of "remoteness" (*paratva*).
This [mention] of the destruction of "remoteness" is an illustration; the same sequence of destruction should be understood to apply to "nearness" (*aparatva*) as well.
Buddhi, upalabdhi, jñāna, and pratyaya are synonyms.
And having concluded [the section on] "intellect and priority and posteriority," he asks: "What is intellect? and says:
"Intellect," and so forth.

The modification of the excellence [of the *sattva* quality] is the internal organ called the Great (*mahat*), which has "intellect" (*buddhi*) as its synonym and "mind" (*citta*) as another name. Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the function (*vṛtti*) of that [intellect], which consists of the quality of *sattva* and assumes the form of external objects through the channel of the sense organs when colored by them. Apprehension (*upalabdhi*) is the taking on of the form of that function by the power of consciousness (*cetanāśakti*) reflected in the intellect, which was previously colored by the forms of ignorance.

And so the Blessed Patañjali said: "For the power of the enjoyer is unchanging and non-transmigrating; yet, as if transmigrated into the changing object, it experiences its fluctuations. Regarding the phrase "the power of the enjoyer," its essential nature has been determined. And [it is] "as if transmigrated" (pratisaṅkrānteva) into the changing object—that is, into the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva)—meaning it is reflected therein. "It experiences its fluctuations" means that, being reflected in the intellect, it takes on the coloring of the intellect's activity and becomes an imitator of the intellect's fluctuations.
The object of cognition (*buddhi*) is the mental state (*pratyaya*) having the form of pleasure and so forth.

Thus, that very Blessed One said: "The person (*puruṣa*), whose nature is cognition, perceives the mental state in order to know it; perceiving it, he too becomes, as it were, of the same nature as that [state], and thus becomes directly perceived. To refute this view of the Bodhya school, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "buddhi" and so forth:
that intellect (*buddhi*) which perceives [objects] such as iron, leaves, or the moon is [merely conventional].

However, that which belongs to one who has seen the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), non-existent due to the very absence of cognitive apprehension (*pratītyabhāva*).

Since activity and cessation would occur due to the superimposition of the body and so forth—conforming to the material cause of the cognition of objects—as being that [cognition] itself, and since its modification would likewise result from the production of that [cognition], both [activity and cessation] are experienced as belonging to the self (*ātman*) and not to any other luminosity. Furthermore, regarding this awareness of cognition, is it different from cognition or not? It cannot be different, because [if it were], there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*anaikāntika*), as it is admitted that even the self possesses the function of hearing.

Furthermore, if the intellect (*buddhi*) were a single entity, then because those [mental states] that possess the forms of objects would also be one, the cognition of a variegated intellect would be impossible, since there would be no perception of mutually distinct forms. This is because the person (*puruṣa*) would merely experience the assistance provided by the intellect and so forth.

As it has been said: "The person is the perceiver of the intellect. And if there is a plurality of mental modifications (*vṛtti*), there must also be a plurality of the intellect, as its unity would be lost; such are the objections to be inferred.
And that [suffering] is of many kinds, because it is determined by various types of notions regarding a self.
He defines the differentiation of cognition (buddhi).
And that [cognition] is of many kinds.
Here he states the reason:
Regarding the phrase "because it is not so":

even if the objects—that is, the referents—are infinite, what follows from that regarding the intellect's having multiple objects? To this, he says: "because it is restricted to each individual object."

Regarding each object and each sense-field, cognitions are restricted; that is, the cognitions therein are individually dependent on their respective objects, as in "this is mine" and "that is not mine. Even if someone were to claim that there is a single cognition with multiple objects, that too must necessarily be seen as consisting of multiple distinct cognitions because of this very restriction; thus, there is no fault.
Due to the imbalance or equilibrium of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, that [intellect] is of two kinds: knowledge and ignorance.
Among these, ignorance is fourfold, characterized by doubt, error, indecision, and dream.
He states the twofold nature of that [intellect] because it must be described as having a distinction even though it does not have a distinction in its objective domain.
Regarding the phrase "of that":
knowledge (*vidyā*) is a cognition consisting of the determination of an abundance of non-existence through the word *vi-*; and ignorance (*avidyā*) is the opposite of that.

Since here only the process of demonstration is intended, he first destroys ignorance even though it follows after knowledge. Regarding the phrase "between those two": between that knowledge and ignorance, ignorance is fourfold, meaning it has four modes, characterized by doubt, error, non-perception, and lack of pervasion.

Even when the fourfold enumeration has been presented, because there remains the possibility of a firm conviction [arising] through the application of reasoning (*tarka*), the wise experience doubt and certainty in the interim.
For instance, some hold that the self possesses the property of being produced (*utpatti-dharma*),
while others hold that it possesses the property of being unproduced (*anutpatti-dharma*).

Then, from that misconception, when there arises a doubt as to whether this [self] possesses the property of origination or whether it is not so, the reasoning (*tarka*) consisting of inquiry proceeds.

If it possesses the property of origination, then neither transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), characterized by the conjunction of a single [self] with multiple bodies and so forth, nor liberation (*apavarga*), characterized by the absolute cessation of that [conjunction], would be possible. However, if the knower is one who does not possess the property of origination, then since transmigratory existence and liberation are observed [to occur], there must necessarily be another [entity] possessing the property of origination.

What is the purpose of the perception of probability (*sambhāvanā-pratyakṣa*)? It is simply the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), for it serves to prevent the arising of other obstacles; otherwise, there would be a lack of firmness regarding the object of both the reason (*hetu*) and the inference (*anumāna*), just as [there is a lack of certainty] regarding a seal-ring [when its existence is merely presumed].

As long as even a hundredfold doubt regarding the non-separation from the extreme [of the probandum] is raised against the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), to that extent the power of the reason's destruction has been established.
Thus it is said.

By this, when the object has been examined—namely, the determination of reality (*tattvanirṇaya*), the unity [of the subject], the unity of the properties of non-arising and persistence, and the possibility [of the object]—inference proceeds because it leads to the realization of the truth. Thus, by way of ascertaining the object, reasoning (*tarka*) serves for the knowledge of reality as an auxiliary to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it is accepted as a cause of the *pramāṇa*; for even that which possesses the characteristics of being sought is dependent upon its own specific function. Indeed, just as a soft clay seal-impression does not produce a hard stone image—even if it is skillfully applied to the interior of a mold—the mere cutting of wood is not sufficient for the production of a statue, however cleverly executed.
And so it has been said:
For there is no such cause in the world or in the Veda for which the desire to bestow favor would not exist, were it not devoid of the requisite procedure (itikartavyatā).
Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, if such reasoning (*tarka*)—consisting of the reduction to absurdity (*prasaṅga*) that establishes what is undesirable for the opponent—is not accepted, then even the *prasaṅga* itself should not be admitted, for it is not distinct from reasoning. Moreover, for the Vaiśeṣikas as well, there exists the [fallacy] of contradiction between the reason and the thesis (*hetu-pakṣa-virodha*) and so forth. To this, it is replied:
Is there an understanding of the non-existence of the opposing position through reasoning, or is there a conviction in one's own position?

Regarding the first alternative, this very [scriptural] authority is the proof: if the knowledge that "transmigration and liberation are impossible for a knower who is impermanent" were not being measured (established), then nothing would be contradicted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that exists at every moment; thus, activity would simply not occur due to the absence of discrimination regarding objects.

Now, if there is an absence of any other alternative [to the second position], then one must admit that something established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is inscribed upon some object among perception and so forth; for there is no means of cognizing anything else apart from those.
Even a doubt regarding this is refuted by contradiction, by demonstrating the possibility of the opposite through the force of some stronger [evidence].
This is done by means of a contrary valid cognition, or by a statement that excludes it.

Now, regarding the cognition consisting of self-examination (*svaprakṣā-bhāvanā*), what is the cause for its arising? Is it that self-examination itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for it? Or is it that when the object has been investigated by inference (*tarka*), self-examination then proceeds; if it were the cause in that case, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*).

If it is argued that the cognition of the non-existence of the object gives rise to the cultivation of self-reflection (*svaprakṣā-bhāvanā*), and thus the cognition of the object’s non-existence is its cause, then the determination of the object’s non-existence would depend upon a prior means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is because when two mutually contradictory [alternatives] are not determined as one, there is an inseparable connection with multiple [possible] affirmations.

Let it be so, provided that one determines the object, assenting that "this is exactly thus," and recognizes this as an object of knowledge rather than mere fatigue; nor is this even a doubt, because of the absence of the two preceding alternatives, but rather it is a descent from doubt and an ascent toward certainty.
This is precisely the cognition of possibility (*sambhāvanā-pratyaya*) for him.

And thus people in the world say, "I shall go tomorrow," where there is no certainty regarding the object [of the action] due to the very nature of that [future time], yet its occurrence is possible through other means; whereas where its occurrence is impossible, there is non-occurrence. Thus, even by way of a different negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), one who understands the absence of an object may consider that which is capable of being produced as something that will come to be. To establish this—that "this object is fit for proof"—the fitness for proof (*pramāṇayogyatā*) of the object is also established; therefore, this is indeed inference (*anumāna*).

And it is precisely in this way that [the statement] "it is grasped by valid cognition" is understood as a cognition of fitness (*yogyatā*), because it serves as the cause for the operation of valid cognition. Otherwise, however, this [statement], being merely a claim of possibility and itself lacking validity, would be useless; for its object's non-existence would have already been established by a subverting valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) which, while stating the two-fold non-connection [of the reason], demonstrates the absence of the object even according to the speaker’s intention.
Others, however, say that this very [statement] is [non-conclusive] because it is not of a definitive nature.

Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is, first of all, a deliberation that does not settle upon any one alternative, arising from the perception of mere similarity between two well-known particulars, the recollection of their respective specific qualities, and the non-perception [of a distinguishing feature].
It is of two kinds: internal (*antar*) and external (*bahir*).

Internal doubt occurs, for example, when a person who has previously seen correctly and seen incorrectly, while wishing to see again at various times, wonders: "Is this seen correctly or incorrectly?"

External [inference] is of two kinds: that which has a perceptible object and that which has an imperceptible object. Regarding the latter, first, doubt arises with respect to a subject (dharmin) from the perception of a common mark and the recollection of the specific characteristics of both [alternatives], as for example, upon seeing only a horn in a forest, one wonders whether it is a cow or a gavaya.

Even regarding an object of direct perception, when one observes the mere similarity between a post and a person, and due to the non-perception of specific features such as curvature and so forth, there arises from the non-manifestation of the specific qualities of being a post and the like, and from the recollection of both specific qualities, a cognition that shines forth within oneself—characterized by a desire for the attributes [of the object]—in the form: "What indeed might this be? Is it a post or a person?"
Regarding doubt (*saṃśaya*): first, by such words [it is meant] "doubt is stated" through the sense of sequential meanings. "Of two well-known particulars" means...

When there is the perception, in a single locus, of a mere similarity—that is, a common property alone—between two things (or two objects) whose specific features, such as thorns and so forth, or heads, hands, and so forth, have been previously known and recognized;
and when, because of that, there is a recollection of those previously perceived specific features of both the post and the person, such as thorns and the like, or heads, hands, and the like;
then the resulting deliberation, which rests upon both possibilities and takes the form "What could this be?", is doubt (*saṃśaya*).

"Is it a post or a person?"—this is doubt (*saṃśaya*), a specific kind of cognition whose object consists of contradictory meanings, characterized by an unsettled apprehension of both general and particular features.
[The phrase] "from the perception of mere similarity":
by the force of the word "mere" (*mātra*), the non-perception of the intended particulars is understood.

The word *darśana* (perception) here denotes apprehension (*upalabdhi*), not the cognition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-mati*), because [the object] is inferable and because commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) is a cause for doubt. Since it expresses the apprehension of similarity (*sādṛśya*), the non-apprehension of the intended object is also implied; for if there were apprehension elsewhere, there would be no apprehension of similarity with that intended object. Furthermore, the doubt resides in the substratum (*dharmin*) alone, not in the similarity, because the latter is already ascertained. Moreover, by the term "similarity," only a common property (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*) is denoted, not a similarity consisting in the cognition of multiple objects. This is because we observe doubts regarding internal and external states—such as pleasure, pain, or whiteness—arising from the cognition of the mere nature of a property and its substratum, even when they reside within the internal organ (*manas*).

Thus, in brief, when a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is perceived in some single locus (*dharmin*), and due to some cause, that specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*) of the locus is not perceived; and when one considers both possibilities—namely, the recollection of what was previously cognized and the object of a contrary characteristic—then, because of this contradiction, doubt arises. Since the common property, which is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with those two states, is observed while their specific objects are absent, there occurs at that time a cognition whose nature is non-ascertainment (*anavadhāraṇātmaka*) regarding the specific aspect of the locus, produced by that very common property; this is doubt.
But is it not the case that it has been refuted that a cognition is non-determinative?
For this [cognition] determines its object as being the inner self in the case of direct perception.
No.

Because both [conditions] are possible: for this [cognition] is produced in the perception of a qualified universal by the assistance of the non-perception of specific properties through that universal, together with the recollection of two distinct particulars. Thus, while there is non-determination regarding the substratum qualified by the universal—such as "Is it a post or a person?"—it would be a cognition whose nature is determination, even while not determining the particular. For it is observed that where the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is distinct, the effect is likewise distinct, as in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
Doubt is also a form of ignorance (*avidyā*), and since that ignorance is blinding for a person, its status as an object of valid cognition (*aprameya*) has been demonstrated.
For it was stated [by others] that [doubt] is not a true [cognition]:

"When some, having perceived a common feature (*sāmānya*), recollects one particular (*viśeṣa*) and then recollects another particular, then—because the perception of the common feature has ceased and because it is the cause of doubt—it cannot logically be the cause of doubt. If this is argued, [we reply]: No, because both particulars are the objects of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and because they are awakened simultaneously, they produce the simultaneous recollection of both particulars. Furthermore, at that time, the knowledge of the common feature—which has reached a state of destruction—is momentary.
The statement "and that is of two kinds" is an enumeration of its divisions.
To the question "by what means? he says:
"internally and externally."

That doubt which was shown by those who hold similar positions— namely, that when a single property is established as existing in reality, there is for the cognizer both the state of apprehension and the state of non-apprehension—
is all subsumed under these two types alone.
First, regarding the internal [doubt], it is expressed by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).

The word "etcetera" (ādi) refers to the astrologer (jyotirvid). Once, he predicted a sign—whether favorable or unfavorable, desired or undesired—concerning a swift, deep, harsh, or terrifying event, such as one designated by the name "mouse. At that time, it was experienced in that very way; later, upon its occurrence, having seen that same sign, he now predicts it again. Consequently, a doubt arises regarding the dream: "Is this knowledge of mine concerning the omen true or false?
External means of knowledge (bahirvidhayah) operate both in the domain of direct perception and in the domain of non-perception.

Among those two, first regarding the object of perception (*pratyakṣa-viṣaya*), there arises [a doubt] such as "Is this a horned animal other than a cow, or is it a gavaya? based on the perception of a common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-liṅga*) and the non-recollection of either specific feature, as previously described.

Since the object here is not directly perceived—being a physical form (*piṇḍa*) concealed by a cloth and inferred through the general perception of horns—it is included among the objects that are not directly perceived (*apratyakṣa*).
Regarding the object of perception as well, he explains it with the words "between a post and a person," and so forth.
Because, upon the non-perception of the mere parts related to both the post (*sthāṇu*) and the person (*puruṣa*), one observes [only] the substratum (*dharmin*) present before one;

and because specific features such as curvature and so forth are not perceived— the word "etcetera" including the head, hands, and so on— and because, in the case of a doubt arising from a stump, there is a lack of perception of the specific features such as the head and hands, which are attributes of a person, equal to those of a post.

In the section on cognition (*buddhi-adhikāra*), there is the determination of the person (*puruṣa*) through the state of being a post, despite the non-manifestation of the specific and general qualities and the absence of attributes and actions, just as in the case of the word "man" [used for a post]. This is the definition of error (*viparyaya*).

Crookedness, hollows, and so forth are the causes for the manifestation of "stump-ness" (sthāṇutva), while the head, hands, and so forth are the causes for the manifestation of "personhood" (puruṣatva). Due to the non-perception of these [characteristics], there arises a state of doubt regarding both stump-ness and personhood. Because the specific attributes of each—whether stump or person—are not brought to mind, one who understands the authority of the statement in both ways, yet observes the object from a distance and desires to determine "it is a stump," is drawn toward the person by the excellence of the person's attributes. Thus, being suspected of being either, his very perception acts as a defect; he does not remain fixed upon a single certainty.

One might as well abandon this unstable [inference] for the sake of the absence of defects; for what indeed does perception actually perceive? It is merely: "Could this be a post, or could it be a person?"
Error (*viparyaya*) also has as its object only that which falls within the scope of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).

First, regarding the object of perception: when one whose sense organs are afflicted by bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*kapha*), or wind (*anila*) perceives an object through the eyes—which have previously grasped many well-known particulars—there arises from the contact between the self and the mind a cognition produced by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the knowledge of objects previously established by hearing. This is perceptual error, such as the cognition "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl.

Even when something is directly perceived, there may arise the conceit of perception, as in the case of the Śabara people who, upon seeing a mass of turtles agitated by the sound of a heavy object—like an ocean whose waters are stirred by the movement of sandalwood leaves carried away by the wind—meditate that it is a *śavara* (a person of that tribe) there.
Likewise, even regarding the object of inference, there is inference when mist and the like are mistaken for smoke, such as the cognition "this is a cow" based on a *gavaya* horn.

In the case of things contrary to what is not-yesterday (i.e., yesterday), the false inference that "substance is [defined by] such qualities as being a bean, speech, curd, or the end" is *viparyaya* (error). It consists of the conceit of self (*ātman*) in the body, the senses, and the mind; seeing permanence in things that are produced; the cognition that an effect arises when there is a deficiency in the causal factors; the cognition of something as beneficial when it leads to harm and suffering; and the cognition of something as harmful when it leads to benefit and happiness. Following the discussion on conjunction, the object (*viṣaya*) is now examined. Even regarding the object, it is understood to be precisely the domain of perception and inference.

And because it is an object of perception and inference just like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that it also occurs when there is a desire for that [conjunction] as its object.
The phrase "it is an object of perception and inference only" is used because there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apart from perception and inference.

Regarding the object of perception, even in the case of things difficult to know, many previously established particulars such as scriptures and so forth are well-known; thus, there is no novelty [in the knowledge] produced by anyone today.

Just as smell and taste are well-known objects [of perception], so too, even when these two [smell and taste] are not present, if there is a cognition of "that" and a cognition of "this," that [cognition] has an object.

Now, if both "cowness" and specific qualities such as color and so forth are included, then it does not occur with respect to the object; but if it does occur, then it is said that this [object] is not included.
Therefore, he says: "because the object is not apprehended."

"Yathārtha" means "according to the object" (yathārtha-artha), that is, the state of being pervaded by the object as it truly is. This means that there is an absence of dependence on anything else, such as scriptures and so forth, for the cognition of [the object] as it is—for instance, "this is a cow.
Therefore, because the cognition "that is in this" arises, its status as the cause [of valid knowledge] has been stated by way of excluding other possible objects.

He asks: "What is the reason that there is no pervasion when the cause is unestablished or contradictory? Or what is the reason for the cognition of an unestablished, undivided [object]? He replies: "Of one whose sense organ is impaired by a mass, a [defective] blade, and so forth. This means: of one whose sense organ (*indriya*)—that is, the faculty—is impaired (*upahata*), meaning corrupted, by a mass (*piṇḍa*), a [defective] blade (*kṛtsna*), or the like, regarding its object (*artha*), that is, the domain (*viṣaya*).
The capacity [of the senses] regarding the non-appearance of unperceived defects such as jaundice (*kāmalā*) and the appearance of perceived objects has been examined.
He says that if the unperceived were to appear solely through the power of defects, then everything would appear to everyone, because there would be no cause for restriction; thus he states:
"From the contact of the self and the mind, depending on the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of a cognition whose object is unperceived."

An object such as sound and the like is not directly perceived; rather, it is known through memory, which arises from a latent impression (saṃskāra) produced by a previously arisen cognition, and which occurs due to the contact between the self and the mind inherent in that impression.

This is its meaning: the sense organ, when in contact with a cow-individual (*gopiṇḍa*), perceives "cowness" (*gotva*) as qualified by the similarity to that individual. Because this is a cause for doubt, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose object is the perceived similarity is awakened by it. That awakened [impression], through the mental application (*manovedha*) directed toward the sense organ upon reaching the undivided individual, produces a cognition possessing both forms in accordance with the similarity to the individual cow. Therefore, there is no manifestation of everything everywhere, because the perceived similarity and the latent impression serve as the restrictive causes.
For this very reason, it is logical that the cognition of those who possess impaired faculties is called an error.

In this way, it would not be sensory cognition at all; for even when the eye is functioning, that which is apprehended as "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva) and so forth—which is devoid of modification—would have to be either the object itself or the locus of the sense organ. But if this [cognition] were not sensory cognition while one is perceiving the connection with a mass of cows through the eye, then what would constitute sensory cognition? It would be something contrary, and so on. Therefore, because it appears through the superimposition of one thing upon another, this error (*viparyaya*) should be understood by the wise as being defined by such a reversal; it is perceived through an aspect that is contrary to its own nature. Thus, it is indeed "contrary manifestation" (*viparītakhyāti*), and not "manifestation of the non-existent" (*asatkhyāti*), because the former is possible as a different form of its own nature, whereas the latter is merely a verbal or mental construct regarding what does not exist.

Where error proceeds through the convergence of many conditions upon a single object, there an external cause is specified; however, in the case of a certainty that is followed solely by a defect of the mind, its occurrence is not possible [due to an external cause]. For instance, when one afflicted by desire perceives a woman here and there in a state of delusion, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) act right there where the conceptualizing error occurs. But in the case of non-conceptual [error], its arising due to the power of a sensory defect is not contradictory, as in the production of the cognition of a yellow conch shell. He states another example of error:
"Even in the case of the sense organ, there is a misconception of it being direct perception," and so forth.

The three eyes of Śiva, agitated by the young *kuṅkuma* trees as they gaze upon the sky, turn back from the face of Umā; yet, as they return, they manifest their own thousandfold excellence by making the sky itself appear to possess a thousand eyes. Thus, the sky—free from clouds, vast, and appearing like Mount Mandara—is directly perceived within the heart, producing a sense of wonder. Having transcended the authority of the senses through its status as the substratum of space, the rule of cognition is established by a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that conforms to that very nature.

For instance, one whose sense organs are impaired by jaundice perceives the sky as if it were covered by a thick film; likewise, due to the presence of cataracts, one sees a black pea as having the luster of silver.

Furthermore, when there is a great, dark, and dense mass of nocturnal gloom before one's eyes, even though the object—the fire within the sacrificial ladle—is not directly perceptible because it is entirely enveloped by that lightless darkness, one nevertheless sees it.

Even regarding the object of inference, when there is a cognition that "this is smoke" in a place where it is not certain—due to steam and the like, or due to a heated needle, a banner, and so forth—and when there is a cognition of a garden and the like from a specific fragrance, this is an object of inference even though it is mistaken. He says that even by means of an extremely distant object, a reversal occurs through non-apprehension: "one should desire the absence of the contrary."
The aggregate of the three Vedas—Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma—is *trayī*; the Atharvaveda, however, is merely a portion of the *trayī*.

That which is perceived through the realization of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is metaphorically designated as "vision" (*darśana*); such vision is called *trayī-darśana*. Regarding those systems of philosophy (*darśana*) such as the Sāṅkhya that transcend this [Vedic] vision, they point out that what is to be known as taught in treatises like Mīmāṃsā—which establishes the distinct parts of the Veda—is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Such a cognition is a false notion (*mithyā-pratyaya*), because in those systems that transcend the scope of the *kṣetra* (the field), there is in every respect a contradiction with the authoritative means of knowledge regarding the nature of the self for those belonging to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*).
Likewise, the misconception that one's own self is not directly perceived is an error (*viparyaya*), because it is the cognizer, distinct from those [objects], who is to be established.
Among the Mīmāṃsakas, the misconception regarding the eternity of the Vedas—which are in fact produced—is an error.

Regarding dharma and adharma, which are effects that cannot be conceptualized, the notion among the Lokāyatikas—that they exist as effects and thus are impermanent—due to their ignorance of the variety of awakened sufferings and so forth, is an error on the part of their disciples.

While the Vedas and Upanishads teach what is beneficial—such as "living beings must not be harmed" and "one should not practice war with poison and the like"—the Jain scriptures (pākhaṇḍa-śāstra) and the Aṅkas teach what is harmful, such as "the supreme dharma is the harming of living beings" and "the practice of war with poison and the like leads to spiritual welfare. Regarding this, the cognition of those [teachings] as causes of harm among the followers of the Jains is a misconception (viparyaya).
On this point, some say:
"There is no misconception, because of the absence of a cause; and that absence [of a cause] is due to the fact that the sense organs produce cognitions that apprehend objects exactly as they are."

If it is argued that defects (doṣas) produce knowledge even regarding an object that has passed away, we say no; for defects can only bring about a failure of capacity, not a change in the nature of the object. Even under the influence of a defect, the sense organ does not fail to perceive the object "mother-of-pearl" as such, but rather fails to manifest the silver that is not present there; otherwise, the principle that defects cause a distortion of perception would be violated. Furthermore, if the visual organ were to manifest even what is non-visual, who could prevent everything from becoming the object of every sense? For in the cognition "this is silver," the visual organ is indeed directed toward the presence of the mother-of-pearl.

For just as this eye, due to the absence of suitability, does not adhere to the object [in the case of an error], and in the cognition of silver, it is silver that appears and not the mother-of-pearl; and since the eye is incapable of grasping silver—which is not its object—the experience "this" has the mother-of-pearl as its object, while "silver" is the form of a conceptual construction (*vṛtti*). Furthermore, the non-apprehension of the form of the mother-of-pearl before one is caused by a defect; thus, the recollection of silver arises from that [defect]. Therefore, these two cognitions have distinct objects. To this, it is replied:

If the cognition of silver does not have mother-of-pearl as its object, but is instead a memory of silver, then, since the aspect of silver in that cognition has been previously apprehended, one would act toward the silver and not toward the mother-of-pearl, because the capacity to induce action resides in the manifesting aspect of the experience.

Now, if you think that the sublation of silver is effected by the sense organ [only] with respect to what is apprehended as mother-of-pearl, but not with respect to the "mother-of-pearl-ness" (śuktikatva) which is a specific property— [and that] when the recollection of silver is presented in a place determined by the cause of the cognition of instruction such as "that [is silver]," due to the similarity between the perceived and the remembered, and because one fails to discern the distinction between the two similar things due to some defect, one proceeds toward the locus of the mother-of-pearl and determines the co-referentiality of mother-of-pearl and silver, thinking "this is silver"— that too is incorrect, because even non-discrimination does not constitute an action.

For it is the cognition of non-difference from silver that is the cause of activity toward mother-of-pearl for one desiring silver, not its similarity; and it is the cognition of difference that is the cause of withdrawal from it. Since both of these are absent, it would follow that one neither acts nor withdraws. However, this is not the case, as there is a rule regarding the determination of error within the scope of cognition:

one invariably acts because of the appearance of the object. This would not even apply to the conceptualizations of universals, since [in those cases] even the notion "this is I" and so forth could arise due to the possibility of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

And likewise, even at the time of the sublating cognition "this is silver," which occurs when the object is being drawn near, it is not the case that the difference between the mother-of-pearl and the silver was not grasped; rather, their identity was not determined, such that one might be deceived in this way. Furthermore, regarding the claim that "this restriction [of the term 'silver'] to the mother-of-pearl arises because it is recognized as possessing qualities such as coolness," this too is possible through the non-grasping of difference, since there can be a non-grasping of a distinction even when other aspects are grasped.

Furthermore, there is indeed an inclination toward the mother-of-pearl and such objects by way of their silver-aspect; there is the cognition of a common substratum in the form "this is silver"; and there is the sublation at a later time, which aims to negate the nature of silver in that which has the character of "this-ness" as its substratum. Therefore, when the sense organ is in contact with the mother-of-pearl, aided by a defect and assisted by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of silver, an erroneous determination (*adhyavasāya*) of silver is produced with respect to the mother-of-pearl due to its similarity and compatibility.
As for what was said—that the nature of the mother-of-pearl contradicts experience—that is incorrect.

Since even the manifestation of nacre—which is restricted to a specific location as "this," and which is characterized by the force of a sublating cognition—is also manifest, it possesses the fitness for linguistic and practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding knowledge and so forth; and this [fitness] is possible even for that object which, though seized by the non-apprehension of the [true] Veda, is the cause for engaging in the practical usage of silver, because that object is accepted at the subsequent moment precisely through its being the objective basis for the engagement in practical usage.

As for the claim that "the defects (doṣas) possess the nature of being causes for the obstruction of capacity," that too is of no consequence. This is because we observe that malevolent spirits (yātus), as perceived by children and others, produce diseases in those afflicted; thus, the restriction of the capacity of all defects toward all [objects] is refuted.

Furthermore, it is not the case that there is a deviation from the pervasion of knowledge [by the absence of defects], such that it would remain unexplained for all [cases]. For where there is no perception of the obstructing causes—the defects which render cognition invalid—the non-existence of those [defects] is established, and trust is justified precisely through the cognition of the absence of the objectivity (viṣayatva) grasped by them.

And if there were no occurrence of error or alteration, what would be the status of the cognition of two moons? For there is no apprehension by means of a single cognition of the form: "This appearance of duality belongs to the pair of cognitions produced regarding the moon and so forth, which arise separately from words that are not intermingled with defects and which fall upon distinct objects. This is because there is no grasping of such a composite cognition.

If it is accepted that this property of cognition, being grasped as non-existent, is grasped by a causeless defect (*ahetuka-doṣa*), then error would have to be admitted, because one property is perceived in another; thus, since the counter-argument is not easily established, we conclude that it is an error, like the perception of two moons.

However, for those who maintain that in the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, it is an extraordinary (*alaukika*) silver existing in the object itself that is being cognized—and who thereby seek to justify the absence of error—for them, there would be no such thing as purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), because the extraordinary [silver] cannot be grasped, cannot serve as a cause, and lacks any correspondence [with the object]. Furthermore, even subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) would pertain only to the objects of perception and inference.

Regarding the object of perception, whether it concerns a well-known or an unknown thing, the *anuvyavasāya* consists merely in the inquiry, "What is this? arising from either the observation of pervasion (*vyāpti*) or from desire;
just as, for example, a person from the forest has a reflective awareness regarding a jackfruit tree and so forth.

In that regard, there arises a determinative ascertainment (*avasāya*) consisting of the cognition of one's own invisibility, earth-ness, the form of the eye, and the series of objects to be abandoned such as odors and so forth.

Even "mango-ness" (*panasatva*), which is invariably concomitant with the mango and excluded from *mātra* and other things, is indeed perceived directly; it is merely rendered distinct through its opposition to specific dissimilarities (*vaijātya*) such as grass, weeds, and so on.

Furthermore, even in the domain of inference, there occurs a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) such as, "Having previously seen a coconut tree and others, and having grasped the non-existence of a crow, this must be a bare tree."
Reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) would also occur only regarding the objects of perception and inference.
This is intended to demonstrate that reflective awareness arises when the objects of perception and inference have been grasped and awakened [in consciousness].
With the intention of stating the reflective awareness first for the object of perception and then for the object of inference in sequence, he employs the word "tāvat," which denotes order.

Anuvyavasāya is merely the reflection "What is this? arising either from the state of being a pervader (*vyāptṛtva*) or from the state of being an object of desire (*arthitva*), with respect to objects that are either well-known (*prasiddha*) or not well-known (*aprasiddha*).

Those objects which were previously known are "well-known objects" (*prasiddhārtha*); because of their status as objects of worldly transaction (*vyāvahārikatva*), there arises—either from the state of being a pervader or from the state of being an object of desire—the mere reflection "What is this? regarding what has been traversed. When [an object] is well-known, such as a rope, it is anuvyavasāya in the sense of a mere cognition, such as "Who has gone by this path? which lacks specific qualities like [the initial] *vyavasāya*.

The meaning is that even when there is a perception of a color or cognition that is not previously established, there is a determinative ascertainment (*avasāya*), just as for one who has never seen a jackfruit tree (*panasa*) before, there arises a determinative ascertainment of the jackfruit’s own nature through seeing it; that is, for one who has not previously cognized it, there is a determinative ascertainment of the jackfruit’s own nature.

In that case as well, the cognition of its being a sentient being, its visibility, its being earth, its being the object of the eye, its having form, and so forth, as well as its having branches and the like, is indeed a determinative ascertainment.

The remainder of the passage, beginning with "it is visible," should be understood as such, because of the exclusion [of other possibilities] by the determinative ascertainment: "it possesses only form and the like, and it possesses branches and the like."

Even the state of being a *panasa* (jackfruit tree), which is invariably concomitant with the *panasa* itself and yet excluded from things such as mats and the like, is indeed indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*).

It is merely because one lacks a specific cognition regarding the word "panasa" and its relation to the quality or substance that there is no determinate ascertainment (*vyavasāya*) or valid cognition (*pramiti*). Since it has not been taught that "this is the name [of this thing]," there arises no realization that "this is what is denoted by the word *panasa*"; rather, there would be only the cognition that "it must have some name. This cognition, which consists in the non-determination of a specific name, is what is called "non-ascertainment" (*an-vyavasāya*).

Even regarding the object of inference, there is non-determination (anadhyavasāya) on the part of an inhabitant of the Coconut Island, who, upon seeing a branch and a trunk, wonders: "What kind of living being could this possibly be in this region? due to his lack of familiarity with branches and trunks.

In the Coconut Island (Nārikela-dvīpa), because elephants are as common as air, the local people are also accustomed to them. When such a person arrives in another land and sees an animal in the forest, he praises its limbs and trunk; however, having merely inferred the existence of a living being in general, he lacks a definitive cognition regarding the specific species of that creature, wondering, "What kind of living being could this possibly be? This is *anadhyavasāya* (non-ascertainment), derived from the etymological analysis of the term as a cognition characterized by the absence of a definitive determination (*adhyavasāya*).

Is it not the case that this is simply doubt (*saṃśaya*), because its nature consists in non-determination, rather than being a distinct category due to a difference in function or a difference in essential form? Rather, doubt arises from the recollection of the specific features of both sides; it is not "non-ascertainment" (*anadhyavasāya*), because the latter can also occur when the specific features of the object are not even perceived. Furthermore, the distinction is that doubt occurs when two opposing alternatives are seen in an unstable state, whereas this [non-ascertainment] does not. Moreover, this is not a form of valid knowledge (*vidyā*), because it does not serve as a basis for practical activity (*vyavahāra*).

For one whose collection of sense organs has ceased its worldly activity and whose mind is dissolved, the mental experience of the state of awakening through the doors of the senses is that dream-cognition.
How so?

When the self (ātman), having willed it, withdraws from the body for the sake of resting during the day for living beings who are weary, and when—depending on the effort of the exertion of the internal organ—the continuity of activity in the mind ceases due to the mental resolve of the instruments, and [the self] remains motionless within the heart-region, then it is designated as "one whose mind is dissolved. When that [mind] is dissolved, the collection of the senses comes to rest. In that state, because the flow of inhalation and exhalation continues through a specific conjunction of the self and the mind distinct from the state of deep sleep, there arises dream-cognition in the form of direct perception regarding objects, produced by latent impressions (saṃskāra) through the doors of the senses.

That [recollection] is of three kinds, to be grasped through the clarity of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), through the intensity of the object, and through constant application. Among these, by way of the clarity of mental impressions: when one, having previously experienced betel, *kārpī*, or saffron through direct perception, recollects them while reflecting, then that very reflection arises as if it were a fresh perception.
One who possesses the nature of power (*śātavaiṣā*) sees such things as traveling through the sky from the ground of the vision of power;

one who possesses the nature of mind (*cittaprakṛti*) sees such things as entering fire and water or flying through the air from the ground of the vision of mind; one who possesses the nature of security (*kṣemaprakṛti*) sees such things as crossing rivers and oceans from the ground of the vision of security.

Regarding things experienced by oneself or not experienced, or things abandoned or not abandoned, whatever brings about auspicious results—such as mounting an elephant or obtaining a parasol—all that arises from the *dharma* of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Conversely, whatever brings about the opposite—such as anointing with oil or entering a brothel—all that arises from what is called *adharma* (non-dharma) of mental impressions.
This refers to things that are absolutely unexperienced, neither seen nor heard.

Even that which is self-evident (*svaprātibha*) to one whose collection of sense organs has been restrained by the power of breath (*prāṇāyāma*), is in fact nothing but memory (*smṛti*) because it consists of a reflective observation of a past continuum of cognitions; thus, this fourfold [type of knowledge] belongs to the undiscriminating person.
He speaks the following for the purpose of defining sleep:
"of one whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased," and so forth.
This refers to the Great Lord of Creatures (Mahāprajāpati) whose collection of sense-faculties—beginning with their engagement in grasping their respective objects—has come to rest.
One whose mind has become thoroughly well-arisen [in concentration] is called "one whose mind is dissolved" (*pralīnamanaska*).

For such a person, whose collection of sense-faculties has ceased and whose mind is dissolved, that mental experience occurring through the doors of the senses—which possesses the quality of awakening, yet is an experience of the cessation of the waking state and consists of the nature of the mind—is dream-cognition (*svapnajñāna*).
It occurs in this manner whenever the previous mind dissolves and the sense-faculties come to rest.
By means of the passage beginning with "How so? and so forth.

When a living being has traveled through the elements in their entirety from one shore to the other, becoming exhausted and weary during the day, sleep occurs at night for the sake of rest and for the alleviation of fatigue. It also serves for the purpose of digesting the food already consumed by transforming it into its various constituents (rasa, etc.), and for the purpose of allowing the limbs to recover their movement. When the self and the internal organ (manas) are disconnected from the external organs, and the mind remains motionless within that internal space which is devoid of sensory activity—being free from the continuous flow of actions, free from the darkness of activity, wakeful yet inwardly withdrawn, and empty of the collection of external senses—then one is said to be in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), with the mind completely dissolved.

When that [mind] has subsided, the collection of the sense-faculties becomes stilled within the mind because the sense-faculties, no longer assailed by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), lack the grasping of objects. In that state of the subsided mind, when an activity characterized by the continuous and frequent subjugation of inhalation and exhalation and the closing of the eyes occurs, dream-cognition arises from the contact of the self and the mind; due to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of sleep—which bears the name "sleep"—there emerges a cognition of dreams in the form of a non-intense awareness directed toward objects previously experienced, even though those objects are separated by place and time.
He states that [the dream] is held to be "awakened" (vinidra) because of the proficiency of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Due to the proficiency of the mental impression,

when one who is lustful or angry sleeps while intensely contemplating a beloved woman or an enemy, then— due to the intensity of the mental impressions— a cognition arises at the beginning of sleep that possesses the form of that [object], being intense with the density of that thought and intense with the clarity of its manifestation, and which speaks as if it were present before the eyes.

Because they sustain the body, the *dhātus*—namely blood, muscle, fat, bone-marrow, bone, and semen—are indeed the body itself. He explains that due to their impairment, specifically through being vitiated by *vāta* and the other humors, the objects of perception become distorted:
one of *vāta*-constitution, or one whose *vāta* is corrupted by some accumulation of worms and so forth, perceives things such as crawling, leaping here and there, or running about.
One of *pitta*-constitution, or one whose *pitta* is corrupted, perceives things such as entering fire, climbing mountains, or traveling across circles of light.
One of a phlegmatic constitution (*śleṣmaprakṛti*), or one whose phlegm is deranged (*śleṣmadūṣita*), sees such things as crossing rivers and oceans, or being struck by snowstorms and the like.

Whether these events have been personally experienced or inferred, or whether they have not been personally experienced but were inferred by another, or even if they are merely imagined at will—whatever auspicious or inauspicious sight is seen in a dream, all that arises from the awakening of latent predispositions (*saṃskāra*).
Whatever is contrary to the auspicious or inauspicious [dreams] arises from such preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*) as anointing with oil, putting on new clothes, mounting a cow, and so forth.

Cognition regarding things that are utterly non-existent—such as eating the moon or the sun—which are unproduced either by themselves or by others, arises solely from a defect; for there is an absence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding such unexperienced objects.

Although dream-cognitions occur due to the intensity of latent impressions, the influence of sleep-defects, or unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), wherein the superimposed form appears vividly, they are mentioned separately because they occur in a specific state [of consciousness], namely, one characterized by moisture (the state of dreaming).

Sometimes there occurs a connection, even within the dream state itself, with an object seen in a dream, such as "this was seen by me. In that case, because there is an awakening—that is, a manifestation—of a previously experienced object, it is called *svapnāntika* (the end of a dream).
For instance, someone has said that dream-cognition occurs when the collection of sense-faculties has ceased;
however, [the author] says this is not so, because there is a perceiver.

Although in dreams and the like, the collection of sense organs has ceased to function, it is nevertheless nothing but memory (*smṛti*), because there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the continuity of dream-cognition, which is past and previously experienced. He concludes: "Thus, ignorance is indeed fourfold."
Knowledge is also fourfold:
through perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony.
They cast away ignorance, [saying] "this is knowledge. Not only is ignorance fourfold, but knowledge as well is fourfold.
[The first is] direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The first is the presentation of perception (pratyakṣa) because it is the primary cause; immediately after that, inference (anumāna); following that, analogy (upamāna); and after that, verbal testimony (śabda). Since [the objects] perceived, inferred, and analogized exist within verbal testimony, the meaning is presented concisely at the end of these worldly sequences, and by means of that, other worlds are fully developed.
In this context, that which arises in dependence on what is designated as the "sense-organ" (akṣa) is perception (pratyakṣa).
The sense-faculties (indriya) are six: the ear, nose, tongue, eye, skin, and mind.
Indeed, that [perception] arises with respect to categories of objects such as substance (dravya) and so forth.

Regarding substance, first, in the case of the sixfold group consisting of the two types of large substances, those possessing multiple substances, those possessing manifested color and light, flowers, existence, and the atom, there is merely the observation of their own form.

However, through the contact of the self and the mind, depending on the qualifiers of generality, particularity, substance, quality, and action, perception arises in the form: "six substances," "earth," "horned," "white," "cow," or "moving.

As for color, taste, smell, touch, number, and so forth, due to their inherence in multiple substances, their own specific qualities, and the contact with their own substrates, the cause of indeterminate perception would arise.
Because sound is heard, its proximity [to the sense organ] consists in its inherence in the auditory faculty; it is perceived by that very faculty.

Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, and sound are perceived by the auditory faculty because they do not inhere in a perceptual cognition.
There is also the apprehension of one's own cognitions.

The perception of cognition (*buddhi*), pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind with their respective substances. The perception of positive entities (*bhāva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth—which are inherent in the substrates that are themselves perceptible—arises from their inherence in those substrates. This "perception of what is located in two" (*dviṣṭheṣuṃ grahaṇa*) constitutes the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of persons such as ourselves. As for the term "us" (*asmad*), however, for other disciplined ones—the *yogins*—when they are in a state of union (*yukta*), there arises through the mind assisted by merit born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*), an unerring vision of the essential nature (*svarūpa-darśana*) regarding their own selves, other selves, ether, space, time, atoms, air, and minds, as well as the qualities, actions, universals, and ultimate particulars inherent in them, and also regarding inherence itself.

Furthermore, for those who are dissociated [from the senses], perception arises regarding subtle, concealed, or remote objects through the assistance of the fourfold contact (*catuṣṭayasannikarṣa*), yogic power (*yogaja-dharma*), and the grace of the Lord (*īśvarānugraha*).

In that context, with respect to universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*), perception as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consists merely in the observation of their own nature (*svarūpālocanamātra*); the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are the categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth; the knower (*pramātṛ*) is the self (*ātman*); and the resulting cognition (*pramiti*) is the knowledge whose object is substance and the other categories.

When the knowledge of universals and particulars arises, perception as a means of knowledge is merely the undifferentiated observation; and there exists another distinct means of knowledge [in this case] because it does not have the form of a fruit [already produced].

Alternatively, with respect to all objects, that knowledge which arises from the fourfold contact—being non-erroneous and non-verbal—is the means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa); the objects of cognition (prameya) are the categories (padārtha) such as substance and so forth; the cognizer (pramātṛ) is the self (ātman); and the result of cognition (pramiti) consists in the perception of qualities, defects, or neutrality.
The definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is direct apprehension (*sākṣātkāra-pramiti*).
In this context, it is called "perception" because it arises in dependence upon (*pratītya*) the sense organ (*akṣa*) and the object (*artha*).
That which arises having reached (*prāpya*) the sense organ and the object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) known as perception.

Even the fact that an effect is produced from a specific instrument (*karaṇaviśeṣaja*) constitutes its essential nature, provided it is not subject to deviation among things of similar or dissimilar classes.
For example, the fact that a sprout of *yakṣa* originates from a seed of *yakṣa* is its defining characteristic; for this very reason, it is designated as a "sprout of *yakṣa*.

If it is argued that pleasure, pain, memory, and so forth should also be considered valid perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*) because they are produced by the senses (*aindriyaja*), we say no, because [the definition of perception] is qualified by the context of the faculty of cognition (*buddhi*).

The cognition that arises in dependence upon a sense organ (*akṣa*) and its object (*artha*) is *pratyakṣa* (direct perception). However, suffering and the like are not of the nature of cognition; if they were, then because they are momentary, their status as a means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) would not be established.
This is true.

Alternatively, [the status of suffering] is obtained here from the perspective of being external to this [cognition]. But if one intends for that [suffering] also to have the status of a means of valid knowledge through the etymological derivation based on the instrument (*karaṇa*), then it is so because it is a cause of determination (*paricchedaka*).
Doubt, error, and transgression [are excluded] because the cessation of ignorance is the subject under discussion.

When it is stated that "perception (pratyakṣa) is that which arises in dependence upon an object," someone might have the misconception—due to its extreme commonality—that perception consists only of what is produced by the sense organs (*indriya*). To eliminate this, the term *akṣa* is to be understood as referring to all the sense organs (*samasta-indriya*), since the capacity for grasping objects belongs to them. Thus, [the word *pratyakṣa*] is explained as beginning with *pra-*, [meaning] "proceeding toward" (*prādiśamāna*).

By the term *pratyakṣa*, meaning "that which has gone toward the sense-organ" (*pratigatamakṣam*), it follows the gender of its referent (*abhidheyaliṅgatā*): direct perception as knowledge (*pratyakṣaṃ jñānam*), direct perception as cognition (*pratyakṣā buddhiḥ*), or direct perception as conviction (*pratyakṣaḥ pratyayaḥ*).
Because the word *akṣa* is conventionally established (*nirūḍha*) in many meanings, there are various interpretations. Here, *akṣāṇi* refers to the sense-faculties (*indriyāṇi*).
And since those six and eleven objects have been mentioned, he enumerates them for the sake of that specific count:
"smell, taste, sight, touch, hearing, and mind.

Since it has been stated here that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*), it might follow that even a mental image (*sphuṭi*) would be perception; therefore, in order to show two distinct meanings [of perception], he specifies the object of perception.
That is twofold.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for emphasis.
That perception consists of the distinction between substance and so forth.
Substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence are absolutely distinct.
Because substance comes first, he first states the production of its cognition:
"directly in substance."
The word *sākṣāt* (directly) signifies sequence.
He asks: for what reason is there direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the great substances—earth, water, fire, and air?
He says: "Because of possessing multiple substances" (*anekadravyavattvāt*).

The state of having multiple constituent substances (*anekadravyatva*) is to be understood as residing in each [substance] that possesses conjunction. The manifestation of what is perceived is declared to be the property of the perceived; that is, when there is no perception of the ungraspable due to the absence of light, the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣabhāva*) arises from this collection of causes: the conjunction of the self with the mind—which consists of four elements and is of a single nature—the conjunction of the mind with the sense organ, and the conjunction of the sense organ with its object. Furthermore, regarding the determination of direct perception, it occurs when there is an excellence of cognition concerning qualities such as sound and smell. Moreover, when there is the capacity for both [the object and the senses], and when all factors such as merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and attention (*avadhāna*) are present, direct perception comes to be.
In the case of a single thread (*māṇu*) and a double-threaded cloth (*drāpyaka*), magnitude (*mahattva*) is perceived because it exists as a perceptible entity.

Since it is perceived through the sequence of hearing, sight, and touch, its pervasion of the entire object—namely, the *sphoṭa*—is established. Because an increase [in magnitude] is observed, the state of possessing multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*) is the cause [of magnitude]. Even when magnitude and the state of possessing multiple substances are present, the state of possessing many constituent substances (*bahudravyavattva*) is the auxiliary cause for external perception.

Since knowledge everywhere has pleasure, pain, and so forth as its effects, it is governed by the capacities of substances such as merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and space; thus, it is produced by merit and demerit. Without the conjunction of the self with the mind, there would be no perception arising from the conjunction of the mind with the sense organs or the sense organs with their objects; therefore, [merit and demerit] are the causes through their functions of assistance and obstruction.

If it is argued that since the contact of the sense organs with their objects is the cause, the apprehension of particulars—just like the apprehension of universals—would necessarily occur, resulting in the production of doubt and error, we say no, because there is no such necessity.

For a universal (*sāmānya*), because its object is manifold, it is possible for it to be perceived simultaneously with the four parts [of the sense organ] due to its extensive nature; however, a particular (*viśeṣa*), because its object is limited, requires contact with the four composite parts of the sense organ and with many of its own constituent parts. Thus, there is no rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) because of this difference in capacity.

For this very reason, there is an indistinct perception of a single horn from a distance; and in the case of a scent, even when the four parts [of the nose] are present, the scattered atoms [of the fragrance] are not perceived beforehand.

Some maintain that there is only one kind of perception, namely conceptual (savikalpaka), because everything is subject to linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) due to its being of the nature of such usage; for even animals, who are devoid of the production of words, engage in activity based on conceptualization of objects. To them, [the author] replies: "It is merely the observation of the thing-in-itself" (*svarūpālocanamātram*).
This means that perception is merely the observation of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), a mere apprehension devoid of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Thus he asserts.

For if the apprehension of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of a real entity by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) were not admitted, then conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) would also be impossible, since the word that grasps that [nature] would not be clearly present. Therefore, one who desires conceptual cognition must also accept non-conceptual cognition. And that [non-conceptual cognition] does not grasp the universal (*sāmānya*) alone, because the particularity (*bheda*) also appears; nor does it grasp the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone, because the form of the universal also appears, and because there is a subsequent synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) upon seeing another individual. Rather, it grasps both the universal and the particular; however, it does not perceive them by discriminating [between them] as "this is the universal" or "this is the particular," because there is no separation from the experience of the other entity. The distinction is that the universal is distinguished by the apprehension of the experience of another individual (*piṇḍa*), while the particular is distinguished by the apprehension of its exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). This is the analysis.

Furthermore, in the state of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpaka*), because there is no experience of other individual objects (*piṇḍa*), the two properties—continuity (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)—which constitute the universal and the particular, are not grasped; yet, due to the non-perception of their similarity, there is indeed a grasping of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) through a distinct apprehension resulting from the perception of suchness (*tathairūpya*).

For this very reason, the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) among universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and necessary properties (*avaśyaka*) cannot be apprehended by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), because that [relation] is based on the comprehension of difference, and difference between universals and so forth is not determined by non-conceptual cognition. Therefore, conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) first perceives the universal, the particular, the substance, and the quality; and having experienced another individual (*piṇḍa*), for one who understands the two properties of continuity (*anuvṛtti*) and pervasion (*vyāpti*), the aforementioned understanding is established through the medium of imaginative construction (*utprekṣā*). Furthermore, there is no sublation (*abādha*) due to defects.

In their view, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), appearing as that which conforms to the exclusion of what is not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), when there is no conceptualization regarding multiplicity or the unknown; it is not conceptual (*savikalpaka*), because the latter—being born dependent on mental impressions (*vāsanā*) and appearing with a superimposition corresponding to a real entity—is erroneous in its occurrence, just like the cognition of momentariness and so forth.
Since those [non-conceptualists] have been refuted, he states that even conceptual cognition possesses the status of perception, beginning with the words "sāmānya... and so on.

Generality, particularity, substance, quality, and action—these are generalities, particulars, substances, qualities, and actions. That contact with the self which has these generalities, particulars, substances, qualities, and actions as its qualifiers is the contact characterized by generalities, particulars, substances, qualities, and actions. From that [contact], there would be perception of the six substances; perception of "earth" as qualified by generality (earth-ness); perception of "horned" as qualified by particularity; perception of "white" as qualified by substance; perception of "the eye" as qualified by quality; and perception of "moving" as qualified by action.

By the phrase "endowed with the fourfold power," although the self is already indicated by its own connection [to the senses], it is mentioned again for the purpose of making it known that there is a different process from the previously mentioned non-conceptual valid cognition (*nirvikalpaka-pramāṇa*). It is stated that conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); for in the cognition "this is a jar," some distinct entity is perceived as the object, and thus it is a real thing. Otherwise, this appearance would be a determination of a non-existent object for the conceptual cognition, and it would be an error. As it has been said: *(Note: The Sanskrit fragment provided appears to be a commentary on the *Tattvasaṅgraha* or a related work discussing the nature of conceptualization and its status as a valid cognition.)*
It is not the case that conceptual construction arises from the firmness of the appearance of an object, like the [illusory] sight of a ghost;
for its activity is non-deceptive.

Now, if it is argued that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) born of experience—which, through the force of its own habituation, superimposes its own appearance [upon the object]—causes a person to act toward the location of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) by concealing the difference between the particular and its appearance, and brings about correspondence (*saṃvāda*) when the jewel is obtained; yet, because it does not provide the actual form of the many substances, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*): [we reply] if the conceptual construction does not touch the real thing (*vastu*), how could it superimpose its own appearance as having the nature of that [thing]? For, according to the maxim "it is not seen for fire," one does not observe the superimposition of water upon a mirage (which is not fire).

Now, the conceptual construction (vikalpa) which is assisted by perception directly perceives the object at the time when it assumes the form of the causal operation; otherwise, activity based on conceptual construction regarding things such as "potency" would be impossible. As it has been said: "From that [perception] as well, activity proceeds toward the object itself through conceptual construction. Thus, this [conceptual construction] is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) with respect to the object, because it is the cause of non-discrepant valid knowledge (avisaṃvādipramiti).

Now, regarding the objection that there is no correspondence (*saṃvāda*) because the momentary object which is grasped by perception is not determined by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and that which is determined by conceptual construction is not obtained through purposeful action (*pravṛtti*): this is not a valid refutation, because those [moments] are indeed momentary. Rather, the correspondence exists with respect to the mere object (*vastumātra*)—which, like a person devoid of egoism, does not distinguish between the differences of moments—such that the very same kind of thing as is grasped by perception is determined by conceptual construction, and the very same kind of thing as is determined by conceptual construction is obtained through purposeful action. In this regard, conceptual constructions are not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) because they grasp what has already been grasped; likewise, the identity of the object is not [grasped anew] by conceptual construction since it has already been grasped by perception itself. And inference (*liṅga*) is not a means of valid cognition because it merely reaches what has already been apprehended by another means of knowledge.
That [exclusion of others] is inexpressible.

For the exclusion of one thing from another is neither of the nature of a non-entity nor is it apprehended by perception as a superimposed, common form that is a mere indicator of the exclusion of others. This is because the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) is its capacity for action (*arthakriyā*), and a non-entity lacks all causal efficiency. A particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), however, being ultimately real and capable of causal efficiency, is the object of perception; and since it does not persist until the time of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), how can there be identity of object?

Even if there were some single object, whose form is not determined by either the eye or conceptual perception (*vikalpa-pratyakṣa*), and which might somehow be fit for primary correspondence, nevertheless, conceptual cognition does not transcend the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because, in the determination of that which is to be known through a cognition possessing an inclusive operation (*vyāpāra-sāhiṅka-buddhi*), it possesses the nature of both a preceding and a succeeding moment, and because it possesses the fitness for the attainment of what has been determined.
