Furthermore, its status as a means of valid cognition being established, it is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*) due to the power of its active engagement and because it conforms to the presence and absence of the object and the sense faculty.

If it is argued that "differences arise through counter-annulment" and thus [conceptualization] does not occur by the mere impact of the sense-faculties as in the case of non-conceptual [perception], because there is an absence of the recollection of expressive words which carries over from the sense-object; and if it is further argued that conceptualization occurs subsequent to another memory, and that memory itself is not produced by the power of the sense-faculty and the object because it is intervened by the memory—then [we ask]: O friend, does assistance extend to the point of covering? For if a seed is obstructed by a stone, its capacity to produce a sprout is blocked. What benefit is conferred upon the sense-faculty and the object by the recollection of the word, such that this [recollection] becomes their auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*)? [The answer is: Just as a conceptualization conforms to the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the object and the sense-faculty for its own production, so too for memory; therefore, this very conformity to the sense-faculty and the object is the benefit to their essential nature (*svarūpopakāra*), namely that these two [the object and the faculty] exist when it exists.

It has been refuted in the section on the denial of the destruction of phonemes that mere [causes], by virtue of their connection with the effect, are not true auxiliaries because they do not produce any excellence in the essential nature [of the object], even though they obtain the assistance of memory.
This might be argued:
"Perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)."
Conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*), however, is determinate (*savikalpaka*); therefore, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to that [object].

Now, if it is argued that conceptualization consists of two types—one consisting of the association with words and another, distinct, consisting of the association with objects, which grasps the qualified [entity]—that is incorrect.
Because conceptual construction is untenable:
does a cognition consisting of the association with a word associate the word with the object, or does it itself become associated with the word?

If, first, it associates the word with the object, then in that case too, does it produce the nature of the word within the object, or does it apprehend the object as colored by the form of the word, or rather, does it designate it by means of the word?
Cognition does not, at the outset, impart a verbal nature to the object;

for the object appears in conceptual cognition precisely in its own form as it was grasped by non-conceptual perception, and because it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Otherwise, there would be no determination of the object that serves as the basis for linguistic usage and practical activity.
Now, if it is argued that [cognition] apprehends an object as colored by the form of the word,
that too is incorrect, because such a thing is not perceived.

When an object has been grasped by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), the inferential word that denotes it—being recalled—determines that object as it truly is by means of two counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) whose own forms have become manifest. However, the object is not grasped as being colored by the form of the word, as a crystal might be colored by blue; for there is no contradiction with the word, since in non-conceptual cognition it is the object alone that appears as "this-ness" (*idantayā*).

Furthermore, there is no obstruction whatsoever to the denoted object’s own nature when it is being recollected within a sentence, such that its status as perception (*pratyakṣatva*) would not occur when there is actual contact of the sense organ with the object.
As it has been said:
For even when a name is being recollected by memory, it does not subvert the perceptual nature of the named object;
for the name stands apart from it and is indeed incapable of covering its true character.
Thus, it is also not tenable to say that cognition designates the object by means of a word for the sake of communication.

For the self is conscious; by virtue of its capacity for synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) and so forth, it remembers the expressive word experienced over a long period of time and designates the object by means of that, thinking "this is a jar. Your [proposed] cognition would not be such, because it lacks the capacity for synthesis and the like.

First of all, perception does not connect with a word, nor does it itself become connected with a word; for cognition—whether as a distinct form (*ākāra*) or as an object (*adhikāra*)—is incapable of being connected with a word because it lacks commonality (*anādhāraṇatvāt*). This is because, according to the principle of visual cognition, there is no designation of the cognizing cognition (*viṣayi-jñāna*) by means of a word through its status as an object (*viṣayatva*) or the like, since that cognition is distinct from the word.

Now, if you think: "Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has as its object an entity conjoined with a word, and that entity, having been conjoined with the word, is designated [by it]. Or: [the other alternative].

The word "grāva" has many meanings; and among those meanings of the word, that which is predominant—namely, its capacity for holding or supporting—is not restricted to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone. Rather, it should be understood as the form (*ākāra*) which is the object of cognition, being both common to others and predominant.

Even the externality of the form of cognition (*bodhākāra*) is nothing other than a determination (*avadhāraṇa*) distinct from that very form of cognition. Furthermore, a universal (*sāmānya*) does not exist in reality, because it cannot withstand analytical inquiry. Within its own nature, when there arises a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding various forms that are produced as determinations, one fails to perceive their mutual difference. Consequently, by superimposing upon them a unity that is excluded from what is other, the notion that "this is external" arises through the power of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this must be understood as inevitable. In that regard, when there is a connection with a word (*śabda-saṃsarga*), a conceptual construction proceeds and conceptualizes an object that is not [ultimately] real; thus, knowledge is defined as "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*).

As it has been said: "Others consider the nature of pleasure, consisting of direct perception and bliss, to be a quality arising from the intellect and other faculties; yet that which appears as its form shines forth as a single, non-dual object of knowledge, when one explains it through tireless investigation and experience."

To this it is replied: If conceptualization (*kalpanā*) consists in the apprehension of an object qualified by a universal (*sāmānya*), because no such real entity as a universal exists— and thus, like the cognition of a "jar-ness" in a jar, conceptualization does not consist in the apprehension of an object conjoined with a word— then, if that appearance of a word is established as a real entity by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then even though there is apprehension of an object conjoined with a word, the conceptual cognition having that as its object would be nothing but perception (*pratyakṣa*), since its cause is the existence of the sense organ and the object.

If something appears as immediate (*aparokṣābhāsi*), it is perception (*pratyakṣa*), just like non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*). And conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) appears as immediate.

Here, the mediacy (*parokṣatva*) of cognitions is pervaded by the absence of contact between sense-faculty and object (*anindriyārthasaṃnikarṣatvena*), as in inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, the presence of contact between sense-faculty and object is perceived in non-conceptual cognition because it arises from both [the sense-faculty and the object]. Thus, there is the apprehension of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

If it is argued that there is also an inference based on a necessary connection (pratibandhānumāna)—such as [the inference] that whatever is preceded by a firm ascertainment regarding the counter-example (vipakṣa) is non-perceptual, like inferential cognition, and that determinate cognition (savikalpakajñāna) is preceded by memory—[we reply: if perceptuality (pratyakṣatva) were the observation of a momentary [object], then its negation would not apply to determinate cognition, because such a negation would have to occur prior to the observation of that [moment].

Now, if it is argued that [the object] is cognized in non-conceptual [perception], but how is it cognized? [We reply: It is cognized through inference based on its being produced by both the sense organ and the object. If that is so, then since the validity of the inference based on its being produced by both—which establishes its status as perception—is established, the inference that functions to negate its status as perception is rendered incapable of proceeding because it contradicts that [established fact]; thus, it is refuted by that very [inference], just as in the case of the statement "sound is necessarily impermanent."

First of all, since cognition consisting of the association with words is not conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), then even that consisting of the association with objects which apprehends a qualified entity is not conceptual construction; for the qualifier, the qualified, their relation, and the state of being clearly perceptible—which indicates their reality—are all real.

Regarding the object as well, I maintain that the cognition arises from the contact of the sense organ with that object; thus it is produced as an unmanifested object, yet it does not engage in deliberation (*vicāra*). Discernment (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), however, is deliberation—namely, "this is the qualifier, this is the qualified, and this is the relation between the two," according to the worldly convention, such as "a man with a staff" and not "a staff is a man. And in deliberation, having made each of these five factors distinct, one apprehends them as "a man with a staff."

If it is argued that even though this distinctness (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is real, a cognition of the qualified object (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) would arise at the very first moment [of perception], yet it does not; therefore, its distinctness does not exist by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), but rather is produced by limiting conditions (*upādhikṛta*), and thus a "cognition of distinctness" is postulated—this is an unwholesome [position] proposed by your long-lived self. For the Self, having directly perceived the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth and supported by them, perceives through the sense organ the distinctness of the object; it is not a cognition of [another] cognition, because [the Self] lacks the capacity for such synthesis (*pratisandhāna*). Having brought about its own operation, the object is indeed distinct due to its connection with the qualifier. However, because the grasping of the qualifier and so forth—which serves as the auxiliary cause—is absent, the object is not grasped in that way by the sense organ during the initial establishment [of the object]. It is grasped only when the qualifiers and so forth have been grasped. Thus, the visual cognition of an object born from the sense-object contact is, if it fails to be perceptual on account of some fault defined by the category of "object-cognition," then it is difficult to resolve; therefore, we shall desist.
They state that the causes for the arising of direct perception (pratyakṣa) with respect to wells and so forth are "the protection of the well," etc.
In the cognition whose object is the eye, substance is inherent; and that [substance] is a multi-substantial entity (anekadravya) by virtue of inherence.

There is a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) in space (*kha*) regarding its nature as space, in odor regarding its nature as odor, and in touch regarding its nature as touch; therefore, from that [specificity], there arises knowledge of the substratum (*āśraya*) of the qualities such as sound and so forth, produced through the external instruments—the sense organs—such as the ear for the sake of form, the tongue for the sake of taste, the nose for the sake of odor, and the skin-organ for the sake of touch.

Because the specific qualities residing in space are the causes, there is a fixed arrangement (*vyavasthā*) of the sense organs; otherwise, there would be a lack of restriction (*parigraha*), since [all] the remaining [qualities] exist [in all].

And the perception of sound, which is not inherent in that [organ], occurs through a sixfold contact (*ṣaḍ-vikarṣa*). Regarding "sixfold contact": although a sixfold contact of the self, mind, and sense organs is observed.

By the phrase "of that which is inherent in the auditory organ" [in the definition], it is stated that [sound] is perceived by that very [organ]; thus, the meaning is that it is perceived by the auditory organ (*śrotra*). Numbers and so forth, which arise sequentially and are inherent in perceptible substances, are grasped because they possess an intrinsic fitness for residing in their substratum.
Regarding the phrase "in succession," this is because no category of entity other than conjunction and disjunction is perceived in a substance moving toward the dark fortnight (the west).
As for the claim that "that which moves is of the nature of an action inferred from conjunction and disjunction," that is answered as follows:

if sequence were imperceptible and inferred from conjunction and disjunction, then, because conjunction and disjunction reside in [the locus of] the inferred object, sequence would also have to be inferred in other substrata.

Nor does the branch, following from the root, go back to the root from an invalid source of knowledge; for even there, the cognition "it moves" arises when it performs conjunction, disjunction, and so forth, which do not belong to the self. If it is held that this [movement] belongs to the tree through its conjunction with the person and other causes, then since the production of that [conjunction] inhering in it cannot occur simultaneously, let it be assumed that the tree possesses sequential movement. In that case, even for the person, there would be a sequence in their conjunctions with different locations; however, the assumption of sequence in the tree itself does not cease.
As a general rule, that which is the substratum of a sequence is the cause of that sequence; however, this is subject to exceptions, such as number itself.

It might be argued: "In the case of a branch being bent, since the sequence is inherent in the branch and not produced by an external agent, there is no need to postulate a sequence of independent effects consisting of conjunctions and disjunctions even when [the action] occurs in another location. But this is not so.

For a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is perceived brings to mind the thing to which it is connected; this is all that is required for the subject (*dharmin*). Since its reality is already established by the very fact of its being connected [to the probandum], what further purpose is served by its formal inclusion?

Nor is it the case that [the earth] acts out of consideration for some purpose like a conscious person; rather, if the conjunctions and disjunctions of a single point in space are postulated as the causes for inferring action, then [the objection is answered]. However, one does not suspect [the existence of] a self-existent creator, because of the impossibility of sensory contact, the impossibility of disjunction, the absence of any means of cognizing non-existence, the impossibility of the power of the terrestrial sphere to produce sprouts, and the lack of consciousness.
Let the action of a bird in flight be difficult to comprehend; let the world go to the various realms of the universe, for the atoms carry away the objects of the multitude of worlds.

If he has perished, let the sign be sought; otherwise, in this altered state, let the external regions, the senses, and the skillful [senses] be appeased. May the arm of that Yakṣa be forgiven, and may my trembling be excused. The cause of his departure is not remembered; his consciousness was unmoored in the sequence of the sacrifice.
They went together in that other form toward the unstable lightning; for one who is not firm, there is no peace.

The cognition of universals such as "substantiality" and so forth, which are inherent in their respective substrates, is apprehended by the same sense organ that apprehends those substrates themselves, in accordance with the manner in which those substrates are established. Thus, these [universals] are grasped by that very [organ].

Furthermore, from the conjunction [of the sense organ] with the visible [object], there is the apprehension of the large; from the conjunction with the conjoined part, there is the apprehension of the white part; and from the conjunction with the conjoined part possessing the quality of whiteness, there arises the cognition of smallness and so forth. From the conjunction with the part inherent in the sound, there is the apprehension of the nature of sound (*śabdatva*); and from the conjunction with the part inherent in the air, there is the apprehension of the nature of air (*vāyutva*), because it is a specific qualifier. Just as the nature of color (*rūpatva*) is a specific qualifier of the conjoined part possessing whiteness, and thus there is the apprehension of the absence of taste (*rasa*) and so forth; likewise, since the nature of sound is a non-specific qualifier of the conjoined part possessing whiteness, there is the cognition of the absence of existence (*sattva*) and so forth. This is the horse [that] destroys the Kṣatriyas. [Note: The text appears to be a fragment of a philosophical commentary (likely Vaiśeṣika) discussing perception (*pratyakṣa*) through various types of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*), specifically regarding the perception of size, color, sound, and elemental properties.]

In the section on perception (*pratyakṣakhaṇḍa*), the nature of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) consists of [the cognition of] letters such as *ka* within [the cognition of] letters such as *kha*; the nature of the qualifier of that which inheres in what inheres (*samavetasamaveta-viśeṣaṇa*) consists of the apprehension of the absence of smell and so forth in space. All of this is subsumed under the category of sound (*śabda*).

Others, however, maintain that what was stated in the sixth [chapter] regarding the eighth [category], namely that the eighth category possesses the status of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of conjunction and inherence, is not accepted by the physicians (*vaidyas*) because it involves many arguments concerning internal relations.
For the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those entities is such that they must be apprehended in that very order;
otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because there would be no restriction regarding their own substratum or another's substratum.
This is what is indicated.
"The perception of those who have given away their wealth and so forth" refers to the perception of those such as the givers of small wealth who are not yogis.
He now describes the perception of yogis.
But for those whose mastery is not yet far off, there is the final stage:
yoga is samādhi. It is of two kinds: cognitive (samprajñāta) and non-cognitive (asamprajñāta).
The sixth chapter concerns the retention (*dhāraṇā*), meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), and concentration (*samādhi*).

For one who has brought the mind under control through the eightfold means, there is a continuous flow; thus, through these coarse [practices] performed in succession, there arises a state of fixedness within the regions of the self. Through the pure [practices] such as the "stone" (*upala*) and so forth, there is the "good yoga" (*suyoga*). For one who is thus engaged, the cycle of births ripens until it is destroyed at its very root; he does not accumulate further merit or demerit. By the destruction of egoism and the like, he no longer directs his attention toward external objects.
Yoga is the application of the mind toward the Self, characterized by the transformation [of consciousness] within the Self itself, which consists of the intention and the ego-sense.

That [yoga], through purity of being (*sattva-śuddhi*) and other qualities, expands among the dharmas; it is by means of that yoga that even those who have fallen away from yoga are said to have attained yoga because they are free from passion (*vītarāgitā*). However, since this is not the case for those who lack awakening and are obscured by veils, he says "of the liberated" (*muktānām*) to address the doubt that might still exist in the minds of some even today.

For those whose [mental] states such as restraint (*yama*) and so forth have been purified, there occurs through a mind sustained by yoga the direct perception (*svapadarśana*)—which is beyond the scope of thought—of the Self within themselves, of the Self within other selves, and of the Self in external objects, in space, in the directions, in time, in air, in atoms and minds, in the qualities and so forth inherent in them, and in inherence (*samavāya*).

By people such as ourselves, the self is perceived within one's own body as an external object of cognition through hunger, thirst, heat, cold, joy, and sorrow. Furthermore, this perception is produced by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of consciousness and so forth; it is not innate. For this very reason, the notion "I am this" or "this is mine" is declared by all disputants to be a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), because it is a knowledge belonging to the contrary dark side (*viparīta-kṛṣṇapakṣa*).

The intrinsic nature (*svābhāvika*) of the six categories is perceived by those yogis when a yogi—through the firm resolve, "I shall truly realize the nature of the Self as proclaimed in the Vedānta"—withdraws the mind from the senses and practices the contemplation of the Self with unwavering one-pointedness upon some support. Then, by the power of that knowledge of reality and through the sequence of one-pointed yoga, the true nature of the Self, which has its sprout-like manifestation rooted out, becomes manifest. Furthermore, when he practices a continuous flow of contemplation upon the Supreme Self, Space, Time, and so forth, then, once his merit (*dharma*)—which possesses inconceivable power and is conducive to the knowledge of the reality of the Supreme and other principles—is augmented, he becomes endowed with knowledge by the force of that merit. Through that knowledge, he becomes connected with external objects such as the Supreme Reality, even though they are imperceptible. From that connection (*saṃyoga*), through *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined), he perceives their qualities; through *saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya* (inherence in what inheres in what is conjoined), he perceives their generic properties (*guṇatva*) and so on. By the power of a specific unseen influence (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*), he also comes to know *samavāya* (inherence) and non-existence (*abhāva*).

Knowledge of even the imperceptible [object] is seen through direct perception by means of a concentrated mind; this is the knowledge of the illustrative example in such cases as "one knows the science," etc.

By contrast, inference establishes that even the self, ether, and so forth are objects of knowledge, because they are causes for the knowledge of reality due to being the result of specific practice, like the practice of sciences, arts, and so on. Likewise, there is a gradation of intelligence, because wherever there is excellence, there is a degree of superiority, just like the gradation of magnitude.
[Objection: But in the case of water being heated, there is a gradation of heat, yet no external sound produced by that heat is observed to arise.
Nor has any instance of this lightness (*laghutva*) being perceived as conjoined [with a substance] been observed, such that one could say of a person who is conjoined with it, "This person is light.
It is replied:
that which, through stable properties, brings about a distinction in its own substratum, reaches the limit of excellence gradually.
The direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the object of cognition according to its qualities is as follows:
the purity of time and whiteness, the ripening of the cooked, the benefit for the eye, and the supreme state of the red stream;
and regarding the utterance of water and snow, even this being spoken of reaches the ultimate limit, for in the case of total effacement, it would be an extreme excellence.

Nor does a subsequent light [penance] possess any capacity to produce a distinction regarding the ownership [of the penance] when there is a prior light [penance]; for, in the case of a settled rule (*nirṇaya*), a subsequent light [penance] is understood even from a stronger [rule] than a prior light one.

For this very reason, when a person has become somewhat withered by three or four [offenses], he is awakened from the previous [state] by a light [penance], because it is capable of removing the obstruction.

But the intellect (*buddhi*), having a stable substratum, brings about excellence in its mastery; for, through repeated study for the sake of grasping what was not previously learned, it draws forth successive excellences of meaning from each preceding state. Thus, by being cultivated over a long period of time, its capacity—once the impurities have been destroyed by the discernment born of yoga—is brought to the highest degree of excellence.
Furthermore, those born of other wombs (animals) are not perceivers of supersensuous objects, because they possess vital breath, just like ourselves.

Thus, if one takes "mere person" as the subject (pakṣa), then, since that [person] is a specific kind of person who is other than the one lying on the bed, this inference by the learned person—based on the observation of grossness—is fallacious.

Now it is argued: "This [objection] is a mere fabrication; and this fabrication is not intended for the purpose of establishing one’s own position through reasoning and so forth, but rather for the sake of refuting the opponent’s position. And since the censuring of another can be accomplished by means of properties (*dharma*) and so forth that are established by the opponent’s own admissions, those [properties] such as *pramāṇa* are not independent for us. Furthermore, the opponent is not capable of standing against us. Therefore, properties and so forth are not fit to be negated even when they are established for oneself. To this we reply:

Is inference that which is connected with a formal syllogism (*prabaddhavākya*), or is it something else? If it is something else, its inclusion within one of the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be described, or else a different definition for it must be provided.

If, however, it is indeed inference, then it proceeds independently as a mere internal connection (*anubandha*), because all inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) functions with the aim of producing certainty in others just as one has oneself attained certainty.

Otherwise, even the statement "the sky-flower is fragrant because it is a flower" would be accepted as valid by the learned who have assented to it, and qualities such as being a living being (*prāṇitva*) would serve as the grounds for [proving] the omniscience of a person of supreme excellence (*puruṣadhaureya*). If even the state of being a living being were to belong to such a person of supreme excellence, then his omniscience would also follow; for there is no contradiction between those two that can be established by the force of perception.

Since omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is not within the scope of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the concomitance (*sahabhāva*) of livingness (*prāṇitva*) and so forth with non-omniscience is merely a matter of verbal assertion. Is it that non-omniscience follows from livingness as a necessary consequence, or is it due to the absence of the quality born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*) which is understood to be the cause of omniscient knowledge? It is impossible to determine this; therefore, since its nature remains undetermined, livingness and the like are incapable of proving it. Furthermore, since the quality born of yoga is not established as the cause of supersensory knowledge, how can the absence of such a quality prove that Candra, Ārya, and others are not omniscient? At the very least, [the existence of] Candra and the others is established; on that basis, one might object: "If the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established through certain determination, how can there be inference?"
Having explained [the perception] of those who are disciplined (*yuktānām*), he now explains that of those who are liberated (*viśṛṅkhānām*). Regarding "of those who are liberated":

those who, through the excellence of qualities accumulated by the practice of yoga, abide in the final stage and perceive objects with their senses even while [in that state], are the liberated ones. Their cause is the direct realization of the universal nature of all objects, which has become established as their very own nature.

Because the establishment of the fourfold nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) results from the application of the depositing of all sleep-remedies within the self, it is said that among the manifestations of the power of mantra, even when objects such as the serpent-demons (*nāga*) or the god-like beings (*brahmabhuja*) are obstructed or separated, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is metaphorically attributed to them.
Thus, having explained the term "direct perception," the result of the means of valid cognition is determined as the completion of direct perception;
therein, direct perception is merely the observation of the universal and the particular as they appear to one's own heart.

The universal (*sāmānya*) consists of existence (*sattā*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth; the particulars (*viśeṣa*) are the individual objects (*vyakti*). With regard to these, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is merely the observation of one’s own heart, or merely the grasping of one’s own heart, devoid of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because it is the most effective instrument for producing valid cognition (*pramā*). Regarding its status as the most effective instrument: when that [instrument] exists, there is the determination of the nature of the knower and the object of knowledge, provided there is no obstruction. When the knower and the object of knowledge exist, valid cognition occurs; however, it does not necessarily occur. But in the case of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), which is the means of valid cognition, valid cognition characterized by the knowledge of particulars and so forth certainly occurs—this is the certainty.

The objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are the categories (*padārtha*), namely the four categories beginning with substance (*dravya*). This means that these four categories—substance and the rest—are the objects of valid cognition (*pramiti*); once they have been cognized, the practical activities of acceptance or rejection proceed with respect to them. The knower (*pramātṛ*) is the self (*ātman*), because it is the agent of cognition.

Valid cognition (*pramiti*) is the knowledge regarding an object such as a sense-organ; when indeterminate knowledge (*nirvikalpaka*) of the general and particular characteristics is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then determinate knowledge (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) regarding substance and the other categories is the valid cognition (*pramiti*).

When others assert that even non-conceptual knowledge of universals and particulars is valid cognition (*pramā*), because it possesses the nature of being an object of expression, then, at the time of its arising, perception is defined as merely the non-erroneous observation of what is present before the eyes.

The reflection "this is that" is merely the non-conceptual (avikalpa) cognition produced by the contact of the sense-organ with its object; it is simply a restatement of the [prior] cognition. As long as the cognition of the universal-particular (sāmānya-viśeṣa) arises, it is a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). Even in the arising of the cognition of the particular, the contact of the sense-organ with the object certainly remains a means of valid knowledge, because it is the cause of valid knowledge. However, it is not independent, as it acts as a concomitant cause for the cognition of the particular. But in the arising of the cognition of the universal-particular, there is only the penetration of the [prior] cognition; such is the conclusion. Having raised the objection regarding the difference in terminology—that "the means of valid knowledge is not the cognition"—he states the justification for this: "That [cognition] does not exist [independently]."

In the cognition of a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) and a qualified (viśeṣya), no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is employed, because the cognition of the qualifier and the qualified is itself perceptual. Since the cognition of the qualified is the fruit of the cognition of the qualifier, and the cognition of the qualifier is not the fruit of another cognition—lest there be the consequence of an infinite regress—it is therefore stated that in the case of the cognition of the qualifier, the sense-object contact alone is the means of valid cognition.

It has already been stated that when non-conceptual knowledge of the general and particular (sāmānyaviśeṣajñāna) is the result, then the sense-object contact is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); and when the knowledge of the qualified object (viśeṣyajñāna) is the result, then the apprehension of the general and particular is the means of valid cognition.

Now, he says that when recollection (smṛti) or cognitions such as "rejection" (hāna) are the results, the knowledge of the qualified object is the means of valid cognition, by saying "Alternatively" (athavā).

When, regarding certain objects, after the contact of the fourfold [senses] and the subsequent apprehension of the fourfold [categories], and in the case of the apprehension of substances following the contact with substances and so forth, there arises a cognition produced by words that is free from doubt and error—whether it be designated (*vyapadeśya*) or undesignated (*avyapadeśya*)—that is the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*).

For from unstable, formless objects, one attains through the cognition of determination (*vyavasthā*) a stable, uniform form; thus they are established by the term "non-cognition" (*avyapadeśya*), as it refers to the cognition of determination. When the eye is engaged with objects that are not subject to doubt or destruction, immediately after verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*), there arises a knowledge such as "this is burning. Although this is caused by the eye, it is not [mere] perception (*pratyakṣa*), because otherwise the discernment of specific features such as lines and strokes would be impossible. Nor is it [merely] verbal, because even in the absence of words, it arises directly through the manifestation of the object, while the sense organ merely serves as its auxiliary cause. Nevertheless, when questioned, one designates it thus: "This was described by him," but one does not say, "I perceived this cow through direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*). It is for the purpose of excluding that [verbal nature] that the term "non-designative" (*avyapadeśya*) is stated.

Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and the like are considered a single [instance of] valid cognition because they function without reaching [their object]. Here, the knowledge that something is "to be acquired" (*upādeya*) arises through the aspect of the apprehended (*grāhya*); the knowledge that it is "to be rejected" (*heya*) arises through the aspect of the instrument (*dvāra*); and the knowledge that it is "neither to be rejected nor to be acquired" (*mādhyasthya*) arises through the aspect of neutrality. Let it be granted that the knowledge of what is to be acquired and so forth occurs once there is a recollection of benefits and the like, following the awareness of the nature of the object, and once there is a determination of its being a means to pleasure and so forth. However, this knowledge of what is to be acquired and so forth is actually the fruit of the very awareness of the object's nature itself, because the recollection of pleasure and so forth constitute its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*). As it has been said: [The text continues with the verse: "Even though the eye is not in contact [with its object], it is established as a means of knowledge; for the result of the sense-organ is the cognition of the object, while the recollection of pleasure and so forth are its intermediate operations. (Pramāṇavārttika 2.3) Thus, even though the eye does not reach its object, it is established as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because the result of the sense-organ is the cognition of the object, whereas the recollection of pleasure and so forth are merely its intermediate operations. Therefore, the cognition of the object's nature is the primary result, and the subsequent knowledge of its being desirable or undesirable is a secondary consequence.
"But in the interval, that activity of the agent is the *prastāva*.
Others, however, say this:

When there is the cognition that something is a means to pleasure, at that very moment there arises, by force of the object being grasped, the cognition that it is to be acquired (*upādeya*); when there is the cognition that something is a means to pain, at that very moment there arises, by force of the object being loathed, the cognition that it is to be abandoned (*heya*). And as for the cognition that "this is neither a means to pleasure nor a means to pain," that is neutrality—the cognition that it is neither to be abandoned nor to be acquired. This is valid knowledge (*pramiti*). When there is the awakening to the true nature of an object, through the recollection of its benefits and so forth, and once the determination that it is a means to pleasure and so on has occurred, the cognition that it is to be acquired and so forth arises; this is the fruit of the awakening to the object’s true nature itself. That which arises from the perception of an inferential mark (*liṅga*)—such as the recollection of pleasure—is worldly [inference].
That which arises from the observation of a mark (*liṅga*) is worldly.

The word "observation" (*darśana*) here signifies apprehension (*upalabdhi*), and not specifically visual perception, because inference based on another inference is also possible. From the observation of a mark, a conceptual cognition (*saṃjñā*) regarding the object of that mark arises; however, this [worldly inference] is not included [in the definition], because it has been qualified by the context of the section on cognition (*buddhy-adhikāra*).

By the word "lineage" (*vaṃśa*), there is the exclusion of doubt, error, and memory by means of the fire of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). The meaning of the sentence is that [knowledge] is "worldly" (*laukika*) because it arises correctly from the perception of a mark (*liṅga*).

Furthermore, because of the correctness of that knowledge, all [cognitions] possess the capacity to determine an object as it truly is; for it is the inherent nature (*kuladharma*) of all [right cognitions] to determine objects according to reality.

Doubt and error are indeed not determinations of reality, nor do they determine [objects] in such a way. As for memory, it too is not a determinative [cognition], because—as we shall explain—it is dependent upon a prior experience (*anubhava*).
Others, however, maintain that doubt and error are eliminated by the operation of valid knowledge (*vidyā*).
They assert that, for the sake of disregarding non-objective cognition and memory, that [valid knowledge] is metaphorically attributed (*upacaryate*) to categories such as substance and so forth.
That is incorrect.
Because the context is not required for the meaning indicated by the sentence;

and because it would follow that Smṛti, Buddhi, and so forth, as well as worldly cognition whose objects are past and future, would also be excluded on the grounds of being ignorant of the [ultimate] reality.

He states the definition of the inferential mark (*liṅga*): "The inferential mark, moreover... The inferential mark, moreover, is that which is known to be connected with the perceived [object] itself and is well-established as being present in what possesses that [property].
And in the absence of that [object], its indicative mark (liṅga) does not exist at all as a means of inference.
Kāśyapa declared that a mark which is contrary to this— whether by one or two [of these criteria]— is a contradictory, unestablished, or doubtful mark, and is therefore not a valid reason.

The meaning is that this very characteristic (*liṅga*) is a property (*dharma*) by which, through the cognition of the inferable (*anumeya*) and so forth, [it is established] that "that which possesses this word exists in that [locus].

For example, even though a *liṅga* existing in a portion of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is said to "subsist in the counter-example," when it subsists in a portion of the subject (*pakṣa*), it is indeed connected with the inferable.
Therefore, one who desires inference regarding the three [types of reasons]—the atom, quality, and conjunction—through the modifications of the intellect, says:

If it is argued that even the *cv*-suffix in the expression "because of being endowed with fragrance" (*gandhayuktatvāt*) would result in the fallacy of the reason being partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*) since the fragrance is not present in all parts of the cloth, this is not so, because there is a difference in nature (*vaidharmya*).

This specific verbal logic regarding the word "endowed" (*yukta*) has as its object the fact that the word "endowed" does not apply to the collection [of parts] as a whole, but rather arises with respect to each individual part; thus, it is intended to refer to each individual part alone.

He [the opponent] maintains that [the subject] exists among the five [types of subjects], just as the verbal property (*śābda-dharma*) is intended to be established by the proponent. However, it is not intended by the proponent to establish the state of being liquid and eternal in an individual earthly atom (*pārthiva-paramāṇu*); rather, since the subjecthood (*pakṣatva*) is established only for atoms as substances in their collective state, there is also the exclusion of [properties] such as being liquid and so forth, because of the absence of the other four types of objects of cognition (*prameya*).
And that [subjecthood] is well-known in the case of the two [types of atoms].
By the word "that" (*tad*), the verbal property is referred to, because of its suitability.

When that [property] is established as being present in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) which is endowed with the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), it is called a "proposition" (*pratijñāna*); thus, this is stated to exclude the contradictory (*viruddha*) and the over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding its absence, it is said that "it does not exist at all";

although the word "that" (*tad*) refers specifically to the property of the subject, by stating that in the absence of that property of the subject it "does not exist at all" and not even a single part of it exists, there is an exclusion of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

That which is contrary to it is the inferential indicator (*anumāpaka*). Having explained the inferential mark (*liṅga*)— which establishes the object of inference— he now explains the fallacious inferential mark (*liṅgābhāsa*).

"Whatever may be contrary to this" means that which is opposed to the aforementioned definition—being devoid of one or both characteristics of a logical mark (*liṅga*). That which is contrary, deficient, contradictory, unestablished, or doubtful is a logical mark consisting of a sequence that fails to bring about the understanding of the object by establishing the inferable. In this regard, [the fallacies] are as follows: the contradictory (*viruddha*) does not exist in the inferable; the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is not excluded from the domain [of the opposite]; thus, each of these is contrary to one of the characteristics of a logical mark.

Since it is contradictory and does not exist in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), yet is not excluded from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it is devoid of both characteristics of a logical mark (*liṅga*).

That which is concomitant with the object to be inferred (anumeya) in a particular place or at a particular time, which is well-known to exist in all or some part of other things possessing the property to be inferred, and which is known by means of valid cognition to be entirely non-existent in everything contrary to the object to be inferred—that becomes the mark (liṅga) that leads to the inference of an unestablished object.
He explains the meaning of the verse, "that which is connected with the object of inference," as follows:
"yadanumeyena" (that which [is connected] with the object of inference).

That thing which is concomitant with the object of inference—the property-bearer (*sādhyadharmin*)—either in a specific place or at a specific time; which is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being present in all or in some instances of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) that possesses the property to be inferred; and which is known through valid cognition to be absolutely non-existent in every instance of the contrary of the object to be inferred, where the property to be proven is excluded—that becomes the logical mark (*liṅga*) for inferring the unperceived property on the subject of inference whose object is not yet established. This was stated—"in a specific place or at a specific time, like the mark of a sword"—in order to demonstrate that the capacity to indicate (*gamakatva*) belongs not necessarily to the mark as it is perceived in the subject of inference, but rather to that mark whose inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the property to be proven has been demonstrated in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) at whatever place or time.

Because it serves as a reason for the non-occurrence [of the probandum] in all instances other than those of the same class (*sapakṣa*), and because it is stated that it is absent from everything else, the term "in all" (*sarvasmin*) is employed to indicate its pervasion over the entire domain of objects, including both the similar and the dissimilar classes (*vipakṣa*). Some logicians, however, previously maintain that a counter-example established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not strictly necessary; for even by the mere statement, "Where this [probandum] is absent, this [probans] is also absent," the pervasion of the probans (*sādhana*) by the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhya*) is understood through the power of implication.
And thus, among them, it belongs to Yama.
Therefore, in this context, the basis for the six [faculties] is that which grasps the object;
for even when those [six] are absent, it is understood to reside there because of the scriptural statement: "In that [case], too."
Thus, regarding the phrase "in the demonstration of that [reason]," the meaning is:
where there is no proof by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparīta*), and not merely by words alone.
For if mere verbal assertion were possible everywhere even when preceded by valid cognition, it would follow that the logical status of being a non-reason (*ahetutva*) could never be established.

If it is argued that this *tiṅulavaṇa* (salt-in-the-tiṅu) is over-pervasive because it exists in both *prakaraṇasama* and *kālātyayāpatti*, [the author] replies: No, for *prakaraṇasama* and *kālātyayāpatti* are included within the category of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) in certain respects. This is because *prakaraṇasama* occurs when the subject (*dharmin*)—the locus of the property to be proven—is such that there is doubt regarding the specific nature of the probandum, and *kālātyayāpatti* occurs when the time [of the reason's application] has passed. Thus, *prakaraṇasama* is so called because it relates to the "equality of the topic" (*prakaraṇasāmya*). A "topic" (*prakaraṇa*) is that which is introduced or set forth as the subject of debate; "equality" (*sāmya*) refers to the investigation (*cintā*) concerning it. That investigation which is conducted results in a lack of determination regarding the object. Since it is common to both sides, it is employed to determine one side or the other when there is equality of the topics.

For example: "Sound is eternal because the properties of the non-eternal are not perceived," and "Sound is non-eternal because the properties of the eternal are not perceived. Since the properties of both the eternal and the non-eternal are unperceived in sound, a doubt arises as to whether it is non-eternal or eternal; consequently, an investigation into that matter ensued, for without adopting one of the two positions, there can be no removal of the doubt through the ascertainment of reality.

In that regard, the non-perception of the properties of impermanence leads to an engagement for the sake of ascertaining permanence; the non-perception of the properties of permanence leads to an engagement for the sake of ascertaining impermanence. That which does not deviate from its respective path while failing to perceive the properties of permanence is not fit for a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*); rather, it functions to negate that [conclusion]. And because it exists in the subject (*dharmin*) as a cause of doubt regarding the object, it is not restricted to a single alternative; thus it is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). Previously, the inconclusive was termed "falling into another time" (*kālāntarāpatti*).

Even if [the reason] were defined as being present in what is perceived (*pratyakṣa*), since "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) exists in fire—which is a counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—[the reason would be fallacious]. In the section on cognition (*buddhyadhikāra*), the desire for the highest [status] regarding qualities is mentioned; that is incorrect. If the probans is considered effective merely by its exclusion from the counter-example—such as when it is said that in the case of "being perceived," there is no deviation from the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) like cognition and so forth, or from the counter-example—then let it be granted that there is a possibility of a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*) regarding the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*). Nevertheless, by the force of the context, the probans is indeed capable of establishing the probandum through its own causal complex (*svayāmagrī*).

Now, if one is unable to establish [the probans] because doubt regarding the counter-example has been introduced, then it follows that there is no capacity for comprehension through the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*). Furthermore, if one maintains that "non-existence in the similar instance" (*asannipadvattva*) is also to be relied upon as another characteristic (*rūpāntara*), then it fails to be a reason (*hetu*) because of its absence in that respect. This same point should be stated previously regarding the fallacy of the "indefinite" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).

If the status of being a logical mark (*liṅgatva*) is based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), then the inference from "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) would result in an invalid inference due to the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).

On the other hand, if [the mark] does not function despite the presence of "being produced" and its exclusion from the subject (*pakṣāvaruṇatva*), because an inference is presented by a counter-argument, then one must also follow another characteristic (*rūpāntara*), namely "having a non-sublated object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), as opposed to the statement "in the absence of contradiction with perception."

Therefore, the final position [pakṣa] is that which is intended to be established; and that which is to be established is that which, while existing therein, is capable of establishing [the point], because it is not a counter-position (pratipakṣa) merely by being cognized as such, since in reality there is no duality of nature. Furthermore, even that which is known through the cognition of the opponent is not a "position" (pakṣa), because it is incapable of being established in its own form, having been already understood in another form. Consequently, that which is connected with the object of inference at the time of the context, but is set aside by something else, is not a valid position.
Because it is the locus for the manifestation of the object of inference (*anumeya*).

Now, one might object that this [reason] is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*) because it does not exclude the contrary; for the reason (*hetu*) is indeed threefold: positive concomitance (*anvaya*), negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).
Among these, the positive concomitance is as follows: "The particular (*viśeṣa*) must be denotable (*abhidheya*), because it is knowable (*prameyatva*), like a universal (*sāmānya*)."

For all its [the inference's] members, such as the subject and so forth, are like the example of a pot: the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). This is because there is no absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that which is not an object of cognition (*aprameya*), since it is unnameable (*anabhidheya*) and lacks the status of being a cognizable object. Furthermore, that which is designated by the term "Buddha" but is unnameable and an object of no-cognition must be regarded as non-existent, like a horse's horn; nor could it be the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), because it would lack intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatva*). And whatever exists must be a similar instance in every respect; moreover, in the case of its existence, it simply does not exist [as a distinct entity], because it pervades through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and lacks negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
If it is argued that "this is one part of that," we say no, because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the final [term].
The logical connection (*anvaya*)—namely, the establishment of another sixfold statement—is its cause; however, its deviation is indeed beginningless.

For instance, there exists the universal concomitance between the state of being cognizable (*prameyatva*), the state of being denotable (*abhidheyatva*), and the state of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*), since denotability is observed in every object of cognition (*prameya*).

Nor is deviation observed, nor does even the suspicion of it arise; for whatever one brings before the mind as being outside the scope of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and wishes to state to another—all that necessarily possesses the properties of being knowable (*prameyatva*) and nameable (*abhidheyatva*). Furthermore, there is no distinction such that non-deviation would be the cause [of validity] when a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) exists, while it would not be so due to the absence of such a scope. Therefore, perceptibility is intended and understood. And the negative instance (*vyatirekin*) is: "The living body possesses breath and so forth, because it has its own self. In this case, all the five members of the syllogism are present.

Nevertheless, because the fallacy of the converse (*viparyaya-prasakti*) and other such defects are impossible, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "selflessness" (*nirātmakatva*) by the possession of properties such as being a pot and so forth is understood; and the absence of "possession of breath and so forth" (*aprāṇādimattva*) is perceived in the living body. Through that perception and that pervasion, there is an inference of the negation of selflessness. Now, [you might argue: "In the case of a horse, that 'horse-ness' is not apprehended, nor is even a single instance of its occurrence grasped; on the contrary, because a logical connection (*pratibandha*) has a positive entity as its object, and since the Self has not been encompassed [in the cognition], how could the cognition of a pot and so forth have grasped the pervasion of that [Self]?"
That is incorrect.

For one who maintains that the self is the witness of all objects, it is not the case that the knower of a jar and so forth lacks the capacity to know the self through his own perception. Once the causal relationship between the effects—such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so on—and the self as their cause is established within the living body, the knower of the jar and so forth, by virtue of the pervasion of the intellect and other faculties, possesses at the moment of their production a direct perceptual determination of his own hidden self.
This is just as the absence of fire capable of producing smoke is established when smoke is absent.

If this were so, the self (*ātman*) would already be established in living bodies when it is being related [to them], because the cognition of a relation is impossible without that which is related; consequently, the inference by exclusion (*vyatirekānumāna*) would be useless, as the means of proof would fail to function as a proof for an action whose sequence has already been accomplished.
This is not the case, because while the self is established for oneself, it is yet to be proved for others, and thus remains the object of proof (*sādhya*).

Nor is there a rule that deviation (*vyabhicāra*) cannot occur otherwise, nor that deviation consists in the non-pervasion of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); therefore, even a reason (*hetu*) that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*) is established as a valid reason, and thus [the definition] is too narrow (*avyāpaka*).

Those who say that in the case of non-comprehension, the inclusion of purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) and purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) reasons—which are unestablished in other systems (*samānatantra*)—is intended, while others state that the definition applies to all types without exception.
"Connected with the object of inference and established as existing where that [object] exists" is the definition of the positive (anvayin) [reason].

"Connected with the object of inference and not existing where that has ceased or where it is absent" is the definition of the negative (vyatirekin). Taken together, this is the definition of the positive-negative (anvaya-vyatirekin). Furthermore, the state of being a means of proving the probandum is the general definition for all three, just as the capacity to produce a cognition corresponding to reality is the general definition for the [three] means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

The second question—“What would it be for one with a perverted cognition?”—is explained by [the author] whose meaning is unimpaired: “That which, however, is contrary to the aforementioned three-fold mark (liṅga) by one or two characteristics, does not serve as a mark for the establishment of the object to be inferred. This very point is stated by the author of the Sūtra: “Non-instruction due to the non-establishment of the cause, non-existence, and the absence of connection” (NS 1.2.4). Regarding the term “non-instruction”: [The commentary continues: “Non-instruction” means that when the reason is not established, there is no instruction [regarding the probandum]. For example: “Sound is eternal because it is visible. Here, visibility is not a property of sound; therefore, since the reason is unestablished, there is no instruction regarding its eternality. Furthermore, even if the reason were established, if it lacks a necessary connection to the probandum, it is also a case of non-instruction. For example: “Sound is eternal because it is produced. Here, although being produced is established in sound, there is no instruction regarding its eternality because there is no connection between being produced and eternality. Moreover, even if the reason is established and connected, if it is contradictory to the intended probandum, it is also a case of non-instruction. For example: “Sound is eternal because it is a product of effort. Here, although being a product of effort is established in sound and is connected to impermanence, it is contradictory to the intended probandum of eternality; thus, there is no instruction regarding its eternality. Therefore, the term “non-instruction” refers to the state of being a non-mark (aliṅga) due to the non-establishment of the cause, the absence of connection, or contradiction. Thus, the three types of fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa)—unestablished, contradictory, and inconclusive—are included within this category of non-instruction. Consequently, these are not separate categories of fallacious reasons distinct from the non-marks. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the word “and” (ca) in the Sūtra implies that other types of non-marks are also included. For instance, when the subject (dharmin) itself is unestablished, such as in the argument “A sky-flower is fragrant because it is a flower,” the reason is a non-mark because the locus of the property is unestablished. Similarly, when the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is unestablished, such as in the argument “Sound is a substance because it possesses color,” the reason is a non-mark because the property to be proven is unestablished. Likewise, when both the subject and the property to be proven are unestablished, such as in the argument “A rabbit’s horn is sharp because it is a horn,” the reason is a non-mark because both are unestablished. These and other such cases are all included under the term “non-instruction. Thus, the meaning is that whatever is contrary to the three-fold mark by one or two characteristics is a non-mark. This concludes the explanation of the second question.
The meaning is that a reason which is "not pointed out" (*anupadeśa*) is a non-reason (*ahetu*).

By "unestablished" (*aprasiddha*), both the contradictory (*viruddha*) and the over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) reasons are included; for these two lack the quality of being a reason because they are not established as proving the object of proof (*sādhyaprameya*).

Even if [the reason] is unestablished, it is considered contradictory; for even if it is established in every respect regarding the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), it is a non-reason if its presence in the subject (*dharmin*) has not been observed.

For when a reason is observed in the subject (*dharmin*) with the notion that it is inconclusive due to its doubtful nature as a property (*dharmatva*), it becomes doubtful whether it is accompanied by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) or whether it is devoid of it; it is not, however, incapable of establishing one [of these] properties. Thus, for one who lacks the knowledge that "this is inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*) with that," there is no desire to know even more regarding the presence of another property in the subject; rather, the very essence of inseparable connection is what constitutes the means of inference (*anumāna*) for the cognition of the inferable object. This he demonstrates:
And the ritual procedure consumes [it].
Wherever there is the absence of fire characterized by smoke, smoke itself does not exist.

Thus, even for that which consists of a well-known location, because smoke is necessarily connected to the undesirable path [of fire], and because one observes the external collection [of causes], there occurs the entry into the connection with the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). In this way, in all cases, that which is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with respect to place, time, and so forth, possesses the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*).

In the treatise (*śāstra*), the fourfold set beginning with "the effect" (*kārya*) is established as an indicator (*liṅga*) of existence, not for the sake of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), because [existence] is understood through two types of excess (*atireka*). For example: the rising of the moon is the cause of the night, of the blooming of the *kuṣuda* flower, and of the swelling of the waters; likewise, the flow of water from a jar is the cause of the rising of fire, and so forth.
All such cases are established by the mere statement that "this is other than that."
That [inference] is of two kinds:
that based on what has been perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and that based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
Among these, *dṛṣ�ṭa* is an inference where there is no absolute difference in nature between the established [reason] and the thing to be established (*sādhya*).
Just as, having perceived only the fragrance in one place, one recognizes it upon seeing only the fragrance in another location;

so too, when there is an absolute difference in genus between the well-known instance and the object to be proven, inference based on the persistence of the commonality of the mark and the property to be inferred is "inference from general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

For example, having observed that the activity of people belonging to the various castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*) possesses a result, one infers a result for those who act without aiming at any visible purpose.
In this context, the perception of the mark (*liṅga*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the resulting knowledge is the valid cognition (*pramiti*).

Alternatively, the resulting knowledge itself is the means of valid cognition, and the perception of qualities, defects, or neutrality is the valid cognition; thus, inference is that which determines its own object.

Regarding the objects [of inference], the manner of cognizing the inferable is as follows: for example, from the statement "there is smoke here, and where there is smoke, there is fire," a person who understands the convention and recognizes the established invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) gains the knowledge that "this is smoke" and "this is a mountain," and so forth. Following this verbal cognition and the subsequent mental recollection—specifically the recollection of the rule "where there is smoke, there is fire"—inference subsequently arises.

Nor is it the case that, in this way, the second consideration of the mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) cannot be obtained; for there is no need for it, since the cognition of the object to be inferred is established by the perception of the mark and the recollection of the pervasion alone. Nor would the cognition of the inferable, following immediately upon memory, be indeterminate in its locus, because the perception of the mark acts as the regulator. Nor is there any pointlessness to this [member], because in the proof for another (*parārthānumāna*), it is presented for the purpose of establishing the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) which has already been indicated by the other members.

Furthermore: what is this so-called "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*), which is non-deviation? Why is it said to arise from identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*)? [The opponent replies: It is a fortuitous relation; just as it occurs, so too might it not occur, and thus there is an absence of a cause for its necessity. Even if, for you, the presence of form and the absence of substance constitute the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), nevertheless, non-deviation cannot be known because the counter-example is difficult to exclude and remains unprevented.

However, when based on "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*), doubt is excluded because an effect cannot arise without its cause. Even when based on "arising from that," the "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*) is established through five instances of perception and non-perception: (1) the non-perception of the effect prior to its arising; (2) the perception [of the effect] when the cause is perceived; (3) [the perception of the effect] after it has been perceived; (4) the excellence or deficiency in cognition regarding the form, bliss, and compassion; and (5) the non-perception [of the effect] due to the non-perception of the substance of the effect. Thus, there is one perception of the effect's non-perception, and two perceptions and non-perceptions of the effect itself.
Thus, regarding perception and non-perception: it is determined that this presence of smoke occurs only when [the fire] exists and its absence occurs when it does not exist.

Furthermore, because the effect arises only when that [cause] exists and its absence occurs when it does not exist, the portion of the name "identity" (*tādātmya*) is also determined through the cognition of identity.

There is no deviation from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, because its establishment as being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) ensures the certainty of identity (*tādātmya*). However, when a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) arises through the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that [certainty] is shattered. But if a subverting factor is merely asserted, who is able to prevent the suspicion that—even though their coexistence has been observed—[the one] might at some time deviate from the other?
As it has been said:
"Either from the relation of cause and effect, or from an intrinsic nature that acts as a regulator..."
The rule of invariable concomitance arises from non-perception [of the absence of the probans where the probandum is absent], but not from perception.

Thus, it is argued that the rule of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva-niyama*) does not arise from the relationship of cause and effect, nor from identity as a restrictive factor, because [the concomitance] is observed in some cases and not observed in others. To this, it is replied: Is it the case that where there is identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*), there is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*)?
Or rather, do [the relations of] identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*) exist only where there is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*)?
It cannot be the first alternative, because even when origination from that exists, there is no certainty regarding the earthiness and other properties of smoke and fire due to lack of investigation.

Even if identity (*tādātmya*) is [the basis of inference], there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because of the particularity of "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*). Now, where there is no deviation, there is identity and origination (*tadutpatti*); thus, non-deviation itself constitutes the nature of a logical reason (*naiyāyikatva*). If that is so, let non-deviation alone be the indicator; what is the use of identity and origination? For even in the case of an effect, it is not the case that "being an effect" alone is what is indicated, nor is it the case that "being an essence" (*svabhāva*) alone is what is indicated. Why is this? Because it is precisely that which does not deviate from it—non-deviation alone is the cause for being an indicator, not identity and origination, due to their deviation.

Nor does one incur the fallacy of non-perception (*apūrvapakṣa*), for smoke is produced by fire and not by its earthiness (*pārthivatva*) and so forth, because the nature of the thing is thus determined.

Nor is this perceived as a qualification, such that "the tree is not the essence of the tree because it consists of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*)," since it is common to barley, mud, and so on; for it is established in that way.

If treeness—which is common to barley and other things—is not the qualifier, then there is no identity between these two, because difference in nature is the defining characteristic of difference. If, however, there were non-difference, then just as treeness is common to all trees, so too would the state of being a qualifier be common to all. Furthermore, a fixed relationship of indicator and indicated is not tenable when there is identity, since that [identity] is the cause of non-difference. If, while the state of being a qualifier is being apprehended, treeness is not apprehended, then even if identity were apprehended, it would be so only sequentially.

Now it is said: just as the property of being visible and the property of being a tree are respectively subsumed within that [notion of] dharma, so too, when dharmas are being subsumed, the state of being an object is subsumed within the nature of cognition (*buddhi*).
As it has been stated:
Therefore, for an entity that is perceived, the quality is indeed nothing other than what is perceived;
what other part could there be that is not perceived and yet is examined by means of valid cognitions?

Thus, when a conceptualization of the object (*viṣayin*) arises and not a conceptualization of the intellect (*buddhi*), this is because the term "intellect" serves to exclude [other things]. Since the word "object-possessor" (*viṣayin*) generates a cognition limited to sensation (*vedanā*), the conceptualization of the object-possessor is defined by the exclusion of non-intellect (*abuddhi*) and so forth, because all conceptualizations have as their objective domain that which stands before them. Furthermore, there is no real ontological distinction between these two—namely, the relationship of the signified and the signifier and the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—because they lack intrinsic existence. Therefore, the exclusions of the conventional and the exclusions of the object-possessor are mutually distinct due to the difference in what is being excluded; thus, as in the case of the seasons, the aforementioned fault does not arise.

"Aha! What supreme skill the scholars possess in connecting what precedes and what follows! [They claim] there is identity (*tādātmya*) between the cognition of inference and the two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) that serve as the probandum and the probans, yet there is mutual difference between them. Is this some sort of sorcery? If it is argued that there is identity between the fire and the smoke, and that they are established as having that nature, such that even though there is a difference between the exclusion of non-fire and the exclusion of non-smoke—which are the objects of those respective cognitions—there is identity according to the conceptual determination (*vyavasāya*)," [we reply: if identity exists, then the exclusion of the subject (*dharmin*) by the exclusion of non-[subject] must be understood; and if that exclusion is not determined by the cognition, then the establishment of identity according to the conceptual determination cannot occur. Thus, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

If it is argued that the establishment of identity (*tādātmya*) between two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*)—which have been determined as having passed beyond the reach of the apprehension of pervasion—is what occurs, then the difference between those two things so determined must be conceptual (*kālpānika*). For if that were so, inference would proceed even by the power of conceptual construction; there would be no such thing as a "non-reason" (*ahetu*), since even for "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*), once they are determined as having a single nature, there is the possibility of identity through the determination of their properties as mental states. If it is argued that because there is no exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there can be no identity between knowability and impermanence, [we reply: True, there is no such identity in the sense of the scriptural meaning; however, an identity supported by conceptual construction certainly exists, and it is precisely this that is employed to justify the arising of inference. Furthermore, regarding the nature of identity and the nature of being that form, if one has a cognition of it despite disagreement, then for one who holds that there is no reason (*hetvābhāsa*), even upon seeing the non-perception of its property, inference proceeds from non-perception. Thus, it is untenable to say that there is a cognition of the absence of that [object] based on the cognition of the absence of the object in the mind, through the cognition of identity with its own negation or through the cognition of its being produced from it, when there is disagreement regarding the reason's absence.

Since it is untenable that every non-apprehension in relation to another cognition constitutes an object of apprehension, [the reason] is vitiated by the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddha*) due to the force of ignorance regarding that [object], or because of its accidental occurrence (*āpātataḥ*). Furthermore, in establishing identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), the essential nature (*svabhāva*) or the effect (*kārya*) serves as the logical reason (*hetu*). Moreover, in cases such as the emergence of a sprout from a seed, the essential nature of the internal state is perceived.

Therefore, the claim that "the restriction [of concomitance] arises either from the relation of cause and effect or from essential nature (svabhāva)" is an unexamined intention. For some thing is necessarily bound by another through its own nature because it is free from conditions (*upādhi*); indeed, a relation produced by conditions ceases when those conditions are removed, but an essential relation does not. If we were to say that the external relation is produced by conditions, then those conditions would have to be perceived; however, this is impossible, as the venerable teachers have already refuted them.

For when smoke and fire are repeatedly perceived externally, there is no basis for [suspecting] anything if their limiting conditions (*upādhi*) are not perceived; nor is it the case that the conditions of a perceived thing must necessarily remain unperceived. For if those conditions were invariably concomitant with their own causes, then even so, the refutation of perception would be established, since the relation [of the condition] to its effect could exist even if it were not produced by that [cause], as long as it is observed to occur. Alternatively, if they were not invariably concomitant, then the causes of those conditions and the causes of those causes would also have to be inferred, and thus one would have to postulate an entire series of words not present in the actual application.
