Furthermore, that smoke which possesses no limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is never perceived independently, just as fire—which has its connection with smoke produced by other adjuncts—is perceived as being produced by dry fuel, whereby these two are clearly observed through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

However, smoke is never seen in this manner within consciousness; therefore, since the non-perception of those limiting adjuncts whose presence would have been reached through perception leads to the cognition of their absence.

When the non-existence [of fire] is cognized through the non-perception of those things that are perceptible, and when it is determined that [non-perception] is not a valid reason because of its deviation (vyabhicāra) in cases where perceptible objects—unqualified by any specific state—are seen again and again at other times, then, for one who does not exclude any spatial or temporal distinctions, there is no fault regarding the perception of the absence of a limiting condition (upādhi). Having ascertained the coexistence (sahabhāva) based solely on the essential nature (svabhāva), which pervades the single object by means of the instrument that has removed all doubt concerning a counter-instance, [the cognizer] determines the necessary connection (niyama) that "this is invariably concomitant with that" through the generality of smoke and the generality of fire.

Although concomitance (*sahabhāva*) is indeed apprehended even at the first sight [of the two things], nevertheless, there is no apprehension of a necessary rule (*niyamagrahaṇa*). For it is not from mere concomitance that necessity arises, but rather from concomitance that is free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhika*). And for one who desires that this freedom from conditions be established through the non-perception of smoke [in the absence of fire], smoke does not arise as a conceptual construction (*savikalpaka*) by the force of the apprehension of concomitance; rather, it arises when the cow is present before one's eyes. This has already been refuted by the argument that since perception occurs moment by moment regarding each existing object, it cannot serve as an auxiliary for the necessity of the effect across individual instances.

For it is not the case that, by abandoning the particular, one grasps the pervasion through the universal alone without first grasping the pervasion as residing in the particular; because that [universal] is the cause of all [cognitions], what [particular] individual would not have entered into the grasp of the pervasion? Rather, it is through the universal. Therefore, since inference is observed even with respect to mere fire—such as "it is hot"—one follows that [universal] and does not take up the particular.

If, however, even when a rule has been ascertained in a general sense, you maintain that there is no violation of the rule because it is not broken, then in your own position as well, what prevents the non-functioning of inference due to doubt regarding the apprehension of that [relation] from causes and effects separated by space and time, even though those external things have been perceived by direct perception and their causal relation grasped? Furthermore, how could the causal relation be determined by your "perception of every instance" (*pratyakṣadarśana*), since smoke, upon being seen, would manifest its specific qualities without being subject to doubt?

If it is argued that perception has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object and is directly apprehended—since it is impossible to perceive individual particulars again and again—and therefore the causal relationship, which has the universal as its object, when determined in a single instance, determines it for all [instances] because the universal is one; we too say: "When [the relationship] is determined for all [instances], why does this restriction not please you?"

Furthermore, for you [the Sāṃkhyas], since the universal (*sāmānya*) is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it cannot experience the relation of cause and effect because it is a non-entity (*avastu*). As for the particulars (*vyakti*), since they are of such a nature, all of them would indeed be grasped by direct perception.

Nor is it logical to claim that there is a mental synthesis (*saṃkalana*) of past and future particulars by means of the mind; for the mind, having abandoned its external state through meditation, lacks the capacity to grasp what is external to it. Even if the relation of cause and effect were established among the particulars seen [in the present], inference could not arise from that, as it would lack generality. Furthermore, it is not tenable for the particulars themselves to be the basis for the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), because they are not mutually concomitant (*anvita*).

Nor can a synthesis based on a single generality be possible at that time, because there is no relationship of probandum and probans between two entities; or else, if it were established through mere verbal artifice, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, they do not understand what the object of the certainty regarding the production of that [inference] is, which is established by perception and from which the operation of inference proceeds. [The answer is:
It is that in which the mark (*liṅga*) of one thing is invariably concomitant with another in terms of place and time.
Just as fire is the mark [of existence] in a lamp;
wherever there is a mark that is inseparable from a place and inseparable from a time, it is a mark for the other which is to be proven (*sādhya*).
For example, the production of gold among the Kashmiris is a mark for the presence of *gāmātika* flowers; and among the Yavanas, the golden limbs of a maiden is a mark for her being a slave-girl.
For example, the breath, the stars, and the movement of birds are invariably concomitant with time; thus, the departure [of birds] at dawn is a mark (*liṅga*) of the king’s awakening.

If the capacity to indicate [a thing] consists in an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with place and time, then indeed it is well known that there are six types of marks in this regard: the effect (*kārya*), the cause (*kāraṇa*), the conjoined (*saṃyogin*), the contradictory (*virodhin*), the inherent (*samavāyin*), and so forth.
The mention of "effect" and the others in the treatise is made for the sake of illustration, not for the sake of being exhaustive.

The phrase "otherwise" means that the mention of the *kūrca* (a bundle of grass) and other such items is intended to illustrate the types of indicative marks (*liṅga*), not for the purpose of defining them as the exclusive set of indicative marks.
To the question "How is this so?", he says: "Why? (kasmāt).
He states the reply:
"Because of the observation of negative concomitance.
Since inference is observed even in the absence of an effect and so forth, it is not for the purpose of non-activity.
In this regard, he demonstrates where there is the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of the effect and so forth:
"Just as, for example, [the word] 'audibility' (*śrāvaṇatva*) manifests in the breast; therein, the cause (*hetu*) is the mark (*liṅga*).

For one who has previously understood that "the taste of mangoes is different from others" and thus hears [the statement], "It is not anything else," if there is an understanding based on the audible mark—the cause—which is to be inferred, then inference exists through the recollection of the cause regarding the object, such as a jar, which is distinct from other things.

Furthermore, there is no statement that [the moonrise] is not a cause, nor an effect, nor a causal factor, nor a conjoined entity, nor a contradictory one, nor [related] by inherence; this constitutes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
He provides another example:
"The rising of the moon [is the cause] of the swelling of the ocean," and so forth.

When the moon rises, the ocean swells and the night-lotuses bloom; since this is certain, one might think that today’s rising of the moon is the mark (*liṅga*) for the swelling of the ocean and the blooming of the lotuses.

However, the rising of the moon is not the effect (*kārya*) of the ocean’s swelling and the lotuses’ blooming; for both are the result of the moon’s conjunction with a specific location, and that [conjunction] is the effect of the moon’s own action, not caused by the swelling of the ocean and so forth.

Nor can it be said that this [the rising of Agastya] is the cause of the increase of the ocean, nor of the blooming of the night-lotuses (*kumuda*), because the blooming of lotuses—characterized by their mutual distinction and arising from excellence, splendor, and beauty—is due solely to other causes existing at that specific time, as they are distinct [from the rising of Agastya].
Furthermore, the flow of water in autumn is [the result] of the rising of Agastya.
The clarity and brilliance perceived in autumn are the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of the rising of Agastya, for there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in other instances.
If there were a logical mark (*liṅga*) distinct from the effect and so forth, then surely all logical marks would be connected to it; therefore, he says:
"As for 'this' and so forth"—that is established by the statement of the capacity of the relationship through the phrase "all this is indeed that.

The intention of words such as "making others hear" and so on is that the logical mark is grasped and established by the statement of the capacity of the relationship through the phrase "all this is indeed that."

It is not tenable to say that "the mark (liṅga) of the subsequent is the subsequent," for [otherwise] there would be the contingency of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). To avoid such an objection, it is stated: "This is the mark because it is seen as the cause. This is a summary statement regarding the specific nature of the object to be expressed as a mark; it does not mean that every other thing is a mark for everything. This is because it is established that a mark is that which possesses a relationship of concomitance. That which is invariably connected to another by way of place, time, or state is said to be its mark; for that very thing is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) with respect to its own object, whereas anything else is not a mark because it exists elsewhere as well.

If you say that the [invariable concomitance] does not apply because one cannot say, "Is this its effect? and so forth, then for what purpose was the set of six [types of] effects and so on mentioned? It was stated for the sake of illustration.
For I suspect that it is impossible for a student to provide an example and then ask, "What invariable mark (*liṅga*) should be shown? Thus, the set of effects and so on serves as an illustration.
There is no general rule (*utsarga*) regarding marks based on such [specific] categories.
He explains the distinction:
"In that case, it is swift in the specific [instance], swift in the general [instance], and swift.
This is for the purpose of supporting the sense faculties, such as the eye.
That inference is indeed a specific instance of rapidity; it is "rapid" by virtue of its unity with rapidity as a universal.
When that [object] is seen in various impure places through the medium of perception, there is an inference regarding the non-difference of the genus.

That which is well-known in the subject (*pakṣa*)—the rapidity to be proven—is slightly less than a moment; when there is knowledge of the unity of that which is to be inferred through its own cognition, that inference is rapid.

Just as, having perceived a horn by means of its scent, one infers a cow in another place—where previously the cow was known only as qualified by the universal *gotva* (cowness)—this is called "inference based on what was seen" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*) because there is no difference in the object of knowledge. Since the specific individual (*svalakṣaṇa*) of that universal *gotva*, which was previously inferred from the sight of the horn, has perished, the inference arises through the medium of what is well-known, following the recurrence of the universal; thus it is an inference based on the universal (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*).

A certain well-known [example] is less than a *saha* (thousand); when there is a perceived [correlation], that which is to be proven (*sādhya*) is the object of inference (*anumeya*). Since these two are of entirely different natures, the mark (*liṅga*) is indeed the object of inference, and thus everything is both mark and object of inference. In this way, regarding their commonality, the mark and the object of inference are the same; regarding their commonality, there is a recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of those two. Since the mark and the object of inference are the same, there is a recurrence of the commonality; therefore, because the commonality of the mark is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāva*) with the commonality of the object to be proven, that inference is "inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

Just as the inference of a result is observed for farmers, artisans, and royal officials who engage in activity without aiming at a visible purpose— such as the result of a farmer’s activity being grain and so forth, that of an artisan’s or royal official’s activity being gold, gems, pearls, charcoal, and so forth, and that of the activities of those belonging to the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramin) being heaven and so forth— the inference of a result follows from their engagement despite the extreme difference in the nature of these activities.

Let this be an inference, because there is an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the generality of activity (*pravṛttitvasāmānya*) and the generality of being fruitful (*phalavattvasāmānya*).
For this very reason, it is called "seen generally" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), since the rule is observed through a general [correlation].

As for that specific fruit characterized by heaven and so forth which is not to be inferred, no such rule is observed for a fruit of this kind; for even the activity of those who know the Veda has as its purpose merely a livelihood, according to the opponent.
To this he replied:
"A visible purpose is not being aimed at.
There certainly exist such persons who, though seeing that many things are fruitless, practice vows such as those of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) and so forth."
Regarding their engagement in this [process], when there is the non-disappearance of these qualities and no modification of the intellect (*buddhi*), there is inference through another word.
The meaning is that one should not know [this] as an "inference of the result" (*phalānumāna*) because it is yet to be established.

The word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), understood through the etymology of the instrument (*karaṇa*), does not reach its full sense without a result; therefore, he demonstrates the distinction between the means of valid cognition and its result.

In this context, it is said that "the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding inference (*anumāna*), the cognition of the mark is established as the *pramāṇa* based on the etymological derivation: "that by which something is correctly cognized (*pramīyate*). The result (*phala*) of the *pramāṇa* is the cognition of the object (*prameya*). Although there is a difference in the objects (*viṣaya*) between the cognition of the mark and the cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) with respect to their production, nevertheless, because the cognition of the mark also functions toward the production of the cognition of the possessor of the mark, it has the mark as its object; consequently, the *pramāṇa* and its result do not have different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatva*).
He states another method with the words "as follows" (*yathā*).

The cognition of the undesirable (*aniṣṭajñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while established consensus (*prasiddhi*) is the fruit of the means of valid cognition. By this, they explain that the perception of qualities (*guṇadarśana*)—the cognition that "this is a means to happiness"—is the perception of the desirable; the perception of defects (*doṣadarśana*) is the cognition that it is a means to suffering; and the perception of neutrality (*mādhyasthyadarśana*) is the cognition that it is neither a means to happiness nor a means to suffering. This is because such a cognition is established through experience.

This is inference with a well-ascertained object (*svaniścitārthānumāna*); the term *niścita* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve niṣṭhā*). Thus, "with a well-ascertained object" means an inference for one's own sake (*svaniścayārtham*).

Verbal testimony (*śabda*) and the other means of knowledge are also included within inference, because they follow the same procedure. Just as there arises inference regarding a supersensuous object for one who possesses a well-established convention, perceives an unambiguous mark (*liṅga*), and has a recollection of its established connection, so too does it arise from verbal testimony and the rest. Even the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) characterized by *śruti* and *smṛti* depends upon the validity of the object; its authority is due to its making that [object] known. For it is stated that the composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by intelligence, and that the creation of the world is likewise preceded by intelligence. Thus, [the Veda] is not eternal, but rather produced through the intention of an intelligent being.

Fearing the objection that proponents might include verbal testimony (*śabda*) and other means of knowledge within their own systems—arguing that these are not distinct from inference because they are "not different" in the case of [the proof of] *kalmā* and so forth—the author states: "Of verbal testimony and the rest.

This means that since verbal testimony and the others are included within inference, there is no separate treatment for them; because they follow the same rule and perform the same process, just as inference proceeds by the force of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*), so too do verbal testimony and the others.

Inference from verbal testimony (śabda) is experienced as being like [other forms of] inference because it establishes its object through the force of pervasion (vyāpti). He demonstrates that they follow the same rule: "Prasiddha... etc. For a person for whom the convention (samaya)—the inseparable connection—is well-known, there is the perception of the mark (liṅga); and through the two processes of following that [mark] and the exertion involved in perceiving it, inference occurs independently of those two. Just as inference occurs even when there is no immediate proximity due to those two [processes], so too does it occur from verbal testimony.

A word such as "lightness" (lāghava) does not convey its meaning so long as it is known to be untrustworthy and its non-deviation [from the truth] is not established; rather, it conveys it like a logical mark (liṅga) that is pervaded [by the probandum], just as effort [indicates the presence of a cause].
Regarding this, someone says:

In that inference where the subject (*dharmin*) is understood through the apprehension of the pervaded property (*vyāpyadharma*), what is the subject in the case of verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*)? It cannot be that which is not yet obtained at that time, because it is [only] being cognized [then]. If you say the word (*śabda*) is the subject, then what is its "verbal-ness" (*śābdatva*)? If it is its very nature, then—just as in the case of [the cognition of] what is already perceived and so forth—how could it be established when it is unconnected by conjunction, inherence, or any other relation with the universal "word-ness" (*śabdatva*) and its particulars such as plurality? For that by which the rule of application is determined must be established as the probandum (*sādhya*). Indeed, the probandum is simply the relationship of the signified and the signifier; this occurs even in the case of words, and it is not an object belonging to a subsequent time.
It is not the case that [the relationship] exists only prior to the utterance of that [word];

nor is there a rule of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva-niyama*) between the word and its object based on their connection with impermanence, because they deviate across space and time. Furthermore, even in that regard, how could there be an absence of deviation?

For usage is grasped through the support of reasoning (*yukti-gṛha*), and even in the case of what is unestablished, it is grasped through usage seen in birth; and even in the case of what is already seen, it is grasped through usage.

Therefore, because it possesses the characteristics of inference, that word is not inference itself, since there is deviation regarding the specific meaning of a place. No other [means of knowledge] deviates from its object, but a word does deviate from its own referent. For instance, the word *cora* signifies "one who desires" among the Southerners (*dākṣiṇātya*), whereas for those dwelling in Āmodavana, it is a designation for a thief.

Furthermore, if there were an inference regarding a word—such as "it is not here" and so forth—there would be a determination of its validity through the cognition of the name or through the cognition of the connection; however, if validity were determined by inference, it would be redundant as a factor of inference, just as in the case of the statement "all is indeed expressible. Or rather, when a specific number has been designated, in the inference of the visible number of objects related to place and time, that [designated] number is not the object of valid cognition, because it is not being perceived there.

Nor can it be [the cause] through the aspect of "that person's knowledge," because that [aspect] is what is being expressed [by the word], and thus it is impossible for it to be related to the number ten as a distinct entity in order to convey the perception of those [ten]. Nor is it [the cause] by way of a portion of the relatum (*anuyogika*), nor is there simultaneity; how then could inference proceed? If it is argued that in the linguistic usage of effect and transformation, the aspect of "that person's knowledge" is the cause for the cognition of the number ten—due to the speaker’s intention to convey such a number, or through the error of a person [mistaking it for such an intention], and so forth—then this is merely a matter of verbal convention.

First, immediately after hearing the word "cow" (*go*), it is understood through inference that this [word] possesses qualities distinct from other words, by means of the mental form (*ākāra*) [of the cognition]. Because the utterance of the word "cow" is perceived as being restricted to those substances [i.e., cows] that possess a dewlap and so forth, there is an inference based on its restriction to those substances. And how is the formal argument (*prayoga*) stated in this case?

If it is argued that a person who possesses unimpeded cognition regarding the utterance of the word "cow" and so forth understands "that is I," then how can there be such an understanding for those whose cognitions are not unimpeded? If you say it is through inference, then how is that established even from a word? Is it because the meaning is understood from the word itself, or because the final phoneme of the word is employed? If you say that the comprehension of the meaning arises from the word itself, then the same doubt applies: does the comprehension of the meaning arise from the word alone, or from something else?
However, although it possesses the nature of an inferential mark (*liṅga*), the deviation of a word from its object across different places and times is not perceived [as it is in the case of smoke].

Therefore, this principle applies: while fire is an inferential mark by virtue of an inherent connection, a word—functioning through a convention (*saṃketa*) created by human will—produces a cognition restricted only to that very object toward which people have established a convention, just as is seen in the case of visible inferential marks.

For this very reason—namely, because it is not dependent on human effort—inference, like the sense organs, would require the ascertainment of its object; yet, since even smoke, which is qualified by properties such as being produced from burning, can lead to the apprehension of fire, there is the possibility of the word's meaning being non-deviant [from its object].

Why then is it not assumed that the communication of the object by the word occurs through its primary function (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*), given that there is no [inherent] relation? Or, if something unrelated were to convey knowledge, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that the relation is natural (*svābhāvika*), we reply: no, because a single word is employed for various meanings across different regions.

If it is argued that when a word is employed according to its respective order, it possesses denotative power (*vācakatva*) in that case, whereas in the other case it possesses the nature of an inferential mark (*liṅgatva*) because it functions in accordance with the meaning of the *Ṛk* verse—then [we reply] that this is equal in both cases. For in both instances, the word "cāra" is considered to be non-verbal (in its primary sense) yet produces a cognition. In that regard, its denotative power consists in producing that [specific] cognition, while its status as an inferential mark consists in its being accepted as such; thus there is no great distinction for one who understands this. Furthermore, even the cognition of the number three from the word "cāra" is preceded by an inferential mark, because it is a comprehension of the number three from the word "cāra," just like the comprehension of the number three from the word "cāra" as used by the Southerners (*Dākṣiṇātyas*), which is accepted by both parties.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of an intrinsic relation (*svābhāvikasambandha*). You assert that the word's status as a signifier is based on its being established in the signified object; since this has already been refuted, you nevertheless call it a "relation.
And so it has been said:
"The relation is indeed the power (*śakti*)."

If it is argued that because the power of a word is by its very nature restricted to the denotable object (*vācyaniṣṭhatva*), the meaning would still be understood from the word even when there is a transposition of the production and the transposition [of the relationship], since the connection between the word, the object, and their relation is possible, and because "the known relation is the cause of the understanding of this object, not its mere existence"—as they have said: "Since the word is the producer of cognition, its own cognition would be the object;
therefore, although it exists, it does not manifest if it is not grasped."
Knowledge is the immutability (*kauṭasthya*) of that which is self-luminous.
If it is argued that this consists in the nature of the relationship such that "this word has this or that as its denoted object," then that [relationship] resides in the very nature of the word.

If it is argued that it is by way of the mode of being a function (*vṛttatva*), then let this—just like the illusory knowledge of a jar or a deity—be understood through mutual worldly convention (*vyavahāradṛṣṭi*). For a child standing nearby, this is perceived as being performed; let this be the cause for the production of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) via the door of the capacity for cognition (*jñaptiyogyatā*). What is the use of a [separate] relation within the word itself?

For the nature of a word (*śabdatva*) resides in its innate capacity (*nija-sāmarthya*), whereas its specific power (*āgantuka-sāmarthya*) arises from a particular cognition. From that very capacity, the comprehension of its meaning is established; since the effect is accomplished by what is observed, there is no room for postulating an unobserved factor, as this would require the assumption of another related entity. Furthermore, if it were argued that the distinction between words [is determined] by the speaker's perception, then the connection with the meaning of Vedic sentences would not be possible due to the absence of such a speaker; therefore, they say: "Even the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), characterized by the Śrutis and Smṛtis, depends upon the authority of a speaker."

Not only do worldly treatises, but even the Vedic tradition characterized by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, conveys its meaning only by depending on the authority of the speaker; the word is dependent upon the speaker, for it has not been observed to possess a nature like that of a foul-smelling four-legged beast.
As it has been said:
Defects such as the deficiency of causes reside in the human speaker with respect to sound;
for sound is not defective by its own nature, just as a jasmine flower is not foul-smelling by its own nature.

Since there is no possibility of defects when the Veda is eternal due to the absence of an author, its validity is established once [the objection] is refuted; however, if it were of human origin, unhesitating validity could never be obtained, because we observe even those statements by persons that have meanings not free from passion, hatred, and so forth.
Thus it is said: "The validity [of the Veda] arises from the authority of its speaker."

The word *tat* (that) refers to the speaker previously established as being devoid of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and free from the joy arising from the view of self, which is empty of scriptural authority (*āgama*). Because [the Veda] was composed by such a distinguished person, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the tradition—the Veda—is established.
This is the intended meaning:

authority is dependent upon the absence of defects, not upon eternality. For even if there were eternality, authority would be undermined by defects that find no room for correction; and even in the absence of eternality, authority exists because the senses and other means of knowledge are free from the defects of the perceiver.
It has been established that defects are simply incapable of affecting a specific person [who is free from them].
Therefore, this [scripture] possesses authority even though it is of human origin, unlike the dice-game and similar things.
For one does not entertain the suspicion that a teacher, who is seen to be free from passion and whose instruction proceeds from compassion and knowledge, would teach something contrary to reality.

How can one know a specific person without perceiving him? This is established by the manner in which perception occurs; for, as if all [persons] were unestablished, the Veda is accepted for its own sake by this [means].

Even if the purpose [of the Veda] were preceded by some knowledge, like sentences concerning the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, there would be an inference regarding its meaning because it is not an object for any investigators, which would result in the contingency of non-authoritativeness for someone, since even non-perception is possible due to the absence of a specific restriction.
And where there is a rule of consensus among all [investigators], that alone is authoritative, as is the case with perception and the like.

The Veda is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for all people because it is non-contradictory and free from error, just like perception. As for the fact that the fruit [of an action] is not seen in some cases despite the inference [of its efficacy] regarding rites with perceptible objects—that does not obstruct its validity. Since *dharma* is also imperceptible, the dependence [of the Veda] upon it is established by the observation of results when what has been stated is possible. Because the sentence expresses a pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no contradiction with the absence of a visible basis at the time [of the action], as the agentship of one whose connection is clear through praise is consistent with that purpose. Thus he says: "It is known by those who understand the absence [of contradiction]."
Regarding the phrase "liṅgadvānvitya":

because of that statement, for the purpose of establishing the authority of what was not previously established, and since the meaning consists merely in what has been stated, it follows from the context that here, in the manifestation of the word, the impermanence of the action indicated by the gender (liṅga) and the number (dvān) is understood.
This is the sense of the phrase "of the expansion of gender" (liṅgaprapañcasya).
"The Veda is a composition of sentences preceded by intelligence.

That is, the composition of sentences—that is, the construction of sentences—is to be understood as preceded by intelligence, because it is a composition of sentences, like the composition of worldly sentences.
He states another inferential mark:

Because it has been stated that "the verb *dadāti* (he gives) is preceded by conscious intent," and because in the Veda the word *dadāti* is stated to be preceded by conscious intent— just like the word *dadāti* used in the context of ordinary giving—
that which is wrongly suspected [by the opponent], namely, "because it was not performed," is unproven (*asiddha*).

"Prajāpati alone existed here at first—speech, mind, and breath; having realized this, he emerged from it. Therefore, from austerity, the four Vedas were born"—since the teacher himself establishes [Prajāpati] as the agent in this way, and because there is no deviation [from this rule] when considering examples such as an old well.

Thus, since the non-eternality of the Veda is established in this way, there arises a doubt regarding the authority of human utterances because of the perception of duality [between truth and falsehood]. For in the case of perceptible objects, action does indeed occur because there is never any doubt; moreover, with respect to a perceptible object, one proceeds only so long as one does not perceive the authority of a contrary statement. And in the world, the authority of speech is understood through the recognition of many excellences; therefore, the same persistence of authority should apply to the Veda as well, provided that the cognition is free from suspicion.
Many say that the authority of speech is not rendered futile by its lack of human authorship and so forth, because all means of valid cognition possess their authority intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
How are they to be questioned?
First of all, what is meant by "validity" (*prāmāṇya*)? Is it conformity with the expression, or is it the determination of an object as it truly is?

It cannot be conformity with the expression, for even if smoke has the capacity [to indicate fire], its validity would remain unestablished in cases where it does not lead to the actual presence of fire; furthermore, there would be an absence of validity in the cognition of a mirage (*marīcikājñāna*) due to its deviation from reality, and because there is a deviation in each case regarding blue, yellow, and so forth. Thus, the eye possesses validity only by virtue of being the generator of a cognition that conforms to reality.
Now, if validity is defined as the determination of an object as it truly is, is that [validity] known intrinsically (*svataḥ*), or is it produced intrinsically, or is it pervaded intrinsically?

If the validity of a cognition were known by itself through that very cognition—namely, as "I am a determiner of reality as it is"—then there could never arise a doubt such as "Is this means of valid cognition a cognizer of reality or of unreality," nor would erroneous cognition ever lead to purposeful activity.

Now, if the cognition of a self does not apprehend its own status as a determiner of reality due to a specific action within itself, then, because it would depend on another for that determination, there would be no comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) without a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); consequently, validity (*prāmāṇya*) itself would fall into the category of being an object of knowledge, since it possesses the nature of an object of knowledge. If it is argued that this leads to an infinite regress—where validity is known by one [cognition], and the validity of that [first cognition] by another, and so on ad infinitum—we say: no, there is no infinite regress, because there is no desire to know validity in every instance.

For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) determines its object by its very arising, not by having its own validity known. However, even when the object has been determined, once the doubt arises—"Is this a valid cognition or an invalid one?"—a person does not act due to uncertainty regarding the object. In that case, for the sake of his activity, there arises a desire to know the validity [of the cognition] through another instrument; yet there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*), precisely because such doubt regarding validity does not arise.

Alternatively, when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises that is indeed devoid of even a slight trace of its own production, due to either the lack of proficiency in its arising or the failure to grasp a specific characteristic (*ākhyaviśeṣa*), then—given the necessity of determining its production—the resulting cognition arises solely from the observer’s scrutiny and so forth.
One does not pursue another means of valid cognition by thinking "it does not exist.

As for one who, even in that case, imposes doubt based on seeing knowledge in both ways, he is unable to override it, because it is overturned precisely by the complete determination of that [absence].
As the Blessed One Auḍulomi said:
"That which is unexpressed is determined by knowledge itself when it is being known.

If the validity (*prāmāṇya*) is sought to be investigated for the sake of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), then since activity proceeds from that very object whose validity has not yet been ascertained, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in that regard; there is no investigation into validity [prior to action]. How, then, can the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) be ascertained through the capacity for activity?

Even in that case, because activity is for the sake of accomplishing an effect, the examination of validity (*prāmāṇya*) is undertaken precisely for the purpose of examining cognition. This [examination] is the very means (*dvāratā*) for that [activity], since for one who has already acted due to a doubt regarding validity, the apprehension of the object occurs through that very activity. Even though the ascertainment of validity arises from the non-disappointment regarding the object produced by that activity, it is not [ascertained] by the power of the thing itself, because the capacity for activity does not invariably entail validity. Thus, in this way, validity is neither known intrinsically (*svataḥ*), nor is it produced intrinsically.

If we subsequently recognize dream-cognitions as being other than those perceived while awake, despite their having the nature of determining objects as they truly are, then we consider that cognition's validity to be extrinsic (*parataḥ*), because we see that its arising from causes depends upon something else, even though it possesses the nature of a cognition that apprehends an object as it truly is. Furthermore, we do not say that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) in the sense that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) produces its own validity by itself; rather, validity is intrinsic in the sense that for the production of validity within a cognition, it depends [on the causes] through the commonality of the excellences (*guṇa*) of the causes that produced it.
This very point remains unestablished.

For if validity (*prāmāṇya*) were caused by those qualities that produce a cognition distinct [from its object], then from what would erroneous cognition arise? If it is argued: "The nature of causes is the production of a cognition that accords with reality (*yathārtha*); when this nature is subverted by defects (*doṣa*), then those very same [causes] produce an erroneous cognition; but when the defects that cause the subversion of their nature are absent, then their nature as the producer of a cognition that accords with reality remains established," then why should all statements possess accordance with reality simply because the cognition of the object is valid?

In this way, there would be the apprehension of the sentence-meaning only through the cognition of the quality (*guṇa*) of the cause, just as in the case of the Dharma-cognition. Now, if validity arises only from the initial cognition produced in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*), then validity does not stem from the mere nature of the cause; rather, it must arise from the excellence (*guṇa*) of that [cause] being observed. Thus, when the word-sound is the cause, its excellence would be its correspondence to reality (*yathārthatva*), and its lack thereof would be a defect (*doṣa*). In that case, if correspondence to reality were the cause of the sentence’s validity, then its validity would proceed solely from the excellence of the cause and not from the mere nature [of the word]; and if validity arose from the excellence of the word, the same would apply to other cognitions as well.

The cognitions under dispute have their validity dependent upon the excellence of their causes, because they are cognitions that are valid, like the cognition of sound and so forth. If it is argued that even in the case of sound, the function of the excellence of the cause lies in the absence of defects and not in the production of validity—because by means of excellence there is an obstruction of defects, and thus the production of the effect of defects (namely, non-correspondence with reality) is prevented; whereas the production of correspondence with reality is already established [by nature], for when there is an absence of a cause, there is an absence of its effect, but not the presence of its opposite, since this [correspondence] arises from the mere nature of the cognition itself. [Response: This is not so.
Because there is no distinction in that [knowledge].

For the distinction of knowledge consists in its being known as the reality of the object; and since that [distinction] is not present when it arises from a nature that is conducive to the production of a cognition whose utility is obstructed in such a way, the sentence would not be restricted to a specific object, because there is an absence of the establishment of a distinction due to the lack of distinction [in the cause]. If, on the other hand, it is argued that a sentence produces a cognition only regarding that object which is the object of the [corresponding] knowledge, then the truthfulness of the sentence is caused solely by the truthfulness of the knowledge; it is not something arrived at through the whim of the Vaiśeṣikas, for its validity arises from excellence (*guṇa*) alone.

Or, let it be that the quality functions in the absence of defects; nevertheless, the extrinsic nature of validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*) is not lost, because in the production of [valid cognition], the absence of defects—which is distinct from the inherent nature of the causes—is ascertained through its capacity for negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with other [invalid cognitions].

If it is argued that the prior non-existence (*prāgbhāva*) of defects is what obstructs [the production of knowledge], while the prior non-existence of the sense organs and so forth—which constitute their very nature—is not so considered because of the duality [of the two cases]: why then is it said that the prior non-existence of defects is an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*)? If you say that such a conceptualization is not made because the superimposed object follows the presence and absence of defects, we reply that this is the same for prior non-existence as well, since it too is observed to follow the presence and absence of the absence of defects. Indeed, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which requires both the prior non-existence and the perceptual absence of defects.

If, by means of effects such as purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), even the non-ascertainment [of truth] belongs to the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) solely from an external source and not through its own intrinsic validity (*svarūpaprāmāṇya*), then faults such as the dependence on assistance or harm and the lack of singularity regarding the effect of purposeful activity and so forth would apply to the directions [of space].
And because one perceives the understanding of a well-known intention through its gesture, that too is indeed inference.

Some maintain that there is another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) for the purpose of avoiding [certain things], such as when a hand, nose, or other limb is observed to have been drawn toward something unwholesome (*akuśala*) by a wicked person, or when one’s own face is turned toward another’s; they claim this is a distinct means of knowledge. To them, he replies:
"Because the intention (*abhinaya*) is well-known.

The intention is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the sense that "this action is performed with this specific intent" based on the movement of hands, feet, and so forth. Since the cognition of what is to be avoided or accepted is seen to arise from the observation of such gestures—such as the movement of hands or eyes—it follows that the knowledge derived from observing such gestures is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*). Thus, there is no separate means of valid cognition.

Since an unestablished prose composition is communicated by means of another prose work through a reliable person, this [prose] is indeed a form of authoritative testimony (āptavacana) based on a comparison.
Establishing that analogy (upamāna) is included within inference (anumāna), they say:
since an unknown object is made known by means of a well-known object through the statement of a reliable person, analogy is in fact nothing other than the word of a reliable person (āptavacana).

*Āptiḥ* (attainment) is like direct perception (*sākṣāddarśana*); *prāptiḥ* (acquisition) is the obtaining of everything as it is. One strives by means of that [attainment], and thus [the words] are those whose application has been directly realized. For one who has seen the actual object, the statement of the speaker—whether desired or fulfilled—is such that, when a city-dweller who does not know what an ox is asks a forest-dweller who knows the word "ox" what kind of animal an ox is, the forest-dweller conveys the meaning of the word "ox" through its similarity to a cow, saying, "An ox is like a cow. This is *upamāna* (analogy). Since the understanding of the object arises solely from the authority of the statement itself, and since the statement that makes something known is *anumāna* (inference), the intention is that analogy (*upamāna*) is also not distinct from inference.

As for those Pūrvamīmāṃsakas who claim that the word of the forest-dweller itself constitutes the means of knowledge known as analogy (upamāna), for them this is nothing but inference (*anumāna*). Regarding the cognition of the property of similarity (*guṇadharmya*), when the camel is being measured, there is no separate means of knowledge called analogy. Furthermore, for those who maintain that the entry of the verbal denotation (*śabda*) [into the process] occurs through the description of the gavaya in the forest by one who knows the cow, the resulting clear reflection in the mind—"My cow is like this"—is merely a form of inference, even though it is not produced solely by the means of knowledge called analogy. It is simply the nature of the thing itself.

For similarity resides in each individual instance among those things possessing a commonality; it does not exist apart from the cognition of conjunction. This is because even when the body of a cow is not seen, the cognition "this gavaya in the forest is like a cow" arises.
As it has been stated by the Mīmāṃsā-pūrvapakṣins:
Similarity is fully established in each of those things possessing commonality,
because it is perceived even when the counter-correlative is not seen.
Thus it is said.

Although similarity (*sādṛśya*) exists as a complete entity in each individual, and although it is merely a figurative construction due to the absence of the application of a [specific] word for it—just as in the case of the cow previously established in the treatises on cognition—nevertheless, through the power of the word that indicates its own substratum, there is indeed the perception of similarity. For example, even though the perception "this is short" does not occur because the counterpart (*pratiyogin*) is not grasped, the dimension [of length] is established as "long" by virtue of its own capacity to convey its own substratum. Otherwise, how could one, having grasped a counterpart located in another place, establish the determination: "compared to this, that is long; compared to that, this is short"?

If the similarity in the cow were not grasped previously by the mere fact of being ungraspable by the senses, then it would not be grasped even when the gavaya is present; furthermore, there would be no restriction that the specific form belongs to the cow alone upon the description of the gavaya, because there would be no distinction between the two cases.

If it is argued that there is a restriction regarding the intrinsic nature [of similarity] because one perceives in the gavaya exactly those common features—such as the capacity for expansion, the presence of dewlaps, and so forth—that were perceived in the cow, we reply: since these very common features are repeatedly encountered, they constitute similarity. If these are perceived individually through their respective similarities, then similarity itself is indeed perceived. Therefore, when the parts are perceived, the cognition of similarity—which depends upon the previously apprehended individual cow—is merely a vivid recollection (*sphuti*) produced by the perception of those parts; it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

Moreover, even that which is apprehended by non-conceptual perception can be the object of clear manifestation, because when one who has not yet mastered [the concept] perceives multiple individual objects, there is a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the universal (*sāmānya*) first conceptualized upon the perception of the first individual during the perception of subsequent individuals.

For those who maintain that when a non-Brahmin hears the extended application (*atideśa*) regarding the description of a *gavaya*, he understands that the word "cow" is not [the name], but rather that the word "gavaya" is the name—thereby intending to express a reversal of the genitive sense in the phrase "the *gavaya* is of the cow"—for them too, the sentence "The similarity between the cow and the *gavaya*" and the cognition produced by it in the world, namely, "That which is indeed heard of as a *gavaya* is similar to a cow," constitutes the verbal testimony (*āgama*).

Even though the cognition that "that which resembles a cow is the denotation of the word *gavaya*" is [for you] an inference—because of your own usage of that term—there is indeed no sublation of a word by those things with which it is grasped through convention.

And since the word *gavaya* is grasped by forest-dwellers and others as being co-referential with the word *go*, therefore that too is certainly denotable by the word *gavaya*. Thus, the cognition [of this] through the meaning of the verbal root is indeed an inference.
In the case of a cow perceived before one's eyes, the cognition of similarity is preceded by the experience of its pervasion by consciousness; thus, it is a result of perception.

Alternatively, when the operation of the senses and the experience [of the sound] occur through the notes such as *ṣaḍja* and so forth, that too is merely a recollection—just like the experience of the denotability by that same word for another individual of the same class, which arises from a mental impression produced by a cognition refined by the object of the universal, that cognition being produced by a mental impression resulting from the projection [of memory] generated by the impression produced by the cognition of the denotability by that word for the parts of the horns and other limbs of the cow, which is manifested by the grasping of similarity.
For in this way, having experienced that very [object] here and now, there arises the immediate experience: "I have already previously understood its denotability by that word."

The term *dru* (presumption) does not apply to the other two [types of presumption, namely *arthāpatti* and *śrutārthāpatti*], because there is no possibility for a subsequent conceptualization (*uttarakalpanā*) [as there is in those cases]. Since the non-apprehension of what is heard (*śrutyagrahaṇa*) is caused by the fact that the door was covered by the back wall, the presumption of the door (*drudropatti*) is established by the possibility of *arthāpatti* according to the opponents. Where a part of what is heard (*śrutaikadeśa*), being otherwise inexplicable, leads to the understanding of another meaning, that is *drudropatti*. For example, in the case "Caitra is alive, yet he is not in the house," the absence of Caitra in the house is cognized through the means of knowledge of non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*). However, because of the statement "he is alive," his presence there is also understood, since for one who is alive, staying outside the house is possible. This is *śrutārthāpatti*. Where a part of what is heard, being otherwise inexplicable, leads to the understanding of another meaning, that is *drudropatti*; as in "Caitra is alive, yet he is not in the house," where the absence of Caitra in the house is cognized by the means of non-existence, but because of the statement "he is alive," his presence there is also understood, since for one who is alive, staying outside the house is possible. This is *śrutārthāpatti*. Furthermore, it is not possible for existence and non-existence to occur in a single thing at the same time, because of the contradiction between their coexistence.

Thus, this non-existence (abhāva), when being perceived, serves as a means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) insofar as it establishes that [Caitra] does not exist elsewhere outside; and when it is logically untenable, it leads to the postulation of that in whose presence it becomes tenable. The absence from the house of one who is alive is untenable unless he exists elsewhere outside, for "being alive" is in contradiction with this very fact. That untenability ceases once his existence outside is perceived: "Caitra is alive, yet he is not in the house"—[this implies] his existence outside. When there is a conflict between two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one of which has scope and the other has none, the untenability of the latter—by way of its lack of scope—establishes a different domain for the former. *Note: The term *jīvati* ("is alive") is used here as a shorthand for the full inference: "Caitra is alive because he is seen by me at another time and place. The "absence" (*abhāva*) is the perceived fact of his not being in the house, which necessitates his existence elsewhere.*
This is the summary of the application for establishing the non-contradiction between these two.

Others, however, maintain that inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of one related object by means of the recollection of another related object, triggered by the perception of that first related object which is restricted to being seen and so forth; this is because there is a difference in the manner in which knowledge arises.
As it has been said:
The fact that [the probans] has its origin dependent on what is illogical is established in inference;
this other [fallacy], however, is the "impossibility" (ayogavyatireka) which functions through exclusion (vyatireka).

Thus, even the master of the Śrutārthāpatti [holds that] where a word is inconsistent, it postulates another word; for example, from the sentence "Yajñadatta does not eat during the day," there is the postulation of the sentence "he eats at night.
Among these, he first includes *dṛṣṭārthāpatti* within inference (*anumāna*).

The arising of non-perception through perception is a specific [type of] non-perception; it is indeed contradictory to the purpose of perception, like an inference based on what is heard following an inference.

In the case of the "visibility" reason (*dṛśyatva-hetu*), the meaning of the observation is that it is observed by means of the five instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇas*) which are themselves observable. Therefore, the cognition of another non-observation—which is invariably concomitant with the non-observation of the object of observation—is indeed a contradiction; it is precisely an inference based on a contradictory [reason]. Whatever has a restriction of a certain kind possesses the nature of a logical mark (*liṅga*) in that very way. But here, since it does not function without the exclusion of another alternative which is contradicted by other means of knowledge, the contradictory itself is the logical mark.
This is the intended meaning:

if, in the absence of the person in the house, his existence outside is postulated merely on the basis of non-perception, then because there is no restrictive cause, another thing might also be postulated. If it is argued that "the absence from the house postulates another thing, and that other thing is not postulated unless its own presence [in the house] is excluded," then by what is it determined that its presence occurs only when he exists outside?

We, however, maintain that even though the substance exists outside, the non-existence in the house is indeed logically untenable; this has been observed: when a visible object is not pervasively present and is found in one place, it is determined by the force of perception itself that the substance does not exist [in the other], just as when rain and wind are perceived together in one place, their conjunction is not absent elsewhere.
The absence from the house of a living person is explained only by his existence outside, and not otherwise.

But if this were so, it would apply excessively to other cases as well; and if that were the case, then *arthāpatti* (presumption) would be nothing but *anumāna* (inference), because its production arises from another [perceived] fact.
We state that it is precisely that [non-apprehension] which operates when there is a contradiction. And thus is the formal argument (prayoga) here:
"Devadatta exists outside, because, while being alive and present, he is not perceived in the house, just as I am."
In this context, he includes presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) [within inference]. Alternatively, it is "inference based on what has been inferred.
For instance, from the authoritative statement of the sentence, "The fat man does not eat during the day," the postulation of his eating at night is an inference based on what has been inferred.

The *liṅga* (logical mark) is the corpulence inferred from this statement, because it leads to the inference of its cause, which is eating at night. This is what is intended: namely, that there is an inconsistency (*anupapatti*) of the means of knowledge regarding the capacity for production [of corpulence] unless one eats at night; and since the statement "he does not eat during the day" is contradicted with respect to its own literal meaning, how could it be consistent?

If it is argued that fatness is the effect of eating, and since this is contradicted when there is no eating during the day—because in the absence of a cause, that [effect] is untenable, and if that is untenable, the sentence itself is also untenable because it arises from a non-connected meaning; then [we reply]: the "untenability" of the sentence refers to the untenability of those two [fatness and the lack of eating]. Furthermore, "tenability" means being logically consistent, not the production of a quality such as fatness. For one who does not eat by day, the perception of fatness, which is the effect of eating, is established through the logical consistency of the meaning—that is, it is consistent with the fact of eating—but it is not established by the sentence regarding eating at night. Now, if the sentence regarding eating at night serves as the cause for the tenability of that [fatness] through the untenability of the other [eating by day], then it would not have the status of being the expressed meaning (*vācyatva*) because it is not the actual probans (*upapādaka*); rather, its status as the probans is understood precisely through the fact of its being consistent. Since there is no deviation—the fatness of one who lacks daytime eating is invariably the effect of eating at night—there is no lack of causal efficacy (*aprayojanatā*) within the scope of the word.

Now, if it is thought that [the meaning] is established only by what is not logically possible (*ayogya*), then even if that were the case, the status of being a verbal meaning (*śābdārtha*) would still be untenable; for a verbal meaning is established only through the word itself, since there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between that [verbal meaning] and being produced by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). Indeed, when it is said "The mountain [is burning]," there is no logical inconsistency (*anupapatti*) regarding the action without an object, because the agenthood of the mountain is perceived directly (*pratyakṣa*). Even when that [perception] exists, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to "What is the mountain? is not yet removed.
However, when the action is presented by the word itself, each person becomes free from doubt, thinking, "This agent is performing the verbal act of moving the mountain.

Even in the case of the statement, "He who does not eat during the day," this is an inconsistency within the meaning of the sentence; therefore, anticipating that this too will be included within the meaning by means of the word itself, one first suspects that it is the very sentence expressing night-eating that is being conveyed through the meaning.

Otherwise, since there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the elements of the sentence regarding daytime and the act of eating at night, the meaning of eating at night would not even become the object of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) within that specific sentence; for that [meaning] is understood from the sentence itself. Nor can it be said that the sentence or its meaning is brought to mind by the sentence regarding the night due to a lack of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), because a sentence can convey meaning even through what is unfit or unknown. Furthermore, presumptive testimony does not require a corroborating instance (*pratyavatti*) like inference, as it functions solely on the basis of the fact that something else is otherwise inexplicable (*anupapatti*).
As it has been said:
"When one object is understood through another object, the second object is not again understood [as a distinct entity],
because it is concealed by the fact that it is grasped by conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*)."
One understands other words through their capacity alone;
by that very means, they are first apprehended as being within the scope of a sentence.
Indeed, it is the sentence itself that is inferred from its meaning, because the sentence is considered to reside in the sentence-meaning.
Thus it is said. It is replied:

Words are employed for the purpose of conveying the meaning of a sentence; yet, being individually incapable regarding the meanings of individual words, they are unable to convey the sentence-meaning [on their own]. Because their function consists solely in denoting meaning, when another word that performs the same function has already arrived, there is no further arrival of another word at that very point where the intended meaning has already been conveyed, since its own object has already been accomplished by the first. This is like the case of those who have already drunk water.

If it is argued that [the contradiction] does not arise, we reply: it does not arise; for even the production of such a contradiction is not possible within inference, whether based on the properties of words or based on the modification of cognition, as it would be included within either the possibility or the impossibility [of the logical mark].

Objection: But how can "being the object to be established" (pratipādyatva) be taken as residing in that cognition? For indeed, even when expressed by the word "night," it is understood as already accomplished from the sentence regarding eating at two times; thus, there is the fault of redundancy (paunaruktya). Furthermore, since there is no activity even for one who has attained certainty through the light of the word "niḥ," the cognition of "arcis" is not subject to doubt. Indeed, in a written record devoid of certainty, the fault of redundancy is not logical because the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) regarding eating at two times is not perceived as untenable; therefore, its inclusion is desired. Moreover, since the application of the word [in a contrary sense] would lead to a contradiction, what occasion would there be for a subsequent assumption?

Nor is there a contradiction between them such that one would be perceived while the other is not; therefore, it is established that the word itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as it does not depend on another word, for there is no deficiency in its own capacity. However, when a word is uttered and its expressed meaning is found to be untenable without a subsequent answer, it strives toward its own justification in accordance with the perception [of the context]; thus, following the use of the word, there is an inference based on an inference (*anumitānumāna*).
Even the occurrence of what is invariably concomitant is nothing other than inference.

Some maintain that the knowledge of a hundred from among thousands arises from "possibility" (*sambhava*) as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because a hundred is contained within a thousand; however, this is refuted here:
possibility is in fact nothing but inference (*anumāna*), because it is based on inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*).
Since a thousand is invariably connected with a hundred—because the former presupposes the latter—the knowledge of a hundred derived from the thousand is indeed inference alone.

Non-existence, too, is indeed inference; for example, an effect that has arisen is a mark for the existence of its cause, and likewise, an effect that has not arisen is a mark for the non-existence of its cause.

Some maintain that when there is a cognition of the absence of an object of knowledge, the non-arising of the means of valid cognition—such as perception and the like—which apprehend existing things, constitutes a separate means of valid cognition called "non-existence" (*abhāva*); however, this is flawed.
Non-existence, too, is simply inference.
To the question "How so?", he says:

Just as an effect that has arisen is a mark for the existence of its cause, so too an effect that has not arisen is a mark for the non-existence of its cause. For one who maintains that non-existence (abhāva) is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), it would follow that the cognition of the absence of an object of knowledge does not arise from the non-arising of a cognition; for even by means of perception whose own nature is established, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving the non-existence of a real entity. Rather, among the causes of cognition, the non-arising of a cognition of a real entity that is capable of being known is the basis for inferring non-existence.

Nor is there any difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) between the non-apprehension of the unqualified (*ayogya-anupalambha*) and the non-apprehension of the qualified (*yogya-anupalambha*), because non-existence (*abhāva*) is devoid of degrees of excellence; therefore, this [non-apprehension] is not a self-luminous sense-organ (*akṣa*), as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakta*). Rather, it is the non-apprehension of the qualified (*yogya-anupalabdhi*) which does not deviate from absence, whereas the non-apprehension of the unqualified (*ayogya-anupalambha*) does deviate, since it is possible for that [latter] to occur even when some Buddhist [entity] is present. Thus, it is specifically the non-apprehension of the qualified that establishes [absence], and no other.

If this were the case, the non-existence [of the probans] would itself be the logical mark (*liṅga*) by virtue of its capacity to grasp the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*); otherwise, it would be impossible to avoid the doubt that the statement of that [non-existence] might, in some instance, cause one to understand the existence of that very non-existence through a negative concomitance.

If it is argued that even when there is no manifestation of the sense organ and its object, the cognition of the absence of a jar on the ground occurs—such as "the eye [perceives] the ground"—then why is it not accepted that the ground itself is the direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) of the absence as well? If you say, "Because there is a connection with the sense organ for all positive entities due to their fitness (*yogyatva*)," this is not established. For fitness is that which is observed in a positive entity (*bhāva*) where the effect follows the presence and absence of the sense organ; it must be so even in the case of a negative entity (*abhāva*). Thus, since the effect [of cognition] is seen even in the absence of the jar, the jar too is fit to be grasped by the sense organ. And from the very observation of the effect, one may infer that it is also graspable by the visual sense organ (*cākṣuṣendriyagrāhyatva*).
And this is not our view:

no absence whatsoever is perceived without a locus, because its occurrence and cessation are governed by spatial and other restrictions. Furthermore, regarding that which serves as the locus for this [perception of absence], the operation of the sense organ is required for the perception of that locus, but the operation of the sense organ does not extend to the apprehension of the absence itself; thus, the cognition of absence arises from perception. To illustrate: suppose someone, having previously perceived a temple or similar place through his own eyes, goes elsewhere and then reflects, "Is Devadatta in the temple or not? At that very moment, one who has already known [the person] and now desires to know, perceives "he is not there" and thereby employs the linguistic convention of absence, saying, "He is not."

Nor should it be argued that the absence of Devadatta was already apprehended by non-conceptual perception at the time of not perceiving his presence in the temple, and is merely being remembered now; for while it is reasonable that jars and the like are apprehended by conceptual cognition through sensory contact because their own nature is independent of anything else, the case of absence is different. Since the very nature of absence consists of the object to be negated (*pratiṣedhya*), its nature itself must be grasped as that which is negated. Therefore, since there is no other nature for that absence apart from the state of being the negation of that [object], it is impossible to define the nature of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) without first defining that [negated object].

For this indeed is the distinction between an affirmation (bhāva) and a negation (abhāva): that one is apprehended as having the form of a positive mark (liṅga), while the other is in the form of the exclusion of another.
As the author of the Nyāyavārttika says:

"The distinction arises from the fact that existence is perceived as an independent specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). For indeed, the object of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is either 'pot,' which is independent, or 'non-pot,' which is dependent and occurs by way of the exclusion of another."
If, however, non-existence were also apprehended independently, it would be indistinguishable from existence.
Therefore, both existence and non-existence are apprehended by non-conceptual [perception].

Furthermore, when there is a conceptualized cognition such as "there was previously a perception of Devadatta’s house," or when one apprehends the contraction of that [cognition], there is a sense of ease regarding the mere recollection of the [house] alone and a lack of delay; thus, it is established that non-existence is subsequently remembered. This is the summary.
That too has been refuted.

Others [hold that] Devadatta is recognized through modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vikāra*), through measurements, and through internal states. Even in the absence of desire and other such factors, because the temple (*devakula*) is perceived in its own essential nature, there is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) associated with prior non-existence; from that non-existence, memory arises.

Furthermore, at that time, even though the cognition produced by another means of knowledge has that [self] as its agent (*ahaṅkartṛ*), there is no apprehension of both [the self and the object] in the counter-correlate known as memory; rather, the means of knowledge is simply the capacity of perception and other such means.

Once non-apprehensibility is established in one case, such as during a state of desire, it is established in other cases as well by that very same reason; thus, for the learned, the status of being a distinct means of knowledge is accepted.
This is what is being said.

Someone who has gone to another country and has not previously seen [Devadatta] understands, by means of a present non-perception regarding that place, the meaning of the name "Deśadatta" as being absent at that time, thinking, "He does not exist now. Or rather, by means of a past non-perception, he understands a past absence, thinking, "He was not there at the time of his departure from the country. In this regard, the present non-perception serves to establish the long-term non-perception; for at the time of the direct perception of the location, the absence of Devadatta is possible because of the presence of others such as Śastra and Kāmagandha. However, the past non-perception—which was capable [of establishing absence] in the moments preceding the past absence—does not persist now, because [the subject] has reached a different state.

Nor can it be the cause of a cognition of a mere absence of an object, nor does that which is called memory operate [therein], because the object was previously known by another means. For non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) cannot be the cause of the existence of an absence, as that would render other means of knowledge redundant; furthermore, for the sake of apprehending such an absence through visual perception, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, this [non-apprehension] is like the cessation of the perception of an object when the sense organ has ceased to function for a moment. They say this, because in that case, the recollection of something produced would be untenable due to its non-existence. Now, you might think:

The non-perception of Devadatta caused by his being in a particular place is set aside by the perception of Devadatta; however, for one who has arrived from another location, that non-perception is not known [to have been negated]. Therefore, the non-perception that has occurred does indeed exist. If, on the other hand, it were the case that even when one has reached another location there is no non-perception, then there would be an infinite regress and no distinction between entities.

Let it be so for the Vaiśeṣikas; however, what remedy is there in cases where, due to the influence of not remembering the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) previously, non-existence was not apprehended, but later, at another time, through the perception of the object and other causes, the cognition of the prior non-existence arises, thinking "it did not exist"? For in that case, the non-perception [of the object] which was desired has indeed been perceived.

Nor can it be argued that non-apprehension (*anupalambha*)—even if not currently existing—is a cause for cognition because it was previously one, for even a functioning sense organ would then be liable to apprehend an object that is not present. Furthermore, the cessation of the non-apprehension of a location (*āyatana*) by means of the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a blade of grass is no different from the case of a previous non-apprehension. If you argue that "the prior absence is not determined by a present non-apprehension which is capable of determining an absence," then you must accept the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*); alas, what skill! For when a living being is perceived by the eye, its presence as a real entity (*vastutva*) is established. And since that [presence] does not differ according to the distinction between the prior time and the location, then while the non-apprehension of the location has ceased, the prior [non-apprehension] has not ceased. Who, then, possessing such meager intellect, can fathom this extremely subtle distinction? What is the point of this stubbornness?

Therefore, we do not consider that [the absence] is determined by us exactly as it is; rather, having grasped the mere nature [of the locus], when there is no recollection of what has gone elsewhere, the cognition of the contradiction with the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) arises through inference. For, when something is being recollected, if another thing—which was capable of appearing and had a very close connection—is not apparent, then its destruction at the time of the original perception is inferred. This is just as, when a bare spot is being recollected, the jar that previously appeared there is not apparent.

When a temple (*devakula*) manifests, even though Devadatta is capable of manifesting and is closely related [to it], he does not manifest; therefore, his non-manifestation is due to the absence of the capacity for grasping that temple, and thus there is an inference of his non-existence. Even in the case of a thing characterized by contraction, the manifestation of one and the non-manifestation of another is observed through the absence of causes such as mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). For example, when a word has arisen, although other words may arise at that same moment, other words do not manifest. In that case, because one manifests while the other does not, the inference of non-existence is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), if you should argue.
