Even when two objects are in close proximity, sometimes only one is perceived due to the influence of causes and not the other; even in that case, since there is perception upon the destruction [of the object], the non-existence of the unperceived jar is established.
Now, if it is thought:

When two things that do not obstruct each other's perception are perceived together, the non-perception of one is the means of proving its absence, but not by everyone. For by whatever cognition a location is grasped, by that very same [cognition] the jar conjoined with it is also grasped. Indeed, when the location is grasped, there is the grasping of the jar as well; for if the jar were present at that location, it too would have been known when the location was being known. Since it is not known—due to the nature of non-examination—it follows that because there is no other way for it to exist, that very thing is unperceived.

Just so, in our position as well, when one of two things that are not separate is manifested, the non-manifestation of the other is the very cognition of its absence. For instance, whatever is the capacity for perceiving the temple is also the capacity for perceiving Devadatta who is conjoined with it; and whatever is the capacity for manifesting the temple is also the capacity for manifesting Devadatta. Since they are cognizable by the same single cognition, if Devadatta had existed at the time of perceiving the temple, he too would have been manifested when the temple was manifested—this is stated because of his proximity.
And it does not flash forth; therefore, Devadatta is [inferred to be] pierced, because that non-flashing cannot occur through any other means—this is the same [logical structure].

However, for that which lasts for a moment, due to the requirement of retaining subsequent words, they are cognized at the end of the words in succession. Even though they are cognizable within a single cognition, there is no inconsistency in the fact that among them, one latent impression (saṃskāra) flashes forth in a subsequent moment while another does not.

In this way, regarding both perception and non-perception of an object, where there is a cognition of prior absence and a cognition of destruction through causes such as striking and so forth—even there, since the previous state does not manifest, there is no manifestation of its reality; therefore, it is inference.

As for those who claim that non-existence is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of existence, for them there is a contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*, which states "non-existence is also the absence of a means of valid cognition," and a contradiction with the *Vārttika*, which states "where the [cognition] of an object does not arise preceded by a means of valid cognition," and so forth; enough of this prolixity.
Furthermore, as for those who say thus:

Since there is no object of cognition (*prameya*) that has non-existence as its cause, verbal [cognition] would lack a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, these [opponents] must be asked: what is the objective support (*ālambana*) for the cognition "it does not exist"? If you claim that some real thing is the objective support, then you are asserting a consciousness without an objective support (*nirālambana-vijñāna*), which is unacceptable to the great authorities on epistemology. If, on the other hand, the ground itself is the objective support, then how could there be the cognition "there is no mat on the ground" when the ground is actually covered by a mat? Furthermore, it would be impossible to avoid [the absurdity of such a cognition] regarding an activity characterized by coming and going that perished in the very moment preceding it.

If it is argued that there is a cognition of "non-existence" whose object is exclusively the bare ground, and that we deny this "bareness" (*kevalya*) even when a jar is not seen—lest it follow that one would perceive [the bare ground] even in such cases—[we reply: Well then, what is this "bareness"? Is it the very nature (*svahṛdutā*) of the ground, or is it a distinct property (*dharmottara*)? If it is its very nature, then since that is not abandoned even in the cognition of a jar and so forth, the aforementioned fault of the undesirable consequence of perception remains uncontradicted. On the other hand, if it is a distinct property, then a separate entity (*tattvāntara*) must be established.

Now, if you think that an entity (*bhāva*) alone experiences the exhaustion of duality—both as solitary and as accompanied by a second—and that its state of being solitary is called "mere" (*kevala*), and that when a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) such as a jar is contemplated, the experience of its non-perception initiates the linguistic usage of "non-existence" (*abhāva*); even here there is an error. Since the jar and so forth do not exist, what meaning for the word expressing negation (*vyatireka*) have you established, which could serve as the objective support (*ālambana*) for the thing that "is not"?

For indeed, without a distinct means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), there can be no arising of a distinct cognition regarding an object, nor is the differentiation of linguistic usage possible. If it is argued that the very unity which belongs to an entity by its own nature is what constitutes its "aloneness" (*ekākitva*), we ask: what is this unity?
Is it the state of being devoid of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), or is it the number one (*ekatvasaṃkhyā*)?
As for the number one, it is perceived as occurring in the cognition [of the object] and persists even when the entity is in a state accompanied by another.

Now, if "being devoid of a counter-positive" is said to be an inherent oneness (*svābhāvikam ekatvam*), that is a different object of cognition (*prameyāntaram*). Even for the cognition of the absence of a jar, the cause is the cognition of the absence co-present with the ground; for it is impossible to have a cognition of the absence of a jar on the ground if the jar is present there. In this regard, first of all, the cognition "the jar does not exist" does not arise from the perception of the ground accompanied by the jar. And if the grasping of the ground as qualified by the absence were the cause of the cognition of absence, then upon grasping the presence of that [jar] at a location where it exists, there would be a grasping of the ground as qualified by its presence.

If it were held that the apprehension of the absence [of Devadatta] arises from the apprehension of the ground as qualified by that [absence], then one would have to admit that the object of its own cognition is the cause of itself.

Therefore, even you must admit some state of "aloneness" (*ekakitva*) of the ground, distinct from the absence and distinct from the non-connection with the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), through the cognition of which the cognition of absence occurs and which initiates the conventional usage, "Devadatta is not here. This has already been stated.
The cognition of non-existence has as its cause precisely the characteristic of the locus (bhūtala) itself.

Nor does it follow that this cognition would occur even in a place where there is a second object (such as a jar), because the capacity to apprehend the non-existence of a jar depends upon the proximity of the sense organ to the locus together with the absence of the jar; since, as in the case of a cloth or similar objects, there is no specific sensory contact with the non-existent jar, the non-existence of the jar is not cognized. For it is not the case that because the eye, light, and so forth—which are causes for perception—exist, the non-existence of lightning is likewise perceived at that very moment. Thus, the non-existence of the jar is not known merely by the presence of these general conditions.

And that [non-existence] is manifold: prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

Prior non-existence is the absence of an effect in its causes; it is the non-existence of the effect prior to its production. Regarding the non-existence of a jar, it is beginningless and eternal, because it is destroyed by the production of the effect; for if it were not destroyed, the production of the effect would be impossible.

What is the destruction of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)? If it is argued that it is simply the arising of an entity, such that when the entity has ceased, the prior non-existence is perceived, we say no; for the destruction of prior non-existence consists in the very nature of the entities that are its objects. The "destruction by annihilation" (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is the attainment of its own form by that which has arisen; and that [annihilation] is destroyed merely by the arising of another entity. The "arising" (*utpāda*) of an entity is its subsequent existence after having been previously non-existent. What, then, is the prior non-existence of that annihilation? The persistence of the entity's own form—that is, the state of the object whose annihilation occurred—is the prior non-existence of that annihilation.

Just as the very arising of a thing is the destruction of its prior non-existence, so too the very arising of its subsequent non-existence (pradhvaṃsa) is the destruction of that [prior non-existence]; since that which lacks its own nature has the power of perishing, this is not to be questioned, because the efficacy of causal factors must be taken into account.

In the case of a horse, there is the absence of the nature of a cow; this is mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*). And that [non-existence] is one, all-pervading, and indeed eternal, because even when one individual body perishes, it is recognized in another body, just as a universal persists and becomes connected with this body after being connected with that. Furthermore, its eternity is established by its very nature.
So too is mutual non-existence. What difference is there between the two?

The transition of a universal occurs through the state of the destruction of the individual instance; however, mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is dependent upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), because it must be defined by reference to another entity.
Absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), on the other hand, is the negation of that which is never present.

If it is argued that mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is like absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), such a view is a delusion on the very royal road [of logic]. For mutual non-existence is an entity established by its own nature, as in the case where there is no negation of the identity between two things, such as a horse and a horn. Absolute non-existence, however, is the negation—unrestricted by space or time—of something superimposed by the intellect as being non-existent, such as "there is no category other than the six categories.
And if absolute non-existence were not admitted, then the restriction that "there are only these categories" would be impossible to maintain.
In the same way, the instruction regarding the end of the movement of the breath (prāṇa) as taught in the Itihāsas becomes awakened.

Regarding the statement "yetihāsamyatihayaprāmopadeśa yat," this refers to the traditional lineage of instruction for one who has mastered the *hetu* (logical reason) and *niyāta* (certainty). All of that is a nominal derivative (*svārthika*) belonging to the category of verbal roots.
"Yetihāsam" means the communication of an object ascertained by oneself through a five-membered syllogism; this is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).

It should be understood that inference for the sake of others consists of communicating an object ascertained by oneself to others—those who are doubtful, mistaken, or possess erroneous knowledge—exclusively by means of a five-membered syllogism.
He speaks for the purpose of explaining inference for others (*parārthānumāna*):
"Inference for others is the communication of an object ascertained by oneself through a statement consisting of five members.

It is said that the six great branches of knowledge (*ṣaḍmahāvidyā*) are the five parts of that collection of words within which the comprehension of the object to be communicated reaches its completion.

A "proven object for oneself" (*svaniścitārtha*) is an object ascertained by oneself as being inseparable from the statement [of the reason]; it is the logical mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant with the statement. The formulation of a five-membered syllogism is the employment of a five-part sentence possessing the capacity to generate the cognition of that [object]. This is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).

For a five-membered syllogism (pañcāvayava-vākya) presents the probans (liṅga) in as many forms as its inseparable connection (avinābhāva) with the probandum is clearly manifested; it is that [complete] form of the probans which brings about the cognition of the object. The establishment of the probandum from the probans does not arise from the sentence itself, because a sentence is merely sound and lacks logical necessity. Therefore, the employment of a sentence that expresses a probans established by inseparable connection is alone called inference for the sake of others (parārthānumāna).

Others, however, explain it as follows: "The word is perceptible; that [word] is the meaning of the word, and the sentence is the meaning of the sentence. Its employment is for the purpose of communicating that [meaning]. But the presentation of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is not its immediate function, because for one who is in disagreement, there is no comprehension of the sentence through the mere utterance of words. They thus explain: "The object ascertained by oneself is the *vācya* (the thing to be expressed). The presentation of the logical mark for that [object] becomes its immediate function. The communication [of it] by means of a five-membered sentence is the employment of the sentence that communicates it; this is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
He clarifies the sequence [of these members] with the words beginning "by the five-membered [sentence] alone," and so forth.
When it is said that "the statement" (*vākya*) refers to the words of the proponent (*vādī*),
others maintain that it refers to what has been formally presented (*vyavahṛta*).
That [statement] consists of five members (*pañcāvayava*), characterized by the form that does not differentiate between the subject and its properties.

One who has doubt regarding the matter to be established is "doubtful" (saṃśayita); one who possesses erroneous cognition is "mistaken" (viparīta); and one who has neither doubt nor error, but possesses only his own [subjective] cognition, is "one who knows otherwise" (anyathājña).

[Vāmana’s view: "An [utterance] is unfit for communication because it lacks internal coherence (*antarvyāpti*). Whoever utters certain words that are individually well-known [to denote specific meanings] possesses the intention to produce doubt or error regarding those word-meanings. Once this rule has been perceived within one's own self, then subsequently, through the employment of a collection of words, the sentence-meaning is inferred from the words by means of the principle: "He possesses the intention to produce doubt or error regarding the word-meanings of the subsequent [words]. Thus, the sentence-meaning is an inference from the words, but not a cognition from the word-meanings; for the Mīmāṃsakas hold that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for word-meanings.

Nor is it accepted that the word-meanings, each being denoted by its respective word for the sake of conveying the sentence-meaning, possess the power to convey that sentence-meaning; for there is an absence of capacity in the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—which has the function of making known—to establish the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Therefore, when word-meanings are conveyed toward the sentence-meaning, they would have to be conveyed either as logical marks (*liṅga*) or through the consistency of their syntactic connection (*anvaya*); otherwise, the sentence-meaning would be a word capable of both.

Now, do words convey the meaning of a sentence as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for each individual word at multiple moments, or do they establish their own respective meanings according to the speaker's intention?
On this point, some first say:
the communication of meaning by words occurs in relation to themselves.

For one who has mastered language through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) in instances such as "Bring the cow" or "Slay the cow," where actions and factors of action (*kāraka*) are expressed, it is established that words convey word-meanings not merely in their own isolated forms, but as factors of action mutually related to an action, or as an action related to its factors of action.
This is now being investigated.

If it is argued that in a sentence such as "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), the word *gām* itself conveys its own meaning as well as the meaning of *ānaya*, then the word *ānaya* would be redundant because its meaning has already been expressed; or, if the meaning of bringing is conveyed by the word *ānaya*, then the word *gām* would merely be reiterating its own meaning which was already implied by *ānaya*, and thus the word *ānaya* would not be redundant. To this we reply: in that case, the word *ānaya* would be expressing only its own isolated meaning and would fail to convey a related (connected) sense, just as before. Furthermore, if one word were to express a connected meaning in this manner, then every other word would be capable of doing so as well. Consequently, the theory of the expression of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāna-vāda*) is abandoned.

If, by the word *ānaya* ("bring"), its own meaning—which is already implied by the meaning expressed by the preceding word—is denoted, then as long as the preceding word has not denoted its own meaning, the succeeding word cannot denote its own meaning as connected with the meaning of the preceding word; and as long as the succeeding word has not denoted its own meaning, the preceding word cannot establish its own meaning as connected with the meaning of the succeeding word. Thus, there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Now, it might be argued that the words themselves indeed exist first, but they merely cause the word-meanings to be remembered; only afterwards does their mutual association arise, which is based on the meaning and brings about the manifestation of its own sense. Therefore, this [theory of] dependence on a sentence (*vākya*) is not tenable. That is incorrect. For words are always perceived as co-occurring with a single word-meaning, and they are not capable of causing the mere word-meaning to be remembered in isolation from its syntactic connection. This is because remembrance proceeds exactly according to prior experience.

Through the usage of elders and by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), a restriction of the word "cow" to that which possesses dewlaps and so forth is apprehended; it is not [restricted] to that which is associated with action, instrument, and so forth, because the word "cow" is seen to be used for each of those individually, as there is deviation from them.

If it is argued that this word "cow" (go-śabda), even when being uttered, due to a lack of clarity, merely recalls some initial state of existence (*ādimattva*) that is invariably concomitant [with the object], but does not recall the action, instrument, and so forth—then in that case, for every word whose restriction to a specific external object has been grasped according to its meaning, that word alone would be its denoter and nothing else; thus, the same fault applies here regarding the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*). Furthermore, it is not well-established that [recollection] proceeds only when there is a restriction of concomitance, as in the case of inference from the nature of a thing (*svarūpānumāna*); for that [recollection] occurs even through the mere deviation from a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), being based solely on latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

For instance, upon seeing a woman, even a location such as her own eyes that was not previously specified is remembered; likewise, the word "cow" (go), upon the mere apprehension of the absence of non-cows, might occasionally remind one of some object that is the counter-correlative of the cow-individual, yet by reminding one invariably of the cow-individual alone, it relies precisely on the nature of a sentence, since such a restriction is possible only in that way.

Furthermore, just as you maintain that words in a sentence denote their meanings as already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*), so too do you assert that within a word, the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) denote their meanings as mutually connected. If, in that case as well, the respective meanings are expressed as being mutually connected, what other "word-meaning" remains that could be remembered by the word subsequently? Thus he says: "The statement falls into the same pitfall as the [theory of] denotation. Let us return to our main subject.

Thus, while the sequential arrangement of words in mutual connection is intended, inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is not [merely] that. Rather, inference is either the inferential mark (*liṅga*) or the cognition produced by it;
and neither the inferential mark nor the cognition possesses the quality of being "for the sake of others."

If it is argued that inference is called "for the sake of others" (*parārtha*) because the verbal expression of an inference is for the sake of others, then perception would also have to be called "for the sake of others," since the verbal expression of perception is likewise for the sake of others.
As it has been said:
"Inference belongs neither to the cognition itself nor to its cause; it does not belong to anything else."
And it is not established in either worldly usage or the Veda that these two have the purpose of another.
Since speech is for the sake of another, verbal testimony is considered inference for the sake of another;
why then is it not likewise assumed that even perception is for the sake of another by means of that [speech]?
To this we reply:

We do not say that it is inference for the sake of others because the word itself is for the sake of others; rather, we say that a statement in a treatise intended for others is an inference because it is a cause of inference by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*).

[Objection: Even so, does it not follow that perception which makes known a logical mark (liṅga) would likewise be an inference? [Reply: No, because there is an absence of the use of the word "inference" for such [perception] in common worldly usage.

It has been stated that a "statement" (*vākya*) consists of a series of animal-like [logical] members (*paśuprabandha*). What, then, are those animal-like members? They are: proposition (*pratijñā*), ground (*apadeśa*), illustration (*nidarśana*), application (*anunaya*), and conclusion (*apratyākhyāya*).

Among these, the proposition (*pratijñā*) is that which is not in conflict with the two [other] inferable factors. It is the firmest means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for making known the subject (*dharmin*) as qualified by the property (*dharma*) one intends to communicate; it is the domain of the instruction (*upadeśa*).
For example: "Substance is air.

By the inclusion of the term "non-contradictory," those [propositions] that contradict perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and the statements of one's own treatise (*svaśāstra*) are excluded. For instance: "Fire is cold" contradicts perception; "Sound is inaudible" contradicts inference; "Wine may be drunk by a Brahmin" contradicts scripture (*āgama*); for a Vaiśeṣika, the thesis that "the effect exists in the cause" contradicts his own treatise; and the claim that "a word does not convey meaning" contradicts one's own statement.
Furthermore, this [statement] is devoid of the formulation of a proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, and is not a refusal to provide assistance.
The word "furthermore" (*punar*) indicates that among those [topics], there is no contradiction regarding the non-duality of the object of cognition (*meyadvaita*), which is the proposition.
He explains this himself as follows:
By the phrase "that which is intended to be explained," and so forth:

the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by that property (*dharma*) which is desired to be established is called the *anumeya* (the object of inference) or the *pakṣa* (the thesis). Its mere mention, or its mere statement, or its presentation accompanied by the means of proof (*sādhana*), is the *pratijñā* (the proposition).
As the virtuous teach:
the status of being a proposition (*pratijñā*) applies to both the statement and its meaning.
If it were a mere enunciation devoid of a reason, it would not truly be a proposition, because, lacking the capacity for proof, it would not deserve to be employed [in an argument].
Just as the Tathāgatas speak.
The cause of that which is capable must indeed be specifically capable;
because it is designated as "Sāṅkhya," the statement of the thesis is not non-existent even through a traditional lineage.
Thus it is said;
regarding this, he says:
"In order to bring [the object] into the domain of that which has no spatial location."

The reason (*hetu*), being without a specific location, requires a locus (*viṣaya*) and a substratum (*āśraya*) in order to be established; for as soon as it is asserted, according to the teaching of the Śākyas, the reason is released [from its state of mere abstraction] because it is already established. However, if a particular subject (*dharmin*) is not presented, the reason does not function, as it would be without a substratum. Thus, the thesis (*pratijñā*)—which is not discarded by the Śākya-vidyut—is like a flash of lightning from the Śākya, for by indicating the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through the subject "I," it brings the subject that serves as the substratum of the reason into proximity. Therefore, the thesis is seen to be like the lightning of the Śākyas, since it causes the reason to function by way of demonstrating its substratum.
And so it is stated in the Nyāyabhāṣya: "If there were dependence upon cognition regarding that which is fit for the qualities [of the probans], the proposition would be rendered purposeless.
For the Adhvaryu priest would proceed only with the reasons and so forth, in order to establish the authority of the proposition.

If it is argued that the locus of the reason is understood from the application (upanaya) itself, we say no; because when the proposition is uttered by the Adhvaryu, that [locus] is likewise not the subject matter [of his specific role].

The application (*upanaya*): The statement of the presence of the probandum in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) indicates its capacity through implication; it does not [directly] instruct the cognizer. For there is no inquiry regarding the probandum at the very outset; rather, because the probandum is the primary element, once the probandum is inquired after, one inquires about its nature through questioning, and subsequently, one inquires about the capacity for that probandum. Therefore, the statement of the probandum itself is established first, and nothing else, since it is appropriate that the capacity for the probandum is expressed as being dependent upon it.

If it is argued that it is contradictory to say "the subject (dharmin) is qualified by the property (dharma) intended to be established," because that [property] is not yet known and cannot serve as a qualifier—[we reply: it is true that an unknown thing does not function as a qualifier; however, the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma), though already known, is stated as a qualification of the subject in the proposition (pratijñā) for the purpose of making it known to those who are in disagreement. For this very reason, the property of being a "subject-property" (pakṣadharmatā) belongs to the logical reason (hetu). Even if impermanence alone were being proven, there would be the fault of the producedness (kṛtakatva)—which is a property of sound—not being a subject-property; but when impermanence is to be proven specifically in sound itself, this fault does not arise.

As Upavarṣa has said: "That very [word] is of a dual nature: it is both the object to be understood and the means of understanding. When its parts have not been individually ascertained, it is the object to be understood; once established, it is not the communicator."
Thus [it is said]. He states an example of the proposition (*pratijñā*):
"Air is a substance" (*dravyaṃ vāyuḥ*).

For one who, even while accepting the *dārvī* (the wooden ladle), does not accept its status as a substance (*dravyatva*), the proposition (*pratijñā*) "Air is a substance" is formulated with the aim of establishing that very point by specifying air as being qualified by substantiality. He explains the purpose of including the term "non-contradictory" (*avirodhi*):

"By the inclusion of the term 'non-contradictory,' those things which contradict the meaning through perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or scriptural acceptance (*abhyupagama*) are excluded."

That which is intended to be established by means of [the reason] and so forth is called the "probandum" (*sādhya*). Even that which is contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition might sometimes be intended as the probandum due to error; therefore, the object of measurement (*prameya*) qualified by its specific attributes is what is intended to be established. If this much alone were stated, even a statement contradicted by perception and so forth would constitute a "thesis" (*pratijñā*); since such a thesis is incapable of establishing its intended object, the term "non-contradictory" (*avirodhi*) was included.

The meaning is as follows: that subject of inference (*anumeya-uddeśa*) for which there is no contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition, or rather, the statement of that [subject] for which there is no such contradiction is the "proposition" (*pratijñā*); that which lacks this twofold quality is not a proposition. What is expressed by this? It is not that whatever one intends to speak is the "thing to be proven" (*sādhya*); rather, only that which is intended to be established is the *sādhya*, and only that is the "subject" (*pakṣa*). Anything other than that is merely a word. An example of contradiction with perception and so forth is as follows: [The text continues with examples.]
"The fire mentioned in the scripture"—
the negation of the meaning stated by the scripture is invalid.

In the view of the *Aṅgas*, [the plurality] is denied, but not in the views of those who do not accept it as a constituent part (*anaṅga*). Nor is there the possibility of a non-injunction stating "there is no plurality for that which is a constituent part," because even if there were plurality, its cognition would not be inferential; for inference does not operate in the absence of perception. Furthermore, when there is a denial of what is perceived by direct perception, the inference of a denial proceeds only after the authority of direct perception has ceased; thus, the statement of an inference of denial is sublated by that very [perception], since its object is already occupied. What deprivation of the object could there be for an inference that is contrary to that [perception] regarding the cognition of that [object]? If an inference is employed to establish something through non-connection (*anupapatti*) but does not produce that cognition because it contradicts direct perception—when the status of being a sense organ such as the eye has been established by a perception whose object is uncontradicted by non-connection, and when that [status] is subsequently determined through the impossibility of its non-occurrence—then this very [inference] is sublated. For if it is employed to demonstrate something through non-connection but fails to produce the cognition of it due to contradiction with direct perception, [it is invalid].
As it has been said:
"In the determination of the contrary, one who does not desire the defeat of another [is acting] at the root; for when that [root] is destroyed, this former object [of debate] is destroyed."

[Objection: "Because there is a contradiction between sublation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), sublation is impossible for that which possesses invariable concomitance. [Response: If by "dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya*) you intend invariable concomitance, then sublation would indeed belong to that very thing possessing invariable concomitance, as in the case of "fire is not hot because it is produced"—wherein the very object of the inference (fire) is sublated. However, if the intention is that dissimilarity constitutes invariable concomitance, then it is said that there is no sublation for that which possesses invariable concomitance; this is what is being stated here.

In some cases, when a reason (*hetu*) has an uncontradicted object, the exclusion of anything contradictory to perception is somehow established; this contradiction with perception—whether it be a fault of the thesis (*pakṣa*) or of the reason—is not a fault of the thesis, because the subject (*dharmin*) is intended as the locus of the probandum (*sādhya*), nor is it a fault of the reason, because the reason possesses efficacy within its own proper domain, while in other domains it lacks efficacy for everyone. Rather, this is a misdeed of the proponent who employs a contradiction within the [proper] domain.

If it is argued that the fault lies in the fact that [the reason] implies the necessity of cognizing the meaning of the thesis, and thus implies its fitness for being established—thereby contradicting what is intended—then this fault applies equally to the sequential order and the formal proof as well. It contradicts wealth, relatives, and one’s own people. By the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through which the impermanence of the sense-faculties (*akṣa*) and so forth is established, by that very same means their eternity and partlessness are also established; therefore, there is no room for doubt. Thus, the thesis is contradicted by the inference based on the pride of self-identity (*ahaṅkāra*).
The statement "wine may be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa" is the first [example], which is non-contradictory.
This is for the sake of the proposition that wine drunk by a Brāhmaṇa becomes a cause of sin.

Now, as for the example of theft: the absence of the status of being a cause of sin in the case of theft is to be understood solely through the authoritative scripture (*āgama*). For by the very same scripture through which the absence of the status of being a cause of sin in the drinking of wine by the Pāṇḍavas is established, by that same [scripture] the status of being a cause of sin in the drinking of wine [by others] is established.
Even in the case of non-duality (*advaita*), when a Brahmin makes a vow to drink liquor, there arises a confusion of examples;
likewise, for the Vaiśeṣika who asserts [non-duality], his position contradicts his own scripture by virtue of the fact that he cognizes objects through the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For the Vaiśeṣikas proceed with regard to sound and other categories by accepting the authority of the Vaiśeṣika scripture. Consequently, for one who says "the effect exists because its cause exists," there is a contradiction between his proposition and the scripture, since it is established in the Vaiśeṣika scripture that [the effect] does not exist prior to its manifestation.
The claim that "a word does not convey meaning" is self-contradictory.
If a word lacks the capacity to convey meaning, then the employment of a word for the purpose of communicating the proposition "a word does not convey meaning" is untenable.
Since a word is employed for the sake of a specific meaning, the very act of employing it establishes its capacity to convey meaning; thus, the thesis is self-contradictory.

The treatise (*śāstra*) is the exposition of the reality of the nature of things according to the seasons; contradiction of that [treatise] is indeed contradiction with perception and inference. Likewise, the justification of an inference that fails to examine the words [of the treatise] constitutes a contradiction with inference for one who denies that a word conveys meaning. Why, then, are contradiction with one's own treatise and contradiction with one's own statement mentioned separately?
It is replied: a treatise, such as those of the Śākyas and others, may also be based on fallacious means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*).

For a Buddhist who asserts the momentariness of all things and so forth, there is indeed a contradiction with his own treatise, not a contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Even his own statement might sometimes be rooted in inference; therefore, its contradiction is not a contradiction with a *pramāṇa*, but rather a contradiction with his own words (*svavacanavirodha*) alone.
The designation by gender and number:
whatever is characterized by a particular mode of occurrence and is established as common to all members of its own class, that gender and number belonging to it is its "designation" (apadeśa).

For example, because of possessing action and because of possessing qualities; and likewise, in that same mode of occurrence, femininity belongs to it, and the possession of qualities belongs to all members of its class, while the possession of action belongs to all substances.
Because there is no implication of a substance through the conjunction of both [qualities], it is established that its mention is an *apadeśa* (designation).
The statement of the indicative mark (*liṅgavacana*) is the *apadeśa* (explanation).
It explains its meaning by means of the verse beginning with "yadvṛttena" and so forth.
That is the compound. He provides an example:
"because of possessing action and because of possessing qualities."

The statement "the action is seen" is the counter-argument (*pratikriyā*). The statement "from substance" is the indicator (*liṅga*) of the action; its verbal expression is the *apadeśya* (the probans). In that very same counter-argument, the statement "from the connection with qualities" is the indicator of the connection with qualities; its verbal expression is the *apadeśya*. This is likewise for the purpose of demonstrating the nature of a logical reason (*hetu*)—both that which is partially present in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and that which is all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*)—by means of examples that are deficient in one or more respects. He says that the definition of a logical mark (*liṅgalakṣaṇa*) has been applied, and that it indeed exists in the case of the action of a substance and the connection with qualities, stating:
"And thus, that..."

That which is characterized by the connection with qualities (guṇabandha) is stated to be inferable; it exists in every substance that belongs to the same class as the subject, namely the sapakṣa, and it is absent from all that is not a sapakṣa. Furthermore, the statement that "action-substance" (kriyā-dravya) pervades each instance within the sapakṣas, while both "action-substance" and "connection with qualities" are entirely absent in the vipakṣa, which is non-substance—this very statement of those two, namely "from action-substance" and "from connection with qualities," constitutes the indication of the reason (hetu). Know this to be established as the "reason" because of its definitive presentation.

By this, it is stated that unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), doubtful (*sandigdha*), non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*), and untimely (*avaśita*) statements do not constitute a valid reason (*anapadeśa*). Among these, the unestablished is of four kinds:

unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*), unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*), unestablished in its existence (*tadbhāvāsiddha*), and unestablished with respect to the object of inference (*anumeyāsiddha*).
Among these, the "unestablished for both" (*ubhayāsiddha*) is that which is unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent, such as: "Sound is impermanent because it possesses parts.
The "unestablished for one of the two" (*anyatarāsiddha*) is, for example: "Sound is impermanent because it is a product.

The "unestablished due to the absence of its existence" (*tadbhāvāsiddha*) is, for instance, when one who is actually a master is presented as a servant in order to prove the presence of fire by means of the presence of ghee; [in this case], he is unestablished as a servant.
The unestablished due to the non-existence in the object of inference (*anumeyāsiddha*) is, for example: "Darkness is composed of earth, because it possesses a black color.

For that which does not exist in the object of inference, yet is absent in everything of its own kind and present in what is contrary to it, is unestablished due to proving the opposite; as in: "Because it has horns, therefore it is a cow. However, that which exists in the object of inference and is common to those of its own kind, being thus indeterminate, is doubtful because it produces uncertainty; as in: "Because it has horns, therefore it is a cow."

Some maintain that [the reason] is "doubtful" (*sandigdha*) because of the presence of two contradictory properties—superiority and inferiority—stated for the same object; this is what is meant by the term "inclusion" (*saṅgraha*).
For example, regarding the death or immortality of a jar, [the reasons would be] its possession of motion and its possession of conjunction.

But if it is argued that there is no such doubt, since we shall state that when two properties are perceived together, the determination of each specific cognition depends on the exclusion of one of the two modes.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the treatises teach in various places that seeing two ways [of viewing a matter] is a cause of doubt? [Response: No, for doubt does not arise merely from seeing two objects. Seeing two objects is a cause for the arising of doubt only when those two are of equal strength; and in that case, because they are mutually contradictory, there would be a non-perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣānupalabdhi*), which is the cause of doubt. However, those two are not of equal strength, because one of them—the inferential cognition—is sublated by scripture. This, therefore, is simply a different kind of contradiction (*viruddhabheda*).

Just as [the reason] is established by being restricted to one of the two limits—namely, by virtue of its being a cause for the ascertainment of existence in the object of inference (*anumeya*) and its non-existence in both the similar (*sajātīya*) and dissimilar (*asajātīya*) classes—as in the case of "the production of an existent effect from an existent cause" (*satkāryasat-utpatti*).
This is understood from the statement that such a [reason] is an "instruction contrary to one's own tenets" (*amataviruddha-anupadeśa*).

Now, an objection is raised: "But was it not stated in the treatise (*śāstra*) that a specific feature (*viśeṣa*) is a cause of doubt, because a specific feature is observed in two ways among things of the same class and among those included within the other? It is not otherwise, because a specific feature is observed in the word (*śabda*)."

When it is stated that "doubt does not arise," this does not mean that the specific property (*viśeṣa*) of any one among the categories such as substance (*dravya*) serves to exclude doubt; rather, it is the commonality (*sāmānya*) alone that is apprehended. Why? Because it has been stated that among substances and so forth—which belong to similar classes yet are distinct from one another—the object of each individual term is observed in both ways (as being similar and as being different). Therefore, the cause of doubt is not [the specific property], for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of doubt arising even regarding many distinct categories. Thus, doubt arises precisely from the cognition of the commonality. By this definition of the probans (*apadeśa*), the definition of the probans is established as a statement that is not contradictory, not inconclusive, not counter-intuitive, and which reaches its conclusion.

By the phrase "being concomitant with the object of inference" (*anumeyena sahacaritatvāt*), it is stated that a statement of what is observed to be undesirable (*aniṣṭadṛṣṭa*) is not a valid indicator (*anapadeśatva*).

By the phrase "established in what is of the same class as that" (*tatsamānajātīye ca prasiddham*), it is stated that contradictory statements (*viruddha*) and statements of what is not established (*apravasitas*) are not valid indicators.
By the phrase "there is simply no contradiction with that," it is stated that a statement of what is doubtful (*sandigdha*) is not a valid indicator; such is the distinction.
Among these—[the] unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), doubtful (*sandigdha*), and non-probative (*anapavahita*)—he explains the "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
It is of many kinds, such as the "unestablished for both" (*ubhayāsiddha*), and so forth.

Among those, the "unestablished for both" is, for example, when there is no establishment [of the reason] for either the proponent or the opponent; as in: "The sound is oily because it possesses the property of being a probandum (*sādhyadharma*). In this case, the state of being a probandum is not established for either the proponent or the opponent regarding the sound; thus, it is "unestablished for both."
"Sound is impermanent because it is a product; this is [an instance of] *anyatarābādha* (non-sublation of either).

Although sound is in fact a product (*kāryatva*), nevertheless, for the sake of the Mīmāṃsaka who holds a contrary view, this [reason] does not prove the probandum (*sādhya*) as it stands; thus, it is employed as *ābādha* (sublated). Similarly, regarding *ābādha*: just as when smoke has disappeared elsewhere, steam arising from heated earth is perceived as having the nature of smoke—that is, as being smoke—it is called *ābādha* (sublated) in that same way.

An example of non-apprehension of the object of inference (*anumeyābhāva*) is as follows: "The sky is earthy because it possesses blackness and movement; there is no other substance called darkness, since the perception of a wooden post or a bean occurs within it; therefore, that substance [of darkness] is earthy because it possesses blackness and movement. This is called non-apprehension of the object of inference because the object of inference is non-existent. Although the compound *abhāvānumeya* could have been analyzed as "that for which the object of inference is non-existent," it is instead stated as *avidvānumeyam* (non-apprehension of the object of inference) because the term *avidvā* (non-apprehension) was mentioned previously.

Just as a reason (*hetu*) may be unknown to one party or unknown to both parties, and just as it may be unknown regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) in either of those two ways; and just as a reason may be unknown to each of the proponent and the opponent respectively—either because its connection with the subject is not perceived or due to the occurrence of doubt and other such cognitions—so too is the locus (*āśraya*). And just as a reason may be unknown to the proponent due to some lack of knowledge, while being "doubtfully unknown" (*saṃdigdhāviddha*) to the opponent.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the basis [of the fallacy] is likewise [threefold]: whether the proponent is ignorant (*ajñāna-avidva*), or the opponent is ignorant due to misconception (*viparyaya-avidva*), or the proponent is ignorant due to doubt (*sandeha-avidva*). Whether the opponent is ignorant due to lack of knowledge, or due to misconception, or whether the proponent or opponent is ignorant due to doubt—in these cases, the basis is to be applied accordingly. The categories such as "ignorant regarding the qualification" (*viśeṣaṇa-avidva*) and so forth are not mentioned separately because they are included within either "ignorant regarding one [of the two]" (*anyatara-avidva*) or "ignorant regarding both" (*ubhaya-avidva*). He now describes the contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetvābhāsa*).
Regarding the phrase "that which [exists] in the subject" (*anumeye*):

when someone, for the sake of demonstrating that a certain hidden cow-individual is a horse, proves it by saying "this individual is a horse because it possesses horns," then the possession of horns—though existing in other individuals belonging to the same class as the horse—is absent in the horse's counter-examples (*vipakṣa*), such as cows, buffaloes, and so forth. Even though it is present in those counter-examples, by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), it establishes the non-horseness which is the opposite of the horse; thus, it is called a "contradictory" (*viruddha*) reason, because it proves a property contrary to the intended probandum (*sādhya*). This concludes the section on the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) within the chapter on cognition.

This is an example of the contradictory reason (*viruddha*) that occurs in only a portion of the counter-example (*vipakṣaikadeśavṛtti*): [the reason] "being cognizable" (*vijñānitva*), because it is impossible in pillars and the like when [the property to be proven] is "knowing everything.
An example of the contradictory reason that pervades the entire counter-example (*samastavipakṣavyāpaka*) should be seen as: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*).

Now, let us consider that which is common (*sādhāraṇa*) to both similar (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar (*vipakṣa*) instances—namely, to the subject (*dharmin*) in all cases of inference; because it generates doubt, it is called "doubtful" (*sandigdhya*).

For example, [the argument] "because it is a *drabhāṇa*, therefore it is a *dru*"— or else, when the object is summarized as "the cow [is this] because of its having horns," if at that time "having horns" were both present in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and observed in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), then due to its being common to both, it would be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) characterized by doubt.

This [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because it pervades both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), yet occurs in only a portion of the dissimilar instances, as in: "Sound is eternal, because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*). It is inconclusive because it occurs in a portion of both the similar and dissimilar instances, as in: "Space is eternal, because it does not exist [as a substance]" (*avṛttitvāt*). It is inconclusive because it occurs in a portion of the similar instances while pervading the dissimilar instances, as in: "Sound is a substance, because it is eternal" (*nityatvāt*). It is "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) to both the similar and the dissimilar classes of things; this is its definition as explained by the term "common. Thus, a property (*dharma*) as previously described, which—by being observed in both the similar and dissimilar instances—produces doubt, would be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) characterized by uncertainty.

When two reasons of equal strength that establish contradictory conclusions are encountered within a single subject (*dharmin*), a doubt arises; therefore, some have stated that this encounter of two contradictory reasons is also a "doubtful" fallacious reason (*sandigdha-hetvābhāsa*). He will refute that later. [Now] he states the definition of the subject (*pakṣa*) and provides an example of it.

For example, regarding whether the mind is corporeal or incorporeal, there is doubt because of the presence of two reasons that establish contradictory meanings: "the mind is corporeal because it possesses action, like the body," and "the mind is incorporeal because it is intangible, like space. This occurs when the two reasons—possessing action and being intangible—encounter one another. For even though both [reasons] are individually valid, they cannot simultaneously establish the nature of a single entity, as it is impossible for them to indicate the same reality.

Nor can both [reasons] be non-probative due to mutual contradiction, because there is no other possibility besides being corporeal (*mūrta*) or incorporeal (*amūrta*). Furthermore, no specific distinction between one or the other reason is perceived by which a determination on one side might occur; therefore, based on the properties of possessing action (*kriyāvat*) and being intangible (*asparśatva*), doubt arises regarding the mind as to whether it is corporeal or incorporeal. This very case is what is seen as the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) among the "non-deviating contradictories" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*); for since it is employed when [the subject] is already doubted, it does not remove that doubt. Thus, its status as "neutralized" consists in its causing doubt.

Now, this [reason] is indeed "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa), because it is based on the force of being restricted to four forms and because it is equal to the wandering of the opponent's counter-reasoning; thus, neither "possessing action" nor "intangible-ness" individually produces a certain conclusion. However, since both are present together, their combination is also uncommon. By means of this combined application, there arises a doubt regarding the nature of "otherness" (anyatva) as distinct from non-pervasion; in such a case, the authority of scripture remains as it was heard, serving as no more than a general rule that lacks firm support.

In each case, when a quality deviates from its locus, the exclusion of that quality (*guṇavyatireka*) constitutes the definition of difference (*anyatva*) between two things possessing abundant properties. Although a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) restricted to a single substance may deviate from contradictory objects, it nevertheless serves as a cause for doubt; for while the negative-only reason (*vyatirekin*) establishes certainty regarding the subject (*pakṣa*) by excluding suspicion of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), certainty arises through the form of a reductio (*prasaṅga*) even by means of an oath, since such a certainty is possible even from that [oath], just as from the counter-example.

In this regard, if the possession of odor (gandhavattva) were to establish the state of being marked by intense impermanence (anityavyāpyotkaṭāṅkitatva), then the rule that it is also necessarily marked by the absence of odor from eternal [substances] would be undermined. Nor can another property be established, because that would entail a duality of the entity; nor is non-difference established, because there is no other alternative mode. Therefore, due to the possession of odor, doubt arises regarding earth: "Is this eternal, or is it impermanent?
As the venerable Bhaṭṭamiśra has said:
Where there is a unique property (asādhāraṇa-dharma), however, in the case of its conjunction with absence,
the mind is the cause of cognition due to its specific nature as a substance.
Thus it is said;
or as the authors of the Nyāyavārttika state:
"That which is produced by disjunction does not have disjunction-produced disjunction as its non-inherent cause."

[The opponent argues: "But [the reason] arises from the word; it is a cause of doubt because it is excluded by the refutation (*khaṇḍana*) and contradicted (*vyāghāta*). Or rather, we shall say that it is established through non-perception (*anupalambha*). [The author replies:

This is not so, because two contradictory [properties] can coexist in the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with their respective counter-correlates (*sapratipakṣa*), and thus there is no exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*). So they say.
What is meant is this: we shall explain that even a unique property (asādhāraṇadharma) does not necessarily bring about [the conclusion]. This is the sense.
Having established that [the reason] which deviates toward contradictory meanings is indeed a cause of doubt, he raises the objection regarding its conflict with the treatise (*śāstra*) by saying,
"Someone... and "because it is seen in both ways."

It is stated in various places throughout the treatises that the perception of a single substratum (dharmin) together with two contradictory properties is a cause of doubt, and this is observed in practice. For instance, perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*) is seen in the self along with incorporeality (*amūrtatva*), just as it is seen in the mind; likewise, possession of action (*kriyāvattva*) is seen in atoms along with corporeality (*mūrtatva*). Therefore, just as perceptibility seen with incorporeality causes doubt upon being perceived, so too does possession of action seen with corporeality cause doubt upon being perceived: "Is the mind corporeal, or is it incorporeal? This is because, just as perceptibility is seen in both ways, there is doubt due to its being seen in both ways. That is to say, the mind is seen together with possession of action, which is invariably concomitant with corporeality, yet it is also seen together with perceptibility, which is invariably concomitant with incorporeality. Since it is seen in both ways, there is doubt: "Is the mind [incorporeal] because of its possession of action? and so forth; thus it should be understood that this is not an answer to such an objection.
By this, those who reject the status of doubt as a cause of cognition on the grounds that it involves deviation (*vyabhicārin*) contradict the treatise (*śāstra*). To this, he offers a rebuttal:
"There is no doubt because two distinct objects are perceived."
Although one's own preferred portion [of the teaching] contradicts the scripture, in that case doubt arises from the perception of two opposing objects.
He explains this very point:
the perception of two opposing objects is the cause for the arising of doubt.

When doubt arises regarding a particular substratum (*dharmī*)—such as "Is this a post or a person?"—the cause of that doubt is the prior perception of two alternatives and the non-perception of one, namely the perception of the object in terms of both "post-ness" and "person-ness. It is not the falling of two contradictory properties upon a single substratum that is the cause; for that would result in a contradiction. Therefore, the intention is that doubt occurs when there is the perception of two objects that have been previously observed together, provided that no reason for the exclusion of one is perceived.
Thus it is said: "The seen and the seen-like are the [cause of] the unseen."

The meaning here is as follows: having previously seen an object—whether a post or a person—and seeing it again in another place or at another time, similar to other posts and persons both seen and unseen, a doubt arises when there is no perception of specific distinguishing features (such as those that have been or have not been considered).

By the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), it is stated that doubt also arises from seeing an object not previously seen, provided it is perceived as being similar to other posts and persons, both seen and unseen.

Furthermore, another indication shows that doubt arises from the recollection of specific imperceptible universals (jāti) corresponding to the various ways in which the objects were previously perceived.

The meaning of the aphorism is as follows: regarding a person seen previously, having been seen in a particular state—whether with his feet together or joined—and then seeing him at another time in a different state, in another manner, or having fallen away from that specific state, one might wonder whether he is now in the same condition as before; thus, a doubt arises as to whether "is he now with his feet together, or has he joined them?
It is not, however, the case that a contradictory non-deviant reason (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is a cause of doubt, because such a reason is never actually employed in practice.

If such a reason, possessing the aforementioned characteristics, exists for the inference, then the comprehension of the object follows from that very [reason] itself; thus, there is no need for a second formulation, because the understanding has already been established.
On the other hand, if this [reason] does not possess the aforementioned characteristics, then this very defect must be stated; what is the use of a counter-inference?

If it is argued that the first reason is called "contradictory and non-deviant" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) because it does not deviate from or exceed its contradictory counter-reason—that is, its sole defect is the capacity for a contrary inference, since when a second counter-position is presented, the first lacks the power to establish its own probandum—then [we reply]: if the second’s non-exceeding of the first’s probandum constitutes its status as a subverter of the first, then what is the point of challenging the other inference? If you say it is because the thing-in-itself (*vastu*) cannot possess two forms and thus [the first] lacks proving power, we ask: who has seen that a thing cannot have two forms? For a thing is real precisely to the extent that it is made known by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, it is clearly observed that a single entity cannot possess two contradictory natures; for one who eats only mung beans cannot, without effort, become otherwise. Likewise, there is no such thing as inequality of strength [between the two options], because that which is established by direct scriptural statement (yathāśruti) is firm; thus, a doubt arises.

Even though there is no difference between the two objects in terms of their reality as perceived, one might still harbor the conceit that they possess equal force due to the perception of some distinguishing feature in one of them. Even if this were so, because they are of equal force, the stronger [cognition] would be obstructed; thus, by obstructing the comparison (*upamāna*), there would be a mutual obstruction such that neither would be a means of establishing its own object, nor would they produce doubt. For doubt arises only when there is a lack of observation of a distinguishing feature that presents both contradictory particulars. Thus he says: "And even if there is equality of force..."

Now, [one might argue that] such [doubt] occurs either by chance or through non-apprehension; however, no other mode [of doubt] equal to apprehension has been observed. Therefore, even when apprehension is not observed, for one who considers the absence of the seer upon the absence of the seen, that very doubt regarding one of the two alternatives certainly arises in the mind.

It is indeed true; however, this is not because of a conflict arising from two contradictory, non-erroneous properties, but rather because, due to the presence of both validity (*prāmāṇya*) and invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), even that which is extremely distant is perceived by the mind as being present in the object of perception. Having accepted an equality of strength (*tulyabalatva*), the status of contradictory, non-erroneous [reasons] as causes of doubt has been refuted. Yet, there is no such equality of strength between these two; for one must consider that the predominance of either one necessarily occurs, since it is said that "the mind perceives it as such" based on the general rule (*utsarga*). However, this is not what is intended here.

Now, if the mind were all-pervasive simply because of its subtle dimension, then there would be no evidence whatsoever for the word "mind" [in that sense]. Thus, the reason—that the mind is formless because it is imperishable—is seen to be contradicted by perception and so forth. If the mind is established through the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions, then it is sublated by the very means of knowledge that apprehend its subject (the mind). For if the mind possesses an atomic dimension, the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is possible; however, if the mind were all-pervasive, it would be in contact with all sense organs at once, and thus the simultaneous arising of all cognitions would result. To this objection, he says the following to show that there is no contradiction regarding the state of intensity (udreka) in this very context.
"But this is indeed a sub-variety of the contradictory (*viruddha*).

This means that while the "contrary to what is to be proven" (*āgamaviruddha*)—which is an excess of the inferable—is called a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) for the purpose of classifying those [reasons] that are contradicted by perception and so forth (and thus opposed to the probandum) through the refutation of the opponent's position, it is nevertheless a sub-variety of the contradictory (*viruddha*), having the same meaning.
The "unascertained" (*anadhyavasita*) is said to be the uncommon fallacy of the reason (*asādhāraṇa-hetvābhāsa*).
He explains that as follows:
"In this way, while existing in these two, [it is] common to both, yet not of the same class," and so forth.

The Sāṃkhyas maintain that the reason (*hetu*)—"because every effect exists in a subtle state prior to its production"—is established by this [statement]. However, this reason fails regarding the six categories, such as space (*ākāśa*), because it lacks the determination of non-existence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), such as a sky-flower. From the perspective of those who seek a specific object, since it is stated that "manifestation occurs in a different form," the very non-exclusion from the subject (*pakṣa*) follows for the Sāṃkhyas. Therefore, for them, the reason "because of production" is not unestablished (*asiddha*) *per se*. This concludes the examination of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) within the section on cognition (*buddhi*) in the *Guṇa* chapter.

He asks: by which statement of the author of the Sūtras is the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) *bahir* (external) included? He replies: "This is the 'unestablished' (*aprasiddha*) [reason], namely the 'indication' (*uddeśa*). With the intention that—as with the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)—the uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) produces doubt, its inclusion under the term "doubtful indication" (*sandigdhāpadeśa*) is appropriate, and not under the term "unestablished," he says: [The text continues: "Because it is not established for both parties, it is called 'unestablished'. This means that since it is not established for both the proponent and the opponent, it is termed "unestablished"; however, because it is not established for one of the two, it is termed "doubtful. Therefore, the fallacious reason *bahir* is included among those [fallacies] that are doubtful, and not among those that are unestablished. Thus, the meaning is that the fallacious reason *bahir* is subsumed under the category of the "doubtful indication. This is the intended sense.
Now, this sixfold classification is a concise summary [of the specific properties] even though they are distinct from those of similar classes.

A specific property of a category arises both from those of similar classes and from those that are subsequent; for example, the possession of odor is the specific property of earth, which exists in relation to other substances as well as to qualities and actions.

Regarding sound (*śabda*), the property of audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is observed as its specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*). Now, is this specific characteristic of sound [distinguished] from things belonging to the same genus (*sāmānyajātīya*), such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, or from those belonging to a different genus (*vijātīya*)? If sound is a quality (*guṇa*), then this specific characteristic distinguishes it from things of the same genus, namely color and so forth; but if it were a substance (*dravya*) or an action (*karman*), then it would be distinguished from things of a different genus. Thus, because of audibility in sound, there arises the doubt whether it is a substance, a quality, or an action. When the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) has thus demonstrated the contradiction with the Sūtra, [the author] says: "Not by other methods," and so forth.

This is not the intended meaning of the Sūtra— that a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is a cause of doubt— but rather its meaning is something else. He demonstrates that very point with the words beginning "Because of the perception of a specific [property] in sound" (*śabde viśeṣadarśanāt*).
Having established that sound is an object perceivable by the ear, the author of the Sūtras stated that there arises a doubt as to whether it is a substance, a quality, or an action.
The meaning of this is as follows: regarding that object perceivable by the ear, the doubt is whether it is a substance, or a quality, or an action.

Regarding this, an opponent has stated: "By you, who assert doubt concerning sound as something perceptible by the ear, the very fact of being perceptible by the ear is declared to be the ground for the doubt. And since 'being perceptible by the ear' is a specific property (*viśeṣa*), doubt is untenable because of its perception; for doubt consists in the simultaneous presence of two contradictory possibilities, and such a presence does not arise from the observation of a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*), because that [unique property] is never observed in association with any specific feature. To this objection raised by the opponent, the author of the Sūtras provides a refutation.

Audibility is not a specific property (*viśeṣa*) of any one among substance and the rest; that is, among substance, quality, and action, audibility is not a specific property of any one—be it a substance, a quality, or an action—but rather this is correctly understood as a common property (*sāmānya*) of them. Why? Because it has been stated that among substances and so forth, which possess homogeneous subsequent parts, a specific property is observed for each individually in both ways.

Regarding the term "in the state of being a composite" (*piṇḍatve*): the "divisions" (*bheda*) are indeed substance and so forth; thus, "substance-divisions" (*dravyādibheda*) refers to substances, qualities, and actions. Among these, just as for a single substance, quality, or action, a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) is observed in two ways from those of a similar class that are subordinate to it: for instance, the distinction of earth from its own similar classes is observed along with "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*); the distinction of color is observed along with "color-ness" (*rūpatva*); the distinction of upward motion is observed along with "upward-motion-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva*); and even for sound, its distinction is observed in the *Śrāva-śāstra* along with "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*). Therefore, by that very nature of being a specific distinction, the commonality (*sāmānya*) of substance and so forth is indeed the basis for the respective word. Consequently, it is logical that a substance serves as a cause for doubt [when it is not further specified]. However, that which is non-common (*asādhāraṇa*)—such as a mere "knife" (*chura*)—is not a cause for doubt there, because of the absence of both the specific and the general [properties], as he says.

"It is not a cause for doubt" [means]: because it is distinguished from both those of the same class and those of a different class—this is to be analyzed. Furthermore, this fault is understood as follows: for those ignorant of the distinctions between substance and so forth, there arises a doubt as to whether sound is a substance or a quality, due to the presence of the two specific properties of "being sound" and "not being sound. This is because the specific property [of sound] is seen to deviate among things of the same class, and because it is difficult to distinguish its specific properties from those that follow [in other categories].

What is being said? [The opponent argues: "In the case of a particular (*viśeṣa*), one observes that it is a substance, a quality, or an action; and in the word [denoting it], one observes the property of being a word for a substance (*dravya-śabdatva*). Therefore, because of its being a particular, there arises doubt regarding whether it is a substance or something else. [The author replies: If even an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) were a cause of doubt, then there would follow the undesirable consequence of doubt regarding the category of "pot" (*ghaṭatva*) among all categories, since they are all equally connected with the state of being uncommon in every respect. Furthermore, this would lead to the consequence of doubt never ceasing. Thus he says: "Otherwise... He concludes as follows.

"Therefore" means that since doubt has its own nature—which is the perception of a non-common property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) that serves as the basis for contradictory particulars and which is capable of producing an effect through inference—doubt arises precisely from what has been stated [above], and not merely from the perception of a non-common property; this is the meaning of the conclusion.
Furthermore, there is a twofold indication of the probandum (*sādhya*), namely by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

In that context, the statement of the property of the probandum (*sādhya*) by way of its conformity with the generality of the mark (*liṅga*) through the generality of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) is the statement of similarity (*vaidharmya-nirdeśana*).
For example: "Whatever possesses action is observed to be a substance, as in the case of an arrow.
Here, the demonstration of the impossibility of the mark where there is the opposite of the object to be inferred is the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-nirdeśana*).
For example, whatever is a substance possesses action, such as a jar.

In order to determine the essential nature of the demonstration (*nirdeśana*), he says: "The demonstration is of two kinds: by similarity (*sādharmya*) and by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). The distinction is as follows: that statement by which the object of inference (*anumeya*) is demonstrated through the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is the demonstration by similarity; whereas that statement by which [the object] is demonstrated through the negation of the probandum and the negation of the probans is the demonstration by dissimilarity.
In that regard, he explains the non-specification of the probandum (sādhya) between those two by means of the words "therein,
of the inferable" (tatrānumeyasya), and so forth.
That is indeed appropriate.
He explains the demonstration by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with the words "in the case of the opposite of the inferable" (*anumeyaviparyaye*), and so forth;
that too is quite clear. Furthermore, in the section on the faculties (*buddhyadhikāra*), there is a demonstration [of this], as well as an investigation into the appearance thereof (*tadbhāsa*).
By this, fallacious positive examples (*sādharmya-nirdeśanābhāsa*) are explained.

For instance: "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal; whatever is corporeal is seen to be non-eternal, such as an atom, such as action, such as a pot, such as darkness, or like a non-sound. And: "Whatever is a substance is seen to possess activity. These are fallacious positive examples based on the mark (*liṅga*), the probandum (*anumeya*), both, the substratum (*āśraya*), the concomitance (*anugata*), the contrary (*viparīta*), and the non-existent (*ajagat*).

Whatever is impermanent is seen to be corporeal, such as a jar, an atom, space, or darkness. Like a pot, whatever possesses action or lacks action is seen to be a non-substance; thus, because they rely on both the mark and the inferable, or rely on one or the other, there are fallacious examples of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-nirdeśanābhāsa*), namely: those where the locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*), those lacking pervasion (*avyāpta*), and those with inverted pervasion (*viparīta-vyāpta*).

By this, fallacious indications (*nirdaśanābhāsa*) are explained. Furthermore, those which are not actual indications appear as if they were indications due to their similarity in form; thus they are called "fallacious indications. By means of this definition of a valid indication, they are refuted because they lack its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

As long as the essential nature of fallacious indications is not known, it is impossible to perform a negative determination (*anupalambha*) of them—like a vajra in its own field or an axe in another's field—as one explains the essential nature [of a wave] in the case of a water-wave.

"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal; for whatever is corporeal is seen to be non-eternal, such as an atom, such as action, such as a pot, or such as darkness, which is like a non-substance; and whatever is a substance is seen to possess motion"—these are examples of fallacious positive instances (*sādharmya-nirdeśanābhāsa*) based on the mark (*liṅga*), the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), both, the unestablished (*asiddha*), the non-concomitant (*ananugata*), and the contrary concomitant (*viparītānugata*). In the case "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like an atom," this is a fallacious instance where the mark is unestablished (*liṅgāsiddha*), because an atom lacks incorporeality.
In the case "like action," this is a fallacious instance where the object to be inferred is unestablished (*anumeyāsiddha*), because action lacks eternality.

For example, "like a pot" is an instance of the unestablished for both [proponent and opponent], because neither the property to be proven (nityatva, eternality) nor the probans (mūrtatva, corporeality) exists in a pot.

For example, "like darkness" is an instance of the unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because in ultimate reality there is no such thing as "darkness"; how then can it be cited as either the property to be proven or the probans?
"Like a sound" is a fallacious example that lacks a commonality.

Although both eternality (*nityatva*) and incorporeality (*amūrtatva*) exist here [in sound], nevertheless, it does not state that whatever is incorporeal is necessarily eternal; rather, it merely states that [sound] is not of the nature of consciousness (*aprakṛticidrūpatva*). Nor is this a case of a valid statement being understood as a non-probative reason due to the lack of comprehension from a faulty expression; therefore, there is no fault because the reference is made to a meaning that is not over-extended (*ananugatārtha*).

The notion that "whatever is a substance is possessed of action" is a case of inverted pervasion (*viparītānugata*).
