Even in the inference "air is a substance because it possesses action," action-possessingness is the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and substantiality is the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Alternatively, the pervasion is restricted to that which is the pervaded; it is not like conjunction, which exists in both [the pervaded and the pervader], for the pervader cannot be the pervaded itself due to the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Although in cases of equal pervasion, such as "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*), the property of being the pervader (*vyāpakatva*) exists even for that which is the pervaded (*vyāpya*), nevertheless, pervasion is established by relying solely on the form of being the pervaded, and not by reference to the form of being the pervader; for it is possible for even a deviant (*vyabhicārin*) property to disregard the latter.
As the teachers state according to the method of formal application (*prayoga*):
"Even though the pervaded is in reality devoid of the status of being the pervader..."
Even if it were dependent [on that], because it is contradictory, it would not establish the object to be apprehended.
Thus [it is said].
In the Vedic scripture (*śruti*), it is observed that [the definition] occurs as residing in the pervaded (*vyāpya*): "That which possesses action is a substance" (*kriyāvad dravyam*).

However, it does not occur there as residing in the pervader (*vyāpaka*), because that [action] is absent in the latter; thus, in the scripture, the application is the reverse [of what one might expect].

And regarding the logical mark (*liṅga*) and the object to be inferred (*anumeya*): those for whom there is an application of the logical mark and the object to be inferred that is not based on the subject (*pakṣa*), they are "those whose application of the logical mark and the object to be inferred is non-ignorant" (*avidyā*). [The compound] *liṅgānumeyopayogādhyāḥ* means those who have applied the logical mark and the object to be inferred. [The text] states that these are either not concomitant with the property to be proven (*tatra viparītānugatāḥ*) or conversely concomitant with it (*tacceti yo janaḥ*).
Furthermore, he explains this by way of the absence of an example through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāvāt*), beginning with the words "that which is solidity" (*yaddravatvam*) and so forth.

"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal; whatever is so is eternal, like action"—this [argument] lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the logical mark (*liṅga*), as there is an absence [of the property to be proved] in the case of action due to its perishability. "Like an atom"—this lacks pervasion regarding the object of inference (*anumeya*), for eternality is not pervaded by the atom.
"Like space"—this lacks pervasion regarding the object of inference, for neither incorporeality nor eternality is pervaded by space.

For example, the argument "darkness" is one where the locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*); for in ultimate reality, darkness itself does not exist—how then could there be an absence of both the probandum and the probans? This is because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to a jar and so forth. Even though there is a pervasion between the probandum and the probans in the case of a jar, one does not say that "the jar is eternal" or "it is corporeal"; nor, when such a restriction is made, does there arise an apprehension of non-pervasion between the probandum and the probans, because the pervasion is established through scriptural analogy.

Because of the reversed pervasion (*viparītavyāpti*)—namely, that "whatever has a mark (*liṅga*) is a substance (*dravya*)"—just as in verbal [inference] the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is the probans (*sādhana*) and the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is the probandum, so too in the case of the unestablished by word (*śābdāsiddha*), the pervaded is the non-existence of the probans and the pervader is the non-existence of the probandum.
As it has been said:
"Both parties should state [the argument] when there is no perception and no trace (*niranvaya*)."
If they are perceived in a contrary manner, that very [reason] is not a prover of that [conclusion].
Thus [it is said].

In that context, the statement "Air is a substance because it possesses motion" is intended to demonstrate the pervasion of the contrapositive (*viparyaya-vyāpti*). When a substance is not associated with qualities, there is no determination of the object of inference and so forth; therefore, it must be stated that [substance] is of two kinds. However, not everything is like that. Regarding duality and earthiness, he says: "That which is subject to modification is suffering. And thus, space does not possess pervasiveness, for even though it is devoid of motion, it is [regarded as] suffering. Therefore, due to this pervasion of the contrapositive, there is an absence of inference by way of dissimilar property (*vaidharmya*).

The mark (*liṅga*), the object to be inferred (*anumeya*), and the object to be known (*bodhya*)—these three, both the mark and the object to be inferred, are [the subjects] not pervaded (*avyāpta*). They have been stated by you as such.

Regarding the one whose validity (*āpti*) is unerring (*akhidha*) through his being an authority (*āpta*), [the term] "unerring validity" (*āptyākhidha*) refers to that which is not pervaded by the mark, the object to be inferred, and both; it is explained as that which is non-pervasive (*avyāpta*) or conversely pervasive (*viparītavyāpta*).

The application of the general mark (*liṅgasāmānya*), which was observed together with the general property to be inferred (*anumeyasāmānya*) in the example (*nidarśana*), to the subject of inference (*anumeya*), is the application of the inference (*anumitisthāna*). That statement by which the general mark—expressed as being present in the property to be inferred and whose actual locus has not yet been perceived—is connected to the subject of inference because it was observed in the example together with the general property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), is the application of the inference. For example: "And thus, air possesses motion."
And since its capacity to prove that [property] was observed only in the absence of the inferable [subject], it is not the case that air is devoid of action.

*Anusthāna* (application) is the bringing forward (*anvānayana*) into the object of inference (*anumeya*) of the general mark (*liṅgasāmānya*) which was previously observed together with the general property to be inferred (*anumeyasāmānya*) in the instance (*nidarśana*).

An instance (*nidarśana*) is an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) in which the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is demonstrated and ascertained; it is that in which the general mark, having been perceived and understood along with the general property to be inferred, is brought forward—that is, superimposed by the intellect—upon the object of inference, the subject of the property to be proved (*sādhyadharmin*), by means of a statement. That [statement] is *anusthāna*.

The indicator (*liṅga*)—which was shown in the example by way of its concomitance with the property to be proven—is subsequently applied to the subject (*pakṣa*) and recalled; this is what is meant by the etymological derivation of "recollection" (*pratisaṃdhāna*). Thus, it makes known the indicator as something to be remembered.
This refers to the "generality of the indicator" (*liṅgasāmānya*) as stated in terms of its presence in the property to be inferred. The intention is as follows:

immediately after the recollection, the indicator is stated by means of the statement of the reason (*hetu*), merely as "the indicator exists in the object to be inferred," but not yet as being connected to the specific locus (*dharmin*). That is the meaning.

The capacity of the *liṅga* (probans) to establish the *sādhya* (probandum) consists in its being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapatti*) and its presence as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Since these two were not previously manifested by the statements of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), that which connects them in the example (*nidarśana*)—where it has been observed together with the generality of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—to the object of inference (*anumeya*) by means of a statement, is the "application" (*anusthāna*).
This is the intended meaning.

Regarding words for the sake of others (*parārtha*), the word is employed in whatever manner the desire to know arises in another; thus, it becomes a means of proof directly presented to the cognizer, fulfilling their expectation by making known that which was to be understood.

But it does not state the five-fold property (*pañcadharmatā*) of the reason within the meaning of the sentence [of the proof], because the sentence-meaning resides in the totality of its own constituent parts (*svarūpasāmagrī*). When the cognition of the sentence-meaning has arisen from the sentence, the statement of the reason functions as a cause for that cognition, just as the mention of "being a cause" [is a cause] for the cognition of causality; however, it does not express the five-fold property of the reason, since a single word cannot function as a denoter in both ways simultaneously. Once the reason is known, one might ask: "How is this its status as a reason? To resolve this, it is understood that the cognition of the reason is established by the totality of conditions (*jñānasāmagrī*), and because it is invariably connected (*avinābhāvaprayojitatvāntarīyakatvāt*) to the formulation of the reason, the lack of invariable concomitance is eliminated by the very statement of the reason. Thus, when a reason capable of such [invariable concomitance] is subsequently applied to the locus (*pakṣa*), it is then recognized as being known.

If it is argued that after the example, the application (*upanaya*) exists for the purpose of understanding the "presence of the reason in the subject" (*pañcadharmatā*), and that this presence is understood through the very force of the statement of the reason—since a reason residing in a different locus cannot be a prover—then [we reply]: the force of that statement is not unobstructed; for where the three-fold character of the reason is absent, even the example cannot be established.

If it is argued that because the status of being a cause can be attributed even to this [subject] as its final basis (*adhāra*), there is no absolute misconception of it as something else, and thus pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be established by means of an example—[we reply: since the attribution of causality through delusion is impossible for that which does not exist at night, the determination of the example's status as a "locus" (*pada*) must be stated separately, based on the ascertainment of the presence of the five-fold property (*pañcadharmatā*). Thus, it should be explained according to what is logically appropriate.

If it is argued: "How can the presence of the five-fold property (*pañcadharmatā*) in the unperforated [subject] be faulty even when it is brought forward by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Therefore, there is no proof of the [logical] member [of the syllogism] from that either. [We reply: How is it that the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding the unperforated inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is also faulty because of its finality? From that, the establishment of the [syllogistic] members follows. If it is argued:

"In the example (*udāharaṇa*), the statement of pervasion is not to be challenged because it follows a means of valid cognition and because it is the investigation of all [instances] in their entirety," [we reply: In the application (*upanaya*) as well, the ascertainment of the presence of that property (*taddharmatā*) arises precisely from following the means of valid cognition that investigates the five-fold property, and not from mere verbal statement.

If it is argued that the conformity to the rule of the five features (*pañcadharmatā*) occurs precisely through the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*) of the statement of the reason (*hetvabhidhāna*), then the conformity to the means of valid cognition regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*) will likewise occur precisely through the impossibility otherwise of that [reason]. If it is further argued that because the statement of the reason has another purpose, it possesses the capacity for application (*upanaya*), and thus its presentation is performed by means of the example (*udāharaṇa*), then let this same method be followed here as well; therefore, the application is established in this manner.
Let it be that the application is redundant when the reason has already been stated.
No.

For when the reason (*hetu*) is absent, because the form of the probandum (*sādhya*) has perished and cannot be understood, there is no possibility of knowing its capacity [to prove]; consequently, there is no occurrence of the statements regarding the example (*udāharaṇa*) and so forth.
And thus says the *Nyāyabhāṣya*:
"When the reason is absent, for what is the status of being a means of proof (*sādhanabhāva*) demonstrated?"
They state an example of *anuvādya* (the subject to be restated) as "and so forth" (*tathā ca*). [The example is:
"The son of Caitra is seen standing. And [they say] "in the absence of that which is to be restated" (*anudheya-abhāve*) as well.

Regarding that which is intended as the object of inference and that which is not intended by others, [the author] states the purpose of the restatement (*pratyāmnāya*) within the section on cognition:
"The restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) for the sake of producing certainty is *pratyāmnāya*.

That is to say, when something has been presented as the object to be established and has been made known through the other members of the syllogism, such as the reason (*hetu*), the restatement of the proposition for the sake of producing certainty by means of a completed sentence is *pratyāmnāya*.
Therefore, it must indeed be stated.

For if this [stating of the reason] were absent, the other members—whether taken collectively or individually—would not possess the capacity to express that meaning, because their meaning would already be understood. If you say "no" [to the necessity of stating it], that is not so, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

To explain: one would have to state only the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), since for those who are learned, the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is remembered [from previous experience].
Since the comprehension of that meaning will occur [through these], the completion of the sense is achieved by the words alone.

By the statement "sound is impermanent because it is subject to destruction," sound is described as qualified merely by the impermanence attributed to it; by the statement "because it follows immediately upon effort," only the mere application of the proof for impermanence is expressed;

and by the statement "whatever follows immediately upon effort is seen to be impermanent, such as a jar," only the concomitance of the general property of the probans with the general property of the probandum is stated.
By the statement, "That which is eternal is seen to be not produced by effort, such as space," the absence of the probans is demonstrated through the absence of the probandum.

And likewise: "Sound is produced immediately after effort," and "Sound is not produced immediately after effort, like space"—the purpose of these two examples, consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), is considered to be the persistence of the general property of the probans (*sādhana-sāmānya*) in sound. Therefore, by the statement "Therefore, sound is impermanent," the completion of the intended meaning—that sound is indeed impermanent—is understood. Consequently, it is established that inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) consists in the communication of an object ascertained by oneself through a syllogism of exactly five members.

He explains [the nature of] perception (*pratyakṣā*) by saying, "when it has been indicated as being inferable. When a thing has been bound by the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), indicated as being inferable—that is, as something to be established—and when its audibility (*śabdatva*) has not yet been determined, that very word by which the designation of the perceptibility of that same audibility is made constitutes a restatement of the audibility of perception. To the question, "For what purpose is this restatement of the audibility of perception? he says:
"For the sake of establishing certainty for others":

first, the verbal [nature of the reason] was stated, but that was not yet established as certain in the mind of the opponent due to an aversion to verbal [reasoning]. Therefore, he speaks of its demonstration; and when the verbal reason is stated, its certainty is produced by means of perception and so forth—this very point he demonstrates with the words "when [the subject] is designated as that which is to be understood," and so on.

Initially, through mere words alone, a verbal certainty regarding others has not yet occurred. For them, by means of the reason (*hetu*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*)—which possess the capacity for the cognition of the probandum to be inferred in the example—the certainty arises through a complete and perfected sentence when the [conclusion] is made for the sake of direct perception (*pratyakṣā*). It is for this purpose that the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) proceeds as a direct perception; here is its illustration: "Therefore, it is unseen. [An objection is raised: "Is verbal certainty determined by the members [of the syllogism], such as the reason and so forth? What is the use of direct perception? To this, he says:
There is no cognition of another reason [in the case of perception].

Even the members of an argument, such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, although each is understood by others for its own specific meaning, are not capable of bringing about the cognition of a single unified object through perception because they are independent.

However, when there is a fulfillment of expectancy following this [proposition], and there is a mutual connection like that of the heart of a wooden mallet and the mallet itself, it is logical for them to lead to perception.
"It has the fault of redundancy" means "because the meaning is already understood.
This is the intended sense: whatever capacity for comprehension exists in inference for oneself, that same capacity exists in inference for others as well.

Now, let there be this distinction: in one's own cognition, this [reason] is connected by oneself; in the cognition of another, it is made known by another, and it is understood by oneself through the power of the logical mark (*liṅga*). For the other person as well, that very same thing is the indicator. The statement, however, has the capacity merely to introduce the logical mark; and when it is presented by the members [of the syllogism], such as the reason and so forth—namely, the five members consisting of positive and negative concomitance—that alone constitutes the logical mark. Therefore, for fear of non-connection or over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), it is sufficient to establish the restriction; thus, the suspicion of over-extension is not tolerated.

Verbal [cognition] makes known only the capacity of the inferential mark (liṅga), not the verbal [object] itself; however, even when that [mark] does not extend externally, there is no contradiction in the case of direct perception, such as when one perceives the specific qualities of a lotus bud through a particular mode of apprehension.

Furthermore, because it produces aversion in two ways, and because its own expressed subject matter is associated with a deviation from its proper scope, as long as the capacity [of the reason] is not established within the compound itself, that word is faulty due to its lack of merit and the corruption of speech; for since there is no certainty regarding the property-bearer (*dharmin*), even if there is a sublation (*bādhana*), the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) is impossible. Thus, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is presented which grasps the absence of contrary evidence. When that [absence] exists, and the capacity has been made known, the proof (*sādhana*) is capable of establishing the probandum. This is the application of a perceptual fault (*pratyakṣadoṣaprayoga*) when the similarity of the case (*prakaraṇasama*) and the non-existence of the thing as it truly is have been determined.

In this regard, if a prohibition is made against the statement "even that which is superior is perceived by virtue of its capacity," then the example (*udāharaṇa*) and so forth must also be prohibited.

For once the statement of the reason (*hetu*) has been made immediately after the thesis (*pratijñā*), [the example] is redundant, since the verbal comprehension of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is possible through the [reason] itself.
This is what is meant:

Inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is not directed toward the person being instructed, because it would be purposeless. Nor is it possible to determine for oneself how much understanding the person to be instructed possesses or how much they lack, since such things depend on the mental deliberations of another, which are inherently inaccessible. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to assume that the capacity of those to be instructed is uniform; for their cognitive powers vary according to their individual discernment. Therefore, having first ascertained [the opponent's state], the probative power of the reason must be established through its actual ontological status (*vastuvṛttyā*); to that extent, it must be communicated by means of speech.
One should not employ words according to one's own inclination, disregarding the distinctions in the practice [of the teaching].
The wise should not state the actual reality to one who is ignorant;
for who would pay heed to the truth for one whose understanding of reality is already perverted?
It brings [the conclusion] near;
therefore, it is called the *upasaṃhāra* (conclusion).

For this very reason—that the capacity (*sāmarthya*) which is appropriate for the purpose is perceived in the *pratijñā* (proposition)—it is from that same [conclusion] that the completion and the cognition of the *upeya* (the goal), namely the *sādhya* (the probandum), are understood. This is the definition of the *nigamana* (conclusion).

Alternatively, the construction is as follows: since the existence of erroneous means of knowledge cannot be understood without an initial [correct] determination, therefore, in this respect, there is the completion—meaning the final culmination—of the capacity of the correct means of knowledge regarding the object to be attained. Having stated the meaning for each part individually, he now explains it by bringing them together in one place, preceded by a question, beginning with "How? and so forth.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether sound is eternal or non-eternal, when there is a desire for specific determination, the particular sound in question is stated to be "non-eternal" by means of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), which is not yet established.

Then, in response to the question "What is the reason (*hetu*)?", the statement of the reason—"because it follows immediately after effort," that is, because it is perceived after effort where it was previously non-existent"—expresses the property that serves as the proof for non-eternality.

This demonstrates the presence of the probans in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) through its coexistence with the probandum, as well as the non-occurrence of these two [the probans and the absence of the probandum] elsewhere.

Regarding the member [of the syllogism] consisting of the statement of the example (*udāharaṇa*), how is this probandum (*sādhya*) understood? When one enters into the capacity of the probandum, the example—stating that "whatever in this world is produced through effort is seen to be impermanent"—merely effects the concomitance (*anvaya*) of the general property of the means of proof (*sādhana-sāmānya*) with the general property of the probandum (*sādhya-sāmānya*); it does not, however, constitute the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that [probandum], as was previously explained regarding the meaning of the word.

"Whatever is not perceived by the senses is eternal"—this [proposition] is redundant, for it demonstrates the absence of a means of proof when there is an absence of the object to be proven. However, when there arises the desire to know whether that [property of being perceived by the senses] exists in sound or not—given that it has been observed that "whatever is perceived by the senses is non-eternal"—it is established that sound is indeed perceived by the senses; just as a jar is perceived by the senses, so too is sound perceived by the senses.

Nor can it be established that sound is non-eternal through the impossibility of its being perceived by the eye, because—due to the equality of the deviation (vyabhicāra) in sound regarding perceptibility by the eye, despite the observed capacity and observed invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) established through positive and negative correlations (anvaya-vyatireka)—it is not understood [as follows]: Just as, although there is an external pervasion (bahirvyāpti) relationship such that "whatever is produced is seen to be non-hot, like a jar," the connection with heat is not absent in what is produced because of the intervention of another means of knowledge (pramāṇa), so too, although there is an external pervasion relationship such that "whatever is perceptible by the eye is non-eternal," there might be a doubt regarding the counter-example (vipakṣa) that sound—which is perceptible by the eye—is not non-eternal. In such a case, since there is no means of knowledge to establish the individual nature of sound itself (pratyātma-āśe) to prove its specific character, the meaning is that sound is not non-eternal.

By this [statement], beginning with the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is presented which apprehends the absence of any contrary means of valid cognition; and once that [absence] has been established and demonstrated, when doubt regarding the contrary has ceased, one understands the probandum (*sādhya*) without hesitation by the force of the means of valid cognition that apprehends the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—since the reason whose inseparable connection has been shown is preceded by the eternal. Thus, nothing further is required. By this, it is understood from the composition of the treatise that the purpose of this work is fully accomplished in order to demonstrate that "sound is indeed impermanent" through direct perception.
Furthermore, the wise have recognized that the conclusion (nigamana) serves a purpose for one who already understands the meaning of the statement to be proven (sādhya).

The nature of a jar and the nature of its being produced are one thing, while that of sound is another. Even if the producedness of a jar is pervaded by impermanence—just as momentariness is—the deluded might think that this same [pervasion] must apply to sound as well. Thus, when there is no cognition of the probandum despite the presence of the two previously shown factors of the reason—its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)—the conclusion (*nigamana*) states "therefore it is so" (*tasmāt tathā*). By following the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that grasps the pervasion as it operates in a general sense, impermanence is established in this sound: "Because this is produced, it is impermanent. This is cognized in a general way and not specifically; therefore, by virtue of its producedness, sound is impermanent.

And in this view, there is no lack of firmness regarding the application of the *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized by the context) rule; for once the [proposition] has been concluded by the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*) itself, there can be no suspicion that it is not a valid thesis, because it possesses the characteristics of a thesis.

Others, however, interpret the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) as referring to the following: because this [sound] is seen to be impermanent when produced, because sound is produced, and because the two opposing [arguments] are impossible to subvert—therefore, on account of its being produced, the conclusion established in the section on cognition is that "sound is impermanent."
He provides a supporting argument: "Therefore.

Because, indeed, in the five types of inference, when the means of proof (*sādhana-sāmagrī*) are understood, the understanding of the probandum (*sādhya*) occurs; since there are exactly these five and nothing else is required, it follows that even elsewhere, the demonstration is made by a sentence consisting of exactly five members through the application of one's own definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Thus, it is established that even in the previous case, a sentence whose meaning is for the sake of another is known as *parārthānumāna* (inference for others).

However, those who maintain that perception alone is the sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and assert that inference is not a means of valid cognition should be asked this: Is it only the single unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of perception, as it is cognized in its own nature, that is the means of valid cognition, or is it the case that all [perceptions] are so? It cannot be the former, because there is no reason for another perception—which possesses the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—to lack validity. If, on the other hand, it is held that every unique particular of perception, whether past, future, or perceived by another person, is a means of valid cognition; [then...]

If it is asked, "How is this determined—that the validity of what is being perceived is established by means other than direct perception (pratyakṣa) and so forth?"—it is through inference; for the validity of inference consists in its being an inference based on essential nature (svabhāvānumāna).

Thus, in the absence of inference as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for whose sake could perception be established as a means of valid cognition, since it is expressible only through conceptual construction? It cannot be for oneself, because one does not need to be established [in a truth] by oneself; rather, it must be for another. Is that other person one who has already understood or one who is in disagreement? It is useless to establish what is already understood. If it is one who is in disagreement, there can be no direct realization [of the truth], and disagreement is not apprehended by perception; if it were inferred from the mark of speech, then the validity of inference based on an effect would be destroyed.

By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it established that inference (*anumāna*) is a means of valid cognition? Perception (*pratyakṣa*) has a positive entity as its object and is not capable of negating anything. If it is argued that [negation] is understood through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), then that would indeed be an inference having apprehension as its logical mark (*liṅga*).
And so it has been said by the Buddhists:
"The establishment of the generality of both the means of valid cognition and its opposite occurs through the cognition of something else."
And because there is a negation of anything that has increased by means of another means of valid cognition.

Thus, because of the establishment of the general categories of valid cognition and its absence, and because this [negation] is a cognition of another [person], and because there is a negation of a particular [object] through perception, the existence of inference— which possesses the three types of logical marks (liṅga) consisting of essential nature, effect, and non-perception— as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) from perception, is asserted by the author of the Vārttika.
Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is a determinative cognition arising from the perception of specific characteristics that is opposed to doubt.

This very [ascertainment] is either perception or inference. That which arises from the perception of specific characteristics and is opposed to doubt is perceptual ascertainment (*pratyakṣa-nirṇaya*).

For example, when a doubt arises—such as "Is this a post or a person?"—due to the perception of common characteristics shared by both a post and a person from a distance, and due to the non-perception of their specific features and the recollection of those features, the resulting determinative knowledge that "this is indeed a person" upon seeing the stone-like hardness and other traits is a perceptual certainty (*pratyakṣa-niścaya*). Similarly, when a doubt arises—such as "Is this a cow or not?"—due to the perception of a mere horn, the resulting determinative knowledge that "this is indeed a cow" upon seeing a dewlap is an inferential certainty (*anumāna-nirṇaya*).
Regarding the determination [of truth], some, however, desire another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for cases where perception and inference fail; to them, he says:
"Arising from the observation of specific features," and so forth.

Just as doubt arises from the non-perception of specific features, so too certainty arises; and that definitive knowledge produced by the observation of specific features is *nirṇaya* (ascertainment).
And that [ascertainment] is the opposite of doubt, because when it is produced, doubt is destroyed.
As Maṇḍana stated in the *Viprama-viveka*:
"Indeed, when [the object] is ascertained, one does not entertain the conjecture 'Is it a post? and so forth"—the meaning is that one does not doubt it.

Although determinate knowledge (*niścayātmaka-jñāna*) is everywhere indeed *nirṇaya* (ascertainment), nevertheless, because it is well-known (*prasiddhi*) as being manifested after the time of doubt and because it arises in opposition to doubt, [the author] explains the summary statement regarding its own meaning and demonstrates the inclusion of *nirṇaya* within perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). [He begins with: "By perception," and so forth.
The knowledge that consists of ascertainment regarding the object of perception is perceptual determination (*pratyakṣanirṇaya*);
likewise, the knowledge of ascertainment regarding the object of inference is inferential determination (*anumānanirṇaya*). This he states by means of the subsequent passage of the text.

Memory is that which has as its objects things seen, heard, or experienced, and which is caused by both the desire and recollection [of those objects] and by a specific conjunction of the self and the mind dependent upon the observation of a mark (liṅga); it arises from impressions (saṃskāra) produced by the cognition of the excellence of an object, and is further assisted by the desire and recollection that serve as the causes for the subsequent determination of the remainder.
The definition of memory [is its arising] when [the object] exists.
Regarding the observation of a mark (*liṅga*), there is a dependence on desire.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "observation of a mark and desire for recollection," the factors such as focused attention (*praṇidhāna*) mentioned in the *Nyāyasūtra* are included; these too [arise] from a specific conjunction of the soul (*ātman*), the mind (*manas*), and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). This is the statement of the causes of memory.
In the cognition of the qualities of the self and the mind, there is a clear exposition of the function of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the signs and substances and that which is not so produced, [the opponent argues] that because memory would otherwise be impossible from this [present] location, and because the latent impression is clearly not produced by the signs and substances alone, they say that the mind (*manas*) is the cause. However, from this [present] cognition, a latent impression is produced by means of a vivid cognition.
A clear cognition is a more distinct cognition; from that, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is known.
Therefore, although a clear cognition arises from the repeated grasping of the syllables of a section (*anuvāka*), a latent impression does not arise for those syllables [if they are not mastered].

For example, even when a section has been recited, because of the repeated grasping of what was already grasped, repetition (*abhyāsa*) is the cause of the latent impression, since the perception of the syllables of the section is observed when that [repetition] exists.

Because of the inclusion [of all objects] within the category of "seen," even when other things are perceived in great variety, there is no lack of connection with the cause of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) due to the manifestation of substances at another time.

This is established by the cognition of the objects through the phrase "in those seen, heard, or inferred. "Seen" means those directly perceived; "heard" means those understood through words; and "inferred" means those deduced through inference.

The definition of the effect is: "The cause of the subsequent favoring [of cognition] is the residual reflective awareness (*anu-vyavasāya*). It is called *śeṣa* because it remains (*śiṣyate*) or is left over. *Anuvyavasāya* is a cognition (*citi*) that occurs subsequently (*anu-paścāt*); thus, it is a residual reflective awareness (*śeṣānuvyavasāya*). With respect to the initial knowledge of the logical mark (*liṅga*), the knowledge of the object to be inferred (*anumeya*) which arises immediately thereafter is its cause—namely, the recollection of suitability (*yogyatā*). The manifestation of being a means to pleasure is the cause of desire; the first presentation is the cause of the recollection of the second term; the recollection of being a source of pain is the cause of aversion; and the clear form [of the object] as "that" is the cause of recognition.
In that case, since the pastness of the object—that is, its having been previously experienced—is cognized, it is a *smṛti* (recollection) whose object is past.

For this very reason, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it functions by presenting the object as being within the domain of a prior experience; thus, in its determination of the object, it merely maintains the prior experience. Inferential knowledge (*anumānajñāna*), however, while apprehending what has arisen, would be like a *smṛti* only if it were independent regarding its own object; but this is not so, because there is no cognition here [in inference] of it as being an experience of a prior experience.
As it is said in the *Tattvaṭīkā*: "All those who possess knowledge of reality are gurus."
A cognition whose object is the object of a preceding cognition is held to be a *sphuṭi* (confirmatory cognition);
its validity is not undermined by that preceding cognition or others.
Thus; as they say in the Veda, [it is stated] in the Kārikā:
In that case, the validity of the preceding cognition is accepted;
its purpose is fulfilled merely by its presence, since the manifestation [of the object] is already clear.
Thus [it is said].

As for those who claim that the Veda lacks authority because it is not clearly perceived, their refutation is as follows: it would follow that cognition whose objects are past or future would lack authority. Regarding the seers (ṛṣis), the authors of the sacred tradition (āmnāya): when knowledge arises—whether based on perception or not based on perception—concerning objects beyond the senses, such as dharma and so forth, whether past, future, or present, through the contact of the self and the mind and by means of a particular merit (dharma-viśeṣa), that knowledge which is intuitive and reports things as they truly are, they call "ārṣa" (the seer's intuition).
But that occurs through the expansion of the divine origins, and only occasionally among worldly beings, as when a girl says, "My brother will come," even though her heart tells her so.
The *ārṣa* [type of knowledge] is to be explained. Regarding the phrase "of the authors of the *āmnāya*":

the *āmnāya* is the Veda; its authors are the creators, such as the Four-faced One (Brahmā). When, through the conjunction of the self (*ātman*) and the mind (*manas*), there arises a prescient cognition (*prātibha-jñāna*)—a presentation of reality, a knowledge of the true nature of things, a cognition devoid of doubt—that pertains to objects beyond the senses, whether they are established through direct perception or not established through direct perception, and which is presented according to the actual state of affairs, the wise call that *ārṣa*.
In the absence of any impairment of the sense faculties (*indriya-pratihati*), that intuitive flash which occurs is *pratibhā*. *Pratibhā* itself is called *prātibham*. And this [intuition] is yours.
Its arising is otherwise untenable due to the absence of a cause; thus, since it would otherwise be useless, it is stated: "from a specific quality of merit" (*dharmaviśeṣāt*).

It is distinguished, hence it is a "specific" (*viśeṣa*); merit itself is the specific, thus "specific merit" (*dharmaviśeṣa*). Knowledge, austerity, and meditative concentration are the preeminent forms of merit; from that, the emergence of intuition occurs.

Generally, through its expansion, this [intuition] occurs predominantly among those of divine nature; yet it sometimes occurs even among worldly people, as when a girl says, "My heart tells me that my brother is coming.

This is not doubt, because there is an absence of the uncertainty characteristic of imagination and the like; nor is it error, because it is confirmed by subsequent correspondence; thus, it is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

In the case of the vision of the perfected ones (*siddha*), why is there no other [separate] cognition? For those who have attained perfection through effort—such as by means of eye-salves, foot-ointments, powders, or pills—the perception of objects that are subtle, concealed, or distant occurs when the heart-lotus is awakened. That perception arises spontaneously; it is not desired as a result of external signs such as the skin, the moon, or flames belonging to celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial beings, nor from the ripening of merit or wealth. This is because, in the section on the faculties within the *Guṇagrāma* chapter of the *Buddhi-adhikāra*, the perception of the perfected ones is described as being produced by the power of their own specific nature, which is not seen in others.
This is precisely the proof.

Now, some maintain that the perception of the Siddhas regarding dharma and other such objects—which is established as being like [ordinary] perception—is actually included within this very category of perception; thus, they consider it to be a distinct type of cognition. To refute that, he said: "The perception of the Siddhas is not a separate kind of knowledge."

This very point is established as follows: by means of immersion, recitation, and so forth, preceded by effort, there exists for those who are learned—the "learned" being those who perceive objects that are visible and capable of being seen—the possession of the essential nature of things. For these learned ones who perceive the visible, when their eyes are obstructed or distant due to immersion and other such acts, the non-visibility [of objects] is merely a cause for the non-functioning of the sense organs and the like.

Now, regarding those beings who possess divine senses that do not exceed [their natural capacity], the cognition of dharma and so forth through their eyes and other organs is indeed inference, because it is produced by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) acting upon the specific parts of the body.

Furthermore, since the perception of dharma and so forth is established for such beings, it is necessarily included within the category of direct perception (pratyakṣa), as its object is directly apprehended.
If the perception of dharma and so forth is born of the senses, then it is direct perception.
Now, that which is independent of the sense organs is the object of inference. Regarding the phrase "instruction" (upadeśa),
it means "cognition in this manner."
Thus, by the immediately preceding [verse],
it is said "intellect" (*buddhi*) among the faculties;
the meaning is that intellect has been explained.
The word "iti" indicates completion.
The source of happiness is the non-perception of objects.

Even when the sense organs are in contact with desired objects, that which arises from the soul’s conjunction with the mind—which is characterized by the absence of pain caused by the bondage of the senses to their objects and the resulting lack of perception—is happiness. Therefore, attachment to those objects is the source of suffering.
In the future, that which is born of conceptualization regarding things not yet present—
namely, the desire to recollect objects and the conceptualizing thereof— is what the wise call dissatisfaction, the cause of desiccation.
Because it has the intellect (*buddhi*) as its object, he explains pleasure immediately after the intellect.
"Pleasure is that whose object is not [previously] perceived.

It is called *anugraha* because one is favored by it; the meaning is that it is characterized by favor, having the nature of favor. For pleasure is the experience of what is agreeable; thus, while making its own object experienced, it favors another person.
It is explained in that very same [work]:
"Pragādi" (beginning with *pra*).

That pleasure which arises from the direct contact (*sākṣāt-pratyakṣa*)—that is, the immediate proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*)—with well-known objects such as women, sandalwood paste, and so forth, produced by the contact between the sense organs and their objects, and characterized by the cognition of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga-upalabdhi*), is pleasure (*sukha*).
It is said that [this] is established by the venerable [teacher].

For those who perceive that the cause [of pleasure] is characterized by a specific quality consisting in the non-appropriation of suffering due to the exclusion of other objects, there is also the understanding that the conceptualization of objects (*viṣayavikalpa*) is a cause, because of the absence of pleasure in one who has departed from that state—
just as, for example, the term "northerner" and so forth indicates a specific direction based on one's own state of being situated.
In cases such as those of Madhupa, Hastin, and others, there is a clarity of the eyes and other senses due to the consumption of very wholesome food;
this favorability consists solely in the object being pleasant. Attachment is passion, and the clarity of the eyes and so forth is the state of being directed toward sense-objects.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the clarity of the mind (manaḥprasāda) is included. These [qualities] produce happiness.

Through happiness, the self-experience of the self is produced; that itself is the favor toward the self. And when happiness has arisen, there would be the manifestation of happiness and the other [qualities].
Attachment to the means of pleasure is the persistence of pleasure.

Regarding past [means], pleasure arises from the recollection of those experienced means of pleasure that have passed; regarding the future, it arises when one thinks, "This will happen to me," as the object is being mentally constructed.

As for that state of non-injury found among the wise who possess self-knowledge—which occurs even when there is a slight inclination toward the recollection of sense objects, or when the recollection is present, or when the object is being slightly constructed—that has its cause in the specific tranquility resulting from the application of knowledge (*vidyā*).

Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the realization of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), by which the senses are conquered. Excellence (*dharma*) is a specific quality consisting of the absence of attachment to the mere substrates that cause the body's persistence; it is a preeminent virtue that removes the stain of worldly activity (*nivṛtti*). These four constitute the cause.

However, for those who assert that pleasure is merely the absence of pain, there is a contradiction with the experience of bliss as the nature of the Self. Furthermore, the occurrence of attraction toward what is beneficial and aversion toward what is harmful—expressed as "this is desirable" and "that is to be shunned"—would be untenable [for them].
Suffering has the characteristic of affliction (*upaghāta*).

When there is contact between the senses and their objects—whether desirable or undesirable—and when there is non-perception of what is desired, that which arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, characterized by distress and dejection, is called suffering (*duḥkha*).
[Furthermore,] regarding past things such as hunger, disease, and grief, it is that which is born of memory.
"In future [births], it shall arise from the Buddhas."
Since pleasure was discussed in connection with its occurrence, suffering should be explained immediately thereafter.
Suffering is characterized by affliction (*upaghāta*). It is called "affliction" because one is afflicted by it; its characteristic is affliction, meaning its nature consists of being harmful.

They perceive the self by producing an experience whose object is the self itself, through a deviation from what was intended regarding suffering and injury. This he clarifies with the words beginning "anigṛhitalakṣya" and so forth.
Intolerance—meaning hatred—is the injury;
the experience of suffering and the loss of luster for those who are objects of hatred are its causes.
When suffering exists, there occurs an injury to oneself characterized by the experience of that [suffering].
Therefore, regarding the many unborn [beings] who are free from desire and devoid of attachment, the previous explanation was that they are born of longing.
Desire (icchā) is the longing for what has not yet been attained, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another.
It is said to arise from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending either upon pleasure and so forth, or upon the essential nature [of the object].
It is the cause of effort, merit, and demerit.

Desire (*kāma*), longing (*abhilāṣa*), passion (*rāga*), attachment (*sakta*), compassion (*kāruṇya*), detachment (*vairāgya*), hypocrisy (*upadhā*), disposition (*bhāva*), and so forth—these are the various types of desire.
Desire for sexual intercourse is *kāma*;
desire for food is *abhilāṣa*.
Attachment (*rāga*) is the desire for repeated enjoyment of sense objects.
Inclination (*sakṛtva*) is the desire for action that is not immediate.
Compassion (*kāruṇya*) is the desire to eliminate the suffering of others without regard for one's own interest.
Vairāgya is the desire to renounce sense objects due to perceiving their defects.
Upadhā is the desire to deceive others. Bhāva is a desire concealed within.
Distinctions in desire arise from distinctions in action, such as the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and the desire to abandon (*jihīrṣā*).
Desire (*icchā*) is the longing for what has not yet been attained, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another.

That desire which is a longing for an unattained object for one's own sake— expressed as "May this be mine"— or a longing for the sake of another— expressed as "May this belong to him"— is said to arise from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending either upon pleasure and so forth, or upon the intrinsic nature [of the object].

When a desire arises for a future object that is pleasant or neutral, and once that [desire] has arisen, pleasure—though future—is perceived by the intellect (*buddhi*) through its causes, such as [the memory of] the excellence of that object.
Thus says the author of the *Nyāyavārttika*:
"Because the fruit is the motivator."

Even when the cause of pleasure has passed away, memory is the cause for its [re-]arising. Effort (*prayatna*) has merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) as its causes. The *Tattvasaṃgraha* states that effort arises from the desire for acquisition; memory arises from the desire to remember. In the case of prescribed rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, merit is produced for one who engages in them out of a desire for the fruit.
In those whose nature consists of activity such as prohibited passion and so forth,
there also exist desire and the like; regarding these,
they say "desire" and so on.

Regarding the statement that desire and the like are merely varieties of longing (*icchā*) and not a distinct reality—that very point is addressed by the term "view" (*dṛṣṭi*). Desire is not the longing for what is not desired; rather, the word "desire" (*kāma*), when used in its defining sense, applies exclusively to the longing for what is not desired, whereas elsewhere it functions through association with other words.
As in the injunction, "One who desires heaven should sacrifice.

*Abhilāṣa* is the desire for consumption—that is, the desire for eating; it is the longing for that. *Rāga* is the desire for repeated engagement with sense objects; the meaning is that *rāga* is the desire for the repeated enjoyment of sense objects.

Desire without attachment is *saṅkalpa*. *Saṅkalpa* is the desire to bring about an object that has not yet come into existence. Compassion (*kāruṇya*) is the desire to destroy the suffering of others without aiming at one’s own self-interest; it is that desire to remove or alleviate the suffering of others when one does not wish to do anything for one's own sake. Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the desire to renounce sense-objects once they have been attained, because their perception causes suffering.
Desire for another's object, desire for the supreme goal, and equanimity;
desire that is not distressed by the lack of gain, and desire characterized by the transformation of the gender—these are *icchā* (desire).
Varieties of *icchā* arise from the distinctions among actions, such as the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and the desire to take (*jihīrṣā*).
The desire to act is *cikīrṣā*, the desire to take away is *jihīrṣā*, the desire to go is *jigamiṣā*, and so forth; these various types of desire follow upon the various types of action.
Hatred has the nature of blazing forth.
That state, in the presence of which one considers oneself as if set ablaze, is hatred.
It arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending either upon suffering or upon its own essential nature.
The cause of the first [unwholesome root] is improper mental application.
Anger, hatred, resentment, and intolerance are varieties of hatred (*dveṣa*).
Hatred (*dveṣa*) consists of burning;
this is indicated by the phrase "one who has destroyed hatred" (*kṣatadveṣaṇa*), as explained in the passage beginning with "in which there is destruction" (*yasmin nu kṣati*).
That is correct.
And that [aversion] arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending either upon suffering or upon its own nature.
When the cause of suffering has been destroyed and the suffering born thereof arises, aversion occurs.

This is the cause of the non-manifestation of the first [type of hatred]: "I shall kill him"—this is the first [form of hatred], arising from aversion (*dveṣa*). Aversion and other such states toward those who are hostile to the meaning of the Vedas and so forth are present at its beginning; indeed, it is through aversion that these offenses arise. From aversion, that which has a manifest form is produced: whoever hates someone remembers the desire to strike them. Anger (*krodha*), malice (*droha*), resentment (*manyu*), and impatience (*amarṣaṇa*) are the varieties of aversion.

Hatred (*dveṣa*) is anger (*krodha*), which consists of an affliction that causes transformations in the body, sense organs, and so forth. Malice (*droha*) is defined as a state of hatred characterized by an intent to harm, accompanied by an inability [to retaliate], a transformation [of the mind], and a persistent attachment [to the injury], resulting in a lack of effort toward the excellence of one's own virtues.
Hatred (*dveṣa*) that is devoid of internal qualities when there is no reciprocal benefit for one who has been harmed is *manyu*.
Hatred toward the excellence of others is *asūyā*.
Hatred arising from the inability to tolerate one’s own virtues is *amarṣa*.
Effort (*prayatna*), agitation (*saṃrambha*), and enthusiasm (*utsāha*) are synonyms.
It is of two kinds: that preceded by life-force (*jīvana-pūrvaka*) and that preceded by desire and aversion (*icchā-dveṣa-pūrvaka*).

Among these, that preceded by life-force is the impeller of the continuous flow of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths in one who is asleep, and at the time of awakening, it is the cause for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) reaching other sense organs.
The existence of this [effort], which is preceded by life, arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on desire.
The other [effort], however, is the cause of an activity capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, and it sustains the body;
it arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending either on desire or on aversion.
*Prayatna* (effort), *saṃrambha* (exertion), and *utsāha* (zeal) are synonyms.

It is of two kinds: that preceded by life (*jīvanapūrvaka*), and so forth. Life is the conjunction or connection of the embodied self—which has as its cause the impressions of past actions (*karma*) regarding sense objects—with the mind. Effort preceded by that [life] performs purposeful activity; therefore, he says:
In that regard, [the argument] "preceded by life" means that the activities of inhalation and exhalation in one who is asleep must have effort as their cause, because they are actions.

Furthermore, at that time, desire and aversion cannot possibly be the causes of effort; therefore, it is understood that effort preceded by mere vitality (*jīvana*) alone is what impels the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. It is not the case that effort preceded by vitality alone is the impeller of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*; rather, at the time of awakening, the internal organ’s reaching toward another sense-organ has as its cause a specific perception inferred from the contact between the internal organ and the sense-organ. This [contact] is produced by an action of the internal organ preceded by effort, because it is a contact between the internal organ and a sense-organ, just like the waking-time contact between the internal organ and a sense-organ. Thus, the [opponent's] proof for [the existence of] effort is unestablished.

The meaning is that from the conjunction of the self and the body, which depends upon the soul-force (*jīvana*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there is activity; and the conjunction of the self and the body, which depends upon the soul-force, is "life" (*jīvana*); therefore, the production of the vital breath arises from that.

The other [type of effort], however, is the cause of exertion and activity—characterized by desire and aversion and capable of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful—and it is that which sustains the body and prevents its falling when gravity is present. This sustaining effort of the body arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on desire and aversion. Among these, effort directed toward the acquisition of the means to achieve what is beneficial is preceded by desire; effort directed toward the abandonment of the means to produce suffering is preceded by aversion.
Gravity is the cause of the action of falling in water and earth;
it is imperceptible and is to be inferred from the action of falling. It is opposed to conjunction, effort, and momentum.

Furthermore, there is a rule that its non-eternality in a substance is like that of color and other qualities in atoms and their aggregates. "Gravity resides in water and earth" is the statement regarding its substratum.
"Causing falling and unification" is the definition of its function; "imperceptible" is the characterization of its nature.
The meaning is that gravity is not apprehended by any sense organ.
As for those who claim that gravity is perceptible by the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*), [they are mistaken].

For them, there would follow the undesirable consequence that weight (*gurutva*) would be perceived just as the touch of a substance situated [on the body] is perceived; for when a property perceivable by the tactile organ is perceived, it is impossible for even a single atom to produce an action distinct from itself. If it is argued that weight is perceived in what is not currently situated [on the body], because one infers the downward movement of things like stones joined to it, then how can this [weight] be perceived if it is beyond the senses? To this, he says: "It has falling as its sole cause."
Gravity, for us, is precisely that which is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) residing in the same substrate as the effect produced by the falling of a substance in a state of melting.
By this, the argument of the Prābhākara school is refuted.

They claim that because no specific downward motion (avanati-viśeṣa) is perceived as the effect of the melting of the whole, there is an absence of gravity in the composite (avayavin); however, this would entail the undesirable consequence that the composite itself could not fall.

Now, if the falling of the whole is due solely to the gravity of its parts, then the falling of those parts must also be due to the gravity of their own parts; thus, the entire causal series would be subject to that same [falling], resulting in its own destruction.

Alternatively, if gravity is postulated in the parts because their falling cannot be accounted for by the gravity residing in different substrata (i.e., their own parts), then it must likewise be postulated in the whole, since the logic is the same.

As for the fact that no additional effect is perceived from the gravity of the whole, that is because the distinction between the gravity of the parts and the gravity of the whole is too subtle to be perceived.
Just as when a large substance is being weighed, there is the perception of the effect of the weight of other subtle substances fallen within it—
this contradicts the Vaiśeṣika doctrine.

There is a great contradiction between weight and conjunction, effort, and the impression (*saṃskāra*) known as velocity (*vega*), because that which is obstructed by them does not produce its own effect.

And likewise, the obstruction of falling occurs through conjunction with a support; the obstruction of falling occurs through effort; and the obstruction of falling occurs through the velocity of the body for one who is carrying it outside during the absence of an arrow.
Furthermore, regarding the production of this [gravity] in earth and the like, there is a rule of non-eternality because it was produced previously.

Just as weightiness (*gurutva*) is eternal in atoms and so forth, so too is it in the atoms of stone and the like. And just as in a substance that is an effect of atoms, qualities such as duality and the like arise through the process of preceding qualities in the causes and perish upon the destruction of the substratum, so too does weightiness.
Fluidity is the sole cause of flowing. It subsists in three substances.
It is of two kinds: natural and incidental.
Inherent [moisture] is the specific quality of water;
occasional [moisture] is the common quality of earth and fire.
Regarding inherent [moisture], there is a rule that it is both eternal and non-eternal, just like gravity.
If it is argued that fluidity is innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) because it exists in mercury, [we reply: no.

For when atoms of water are conjoined with fire, their mutual conjunction—which is the cause for the production of a substance—is obstructed by the fluidity of those atoms; consequently, the effect, such as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, does not produce fluidity.
Furthermore, adventitious (*naimittika*) fluidity arises from the non-eternal conjunction of earth and fire.

How is it that, from the sixfold causes, fluidity arises in independent atoms? When, due to the conjunction of impermanent [fire] with the atoms—the causes of substances like dregs and the like—there is the production of an effect depending on a quality, there arise disjunctions produced by that [conjunction]; from these disjunctions, the conjunctions that initiate the substance are destroyed. Upon the cessation of the causal substance, fluidity arises in the independent atoms depending on the impermanent conjunction and other factors. Then, because the enjoyers are not separate from those [atoms], through the conjunction of the self with the atoms, an action is produced; from the conjunctions produced by that action, the causal substance is produced by the process beginning with the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). And in that [substance], at the same time as the production of color and other qualities, fluidity arises by the process of the qualities of the cause.
Fluidity (*dravatva*) is considered the cause of the action of flowing; the meaning is that fluidity is that which causes the action of flowing.
"In the three—earth, water, and fire"—this means in these three.
[The objection] "But it is of two kinds" [is raised].
The meaning of the words of the aphorism is that gravity is a single substance, yet it is of two kinds:
incidental (*naimittika*) and natural (*sāṃsiddhika*).
It is called "incidental" because its effect arises from an external cause, namely conjunction with fire (*bahiḥ-saṃyoga*).
One should consider that which is innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) as established by its very nature and independent of external conjunction.
Even though it is innate, it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) because it exists only at the final stage; whereas in earth and fire, it is occasional (*naimittika*).
It is a general quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*) because of its commonality.

Regarding the division of innate fluidity (*sāṃsiddhika-dravatva*) into eternal and non-eternal, just as gravity (*gurutva*) is eternal when inherent in an eternal substance, whereas when inherent in a non-eternal substance it is produced by the qualities of its causes and perishes through the destruction of its substratum, so too is innate fluidity. Here, an objection is raised:

If it is argued that since the six-fold quality of water is observed in substances such as hailstones when they have ascended into the sky, and since solidity is seen [there], it follows that the fluidity of water is established by its own nature; [the author] answers: "By the divine... and so forth.

All water possesses fluidity that is established by its very nature (*svabhāvasiddha*), because it is conjoined with the quality of being a substance established by its own nature; this fluidity is not something distinct [from the substance]. However, in cases such as snow or hail where fluidity does not arise in the effect, there occurs a mutual conjunction of the atoms of water (*āpya-paramāṇu*) which have been conjoined with celestial fire (*divya-tejas*); this conjunction is the initiator of the substance. Because of this, the fluidity of the atoms—which is the cause for the production of the substance (snow/hail)—is obstructed. Thus, by the conjunction with fire, the fluidity of the atoms is impeded. Furthermore, lightness (*laghutva*) is also inferred through the obstruction of fluidity by external conjunction, just as the melting of substances like snow and hail at another time allows one to infer their lightness. Water, however, is the substratum of snow, hail, and so forth, and is perceptible by the sense organ. If there is lightness in a solid substance, it is understood to be due to external conjunction, as in the case of gold and other metals. Even the melting of snow, hail, and the like is indeed a process of liquefaction.
Therefore, here too, it is precisely the external conjunction with the collection of causes for perception that is designated as the efficient cause (*nimitta*).
Having explained the substantiality (*dravyatva*) according to the Grammarians, he now explains the occasional (*naimittika*) [quality]:
the occasional is produced by the conjunction with fire following the [initial] contact.
How so? It is explained by the verse beginning with "saṃbheda" and so forth.

In the case of substances such as a jar, when action arises due to the conjunction of atoms—the causes of stones and so forth—and through successive disjunctions, the originating conjunctions of the jar are destroyed; once the substance of the jar has ceased to exist, substantiality (*dravyatva*) arises in the independent atoms through external conjunction. Immediately thereafter, when action arises in those atoms in which fluidity has been produced—due to the contact between the soul and the atoms for the sake of favoring sentient beings—then, through the successive mutual conjunctions of the atoms, a causal substance is produced in the form of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so on. At the very moment that qualities such as color arise in that effect-substance, substantiality arises from its causal substances.
The same principle applies even to the melting of snow, hailstones, and the like.
This specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) is of two kinds:
it is the cause of cohesion, flags, and so forth.
Like gravity (gurutva), it is also subject to the rule of being either non-eternal or eternal.

This specific quality (*viśe�ṣaguṇa*) is twofold, being the cause of cohesion (*saṃgraha*) and so forth. Cohesion is a particular kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*) that is the cause for the attainment of a solid mass (*piṇḍībhāva*) by soft substances such as flour and the like. Purity (*śuddhi*), which consists of the removal of impurities from an object, and the property of fluidity (*anudravatva*)—indicated by the word "and so forth" (*ādi-śabda*)—are also caused by it. Regarding both types [cohesion and fluidity], there is a rule concerning their eternity and non-eternity similar to that of gravity (*gurutva*): gravity is eternal in atoms (*paramāṇu*) and in its effects (*kārya*) it is preceded by the qualities of its causes, while it is destroyed by the destruction of its substrate and so forth; likewise, both [cohesion and fluidity] are twofold [in this respect].
Impression (*saṃskāra*) is threefold: velocity (*vega*), mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*).

Among these, velocity arises in the five corporeal substances from the conjunction of action, depending on specific causes; it is the cause of a continuous series of actions in a fixed direction. [This concludes] the definition of impression among the five qualities. Velocity is a quality that produces action; it is contrary to the non-distinction of contact with resistance up to the increase of touch, and it is produced by a prior action.

Because it is the agent of the word "cultivation" (bhāvanā), the person (puruṣa) is the cause of memory and recognition regarding what has been seen, heard, or experienced; this cognition is contrary to [the notions of] the unseen (adṛṣṭa), space (kha), and so forth.
He explains the term "padma": it is born from a cognition (pratyaya) and depends upon the cognition of the word (pada).
And it arises from the conjunction of the self with the mind (manas).
An excellence of mental impression (*saṃskārātiśaya*) arises regarding an object that has been perceived [previously],
as in the case of one who has heard the speech of a person from the southern or northern regions.

In the case of those who have studied under teachers, whose fathers are learned, or who have performed meritorious deeds, an excellence of mental impression arises from the repeated conjunction of the self with the intellect, based on subsequent cognitions that depend upon each preceding mental impression regarding that very same object.

Having fixed the mind through effort upon an unprecedented object, for one desiring to see it, there arises a cognition of intense clarity, like a flash of lightning or a sudden vision. From that very [cognition] and from the conjunction of the self with the mind, an excellence of latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced, as in the case of seeing the silver peak and lotuses at Lake Daiva-hrada.

As for elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*), however, it resides in tangible, solid substances characterized by a dense arrangement of parts and persisting over time; it restores its own substratum, which has been altered, back to its original state.
The function of *sthiti-sthāpaka* (elasticity) is observed in stationary and moving modifications—such as bows, branches, hands, bones, threads, and garments—which have been bent or coiled;
this applies to both eternal and non-eternal substances, just like gravity (*gurutva*).
Impression (*saṃskāra*), however, is of three kinds: velocity (*vega*), mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*).
Among these, velocity arises from action dependent upon a specific cause in moving substances such as animals and material objects.

In animals and material objects—namely earth, water, fire, air, and mind—action produces velocity and not elsewhere, according to its own measure; it depends upon specific causes such as pushing or striking, and is not merely a slow motion.
Because of the absence of momentum (*vega*).

It is the cause of a continuous series of actions directed toward a fixed direction. The meaning is that it is the cause of a continuum of action precisely in the same direction as the momentum was produced by the action.
Regarding "the tactile organ" (*sparśendriya*): [it is]...

Velocity is destroyed by a specific conjunction with a tangible substance (*sparśavad-dravya*), occurring when its constituent parts have reached a state of extreme density; this [destruction] is specific to itself. However, a slow velocity is destroyed by mere conjunction with a tangible substance, as in the case of a reed that has traveled a great distance and is bound by the moisture of the earth.
[The text says] "kṛcchriti"; thus, velocity is indeed gradual due to the nature of the wind.
Even in a reservoir of water situated on rugged, steep, and precipitous ground, a cause for movement arises through the force of its own momentum.
Regarding the phrase "mental cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) and so forth:
mental cultivation is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), which is a quality of the self (*ātman*).
Regarding the phrase "in regard to things seen, heard, and experienced":
it is stated that [memory] is the cause of recollection (*smṛti*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) with respect to objects seen, heard, and experienced; this is a description of its function.

Furthermore, the qualification "in regard to things seen, heard, and experienced" should be understood as the coloring (*uparāga*) by the object, since it is observed to be clearly manifest even in that case.
Regarding "knowledge":
through the knowledge that serves as the antidote, latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*) are destroyed;
and calamities such as gambling and other vices [are eliminated] because of the thorough forgetting [of them] upon awakening.
Even by intoxication, there is the destruction of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), as in the case of one who has drunk liquor due to a particular location.
Even by sufferings such as death, the mental impression perishes, because of the absence of recollection of what was experienced in another birth.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), pleasure and so forth are included.

Because one who is in a state of intense emotion or anger lacks the recollection of prior occurrences; "due to the presence of intensity" means that because of the presence of intensity, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is subsequently produced regarding the path and so forth, due to the absence of misapplication.

From a specific conjunction of the self and the mind, when the sense organs are sharp, a sharp latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—which is a quality of the self—is produced. As for the word "sharp": in the case of a Southerner who has experienced a certain thing intensely, a sharp latent impression is produced from that experience because it generates a seed capable of producing memory at a later time.
He demonstrates the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the force of practice with the words "learning, art," and so forth.

Learning (*vidyā*) consists of the mastery of sciences such as grammar; art (*śilpa*) refers to activities such as the carving of leaf-patterns; and physical exercise (*vyāyāma*) refers to practices such as breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). These [impressions] are intensified within specific mental dispositions (*sattva-viśeṣa*) that are about to arise through them.
"From the beginning," and so forth.

Since [the memory] persists for a very long time and produces a much clearer recollection, it is not the case that the initial experience itself brings about a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*), because there is no recollection of that [initial object] at first. Nor is the intermediate [experience] the cause, because of the difference between the prior and subsequent states. Therefore, through a sequence in which each successive experience—dependent on the preceding latent impressions—produces an additional latent impression of the object, there is an accumulation of impressions; from this accumulation of impressions, [recollection] arises from the final experience.
This indicator (liṅga) is now examined.

When there is a doubt as to what is being conveyed by the sentence regarding the meaning that exists [in the mind], is it the "suitable" (*tadyogya*) that is expressed, or is it the *sphoṭa*? There is disagreement regarding this doubt;
for some say that the *sphoṭa* is what conveys the meaning.
Others, however, say that the *sphoṭa* is the conveyor of meaning.
Therefore, the doubt is justified: what is it that is grasped—the *sphoṭa* as the conveyor of meaning?
For if the word were distinct from the letters, and the sentence distinct from those words, then there would be no cognition of meaning at all.

For instance, individual phonemes (*varṇa*) do not each convey a representation of meaning or a mere manifestation, because they are only capable of being understood as words; nor is it possible for them to possess accents such as the *anudātta* (unraised tone) and so forth, since a similar cognition would arise when their mechanical sounds are identical. If it is argued that this [property] exists in the aggregate (*samudāya*) which is eternally connected with its own meaning, even so, no cognition of those [individual phonemes] is experienced. And if those which are not being cognized were perceptible, there would follow the consequence of their never being cognized at all.
