For there is no establishment of the six parts of a lute-neck (*ṣaḍvaṃśa*) by means of what is not being perceived, nor any proof for things that remain unperceived.

If it is argued that "the phonemes previously perceived, flashing forth with an ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), are the causes of cognition," then [we reply]: if even this flashing forth occurs sequentially, then at the time of the ego-sense of the third phoneme, the resonance of the first phoneme would have vanished; thus, this [first] phoneme would no longer exist. Furthermore, the simultaneous production of flashing cognitions is not even to be suspected, because of the impossibility of the simultaneity of cognitions.

Now, if it is argued that first there is the perception of the first phoneme, followed by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), then the perception of the third phoneme, and by that previous impression another distinct impression is produced—thus, in this sequence, at the end, an impression having all the phonemes as its object arises and produces a single simultaneous manifestation of all the phonemes at once; then the sequence would be lost. For sequence is priority and posteriority, and that must be determined either by space or by time. Neither of these two obtains scope here, because those [phonemes] are all-pervading and eternal.

Let the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*) be governed by the process of the intellect, and let there be a sequence within a single manifestation-consciousness (*sphūrtibuddhi*). Since the measure of words and phonemes has subsided in that single consciousness, it is only the imperishable [phonemes] themselves that possess the capacity to convey meaning.

Consequently, in cases such as *khare*, *rathaḥ*, *vane*, *carma*, *madhau*, and *daurṇaḥ*, there would not even be a single unified cognition, because the objects [of these words] are not identical and because the sequence is not perceived. Yet, this difference in cognition does exist; since no other cause can be pointed out that is not sublated by its universal utility for all people, the existence of the *sphoṭa* is established.
Now, even the *sphoṭa* cannot signify an object without having a name as its qualifier, because otherwise it would follow that it would be perceived at all times.

Furthermore, its manifestation from the phonemes (*varṇas*) is impossible according to the reasoning already stated, since neither the individual nor the combined phonemes can effect such a manifestation. Therefore, the comprehension of meaning is difficult to obtain even from the *sphoṭa*.

On this point, those who know the truth speak as follows: those who follow the first [view] maintain that each individual phoneme, being independent, manifests the sphoṭa—which is its own function—in an indistinct manner; yet, by attaining an uninterrupted refinement of the object through the preceding [phonemes], they cause the sphoṭa to appear clearly at the end.

And likewise, at the end, when all distinctions between phonemes have subsided, there is experienced a single, partless, indivisible, and unitary auditory object, which is Viṣṇu, acting as the author [of the word]. For if the word were merely the phonemes, it would not be the object of a single cognition; thus, the cognition would result in being without a support, and the designation "we comprehend the meaning of the word" would not be possible. Therefore, there exists some single entity distinct from those [phonemes], from which the meaning becomes manifest.
This is because when the meaning is attained, [the phonemes] are negated.

In words such as *guṇaratnākaragataḥ*, *kāyasthakulanindakāḥ*, and *pāṣaṇḍudāyaḥ*, only the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves are perceived in their sequential order, like those moving swiftly toward Naimiṣa; there is no perception of any object distinct from the phonemes even in a dream.

For if the preceding [cognition] were truly perceived in the form of the utterance of phonemes, then at its conclusion, the subsequent cognition would lead to the realization of the falsity of that prior utterance—just as one whose visual faculty is affected by red perceives a mother-of-pearl shell as silver. Yet, there is no such realization that "this is not a phoneme, but rather the *sphoṭa*."

Furthermore, this cognition which is inconsistent regarding a single object does not establish another [permanent] Lord; rather, it relies solely upon immediate experience. When people say, "We understand the meaning from the word," they employ such language by taking as their basis the sequential appearance of the phonemes. Nor can that [word] which is not perceived individually be determined through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), due to the absence of any such method.

If it is argued that the sphoṭa is established because its existence is otherwise inexplicable (anyathānupapatti) in the absence of the cognition of meaning, we ask: have you established that the sphoṭa is the cause of the manifestation of meaning while it is itself unperceived, or while it is perceived? If it were the cause while being unperceived, then the light of a firefly would have to be denied [as a cause for illumination]. As for the case of it being perceived, it has already been stated that such a thing does not exist. Furthermore, the cognition of meaning merely supports the perception of the actual existence of the phonemes themselves; therefore, let some supporting factor be relied upon for the communication of meaning that follows the phonemes, such as the eyes and other senses. However, it is not logical to postulate something that is not perceived, any more than one would postulate the fragrance of a flower in the sky.
Nor is this external phoneme-series the nature of the cognition itself when it functions as the signifier, whether there be a difference in sequence or an intervention [by other elements].

For those [phonemes] in a reversed order, or those situated in different places and times due to a difference in sequence, are not capable of being the cause based on the experience of that specific sequence. Indeed, the potencies of entities are differentiated according to their effects; their potencies are described exactly as their effects are observed from them.
Thus do the wise teach.
However many phonemes there are, of whatever kind they may be, and for the purpose of conveying which meaning, their conjunction with wisdom is the very means by which that [meaning] is understood.
Thus, because phonemes (varṇas) are all identical and eternal, their sequential existence [is established].
For this very reason, the distinction [between words] such as *nadī* and *dīna* arises from the difference in sequence.

There is no sequence among the phonemes; it would follow that sequence is merely non-sequence, since for those phonemes when uttered by one who is teaching, a priority and posteriority produced by space and time is possible. As for the statement that "neither individually nor collectively do they possess the capacity to produce verbal cognition," that too does not reflect an examination of the opponent's position. Even though the phonemes themselves are non-durable, the mental impressions (*saṃskāras*) arising from the cognitions of them—which are momentary—bring about the cognition of the word-meaning.

Alternatively, the letters are perceived through the successive cognitions refined by preceding impressions (*saṃskāra*). This has been established in the case of duality (*dvitva*), just as the impressions produced by a previous perception generate a recollection upon contact. Now, you might think that it is illogical for the letters to produce a cognition of meaning through impressions; for an impression, when it brings about a clear manifestation, manifests only that object which was its basis, and not some other effect. As Maṇḍana, a knower of the *sphoṭa*, said: "An impression indeed manifests that which was previously perceived, even if it was not [then] fully manifested."
It is conceived that it produces its fruit in that very same [moment], even though [the action] has passed away and ceased.
Thus it must first be urged:

since, in accordance with the comprehension of word-meanings, mental impressions (*saṃskāras*)—which are objects [of cognition] produced by letters when perceiving inferable things—are deposited internally as being distinct from the impressions that cause memory, because such effects are indeed apprehended; and whether these impressions consist of the object itself or have the nature of a mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), nevertheless their dependence on the influence of the presentation of the object is established, because they arise through that medium.

For those who postulate the *sphoṭa*, they must also postulate that it possesses the capacity to manifest [the word], which results in a complexity of postulation (*kalpanā-gaurava*). However, in the case of postulating the mere capacity of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of the word, there is simplicity (*lāghava*); therefore, this alone is appropriate to postulate.
As it is stated in the *Nyāyavārttika*:
"Even though the status of the mental impression as the cause of memory is established..."
Its capacity is not obstructed even in other tasks.
Thus, since the cognition of meaning is possible from the phonemes themselves by means of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), the postulation of *sphoṭa* is incorrect.
[The author] demonstrates the mental impression in the cases of respect and intensity.

By the words "by the first," and so forth: zeal consists of initial exertion, capacity, and freedom from aversion; it desires what is seen. Just as there is lack of fortitude regarding the touch of each object, there arises a connection with latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) through contact with those things that are not useless, because of the endurance of the context of their state; for even when a long time has elapsed, that [impression] is not cut off. This is the illustration.
As in the case of "Devahūda" and so forth:

at Devahūda, on the full moon day of the month of Caitra conjoined with the *Citrā* nakṣatra, silver and lapis-lazuli lotuses are seen at midnight. For those companions of Bālī who stood there on that lunar day with a desire to see them—even though they were not close enough to hear a verbal instruction—they fixed their minds with the utmost effort and remained there; consequently, from seeing those lotuses for even a moment, an extremely intense latent impression (*saṃskāra*) was produced, which serves as the cause for a clear recollection even at a later time.
The *sthitisthāpaka* (elasticity) is explained as follows:
*Sthitisthāpaka*, however, is distinct [from momentum].

The word "grass" (*tṛṇa*) is used to express the specific quality of *sthitisthāpaka* by virtue of its own firm restoration from an extremely firm displacement, whereas [momentum] arises from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, those specific sounds produced by the force of striking are dense; when all desired objects are perceived, the *sthitisthāpaka* (elasticity) present therein causes its own substratum—which had been altered from its state, such as being bent—to be restored to its original condition, making it function as it did before.
To those who, due to the non-perception of [the cause], maintain that *sthitisthāpaka* does not exist, he demonstrates its existence through its effects in various ways, saying:
"The [sounds] are turned away and experienced," and so forth.

Those who were asleep and bent over with their own bodies have returned to their former state; those who were sleeping and prostrate on the ground have likewise recovered. In these cases, the effect of *sthiti-sthāpaka* (elasticity) is observed.

When a bow, a branch, or similar object is bent and then released, that which—due to previously mentioned causes such as a tiger—is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) residing in the same substrate as the action (*karman*), is called *sthiti-sthāpaka*, because it is established through its designation as a type of *saṃskāra* (latent impression).

Others, however, considering the qualification "moistened by earth" (*bhūmyadhalipta*) to be excessive—interpreting it as "those trees and the like which are moistened by the earth"—explain that it refers to those [trees] such as the *vṛṣa* and others that are rooted in the ground.
The determination of its permanence or impermanence is like that of gravity (*gurutva*).
Just as gravity is permanent in atoms and impermanent in effects, being preceded by the qualities of its causes, so too is elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*). This is the meaning.

Dharma is a quality of the person (*puruṣaguṇa*). It is the agent; it is the cause of action and the cause of liberation. It is contrary to the knowledge of the final pleasure of women. It arises from the conjunction of the person and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) when that conjunction is not impure and is born of intention. Its specific characteristics for those belonging to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*) consist of particular duties, wealth, and emblems.

Its means of accomplishment, as prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, are substances, qualities, and actions, which exist in the relationship of general and particular for those belonging to the castes and stages of life.

In this regard, the common [virtues] for all are faith, non-violence, benevolence toward living beings, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, freedom from guile, avoidance of anger, ritual bathing, purity, accumulation of necessary materials, devotion to a specific deity, supreme absorption, and vigilance. For the Brāhmaṇa, these are his stations; his specific duties are study, giving, and [receiving] gifts; his specific occupations are receiving gifts, teaching, and officiating at sacrifices; and his sacraments are those prescribed for him. For the Kṣatriya, they are the proper protection of subjects, the restraint of the wicked, and not retreating in battle; his sacraments are those prescribed for him.
For the Vaiśya, [the duties] are buying and selling, agriculture, and cattle-rearing; his own purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are as prescribed.
For the Śūdra, [the duty is] dependence on the preceding classes and performing rites without mantras.

As for those belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*), the student (*brahmacārin*) dwelling in the teacher’s family has the following duties ordained by his own scripture: service to the teacher, tending the sacred fires, and wandering for alms; he must avoid honey, meat, sleeping during the day, applying unguents, and other such things censured by the righteous.
And excluding meditation (*jñāna*) and the like:

for a householder who has completed his study of the *Vicarashataka* and whose debts have been paid, there is the performance of the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajñas*)—to the *ṛṣis*, ancestors, humans, gods, and *brahman*—as well as the morning and evening burnt offerings (*agnihotra*), according to the rule of the single fire (*ekāgni*). This applies to the constant performance of the *pākayajña* rites, the *haviryajña* rites such as the *anvaṣṭakya* and others, and the *somayajña* rites such as the *agniṣṭoma*. During the intervals between these seasons, he should observe celibacy and procreate offspring.

For the student (*brahmacārin*) or the householder (*gṛhastha*), there is dwelling in the forest after having previously established the sacred fires, as well as the wearing of bark garments, skins, and the keeping of medicinal herbs, along with the maintenance of the beard, nails, and body hair.
For the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), there is the eating of forest-grown food and the remnants of hospitality.

For the wandering mendicant (*pravrajita*), who is one of these three [stages] and has gone forth, having granted perpetual fearlessness to all beings and renounced his own ritual duties, there is the cultivation of yoga through the contemplation of the six categories, remaining vigilant in the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*).
When the purpose is perceived, those means of accomplishment and the clarity of disposition are required; from the conjunction of the self and the mind, dharma arises.
Dharma is [attained] by men.
That which is Dharma is for the benefit of man; it does not consist in the engagement of the senses with their objects through successive stages.
Sacrifice is the cause for obtaining what is dear and beneficial.

"Priya" (the pleasant), "sukha" (happiness), and "hita" (the beneficial) are said to be the means of happiness; it should be explained that *dharma* is that which is the cause of these very things—namely, the pleasant and so forth—which is one among the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self (*ātman*), and which bestows non-affliction (*akleṣṭadatva*). It should not be explained as: "Dharma is that sacrifice (*kratu*) alone which is the cause of the pleasant and so forth."
Just as for a man, by the power of the body protected by his ancestors,
there is a certain state resulting from what has been done, so too, through the force of instruction, even another person performs it when it is made with cow-dung cakes by one desiring a sacrifice;

because the connection between the sacrifice and its fruit is observed in such scriptural statements as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," they apply, by means of logical connection (*yoga*), the status of being a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatva*) to rituals, [interpreting them] as "one should produce heaven" through those actions.

However, that which connects a person with [a result] is *dharma*; thus, only the sacrifice and other means of achieving it are *dharma*, and not a quality of the person. For instance, they call one who performs a sacrifice "righteous" (*dhārmika*).
This is incorrect, because since an action performed at one time must necessarily yield its fruit at another time, [the connection between the act and the result requires an intermediate principle].
Regarding the removal of debt:

momentary action, having ceased its own activity which occurs at a later time, produces a cause that brings about the effect; yet the causal status of sacrifices and the like would be both illogical and untenable [if it were otherwise]. Therefore, by me, some capacity of the action (*karma-sāmarthya*) is postulated—which persists until the state of the production of the fruit—and by means of which the actions, through the bestowal of the fruit, are brought to completion.
And because this [apūrva] falls within the scope of other means of knowledge, it is designated as "difficult to understand," as it has been said:
"An action enjoined for a result that occurs after a long time cannot be accomplished by any other means;
thus, even the apūrva is postulated."
[The opponent] replies: "It is consumed. [We respond:

No, because the capacity of an action does not persist in the action once it has ceased. For when that which possesses the power (the agent) has perished, it is impossible for the capacity to remain without a substratum.
Furthermore, at that time, the fruit—such as heaven—is yet to come; thus, the capacity cannot be its substratum.
If heaven were to occur immediately after your city, then the purposelessness of the Vedic injunctions (*ṛṣu-vidhāna*) regarding its attainment would be unavoidable.

If it is argued that there is no experience [of heaven] due to the absence of a specific body, sense organs, and so forth, then it must be admitted that at that time heaven has not yet arisen; for even during a single moment, a portion of suffering exists which is incompatible with heaven, and thus it must be acknowledged as such.
Therefore, heaven arises in a location other than the place where the fruit [is currently being experienced].

Furthermore, it is not possible for a result that accrues to the self to arise from an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) inhering in space and so forth. Moreover, in the nature of things, an effect cannot occur without a cause; therefore, its production and persistence must follow a sequence inherent in the self alone. Thus, the capacity for that action would exist [in the self], because otherwise, a capacity existing in one thing could not produce an effect in another due to the lack of inherence. If it is argued that the power of one thing may be admitted to inhere in another, since that [power] is to be inferred from its effect—then it has already been stated [in response].
For power is indeed to be inferred from its effects;
it is perceived as residing either in its own substratum or in another substratum.
This is incorrect.
Since it is logically untenable for that mere capacity to produce an effect once the possessor of the capacity has perished, this [objection] is also refuted thereby.

As it was stated by Maṇḍana in the *Vidhiviveka*: "Because that [efficacy] is deposited [in the substrate], its power [resides there]; since the sacrifice is not deposited in the *apūrva*, the power of the sacrifice would reside in the *apūrva* as its effect. For, since the fruit does not arise from the action [once completed], and because the action perishes immediately after its performance, it is logical that the fruit arises solely from the *apūrva*, which remains as the sustainer of the power. Thus, the three [means of knowledge] are verbal.
Furthermore, the operation of the cause—such as the sacrifice—is through the mediation of the production of the *apūrva*, and not directly, even though this is not contradicted by the evidence.
All this is thus correct.

Regarding the term "this apūrva": even that which is the locus of dharma in sacrifices and the like is [defined] by its being the vehicle for the apūrva, and it involves the rejection of the attribution of qualities as dharma.
However, according to the Prātiśākhya, there is the application of what was proclaimed by oneself.

For in the chapter on *svaprokṣa* (self-sprinkling), the Buddhist principle of *jyotirgupta* [is established] because there is constant praise through the *arthavāda* of the *Prātiśākhya*, and because elsewhere, in the case of grasping the *prauna*, the intellect (*buddhi*) is employed; since there would be a failure of the sentence (*vākya*) in its absence, the *svaprokta* is based upon *prauna*.

Since its application in the *Prātiśākhya* occurs according to its specific definition, it is understood from the *Prātiśākhya* teachers that it arises as such; therefore, one must resort to the assumption of a denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) for the *samprayā*.

In this way, the word *dharma* is also used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇayā*) to denote its accomplishment. Since the cognition "he looks" arises from the denotation of the suffix *-ika* alone, there is no need to postulate a dual denotative power. This is the procedure for the three [suffixes].
That which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) is not grasped by ordinary sense organs; thus, *dharma* is beyond the senses. It is an object of supersensuous direct perception (*anubhava-vijñāna*).

If destruction were caused by a factor (dharma), it would be possible for it to arise at a specific moment; however, destruction cannot be causeless. Furthermore, if destruction were due to something else—as in the case of a flash of lightning—it would follow that the object would necessarily persist until the time of its destruction, as long as no other cause for its cessation exists. Moreover, the fruit of a phenomenon (dharma) is to be experienced over many moments, like a flash of lightning; if its destruction followed immediately after the first moment of experience, there would be no production of the fruit in subsequent moments. And yet, there can be no total annihilation of a single entity.
Therefore, destruction is possible; thus, there remains a substance.
By means of ninety-six qualities, dharma perishes.
As for those who assert that dharma is eternal, for them the attainment [of results] is untenable, because there would be no change in its nature.
[It is] by means of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of the person (*puruṣa*).
Because it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self (*ātman*), like pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth.
[The term] "pure" (*viśuddha*)...
Even when pure, it is devoid of sound and the hollow of the bell;
from that specific kalpa, the vowels and so forth are born;
it possesses the function of destruction.
Killing and striking are not objects of knowledge for them.
For students (*brahmacārins*), forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*), and householders (*gṛhasthas*), there is no darkness of ignorance.
Their duty is that which has been specifically enjoined; having approached their respective teachers, they are distinguished by the injunctions prescribed in the scriptures—this is the meaning.
Regarding the supersensuous *dharma*, the scriptures (*śāstra*) and so forth are the means by which it is to be understood;
these are its causes.

It is not apprehended through the grasping of a specific latent disposition (*anuśaya*), nor is it grasped by means of inferential marks (*liṅga*). Thus, the Veda is the scripture that accords with the revealed truth (*sphuṭi*). The duties (*dharma*) prescribed and established for the various classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśramin*) exist without distinction; they are the duties whose qualities and actions are perceived, and they constitute the wealth of all.
For you and for all those belonging to the social classes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*), the scriptures describe the duties to be performed as the means for achieving *dharma*.
Faith in these, mental clarity regarding *dharma*, non-violence toward living beings, and a disposition free from malice— these are the characteristics [of *dharma*].
For one who has realized non-malice (*anabhidroha*), the cessation of malice does not constitute unrighteousness (*adharma*), nor does it give rise to righteousness (*dharma*).
However, non-malice that is practiced with effort would indeed be a means to righteousness because it is prescribed [by the scriptures].
The welfare of beings is the favoring of living creatures; truthful speech is speaking in accordance with reality.

Non-stealing consists of not taking the property of others without it being offered and without asking; it is forbearance and the absence of the volitional intention to take what belongs to another, and not merely the physical abstention from seizing another's property. Regarding celibacy, it is the total avoidance of women as objects of passion;
it is the absence of pride and the absence of volitional intention.

Because actions performed with a mind purified by the absence of malice serve as the means for attaining Dharma, one should not harbor malice. The avoidance of anger is the total renunciation of anger;
for anger is essentially nothing but a form of mental resolve.
*Abhiṣecana* means bathing.

*Śucidṛṣṭa* refers to the prescribed use of pure substances such as sesame seeds and so forth, along with *kuśa* grass and leaves, as a divine means for accomplishing dharma. The meaning is devotion to the deities intended for practice according to the ritual procedures of the Tāntrika tradition.
Fasting (*upavāsa*) is the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to abstain from eating on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and other such occasions.
Primacy (*agramāda*) is the cause for the inevitable performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.
All these are equal means for the accomplishment of dharma.
The performance of sacrifices and oblations according to one's desire;
study, which is the recitation of the Vedas;
and giving, which is the specific mental resolve to transfer one's own property to another.

Giving indeed exists even for pure substances; therefore, that giving which occurs in sacrifices and the like is declared to be a means of accomplishing *dharma* through the ritual procedures of shrines and so forth.
It sets forth the specific practices of a Brahmin as means of accomplishing *dharma*:
receiving gifts, causing others to give, and accepting what is offered.
Receiving gifts (*pratigraha*) is the acceptance of distinguished objects;
teaching (*adhyāpana*) is well known;
officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) is the honey of the *Anvīkṣikī*.
These are the means for accomplishing the dharma of a Brāhmaṇa; among these, the investigation [of the Veda] is the application of wealth acquired through the three types of seeking toward dharma.

The four [types of] learning prescribed by one's own branch of the Veda constitute the means for accomplishing the dharma of a Brāhmaṇa by way of producing proficiency through the performance of Vedic rites.
As for the Kṣatriya, his specific means for accomplishing dharma are as follows.

Forgiveness consists in the protection of subjects and the preservation of subjects who are established in righteousness; lack of forgiveness is the punishment of the wicked according to the scriptures. In battle, it is the non-retreat from combat, the attainment of victory, and being intent on not fleeing even at the cost of one's life.
The cultivation of one's own field;
for a Vaiśya, agriculture, trade, and the tending of cattle;
and buying is the taking of goods from another after giving a price.
Taking a price and giving one's own goods to another is trade (*vikraya*).
Agriculture consists of sowing and planting seeds in tilled soil, as well as the tending of cattle—the protection of cows, goats, sheep, and so forth.
These are the means for fulfilling the duty of a Vaiśya.
In that regard, because wealth acquired through reflection and seeking is a constituent of dharma,

for a Śūdra, service to the preceding castes— such as obedience and so forth— is the means for accomplishing dharma; however, for those who possess self-mastery, [independence] is said to be the means for accomplishing dharma.

"Students living in the teacher's household" refers to those who, having been initiated (*upanīta*), study the Veda along with its auxiliary branches (*sāṅga*) and secret doctrines (*sarahasya*). For such a student who is habitually residing in the teacher's family or house, there are duties prescribed by the scriptures specifically for students, beginning with the word *svadhā*.

These include service to the teacher (*guruśuśrūṣā*), which is the attendance upon the teacher; as well as reverence toward the sacred fire (*agninamaskṛtya*) and purity (*śauca*). These are considered the extraction of the essential duties for them.

The practice of the causes of *sthāna*, *guhūṣu*, *gumpha*, *śeṣa*, and *agrya* is indeed the conduct of the beautiful (*kamanīyācaraṇa*). The distinction is that daily practice regarding these [causes] is the conduct of the golden [nature], while the practice of the other [causes] such as *kuñcana* and *atyanjana* is the conduct of the forest-dweller (*vanādin*). This explains the means for accomplishing the dharma of the householder.
Regarding the phrase "consisting of the essence of knowledge" (*vidyātattvātmaka*):

he who, for the purpose of studying the Vedas, has completed his studies under a teacher and, having transcended that [stage], desires to know the subject matter of the Vedas—that is the *vidyābrahmacārī*. For him, once he has become a householder by taking a wife, there is the performance of the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*)—to the gods, ancestors, humans, beings, and Brahman—at both evening and morning, as undertaken by the *śālīna* and *yāyāvara* types of householders.

The amount of grain sufficient for the maintenance of a household, whether taken as a single measure (kumpīpāka) or enough to sustain one for a day—one who accepts such a quantity, whether it is brought to him spontaneously or given out of faith, his acceptance of this constitutes the *śālīna* mode of life (*vṛtti*). Taking a single measure from another without asking, or what is subtle or obtained by going forth (*niṣkāmya*), is the *yāyāvara* mode of life. Having acquired wealth through these means, the performance of the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*) either in the morning or in the afternoon is the means for fulfilling the duty of a householder.
The offering of oblations at the dwelling place (*pratiśraye balipradāna*) is the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*).
The honoring of guests is the sacrifice to humans;
the burnt offering (homa) is the sacrifice to the gods; the ancestral rite (śrāddha) is the sacrifice to the ancestors.

The *brahmayajña* is the recitation of the Vedas. According to the rule "by means of this [Veda], there is the support of the five classes of *pākayajñas*," it is fourfold. The author of the *Śrībhāṣya* states that at the time of marriage, one should accept a learned man; by him, when capacity exists, there is the fourfold performance of the *pākayajña-saṃsthās*—that is, the specific *pākayajñas* such as the *ahṛta*, *pravargya*, *iṣṭi*, *aṣṭakā*, *graha*, and so forth—which are obligatory and intended for self-purification.
Regarding the phrase "of the *kumbhī-ādheya* and so forth":
the wealth for the sake of Dharma is fourfold.
By the term *kumbhī-ādheya*, there is intended that which will be described as eightfold, pertaining to the stationing of others in an improper manner. This [eightfold wealth] is what is performed.
By the term *haviryajñasaṃsthā*, the specific types of *haviryajña* sacrifices—such as the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*, the *Cāturmāsya*, the *Āgrayaṇa*, and so forth—are described.

By the phrase "the Agnihotra and others," the specific types of *somayajña* sacrifices—the *Agnihotra*, *Iṣṭi*, *Agniṣṭoma*, *Aptoryāma*, *Paurṇamāsa*, *Iṣṭiyāga*, *Goṣṭoma*, *Ukthya*, *Atirātra*, and *Agniṣṭoma*—are designated by the term *somasaṃsthā*.
[The phrase] "in other *kratus*" refers to...

At a time other than that prescribed by the injunctions for ritual action (*kratu*), the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and the observance of vows, as well as the avoidance of women and poison, are means for attaining *dharma*.
Furthermore, the production of a *caṇḍāla* [through forbidden union] is a means for attaining *dharma*, because of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "Through a son, one conquers the worlds.
He now explains the means for attaining *dharma* for one who dwells in the forest (*vanastha*).
"Whether one is a student (*brahmacārin*) or a householder (*gṛhastha*).

Because of the scriptural injunction, "On whatever day faith arises in a person, on that very day he should go forth into the forest," when faith arises, the forest-dwelling belongs either to the student or to the householder. For him, being peaceful, humble, and modest, wearing bark garments and skins, having undergone initiation, with shaven head or matted hair, his dwelling is the forest; his food consists of wild fruits and roots, as well as the remnants of the sacrificial oblation (*huta-śeṣa*) and the remnants of the offerings to guests (*atithi-śeṣa*), which constitute the means for achieving dharma.

He who, having extracted the prosperity pertaining to Prajāpati and given it as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) among the years, having deposited the fire within himself, and having cast it forward onto the path, should then cast it away—for him there is no burnt offering (*homa*), nor for him the acceptance of what has not been cast away. But he who, though possessing much or little, is concealed by the power of the sacrifice to the gods (*havyahāni*), for him the maintenance of the lineage, the performance of the *śrāddha*, and the feeding of guests are the means of accomplishing Dharma. This is that self-restraint which the ascetic practices.

Regarding the phrase "as it is not prescribed" (*yathānāmiti*): for one who has no fixed rule even regarding this non-acceptance [of worldly ties], when faith arises—whether he becomes an ascetic (*yati*) in the stages of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), a householder (*gṛhastha*), or a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*)—it is with this intention that it is said, "of any one of the systems of logic" (*nyāyānām anyatamasya*).

One whose strength is faith, whose strength is knowledge, and whose strength is the sacred word, having given all this away at the proper time, and having taken up the fourfold vow (*caturhotṛkalpa*) thinking, "I must never harm living beings," and having gradually renounced and abandoned even those optional rites (*kāmya*), remaining steadfast in the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) such as non-violence and the rest—these [non-violence and so on] are the *yamas*.
As the Blessed Patañjali said:
"Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the *yamas*.
Austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the *niyamas*."
And as the Blessed Lord Yama said:

"Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (niyamas). However, the author of the Nyāyamālā states that the observances are the determination of the means for accomplishing dharma based on proximate causes.
For one who is vigilant regarding these [six categories], there is constant vigilance.

By means of the non-confusion of the six categories, for one who casts in the practice of dharma— which consists of the taking up and giving up corresponding to the bestowal of a specific forbearance capable of producing knowledge consisting of the realization of the true nature of the six categories—
it is said how these accomplish dharma.
And [it is] "defiled" (duṣṭam).

Defiled means that when these means are performed without intending them for the sake of merit or compassion toward unseen things (adṛṣṭa), those means arise from the conjunction of the self and the mind, depending upon the predominance of the state [of the action] and the purity of intention.

For one who is repeatedly struck by sufferings for every object, who through investigation into reality has become detached from sense-objects that invariably bestow only suffering, and who perceives within himself a desire for that which opposes suffering—since no other means of abandonment exists apart from the Self—he, having heard this, renounces all actions performed out of desire and practices forbearance (*kṣamā*). For him, who has abandoned the vehicle of the self that is not purified by truth, and who has refined his own being through restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), Dharma arises from the cultivation of forbearance and the discernment [of the Self].

Therefore, self-restraint (*yama*) is excellent; beyond that, forbearance (*kṣamā*) is more excellent; and superior even to that, it is most excellent and supreme. One who possesses forbearance eventually wanders among the virtuous through specific acts of forbearance.

That which cannot be accomplished by visible means is indeed seen [to be achieved] by one who contemplates the objects of the senses without attachment; for one whose mind has become one-pointed, there will be an entry into the causes of purity regarding the qualities of sense-objects, which leads to the proclamation of the concealment of unrighteousness (*adharmanihnavāda*).
And it has been said that one who possesses the yoga of the self through the attainment of what is to be attained, even while moving at will within the Lord, does not perceive even a king passing by.
And so says the venerable Patañjali:
"Its cessation [of mental fluctuations] occurs through practice and dispassion."
When concentration has thus matured, a discernment that brings about mastery over the nature of the self arises.
As the followers of Kapila have said:
"From the practice of the principles [of reality], there arises the complete realization: 'I am not, nothing is mine, I do not exist.'"
Knowledge arises that is exclusively pure, being free from error and the like.

Thus, for this reason, the ascetic who seeks self-knowledge practices the science of Yoga. Knowledge is the fruit of the means for attaining the desired goal; and since the true nature of the Self is attained even through the knowledge of the Self heard from scripture, one might ask: "What is the use of examining it through the practice of meditation? To this, we say: No.

Because it is impossible for that which is beyond perception to possess the capacity to produce direct perception, the self (*ātman*) is, by its very nature, neither an agent nor an enjoyer, but rather entirely indifferent. Likewise, the notion of agency and enjoyment—expressed as "I" and "mine"—is a false attribution produced by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the body, senses, mind, and so forth; this is the intended meaning.

As for that which has been said: attachment toward things experienced as favorable and aversion toward those that are unfavorable; from these two arise engagement and withdrawal, from which follow merit and demerit, and from those, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
As it has been stated by the Vaiyāsikas:
"Indeed, when the Supreme Brahman perceives a distinction between self and other within the Self, [transmigration begins]."
From the conjunction of these two, all states of being are produced.

The continuous stream [of existence], conditioned by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), has been suppressed by all [schools] such as the Sāṅkhya and Buddhists; this very notion of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is a [mere] mental construct. However, the knowledge of the reality of the Self derived from the Vedas (*śrauta*) is most excellent, yet it lacks corroboration through perception and is indirect (*parokṣa*). Furthermore, there is no greater calamity than the state of transgression (*pratyavāya*); for that which exists indirectly cannot be prevented by the absence of [direct] experience. Indeed, even with effort, in the absence of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the bitterness produced by a defective sense organ does not cease, nor does the experience of suffering resulting from thirst [disappear] merely because the sweetness of molasses is [only] indirect.

Therefore, concentration (samādhi) is undertaken for the sake of direct perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*). When that concentration has brought about the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkṛti*), and the true nature of the self (*ātmatattva*)—which is distinct from being an agent or an enjoyer—has become manifest, then, because of the opposition between knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) regarding the same object, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and possessiveness (*mamakāra*) no longer touches the self.
Thus is the illustration according to the Sāṃkhya view:
"By that [knowledge], when the power of the name and form has ceased its productive activity, there is a withdrawal from the nature of existence."
The Puruṣa, established in its own state, observes Prakṛti like a spectator.

By means of that true knowledge being present, she [Prakṛti] has ceased her procreation—that is, her capacity to generate experience has ceased. Having understood through the authority of the scriptures that liberation consists in the cessation of the impulse toward worldly enjoyment, when there is the withdrawal of the existent form [of Prakṛti], the Puruṣa remains established in his own nature; the meaning is that he beholds, being independent, free from the influence of *rajas* and *tamas*, and unmixed with the intellect (*buddhi*).

Or rather, even if the latent impression for liberation is not intense, yet the teacher of those who possess true knowledge from beginning to middle is such that, by this very means, one becomes free from the pairs of opposites; for the awakening to reality is indeed the supreme strength of the intellects.
Adharma is also a quality of the self.
It is the cause of agency, disadvantage, and sin; it is supersensible and is opposed to the final consciousness of pain.

Its means of accomplishment, as prohibited in the scripture and contrary to the means of accomplishing dharma, are violence, theft, robbery, and so forth, as well as the non-performance of prescribed duties and negligence. Due to these defects, and depending upon the conjunction of the self and the mind, adharma arises.
"Unrighteousness" (adharma) is a quality of the self;
not only dharma, but adharma as well, is a quality of the self.
"Kanūri" means so.
That which is devoid of desire is a means to suffering; transgression is suffering, and unrighteousness (*adharma*) is the cause of those two.
"The thorough cognition of the final suffering":
it is the thorough cognition of the final suffering, and by means of that, its destruction [is achieved].
However, its means of accomplishment are not those prohibited in the scriptures, such as violence, theft, and robbery, which are the opposites of the means for achieving dharma.
Violence is the desire for the misfortune of others;
untruth is false speech.
Theft is the taking of another's property not in accordance with the scriptures.
Renunciation and the like are the opposites of the means for achieving dharma—those acts which are prohibited by the scriptures and yet are not themselves means for achieving adharma.
Non-performance of what is enjoined is the failure to perform that which has been prescribed as a necessary duty.
Heedlessness (*pramāda*) is a lack of application that is not preceded by conscious intent;
it also refers to that which is observed to be a means for unrighteousness (*adharma*).
It prevents the arising of unrighteousness even from [ordinary] efforts.
And these [are the causes].
Where there is the performance of unrighteous means for the sake of fulfilling desires, there the corrupt intention (*abhisandhi*) is the cause of unrighteousness;
however, when it is done without desire, negligence (*pramāda*) is its cause.

For the ignorant person possessed of passion and hatred, from a preponderant dharma mixed with a small amount of adharma, there arises a connection with the worlds of Brahmā, Indra, Prajāpati, the ancestors, and humans, through the experience of the most intense pleasures of the objects of the senses and so forth.

Likewise, from a preponderant adharma mixed with a small amount of dharma, there arises a connection with the states of hungry ghosts and animals, through the experience of the most intense suffering of the objects of the senses and so forth; thus, in this group of eight and six [worlds] characterized by the mixture of dharma and adharma, there is a dual connection.
Thus, due to the characteristic of active engagement associated with the phenomena of grasping, there occurs again and again the bondage of rebirth among gods, humans, animals, and denizens of hell.
The scripture speaks with the intention of suppressing unrighteousness,
beginning with the words "of the ignorant," and so forth.

The agent who, though in the ultimate sense subject to the affliction of suffering, conceives of himself as a hearer or a non-hearer, and conceives of external and internal objects—which are actually instruments of suffering—as means to happiness; and who, being possessed by the thirst for his own enjoyment, becomes attached to an object satisfied as a means to happiness and becomes averse to it when it is tainted—such a person, through the force of merit (dharma) performed for the sake of rebirth, whether as a human, a preta, or a gandharva, enters into a connection with subsequent actions that correspond to his nature and are adorned by excellence, which serve as causes for superior fruits. Even among those such as Brahmā, Indra, or Āditya, there exists the experience of suffering.

Furthermore, there is no experience of suffering arising from unrighteousness (*adharma*), nor is there any cause for suffering arising from unrighteousness; therefore, it has been stated that even a small amount of righteousness is beneficial.

To demonstrate that for one whose righteousness is preeminent, the body and other factors become preeminent; for one whose righteousness is more preeminent, they become more preeminent; and for one whose righteousness is most preeminent, they become most preeminent—it was said, "conforming to their substratum" (*āśrayānurūpaiḥ*).
The word *kṣudra* (small) is to be connected with each of the items beginning with the body.
It is more elevated than the substance because of its application.

Likewise, from preeminent merit (*dharma*), there occurs a conjunction with bodies and so forth as Indras in the abodes of the *preta* and animal births; thus, in the state of being a *preta* and so on, it exists in accordance with the disposition of the being. Therefore, it has been said that even a small amount of merit is effective.
He concludes:
"Just as this," so it is said.

But for one who has acted with prior knowledge, the result is the exhaustion of the remaining karma; for one born into a twice-born family, desiring to know the means for the ripening of suffering, having attained the knowledge of reality through the six steps arising from contact with a teacher and a peer, and being dispassionate due to the cessation of ignorance, there occurs the destruction of passion and hatred. Through that victory, by means of successive stages of yoga equal to those above, and through the exhaustion of previously accumulated demerit by experience, merit alone remains. When the body is discarded, and the senses such as hearing are withdrawn along with their respective objects, that absolute merit ceases after producing the happiness born of the vision of the ultimate truth.

Then, due to that cessation, for the self which is rendered seedless, there is the cessation of the body and so forth; because it never again falls back into a body, liberation is defined as the state whose nature is the non-experience of suffering.

Having thus established that cyclic existence arises from phenomena (*dharma*), he now establishes both [the means and the result] through the passage beginning with "preceded by knowledge" (*jñānapūrvaka*). One for whom the knowledge has arisen that all objects—whether external or internal, pertaining to heaven or liberation, and whether serving as instruments of pleasure or pain—are essentially means to suffering, is one who possesses "dispassion toward seen and heard-of objects. Such a person, being free from desire for fruits, performs prescribed actions that are to be done and are conducive to the goal, by way of engaging in the means of practice without expectation of reward. This is what is meant by "illuminated" (*prabhāsūri*).

Therefore, from action performed preceded by knowledge, one’s birth occurs in a pure family; for one who is not of slender means, faith does not arise; nor does inquiry come to pass for one lacking material resources; nor does the knowledge of reality accrue to one who lacks inquiry; and for one who is not liberated from that [lack of knowledge], there is no attainment of liberation.

Therefore, because it bears fruit in accordance with the dharma conducive to liberation, action results in birth in a pure family. For one born in a pure family who is daily assailed by sufferings, a desire for inquiry (*jijñāsā*) arises for the sake of liberation from suffering, thinking, "Even though this [inquiry] has been undertaken by me, may there be an end to my suffering. Thus, having become one whose inquiry is well-born, he approaches a teacher. And from the teacher's instruction regarding the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), the knowledge of the reality (*tattvajñāna*) of pleasure arises.
Following that, through the sequence of tranquility (*praśama*), self-restraint (*damana*), meditation (*nididhyāsana*), and so forth, it becomes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For one in whom the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) has arisen, there is the cessation of ignorance (*ajñāna*) and the cessation of doubt; and upon the cessation of ignorance, because of the absence of passion and aversion—which are like long-held impressions of objects previously grasped—there is no further production of *dharma* and *adharma* through the power of action. For activities bound by those [past] actions proceed like men bound by ropes; when those actions have ceased, like men whose bonds have been released, they are no longer obstructed in their purpose.
As the Blessed Lord Patañjali said:
"When the substrate (*dharmi*) is destroyed, its modifications (*vṛtti*), namely birth, lifespan, and experience, are also destroyed."
As the Blessed One Cakrapāda said:
"There is no further activity for those who have severed the bonds of rebirth and whose field is inferior.
This concludes the examination of the auxiliary factors regarding merit and demerit produced by prior states within the category of wholesome phenomena.

Cessation is characterized by withdrawal due to the causes of stillness through the application of means and so forth; likewise, having experienced the happiness of contentment regarding the arising of karma and the like, and having undergone the dissolution of the body, one turns away from passion and the rest. Thus, the affliction characterized by withdrawal ceases once the vision of ultimate reality has been made into happiness.

*Samsāra* is that by which one turns back; thus, *nivṛtti* (cessation) is characterized by turning back. That which is characterized by cessation, whose nature is cessation—just as when one has turned away from passion (*rāga*) and so forth—the affliction (*kleśa*) comes to rest. Having experienced the happiness of contentment and the dissolution of the body, and through the vision of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-darśana*), it produces the happiness of the vision of the Self (*ātma-darśana*). Having produced that, it ceases. Because of the obstruction of the objects of ego-inflation (*ābhimānika-artha*), then, for the bound soul (*nirbandhya-ātman*), there is no further production of a body and so forth; thus, there is the end of sorrow, which is the suffering of being dependent on the cycle of miserable states (*durgati*).

When one has turned away from rebirth by realizing the ultimate truth as described, then, because the self—which is essentially ungraspable—is free from the destruction of the body and so forth, and because there is an absence of causes for the non-arising of future bodies and such once the bondage of karma has ceased, there is no further production; thus, like one who has descended from a precipice and grasped a support, there is no sorrow regarding the non-production of a body again.

This, however, is being refuted. Is it the cessation of mere knowledge? Or rather, do we say it is from the combination of knowledge and action? Even regarding cessation—that is, the disappearance [of bondage]—even for one who has desisted from optional (*kāmya*) actions, the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties do not cease to assist him; for these were prescribed specifically for a *brāhmaṇa* who has been initiated (*upanīta*), and they remain binding as long as the status of the *brāhmaṇa* caste is not severed. Just as one who is eligible for the thirty-six duties must perform them, otherwise there is sin; and since that sin is exhausted by the performance of those duties once he is initiated, the bound man is not liberated [merely by knowledge].
As it has been said:
"Those actions performed for the sake of desire, as well as those that are prohibited— even the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites— bind him who does not perform them."

[Objection: "Thus, the efficacy of the non-performance of what is prescribed is not a cause for the existence of demerit (*pratyavāya*), because non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot be the cause of an entity (*bhāva*).

Therefore, demerit does not arise from the senses. [Response: This is not so, because demerit can occur due to other causes even when there is non-performance of what is prescribed; for it is not accepted that non-existence is a cause in its own right, but rather as subordinate to an entity. Furthermore, at the time of the *ṣaṇḍhya* rite and so forth, one does not perform anything with body, speech, or mind in their entirety, since even acts such as maintaining the body are being performed.

As it has been said: "That which is momentary in the case of prior non-existences, such as the non-performance of prescribed duties, is not deprived of its status as a real entity (vastutva) merely because it brings about what is undesirable."
Whatever activity a thing performs at its own time, that it performs as something insentient;
its cognition is likewise produced by that very name.

Thus, the meaning is that destruction is produced by a momentary [act] alone. Or, if there is doubt as to whether the transgression (*pratyavāya*) and the maintenance of the body (*śarīradhāraṇa*) and so forth result from the superimposition of a reflection (*pratibimba*), or rather from the substance that is the reflection itself being the agent—[if one asks], "If one casts away even what is appropriate, what is the fault?"—then at that time there is the loss resulting from the non-performance of what is prescribed; and since there is no distinction [in that regard], there is the transgression of performing the mere maintenance of the body and so forth when it is not [properly] reflected upon.
In that case, there would indeed be a transgression caused by the performance of what is prohibited, such as [the act of] reflecting an image.
How is this explained?

If it is argued: "Because it has persisted for a long time, even the knowledge of the Self—which consists of the cultivation of the opposite [of ignorance] when it was previously dense and unperceived—overcomes passion, hatred, and delusion, and likewise overcomes even the transgression caused by failing to perform prescribed duties while enduring hunger and thirst."
That is incorrect.

When [the scriptures] declare that "those who have known thus become serene," they determine that "I have become That Reality" and that this is an object of certainty; however, their capacity should be seen as directed toward the things to be perceived, not toward the pointing out of another doubt.

If, on the other hand, self-knowledge were established as being capable [of liberation] independently, and if liberation were determined to occur through the abandonment of effort, then the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) would be far removed from reality; for one whose entire karma has been exhausted immediately after the vision of Truth would simply fall away from the body.

In what sense? In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), although all names and forms have been entirely destroyed and stilled, all worlds are perceived as if painted by a thought, devoid of any sense of substantiality. They experience the specific fruits of their *prārabdha* karma, like the rotation of a potter’s wheel that continues due to the momentum of the initial impulse even after the sound of the potter has ceased. Thus, they await the fall of the body while regarding the forest-thicket of worldly existence with indifference. Accordingly, the Śruti says: "Indeed, the wise man is liberated even while living, having cast off the bonds accomplished through effort.
And so say the followers of Kapila:
On the path toward liberation, which begins with the cessation of ignorance and other afflictions,
there occurs a withdrawal [of the mind] due to the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), preceded by a state of meditative absorption that resembles that delusion.
Thus [it is said].

Even on the path where dharma and the other causes have been severed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the meaning is that dharma and the rest cease to exist because the sixfold causal capacity (*ṣaṭkāraṇa-śakti*) of dharma and so forth has been destroyed. If it is argued that "karmas whose fruits have not yet begun (*anārabdha-phala*) are removed through the knowledge of reality," even so, because they are karma, those whose fruits have already begun (*ārabdha-phala*) cannot undergo destruction merely by one's will.
Even for one who has been awakened [to reality], when that which is both higher and lower is seen, there is the instruction: "even his [past] actions perish.

This is because, when knowledge exists, actions are not performed due to the realization of the non-substantiality (anātmatva) of the self; it does not mean, however, that existing actions are destroyed by knowledge. Thus, it is said: "As fire consumes its own fuel... (Gītā 4.37).

"Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of aeons unless it has been experienced," and so forth. If knowledge does not destroy karma, then how can there be the exhaustion or total destruction of karmas accumulated over thousands of births? If you argue that liberation results from the destruction of karma because the exhaustion of all karmas occurs in a single birth through the impelling force of [knowledge], we say no, because there is no fixed rule regarding time.

Just as actions are exhausted with each successive birth, so too are they exhausted from the state of a preta; however, if those actions are not yet exhausted, then through the experience of one's own consciousness and external reflection, they enter into the yoga of action itself, and thus the actions are quickly destroyed.
As it has been said:
"One who knows the true nature of the self effects the exhaustion of karma through liberation."
Out of thousands of millions who sleep, perhaps one is liberated.
Thus.

Thus, for one who fails to perform what has been enjoined, there is transgression (*pratyavāya*); and since that transgression is a cause of bondage and cannot be ceased through any other means, those who desire liberation must, while not contradicting the practice of yoga, perform the enjoined duties—such as eating and so forth—at the appropriate times without desire, until the inner essence (*adhyātmasattva*) becomes manifest. Even for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) who has manifested the reality of the Self, actions continue as long as their momentum persists. However, for one who is firmly established in the Self alone, whose mind is not distracted by external objects, and whose karma is nearly exhausted, those actions simply perish, as outward consciousness has become vastly expanded.

When the power of matured *samādhi* has clarified that which resembles deep sleep (*suṣupti*), and when the state of being a subject (*viṣayitva*) and so forth—which depend upon effort and have been brought to full development—is abandoned; then, for one who is not insane, there arises only the pure, eternal bliss of the Self’s own knowledge, having made the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) its manifold support and taking as its object only the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*). There is no external perception, because the activity of the external senses has ceased. Thus, who can fear whom? What can afflict whom? And so says the Śruti: "They say he does not sacrifice," "they say he does not see," "he becomes one," and so forth.

And at that time, there is no visual cognition such as "this object is present before me," nor is there any recognized notion such as "I am a Brahmin," because for one devoid of the realization "I am a Brahmin," the eligibility for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*) is excluded.
As it has been said:

One who pursues the state of a Brahmin brings his karmas to exhaustion and sleeps; yet for him, whose every activity has ceased and who has chewed the essence of the Kṣatriya stage, there arises the awakening of oneness through the realization that living beings do not fear one another. Because he possesses the knowledge of suffering, even though the body appears clearly before his eyes, it is no longer a source of wonder. As long as that body persists, his karma—which acts as the regulator of its existence—continues to function until the end of time.

Alternatively, since the body is pervaded by the action associated with a previous time—as expressed in the statement regarding the duration of that time—let it continue to run about for that long; then, upon the exhaustion and cessation of the action through the performance of its own effect, there is the cessation of the body which is that action's effect. Thus, because of this cessation, even the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), being the cause of that [cessation], becomes a qualification of the self once it has perished.

The knowledge of reality possesses a powerful efficacy because it obstructs the operation of prescribed duties at moments other than the *saṃdhyā* periods; this is due to the fact that the various constituents of the body and so forth are characterized by both assistance and injury to knowledge. Furthermore, since the knowledge of reality destroys the notions of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) and "mine" (*mamakāra*), as well as the two types of attachment toward objects that assist or injure, and since it eliminates the capacity for perception regarding the sphere of the intellect—thereby acting as the cause for the exhaustion [of karma]—and since the sin resulting from the non-performance of what is prescribed is itself obstructed by the performance of those very duties, there remains no other cause for the continued existence of the body once its connection to karma has ceased. Consequently, when the body has perished, there being no further cause for its re-emergence, the soul abides in its own essential nature.
As it has been said:
"Performing obligatory and occasional rites, one effects the destruction of evil;
purifying knowledge, one exerts oneself for the sake of liberation."
Gradually, through the aforementioned consciousness, a person attains absolute liberation.
Thus it is said;
likewise, this path has been adopted by others as well:
"The determination of the self [is achieved] through the action of the wood-boring insect."
By this very method, the moon-marked [mudrā] would become the renunciation of the sage in this world.
Thus [it is asked]: what, then, is the nature of the self by virtue of which liberation while abiding [in this world] is spoken of? Some say it is the self consisting of bliss (*ānandātman*).
That is incorrect,
because it leads to a dilemma:
is that bliss experienced through the mouth or not?
If it is not experienced, then even while existing, it is no different from being non-existent, because it would be unfit for enjoyment.
If it is experienced, then experience must be said to be an effect; yet, there is no possibility of its production within the distinction between cause and effect and so forth.

If it is argued that the conjunction with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the cause [of experience], we say no; for the mind’s capacity for non-distinct functioning is due to its manifold latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Consequently, there would be no cessation of the seeds of diverse experiences, nor would there be a state prior to the Self. Even if one were to favor the nature of the Self through the grace of yoga, since all yogis have already accomplished their purpose, who among them would still experience [the world] within the three principles?

This is the mind. Because it is insentient, even if the Self were mute, it would be no different from a stone and the like; for even a mute person does not experience pleasure or pain in that same way [as the mind]. What, then, is the distinction between the two?

Therefore, that which is the natural modification of the self—namely, when the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) functions through aversion to the senses—it then becomes extroverted. But when the senses become intent upon their own objects, then it immerses itself in the state of bliss within its own self. For this conscious self, if it illuminates something whatsoever, yet if it remains in a state of silence like a mute, then even though it exists, it is as if non-existent; if it were so, one might ask, "Why then should the self not be regarded as inert? To this it is replied: [The text continues with the response to this objection.]

Is this [bliss] innate to the nature of the mind as its essence, or is it produced by some other cause? First of all, it cannot be the cause of manifestation; for it has been stated that the causes of such manifestation—such as speech, instruments, and so forth—are absent in the state of a mute person. If it were innate, then bliss would be experienced even during the state of worldly bondage (*saṃsāra*), since there would be no obstruction to its presence even when one is not in a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). If it is argued that there is no experience because of a lack of consciousness (*acittatva*), that is not so, because there is no absence of the experience of bliss for eternal consciousness (*citi*).

Because there is no falling away from one's own nature (*svarūpa*). What would be the meaning of an obstruction? Or, if it had fallen away from its own nature, what permanence could there be? Therefore, bliss (*ānanda*) is variable; being perceived by eternal consciousness (*cityā*), it is perceived without distinction between the states of seeing and not-seeing. But this is not so, because in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), pleasure is experienced as a cognition dependent on objects and the senses for the cognizer who has arisen [in that state]. Consequently, there is no eternal bliss belonging to the Self. And due to the absence of such [eternal bliss], the experience of it in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*) does not exist; rather, even when all the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the Self are destroyed, it is the persistence of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) through ignorance (*avidyā*).
And by her, this purpose of man has been accomplished accordingly.

Sound has the qualities of being imperceptible to the senses, is graspable by the ear, is momentary, is opposed to both its cause and its effect, is born from conjunction, disjunction, and sound, exists in a specific location, and has causes that are both similar and dissimilar.
It is of two kinds: characterized by phonemes (*varṇa*) and characterized by resonance (*dhvani*).
Among these, that characterized by phonemes consists of *a*, *ka*, and so forth; that characterized by resonance is caused by the striking of a drum and the like.

In that regard, the production of phonemes (varṇa) characterized by specific qualities arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, followed by memory, indifference, cognition, effort, and desire. Immediately thereafter, depending upon effort, an action is produced in the air due to the conjunction of the self and the air. That [air], moving toward the throat and striking the palate and other locations, produces the phoneme through the conjunction of the location and space, depending upon the conjunction of the location and the air.

Furthermore, even upon the conjunction with the auditory organ, a distinction [of sound] is produced from the conjunction of the air and space, depending upon the impact of the stick [or articulator].

Due to the division of specific locations, the threefold division of space, and sound produced by conjunction and disjunction, there is a demarcation of air in a continuous stream (*santāna*); thus, when [the sound] has reached the region of the ear by means of this stream, it is perceived. Since there is no mutual contact between the ear and the sound, there is no perception of that which is not reached; therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the existence of the stream is established.
Thus ends the category of quality in the Praśastapādabhāṣya.
Sound is also its quality; it is a quality of space (*ākāśa*).
Now, one might object: "Since there are six qualities belonging to space even though it is a single substance, how does this definition of sound avoid contradiction? To this he says:
"That which is perceptible by the sense of hearing."
The meaning is that sound is that which, while being perceivable by the ear, is a quality of space (*ākāśa*).
He says "manifesting" (*vyañjaka*) in order to refute the opponent's assertion of a double application [of the term].
Regarding the view of the Teacher (Ācārya) that the form (*ākṛti*) is indestructible while the word (*śabda*) is not eternal, he states the inference as follows:

That which is a substance [is not eternal], because there is no ground for postulating its manifestation due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because this would contradict recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), and because, since it would have only the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, it would entail the cessation [of the individual] and the suspicion of a difference between manifestations in the case of the subsequent mantras and the Veda.
This [inference] contradicts the distinction between cause and effect.

The first sound perishes in its own cause; another [sound] perishes through a sound produced by its own cause; and even when the causes of destruction for others are present, they perish only upon the debtor's [final] payment.
This is like the case of conjunction and disjunction producing sound.
The distinction is that the first sound arises from conjunction and disjunction, whereas the subsequent ones arise from sound alone.
The term *pratyaughani* means "one who has studied the *oghani*" (or *adhyāpyaughani*);
this has already been established.
This [term] belongs to the same class as *samrāj*.
Sound is a cause of its own kind through [its] sound-ness;
it is a cause not of its own kind through conjunction and disjunction.
It is of two kinds: characterized by phonemes (varṇa) and characterized by the sphoṭa.
The [word] characterized by *sphoṭa* is caused by sounds such as phonemes beginning with 'a' (*akāra*).
Among those two, the production of that which is characterized by phonemes is now described.

Inherent in the self, there arises a desire (*icchā*)—which is the cause of the effort (*prayatna*)—to produce the various distinctions of sounds that are to be understood through the reality of words. From that [desire], effort arises; that effort is the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). Due to the impact of that effort upon the vital air (*prāṇa*), an action (*karman*) is produced in the abdominal air (*koṣṭha-vāyu*) by way of conjunction. Then, that air, following the sequence of the throat and so forth, strikes locations such as the heart, the throat, and the palate. Immediately after that impact, there occurs a conjunction of the abdominal air with the location (such as the throat); this conjunction is the instrumental cause, and from the conjunction of the location with space (*ākāśa*), the production of the phoneme (*varṇa*) occurs by way of its arising.

Even though there is a distinction between the parts [of the drum], the disjunction [of the drum from the air] arises from the conjunction of the drumstick; the disjunction of the air [from the drum] arises from the conjunction of the air with the velocity [imparted by the stick]. Disjunction is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of disjunction; the conjunction of the drumstick and the substance [the drum] is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and velocity is the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
From the disjunction of the air [from the drum] produced by that [initial] disjunction, a further disjunction with space arises, and from this, sound is born.
And from sound, the production of further sounds proceeds.

Regarding sound, just as when waves are produced by conjunction and disjunction, in the case of waves that are unobstructed or obstructed, another wave arises in a location separated from the first, and from that yet another, and from that yet another—in this sequence waves arise; so too, from a sound that has been produced, another sound arises in a location separated from it, and from that yet another, and from that yet another, until reaching the point of non-perception—by this sequence sounds arise.
The sound is grasped by the dense [air] as it reaches the location of the ear; this refers to the apprehension of the final sound.
But from where does this conceptualization arise? He says: "Of the ear and the sound," as the lightning-like [sound] vanishes.

The ear does not go to the location of the sound, nor does the sound go to the location of the ear; for, due to the sequence of their production, there is no perception of what has not been reached, and so forth—this is because [the sense organ] functions by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*). Furthermore, it is not possible for the sound to reach [the ear] in any other way. Indeed, it is observed that when sounds perish at their own place of origin, they are perceived individually as they arise; then, through a succession of initiations of sound-impulses in intervening spaces, there is an arrival at another location. Therefore, the propagation of sound-pulses is postulated.
Nor does this lead to an infinite regress; for as far as the air within the body (koṣṭhavāyu), acting as the efficient cause, persists, so far do the sounds of the word persist.
For this very reason, there is no perception of the sound in each subsequent echo, due to the obstruction of the internal air.
Therefore, the intent of the Bhāṣya regarding the roar of the ocean and so forth has been explained solely by means of the wood-boring insect (ghuṇa) analogy; no other argument has been stated.
One who is enriched by virtues, whose non-duality is established through reason and logic,
and who is as pure as a string of pearls— such a sage should be meditated upon in the heart for the sake of bliss.

Thus ends the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*) in the *Nyāyakandalī* commentary on the *Padārthapraveśa*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Bhodhava. Now begins the exposition of the category of action (*karmapadārtha*).
The five actions, beginning with upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), possess the common relationship of being "action" (*karmatva*).

The specific characteristics [of action] are: subsisting in a single substance; being external; subsisting in substances that are not eternal; having the nature of an atom; being produced by gravity, fluidity, effort, and conjunction; being opposed by the conjunction that is its own effect; being a cause independent of conjunction and disjunction; being a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); being a non-inherent cause of effects inherent in itself, in another, or in both; not initiating [an effect] of the same class; not initiating a substance; possessing a restricted genus;
and being a non-inherent cause of two kinds of qualities. These are the distinctions.
Samsara is described for one who has understood its consequences.
Homage to the moon-crested Lord, whose head bears the moon that flows with the nectar of knowledge.
Explaining the mutual similarity among throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the others, as well as their distinction from other categories of entities, he says:
"Of throwing upwards and so forth.
That which is called "action-ness" (*karmatva*) is a generality (*sāmānya*); it is with this that throwing upwards and the others alone have a manifold connection.
The property of subsisting in a single substance (*ekadravyavṛttitva*) means that at one time, only one action subsists in one substance, and one action subsists in only one substance.
