If, in a single substance, there were a co-inherence (*samavāya*) of multiple actions due to [multiple] qualities, then, because those two would not mutually obstruct each other, there would be no production of specific conjunctions and disjunctions; consequently, action—which is defined as the dependent cause of conjunction and disjunction—would lose its defining characteristic.
Moreover, since only one [action] arises from a single substance as the conjunction and disjunction of that substance with two other substances, the postulation of a second action is redundant.
Likewise, a single action does not reside in multiple locations, because when one [action] arises, no movement is perceived elsewhere from the action situated there.
Its externality consists in its perishability immediately upon its production.
The state of residing in substances that are not composed of cognition; the state of residing in substances possessing non-cognitional dimension; the absence of possession of qualities in atoms;
and the state of being produced by gravity, fluidity, effort, and conjunction.
"By its own effect" means that it is destructible by conjunction, which is its own effect, and not by disjunction; nor is it subject merely to a subsequent conjunction.
"Conjunction and disjunction," etc.

Just as motion does not possess the status of being a quality due to its departure from [the category of] qualities, so too motion does not possess the status of being a substance due to conjunction and disjunction; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, while qualities possess the nature of being non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), motion does not; rather, it is the atom that is fit to be a non-inherent cause of motion, as stated in the commentaries on the Upaniṣads and other texts.
This is the very distinction between these two.
Regarding the phrase "of the two intrinsic natures":

unity consists in the fact that these two qualities—namely, those characterized as conjunction and disjunction which exist in the states of deep sleep (*svāpya*) and tranquility (*prasanna*)—are identical in essence.
It is distinct [from them].

If it is argued that, "In the case of the commencement of another action (*karmāntara*) in succession, there is the destruction of motion and [the subsequent] pervasion by sound, space, and so forth, according to the previously stated directions," we say: no. This [succession] consists merely of the nature of volition (*icchāmayatva*) and so on, even for a single conjoined effect; it is not an action (*karman*) superimposed upon a specific sequence, nor is it a commencement of another action, because such a claim is simply untenable. Alternatively, this [succession] is merely what is designated as a specific action and its purposeful engagement, as explained by the opponent.
"Visible" (dṛśya) means that it is produced as an object of action (karman) which continues through subsequent conjunctions (yoga). "Specifically determined" (pratiniyata) means...
The meaning is that within each of the aforementioned [types of] seeking (*eṣaṇā*), there is no exclusion of the seeking of liberation (*mokṣaiṣaṇā*).
This [point] regarding the *yajus* formulas should be explained by Dhanañjaya.
There are two kinds of satisfaction (*juṣṭi*).
The body is of two kinds, depending on whether it is the agent of what is desired or what is not desired;
thus it is said.

In that context, the upward movement of the aforementioned [bodily humors] within the limbs of the body and their similar parts—caused by conjunction with regions possessing excessive heat and characterized by disjunction from those same regions—is called *utkṣepaṇa* (upward throwing). It consists of both conjunction and disjunction resulting from the accumulation of successive [motions].

In the case of the limbs of the body, such as Indra and others, and in things like flowers that resemble them, that which is produced by conjunctions with parts possessing superior qualities and by disjunctions from parts possessing inferior qualities—measured precisely by the extent of the conjunction—is called *ukṣepaṇa* (throwing upwards).
Action that is the cause of conjunction and disjunction contrary to those [previously mentioned] is called *apacayaṇa*.

"Contrary to that" means that the action which is the cause of conjunction with an iron substance and the cause of disjunction from the very same [substance] is called *apaveśana*. This is the meaning.

When the two parts of the visible object possess a downward motion, there is a separation from their cause; by means of a motion directed upward from the base region, the support becomes curved, and that is called *apakṣepaṇa* (throwing downward). It is produced by substances such as *khadira*, *aśvakarṇa*, *rudrākṣa*, and so forth—this is the connection with the phrase "by which action."
In the opposite case, when conjunction and disjunction arise, that action by which a previously contracted mass is expanded is called *prasāraṇa* (extension).
The meaning is: when the production of conjunction occurs in accordance with the division of the fundamental regions of the atoms.
That which is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions with indefinite spatial directions is the motion of the tree.

This action, which is of five kinds, also exists in the parts of the body and in those things connected to them; and because it inheres in similar [substances], that which is other than these exists only in those others as well.
The fact that there are five classes of actions has not been explicitly stated here, because they are included within the specific types such as "going" (*gamana*) and so forth.

For in all corporeal actions, what is produced is merely "going," which brings about conjunctions and disjunctions with spatial points (space-points) above, below, or across the path of the wind; since the cognition of "going" is indistinguishable everywhere, all [action] is indeed nothing but "going."

The [five] classes and so forth are not [the causes], because we observe the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions. Here, in cases such as "throwing upward," "falling," and "not falling," the recurrence and exclusion of cognitions are observed everywhere; from this, a distinction between universals and particulars is understood to be their cause.

Since these [classes] produce specific effects in specific directions due to the particularities of their *udātta*, *anudātta*, and *sarga* [qualities], they are established as distinct even though [the sounds] are perceived as identical.
Thus, the restriction that "everything consists of only five" is untenable.
If it is argued that even in cases such as entering a desireless village, the recurrence and cessation of notions like "class" (varga) and so forth are observed;

and that since the recurrence of notions such as "class" and the manifestation of distinctions are seen everywhere in actions like lifting and so forth, a difference in genus (jāti-bheda) must be admitted for all of them—even in the case of entering a desireless village and the like—and that the recurrence and cessation of notions in those instances are due to a difference in the effects (kāryabheda), [we reply: no, for then the consequence would follow that in the case of lifting and so forth as well, the recurrence and cessation of notions would occur solely due to a difference in the effects.

If it is argued that, while the persistence of the same cognition occurs equally for both groups, the specific reason for why there is a distinction of genus (*jāti*) only for throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth, and not for pushing out (*niṣkāsaṇa*) and so forth, is stated [by the opponent], we reply: because this would lead to the undesirable consequence of a confusion of genera (*jātisaṅkara*).
Since the persistence of the cognition is interrupted by the distinction of genus in the case of pushing out and so forth, a confusion of genera results.

How so? When a substance intended as the object of throwing upwards moves from one room to another room, the simultaneous cognitions of "standing," "sitting," and "entering" are observed; likewise, regarding the entry through a door, the cognitions "he enters" and "he goes out" are observed.
But when it is perceived as being carried by an opponent, there is neither the cognition of entering nor the cognition of exiting, but rather only the cognition of moving.

Similarly, in the case of a bamboo basket, when many objects fall together, one observes the simultaneous cognitions of whirling, falling, and entering; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of a confusion of genera (*jāti-saṅkara*).

However, such a confusion of cognitions is not observed in the case of upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the others. Therefore, while the persistence and exclusion of cognitions for upward throwing and the rest are due to a difference in their genera, those for exiting and the rest are due to a difference in their effects (*kārya-bheda*).

If it is asked how there can be a simultaneous diversity of cognitions [regarding a single action], and if it is thought that just as there is no confusion of genera (*jāti*), so too there is no simultaneous entry of multiple inherent properties—then how can there be, in a single action, the simultaneous cognitions of two [different agents] performing whirling, falling, and entering?
To this we reply: it is not because of a transformation (*vivarta*) of the parts and the whole, but rather due to the distinction between various applications and divisions.

For one who perceives the conjunctions and disjunctions of the constituent parts of a substance occurring on its sides in succession at various points of displacement, there arises the cognition of "moving.
For one who observes the disjunction from a lower point and the conjunction with an upper point of a substance, there arises the cognition of "falling.

Furthermore, for one who perceives the conjunction [of a substance] with an internal location and the disjunction from an external location, there arises the cognition of "entering. Thus, it is established that the difference in cognitions regarding effects such as motion and so forth is based on the observation of these [conjunctions and disjunctions].

The distinction in the conditions for [the cognition of] things such as the remnants of food is due to the difference in their genus (*jāti*), whereas for things such as the act of depositing, it is due to the difference in their effect (*kārya*).
"Dependent on that" (vatpratyayam) means that there arises both direct observation and indirect observation.
"That which is seen" (yaddṛśyam).
This [wind] also exists in substances that are subtle, such as the body and so forth, which are extremely thin;
whatever effect characterized by motion arises therein, and that which is inferred from its cognition,
it causes to move.
Regarding the phrase "by action":

it has been stated that actions such as throwing upward (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth are connected to their respective classes (*jāti*). If it is argued that this is incorrect because there is no distinction among all of them due to the commonality of "going" (*gamana*), [we reply: heaven is likewise spoken of without distinction due to the act of "going."
By the words "all indeed," etc.:

because we observe the cognition "it moves" even when [actions] such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) are seen, all these—upward throwing and so forth—are nothing but movement (*gamana*). Thus it is with those beginning with downward throwing (*avamardana*).

This is not so. Where, however, there is upward motion, as in the case of throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the rest, the color [of the action] is described. Because it conforms to the internal [quality], it is subordinate; because it conforms to the internal [quality], the genus "upwardness" (*ūrdhvatva*) is postulated. Just as that is the case, so too in the case of throwing upwards and the rest, because they conform to the internal [quality] and because of the doubling of the conformity to the internal, the postulation of the universals such as "throwing upwards-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva*) is unavoidable; thus there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*).
The explanation of "the eye" (*cakṣuḥ*) is easy to understand.
Regarding the word "of these" (*eṣām*):
in the context of the non-perception of the apprehender, the word "after" (*paraḥ*) should be understood as following the perception of the effect, such as the body.
It is perceived as distinct from others when it is apprehended; thus, the individual (*vyakti*) is perceived, and that [perception] is the universal (*jāti*). This is the Master’s [view].

Not only is the distinction between universals established through the two cognitions of persistence (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), and through throwing upward (*utkṣepaṇa*), throwing downward (*apakṣepaṇa*), and so forth, but they also know [the distinction] from specific causes such as effects, based on specific marks (*liṅga*) and the difference in examples.

Others, however, maintain that there is no difference in the examples of these [actions] such as throwing upward, because there is no difference in the production of specific qualities or effects, nor even in the difference of cognition; this is for the purpose of excluding [the notion of] "going" (*gamana*) as a separate category.

Regarding the word "vidvan" (the knower): for if there were a difference in action, then even the cause of the production, non-existence, conjunction, and disjunction of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) would result [as the object]. Regarding "it is produced again," [it refers to] "made of barley."

If the persistence of the notion of obstruction and its constant recurrence do not conform to a commonality within "I-ness" (*ahaṃtva*) and so forth, then in the case of extraction (*niṣkarṣaṇa*) and other such acts as well, the persistence of the notion of obstruction and its constant recurrence would have to conform to a commonality such as "extractiveness" (*niṣkarṣaṇatva*). Consequently, the restriction [implied by the term] "only this" (*evaitat*) would be untenable.

Alternatively, if it is argued that in extraction and the like there is a difference in notions due to a difference in effects, and not due to a difference in genus (*jāti*), then the same would apply to pressing (*utpeṣaṇa*) and so forth.
To this he says: "It is established from the difference in effects."
And [the author] says "and he composes" (*samādhatte*).
If [these] were intended to be of the same genus as "extracting" (*niṣkarṣaṇa*) and so forth, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a confusion of genera (*jātisaṅkara*).
The meaning is that it is impossible for [such properties] to coexist in a single individual (*vyakti*), because they are mutually exclusive.
The word "kāryam" (the effect/task) is to be supplied as the subject matter. It is seen or unseen;
that is, because it is not seen in one room, it is [inferred to be] in another room.

When a man is walking, two things are perceived by the observer: the explicit acts of exiting and entering. To one standing where he has already exited, there arises the cognition that "he is exiting"; to one standing where he is about to enter, there arises the cognition that "he is entering. If these cognitions were produced by universals (*jāti*), then, given the observation of these two distinct acts, it would be impossible for two mutually contradictory universals—namely, "exiting-ness" and "entering-ness"—to coexist in a single manifest individual (*vyakti*).

Just as one says "he enters" or "he exits" regarding a substance's location, so too, when a person moves from one room to another within a single large compound, there arise the two cognitions "he emerges" and "he enters" between the two visual perceptions situated in the preceding and succeeding rooms.

However, when the [person] is obstructed in the middle and the [perceptions] are not unobstructed, then there is neither the cognition of entering nor the cognition of exiting; rather, there is only the cognition of mere movement. Therefore, all logical consistency is established solely through the sequence [of moments].
The intended meaning is that there is a difference in the conditions for what has been produced.
He states another example:
"And likewise in the case of a painting," and so forth.
"Cālikā" refers to vehicles situated in a pit.
He states a distinction regarding his own position:
"And it is not thus."
Regarding the terms "above" and "below":
as for the phrase "therefore," he explains how multiple actions could be conceived simultaneously when, in a single substance occupying a single location, there can be only one action at a time.
How so?
[It is] "pertaining to the visible world" (*sāṃdṛṣṭika*), etc.; now, [the author] begins with the differences of opinion (*matabheda*).
To this we reply: the introduction is made by the learned one [the author].
Since you have stated that there are three [types of sound] according to the specific designations, due to the difference between the conjunctions and disjunctions of those situated in two locations;
now follows the easy explanation.

Furthermore, when the sides [of the body] are capable of conjunction and disjunction, there arises the cognition of "whirling"; the meaning is that from the difference in the effects of that action, there arise the cognitions of "falling" and "entering."

Thus, there is no fault; the difference in cognition arises from the difference in the types of birth (jāti). Now, is "going-ness" (gamanatva) a synonym for "action-ness" (karmatva), or is it a distinct generality (sāmānya)?
Why do you have this doubt?

Because, just as there is a cognition of "action" in all [four types of action] such as upward throwing (utkṣepaṇa) and so forth, there is no distinction in the cognition of "going"; therefore, it is understood that "going-ness" is a synonym for "action-ness."
If it is argued that because it is designated by a specific name like "throwing upwards" (utkṣepaṇa) and so forth, it must therefore be another [lower] generality (sāmānya),
we say no;
for it is a synonym for "action-ness" (karmatva).

Just as "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) and "personhood" (*puruṣatva*) are synonyms, so too is "going-ness" (*gamanatva*) a synonym for "action-ness" (*karmatva*). Now, one might ask: for what purpose is the term "going" (*gamana*) specifically mentioned? It is not for the sake of confusion; rather, the mention of "going" is made in order to include within its scope actions such as whirling, falling, and vibrating, which would otherwise not be included by the specific terms "throwing upwards" (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth. Thus, the mention of "going" is intended to encompass those movements that lack fixed [specific] names.

Otherwise, it would follow that those very four which were designated by the term "particular" (viśeṣa-saṃjñā) would themselves fall under the scope of the term "general-particular" (sāmānya-viśeṣa-saṃjñā).

Alternatively, let there be another generality called "going-ness" (gamanatva), which exists only in these [motions] such as whirling and so forth, characterized by the form of conjunction and disjunction with indefinite directions and locations; the word "going," however, should be understood as being used figuratively for upward throwing and the rest, on the basis of the commonality of being the agent of conjunction and disjunction with its own substratum.

Now, the learned person asks: "Is 'the state of going' (gamanatva) a synonym for 'the state of being an object' (karmatva), or is it another distinct generality (sāmānya)? [The opponent replies: "Why do you have this doubt?
Such a doubt is untenable. This is the meaning of the first part.
The opponent raises a doubt:
"In all [of them]" and so forth.

Just as there is indeed a cognition of action (*karmapratyaya*) consisting of throwing upwards and the other three, so too in those [motions] there is a cognition of going (*gamanapratyaya*), such as the cognitions: "the ox goes," "the horse goes," "it goes in the eastern direction," or "it goes in the western direction. Therefore, it is understood that "go-ness" (*gamanatva*) is a synonym for "action-ness" (*karmatva*), because of the statement "in all of them" which follows immediately after.

Since "going" (gamana) is also mentioned separately by a specific name, just like "throwing upwards" (utkṣepaṇa) and so forth, therefore "the nature of going" (gamanatva) would be another lower generality (apara-sāmānya). Now, [the opponent] might object that this is not a proof for the existence of action (karman), because it is mentioned among the internal sensations (antarvedanika) as being distinct from the [five] sense-objects. To this we reply: no, because it is mentioned there as a subordinate [quality] of that [action].
As for the doubt raised by the opponent, the Sūtra says: "No.
No doubt should be entertained, because "going" (*gamanatva*) is synonymous with "action" (*karmatva*).

For it has been observed that the state of being a self (*ātmatva*), the state of being a person (*puruṣatva*), and the state of being an agent of action (*satkarmatva*) are indeed synonyms for the state of motion (*gamanatva*).

Just as the state of being a person is a synonym for the state of being a self because it pervades all knowable objects, so too the state of motion is a synonym for the state of being an agent of action.
Now, if it is argued that the term "separate movement" (*pṛthag-gamana*) is used because there is a specific designation for a specific [object],
he states the reply: "It is drawn forth" (*kṛṣṭi*).

No; for if the ascetics (*śramaṇa*) and others were not included by means of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), which is used as a figurative designation (*utprekṣaṇa*), then they would not be included as objects (*karman*) if the act of going (*gamana*) were not the primary topic.
Rather, only those specifically named items, such as "looking about" (*utprekṣaṇa*) and the rest, would be subject to the status of being objects.

Furthermore, since ascetics and others are also well-known in the world as objects of going (*gamanatvena*), the word "going" was used separately in order to include them; such is the opinion of some.
Alternatively, let there be another [type of] going that consists of sensual desire (*kāmānyam*); it is said in response to that:
"unrestricted" (*aniyatā*).
Because [the term] has already been used for such things as "looking upwards," there arises the notion of "going" [in those cases]; therefore, he says:
"But the word 'going'...

Since the word "going" has the sense of indicating a connection (*yoga-lakṣaṇārtha*), the notion of "going" appearing in relation to "looking upwards" and so forth should be understood as metaphorical.
He states the purpose of the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*):
"Because it shares the common property of being the agent of conjunction and disjunction with its own substratum.

Motion causes conjunction and disjunction of its own substratum; since looking upward (*utprekṣaṇa*) and so forth also do the same, by this commonality of action, the conventional usage of the term "motion" occurs for looking upward and the like. By this same commonality of action, why does the conventional usage of "looking upward" and so forth not occur for motion? However, in states such as yellowness (*paiṅgalya*) or whiteness (*pāṭatva*), various kinds of verbal expressions (*māṣaṇaka*) arise due to the specific action (*kṛtya*).
It is said:

the conceptualization of an effect does not occur when the cause is absent; rather, the conceptualization of a cause occurs only when the conventional usage [of the effect] is already established. The same applies to sensation (*vedanā*); that is the rebuttal.
This is the procedure for the manifestation of true reality.

How is it that when one desires to move or to withdraw the hands during sacrifices, Vedic study, giving, or other such activities, then a specific region of the self (*ātman*) is perceived as being exerted, like the hand? Depending upon that effort and conjunction (*saṃyoga*), action occurs in the hand due to the conjunction of the self and the hand; and just as it does in the hand, so too does it occur in all the constituent parts supported by it, such as the feet and so forth, or in the body as a whole.

How does it occur even in relation to those things connected to it? When one, having grasped a pestle with the hand, forms the desire "I shall lift the pestle with my hand," immediately thereafter, due to the conjunction of the self and the hand depending upon effort, an act of upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa-karma*) arises in the hand at that very moment; and at that same moment, due to the conjunction of the pestle and the upper part [of the mortar] depending upon that same effort, an action also arises in the pestle.

Then, when the upward motion (*utpatti*) has arisen in the arrow (*subala*), the desire for that [motion] ceases; subsequently, another imperceptible impulse (*apadeśa*) arises. Immediately after that, from the aforementioned conjunction which depends upon effort, two simultaneous actions of throwing upward (*utkṣepaṇa*) occur in the upper and lower parts of the arrow. Then, by means of another action of the arrow, a conjunction called "impact" (*abhighāta*) is produced between the upper and lower parts of the arrow. That conjunction, depending upon the momentum (*vega*) inherent in the arrow, produces an upward motion in the arrow that is independent of any further cause.

Depending upon the impact of that action, the hand initiates a momentum (*saṃskāra*) toward upward motion; and due to that [impact], the conjunction of the hand with the ball produces an upward-moving action in the hand as well, even though the previous momentum has been destroyed. Nevertheless, because it is a specific kind of conjunction, the conjunction between the ball and the hand is capable of producing an upward action and is thus able to assist in the initiation of that momentum. Alternatively, the very same previous momentum perishes due to the impact, as it is not stable.

Therefore, since there is no further commencement of an impression (*saṃskāra*) once one already exists, at the very moment when the effortless action of upward motion arises in the arrow due to an impact dependent on an [existing] impression, at that same moment, due to the contact between the hand and the arrow which depends on that very same impression, an effortless action of upward motion also arises in the hand. [This occurs] even against the will of one who desires to manifest heaviness in the midst of the action.

When one desires to raise the hand, an effort arises in the self's region due to the lightness of the hand; taking that effort as the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), from the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*)—namely, the conjunction of the self and the hand—the effect, which is motion, arises in the substance [the hand]. Furthermore, in the case of raising or lowering the hand and so forth, when there is effort, gravity, and external contact, the quality of momentum (*vega*) is also a cause. This applies to the velocity of the action maintained by the lightness of the hand, or to the motions in the feet and other limbs.

Regarding the production of action in the foot: effort (*prayatna*) residing in the self-part of the foot is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), while the conjunction of the foot and the self (*pādātmasaṃyoga*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Previously, lightness and effort in the body should be understood in the same manner as in the case of jumping. Furthermore, regarding the production of action in the body: the conjunction of the body and the self is the non-inherent cause, and effort residing in the self-part of the body is the efficient cause.
One must ask: even when there is the perception of that intrinsic nature, the perception of the body, and the perception of light effort in the body, how does the action of karma arise?
For instance, when one grasps a heavy object with the hand and exerts an upward effort, thinking, "I am lifting the heavy object with my hand."

Immediately after the desire to lift [the pestle], an effort arises from that desire due to the intermediate weight between the hand and the pestle; this results in a specific conjunction with that intermediate weight. Taking that specific effort as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the soul-hand conjunction as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), the action of upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) arises in the hand at that very moment. At that same time, due to the gravity and effort of both the pestle and the effort, and taking the conjunction with the pestle as the non-inherent cause, an action also arises in the pestle. Because of the simultaneity of these causes, the pestle moves away to a distance. When that upward throwing ceases and the desire to throw it up ceases, then, in the absence of further effort, the desire to cast the pestle down with the hand arises. This is the meaning.

Immediately thereafter, even as the effort arises, it arises specifically distinguished like the effort of throwing upward. Taking that effort [as its cause], from the conjunction of the hand and so forth, and from the conjunction of the self and the hand, and from the conjunction of the upper and lower arms, there arise the actions of gravity and effort in the upper and lower arms respectively. Then, by another action of the upper arm, a mutual conjunction characterized by the nature of "upward" is produced between the upper and lower arms. The meaning is that, having thrown [the object] upward, by the action within the upper arm, a conjunction is produced which is the cause for the production of the upward motion in the lower arm.

That conjunction, while producing an upward action in the arrow (*subala*) through the impulse (*vega*) that has reached it—which is a causal condition (*pratyaya*) not preceded by volitional effort (*aprayatnapūrvaka*)—has the impulse as its non-inherent cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) and the arrow as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

Upon the arising of that action, a momentum (*saṃskāra*) is initiated in the arrow; however, the action of leaping (*utpatanakarma*), being non-material and dependent on a conjunction, initiates an impulse in the arrow.

Depending upon that impression (*saṃskāra*), this conjunction with the hand—which is an inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*)—produces an action of upward motion in the hand that is independent of cognition and not preceded by volitional effort (*aprayatnapūrvaka*). This [action] is produced by the same series of successive impulses (*eṣaṇa-paramparā*) as that which was previously mentioned, and it possesses qualities such as being directed toward the target. In the absence of that [volition], the action of upward motion arises in the hand independently of cognition, initiating the momentum of the flight; and because there is no other efficient cause (*apekṣākāraṇa*), it does not continue indefinitely.

Although the previous latent impression (*saṃskāra*) has perished, nevertheless, Padmanābha spoke in the *Ṣaṭkarmopadeśamādhyama* regarding the conjunction of the *subala* and *utkabalas*. The author of the *Ṣaṭkāraka* also stated: "From a specific conjunction alone, due to the particularity of the two [factors], that which is produced by action is indeed what it is. Its sequence consists of the performance of the sixfold nature; it occurs in the state of union with ignorance (*avidyā*), and it occurs in the state of assistance (*sāhāyya*).
In the movements [of the hands], the two [hands] occur sequentially according to the sequence of moving the hand and the mouth;
however, due to their rapid occurrence, they are perceived as simultaneous.
He states another method:

Alternatively, the very same prior impression (*saṃskāra*), due to its impact by a refinement (*saṃskārābhighāta*), remains situated in consciousness because it lacks a [new] object; thus, there is a rule regarding the production of specific cognitions and so forth. An impression does not perish even through conjunction with its own substrate. Therefore, while the impression exists, there is no apprehension of another impression, because the impression depends upon the prior one and is not lost. Consequently, it is understood that when the pleasure possesses the prior impression, there is no apprehension of another impression.

At the very moment when the sequence of upward motion arises in the hand due to the causal condition of the impact and destruction of the [original] formation (*saṃskāra*), at that same moment, the sequence of upward motion also arises in the foot due to the causal condition of the conjunction with the pleasure of the body resulting from the impulse imparted by that same formation.
In the case of movements such as walking, the simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) of the sequences of upward motion in both the hand and the foot is merely a matter of their being perceived together;
this is the procedure regarding the movement of the hands and feet.

When a person, having grasped a javelin with the hand, wishes to throw it and subsequently releases it, then—due to the conjunction of the soul and the mind observing that [intention]—two simultaneous actions of throwing arise in both the javelin and the hand.

When the hand has been discharged, the first action ceases for the purpose of pulling it back; immediately thereafter, a desire arises, "I shall throw it sideways, upwards, far away, or downwards. Following that, an effort associated with that desire arises, and the conjunctions of the hand with the javelin (*tomara*)—depending upon that effort—are called "impulses" (*nodana*). From that, an action is produced in the javelin depending upon the impulse, and from that, a momentum (*saṃskāra*) alone arises. Then, actions of that same kind occur due to the momentum and the impulse, as long as there is no separation from the javelin as previously described. Once the impulse has ceased due to that separation, actions of the hand occur upwards, sideways, not far, or downwards, conforming to the effort, until the fall. This is the procedure for the movement when the hand is released.
To the question, "How is there a process of motion for a substance released from the hand? How does the cause of motion continue to operate? we reply:
It is by means of [the momentum] of the *tomara* (javelin) and so forth.
Regarding the objection to the wording of the Sūtra:
even though both the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) are present [as possible meanings],
the first [the object] is excluded.
Of these two, when one exists, the first—the purpose of the objection—ceases and not the second, according to statements such as "the first to be propitiated" and "the first to arise.
"Immediately after that."

Immediately after the *pravāraṇā*, in the first *niṣeṇu* or in the first rapid *āghaṭṭa*, with the intention "I shall cast [it]," thereupon a corresponding first [movement] is known—sideways, upwards, and downwards; even when the first [movement] sideways, upwards, and downwards is known, and even when the downward-first [movement] is well-established in the absence of [other] directions, the first [movement] is known as having traversed the path in a distant place, and likewise in drawing [it] toward oneself and in space, according to the rules. Thus it is known through words and meanings corresponding thereto.

In that context, the conjunction of the hand and the javelin (*tomara*)—which is called "impulsion" (*nodana*)—is the cause of the javelin’s being impelled and the hand’s acting as the impeller. Because it serves as the cause for the javelin’s initial state corresponding to the [agent's] desire, when the javelin arises sequentially, its action, depending upon that impulsion, initiates a momentum (*saṃskāra*) within the javelin. Consequently, it moves like a sword;
the meaning is that the successive movements of the javelin occur in accordance with the [desired] trajectory of a sword.
Likewise, there is the method of movement for those discharged from a mechanical device (yantra).

When one who has exhausted his strength and whose exertion is spent takes up a bow with his right hand—using a blade as sharp as a razor—and having drawn the string back to the ear, he forms the desire to pull it; this is called the "pulling of the bowstring" (*vajreṣṭhākarṣaṇāstrīhatanu*).

Immediately thereafter, at the very moment that action arises in the hand due to the conjunction of the hand and the thumb—which depends upon the first [action]—at that same moment, actions arise in the bowstring and the two ends of the bow due to the conjunction of the thumb and the other [hand], depending upon that same first action of the hand and the conjunction of the bowstring and the hand; and actions arise in the two ends of the bow due to the conjunction of the string and the tips of the bow, depending upon that same previously specified conjunction of the hand and the bowstring—all of this occurring simultaneously.

Thus, regarding the drawing back [of the bow] for the purpose of discharge, the knowledge that "one must not go beyond this point" arises from the previous drawing back; consequently, the first [moment] of the object's [motion] perishes. Thereafter, it is no longer produced by a subsequent awakening. Immediately following that, independent of the first [moment], the portion [of the action] that constitutes the cause for the production of the self [in the next moment] settles upon the hand with the tips of one's own thumbs, having reached the front.

Then, from the separation [of the bowstring], when all [the fingers] are positioned with the tips of the thumbs placed [on the string], and the obstructing [fingers] are held back, the stabilizing impression (*sthitisthāpaka-saṃskāra*) keeps the curved bow in its original state. At that time, depending upon that very impression, through the contact of the hand and the fingers joined with the bowstring, the string is gradually released toward the arrow; by means of that impression, it first produces an impression on the string. Subsequently, the contact of the arrow with the string and so forth is the impulsion (*nodana*); from that, the action of the arrow proceeds, and depending upon the iron [of the arrow], it brings about an impulse (*saṃskāra*) in itself.

Therefore, actions arise from the impulse assisted by the residual potency (*saṃskāra*) for as long as the collection of factors such as the arrow and the bowstring remains; that is, until the impulse has ceased after three parts [of the flight], subsequent potencies of the arrow arise from the action [itself] until its fall.
Many actions occur sequentially due to the multiplicity of conjunctions; however, a single residual potency is appropriate, because there is no cause for requiring further actions in the interval.

Having performed the obstruction (*vyāghāta*) and the favoring (*anugrāhya*) and so forth, with the hand of tranquility (*śama*), one should grasp the bow firmly by its lower end (*prajanitrī*). With the right hand, having joined the arrow with its point directed forward to the bowstring, and having released the string that was in contact with the arrow, one takes hold of it and performs the subsequent action. Following with the raised end is the "following" (*anuvṛtti*).

"Light" (*jyotis*) refers to the bow; "bow" (*dhanus*) is the designation for the weapon. Since the string (*jyā*) and the arrow (*iṣu*) exist together for the sake of victory (*jeṣa*), they are called "victory-string" (*jeṣujyā*). Thus, the form of the composite bow (*saṅgrahadhanus*) is the right shadow, being consistent with the eightfold action (*aṣṭakriyā*).

Immediately thereafter, from the conjunction of the self and the hand depending upon effort, action arises in the thumb and the fingers of the hand at the very moment of striking the self; simultaneously, from the conjunction of the bowstring and the arrow depending upon that effort, action arises in the bowstring and the arrow. Furthermore, from the conjunctions of the bowstring and the hand—depending upon the conjunction of the bowstring and the fist characterized by effort—action arises in the bow. All of this occurs through the simultaneous application of its causes.

Thus, from the drawing back [of the bow], there is the cognition: "I am grasping the arrow with this hand which has drawn the bow. Therefore, by that drawing back, there is the destruction of the effort consisting of the drawing back of the bow.

Then follows the desire for the release of the arrow and the string, and immediately after that, an effort for the sake of releasing them. Following that, from the conjunction of the self and the hand, there is the instruction on the action of the sense organ of touch regarding the action of the fingers.

In the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), there are divisions consisting of the principles (*tattva*), reflections, forms, and the qualities of the arrow; from that division, there arises the state of conjunction and disjunction with the bowstring. When the conjunction [with the string] is destroyed, due to the absence of an obstructing factor, the elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*)—which is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) residing in the wood—is activated. That elasticity, having become manifest, establishes the arrow in its state. Through the continuous succession of that latent impression, and due to the connection with the shadow (the reflection), a sequence arises in the shadow as well. At that moment, the prior cause—the prior conjunction of the arrow with the string—produces a latent impression called "velocity" (*vega*) within the shadow. Depending upon that latent impression, the conjunction of the arrow with the string acts as an impulsion (*nodana*); because it is the cause of the arrow's repeated movement, it is called impulsion. From that impulsion, a sequence of subsequent actions is initiated through the medium of the latent impression. From that latent impression, which originates from the impulsion and the shadow, successive actions occur directly until the desire for the aim is fulfilled. Once the impulsion has ceased due to the occurrence of disjunction and other factors, the subsequent actions arise solely from the latent impression known as velocity, continuing until the fall. And the fall occurs due to the cause of gravity (*gurutva*) and the exhaustion of the latent impression.
Now, an objection is raised: "Why are there many steps occurring sequentially?

The intention [of the objection] is this: since there are many steps occurring sequentially during the interval between the yoga and its result despite the absence of deviation, why is it postulated that they occur in sequence? Why is it not rather postulated that the action itself is non-sequential?
As it is said: "Because of the multiplicity of conjunctions.

It is established that action ends with the final subsequent conjunction; however, in the interval between [the first and last points], many conjunctions are observed. Therefore, it is accepted that there are many successive steps.

However, because there is no cause for action in the subsequent parts [of the body], action initiated by impulsion or impact does not produce momentum (*saṃskāra*) in those subsequent forms; it produces only action, because of the absence of that which is called velocity (*vega*).

In the interval [of flight], there is neither a push nor an impact at that time; rather, a specific *saṃskāra* (impulse) produced by the action of the arrow upon the contact with the bowstring at the first moment persists until its fall. And as its capacity for performing its function gradually diminishes, its effect arises in a progressively slower sequence—slower, slower still—and so on, until it finally ceases, just as the fruit of crossing a river is either advanced or delayed as one grows old.
Thus, even among external things denoted by such terms, internal [mental] construction does not apply.
Regarding external things not so denoted, there are four types of action—namely, those caused by water, air, fire, and effort—which consist solely of motion arising from impulsion and the like.
Their differentiation arises from gravity, fluidity, velocity, and effort; it is manifold, depending on various factors and being independent of superimposition.

And a particular conjunction is not the cause of the action of the sense organ (*akṣa*) which is the reason for the division of the sound; therefore, even though there is a multiplicity of great elements (*mahābhūta*), action occurs [in them].
He brings forward [the argument] with the words "that which...
(*yad iti*).

Regarding the four external great elements (*mahābhūta*) when they are not [otherwise] denoted, movement occurs from impulsion (*nodana*) and so forth, and it is of the nature of going by itself; thus, according to the second view mentioned by the Sāṅkhya, action consists solely of the nature of going in a sequential manner, and not of throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*), throwing downwards (*apakṣepaṇa*), and so on. It has been stated that at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), action arises from impulsion and so forth. Now, what is "impulsion" (*nodana*) in this context? He says:

In this context, *nodana* (impulsion) is said to be a particular kind of conjunction produced by gravity, fluidity, and velocity—either collectively or individually—as well as a particular conjunction with the agent. Regarding this, it is stated:
"Impulsion is the cause of the action that does not result in disjunction.
This means that impulsion is directly perceived as the cause of that action which does not produce mutual disjunction between the object being impelled (*nodya*) and the impeller (*nodaka*).

Just as in the case of earth situated in mud: that particular conjunction which depends on velocity (*vega*) and is the cause of a single action that results in disjunction is called "impact" (*abhighāta*). From that as well, action arises in the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), as when hard objects such as stones and the like are struck. Likewise, in the case of earth situated in mud being stepped upon or struck by feet and so forth, there is a conjunction—dependent on either impulsion (*nodana*) or impact, or dependent on both—which is a "conjunction with the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*). From that as well, action arises in earth and the other elements.
Action also arises in those regions which are neither pushed nor struck.
When there is an absence of conjunction with the earth, water, gravity, disjunction, weight, effort, and velocity, downward motion occurs due to gravity,
as is observed in the case of a body such as that of Subala.
Even there, however, the second and subsequent [motions] depend upon gravity and the impression (*saṃskāra*).

What is meant by this conjunction? It is that which impels, is impelled, or causes impulsion, and not otherwise; therefore, it is called "impulsion" (*nodana*). However, he does not state that impulsion is the cause of action, as in the example: "on the earth situated in mud. When a small wooden block placed gently on top of mud in the earth is capable of moving due to its prior momentum, then the conjunction with the wooden block, depending upon gravity, is impulsion.

When a clod of earth is struck with effort from a distance, then the conjunction dependent on gravity, effort, and velocity is *nodana* (impulsion); when it is struck by water, then the conjunction dependent on all [three] is *nodana*. This should be understood according to the circumstances. Thus ends the description of perceptible action among actions.

That conjunction which is the cause of a single action that produces disjunction is dependent [on other factors]. For instance, the mutual disjunction of earth, water, fire, and air arises from a specific conjunction which is the sole cause of that very action; that specific conjunction is dependent [on other factors]. Therefore, action also occurs among many great elements (*mahābhūta*), as when stones and other objects are struck at a distance.

Impulsion (*nodana*) is the cause of only that single action which has mutual non-separation as its effect, not of that which has mutual separation as its effect. Likewise, impact (*abhighāta*), fire, and wind are also causes of only that single action which has mutual separation as its effect, not of that which has mutual non-separation as its effect; thus they are the causes of an action that is to be inferred. Conjunction through conjunction (*saṃyukta-saṃyoga*) is now to be explained.
[This occurs] when [the body] is being moved by the feet and so forth.
Furthermore, when the earth is being pushed or struck by a foot, action is observed even in those parts that are neither pushed nor struck.
In that case, the cause is conjunction itself, which consists of the conjunction of those other parts with the parts being pushed or struck.
For example, when a striker strikes a patch of ground and does not rise up slightly, the cause for the action in those other parts is the conjunction of what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*).
He states that gravity is the cause of action:

when there is an absence of conjunction—which maintains the unity of earth and space—then falling occurs due to gravity; this is indeed downward motion, as in the case of a muñja grass stalk or a rope being devoid [of support].
In the absence of contact with the hand, which prevents gravity, the upward motion of a clay ball is due to the manifestation [of action] from gravity.

Similarly, in the absence of a stream that counteracts gravity, the falling of the body occurs because of the absence of any other effort or velocity; thus, the falling is due to gravity. Among these, the first [instance of falling] arises from gravity alone, while the second and subsequent instances arise from both gravity and momentum (*saṃskāra*).

Among those [actions], such as the throwing of a deer and so forth, the first action arises due to gravity; by that action, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced. Immediately thereafter, subsequent actions arise from both gravity and the latent impression. Furthermore, in each case, there is another [action] due to the maintenance of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Regarding the threefold movement of water that has become a stream, its motion occurs because of its solidity; how then can there be a fault regarding momentariness? The fluidity of the parts is obstructed by its conjunction with the solid [earth], and the fluidity inherent in the substance is likewise obstructed by that very same [solidity]. Furthermore, the fluidities of each successive part are obstructed by the conjunctions of those [parts] with one another.

But when the central part is destroyed by the blow, then, because the whole substance (*avayavidravya*) is obstructed, there is no cause for the production of the effect; however, for the constituent parts (*avayavadravya*) situated nearby and for the successive subsequent parts, activity is attained due to the absence of any obstruction.

Then, through the successive conjunctions of those very [atoms] facing one another, and upon the destruction of the previous substance, a new substance is commenced by the constituent parts (*avayava*) abiding in the manner that will be described hereafter. In that case, substantiality (*dravyatva*) arises preceded by the qualities of the causes; and therein, when the conjoined causes move with great force, the action that arises in the constituent part is called "spontaneous motion" (*ispandana*).
It explains the causality of substance (*dravya*).

The meaning is as follows: when atoms that desire earth and so forth move toward the attainment of a location such as a field, there is a vibration (*spandana*) in the atom due to the substance [of effort]; that vibration which results in the attainment of a location such as a field is supported by the substance.
The question is: "How so?"
The state of being bowed down in all directions.

When there is a conjunction with silver on all sides—that is, a complete conjunction—the substantiality (*dravyatva*) or the motion [of the parts] does not act, being obstructed by the wheel-like substance. That which is inherent in the wheel-like substance is itself obstructed by that very [conjunction]. In the first part where the conjunction with silver occurs, the substantiality of that first part-substance is obstructed by that very conjunction with silver. However, the subsequent part-substances are obstructed by "conjunctions of the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*). Because of the conjunction of another part with the part already conjoined with silver, the substantiality of that other part is obstructed.
By this very principle—that [the power] of the subsequent [element] is obstructed due to conjunction with that [preceding one]—the successive substances are obstructed.

But when a distinction in the cause is made, then even for that which is obstructed on all sides and non-fluid, there is no fault regarding the production of the effect; for although it is obstructed on all sides, there is no exit by way of a very small path created in one part of a large dimension. However, for that which possesses fluidity due to the presence of a distinct cause, there is the attainment of functional activity, because even a small amount of fluidity can possibly exit through that path.

When that [mind] attains its functional activity (*vṛtti-lābha*), since there is no longer any obstruction even for the substances located at a distance of hundreds of *yojanas*, they too attain their functional activity and perform their own respective effects.
Consequently, among those [substances] in conjunction, only those situated directly in front [are affected].

Just as the one situated nearest to the cause is the first to face it, so too the one situated near that, and the one situated near that; in this manner, all [substances] successively face it. And these states of facing one another are not mutually obstructed; rather, they possess a specific directionality (*diṅ-niyama*) according to the sequence of their respective actions.

But they explain that there is an intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) such that they become mutually conjoined; this has been stated [previously]. Or rather, it was said that the intention belongs precisely to those who have spoken.
Furthermore, there is no deficiency in the immeasurables; they are designated through a combination of one and a half [units], and "Niṣadhiṣaṇa" is found as another numerical designation.

Then, upon the destruction of the previous conjunction of parts and the non-destruction of the [resultant] whole, it is designated as a substance by means of its connection with the qualities residing in a continuous series. When that [substance] is produced from causes whose qualities are prior [to it], it is called "substantiality" (*dravyatva*). Furthermore, when there is a manifestation of length and so forth through the substantiality of the constituent parts, that is called "substantiality"; and when, due to the continuity of the conjoined causes, a certain action arises in the composite whole, that is its "flowing" (*syandana*) because of its substantiality.

And when that substantiality (dravyatva) has arisen in it, the continuity of the parts of the causes is perceived as a manifestation of the process of becoming a mass; and since there is fluidity in the composite whole, its sequential movement is perceived through the act of flowing.
The sūtra beginning with "From volitional formation (saṃskāra), there is karma," and likewise the wheel and so forth;
[this refers to] the conjunctions and disjunctions of its own parts with specific directions and locations on its sides.

[The definition of] action (*karman*) is that which, being a whole (*avayavin*) by virtue of its nature as "cowness" (*gotva*), is the cause of conjunctions and disjunctions in indefinite directions and locations due to *saṃskāra*, and which consists in conjunction with many substances.
Thus [it is said].
The stages of life are specific modes of movement.
The sūtra beginning with “From formative forces (saṃskāra), karma arises” [is cited].
Likewise, in the case of the wheel and so forth, the word “likewise” (tathā) depends upon the word “just as” (yathā), because it is a conditional correlative. (4)
The meaning is that just as work is produced from the preparation of wood in the case of walls and so forth, so it occurs in the case of wheels and other such things;
it should be viewed as being like a wealth-giver.
[This applies] to each of the parts on both sides.

In the production of conjunctions and disjunctions with fixed directions and locations, that action which arises from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the whole (*avayavin*) and serves as the cause for conjunctions and disjunctions with non-fixed directions and locations is to be understood. [This occurs] with those specific directions and locations situated on the sides.

When conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts have arisen, that action which is known to be the cause of the conjunctions and disjunctions of the whole with objects in indefinite directions due to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) should be observed.

First, an action arises in the whole, such as a wheel, from its conjunction with a stick; thereafter, subsequent actions arise from the impulse (*nodana*) and other determinate causes, as well as from the latent impression.
Thus, due to momentum (*vega*), when the stick is conjoined [with the wheel], action arises in the parts of the wheel conjoined with the stick;

and in other parts, due to conjunction-with-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*), actions arise in the parts of the wheel conjoined with the stick. Furthermore, due to the impulse (*saṃskāra*) of others and due to disjunction-with-the-conjoined (*saṃyuktavibhāga*), there is no action in the wheel itself or in its own constituent parts, but rather [action arises] solely from impulse.
He summarizes:

"These and others are the specific types of motion. However, action in the wind known as *prāṇa* arises from the conjunction of the self and the wind, depending upon an effort preceded by desire or aversion, because its conformity to desire is observed; whereas in deep sleep, it arises depending upon an effort preceded by the mere maintenance of life.

Although ether (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*dik*), and the self (*ātman*) possess the status of substances, they are inactive, because they lack rapidity, like [the qualities of] being small and so forth.

Since a corporeal form possesses the dimension of a substance that can occupy multiple locations, its action follows accordingly; however, such [action] does not exist in space and the other [substances], and therefore they have no connection with action.
In the wind called *prāṇa*, action arises from the conjunction of the self and the wind, depending upon an effort preceded by desire or aversion.

How is this known? To this he says: because it is observed to follow desire. In the performance of actions such as bending the body, the activity of *prāṇa* is perceived as following one's desire; it does not occur in the absence of effort toward that object, nor in cases contrary to it. Furthermore, the activity of *prāṇa* also occurs through aversion toward an object contrary to one's will; therefore, it depends on a specific kind of effort.

In deep sleep, the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) depends upon an effort preceded by the [desire for] life; the activity of the vital breath in deep sleep is the effect of an effort, because it is an activity of the vital breath, just like the activity of the vital breath during the waking state. And that [effort] is not preceded by desire or aversion, because of the absence of desire and aversion in deep sleep; therefore, it is determined to be preceded solely by the [desire for] life, since the maintenance of the vital breath is dependent upon that. He explains why the production of activity is not observed in the four great elements, beginning with air: *In the four great elements, excluding space and the others, why is the production of activity not seen?* He says: [the answer follows].
Regarding the phrase "of space, time, direction, and the self":
action is pervaded by corporeality, and since corporeality does not exist in space and the others, it follows that the existence of action also does not exist there; this is the meaning.
He explains this very point as follows:
By the words "of the form," etc.,
it is caused by that.

Action arises in the mind, which is its own object, merely from the connection between the sense organ and the self; [action] arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind depending on effort preceded by desire or aversion, because [otherwise] there would be the perception of other objects even without the accomplishment of another's intention;
[action arises] from effort preceded by the impulse for life at the time of awakening for one who is asleep;
and action occurring outside of the prescribed occasions (aparva) and occasional action arise from the conjunction of the self and the mind depending on no [external] cause.

How is it that when there is awakening due to the operation of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are concomitants of life, and the conceit "I am" arises—then, because of the deficiency of those two [merit and demerit] as concomitants of life, and because of the deficiency of the previous single effort, there arises from the contact of the self and the mind, aided by the two [merit and demerit] which have obtained their function and by the vital breaths, a cause for the production of the parts of the body and so forth, which is capable of liberation (*apavarga*).

Then, having emerged from the body, it becomes connected by those very two—the dharma and the medicinal herbs—with the *ativāhika* (conveying) body; and having transferred there and reached heaven or hell, it becomes connected with a body characterized by its specific gravity (*āśraya-gurutva*). The movement of karma is for the purpose of that conjunction.
Furthermore, for yogis, there is the outward and inward movement of the mind—that is, the mental faculty—to the intended location and back again.
Likewise, at all times, karma produced by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) acts to bring about connection with the body through direct perception.

In the same way, whatever else among the great elements (*mahābhūta*) has an unperceived cause according to both scripture and inference, yet is capable of performing benefit or harm, that too is brought about by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). For example: the arousal of the great elements when there is the upward or oblique movement of sound and musical instruments as described in the *Saṃgīti*;
and the movement of consecrated gems toward the hand that holds them.
And this is the non-approaching of iron toward a magnet.
Thus ends the category of action (*karma*) in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*.
He states the cause of action in the mind: "In the sixfold apprehension.

For a waking person, when there is a sixfold apprehension in the mind—that is, when the mind is directed toward the body—there arises an action for the purpose of connecting the mind with another sense organ; this consists of the persistence of an impulse preceded by a desire to project [the mind], and an effort preceded by will and aversion, originating from the conjunction of the self and the mind, and so forth.
"Action has the mind as its cause. To explain this statement, he says:

because the perception of objects by means of one sense organ is observed even when there is no contact with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); for in the waking state, the perception of objects by means of one sense organ, such as the eye, is seen to occur through the sequence of other sense organs.

When a person desires to perceive a form, then he sees the form; when he desires to perceive a taste, then he tastes the taste, not otherwise. Since it has been stated that the external sense organ possesses the capacity to grasp its object only through the mediation of the internal organ (manas), it is understood that activity arises preceded by desire and aversion. As for the phrase "of the seen": in the case of one who was asleep and then awakened, the activity of the mind at the time of waking occurs due to the conjunction of the self with the life-force (jīvana) and the specific recognition [of the object].
"He says 'capaṣapeṇa'.
He explains this as well, preceded by a question beginning with "How so? and so forth.

The conjunction of the self with the vital breaths constitutes its life. When these [vital breaths] act as auxiliaries for the performance of their own specific functions, just as [the body acts] together with the self, then from the exhaustion of those [functions], there is awakening and destruction. Or, when they are mutually facing one another, there is a mutual obstruction, or the performance of their own specific functions; thus, due to the deficiency of the two which assist life—just as in the case of the two [eyes]—there is an absence. This is because of the non-perception of the prior perception of life, following the observation of that very state. Since it has been established that the fruit must be experienced in another body upon reaching this body, it follows that the fruit is to be enjoyed in a subsequent body according to the respective suitability of those two.

When the functioning of those [latent dispositions] that are to be experienced in this present body has been obtained—because they have become weak due to being experienced according to their nature—and no further effect is produced for those to be experienced in another body; and when there is awakening to the experience of this present body according to its nature, then the obtaining of the functioning of those to be experienced in another body is known to be obstructed by the absence of such conditions. When their functioning has been obtained and delusion is destroyed, the karma that was to be experienced in the body ceases through liberation. Furthermore, the cause of the separation from the body, which is the conjunction of the self with the mind, is exhausted through liberation.

When the mind, having obtained its activity through the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) of the conjunction between the self and the mind—which is characterized by the absence of pride and patience—and having the self as its inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), becomes a contributory cause (nimittakāraṇa) for the knowledge of reality; immediately thereafter, the knower of reality, having cast off the gross physical body, causes that mind—which has already attained its activity—to become connected with the subtle body (ātivāhikaśarīra). Following that, the mind, having reached the end of that subtle body, goes to heaven or to hell, and having gone there, it becomes connected with a body corresponding to its support and corresponding to its karma.
Whether one goes to heaven or to hell, the body must necessarily be connected with the mind, for otherwise enjoyment in those regions would be impossible.
Nor can the mind's connection with another body be said to be merely accidental, as it is not all-pervading.

Furthermore, such a description of the mind is not possible for it in isolation, because apart from the state following the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), there is no activity of the mind without a body.

Therefore, prior to the acquisition of a new body, another body—extremely subtle, imperceptible, and produced by the excellence of the conjunction of the soul with the mind, the qualities, the residual impressions (*anuśaya*), and the life-force (*āyuṣ*)—is postulated.

That body, moreover, because it enables the movement of the mind to regions such as heaven or hell and because it is singular at the beginning [of that journey], is called the *ativāhika* (conveying) body.

In the interval between death and birth, the movement of the mind occurs through its conjunction with the body; this is established by the fact that it transcends the state following the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), provided that karma is something distinct [from the mind]. Because it is the action of the mind, it is observed in the actions of the visible vehicle-body. This is the definition of the category of generality (*sāmānya*).
It is "observed" (*dṛśyate*);
and for the sake of connecting the true nature [of things], there is the sequential application of prefixes.

Therefore, for us who possess the capacity for vision, there is a sequential movement [of the mind] for the sake of conjunction with the mind by means of the body produced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And for yogins, there is the going to and returning from their desired location by means of the mind, which has left the body and is situated externally.
Likewise, it is established that the sequential movement of the mind is undertaken for the sake of connection with the body through direct perception at all times.

Not only this much, but everything else as well—namely, that which among the great elements (*mahābhūta*) has an unperceived cause through both direct perception and inference, yet functions as a causal factor—that too has been explained by the diligent [author].

Just as in the case of sound and the sequence of atoms, an unutterable [force] has been explained by the diligent; likewise, in the case of movement, there is the motion of the great elements and the mountains and so forth due to their awakening.
At the time of examination, there is the movement toward the mass of fire for those who have received the consecration.
And because it is not pleasing even to the eye, it is joined with the state of being devoid of consciousness.
Action is the supreme reality, being the basis for the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful; once this is understood, let your intellect act accordingly.
Thus ends the section on the sequential meaning of the categories in the *Nyāyakandalī* commentary on the *Padārthapraveśa*, composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Mīmāṃsaka.
Now follows the definition of the category of generality (*sāmānya*).
Generality is of two kinds: lower (*apara*) and higher (*para*).

It pervades all its own objects, possesses a non-different nature, and subsists in many [individuals]. Because it consists of a single substance and yet has a manifold nature, it produces a cognition that conforms to its own form; existing continuously in its substrates without distinction from its own form, it is the cause of the cognition of recurrence (*anuvṛtti*).

How is it that a specific [cognition] depends upon a universal? Because when knowledge arises in a continuous stream, there are latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated cognitions; and through the examination of this continuity, that which persists [through change] is not found to exist as a [real] universal.
In that regard, in the case of a jar and so forth, the cause of the recurring cognition is simply something else.

Just as there is a recurrence of the cognition "blue, blue" with respect to various distinct substances such as cloth, wood, or *kṛṣṇala* seeds, based on a single substance that is blue, so too there is a recurrence of the cognition "substance, substance" with respect to substances, qualities, and actions which are themselves distinct from one another. And since that [recurrence] arises from a different entity (*arthāntara*) called "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), it is established that this "different entity" is substance-ness.

Furthermore, because of its connection with existence (*sattā*), there is a recurrence of the cognition "substance, substance"; therefore, it (substance-ness) must indeed be denoted by a separate word.

Furthermore, substance-ness (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth, are both universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*), because they are inclusive, pervasive, and serve as causes [of cognition].

Among these, substance-ness is a universal because it is the cause of inclusion among earth and the other substances which are mutually distinct; it is a particular because it is the cause of exclusion from qualities and actions.

Likewise, quality-ness is a universal because it is the cause of inclusion among color and the other qualities which are mutually distinct; it is a particular because it is the cause of exclusion from substances and actions.

Similarly, "action-ness" (*karmatva*) is a generality because it is the cause of a recurring cognition among mutually distinct actions such as upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*), and it is a particularity because it is the cause of the exclusion [of those actions] from substances and qualities.

In this same way, the status of being both a generality and a particularity is established for earth-ness, form-ness, upward-throwing-ness, cow-ness, moon-ness, cloth-ness, and so forth, according to whether they are encountered in the east or the west, by virtue of their being causes of recurrence and exclusion.

However, these [higher categories] such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) are primarily generalities because their scope is extensive; yet they are designated as "particularities" (*viśeṣa*) in a secondary sense because they differentiate their own substrates.
Victorious are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— the Supreme Selves of the universe— who are the causes of the creation, preservation, and destruction of the world.
The universal (sāmānya) shall be explained.
The universal is of two kinds: the higher and the lower.
The explanation of the lower has already been provided without fault.

Some maintain that all particulars are identical; in order to refute this, he says: "The determination of the validity of a particular belongs to the universal itself, because it consists in the cognition of its own object. That universal which is perceived in a particular instance—that instance is its own object. Since the cognition of the property [the universal] therein occurs through the perception of its own remainder (the particular), it is established as such.
When there is the state of being a sensation remaining in the void, non-apprehension itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Since the universal exists in one individual (*piṇḍa*) by a certain nature that constitutes its own cognition, it exists in another individual by that very same nature; this is because there is no distinction in the cognition of it. That it exists in many individuals as the cognizer of them—that is, that it exists in multiple locations with a certain nature—is to be established by the force of common experience.

Indeed, there is no such thing as an "inconsistency" regarding an object already apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, duality and so forth do not reside in a single [individual] due to its being non-different from its friends [or similar instances]. Therefore, the particular (*viśeṣa*) does not touch upon the universal (*sāmānya*). To explain: that which is the cognition of a substance is the universal. When an observer perceives it in one individual (*piṇḍa*), he produces the notion "this is the same" because he perceives the persistence of its own nature even in another individual. If it were merely a signifier for what was not seen in the observed individual, then—since the cognition "cow" occurs—the universal would not exist; however, duality and so forth do not function in this manner, and thus they constitute the distinction.

Regarding the suffix *vati* [denoting "that which exists in many"]: when a single substance, by virtue of following its own essential nature (*svātmasvarūpa*), is the cause of cognition, that is the definition of a universal (*sāmānya*). He explains this very point through the words:
"by means of the distinction of its own nature" (*svarūpabhedeneti*).

In whatever individual object (*piṇḍa*) a certain essential nature (*svarūpa*) exists, that same nature exists in other instances of its manifestation as well; therefore, that which—by means of verbal instruction (*pravacana*)—subsists immediately following [the perception of] the aforementioned particulars without abandoning them, and which serves as the cause for the cognition and conceptualization of one's own observation, and the cause for the recognition of the persistence of the essential nature, is *sāmānya* (the universal).
"How so? is the question of the opponent.
The meaning is: "How does the universal subsist in multiple individual objects?"
He states the answer:
"With respect to each individual object" (*pratipiṇḍam*).

Just as there is a dependence upon a universal with respect to each and every individual object (*piṇḍe piṇḍe prati*) when cognition arises, that which the intellect attains by means of this [process]—namely, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced—and through the review and recollection of the stream of cognitions thus established, that which persists as a continuous concomitant is the universal (*sāmānya*).

What is meant is this: when a universal is perceived in one individual object (*piṇḍa*) and that same universal is recognized (*pratyabhijñāna*) in another individual object, it is understood that a single entity subsists in many.
For this very reason, any arguments that might contradict this are set aside due to their conflict with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Indeed, those who possess true knowledge declare, based on direct perception, that the universal is of two kinds: the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*).

In that regard, the supreme eternal universal (*sanātanasāmānya*) is precisely the cause of the cognition of persistence (*anuvṛttipratyaya*). Although it is perceived in each individual instance, it nevertheless serves as a basis for inference with respect to particular locations (*viśeṣapada*),
just like the production of mutually distinct [entities].
That is equivalent [to the previous argument].

The persistence of the cognition "this" with respect to the six categories beginning with substance is based on a distinct [underlying] cognition, because it is a persistent cognition across three [categories], just like the persistence of the cognition of "blue" and so forth in the case of "substance-ness" and the rest.

Since the suffix *san* produces a persistent cognition regarding substance and the other categories without contradicting it, it is therefore a universal (*sāmānya*) and not a particular (*viśeṣa*), according to the Teacher [Uddyotakara].

Furthermore, with respect to substance-ness (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), and so forth, they are both universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*), because they are the causes of inclusive cognition (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusive cognition (*vyāvṛtti*). Substance-ness is a universal because it is the cause of the inclusive cognition [of "substance"] among substances; it is a particular because it is the cause of the exclusion [of substances] from qualities and actions.
