Quality-ness is a universal because it is the cause of the inclusive cognition [of "quality"] among qualities; it is a particular because it is the cause of the cognition of the exclusion [of qualities] from substances and actions.

Likewise, "action-ness" (*karmatva*) is a generality (*sāmānya*) because it is the cause of a recurring cognition through its mutual qualification [of individual actions], and it is a particularity (*viśeṣa*) because it is the cause of the exclusion [of actions] from substances and qualities.

He states that even for those things not conjoined with [the universal] "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth, there exists the state of being both a generality and a particularity, because they are the causes of recurring and exclusive cognitions; thus he says: "If this... and so on.
Universal properties (*sāmānya*) pertaining to living beings include "cowness," "horseness," and so forth; those not pertaining to living beings include "jar-ness," "cloth-ness," and so forth.

Is the status of universal properties such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) on the level of reality like that of universals, or like that of particulars (*viśeṣa*), or like that of ultimate particulars (*antya-viśeṣa*), or is it non-existence? [The author] says:
"Because they do not exist [ultimately]."

The state of being common is "generality" (*sāmānya*); thus, the definition of generality exists in [categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*). However, the definition of a particular (*viśeṣa*)—namely, that which is cognized in its own object and distinguishes it—does not exist [in them]. Therefore, by primary application, they are only generalities and not particulars; they obtain the definition of a particular only through metaphorical usage.

For a particularity (*viśeṣa*), which perceives its own object, distinguishes even [categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) from those of a different class; it is by this much capacity that the application of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) proceeds.
The distinctness of *sāmānya* (universality) as a category separate from substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*) is established by the difference in its characteristics.
For this very reason, it is eternal.

Furthermore, because of its restricted occurrence within substances and so forth, and because of the difference in the cognitions [it produces], it is both distinct from and not other than those [substances, qualities, and actions].
Each [universal] is a unity because it possesses its own specific characteristics and lacks any further specific characteristics.
For this very reason, universals occupy limited spaces; nevertheless, due to the restriction of perception and the restriction of causal complexes, they function toward their own respective objects.
Furthermore, in the intervals between them, they are designated as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), production (*utpatti*), and so forth.

Thus ends the section on the category of generality (*sāmānya*) in the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*. [The following is] the determination that generality is not distinct from substance and the other categories. [An objection: "Generality-ness" (*dravyatva*) and the like are not distinct from substance and the rest, because they do not possess a form separate from the individual (*vyakti*). To this, he says, in accordance with the logic for determining the meaning of separateness: "Because of the difference in definition" (*lakṣaṇabhedāt*).

Since the four categories—substance, quality, action, and generality—are distinct from one another, and since the properties such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth are cognizable by their own specific intellects and are distinct from the substances themselves, these properties such as "substanceness" must be separate entities from substance, quality, and action due to the difference in their definitions and the difference in their cognition.
For this very reason, they are eternal.

Precisely because the generality is distinct from substance and the others, it is therefore eternal; for if there were no distinction between the generality and the substance and so forth, then upon the destruction of the substance, the generality would be destroyed, and with the non-production of the substance, the generality would not be produced. However, since there is a distinction, this [consequence] does not apply, as is asserted.

Now, some say: "The cognition that follows through diverse individuals is the universal (*sāmānya*)," and they define it as "ascertainment" (*vyavasāya*). Furthermore, this [cognition] does not manifest two distinct entities—one as the universal and the other as the particular—within each individual substance such as a cow or a person, independently; nor does it manifest a relationship of qualifier and qualified, because [the cognition] does not arise in the form "cowness" or "that which possesses cowness."

However, this cognition which grasps identity [is established] because of the observation that Caitra’s nature is not distinct from his self, and because the two are perceived as mutually inclusive, thereby precluding the possibility of any other intrinsic form. For the nature of "cowness" itself—and indeed of any other universal—is both the exclusion of what is other and the inclusion of its own particulars; likewise, the nature of the individual cow is both the inclusion of its own members and the exclusion of others. Apart from this mutual identity, no other distinction can be specified.

Furthermore, it is not tenable that its very nature is the same as its relation, because for that which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), there can be no correlate. Therefore, the connection with its own genus is its reality by virtue of its own essential identity. In this way, even the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) is contradicted;
for just as the brindled cow (*śāvaleya*) is perceived in the cognition "this is a cow," so too is the black-spotted cow (*bāhuleya*).

Furthermore, there is no learned person who would say that only a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow) is a cow and not a *bāhuleya* (a black cow); rather, for all of them, there is a single genus (*jāti*), such that "this is a cow" and "that too is a cow.

In that case, once it is established through the force of cognition that the cowness (*gotva*) inherent in the *śābaleya* is also inherent in the *bāhuleya*, even its difference from the *śābaleya* is contradicted.
For this indeed is the difference of a universal from a previous individual: namely, that it consists in being the very nature of another individual.
And this very nature of being a universal consists in having a dual nature.

If it is argued that this is contradictory because it depends upon both difference and non-difference, we reply: no, for it is not possible for you to assert this contradiction through logical reasoning.

That which is contradictory is only so-called where it is always perceived by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as such; however, where it is perceived by the intellect (*buddhi*) in exactly that way, the assertion of contradiction itself is contradictory.

If you argue that "it was seen in one way [previously] but not so now," then is even perception (*pratyakṣa*) merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) like inference (*anumāna*) and other means? This is a mere assertion of a partial truth.

If one proceeds toward an object always as it is perceived by many, then that object cannot be rejected on the grounds of being merely seen for one's own sake; for there would be no stability of the self for anyone who has attained anything. Therefore, the universal (*sāmānya*) is pervasive, inseparable from others, and exists in the intermediate state between them; it is both eternal and non-eternal, and is not restricted to a single point.
This has been explained in the *Viśeṣa*:

does the cognition grasp a non-distinct form for both the universal (*jāti*) and the name (*saṃjñā*) because of the perception of them as such; or does it grasp them as being non-different from one another; or rather, does it grasp their forms as mutually distinct?

In the first case, there would be only a single entity, for two things cannot possess a single nature. This is because the diversity of cognitions regarding non-distinct forms would otherwise result in a lack of distinction [between the entities].

In the second case, however, there is indeed a contradiction. For it is by means of abiding in two distinct forms that the distinction [of those forms] is established; when that [distinction] is possible, and because their identity would be understood, how could they be established as distinct at one and the same time? How, then, can there be a cognition of identity? We say: not in any way. If, first of all, a single form is experienced, this is the cognition of a single object, not of two.
Now, if two forms are experienced as identical in essence, their cognition is simply impossible.

Furthermore, as for this expression "cow," it is not a cognition of the individual (anna-saṃvedana), because of the power of inherence (*samavāya*). For in conjunction (*saṃyoga*), there is merely the state of being conjoined between two things; but the majesty of inherence is such that the two related entities—the universal and the individual—are perceived as both distinct, like a ball of clay, and yet as non-distinct. Moreover, the universal is not the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the individual; therefore, even though there is a difference, just as with a water-pot and its base, the nature of the individual is determined as separate from the universal. However, their form is perceived as mutually dependent. Even when one is at a distance, although the individual cow is grasped before the universal "cowness" (*gotva*), and the universal "cowness" is grasped even before the individual in another [cow], the universal is nonetheless distinct from the other. This is the method of the Logicians (*Tārkika*) and the followers of Kaṇāda.
Because of the restriction of their occurrence to substances and so forth, and because of the difference in their cognitions, these [categories] are mutually distinct.

Substantiality (*dravyatva*) and the others are each restricted to substances and so forth respectively, and a difference in cognition is observed regarding them; therefore, due to the restriction of their occurrence to substances and so forth, and due to the difference in their cognitions, there is a mutual distinction among substantiality and the rest.
Previously, it was stated in general that "the universal has the nature of non-difference"; now, he establishes its distinction by means of proofs (*pramāṇa*).
Because each is connected with its own object. "By means of characteristics" (lakṣaṇaiḥ) means by means of the knowledge that characterizes and subsequently defines.

One should apply [the definition] to each individual instance (*piṇḍa*). In the case of a distinction such as "one," "full," "effort," and so forth, there is the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) upon the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and the universal (*sāmānya*) possesses unity through its connection with its own object and is not separated from its own particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding that which was stated—that every universal inheres in its own object and nowhere else—he states the reason for this:
"as has been said."

As it has been stated: others [hold that] generality (*sāmānya*) is distinct from substance (*dravya*). Even though it is not delimited by its connection with the individual object (*piṇḍa*) as it arises there—and even though it is not restricted to that [object] alone—it is nevertheless perceived through its manifestation; because the specific arrangement of its parts is restricted, and because it is fixed [in its nature], all [generalities] inhere in their own respective objects and nowhere else, starting from the very moment the individual object is produced, and not before. For it is exactly so in this case as well.

In specific configurations such as those of a *ḍākṣā* (a type of ox), the *kaivara* (a specific individual) is the manifester of "cowness" (*gotva*); in specific directions and locations, it is the manifester of "horseness" (*aśvatva*); and in specific places characterized by qualities such as whiteness, it is the manifester of "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), due to the restriction of their cognition.
Furthermore, these specific configurations are not common to all individuals; rather, they occur only in particular ones.

In that regard, although every universal is capable of being connected to other individuals within its own domain by virtue of its arising [therein], nevertheless, the inherence (*samavāya*) of a universal in a particular individual occurs only where its manifester is perceived in that individual, and not elsewhere.
Thus, even from the restriction of inherence (*sāmānya*), there is a restriction regarding the relation of the universal (*sāmānyasambandhaniyama*).

For instance, it is the very nature of causes such as threads that the state of being a cloth (*paṭatva*) inheres only in a single primary substance and not elsewhere; just as it is the nature of earth and other elements that the state of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) inheres only in the substance produced by them and not elsewhere. Now, the universal does not go elsewhere to be expressed, because it has no desire to depart.

Nevertheless, if there were no destruction [of the previous entity] beforehand, there would be no connection between it and the body being produced therein; yet, in the case of a bad argument (*durukte*), there would be a connection with every body being produced everywhere. Therefore, the thought that "all [entities] belong to all" is like drinking water from a mirage. This is because, in the intervening space, there is no basis for designation due to the absence of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*).

By "intervening space," one might mean ether (*ākāśa*), or a dual substance, or the absence of substance (*adravyabhāva*) existing in the middle of the hands and so forth; however, in these cases, there is neither conjunction nor inherence of universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*).

Furthermore, there is no evidence for their persistence in those very [substances] that are incapable of transformation; therefore, universals are not designated as existing in the interval, nor do they arise anew therein.
Rather, they become connected with the lump that arises there by virtue of the causal capacity [of the material].

Conjunction occurs from another [entity], or it occurs for that which is already situated in conjunction; therefore, inherence (*samavāya*) is indeed distinct. Just as the causes operate toward the production of a composite whole (*piṇḍa*), so too, by the power of those causes, there occurs in the whole—inhering therein though not arrived from elsewhere—the universal (*sāmānya*), because the capacity of things is immeasurable. This is the meaning.
"That non-existence is [the case] for those who have not reached [the truth].
Since no single form is perceived among the various distinct things that are being perceived, there is no universal at all.
This is incorrect.
Because, when multiple individual cows (*govyakti*) are being perceived, there arises a cognition of a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*) due to their being distinct from individuals such as horses;

for if there were nothing experienced among the individuals such as Śābaleyas that is independent of one another—just as the mutually distinct natures of a cow and a horse are individually cognized, so too would the individual cows be cognized [only in their particularity]—or just as the individual cows are perceived through six [sensory means], so too would the individuals of both cows and horses be perceived, since there would be no distinction [between the two cases].

However, since individual cows are invariably perceived as being distinct from one another, they must depend upon some single entity—such as the heart and so forth—which is expressed by the common term "cow" and which serves as the cause for their mutual exclusion and their shared characteristics.

If it is argued that there is a unity among the individual cows, we reply: no, because unless a universal exists, it is impossible for the causes of individuals or the effects of individuals to be non-distinct from one another, given that individuals themselves are mutually exclusive.

Furthermore, if identity were to result from having a single cause, there would be no mutual distinction between the individual instances of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); yet a difference in causes is observed, such as the eye, the visual faculty, inference, and so forth—as seen in the production of sight and other effects, or as when the sun’s rays are applied to a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*) and the like.

Moreover, if identity were based on having a single effect, it would follow that even heterogeneous things would become one, since external activities such as moving the body are seen in both classes of individuals—just as they are in cows and the like, so too in fish and the like—and furthermore, that which is seen in the genus "cowness" (*gotva*) would not be absent in the individual cow.

Furthermore, in the absence of a universal (sāmānya), what object could be the referent of the association with words? It cannot be the particular (svalakṣaṇa), because that which is momentary is cognized by itself and lacks the nature of being an object for the six [sense] faculties.
Nor can conceptual construction (vikalpa) be the word-meaning, because it does not possess the determination of momentariness and so forth.

If it is argued that the object of a word is the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*), is this form of conceptual construction distinct from the conceptual construction itself or non-distinct? If it is distinct, is it common to all conceptual constructions or does it differ with each individual conceptual construction? First, regarding its being common: it would be non-different from a universal (*sāmānya*). If the former [is the case], then according to some who maintain that "this [form] is the support for both cognition and mental factors" and is perceived only by way of its capacity (*śakti*), [it would follow that it is not the object].

If this mental form (*ākāra*) is distinct [from cognition], it would differ with each individual cognition; or if it is non-distinct from cognition, in either case, its capacity for association with words is not faultless because it lacks the nature of being an external object. Thus, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), by determining that [external] form through mutual exclusion, superimposes its own form and conceptualizes it as having the nature of an external referent.

If it is argued that this [conceptual image] is associated with words because it is superimposed as being external, [we reply: since the form of the conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*) possesses both unity and multiplicity, it perishes at the very moment it arises when a conceptual construction occurs; though appearing as if it were perishing, it remains distinct in every individual conceptual construction.
Furthermore, the non-perception of its difference is not capable of negating it, for it is experienced as being excluded (*apohyate*).

Just as one conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) superimposes its own appearance as being an external object in the form of a cow, another conceptual cognition likewise superimposes that very same form. Because each conceptual cognition has the power to grasp only its own specific internal aspect, they are not capable of perceiving the difference between the mutually superimposed aspects.

Because that [cognition] is dependent upon the apprehension of what is to be attained (*upeya*), or because of the non-apprehension of that [external object], various forms (*ākāra*)—which are conceptualized and superimposed—are projected as one; thus, a single object is spoken of for these conceptualizations. That very thing is the universal (*sāmānya*). Even though it is external, it is conceived by those who grasp internal differences as the cause of the appearance [of identity]. Among those things which are superimposed with dissimilar forms upon the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is called a "common form" (*samākāra*). This superimposed externality is the denotation of words and the object associated with verbal expression. Precisely for the sake of grasping that object, it is for the sake of grasping the object as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); for it is always superimposed upon that [particular] as being identical to it. Furthermore, it possesses the nature of not applying elsewhere, and it is common to both existence and non-existence, as seen in the usage: "Is there a cow? or "Is there no cow? For if this [universal] were of the nature of existence, then from the usage "there is a cow," the usage "there is no [cow]" would be a redundancy; and "there is no [cow]" would not be employed due to contradiction. Likewise, if its nature were non-existence, then "there is no [cow]" would be redundant, and "there is [a cow]" would be contradictory.
As it has been stated:
"One must say 'the jar does not exist,' for the jar is indeed that which is said not to exist;
yet even this must not be said, because of the contradiction between the jar and its absence."
Thus, for this very reason, there is an absence of unity among individual names even for those that are false.

For this [unity] is in every way the object of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); since these [constructions] consist of the imagination of unity and so forth, they are manifold. Because they are manifold, their causes—the non-conceptual cognitions (*nirvikalpaka*)—which occur in a specific, restricted manner, are also manifold. And because those causes are manifold, there is an absence of unity among the individual names.
As has been stated.
Because it is the cause of the liver, skin, and urine, it is the "divider of enemies" (vairibhedinī);
likewise, because it possesses the cause [of being] the liver, there is no difference even in the names of the individuals.
This too is incorrect, because conceptual construction is untenable.
Falsifiers claim that a single, superimposed universal is denoted because they perceive the forms of various conceptual constructions as distinct; or else, it is we who say so.
Is the superimposition of non-difference merely the non-apprehension of the difference between mental images (*ākāra*), or is it the apprehension of non-difference itself?
The first alternative is not tenable, because activity would proceed even toward that which is superimposed as different.

Just as the difference between conceptualized images is not apprehended, so too their non-difference is not apprehended; for if, due to the non-apprehension of difference, there were a superimposition of difference, then likewise, due to the non-apprehension of non-difference, a superimposition of difference would also have to be admitted, which would result in the impossibility of engaging in practical activity based on the unreality of non-difference.

Nor is it tenable to say that there is a superimposition of difference upon the apprehension of non-difference; for, according to you, since a single entity is the perception of many things, it is that [single entity] which perceives their difference and non-difference. But in the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavāda*), there is no one at all who perceives multiple objects, because each conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is restricted solely to its own internal form. If it is argued: "Let it be so; there exists a cause for the exclusion of the form of 'non-cow'—namely, the specific nature of the form of 'cow' and so forth, as seen in your own experience"—then what are these "non-cows" such that, by the production of our own cows, the unity of the form of 'cow' is superimposed?

If it is argued that "those which are not cows are non-cows," then [one must ask] what those cows are which are not non-cows? If the nature of the cow is established by the exclusion of its opposite, then the nature of that non-existence is established through the production of the cow; and if the nature of that non-existence is established, then the nature of the cow is established through the production of that [non-exclusion]. Thus, even when there is no mutual dependence, a lack of comprehension persists. As the venerable [author] has said:
"Because the determination of a cow occurs through the exclusion of the non-cow, the nature of the non-cow is established by the production of the cow."
In that case, it must be said that the cow itself is what is negated by the negative particle.
When the cow is sacrificed, there is no sacrifice of the self; but in the absence of that [cow], the sacrifice is performed by means of a cow.
Thus, regarding the application of discourse, even from the conjunction of words, the true nature of the constituent parts of speech is expressed:
"Is there some 'cow' (go) or not? Is it a cow, or is it not a cow? Is it an entity (bhāva) or a non-entity (abhāva)?"

If it is an existent (bhāva), is that nature identical to the individual cow (gopiṇḍa), or is the non-existent (abhāva) identical to the individual? If, first of all, it is identical to the individual cow, then its uniqueness (asādhāraṇatā) cannot be asserted; for it has already been stated that the application of a word does not occur toward an object that is unique. Furthermore, the claim that "it is identical to the individual cow" is difficult to establish in another way as well. If this were so, the meaning of the word "cow" would not be attained [as something distinct]. On the other hand, if a real entity (vastubhūta) distinct from the individual, which is not unique and serves as the basis for the word "non-cow," is denoted by the word, then the production of a conceptual determination (vidhṛtipatti) would have as its object merely the word itself.

If it is argued that non-existence (*abhāva*) is described as having the nature of being preceded by non-utterance (*avyāhṛti-pūrvatva*), then there would be no doubt regarding its status as a cognition (*pratyaya*), since it possesses the characteristic of an external object (*bāhya-lakṣaṇatva*) by virtue of producing knowledge; and because non-existence is characterized by the total absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Furthermore, there can be no grasping of linguistic convention (*saṅketagrahaṇa*) with respect to an object that has been made the basis of a cognition, for this [non-existence] is simply the non-operation of the word. Nor would activity directed toward the object of the hearer’s intellect occur when that [non-existence] is perceived, because existence and non-existence are distinct and because such a consequence is untenable.

If it is argued that, because there is a cognition of non-existence as having the nature of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), activity proceeds toward the particular characteristic through non-discrimination—[the opponent replies: "Having conjoined the perceived and the conceptualized, there is the comprehension of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as the non-conceptualizable; this is the 'perfected stage' (*pratipūrṇabhūmi*).
This is incorrect, because when something is non-existent, the application of a mode of being characterized by that nature is untenable.

Furthermore, there is no complete determination [of an object] by means of a word at this time, because the word does not possess that form [of the object] and because there is an absence of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Moreover, since activity toward an object arises from a word, the non-existence of the agent is also the meaning of the word.

There is no cause such as knowledge, desire, or the like; rather, this entire collection of objects is mutually dependent, momentary, impermanent, inferable, and cognized through words—not through direct perception, even when the object is not grasped, because the specific causal efficiency (*sāmarthya*) for the production of knowledge remains unimpeded despite the difference [in the object].

There exists the linguistic usage of words, and there exists the worldly course of life—which is preceded by perception and follows the distinctions between the superior and the inferior—consisting of the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful; and it is by this that one establishes the uniformity of falsity in a particular instance, since the cognition arising from a word serves as a non-prohibition [of the object] through its belonging to that same class. Thus, even in the case of inference regarding an unknown object, people proceed toward the goal with hesitation.
The cognition characterized as inference, which arises based on a causal connection, is false;
yet, even without that [inference], this worldly course of affairs proceeds.
Thus ends the section on the general categories (*sāmānyapadārtha*) in the *Tantrāloka-vyākhyā* titled *Padārthapraveśanyā*, composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Śrīdhara.

Now follows the definition of the category of particularity (*viśeṣa*). Existing in the ultimate [entities], they are "ultimate" (*antyāḥ*); they are "particularities" (*viśeṣāḥ*) because they differentiate their own substrates.

In eternal substances—which are devoid of the capacity for destruction—namely the atoms, ether, time, space, and self, they reside in each individual substance in its entirety as spatially distinct parts, serving as the cause of the cognition of absolute differentiation.

Just as, for those who hold the self to be great and so forth, a perceptual exclusion is observed based on the specific differences in form, quality, action, and parts [of objects] such as existence and the like—for example: "a cow," "white," "swift-moving," "having full dewlaps and humps," or "a great bull."

Likewise, for yogins who perceive the self, there arises a non-contradictory cognition based on mutual causes regarding atoms—which are eternal and identical in form, quality, and activity—as well as regarding liberated selves. This consists of a perceptual differentiation such as "this is distinct" and "that is distinct," as well as recognition regarding objects distinguished by place and time, and regarding the ultimate nature of things; these are the particulars (*viśeṣas*).

If, however, without an absolute distinction, there were for yogins both the cessation of perception through the power born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), what would follow? It would be as follows:

just as a cognition of a white object does not arise toward something that is not white, nor is there recognition toward something other than what was previously perceived; if these were to occur, they would constitute a certainty. Thus, in this case, without an absolute distinction, neither the cessation of perception through the power born of yoga nor recognition can possibly exist for yogins.

If it is asked, "Why is the self-exclusion of perception (*pratyakṣavyāvṛtti*) postulated for atoms (*paramāṇu*) as it is for other particulars (*viśeṣa*)?"—the answer is: because of identity (*tādātmya*).

In this world, even regarding things that do not possess that nature, a cognition occurs without an external cause, as when [the cognition of heat] arises from a lamp in the case of jars and the like, but not from another lamp in the case of the lamp itself.

Just as cows, horses, buffaloes, and so forth are inherently impure, and others [are pure] by contrast, so too here, due to identity, there is self-exclusion of perception in other particulars; and because of their connection with that [exclusion], atoms will be designated as such.

Thus ends the category of *viśeṣa* (particularity) in the Praśastapādabhāṣya. Regarding the position on *viśeṣa*, there is an investigation into its distinctness from substance and the other categories.
To explain *viśeṣa*, he says:
"Those which exist at the ends (*anteṣu*) are the ultimate (*antyāḥ*)."
Because they exist at the end of production and destruction, eternal substances are denoted by the word "end" (anta); the meaning is that they reside within them.
This is because, for the reason that they are particularizing factors in every respect for their own substratum and because they are non-substances, they are called "atoms" (aṇu).
"By manifestation and so forth, which are devoid of destruction and origination" is the explanation of the phrase "devoid of destruction and origination.
And "causes of cognition through extreme recurrence" is the explanation of the phrase "because they differentiate their own substratum."

"Existing one by one in each substance" means that a distinct particular (*viśeṣa*) resides in each and every substance. For if the cognition of the exclusion of a thing's own substratum were produced by the particular alone, the postulation of a separate category called "particularity" would be useless.
And how these qualifiers constitute the definition has been explained previously.

Anticipating the objection that it would be appropriate to state the definition of those [letters] only when they possess the *bindu* (the nasal dot) as a specific cognition, and not when they lack the *bindu*, he introduces another section beginning with "yathā" (just as) in order to demonstrate the multiplicity of the qualifiers.

Just as, among cows and other animals, the cognition "cow" is seen to be based on the genus (*jāti*), the cognition "white" is based on a quality (*guṇa*), the cognition "swift-moving" is based on an action (*kriyā*), the cognition "long-nosed, long-eared, large-eyed" is based on parts (*avayava*), and the cognition "large-bodied" is based on conjunction (*saṃyoga*), so too is the exclusion of cognitions regarding limbs and the like observed.

Likewise, for us [ordinary people] and for yogins, regarding atoms that possess identical forms, qualities, and actions—meaning those with identical forms, identical qualities, and identical actions—a distinction in cognition arises from ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*). Since no other cause is possible for liberated souls (*muktātman*), these ultimate particulars serve as the cause for the exclusion of cognitions based on the substances inherent in their respective substrates. Just as for people like us there is a difference in cognition regarding individual cows and the like, so too must there be a difference in cognition regarding atoms and the like, even without such [external] factors, because a difference between individuals must exist.
Nor is the difference between individual instances (*vyakti*) alone the cause [of doubt],
because doubt is observed even regarding qualities and actions similar to those [of the object] in cases such as a post (*sthāṇu*).
Furthermore, there is no other cause, since the form (*ākṛti*), appearance, and action are identical [in both cases].
Furthermore, no difference in conditions is observed without a cause; therefore, there must necessarily be a cause and a specific distinction.
Due to spatial distance and temporal distance, atoms would be perceived by some and not by others, because they possess both generality and particularity, just like jars and other such objects.

Furthermore, even regarding what was previously seen, the cognition of a specific distinction does not occur without [an external factor]; therefore, there exists a specific characteristic that serves as its cause. To this, an objection is raised: "But if... and so forth.

The meaning of the objection is this: just as for practitioners of yoga there is perception of supersensuous objects through the practice of yoga, so too there will be recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and repeated cognition (*pratyabhyāvṛtti*) by means of another specific [means]. He answers: "It is not so.

Just as for yogins there is no [perception] of the color white or the stars when they are not joined [with their causes], and there would be no recognition of that which is absolutely unseen; if it were to occur, it would belong to animals and the like.

Likewise, without the ultimate particularity (*antyaviśeṣa*), there would be no repeated occurrence or recognition; thus, according to the view of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, the connection between sense faculty and object will not result in cognition as we maintain—this is the intended meaning. [This is stated] because of the fault of tautology, and because of the phrase "and by the ultimate particularity."
There is no specific property of "sound-ness" (śabdatva); rather, there is only another specific property [of each individual sound], because it is not a genus (jāti).

And just as for yogins, perceptual pervasion occurs among those [sounds] by their very nature without any other specific property, so too will it be for atoms; what is the use of postulating a specific property? Thus he states the internal [objection].
"No," [he says].
For what reason? Because of identity with that which remains of the text. He explains this very point:

Regarding the word "here": this cognition arises with reference to that which does not have that nature as its cause, and not toward things that do possess that nature—just as, for example, from a lamp whose nature is luminosity, illumination occurs among objects such as jars which do not possess that nature; yet illumination does not occur in the lamp itself from another lamp, but rather from itself alone.

Just as elephants, horses, buffaloes, and the like possess an inherent connection (*anuṣakti*) such that their own nature (*svaguḥ*) is the mode of perception (*pratyakṣaprakāratva*), so too for yogins there is distinctness from those [objects], while for others there is non-distinctness. Likewise, because of identity (*tādātmya*) and because substances have the nature of being produced from threads and so forth, there is a direct perception (*pratyakṣavyāpti*) of specific substances through their own essential form (*svarūpa*) alone, and not from the nature of other particularities (*viśeṣa*). However, in the case of atoms (*paramāṇu*) which do not possess that identity, and in the case of general properties (*sāmānyadharma*), it is logical that direct perception occurs only through the connection with a particularity (*viśeṣayoga*), and not from the mere essential form itself.
In eternal substances, when there is a mutual conjunction among substances,
the *viśeṣas* (particularities), which reside individually in each, are the causes of differentiation.
Thus ends the fifth [section] on the category of *viśeṣa* in the *Samandalī-ṭīkā*, a commentary on the *Padārthavivecanavyākhyā* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Bhāskara.
Now follows the definition of the category of inherence (*samavāya*).

Inherence is that relation between things that are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relationship of the supported and the support, which is the cause of the cognition "this [is] here. Whether they stand in a causal relationship or not, substances, qualities, motions, universals, and particulars exist as inseparable entities in the form of the supported and the support; from that [relation] arises the cognition "this is here," and because it is distinct from conjunction (*saṃyoga*), that relation, which possesses its own specific power, is called inherence.

Just as the cognition "there is curd in this jar" occurs when a relation exists, so too—based on the observation of such cognitions regarding perceptible substances—we know that these [categories] possess a relation: "here is a cloth in the threads," "here is a mat in the *vīraṇa* grasses," "here are quality and action in the substance," "here is existence (*sattā*) in the substance, quality, and action," "here is substantiality (*dravyatva*) in the substance," "here is quality-ness (*guṇatva*) in the quality," "here is action-ness (*karmatva*) in the action," and "here are ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*) in the eternal substance. Thus, because we observe such cognitions, their relation is known to exist.
Salutations to Śambhu in his form as Vāma, who dispels the inner darkness, whose cause is the form of the enemy of all worldly activity, and whose body is stainless knowledge.
He states [the definition of] inherence (*samavāya*) at the very beginning:

"Inherence is that relation which, among things that are inseparable (*ayutasiddha*), standing in the relationship of container and contained, and whether they be cause and effect or not cause and effect, is the manifestation as 'here'.
I shall now examine this explanation provided by him.
Which are those things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*), such that their relation would be inherence (*samavāya*)? To this he says:
"Of substance, quality, action, generality, and particularity.
This is the definition of the rule: [it applies] to those things that stand in the relation of cause and effect, as well as to those that do not stand in the relation of cause and effect.

Regarding the phrase "the destruction of non-separation" (*ayutavākyavināśam*), there is a rule stated by way of contrast (*vyatirekamukhena*): conjunction (*samavāya*) is that which exists between eternal substances and the impermanent qualities inherent in them, as well as between actions and their subsequent effects; and it is the conjunction of those things that are not related as cause and effect—such as eternal substances, the eternal particulars (*viśeṣa*) inherent in them, or any other eternal entities—that constitutes "non-separability" (*ayutasiddha*).
Although this is indeed a restrictive rule, it is also a rule that applies to those things situated in contact with one another despite being incapable of such union.

The cognition "this is here" arises from a cause; that which is the non-difference, the non-distinct existence, the unity, and the infinity of things—such as a son and so forth—which, though residing in fixed locations and though their individual natures are distinct, is perceived through the cognition of a relation by means of a cognition of mutual dependence, that is *samavāya* (inherence).
He establishes this very point by means of a question beginning with "How is this so?
Just as the cognition "there is curd in this jar" is observed when there is a relation between the jar and the curd.
Likewise, because we observe cognitions such as "the cloth is here in these threads," it is known that there exists a relation between these [entities], such as the threads and the cloth.

Cognitions such as "the cloth is here in these threads" are caused by a relation, because they are cognitions of a whole [in its parts], like the cognition "curd is in this jar. Nor is this relation conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because the related entities are not established separately; because it does not arise from causes such as the action of one of the two; because no end in separation is observed; and because it exists only when there is a locus and that which is located. This [relation] is inherence (*samavāya*).
[An objection is raised: "Surely this will be a conjunction. To this he says: "And that is not a conjunction.
That relation between those two bowls is not a conjunction; why is that? To this he says:

"Because relations consist of things that are not established separately. For conjunction occurs only between things that are established separately; this [relation], however, belongs to things that are not established separately.
Likewise, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) may arise from the action of one of two things, from the action of both, or from another conjunction.
However, in this case, since there is an absence of causes such as the action of one of the two, one should understand it through the capacity of its lack of a [material] cause.

It is observed that conjunction ends in disjunction (*vibhāga*), meaning it has disjunction as its destruction; this is not the case for inherence (*samavāya*). Conjunction occurs even between two independent things, such as two fingers held apart; this [inherence], however, occurs only between a substratum and what is to be supported. Therefore, this is not conjunction, but rather something distinct from it.
And that [inherence] is a distinct category from substance and the others, due to the difference characterized by its own existence (*bhāva*).

Just as existence (*bhāva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth, have a state of being dependent on their own substrates and mutually on one another because they produce cognitions corresponding to themselves within their respective substrates, so too inherence has a status as a distinct category from those [other categories], since the cognition of "non-separation" (*ahetitva*) is observed among the five categories.

Nor is it like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because of the distinction characterized by its own existence and because there is no specific mark [of conjunction] present; therefore, inherence is one and the same throughout all things.
When inherence (samavāya) is established, he demonstrates its distinction from substance and the other categories,
asserting that it is a category distinct from substance and so forth.
To the question "Why?", he says:
"Because of the distinction between the characteristics of existence and power. For it is said: "Since it is not a substance... as has been stated.
"Being" (bhāva) refers to the general property of "pot-ness" (ghaṭasāmānya). By the word "and so forth" (ādi), "substance-ness" (dravyatva) and "quality-ness" (guṇatva) are included.

Just as for a category (bhāva), there is a cognition corresponding to its own nature among its own substrata—namely, substances, qualities, and actions, such as the cognition "this is a jar" for the universal "jar-ness"; for the universal "substance-ness," there is a cognition corresponding to its own nature among its own substrata, the substances, such as the cognition "this is a substance, this is a substance"; for the universal "quality-ness," there is a cognition corresponding to its own nature among its own substrata, the qualities, such as the cognition "this is a quality, this is a quality"; and for the universal "action-ness," there is a cognition corresponding to its own nature among its own substrata, the actions—and likewise for inherence (samavāya), because it is distinct from substances and so forth, and because it is eternal and lacks qualities.

*Pratyaya* (cognition): the cognition of "effect" [arises] with respect to an effect; because it is its agent, there is a mutual dependence on their own substrates regarding properties such as existence (*bhāva*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*). Likewise, since the cognition of "inherence" (*samavāya*) is observed within the six categories (*padārtha*), it is a distinct category separate from them.
There is an inquiry as to whether this [inherence] is one or many; however, its multiplicity is not established like that of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Just as conjunction is manifold, inherence is not so.
For what reason? To this he says:
because there is no distinction for those who perceive existence (*bhāva*), and because of the absence of a substance (*dravya*) as a mark (*liṅga*) of existence.

Just as, although all [perceive] the characteristic of being composed of *sattva* and so forth without distinction in their perception produced by seeing, there is no difference in the characteristic; and because of the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that characteristic, existence is one and the same in all things. Similarly, because the characteristic that serves as the cause for the cognition of its specific distinctions is identical in all cases, and because of the absence of a means of valid cognition [for any difference], inherence (*samavāya*) is one and the same.
He concludes:
"Therefore."

Now, if inherence (*samavāya*) were one, then because it would be the same relation for substances, qualities, and actions with their qualifiers such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*), "qualitiness" (*guṇatva*), and "actionness" (*karmatva*), there would follow the consequence that there are only six categories of entities. This is not so, because of the restriction of the relationship between the container and the contained (*ādhārādheya*). Even if inherence is one and independent everywhere, there still exists a restriction of the container and the contained:
how is it that substanceness exists only in substances, qualitiness only in qualities, and actionness only in actions?
Why is it so in such cases? Because of the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Here, because the positive concomitance of the cognition whose cause is inherence (*samavāya*) is observed, it is understood that inherence is one and the same in all instances.
Because the positive concomitance of the causes for [cognitions of] "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth is not observed, their specific restriction is known.
Just as in the case of a bowl and a staff, despite the oneness of their conjunction, there is a fixed rule regarding the relationship between the locus and the located;

so too, although inherence (samavāya) is one, there is a fixed rule regarding the container and the contained among substance-ness and the rest, due to the distinctions of the manifested and the manifestor, and the subtle and the gross.
It explains: "When it is one.

If inherence were one, then this very same connection of substantiality (*dravyatva*) with earth and the other [substances] would be the same as the connection of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) with qualities and action-ness (*karmatva*) with actions. Just as the connection of substantiality exists in earth and the others, thereby establishing their status as substances, so too, since that same connection is possible for qualities and the rest, they too would possess substantiality.

Just as the connection with "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) is said to exist in color and so forth, thereby establishing the quality-status of color and the rest, so too, since that same connection exists in substances and actions, they too would possess the status of quality. And in this way, there would be a confusion of categories among all things, rather than [the restriction] to the six categories beginning with substance, including inherence (*samavāya*).

Nor is there any confusion among categories, because of the restriction between the locus and the located. Substantiality (*dravyatva*) does not inhere in inherence (*samavāya*), but rather, through its inherence in substance, substantiality [is established] in substance; and through its inherence in inherence, [substantiality is established] in the cognition of substance, as well as in qualities and actions and the cognition thereof—thus they possess substantiality.
This should be explained in the same way for qualities and actions as well.
He explains this summary verse with the words beginning "Even though inherence is one," and so forth.
The meaning is that it is independent, in the sense that, like conjunction, it is not bound by any other relation.
The other [alternative] is untenable because of the fault of tautology,
and so forth, as explained in the *Kalpa*.
"Substantiality (dravyatva) exists only in substances, quality-ness (guṇatva) only in qualities, and action-ness (karmatva) only in actions"—such is the conceptual construction (kalpa).
By this, you mean "knowledge. He states the reply:

"Because of the mutual exclusion of the single substance. This means that when the perception caused by the universal *dravyatva* (substanceness) is present in substances, there is an absence of it in qualities and actions; when the perception caused by the universal *guṇatva* (qualityness) is present in qualities, there is an absence of it in substances and actions; and likewise, when the perception caused by the universal *karmatva* (actionness) is present in actions, there is an absence of it in substances and qualities. Therefore, because of this mutual exclusion regarding the single substance, the restriction of *dravyatva* and the other universals is known. Now follows the commentary on the [next] verse.

Since there is no difference in their inherence, the restriction of meaning is indeed established: that the inherence of *dravyatva* (substance-ness) occurs only in earth and so forth, that of *guṇatva* (quality-ness) only in color and so forth, and that of *karmatva* (action-ness) only in upward throwing and so forth, and not otherwise.
To this he says: "If [it were so]...

Even though conjunction is one and the same, a restriction is observed—such as between a bowl and a jujube fruit, or between a red cloth and the eastern direction—due to the restriction of capacity (*śakti*).
Just as in the case of a jar and its color,

when inherence (*samavāya*) is asserted, there is likewise a restriction of the locus and the located for *dravyatva* (substance-ness) and so forth, due to the difference in their own expressive capacities (*svajñāpakaśaktibheda*).
What would be the consequence?
The power that manifests [the universal] through substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so forth belongs to substances alone; therefore, substance-ness inheres only in substances and not elsewhere.
This should be explained in the same way for qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*) as well.
Even though the relation is eternal, it does not possess non-eternality like conjunction, because, like an existent entity (*bhāva*), it is without cause.
Just as it was stated that an existent entity is eternal because no cause for it is perceived through logical consequence (*prasaṅga*), so too is inherence (*samavāya*).
For no cause whatsoever is perceived for this [inherence] through logical consequence.
Furthermore, where does inherence (samavāya) reside in relation to substances and so forth?

Conjunction (saṃyoga) is not possible, because, being a quality (guṇa), it must depend upon a substance. Nor can it be inherence, because that has already been ruled out. And there is no other mode of existence (vṛtti) such as "universal" (jāti).
No; because of identity (*tādātmya*).
Just as there is no other conjunction for the nature of existence (*bhāva*)—namely, the intrinsic form (*svarūpa*) of substance, quality, and action.
Thus, for inherence (*samavāya*), which is of such an indivisible nature, there is no other mode of occurrence; therefore, its occurrence is within itself.

For this very reason, it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), because, like existence (*sattā*) and the like, there is an absence of self-referential cognition regarding perceptible substances, qualities, and so forth.
Therefore, inherence is inferable from the cognition "here" (*ihabuddhi*).
Thus ends the category of inherence in the Praśastapādabhāṣya.
Furthermore, regarding the doubt as to whether this [inherence] is impermanent or eternal, we reply:
"Even though the related members are impermanent.

Just as conjunction is impermanent when its two related members are impermanent, inherence is not impermanent when its two inherent members are impermanent, because it is the cause of the manifestation of existence.
He explains this with the words "Just as," and so forth.
For it is logical that conjunction is destroyed when its relata are destroyed, because the two relata are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of its production.
Intrinsic inherence (*samavāya*), however, is not a cause for its relata, because it is merely a relation;
how it is not a cause has already been demonstrated.
Therefore, even upon the destruction of its relata, it does not perish.
Because it is recognized even at another time, despite being beginningless. Furthermore, inherence must either be unrelated to its relata and yet connect them, or it must already be related.
It is not logical for that which is unrelated to possess the capacity to relate things, as that would lead to the absurdity of [everything] being a causal power.
This relation cannot be of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because that depends upon substance;
nor can it be inherence (*samavāya*), because [inherence] is unitary;
and there exists nothing distinct from both conjunction and inherence.
To the question, "In what manner, then, does its subsistence occur?", he says:
"Action, moreover, subsists as non-action through inherence in substances and so forth; or rather, it subsists by virtue of the existence of another. This is the intended meaning.
The opponent replies:

"It is not so. [The Self] does not exist as a function because of the absence of functioning; nor does it exist through identity, because it is devoid of functional parts. Therefore, this is functioning by its very own nature.

For conjunction exists only among produced things; even for that which has the nature of inherence (*vṛttyātmaka*), there is no further mode of existence (*vṛttyantara*), because inherence is defined as the subsistence of a cause in its effect.
Inherence, however, has no other mode of existence.
Therefore, its existence is by its own self, by its very essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*), and not by way of another mode of existence.
For this very reason, inherence (samavāya) is beyond the senses;
for, unlike forest-trees and the like, it lacks a presence within perceptible objects.

Just as jars and the like possess a presence even within perceptible things—and are therefore perceived by the sense organs through their conjunction with a substance in which they inhere—such a possibility of presence does not exist for inherence itself.
Therefore, this [ether] is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*),
because the capacity of the sense organ to apprehend an existent entity is observed only in dependence upon conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*).
If there were a sensory perception of ether as its object, it would follow that there is no direct perception of the relation [between the sense organ and the object].
Now, they say that it is precisely this [inherence] which is inexpressible, because it is not perceived as residing within its own self.

Just as the manifestation of a substance occurs through conjunction with a sense organ, such is not the case for the manifestation of inherence, since the two related entities are never perceived separately. Therefore, this [inherence] is non-empirical (alaukika).
He concludes:
"Therefore."
That mutual alliance which is formed by friends should be understood as a coalition that obstructs independence.
The state of Khavetāra consists of gold, silver, and copper;
it is golden, with Śakra as its seed, and is the commentary on the Nyāyacandrikā.
Proclaiming their virtues upon the nails— which are like campaka flowers produced without effort—
the followers of Nyāyacandrin dance five times within the courtyard of the intellect.
Born from the body of King Dviṣaṇa, he was a twice-born of the Bhr̥gu lineage;
his knowledge brought about great prosperity and welfare, and his fame was exceedingly vast.
From the ocean of the two lineages arose the moon of both families,
a twice-born one who brought joy to the world like Bṛhaspati.
Therefore, in this great ocean of the multitude of faults, for the sake of providing a firm support to those seeking the knowledge of liberation,
there is one named Baladeva, who— by the power of destiny— is the flow of the river of fame, ageless and unyielding, appearing as his own reflection.
To him there appeared this pure silk garment,
possessing the virtues of lotuses and mountains, a household for the domestic fire; it was cool-shaded, yielding fruit on its surface, rich in many flowers, a refuge for birds,
and known as the "Bearer of Wealth"— it became his wish-fulfilling tree.
When the composition of this work was undertaken,
the *Nyāyakandalī* was indicated by the six-footed bees who were drawn to its fragrance.
This *Nyāyakandalī* was composed by Śrī Pātrakesarin on the 103rd year from the time of the binding of the branches [of the Nyāya tree],
under the patronage of the illustrious Pāpaḍu.
This Nyāyakandalī commentary on the Padyārthapraveśa is completed.
This work is completed.
